# Clean room

### JPEG 2000 Part 1 decoder (decoders/jpeg2000-kernel, 2026-11-27)

Conformance and ICC (2026-11-27): the tables and constants first written from memory (Table C.2, Tables D.1 to D.4
and D.7, Table F.4, Equations E-6, E-8, G-6 to G-14) were checked against the text of Rec. ITU-T T.800 (11/2015) and
agree. The decoder tests, their procedure and tolerances are those of Rec. ITU-T T.803 (11/2002) | ISO/IEC 15444-4,
"JPEG 2000 image coding system: Conformance testing", <https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-T.803-200211-S>; its
codestreams and reference outputs are data, run and never committed. They showed that the markers 0xFF30 to 0xFF3F of
A.1, which carry no segment, were read as segments, and that the restricted ICC method (I.3.2 and J.8, ICC.1) was not
applied: the profile now goes through the package's own ICC reader (`src/icc.ts`). A reader also ignores a colour
specification box of a method Part 1 does not define (I.5.3.3). No other decoder's source or output was used.

`packages/decoders/jpeg2000-kernel` is a Margo-authored Rust crate, built in pieces: the codestream syntax of Annex A
(SIZ, COD, COC, QCD, QCC, RGN, POC, PPM, PPT, SOT and SOD; the tile-part rules; the precedence of tile COC over tile
COD over main COC over main COD, and the same for QCC and QCD), and the canvas geometry of Annex B (tiles,
tile-components, resolutions, sub-bands, precincts and code-block sizes), from Rec. ITU-T T.800 | ISO/IEC 15444-1,
"JPEG 2000 image coding system: Core coding system" (ITU, 2002 and 2015 editions),
<https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-T.800>; David S. Taubman and Michael W. Marcellin, *JPEG2000: Image Compression
Fundamentals, Standards and Practice* (Kluwer, 2002), <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4615-0799-4>; and David
Taubman, "High performance scalable image compression with EBCOT" (IEEE Transactions on Image Processing 9(7),
2000), <https://doi.org/10.1109/83.847830>. No decoder's source (OpenJPEG, Kakadu, Grok, jpx.js or any other) was
read. Tier-2 (B.9 to B.12): tag trees decoded node by node from the root, the packet header bit reader with its
0xFF stuffing, Table B.4's pass counts, Lblock and per-segment lengths, SOP and EPH, packed headers, and the five
progressions with POC changes; the position-driven orders sort each precinct by where B.12's loops first reach it
(the tile corner for a precinct its resolution starts inside). Tier-1 (Annex C and D): the MQ decoder's INITDEC,
BYTEIN and DECODE with Table C.2's 47 states, the bypass's raw bits, and the significance propagation, refinement
and cleanup passes with Table D.1's zero coding, D.3's sign and D.4's refinement contexts, run-length coding, and
every Table A.19 style (bypass, reset, termination on each pass, vertically causal contexts, segmentation
symbols). The unit tests hold it against a test encoder written from C.2 and D.3. Annexes E to H: Equation E-2's bit-planes and E-3's step sizes (derived and expounded), reconstruction at the middle of what the cut planes leave (r = 1/2, Equation E-6), H.2's Maxshift, the 2D_SR of Annex F with whole-sample symmetric extension and band parity from absolute canvas coordinates, the 5-3 lifting of Equations F-5 and F-6 and the 9-7 lifting of Equation F-7 with Table F.4's constants (the unit tests pin K by Table E.1's gains: low-pass 1 on a constant, high-pass 2 on the alternating signal), and the RCT, ICT and DC level shift of Annex G. Annex I: the JP2 signature, file type, header (image header, the first colour specification, palette, component mapping, channel definitions) and contiguous codestream boxes, with XLBox and to-the-end lengths, and the mapping to straight RGBA (palette lookup, channel order by association, premultiplied opacity divided out, sYCC to RGB by IEC 61966-2-1 Annex G). The whole decode runs per tile: tier-2 to the requested layers and resolution, tier-1, dequantization, the wavelet up to the kept resolution, the component transform and the level shift. Part 2 extensions (marker range 0xFF70 to 0xFF7F, MCT above 1, arbitrary kernels) and the HT block coder of
Part 15 are refused as unsupported, not skipped. The Wasm interface, the `decoders/jpeg2000` entry and its module
workers are Margo's own code over the W3C WebAssembly JavaScript Interface
(<https://www.w3.org/TR/wasm-js-api-2/>).

### A membrane shell for soft volumes (P8, SOFT-04 and SOFT-06, point 2, 2026-11-28)

`SoftVolumeOptions.membrane` (`packages/physics/soft-kernel/src/membrane.rs`, the rest shapes in `membraneRest` of
`soft-volume.ts`) makes the surface tier's shell an incompressible neo-Hookean membrane: per triangle the 3 x 2
deformation gradient F of its rest shape in its own plane, C = F^T F, area stretch J = sqrt(det C), the thickness H / J
from incompressibility, and the energy (mu H / 2) (tr C + 1 / J^2 - 3) per rest area. The law and its closed form for a
sphere, p = 2 mu H / R (1 / lambda - 1 / lambda^7) with its maximum at lambda = 7^(1/6), are from J. E. Adkins and R. S.
Rivlin, "Large elastic deformations of isotropic materials IX. The deformation of thin shells", Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A
245 (1952) 505-531 (<https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1952.0030>), and L. R. G. Treloar, *The Physics of Rubber Elasticity*
(3rd ed., Oxford 1975); the general thin-shell form p = (H / R) W'(lambda) / lambda^2 and the balloon models it is
compared with are in Robert Mangan and Michel Destrade, "Gent models for the inflation of spherical balloons",
International Journal of Non-Linear Mechanics 68 (2015) 52-58 (arXiv:2009.08752), read for its equations only. The
sheet and its gas are solved together by Anka He Chen, Ziheng Liu, Yin Yang and Cem Yuksel, "Vertex Block Descent", ACM
TOG 43(4), 2024: the gas enters as its isothermal energy -nRT ln V + p_out V, so the sheet and the gas share one
stationary point; each particle's Newton step uses a majorizer of the membrane's Hessian (the area-stretch term's
curvature is dropped, which is negative because J is the norm of a function affine in one particle) and is cut back
until the potential falls. The tests hold a sphere to the closed form at three fills, its stiffness dp / dlambda and a
held-out sheet near the peak (`packages/physics/tests/soft-membrane.test.js`). No code was read.

### Directing soft volumes: cues and target shapes (P8, point 7, 2026-11-28)

`SoftBody.cue` and `setTargetShape` (`packages/physics/src/soft-direct.ts`) are Margo's own scheduling over the existing
impulse, vent and target calls. The target pull is shape matching's goal from Matthias Müller, Bruno Heidelberger, Matthias
Teschner and Markus Gross, "Meshless Deformations Based on Shape Matching" (ACM TOG 24(3), SIGGRAPH 2005): the target's
offsets from its mass-weighted centre, turned by the rotational part R of A = sum m p q^T and placed at the particles' centre
of mass, which makes the springs m omega^2 (g - x) add to no force and, since A R^T is symmetric, to no torque. R comes from
Matthias Müller, Jan Bender, Nuttapong Chentanez and Miles Macklin, "A Robust Method to Extract the Rotational Part of
Deformations" (MIG 2016), warm-started from the last step's. The pull is a kick at the step's start, so the sums are exact
at the instant they are found. No code was read.

### Venting and bursting soft shells (P8, SOFT-06, 2026-11-28)

`SoftBody.openVent` (`packages/physics/src/soft-vent.ts`) lets a shell's gas out by the isentropic orifice flow of an ideal
gas, subsonic below the critical pressure ratio (2 / (gamma + 1))^(gamma / (gamma - 1)) and choked above it, and the jet's
thrust mdot u + (p_t - p_a) A_e: Ascher H. Shapiro, *The Dynamics and Thermodynamics of Compressible Fluid Flow*, vol. 1
(Ronald Press, 1953), ch. 4, and John D. Anderson, *Modern Compressible Flow* (3rd ed., McGraw-Hill, 2003), ch. 5. The
default discharge coefficient, 0.61, is the contraction of a free jet from a sharp-edged hole in a thin wall: G. Kirchhoff,
"Zur Theorie freier Flüssigkeitsstrahlen", Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 70 (1869), whose free-streamline
contraction is pi / (pi + 2) = 0.611, against the 0.596 the Reader-Harris/Gallagher equation of ISO 5167-2:2003
(*Measurement of fluid flow by means of pressure differential devices, Part 2: Orifice plates*) gives as its diameter
ratio and inverse Reynolds number go to 0. The gas inside stays isothermal (the shell's own model, Matyka and Ollila 2003
below), so a blowdown is the isothermal tank's: choked, p(t) = p_0 exp(-Cd A sqrt(gamma R T) (2 / (gamma + 1))^((gamma +
1) / (2 (gamma - 1))) t / V), which the tests hold it to. A membrane bursts once a triangle's greater principal stretch,
the root of the larger eigenvalue of C = F^T F, reaches its burst stretch. No code was read.

### Soft volumes from a mesh (P8, SOFT-04 and SOFT-06, 2026-11-27)

`SoftBodyDesc.volume` (`packages/physics/src/soft.ts`, `weldMesh` in `soft-volume.ts`) welds a mesh's split vertices
into particles by a spatial hash of cubes one weld tolerance across, each vertex compared with the 27 cubes around it,
as Matthias Teschner, Bruno Heidelberger, Matthias Müller, Danat Pomeranets and Markus Gross, "Optimized Spatial
Hashing for Collision Detection of Deformable Objects" (VMV 2003), hash points into a uniform grid. The surface is
held by the XPBD distance springs of Miles Macklin, Matthias Müller and Nuttapong Chentanez, "XPBD: Position-Based
Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics" (MIG 2016), whose compliance and damping a natural frequency and damping
ratio set, and keeps its volume by the closed-mesh volume constraint of Matthias Müller, Bruno Heidelberger, Marcus
Hennix and John Ratcliff, "Position Based Dynamics" (VRIPHYS 2006; JVCIR 18(2), 2007, section 4.4), the same volume
energy Teschner, Heidelberger, Müller and Gross give in "A Versatile and Robust Model for Geometrically Complex
Deformable Solids" (CGI 2004). With `pressure` the shell holds an ideal gas at fixed temperature, p V = n R T, as the
pressure soft bodies of Maciej Matyka and Mark Ollila, "Pressure Model of Soft Body Simulation" (SIGRAD 2003); the
survey of Andrew Nealen, Matthias Müller, Richard Keiser, Eddy Boxerman and Mark Carlson, "Physically Based
Deformable Models in Computer Graphics" (Computer Graphics Forum 25(4), 2006) places the three models. A closed body's
air load takes each windward face at a cube face's pressure coefficient, 1.05 (Sighard F. Hoerner, *Fluid-Dynamic
Drag*, 1965, chapter 3), checked against Elmar Achenbach, "Experiments on the flow past spheres at very high Reynolds
numbers" (Journal of Fluid Mechanics 54(3), 1972), 0.47 below the drag crisis. Written from the papers; no engine's
source was read. [Teschner et al. 2003](https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/publications/tetraederCollision.pdf),
[Macklin et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1145/2994258.2994272),
[Müller et al. 2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvcir.2007.01.005),
[Teschner et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.1109/CGI.2004.1309199),
[Matyka and Ollila 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0407003),
[Nealen et al. 2006](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2006.01000.x),
[Achenbach 1972](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112072000807).

The `'cells'` tier (`packages/physics/src/soft-stuffing.ts`) fills the mesh by isosurface stuffing, from François
Labelle and Jonathan Richard Shewchuk, "Isosurface Stuffing: Fast Tetrahedral Meshes with Good Dihedral Angles" (ACM
Transactions on Graphics 26(3), SIGGRAPH 2007): the body-centred cubic lattice, cut points on the edges that cross the
surface, the warp of a lattice vertex onto a cut point nearer than 0.24999 of a long edge or 0.41189 of a short one, and
the stencils by sign. Where a stencil leaves a quadrilateral, its diagonal runs through its lowest-numbered vertex, and
prisms split by the rule of Julien Dompierre, Paul Labbé, Marie-Gabrielle Vallet and Ricardo Camarero, "How to
Subdivide Pyramids, Prisms and Hexahedra into Tetrahedra" (8th International Meshing Roundtable, 1999), so neighbouring
cells agree; that rule is not the paper's parity rule, so the paper's angle proof does not carry over, and the tests hold
the paper's bounds on the meshes they build. Cut points are where the edge meets a triangle (Tomas Möller and Ben
Trumbore, "Fast, Minimum Storage Ray/Triangle Intersection", Journal of Graphics Tools 2(1), 1997). Constrained
Delaunay refinement (Hang Si, "TetGen, a Delaunay-Based Quality Tetrahedral Mesh Generator", ACM TOMS 41(2), 2015;
Jonathan Shewchuk, "Tetrahedral Mesh Generation by Delaunay Refinement", SoCG 1998) was weighed: it keeps the input's own
vertices on the boundary, but a lattice fill is linear in the cells, needs no exact predicates and conforms by
construction. The tier is checked against Heinrich Hertz, "Über die Berührung fester elastischer Körper" (Journal für
die reine und angewandte Mathematik 92, 1882), with K. L. Johnson, *Contact Mechanics* (Cambridge, 1985), chapter 4, for
its range. Written from the papers; no mesher's source was read.
[Labelle and Shewchuk 2007](https://doi.org/10.1145/1276377.1276448),
[Möller and Trumbore 1997](https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.1997.10487468),
[Si 2015](https://doi.org/10.1145/2629697),
[Shewchuk 1998](https://doi.org/10.1145/276884.276899).

The vertex-block and fem passes start from the adaptive first guess of Anka He Chen, Ziheng Liu, Yin Yang and Cem Yuksel,
"Vertex Block Descent" (ACM Transactions on Graphics 43(4), SIGGRAPH 2024), section 3.6, and the fem solve holds a particle
resting on a still body by the constraint filter of David Baraff and Andrew Witkin, "Large Steps in Cloth Simulation"
(SIGGRAPH 1998), section 5.3. Huamin Wang, "A Chebyshev Semi-Iterative Approach for Accelerating Projective and
Position-based Dynamics" (ACM Transactions on Graphics 34(6), SIGGRAPH Asia 2015) was built for the sweeps and dropped
(KB-SOFT-VBDGUESS1). [Chen et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1145/3658179),
[Baraff and Witkin 1998](https://doi.org/10.1145/280814.280821), [Wang 2015](https://doi.org/10.1145/2816795.2818063).

### Breakable objects and Voronoi fracture (BREAK-01)

Saty Raghavachary, “Fracture Generation on Polygonal Meshes Using Voronoi Polygons” (ACM SIGGRAPH 2002 Conference
Abstracts and Applications, p. 187), introduces Voronoi-cell partitioning of polygonal solids into convex fracture
pieces with newly capped interior cut faces. Eric G. Parker and James F. O'Brien, “Real-Time Deformation and Fracture
in a Game Environment” (ACM SIGGRAPH/Eurographics Symposium on Computer Animation, 2009, pp. 165–175), formulate
structural connectivity graphs, cumulative impulse damage, and support-anchor detachment so grounded sections remain
standing while unsupported overhangs break away (`X-42`, `X-43`). Matthias Müller, Nuttapong Chentanez, and Tae-Yong
Kim, “Real Time Dynamic Fracture with Volumetric Approximate Convex Decompositions” (ACM Transactions on Graphics
32(4), SIGGRAPH 2013, Article 115), describe impact-clustered fracture site distributions around the hit point and
fast runtime rigid-body fragment spawning with inherited rigid velocities (`v + ω × r`). Brian Mirtich, “Fast and
Accurate Computation of Polyhedral Mass Properties” (Journal of Graphics Tools 1(2), 1996, pp. 31–50), provides the
exact tetrahedral volume, centroid, and inertia tensor integrals used per Voronoi cell and combined across compound
islands via the parallel-axis theorem and cyclic Jacobi principal-axis diagonalization. Carl B. Barber, David P.
Dobkin, and Hannu Huhdanpaa, “The Quickhull Algorithm for Convex Hulls” (ACM TOMS 22(4), 1996, pp. 469–483), supplies
the convex-hull construction used for arbitrary input meshes and fragment colliders. `@margoengine/physics/breakable`
is written clean room in pure TypeScript over Margo's own `@margoengine/physics` kernel (`packages/physics/src/breakable/`).
[Raghavachary 2002](https://doi.org/10.1145/1242073.1242200),
[Parker and O'Brien 2009](https://doi.org/10.1145/1599470.1599492),
[Müller et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.1145/2461912.2461934),
[Mirtich 1996](https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.1996.10487458),
[Barber et al. 1996](https://doi.org/10.1145/235815.235821).
### Live FFT ocean wind retuning, synchronous CPU wave queries, and reflecting water ripples (PA-11, PA-16, 2026-11-26)

- **Live `FFTOcean.setWind` & synchronous CPU spectral sampling (`packages/water/src/fft.ts`, `packages/water/src/fft-cpu.ts`, `packages/water/src/fft-shaders.ts`)**:
  Jerry Tessendorf, *Simulating Ocean Water*, SIGGRAPH Course Notes (1999–2004, §§3–4, Eqs. 36–45, [course notes](https://people.computing.clemson.edu/~jtessen/reports/papers_files/coursenotes2004.pdf)), defines the Phillips spectrum, Hermitian time-domain synthesis $\tilde{h}(\mathbf{k}, t)$, choppy displacement $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{x}, t)$, and folding Jacobian $J$. Klaus Hasselmann et al., *Measurements of Wind-Wave Growth and Swell Decay during the Joint North Sea Wave Project (JONSWAP)*, Ergänzungsheft zur Deutschen Hydrographischen Zeitschrift, Reihe A, No. 12 (1973), defines the fetch-limited JONSWAP spectral density $S(\omega)$ with fetch-dependent $\alpha$, $\omega_p$, and peak enhancement $\gamma$. James W. Cooley and John W. Tukey, "An algorithm for the machine calculation of complex Fourier series", *Mathematics of Computation* 19(90), 1965, pp. 297–301 ([doi:10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0178586-1](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0178586-1)), supplies the radix-2 butterfly decomposition used by both the GPU compute passes and the lazily allocated CPU evaluator (`CpuOceanEvaluator`), which packs pairs of Hermitian-symmetric real fields into three complex 2D IFFTs and inverts horizontal choppy displacement via damped Newton/fixed-point iteration. Retuning wind via `setWind` re-dispatches the existing `initial` compute pass into the retained GPU spectrum buffer without allocating buffers or discarding foam history. The GPU debug overlay (normals, Jacobian determinant/foam mask, anti-aliased `fwidth` grid wireframe, cascade patch-domain rings, and sample-point markers) is Margo-own.
- **Synchronous CPU analytical `Water.sample` / `sampleHeight` (`packages/water/src/index.ts`)**:
  Alain Fournier and William T. Reeves, "A Simple Model of Ocean Waves", *Proceedings of SIGGRAPH 1986*, pp. 75–84 ([doi:10.1145/15922.15894](https://doi.org/10.1145/15922.15894)), defines Gerstner/trochoidal wave displacement, surface tangents, and orbital velocity. Margo evaluates its three-component bent-crest swell trains, `SpectralSea` linear wave components, and incoming far-field profile identically to the WGSL vertex shader, and inverts horizontal Gerstner displacement $(u, v) + \mathbf{D}_h(u, v) = (x, z)$ by 2D Newton-Raphson using the exact analytical horizontal Jacobian (guaranteed invertible by Water's non-folding steepness bound).
- **Interactive water ripples: solid obstacle Neumann reflection, moving-body coupling, ray disturbance, and debug overlay (`packages/water/src/ripples.ts`)**:
  Michael Kass and Gavin Miller, "Rapid, Stable Fluid Dynamics for Computer Graphics", *Proceedings of SIGGRAPH 1990*, pp. 49–57 ([doi:10.1145/97879.97884](https://doi.org/10.1145/97879.97884)), and Matthias Müller, "Fast Water Simulation for Games Using Height Fields", GDC 2008 ([slides](https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/talks/GDC2008_HeightFieldFluids.pdf)), describe explicit 2D height-field wave integration and rigid-body displacement coupling. Cem Yuksel, Donald H. House, and John Keyser, "Wave Particles", *ACM Transactions on Graphics* 26(3), 2007, Article 99 ([doi:10.1145/1276377.1276501](https://doi.org/10.1145/1276377.1276501)), motivates solid boundary wave reflection and moving-object wakes. Moshe Israeli and Steven A. Orszag, "Approximation of radiation boundary conditions", *Journal of Computational Physics* 41(1), 1981, pp. 115–135 ([doi:10.1016/0021-9991(81)90082-6](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(81)90082-6)), supplies the outer absorbing sponge damping layer. Solid obstacles (spheres, cylinders, oriented boxes, and walls) impose a homogeneous Neumann boundary condition ($\partial h / \partial n = 0$) on the 5-point discrete Laplacian by substituting the centre fluid cell's height for any solid 4-neighbour and clamping solid cells to `(0, 0)`, preserving symmetry and the existing CFL stability limit while reflecting waves with zero transmission. Wall obstacles enforce a minimum half-thickness of `0.72 * cell` so diagonal walls remain 4-connected with no diagonal leakage. Moving-body splash/wake heuristics (`trackBody`), ray-plane intersection (`disturbRay`), and the fragment heatmap/bounds debug overlay (`setDebug`) are Margo-own. No other engine's source code was read.
- **The ripple field on the CPU (`RippleField`, `Ripples` `cpu: true`, `packages/water/src/ripple-field.ts`) and its tests (2026-11-27, Claude laptop, taking SEA-02 and SEA-04 over from Gemini)**:
  the step is the shader's own (velocity first, then height: symplectic Euler, equal to leapfrog on the height), whose
  discrete dispersion relation sin(omega dt / 2) = (c dt / dx) sqrt(sin^2(kx dx / 2) + sin^2(kz dx / 2)) and its
  start-up phase come from John C. Strikwerda, *Finite Difference Schemes and Partial Differential Equations*, 2nd ed.,
  SIAM (2004), chapter 8 (second-order equations, the leapfrog scheme for the wave equation)
  ([doi:10.1137/1.9780898717938](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717938)). The wall test is the method of images for
  the Neumann problem (a reflecting wall is the free field plus the mirror source), as in Philip M. Morse and Herman
  Feshbach, *Methods of Theoretical Physics*, McGraw-Hill (1953), part I, chapter 7 (Green's functions and the method of images).
  `seaSurface` (`packages/water/src/sea-surface.ts`) writes the drawn water into the physics framework's `SeaSurface`
  contract (docs/physics-framework.md) with hydrostatic gauge pressure rho g (eta - y); the band-edge test of
  `fft-cpu.ts` follows the shader's binary32 wave number so both include the same modes. Margo's own; no engine read.

### Joint axes, the joint debug view and joint errors (DYN-03)

Limits and motors on every free axis of every joint reuse the kernel's joint rows of PK24 below, unchanged: a limit is
rigid up to its edge and soft past it, a motor a soft row in implicit form (Erin Catto, "Soft Constraints", GDC 2011),
and a rope's or spring's distance row with a least and a greatest stop is the maximum-distance row of Matthias Müller,
Miles Macklin, Nuttapong Chentanez, Stefan Jeschke and Tae-Yong Kim, "Detailed Rigid Body Simulation with Extended
Position Based Dynamics" (SCA 2020, Eq. 25) bounded on both sides. Reduced-coordinate chains are the existing multibody
(Roy Featherstone, "Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms", Springer 2008). The debug view's arcs are the turn of a frame axis
about another (a rotation of axis i + 1 toward i + 2), and a cone's rim the swing ellipse of its rotation vector, as the
cone row measures it (Dobrowolski 2015, PK24); both own geometry. The three.js migration note names Rapier's JavaScript
API calls as its public user guide lists them (rapier.rs, "Joints" and "Multibody joints"); no Rapier, three.js, Ammo,
Bullet, Havok or Babylon source was read.
[Catto 2011](https://box2d.org/files/ErinCatto_SoftConstraints_GDC2011.pdf),
[Müller et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14105),
[Featherstone 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-7560-7).

### Volumetric solids and vertex block descent (SOFT-04)

Anka He Chen, Ziheng Liu, Yin Yang and Cem Yuksel, “Vertex Block Descent” (2024), §3.1–3.3, describes implicit
Euler as minimization of the inertia and elastic energies and visits one vertex at a time. Breannan Smith,
Fernando de Goes and Theodore Kim, “Stable Neo-Hookean Flesh Simulation” (2018), Eq. 13 and §4.2, gives
`μ(‖F‖²−3)/2 − μ(J−1) + λ′(J−1)²/2`, where `λ′ = λ + μ` recovers the input Lamé constants at rest.
The gradient of the shape function is `g`. A single vertex displacement changes `F` by the rank-one product
`Δx gᵀ`, so `J = det(F)` is affine in that displacement and `dJ = cof(F)g`. The exact per-cell block is
`μ(g·g)I + λ′ dJ dJᵀ`, with the positive inertia term added per vertex. The native LDLᵀ solve minimizes that
quadratic without eigenvalue filtering. The dissipative potential uses squared differences in `F` and `J`
from the start of the substep, scaled by the existing stiffness damping coefficient divided by the step
length. Its local Hessian has the same form. The VBD paper's §3.3 uses a block-local Rayleigh force.
Sofien Bouaziz, Sebastian Martin, Tiantian Liu, Ladislav Kavan and Mark Pauly, “Projective Dynamics: Fusing
Constraint Projections for Fast Simulation” (2014), §3.3, describes the alternating independent projections
and global linear system of the X-33 method. The implementation uses its Eq. 10, Eq. 15 and Appendix A
for a second optional mode. A signed spectral basis puts inversion on the least singular axis and keeps
the rotation proper. The volume projection solves `qᵢ(qᵢ − σᵢ) = −λₚ` with product one in the signed
singular basis. Compression has a monotonic multiplier. Expansion checks the large roots and searches
the smaller root of the least singular axis when it can be closer. The per-tet elastic weights are
`2μ` and `3λ`. The latter follows because the squared distance to unit determinant is
`(tr ε)²/3` to quadratic order near rest. A matrix-free preconditioned conjugate-gradient solve
uses the same rest-gradient operator for each global iteration. Floating positions are stored as
corrections to the inertial prediction in the solve.
[Chen et al.](https://doi.org/10.1145/3658179),
[Smith et al.](https://doi.org/10.1145/3180491),
[Bouaziz et al.](https://doi.org/10.1145/2601097.2601116).

Brian Mirtich, “Fast and Accurate Computation of Polyhedral Mass Properties” (1996), formulates rigid
mass as a volume integral over a solid bounded by its surface. Molino, Bao and Fedkiw (2004) distinguish
the split material from its collision geometry. Rebuilding a fragment keeps an existing volumetric
collider's density only when the new collision mesh remains a closed and outward-wound volume.
A query-only parent and an open fragment use triangular surfaces without volume mass.
[Mirtich](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~jfc/mirtich/massProps.html)
[Molino et al.](https://physbam.stanford.edu/papers/stanford2004-01.pdf)

Ellen M. Arruda and Mary C. Boyce, “A three-dimensional constitutive model for the large stretch behavior
of rubber elastic materials” (1993), gives the five-term inverse-Langevin chain expansion. Alan N. Gent and
Alan G. Thomas, “Forms for the stored (strain) energy function for vulcanized rubber” (1958), contributes
the logarithmic second invariant. The combined law uses raw invariants `I₁ = ‖F‖²` and `I₂ = ‖cof F‖²`.
For shear contributions `u = W₁′(3)`, `v = W₂′(3)`, its volumetric energy is
`(λ + 2u − 4W₁″(3) − 16W₂″(3))(J−1)²/2 − (2u+4v)(J−1)`. Differentiation at identity gives zero
stress and `μ = 2(u+v)`. At `I₂ < 3` the second-order continuation at 3 preserves the energy and its
first two derivatives while keeping collapsed cells finite. Both cofactors and the determinant are affine
in a single vertex's displacement. A tangent majorizer represents the concave logarithmic term, and the
finite-strain block uses backtracking to accept a decrease of the physical objective.
[Arruda and Boyce](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-5096(93)90013-6)
[Gent and Thomas](https://doi.org/10.1002/pol.1958.1202811814)
[Chen et al.](https://doi.org/10.1145/3658179)

L. R. G. Treloar, “Stress-strain data for vulcanised rubber under various types of deformation” (1944),
measured the 8% sulfur sample. The test uses nominal tensile stress, converting one kgf/cm² to 98,066.5 Pa.
The measured stresses used for calibration are the even-indexed uniaxial readings and the planar series.
A grid over chain-link parameter `N` from 5 to 25 in 0.05 steps and spread from
`[1,2,3,4,6,8,10,13,16,24,40,64]` minimizes the calibration squared relative residual. Each candidate
fits the nonnegative chain and second-invariant coefficients by two-variable least squares. It selects
`N = 20.45`, spread 6, a chain coefficient of 239,299 Pa, and `W₂′(3) = 54,155 Pa`.
These give `μ ≈ 354,972 Pa` and transverse fraction 0.3051. For the prediction envelope, normalize
each calibration residual by its measured stress plus the first 0.6 kgf/cm² recorded load.
The residual at 21 degrees of freedom is 0.09164 of that scale. Use the 95% Student-t factor 2.080
and the independent numerical traction bound described in the test. Eleven withheld uniaxial and
twelve equibiaxial observations at 20% extension or more exercise the native solver. Both the held-out
stresses and the small-strain mismatches are separate from the coefficient fit.
[Treloar](https://doi.org/10.1039/TF9444000059)
[Experimental measurements and units](https://abaqus.uclouvain.be/English/SIMACAEBMKRefMap/simabmk-c-rubberfit.htm)

Senalik and Farber, “Mechanical Properties of Wood” (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, 2021),
Table 5–1, gives different longitudinal, radial and tangential moduli. The directional regression
uses the printed Douglas-fir tangential/longitudinal ratio 0.050. Hernandez et al., “Anisotropic
Strain Limiting” (2013), motivates authored rest-space directions. For the two tetrahedron solvers
Margo adds `κ(‖Fa‖−1)²/2` for a unit material axis `a`. Its local target is the nearest unit
vector to `Fa`. In the projective global solve this adds the constant stiffness entries
`κ (gᵢ·a)(gⱼ·a)`. In a vertex block the frozen target majorizes the directional energy and adds
the scalar `κ (gᵢ·a)²` to the three coordinate diagonals. A projection refresh follows the local
solve. Both routes use the same rest-volume and stiffness-damping scaling as the bulk modes.
[Wood Handbook](https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/62244),
[Hernandez et al.](https://filedn.eu/l8vDXhPLwQPyaW6XewVeXCk/publications/anisotropic_strain_limiting/paper.pdf).

Eftychios Sifakis and Jernej Barbič, “FEM Simulation of 3D Deformable Solids: Theory and
Discretization” (2012), uses Green strain `(FᵀF−I)/2` to remove dependence on rigid rotation.
The full orthotropic material evaluates that strain in the authored axes. Its three engineering
shears are twice the corresponding off-diagonal strains. The normal compliance has diagonal
`1/Eᵢ` and symmetric off-diagonal `−νᵢⱼ/Eᵢ`; its inverse gives the normal stress coefficients.
The shear stresses use the three independently supplied shear moduli. Tables 5–1 and 5–2 in
C. Adam Senalik and Benjamin Farber, “Mechanical Properties of Wood” (2021), supply the
Douglas-fir ratios for an independent numerical specimen.
[Sifakis and Barbič](https://viterbi-web.usc.edu/~jbarbic/femdefo/sifakis-courseNotes-TheoryAndDiscretization.pdf)
[Senalik and Farber](https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/62244).

Green strain also vanishes under a reflection. Geoffrey Irving, Joseph Teran and Ronald Fedkiw,
“Invertible Finite Elements for Robust Simulation of Large Deformation” (2004), describes this
inversion problem. The implementation here adds `c max(0,1−det F)⁴/4`, where `c` is the mean
normal stiffness. Each vertex block uses a positive curvature approximation and accepts a position
only if the total incremental potential evaluated at that stored position preserves or lowers the
prior value. Both the compression term and its tangent vanish at the rest volume.
[Irving et al.](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~jteran/papers/ITF04.pdf).

P. Areias and T. Rabczuk, “Steiner-point free edge cutting of tetrahedral meshes with applications
in fracture” (2017), gives the affine edge intersection and motivates globally consistent subdivision
across adjacent elements. Each side of one plane is convex. Margo constructs both clipped polyhedra
and cones over faces that omit the smallest vertex, triangulating each such face from its own smallest
vertex. This is the pulling triangulation described by Jesús A. De Loera, Jörg Rambau and Francisco
Santos in *Triangulations* (2010), §4.3.2. A shared edge receives one global vertex ID, so both
neighbors choose the same diagonal on any clipped face.
[Areias and Rabczuk](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.finel.2017.05.001)
[De Loera, Rambau and Santos](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-12971-1).

The child tetrahedron's edge matrix in parent coordinates is `A`. Its rest inverse is
`A⁻¹ Dₘ⁻¹` and its rest volume fraction is `det A`. The current gradient therefore agrees with
the parent's, including its plastic deformation. Lumped child quadrature integrates each affine
parent shape function with its usual `V/4`. Applying those same nonnegative fractions to nodal
mass and momentum preserves their sums. Neil Molino, Zhaosheng Bao and Ronald Fedkiw (2004) and
Eftychios Sifakis, Kevin Der and Ronald Fedkiw (2007) describe virtual nodes for multi-plane and
partial incisions. Those methods embed material in replicas of the uncut tets. The conforming plane
operation uses actual subdivided tets so its particles and faces can use the existing contact path.
[Molino, Bao and Fedkiw](https://physbam.stanford.edu/papers/stanford2004-01.pdf)
[Sifakis, Der and Fedkiw](https://physbam.stanford.edu/papers/stanford2007-04.pdf).

Franziska Seeber, Ani Khaloian-Sarnaghi, Taoyi Yu, Fabian Duddeck and Jan Willem van de Kuilen,
“Development and validation of an orthotropic 3D elasto-plastic damage model for wood,
considering fiber deviations” (2024), compares Tsai–Wu, Hashin, Sandhaas and separated modes.
Equation 26 gives the separated stress-to-strength ratios, with distinct positive and negative
normal strengths in each direction and three independent shear strengths. The native solve
uses Green-strain-conjugate stress and shear magnitudes in the material frame. It carries
one filtered utilization per failure mode and selects whole-cell tear events using the
largest utilization and the existing interior-strength factor. This uses their initiation
criterion with the existing topological split. Directional post-peak softening requires a
separate fracture-energy law. Table 1 supplies the elastic and shear inputs, and the observed
strength intervals in Table 2 supply independent axial fixtures.
[Seeber et al.](https://repository.tudelft.nl/record/uuid%3Afe38cfa8-6c48-4832-8906-bbbc1e87cd89).

The optional progressive law uses their Eqs. 30–33 and 47 and Sandhaas and van de Kuilen's
Eq. 9. With `h = (6V₀)^(1/3)`, `β = 2EG/(f²h)` is the utilization at zero tensile or
shear stress. The fraction of stiffness left on the descending branch is
`(β−κ)/((β−1)κ)`. The uniaxial loading work per area is `hf²β/(2E) = G`.
Compression follows the separate stress plateau, with remaining stiffness `1/κ`.
The history is irreversible. The stress sign for each normal axis is held fixed during a
native substep and refreshed from the undamaged stress after it. Diagonal compliance
increases implement Eq. 33. If `r` is the vector of remaining normal stiffness fractions,
scaling the damaged compliance by `diag(sqrt(r))` on both sides makes inversion well
defined at a fully damaged axis. The volume-derived length is Margo's tetrahedron convention
for the Bažant–Oh crack band regularization. The cell then separates using the existing
face topology.
[Sandhaas and van de Kuilen](https://heronjournal.nl/58-23/5.pdf)
[Bažant and Oh](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02486267).

For finite incisions, Sifakis, Der and Fedkiw (2007), §3.3, describes testing material
contiguity across shared polygons. Yuting Wang, Chenfanfu Jiang, Craig Schroeder and
Joseph Teran, “An Adaptive Virtual Node Algorithm with Robust Mesh Cutting” (2014),
§5, organizes intersections in a shared registry and handles cuts through vertices,
edges and faces. Margo partitions the planar section using the three blade edges,
sharing all inserted nodes on intersected cell faces. The restricted polygon
triangulation adds an interior node to the released lip and to a released seam whose
endpoints both lie on the crack front. Cones from the interior repopulate each convex
half with positive-volume tetrahedra. Shared face polygons outside the blade continue
to join their cells and corresponding particle slots. The conservative affine state
transfer is the same as for a complete plane cut.
[Sifakis, Der and Fedkiw](https://physbam.stanford.edu/papers/stanford2007-04.pdf)
[Wang, Jiang, Schroeder and Teran](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~jteran/papers/WJST14.pdf).

Geometric cuts and face tears transfer a live point attachment to every surviving copy of its
original material vertex. Molino, Bao and Fedkiw's 2004 virtual-node construction describes
duplicating the material degrees of freedom at a cut. Macklin, Müller and Chentanez's 2016
XPBD formulation uses constraint gradients to update both linked bodies. Margo retains the
authored rigid-local point through the split and solves its existing reciprocal point rows
on the live descendants without deriving a new anchor from the current, possibly stretched pose.
[A Virtual Node Algorithm for Changing Mesh Topology During Simulation](https://physbam.stanford.edu/papers/stanford2004-01.pdf)
[XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics](https://mmacklin.com/xpbd.pdf).

Chen et al.'s 2024 vertex-block objective has a mass-weighted quadratic term about the inertial
prediction. Elastic and internal damping terms are invariant under uniform translation. After the
local sweeps, minimizing that objective along a translation gives the mass-weighted mean
of the inertial position minus the solved position. Margo applies that common displacement
to every unpinned vertex in a free body before rigid contact. The linear momentum correction
has the same mass weighting as Dahl and Bargteil's 2019 Eq. 3. The correction is in position
space so translational velocity reconstruction and subsequent reciprocal contact both see it.
[Vertex Block Descent](https://www.cemyuksel.com/research/papers/vbd-siggraph2024.pdf)
[Global Momentum Preservation for Position-based Dynamics](https://cal.cs.umbc.edu/Papers/Dahl-2019-GMP/).

Section 4 of Sifakis, Der and Fedkiw (2007) constructs the collision surface from faces with
one incident material tetrahedron. Margo uses that cut boundary to rebuild configured query
colliders and carries their live contact and filtering settings. The triangles continue to
receive their fragment's current vertex positions and velocities, as moving contact geometry
in Bridson, Fedkiw and Anderson (2002).
[Arbitrary Cutting of Deformable Tetrahedralized Objects](https://physbam.stanford.edu/papers/stanford2007-04.pdf)
[Robust Treatment of Collisions, Contact and Friction for Cloth Animation](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~rbridson/docs/cloth2002.pdf).

Li and Barbič (2014), §3, define Green strain as `E = (FᵀF − I)/2`. For a patch normal
`n` in the rest solid, the opening measure is `nᵀ E n = (|Fn|² − 1)/2`. Margo compares it
with the authored tensile strain at the end of the soft tick. The patch's three points stay
at their exact affine coordinates in the changing cell until the finite cutting planner opens it.
Romanowicz and Grygorczuk's 2024 pinewood Mode I experiments motivated the choice of a
specified material plane. The option does not emulate the paper's cohesive crack-growth law.
[Stable Orthotropic Materials](https://viterbi-web.usc.edu/~jbarbic/orthotropic/LiBarbicStableOrthotropicMaterials-SCA2014.pdf)
[The effect of crack orientation on the mode I fracture resistance of pinewood](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10704-024-00798-z).

O'Brien and Hodgins (1999), §4.2, use local directions computed from FEM stresses to guide
crack nucleation. Margo's brittle tensile option instead diagonalizes the current
`F Fᵀ` after a native step. Its spectrum equals that of `Fᵀ F` in Li and Barbič (2014), §3,
and `(largest eigenvalue − 1)/2` is the maximum elastic Green strain. The eigenvector is a
world-space normal. The winning cell opens a centroid section while compatible faces on
neighboring cells retain material continuity. A native flag follows the subdivided parent
region and prevents the same material from nucleating repeatedly.
[Graphical Modeling and Animation of Brittle Fracture](https://doi.org/10.1145/311535.311550)
[Stable Orthotropic Materials](https://viterbi-web.usc.edu/~jbarbic/orthotropic/LiBarbicStableOrthotropicMaterials-SCA2014.pdf).

O'Brien and Hodgins (1999), §4.3, describe sharing the edges split by the fracture with
the original tetrahedron's face and edge neighbors. Margo registers those edge nodes and the
split faces once. A neighbor matches the registered facets and makes its interior tetrahedra
from that boundary. The center nodes do not insert new points on any other old edges.
[Graphical Modeling and Animation of Brittle Fracture](https://doi.org/10.1145/311535.311550).

The tensile continuation follows the crack-front idea in O'Brien and Hodgins (1999), §5.
For an existing material edge with unit tangent `e`, a candidate uses the projection
`n − (n·e)e` of its current principal direction `n`. Its plane must cross the other two
corners of the adjacent tetrahedron. The front is a set of edge slots in the native cell
flags. A conforming midpoint on the previous edge gives the two advancing lips independent
degrees of freedom. The released edge is removed from every incident child's front slots.
This follows the separation of shared crack degrees of freedom in O'Brien and Hodgins §4.3.
A loaded rung fixture independently pairs boundary faces in rest space and checks that
each tracked edge still shares its endpoint particles between the real lips.
The published mixed-mode approach of Erdogan and Sih (1963) describes
crack direction under stress-intensity loading. The implemented rule uses tensile Green strain.
[Graphical Modeling and Animation of Brittle Fracture](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.02934)
[On the Crack Extension in Plates Under Plane Loading and Transverse Shear](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3656897).

Sifakis, Der and Fedkiw (2007), §4, use the connectivity of released material to
represent incompletely separated incisions. For prescribed finite cuts, Margo pairs
the two triangles with the same pre-release material face after assigning the new
particle identities. Exactly two common particles identify a bonded lip edge. This
avoids interpreting an exposed edge on a fully separated fragment as a front.
[Arbitrary Cutting of Deformable Tetrahedralized Objects](https://physbam.stanford.edu/papers/stanford2007-04.pdf).

O'Brien and Hodgins (1999), §4.3, retain the orientation of a material crack while updating
its neighbors. When the propagation plane equals an existing bonded facet, Margo releases
the two incident sides of that facet directly. Only cells that contain the released edge
insert its midpoint. The native side test treats sums within their arithmetic roundoff
as lying in the plane. No geometric offset is introduced to split a coincident face.
[Graphical Modeling and Animation of Brittle Fracture](https://doi.org/10.1145/311535.311550).

Avecillas-Leon, Singh and Duarte (2025), Eqs. 20–22, give the stress intensity factors
from the displacement jumps on the paired lips behind a straight crack. Margo uses the
leading term with the isotropic plane-strain modulus `E′ = E/(1−ν²)`. Substituting into
Okada and Kamibeppu (2005), Eq. 5, gives `Gᵢ = π E′ δᵢ²/(32r)` for I/II and
`Gᵢᵢᵢ = π μ δᵢᵢᵢ²/(16r)` for III. `r` measures undeformed distance behind the front.
The opening term is zero under compression. The mode basis follows the current bonded
facet, preserving its values under rigid rotation. Reeder (2006), Eqs. 6–7 with `η=1`,
gives the critical energy as the arithmetic mean of the three authored toughnesses
weighted by their fractions of total released energy. The native solver releases the
bonded facet when the total exceeds that critical value.
[Validation and Improvements of a Generalized/eXtended Finite Element Method for 3-D Fatigue Crack Propagation](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10704-025-00888-6)
[A Virtual Crack Closure-Integral Method for Three-Dimensional Crack Problems Using Linear Tetrahedral Finite Elements](https://doi.org/10.3970/cmes.2005.010.229)
[3-D Mixed Mode Delamination Fracture Criteria](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20060048260).

Gravelle and Marangoni (2021), Table 1, measured a Young's modulus of 10.57 ± 0.64 kPa
for unfilled 4% B-type gelatin at pH 6. Geerligs et al. (2008) reported 7.5 kPa shear
modulus for porcine subcutaneous tissue at 10 rad/s and 37 °C in the small-strain
regime. These are elastic inputs for independent one-step simple-shear tests, with
Poisson ratio 0.45 authored for both. The tested backward-Euler displacement uses
the exact stiffness `μV/L²` of a tetrahedron sheared with its base fixed.

Frederking and Timco (1983), Table I, series 1, test 1, measured 84 N/mm stiffness
and 135 N peak force in a 600 × 123 × 62 mm freshwater ice cantilever. Their Eqs. 1–2
give an apparent modulus of 2.476 GPa and a flexural stress of 1.028 MPa. The resulting
outer-fiber strain `σ/E = 0.00041518` sets the threshold for a separate uniform-extension
sheet fixture. The solver holds at 90% and opens at 110%, conserving mass in the cut.
[Dataset on the small- and large deformation mechanical properties of emulsion-filled gelatin hydrogels](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dib.2021.107410)
[Linear viscoelastic behavior of subcutaneous adipose tissue](https://doi.org/10.3233/BIR-2008-0517)
[On Measuring Flexural Properties of Ice Using Cantilever Beams](https://doi.org/10.3189/S0260305500005243).

Shewchuk's 1997 work on robust geometric predicates motivates checking the determinant
in the coordinates that the native kernel will hold. An automatic crack is eligible only
when the replacement has representable f32 vertex positions, affine rest bases and nodal masses.
The rung fixture derives its 0.015 strain contrast from the fixed-end moments in Connor and
Faraji (2016), Table 9.1, and the elastic outer-fiber strain `Mc/(EI)`.
[Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~jrs/jrspapers.html)
[Fundamentals of Structural Engineering](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-24331-3).

Camanho and Dávila (2002), Eq. 27, combine the positive opening and two signed shear
tractions in a quadratic failure envelope. The Abaqus cohesive-element reference gives
the corresponding nominal-strain form. Margo uses the envelope with the rest-frame normal
Green strain and engineering shears `2nᵀEt` and `2nᵀEe`, where `e` is the first edge of
the authored triangle and `t` is perpendicular to it within the seam. Compression
contributes zero to the normal term. The tests prescribe an affine deformation and
independently verify both shear modes and their interaction with tensile opening.
[Mixed-Mode Decohesion Finite Elements for the Simulation of Delamination in Composite Materials](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20020053651/downloads/20020053651.pdf)
[Quadratic nominal strain criterion](https://docs.software.vt.edu/abaqusv2026/English/SIMACAEELMRefMap/simaelm-c-cohesivebehavior.htm).

### Soil pressure, shear and permanent footprints (EARTH-05)

M. G. Bekker, *Introduction to Terrain-Vehicle Systems* (1969), supplies the plate fit
`p = (kc/b + kphi) z^n`, verified against J. Y. Wong, *Theory of Ground Vehicles*, 3rd ed. (2001), Eq. 2.47.
J. Y. Wong and A. R. Reece, “Prediction of rigid wheel performance based on the analysis of soil-wheel stresses”
(1967), integrates normal and tangential stresses around a wheel. The mean tier applies uniform pressure to a
measured contact patch and uses DYN-04's suspension. Z. Janosi and B. Hanamoto, “The Analytical Determination of
Drawbar Pull as a Function of Slip for Tracked Vehicles in Deformable Soils” (1961), gives
`τ = (c + p tan φ)(1 − exp(−j/K))`, verified against Wong Eq. 2.56.
[Bekker](https://books.google.com/books?id=N694AAAAIAAJ),
[Wong](https://courses.minia.edu.eg/Attach/9775Theory%20of%20Ground%20Vehicles%20-%20J.%20Y.%20Wong%203rd%20Ed.pdf),
[Wong and Reece](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-4898(67)90105-X),
[NASA report with the Janosi and Hanamoto proceedings citation](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170010706/downloads/20170010706.pdf).

R. W. Sumner, J. F. O'Brien and J. K. Hodgins, “Animating Sand, Mud, and Snow” (1999), models compression and
redistribution into the first unoccupied ring. Margo integrates volume with the exact nodal areas of the existing
height-field triangles and weights the berm in the direction of mobilized shear. The ledger separates compacted
volume, dry mineral fines and loose soil that leaves the modeled patch. Native state retains the peak indentation.
[Sumner et al.](https://www.ri.cmu.edu/pub_files/pub4/sumner_robert_1999_1/sumner_robert_1999_1.pdf).

R. Krenn and G. Hirzinger, “SCM – A Soil Contact Model for Multi-Body System Simulations” (2009), Eqs. 2–4,
defines equivalent width as twice a footprint's area divided by its perimeter. The resolved tier uses that width
and solves one peak depth from the force integral `F = Σ (kc / b + kphi) (z_peak q_i)^n A_i`.
For a rectangular rounded footprint the profile `q_i` is one minus the squared maximum normalized coordinate.
For an ellipse it is one minus the squared normalized radius. The per-vertex area is the TerrainBed nodal
area. The local repose pass conservatively transfers only the current step's new loose material.
[Krenn and Hirzinger](https://elib.dlr.de/60535/1/elib_ISTVS2009_KrennHirzinger.pdf).

Liang Ding, Haibo Gao, Zongquan Deng, Kazuya Yoshida and Keiji Nagatani, “Slip Ratio for Lugged Wheel
of Planetary Rover in Deformable Soil: Definition and Estimation” (2009), Eq. 22, gives independent
drawbar force and axle moment from the angular forces. After balancing the vertical load, the
resolved rolling option projects the tangential stress forward and the normal stress rearward.
The axle moment is the tangential force times its effective radius. The native integration uses
24 midpoint samples on each side of the pressure peak. For a smooth wheel with symmetric pressure
and no shear, drawbar equals the vertical load times the negative tangent of half the entry angle.
At full slip with constant cohesion and zero internal friction, the shear exponential gives exact
axle moment and sine/cosine force integrals, which the tests compare to the native midpoint error bound.
[Ding et al. (2009)](https://vigir.missouri.edu/~gdesouza/Research/Conference_CDs/IEEE_IROS_2009/papers/0739.pdf).

The held-out Wh2 high-slip comparison uses the 10 mm lug at 80 N and 10 mm/s in Fig. 6(a,c).
Equation 8 converts the 0.6 tip slip to 0.58768 at the model's half-lug effective radius.
The bounds come from the plotted red marker edges (216.54–217.92 and 308.58–310.217 PDF
points) divided by the labelled tick scales. They give approximately 24.37–25.19 N and
7.22–7.45 N·m. The solver predicts 24.67 N and 7.39 N·m. These points were held out from
the 2010 slip-sinkage fit and use the same soil family and wheel dimensions. The test
also checks a permanent rut. The source's high-slip sinkage and transient digging force
remain separate comparisons.

Catherine Pavlov and Aaron M. Johnson, “A terramechanics model for high slip angle and skid with
prediction of wheel-soil interaction geometry” (2024), and Pavlov’s 2023 CMU dissertation, Eqs.
5.3–5.6, 5.11 and 5.15–5.20, distinguish driving slip from braking skid. The optional skid arc holds
the pressure peak and exit angle at the load-matched free-rolling geometry. It increments the
bearing exponent by the magnitude of skid times the measured coefficient. The rear and front
shear distances integrate distinct velocities. The front bias is the mean cosine between the
first contact and the transition. The code splits integration where the local shear changes sign.
At zero spin, all nonzero shear distances reach their signed saturation. The exact test integrates
the locked smooth wheel’s constant-cohesion moment over both signed regions. The live fixture
uses the sand fit from dissertation Table 5.3 with its own wheel geometry and verifies a negative
drawbar impulse, a positive wheel spin impulse, no energy gain in the paired tangential impulse
and exact seek. It uses the signed speed ratio even below 1 m/s.
[Pavlov and Johnson (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jterra.2023.08.004),
[Pavlov (2023), Chapter 5](https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/amj1/papers/Pavlov2023.pdf).

Catherine Pavlov and Aaron M. Johnson, “Soil Displacement Terramechanics for Wheel-Based
Trenching with a Planetary Rover” (2019), and Pavlov’s 2023 CMU dissertation, Eqs. 4.1, 4.2
and 4.4, split excavated soil across travel and derive initial pile height from triangular
cross-sections at the angle of repose. The wheel face projects a circular segment across
the direction of travel, and the rim projects a rectangle. This optional depositor uses their
area ratio between 10° and 80° and equal shares at other angles. It builds each side from the
actual cut volume after compaction and dust. Separate quadrature over the physical terrain
areas closes both banks' volumes. Each vertex integrates its partial overlap with the wedge.
The coupled fixture verifies both banks, a deliberately missing bank at an open boundary and exact seek.
Equation 4.3 gives transport area per metre of advance as
`r (ω/v) ζ μ h_g b`, with `ω` in radians per second. The optional `grouserFill` supplies
`ζ μ`. The native ratio uses the signed forward slip definition with the same effective shear
radius as the rolling model. The transported fraction is bounded by the actual loose cut,
and oblique travel draws it only from the source-side bank.
When the front and rear corners align, the article's high-obliquity rule moves the transported
portion to the opposite bank. Otherwise it returns soil into the rear contact area, limited by
the present net depression accumulated by this solver, including its earlier cuts and repose
redistribution. The excavation maximum is a separate history. Returning earlier material
therefore preserves the original cut ledger. A moving-carriage case checks two filled trailing
stations against the same wheel without transport, net volume, zero export and snapshot replay
in plain and shared memory.
[Pavlov and Johnson (2019)](https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/amj1/papers/ICRA2019_Wheel.pdf).

For straight travel, Pavlov's Eqs. 4.11 and 4.12 describe the same area balance for pointed and
flat-bottomed trenches. The native raster uses their common volume condition directly. It
raises the deepest available rear vertices up to one elevation and integrates
`max(0, elevation - old height) × vertex area`. The volume is piecewise linear in the new
bottom. A bounded Newton solve removes vertices as they become dry, then distributes the
requested volume over the resulting profile. The fixture checks three partial fill amounts and
independently computes the swept area from Eq. 4.3. [Pavlov (2023), Chapter 4](https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/amj1/papers/Pavlov2023.pdf#page=45).

At intermediate angles, Figure 4.2f and Eqs. 4.13–4.18 describe a step under the trailing
edge of the rotating grousers. Its initial band is the projection of the wheel width
`b cos β` about that edge. The solver uses node coverage for partly intersected band cells.
It fills the deepest cells of the band and then uses any remaining trailing room if that
band reaches the original terrain. A mirrored ±22.5° test verifies the plateau, the band
boundary, the projected face-plus-rim transport volume and conservation.
[Pavlov (2023), Figure 4.2 and §4.2](https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/amj1/papers/Pavlov2023.pdf#page=42).

The optional phase-driven excavation applies the angular sweep as a volume budget. Over a
wheel's angular change `Δθ`, Pavlov's Eq. 4.3 gives `r b h_g ζ μ |Δθ|` independently of
translation, because the forward travel cancels in the volume integral. Ibrahim et al.'s
relative rotation construction uses actual rotation minus the rotation implied by travel.
In the solver this gives a multiplier equal to positive slip. The normal-contact weights
distribute that cut. Bedrock and the modeled axle depth limit the volume actually removed.
The swept soil joins the external loose deposit rather than filling the same cut on the same
step. Omura and Ishigami's test provides the 10°/s control rate for the exact-volume fixture.
A real held vehicle also sends its rigid wheel phase to create a deeper rut. The measured
time history of contact angles remains a separate comparison.
[Pavlov (2023), Eq. 4.3](https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/amj1/papers/Pavlov2023.pdf#page=43),
[Ibrahim et al., “The Effect of Assistive Anchor-Like Grousers on Wheeled Rover Performance over Unconsolidated Sandy Dune Inclines” (2016), Figure 10](https://doi.org/10.3390/s16091507),
[Omura and Ishigami, “Wheel Slip Classification Method for Mobile Robot in Sandy Terrain Using In-Wheel Sensor” (2017), §3](https://doi.org/10.20965/jrm.2017.p0902).

The cross-track banks settle with a conservative face flux from a common elevation state.
The dry granular finite-volume treatments by Roger P. Denlinger and Richard M. Iverson (2004)
and A. Mangeney-Castelnau et al. (2003) motivated equal and opposite transfers that stop at a
Coulomb slope threshold. The solver divides each equalizing transfer and the donor's available
loose volume by the four possible outgoing faces. It applies the resulting transfers
together and saves the touched neighborhood for the next step. The original moving-carriage
case reached 21 mm of numerical left-right difference. The mirrored case now compares the
full interior at roundoff, settles after unloading and preserves the volume ledger and replay.
[Denlinger and Iverson, “Granular avalanches across irregular three-dimensional terrain,” §4](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003JF000085),
[Mangeney-Castelnau et al., “Numerical modeling of avalanches based on Saint Venant equations using a kinetic scheme,” §3](https://doi.org/10.1029/2002JB002024).

The measured locked-wheel check takes the nominal 48 mm wheel radius, 50 mm width, 5 mm
grousers, 29° repose angle and 30 mm/s carriage travel from Pavlov's Table 4.2 and §4.3.
A fixed normal load matches the requested 15 mm setup sinkage. The aggregate 5.76% lockup
compaction from Table 4.3 supplies the single fixture's soil input. The held-out quantities
are the two crest-to-trough ratios from the blue traces in the top left of Figure 4.5.
In the embedded 1,500 × 562 RGB image, flat-ground row is 52 ± 1 from columns 100–140.
The left crest spans rows 38–41 near column 176, the right rows 36–40 near column 284 and the
trough rows 70–74 near column 232, allowing for the raster marks around the visible medians.
The common vertical pixel scale cancels in the ratios. Both simulated crests are about 10.64 mm
and the trough about 14.74 mm at the central station, giving 0.72 on each side within both measured
envelopes. This check establishes relative locked-wheel relief at one condition. Absolute
trench geometry across powered slip and obliquity remains open. [Pavlov (2023), Figure 4.5](https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/amj1/papers/Pavlov2023.pdf#page=49).

Ryota Matsumura and Genya Ishigami's 2021 in-wheel imaging measured distinct sinkage across
a tilted wheel, and Yuankai Li, Liang Ding and Guangjun Liu's 2016 wheel-attitude model
describes lateral inclination relative to the ground plane. The cylindrical raster projects
its width by `cos γ`, samples the current triangulated bed at both limits, then adds
`lateral distance × (bed grade - tan γ)` to nominal depth. The positive-depth mask controls
pressure and excavation, and the pressure quadrature integrates exactly to normal load.
The live slope case evaluates level, slope-aligned and oppositely cambered wheels and
checks the cross-width difference directly from plane geometry. The along-wheel force
arc uses its cylindrical reference. Full dynamic camber forces remain a separate comparison.
[Matsumura and Ishigami, “Visualization and analysis of wheel camber angle effect for slope traversability using an in-wheel camera” (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jterra.2020.09.002),
[Li, Ding and Liu, “Attitude-based dynamic and kinematic models for wheels of mobile robot on deformable slope” (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.robot.2015.10.006).

Ishigami, Miwa, Nagatani and Yoshida (2007) use independent longitudinal and transverse
displacements and shear lengths in Eqs. 12–15. An optional lateral length enables those
forward rim expressions and projects total mobilization onto the Mohr–Coulomb yield circle
when both axes would exceed it. The existing passive wedge supplies the sidewall contribution.
The FJS-1 wheel uses the published radius, width, speed, load, soil properties and the
Table 1 expressions for both shear lengths in radians. An angular exit fraction of
`-√0.9` is the small-angle equivalent of the lower reported rear/fore sinkage ratio.
Figure 12 in the author PDF has 0–0.9 slip across 160.649 pt and 10 N across 20.645 pt.
The test uses four published marker centres near 0.6 slip and the bounds of the paired
experimental marks at 5°, 10°, 15° and 20°. No plotted forces supplied the material fit.
The test checks one slip neighbourhood. The high-slip endpoint and full dynamic camber
loads need additional measured comparisons. [Ishigami et al., “Terramechanics-Based Model for Steering Maneuver of Planetary Exploration Rovers on Loose Soil” (2007), Figure 12](https://k-nagatani.org/pdf/2007-JFR-Genya-online.pdf#page=14).

Pavlov and Johnson's oblique contact combines the longitudinal and transverse displacement
magnitudes in the shear law and projects the force in the direction of the local slip velocity
(dissertation Eqs. 5.10–5.14 and 5.20–5.21). The sidewall depth is measured from the chord between
entry and exit, and the depth-integrated passive wedge pressure follows Eqs. 5.22–5.27. Specific
weight is material density times the configured gravity. At 45° with zero cohesion and friction,
the symmetric arc's sidewall integral reduces to a polynomial in sine and cosine. The tests bound
the native midpoint error from its second derivative and check exact mirror symmetry. The live
oblique rig verifies that the previous side reaction gives the chassis an impulse opposing slip
at the actual contact and reproduces the coupled state after seek.

Blake Hannaford and Jee-Hwan Ryu, “Time-Domain Passivity Control of Haptic Interfaces” (2002),
Eq. 12, motivates accounting for work across all ports in a sampled coupling. For longitudinal
contact impulse `J`, signed axle impulse `L`, tangential relative speed `v`, angular speed `w`,
contact inverse mass `M` and spin inertia `I`, the exact rigid kinetic-energy change is
`s (Jv + Lw) + (s²/2)(MJ² + L²/I)`. The application chooses the largest scale `s` up to one
that keeps this change nonpositive and does not reverse speed. Both impulses retain the same
scale after the measured load and optional grip bounds. The fixture checks actual shaft and
chassis impulse with the changed collider normal, and an active force sample is refused.
[Hannaford and Ryu (2002)](https://cim.mcgill.ca/~hayward/Teach/papers/Part-II/Hannaford-Ryu-02.pdf).

Krenn and Hirzinger's Fig. 9 gives a discontinuous projected footprint. The resolved tier accepts projected
depth sampled from a shape. It rotates the sample grid with the contact and bilinearly interpolates local depth
before applying the force integral. Supplied area and perimeter retain the geometry's effective width when
the model is rotated or the bed is resampled. The two-lug fixture uses independently calculated depth
and verifies that its gap stays unloaded.

M. Apfelbeck, S. Kuß, B. Rebele and B. Schäfer, “A systematic approach to reliably characterize soils based on
bevameter testing” (2011), gives fits for circular plates in Table 5 and observed square profiles in Fig. 8.
Both tiers reproduce the held-out square-plate sinkage for the dry quartz sand at 41.21 kPa (18.6–21.2 mm)
and fire clay at 2 kPa (24.3–30.7 mm). The test bands use the plotted error bars with one pixel of graph read-off
allowance. The circular-plate fits used for the check are the slow quartz and fast clay measurements in Table 5.
[Apfelbeck et al.](https://elib.dlr.de/69724/1/Apfelbeck_BevameterTest_JTerra2011.pdf).

N. D. Salman, G. Pillinger, M. M. Hanon and P. Kiss, “Design and performance evaluation of bevameter
equipment” (2020), Eqs. 6–7, computes the breaking depth as soil thickness minus the footing radius times
`tan(π/4 + φ/2)`. Margo uses the area-perimeter equivalent radius for noncircular profiles. The two
pressure laws are joined continuously at that depth by adding the upper law's pressure there and
subtracting the lower law's value there. The resolved tier integrates the piecewise pressure at each vertex
with a bracketed force solve. The test for the 200 mm plate uses the authors' Table 2 pressure fits for
sandy loam. At 110 kPa it compares with the adjacent Fig. 6 marker centers at 118.5 and 122.2 mm,
allowing one rendered PDF pixel. This checks the published fitted example. The quartz and clay examples
above use held-out plate geometry.
[Salman et al.](https://doi.org/10.1299/jamdsm.2020jamdsm0084).

Hardpan thickness can vary by vertex. The contact samples it with barycentric interpolation using TerrainBed's
triangles. The excavation floor uses bedrock values at the same vertices and clips the cut before the native
soil ledger divides the displaced volume. The two-sided tests use independent exact thickness and mass cases.

L. Ding, H. Gao, Z. Deng and J. Tao, “Wheel slip-sinkage and its prediction model of lunar rover” (2010),
Eqs. 13–19 and 22, supplies the slip-adjusted exponent, lug entry and shear geometry, asymmetric Wong–Reece
normal stress and lug bearing offset. The implementation integrates each side of the pressure maximum
with 24 midpoint ordinates and brackets the axle load against the vertical components of normal and shear
stress. It projects the loaded arc onto the bed using 33 stations and normalizes the rasterized vertical
load. The assumed peak fractions 0.4 and 0.3 use the published empirical range in K. Nagaoka,
*Study on Soil-Screw Interaction of Exploration Robot for Surface and Subsurface Locomotion in Soft Terrain*
(2011), Appendix B.2.
The exit angle is zero by default, a reported simplification in L. Ding, H. Gao, Z. Deng, K. Nagatani and
K. Yoshida, “Experimental study and analysis on driving wheels’ performance for planetary exploration
rovers moving in deformable soil” (2011), Sec. 2. The material values come from its separate plate and shear
tests in Table 2. The rod carriage replays the Wh32 geometry and an 80 N load. The 2010 rolling coefficients
are 0.84 at zero slip and 0.72 per unit slip, with 1.5 mm lug support. The 2011 observation at zero slip
is 2.89 mm, checked against a 0.25 mm comparison band from the same wheel's reported Table 4 scatter.
At 20% slip, the rounded 0.25 mm absolute and 2.89% relative scatter give a mean range of 8.46–8.84 mm.
The test extends that range by two 0.25 mm scatter widths, giving 7.96–9.34 mm. These cases check
the two publications’ related rigs and settings.
[Ding et al. (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11771-010-0021-7),
[Ding et al. (2011)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022489810000601),
[SOKENDAI thesis appendix](https://ir.soken.ac.jp/record/2467/files/%E7%94%B21413_%E6%9C%AC%E6%96%87.pdf).

K. Skonieczny, S. J. Moreland and D. S. Wettergreen, “A Grouser Spacing Equation for Determining
Appropriate Geometry of Planetary Rover Wheels” (2012), Fig. 8, relates tire and lug geometry to the
point where a rotating lug enters the soil. Ding et al. (2010), Eq. 2, gives the corresponding periodicity.
The resolved phase path projects each effective lug tip, with radius `R + h`, onto the bed. A tip at
signed angle `θ` reaches `(R + h)cos(θ)` below the axle and lands `(R + h)sin(θ)` along travel.
Its projected width is an authored strip. The phase fixture checks exact vertical contact at zero phase,
an unloaded gap at half a pitch, and identical terrain after a full pitch across native memory variants.
[Skonieczny et al.](https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/2012/10/SkoniecznyIROS2012.pdf).

Rainer Krenn and Gerd Hirzinger, “SCM – A Soil Contact Model for Multi-Body System Simulations”
(2009), §3.2 and Fig. 6, use transformed polygon geometry and the lowest point at each soil-grid
column. The indexed tread path rotates triangles about the axle by the live spin angle and solves
two horizontal barycentric coordinates at each candidate profile sample. The weighted vertex
heights give the contact depth, and the lowest intersecting triangle wins before the rim and tread
pressures are normalized to the prescribed vertical load. The projection uses the local horizontal
bearing plane. The test places a tread outside the rim width and checks its exact downwards cut,
the unloaded opposite side and quarter-turn clearance in both native memory modes.
[Krenn and Hirzinger](https://elib.dlr.de/60535/1/elib_ISTVS2009_KrennHirzinger.pdf).

R. Matsumura and G. Ishigami, “Visualization and analysis of wheel camber angle effect for
slope traversability using an in-wheel camera” (2021), measure unequal sinkage across a tilted
wheel. The indexed geometry now rotates about the axle by its live spin and about the travel
axis by its signed camber. The rigid field publishes the vertical component of the true steered
right axis. An independent plane fixture tilts an off-centre tread through both directions and
solves its height at a bed vertex outside the upright rim. The analytic bearing arc remains the
load reference, and measured slope-dependent soil failure stays separate from this projection.
[Matsumura and Ishigami](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jterra.2020.09.002),
[Keio Space Robotics Lab](https://www.srg.mech.keio.ac.jp/research/matsumura2021visualization/).

### Resistive force on rotating legs (EARTH-05)

Chen Li, Tingnan Zhang and Daniel I. Goldman, *A Terradynamics of Legged Locomotion on
Granular Media* (2013), Eq. 1, Eq. 2 and supplement Eqs. S8–S9, give the force on
an immersed element of a moving surface. The four horizontal and five vertical
Fourier terms depend on element attack and intrusion directions. They multiply the
wet element's area and vertical depth; the force at each midpoint produces a moment
about the rigid body's centre of mass. Angles follow Fig. 2A, with the positive
intrusion direction pointing down. The sign and magnitude of vertical extraction force
can differ from intrusion. The implementation uses angle-addition products of unit
directions and deterministic two-element SIMD batches.
[Paper and supplement](https://goldmanlab.gatech.edu/pages/publications/pdf/Science-2013-Li-1408-12_ALL.pdf).

Tingnan Zhang and Daniel I. Goldman, *The effectiveness of resistive force theory in
granular locomotion* (2014), reviews the independent strip superposition and where speed
and adjacent elements limit it. Laura K. Treers, Cyndia Cao and Hannah S. Stuart,
*Granular Resistive Force Theory Implementation for Three-Dimensional Trajectories*
(2021), tests a three-dimensional extension to the vertical-plane law used here.
[Zhang and Goldman](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4898629).
[Treers, Cao and Stuart](https://doi.org/10.1109/LRA.2021.3057052).

Table S2 gives coefficients in N/cm³ from linear measurements on a 38.1 × 25.4 mm
plate. Multiply by 10⁶ to obtain N/m³. The held-out targets come from the separate
Fig. S5 A and D rigid C-leg rotation runs by the apparatus at a 20 mm hip height
and 0.2 rad/s. The fixture divides the 76.2 mm long, 25.4 mm wide C-leg into 30 strips
and computes force and moment from the actual kinematic body in the live TerrainBed.
The model input consists of geometry, motion and nine coefficients from the plate tests.

The test digitizes the green solid thrust and blue solid lift paths on supplement
page 11 every π/8 over ±π/2. In top-left PDF points, panel A uses θ = 0 at x = 263.307,
π/2 spans 35.309 pt, and the 0 N and 10 N grid lines are at y = 166.277 and 82.555.
Panel D uses θ = 0 at x = 263.195, π/2 spans 34.724 pt, and its 0 N and 20 N grid
lines are at y = 270.534 and 182.585. The independent peaks are [4.619, 9.357] N
and [6.981, 15.175] N in thrust, lift order. The tests use the paper's C-leg
10% and all-leg 33% peak error envelopes, plus the 0.05 N instrument precision
and up to 0.13 N from half the 1.1 pt PDF curve stroke. The phase comparisons use
the wider published envelope relative to each measured peak. These bounds account
for model error separately from instrument precision.

Run `node --test packages/physics/tests/coupling/resistive-soil.test.js` after building
Physics. The analytic fixture independently integrates a translating strip's force and
moment, verifies the rigid body's resulting velocity and checks snapshot hash parity.
The browser repeats that test with both native memory variants.

### Cyclic soil bearing (EARTH-05)

J. Y. Wong, M. Garber and J. Preston-Thomas, *Theoretical Prediction and Experimental
Substantiation of the Ground Pressure Distribution and Tractive Performance of Tracked
Vehicles* (1984), distinguish permanent settlement and elastic rebound for repetitive
normal loading. J. Y. Wong, *Terramechanics and Off-Road Vehicle Engineering*, second
edition (2009), gives the mineral-soil relation in Eqs. 4.23–4.24. The unloading and
reloading line starts at the largest pressure and has slope `k₀ + Aᵤ zₘₐₓ`. Given
pressure instead of prescribed depth, the recoverable part is pressure divided by that
slope. The loading envelope resumes when a new pressure exceeds the stored maximum.
[Wong, Garber and Preston-Thomas](https://doi.org/10.1243/PIME_PROC_1984_198_155_02).
[Wong's book](https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/monograph/9780750685610/terramechanics-and-off-road-vehicle-engineering).

S. J. Antony and Z. K. Jahanger, *Local Scale Displacement Fields in Grains–Structure
Interactions Under Cyclic Loading* (2020), show reversible rebound in dense silica sand
under multiple controlled cyclic programmes. Haibo Gao, Liang Ding and coauthors'
separate Wh12 repetitive-pass tests (Ding et al., 2011, Figures 22–23) report further
absolute sinkage when a wheel follows the same path. Those tests guide the next
material validation, including its reference to the undisturbed surface.
[Antony and Jahanger](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10706-019-01088-5).
[Ding et al.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jterra.2010.08.001).

The current fixture uses a square 300 mm plate covering nine equal-area vertices.
It prescribes 10, 5, 0, 7.5, 10, 15 and 0 kPa in turn. The specified 100 kPa/m
loading slope, 400 kPa/m unloading stiffness and 2,000 kPa/m² hardening give exact
full-load peaks of 100 mm and 150 mm, with recoveries of 16⅔ mm and 21³⁄₇ mm.
The tests compare the live bed, cumulative plastic cut and restored state to those
closed forms. They also check release on travel and a bedrock-limited, dust-producing
plate. This evidence is analytic.
Run `node --test packages/physics/tests/coupling/soil-unloading.test.js` after building Physics.

### Synoptic weather and moisture (ATMO-10)

J. G. Charney, R. Fjørtoft and J. von Neumann, “Numerical Integration of the Barotropic Vorticity Equation”
(1950), supplies the rotating-vorticity model and the inverse horizontal Laplacian. James R. Holton,
*An Introduction to Dynamic Meteorology* (fourth edition, 2004), gives geostrophic balance, curvature and the
moist lapse. Margo inverts the periodic discrete Laplacian by FFT, advances the linear beta term by
Crank–Nicolson, and transports the regional fields with either upwind or limited piecewise-linear face fluxes
following Bram van Leer, “Towards the Ultimate Conservative Difference Scheme. IV” (1977).
[Charney et al.](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2153-3490.1950.tb00336.x),
[Holton](https://webspace.science.uu.nl/~delde102/Holton_2004.pdf),
[van Leer](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(77)90095-X).

Helen Dacre et al., “How Do Atmospheric Rivers Form?” (2015), defines the column vapour budget and transport
vectors. Ronald B. Smith and Idar Barstad, “A Linear Theory of Orographic Precipitation” (2004), equations 1–2
and 10–19, give separate cloud and falling reservoirs and the wave-filtered lifting of the prescribed mean wind.
Appendix A's saturation pressure and exponential vapour profile give the column capacity `ρs Hw`. The local
advected temperature sets that capacity and the uplift sensitivity `ρs Γm/Γ`. The phase change compares the
displaced saturation column with the available vapour. It bounds evaporation by cloud storage and the humidity
deficit. A manufactured test checks both sides of the saturation threshold and the warm and cool responses. The
stratified wave test uses the phase and amplitude of `1/(1 − i m Hw)` from equation 16. Equation 19 covers its
separate neutral limit. The existing
precipitation service uses the land rain-to-snow transition from Aiguo Dai (2008).
[Dacre et al.](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-14-00031.1),
[Smith and Barstad](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469%282004%29061%3C1377%3AALTOOP%3E2.0.CO%3B2),
[Dai](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008GL033295).

Norman Phillips, “Energy Transformations and Meridional Circulations associated with simple Baroclinic Waves
in a two-level, Quasi-geostrophic Model” (1954), supplies the shear-growth mechanism. Margo solves the mean and
thickness modes separately in the FFT and integrates their coupled linear tendency with a 2×2 Crank–Nicolson solve.
Conservative limited fluxes transport both vorticity fields, and the hypsometric relation converts their thickness
to temperature. J. R. Garratt (1977) supplies the neutral wind-drag coefficients through 21 m/s. M. A. Donelan et al.
(2004), Figure 2, motivates the prescribed high-wind plateau. The coefficient joins these two domains linearly,
and the stress uses the relative velocity of air and water. The existing test verifies the implemented curve through
the water port. An independent high-wind observation remains a separate requirement.
[Phillips](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2153-3490.1954.tb01123.x),
[Garratt](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493%281977%29105%3C0915%3ARODCOO%3E2.0.CO%3B2),
[Donelan et al.](https://doi.org/10.1029/2004GL019460).

### Divergence-free particle liquid (FLUID-01)

Jan Bender and Dan Koschier (2015, 2017), *Divergence-Free SPH for Incompressible and Viscous Fluids*,
section 3 equations 7–12 and Algorithms 1–3, supply the two implicit pressure projections, warm starts and CFL
scheme. The kernel gradients are normalized by reference density. The positive density-prediction residual is
divided by the step duration, so the two passes use the same symmetric velocity update. The bounded line step maximizes the quadratic pressure dual within the nonnegative multipliers.
Previously applied pressure can relax as the other constraints converge. Boundary reactions follow the same
velocity correction. Margo uses the cubic spline for both kernel value and
gradient and shares the position-based entry's 27-cell sparse hash. [2015 paper](https://animation.rwth-aachen.de/media/papers/2015-SCA-DFSPH.pdf),
[2017 paper](https://dankoschier.github.io/resources/papers/BK17.pdf).

Nadir Akinci, Markus Ihmsen, Gizem Akinci, Barbara Solenthaler and Matthias Teschner (2012), *Versatile
Rigid-Fluid Coupling for Incompressible SPH*, equations 4–10, supply inverse kernel-sum boundary volumes.
Each sample takes the rigid velocity at its world point. It receives the negative fluid impulse and its
moment about the rigid body's centre of mass.
[Akinci et al.](https://cgl.ethz.ch/Downloads/Publications/Papers/2012/Sol12/Sol12.pdf).

Marcel Weiler, Dan Koschier, Magnus Brand and Jan Bender (2018), *A Physically Consistent Implicit Viscosity
