Solver for SPH Fluids*, equations 7–12, supply the central Laplacian, backward-Euler system and moving-body
boundary term. The same matrix-free system is solved with a coordinate-Jacobi preconditioner. Each fluid pair
has one central interaction, so a rigid rotational velocity contributes no viscosity on its own.
[Weiler et al.](https://dankoschier.github.io/resources/papers/WKBB18.pdf).

Rene Winchenbach, Rustam Akhunov and Andreas Kolb (2020), *Semi-Analytic Boundary Handling Below Particle
Resolution for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics*, use the closed plane integral of a radial kernel. Margo
integrates its cubic spline with circular sections, yielding the dimensionless half-space density
`2*pi*integral[q,1] W(r)*r*(r-q) dr` and its derivative. At perpendicular walls the product of missed
fractions approximates overlap, so the gradient matches the same density model.
[Winchenbach et al.](https://www.cg.informatik.uni-siegen.de/sites/www.cg.informatik.uni-siegen.de/files/data/Publications/2020/semi-analiticBoundaryHandling.pdf).

Rustam Akhunov and Andreas Kolb (2024), *Decoupled Boundary Handling in SPH*, section 3, identifies
excess boundary density as a cause of still-water motion. The default Margo box uses the discrete
complement of the same rest lattice that samples the fluid. For each lattice point outside at least one
closed face it accumulates rest volume times the same value and gradient as the liquid kernel. Face,
edge and corner samples each enter the sum once. The closed-box regression forms the full reference
kernel sum independently and measures zero change of velocity and position in the absence of forces.
[Akhunov and Kolb](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-023-03212-2).

For viscosity, the same exterior lattice contributes the Weiler et al. boundary matrix with solid
velocity zero. Each sample adds a positive rank-one tensor in its radial direction. The analytic limit
integrates the tangential and normal angular moments of the kernel cap. Its radial integral uses a
five-point Gauss rule on each cubic spline piece. These tensors enter the backward-Euler system
before its conjugate-gradient solve.

Timo Probst and Matthias Teschner (2025), *Unified Pressure, Surface Tension and Friction for SPH Fluids*,
equations 5–12 and section 5.2, supplies the capillary surface energy gradient. Margo uses the recommended
cubic surface kernel of three spacings, interface smoothing of 0.05 and rest area of π/4 times the spacing
squared. Unlike the older cohesion kernel evaluated in Akinci et al. (2013), the contribution drops away
in the liquid interior. The capillary force is split from the density solve, with substeps bounded by the
maximum represented wave number on the discrete spacing. Sampled solid interfaces use both half
energies and publish matching reactions. Analytic planes use the same kernel fraction for the solid
energy difference. The SI example uses the IAPWS tabulated 0.07274 N/m for pure water at 20 °C.
[Probst and Teschner](https://cg.informatik.uni-freiburg.de/publications/2024_TOG_unifiedPressureSurfaceTensionFriction_v3.pdf),
[Akinci et al.](https://cg.informatik.uni-freiburg.de/publications/2013_SIGGRAPHASIA_surfaceTensionAdhesion.pdf),
[IAPWS](https://iapws.org/technical-guidance/release/Surf-H2O).

The lab diagnostic follows J. C. Martin and W. J. Moyce (1952), *An Experimental Study of the Collapse of Liquid
Columns on a Rigid Horizontal Plane*, section 3 and Table 2. The measured spread intervals exclude the unknown
diaphragm release time. At 18 particles across the short initial cross-section, the accurate profile reaches the
two stations in 0.709754 and 1.183967 normalized time units. Both fit the unchanged experimental ranges
and time-quantization allowance. The 12-particle and interactive cases retain their earlier discrepancy.
[Martin and Moyce](https://www.math.ntu.edu.tw/~shyue/orch08/benchmarks/lowmach/broken-dam/91519.pdf).

Nils Thürey, Matthias Müller-Fischer, Simon Schirm and Markus Gross (2007), *Real-time Breaking Waves for
Shallow Water Simulations*, sections 5–7, describes creating overturning liquid from a height field and
absorbing it on return. The optional parcel fields implement the exchange side of this division with
signed whole-particle volume and a three-component momentum receipt. The second endpoint applies the
conserved quantities only after a clocked acceptance.
[Thürey et al.](https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/publications/breakingWaves.pdf).

H. Norman Abramson, ed. (1966), *The Dynamic Behavior of Liquids in Moving Containers*, NASA SP-106
section 2.2, gives the independent first free-surface mode for a rectangular tank,
`omega² = g k tanh(k H)` with `k = pi / L`. The regression initializes the associated potential-flow velocity
on an undisturbed surface and estimates one full period from the phase at the two ends. At 0.36 m depth
and 0.9 m length, the result is 1.168 s against the 1.165 s reference, a difference of 0.0033 s at 120 Hz.
[NASA SP-106](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19670006555/downloads/19670006555.pdf).

### Position-based particle liquids (FLUID-02)

Miles Macklin and Matthias Müller (2013), *Position Based Fluids*, equations 1–14 and 15–17, supplies the
Jacobi density constraint, kernel-relative artificial pressure, vorticity confinement and XSPH transport.
Matthias Müller, David Charypar and Markus Gross (2003), *Particle-Based Fluid Simulation for Interactive
Applications*, equations 20–21, gives the three-dimensional Poly6 and Spiky kernels. The PBF solve works
in support-normalized coordinates, with particle rest volume as its kernel weight. The artificial pressure
exponent is four and the reference distance is 0.3 support radii. A global correction scale limits a single
Jacobi update to the 0.4-support advective interval without disturbing paired pressure reactions.
The artificial pressure coefficient uses a 60 Hz reference step. Scaling it by the squared step relative to
that reference keeps its acceleration scale fixed across dyadic rates and subdivisions. In free-water mode
the artificial pressure acts on a pair while either density constraint is active. Miles Macklin et al. (2019),
*Small Steps in Physics Simulation*, §6.4 discusses substepping for position-based liquids.
[Macklin and Müller](https://mmacklin.com/pbf_sig_preprint.pdf),
[Macklin et al.](https://mmacklin.com/smallsteps.pdf),
[Müller, Charypar and Gross](https://cgl.ethz.ch/Downloads/Publications/Papers/2003/Mue03b/Mue03b.pdf).

Matthias Teschner, Bruno Heidelberger, Matthias Müller, Danat Pomeranets and Markus Gross (2003), *Optimized
Spatial Hashing for Collision Detection of Deformable Objects*, section 4.1, supplies the coordinate hash.
The native grid matches the complete keys after a collision and clears only touched buckets. Its 27-cell
support covers the entire kernel because a cell's edge equals the smoothing radius.
[Teschner et al.](https://cgl.ethz.ch/Downloads/Publications/Papers/2003/Tes03/Tes03.pdf).

Nadir Akinci, Markus Ihmsen, Gizem Akinci, Barbara Solenthaler and Matthias Teschner (2012), *Versatile
Rigid-Fluid Coupling for Incompressible SPH*, equations 4–10, gives the inverse kernel-sum volume for each
boundary sample and the action-reaction exchange. Margo applies those weights to the PBF constraint, rotates
them from actual body poses, and records the positional correction as a momentum change over the substep.
Matthias Müller, Bruno Heidelberger, Marcus Hennix and John Ratcliff (2007), *Position based dynamics*, gives
hard contact projection for separate geometric overlaps. A sphere projects along its radial normal, while
a capsule uses the nearest point on its spine to find the same radial normal. The confinement option subtracts the
net linear mode and limits restored kinetic energy to the available XSPH loss. Static contacts only have the
incoming kinetic energy and work of gravity available to redistribute.
[Akinci et al.](https://cgl.ethz.ch/Downloads/Publications/Papers/2012/Sol12/Sol12.pdf),
[Müller et al.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvcir.2007.01.005).

J. C. Martin and W. J. Moyce (1952), *An experimental study of the collapse of liquid columns on a rigid
horizontal plane*, Table 2, supplies independent surge arrival readings. The fixture uses their rectangular
column with aspect ratio two, 2¼ inches wide and thick. It subtracts the time at the first measured front
station from the subsequent readings within each trial, so camera release offsets cancel.
[Martin and Moyce](https://www.math.ntu.edu.tw/~shyue/orch08/benchmarks/lowmach/broken-dam/91519.pdf).

### Atmospheric lightning (ATMO-07)

Luciano Niemeyer, Luciano Pietronero and Hans J. Wiesmann, “Fractal Dimension of Dielectric Breakdown”
(1984), supplies the field-powered stochastic growth law. Theodore Kim and Ming C. Lin, “Physically Based
Animation and Rendering of Lightning” (2004), §4, supplies the potential boundary and growth weighting and
extends Laplace to Poisson for volume charge. Margo uses a cubic seven-point finite difference and native
masked Jacobi with insulating side faces. A leader bond is eligible where its cloud-normalized potential
drop is positive and is drawn with probability proportional to that drop raised to `exponent`. The first
grounded path is traced back to the cloud before the side branches are packed for Sky.
[Niemeyer et al.](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1033),
[Kim and Lin](https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~misha/ReadingSeminar/Papers/Kim04.pdf).

Mansell, MacGorman, Ziegler and Straka, “Simulated three-dimensional branched lightning in a
numerical thunderstorm model” (2002), §3.2.2, separates initiation and growth field thresholds.
For an authored seed and our unipolar channel, the optional threshold is subtracted from the
forward potential drop per metre before drawing a bond. This uses the magnitude of the configured
cloud potential to convert V/m to the normalized drop. An exhausted bond set is a halted leader.
The finite-difference Laplace field between planes and its discrete maximum principle determine
the exact ignition and propagation bounds used in the regression. A nonfinite native correction
rejects the trial, since a max that ignores NaN cannot establish convergence.
[Mansell et al.](https://doi.org/10.1029/2000JD000244) ·
[Long Chen, Finite Difference Methods for Poisson Equation, §3](https://www.math.uci.edu/~chenlong/226/FDM.pdf).

Each Jacobi sweep reads the previous field after reflecting the insulated side halos. A shared
worker processes complete transverse rows with the same two-node SIMD stencil as serial. The
next sweep begins after each partition publishes its maximum correction. The result retains the
ordering of every field update, including the discarded odd-width SIMD lane. The counted work
is one native pair per two nodes (rounded up per row) per completed sweep.
[Randall J. LeVeque, Finite Difference Methods (2007), §4.1](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717839.ch4) ·
[HTML Standard, agents](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#agents).

Vladimir A. Rakov and Martin A. Uman, *Lightning: Physics and Effects* (2003), describes the downward leader and
upward return stroke. James D. Hill, Martin A. Uman and Douglas M. Jordan, “High-speed video observations of
a lightning stepped leader” (2011), gives the measured order of leader speed. J. Jerauld et al., “Electric and
magnetic fields and field derivatives from lightning stepped leaders and first return strokes measured at distances
from 100 to 1000 m” (2008), gives the initial order of return speed. Arthur A. Few, “Power spectrum of thunder”
(1969), motivates treating the tortuous return channel as separate acoustic line sources. Margo timestamps each
segment at its midpoint arc length divided by the return speed. Its acoustic weights and light envelope are
relative, with propagation and arrival handled by the outdoor acoustics solver.
[Rakov and Uman](https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/83275/sample/9780521583275ws.pdf),
[Hill et al.](https://doi.org/10.1029/2011JD015818),
[Jerauld et al.](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008JD010171),
[Few](https://doi.org/10.1029/JC074i028p06926).
The relative leader light control defaults to 0.1, the mean optical ratio measured for triggered
dart leaders near ground by Idone and Orville (1985). It sets the appearance of the seeded channel;
photometric validation of a stepped leader remains open. The renderer consumes the accepted
records at the simulation's world time, and leaves the Weather light schedule independent.
[Idone and Orville](https://doi.org/10.1029/JD090iD04p06159).

### Cyclone and compact-vortex forcing (ATMO-05)

Greg J. Holland, “An Analytic Model of the Wind and Pressure Profiles in Hurricanes” (1980), gives the
radial surface pressure and gradient balance. Willoughby, Darling and Rahn, “Parametric Representation
of the Primary Hurricane Vortex, Part II” (2006), compares radial decay and secondary wind maxima.
Margo keeps the existing pressure-balanced Holland profile and can include the existing Sky secondary
eyewall. Compact vortices retain the combined Rankine or Burgers–Rott velocity and its integrated
cyclostrophic pressure. The E1 pressure integral is shared with Sky. Fiedler and Rotunno (1986) and
Orf et al. (2017) describe the vertical structure and nonaxisymmetric flow missing from a prescribed
axisymmetric vortex. Margo adds a logarithmic surface profile and tapered vertical velocity.
[Holland](https://impacts.ucar.edu/en/publications/an-analytic-model-of-the-wind-and-pressure-profiles-in-hurricanes/),
[Willoughby et al.](https://doi.org/10.1175/MWR3106.1),
[Fiedler and Rotunno](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469(1986)043%3C2328:ATOTMW%3E2.0.CO;2),
and [Orf et al.](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-15-00073.1).

John D. Holmes, “Trajectories of spheres in strong winds with application to wind-borne debris” (2004),
supplies quadratic relative drag. The rigid adapter analytically averages that drag over a world
tick with frozen wind and a fixed pressure lever. The surface-water source uses the pressure-gradient
term from Luettich, Westerink and Scheffner's ADCIRC formulation (1992). Garratt (1977) supplies
the linear 10 m drag fit. Milan Curcic and Brian K. Haus, “Revised Estimates of Ocean Surface Drag
in Strong Winds” (2020), report a 0.0026 plateau in their new short-fetch measurements and revise a
10 m extrapolation error in the original Donelan et al. data. The existing Garratt ramp intersects
that new laboratory plateau at about 27.6 m/s. It remains a simple short-fetch stress closure.
[Holmes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jweia.2003.09.031),
[ADCIRC](https://adcirc.org/home/documentation/adcirc-related-publications/),
[Garratt](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/mwre/105/7/1520-0493_1977_105_0915_rodcoo_2_0_co_2.xml),
[Donelan et al.](https://doi.org/10.1029/2004GL019460), and [Curcic and Haus](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020GL087647).

The optional water kernel evaluates four pressure points and an optional wind sample per wet cell. It
pairs the independent horizontal radius evaluations in f64x2 lanes and uses the same pinned scalar
functions for Holland and compact profiles. Each worker writes disjoint rows. Accepted probes, loads and
water all publish after the candidate succeeds.

Michael T. Montgomery, Michael M. Bell, Sim D. Aberson and Michael L. Black, “Hurricane Isabel (2003):
New Insights into the Physics of Intense Storms. Part I” (2006), supply the held-out dropsonde speeds
and radial direction. The separate NOAA/NHC B-deck supplies only pressure, radius of maximum wind
and latitude. Mark D. Powell, Peter J. Vickery and Timothy A. Reinhold, “Reduced drag coefficient for
high wind speeds in tropical cyclones” (2003), supply independent field drag over four wind bins.
None of those observed upper winds or drag values set model parameters. [Isabel observations](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-87-10-1335).
[NOAA best-track archive](https://ftp.nhc.noaa.gov/atcf/archive/2003/bal132003.dat.gz). [Field drag](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature01481).

### Seismic waves and ground shaking (EARTH-08)

Jean Virieux, “P-SV wave propagation in heterogeneous media: Velocity-stress finite-difference method”
(1986), gives the spatially staggered velocity and stress equations, face coefficients, and their
two-dimensional wave dispersion. Margo uses the second-order stencil with the corresponding Courant
bound and native pairwise SIMD across the section. Dimitri Komatitsch and Jeroen Tromp,
“Introduction to the spectral element method for three-dimensional seismic wave propagation” (1999),
describe a traction-free surface, source moment tensors, and physically heterogeneous propagation.
The surface uses an odd normal-stress extension and zero tangential traction.
<https://doi.org/10.1190/1.1442147> and <https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1365-246x.1999.00967.x>.

James N. Brune (1970), “Tectonic stress and the spectra of seismic shear waves from earthquakes,”
motivates the single-corner source spectrum. Margo releases a prescribed moment with the normalized
causal double-pole pulse whose rate is proportional to time times an exponential. The integrated
moment is independent of world rate. Cerjan, Kosloff, Kosloff and Reshef (1985),
“A nonreflecting boundary condition for discrete acoustic and elastic wave equations,” motivates
the absorbing strip. Margo uses diagonal implicit damping with a quadratic profile.
<https://doi.org/10.1029/JB075i026p04997> and <https://doi.org/10.1190/1.1441945>.

H. B. Seed and I. M. Idriss, “Simplified Procedure for Evaluating Soil Liquefaction Potential” (1971),
and the Youd and Idriss workshop report (2001), give cyclic stress demand as 0.65 times the peak
horizontal acceleration in g, times the total-to-effective stress ratio and depth reduction.
Nathan Newmark, “A Method of Computation for Structural Dynamics” (1959), supplies the
constant-average-acceleration update used for base-excited single-mode structures.
<https://doi.org/10.1061/JSFEAQ.0001662>, <https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)1090-0241(2001)127:10(817)>,
and <https://doi.org/10.1061/JMCEA3.0000098>.

### Outdoor sound propagation (SOUND-01)

The absolute air losses implement ISO 9613-1:1993 equations (3)–(5) and the Annex B humidity conversion.
Table 1(e) provides an independent rounded check for 1 kHz at 0 °C and 50% relative humidity.
ISO 9613-2:2024 defines the outdoor engineering terms for divergence, atmosphere, ground and screening.
<https://www.iso.org/standard/17426.html> and <https://www.iso.org/standard/74047.html>.

Erik Salomons, *Computational Atmospheric Acoustics* (2001), and Kenneth Gilbert and Michael White,
“Application of the parabolic equation to sound propagation in a refracting atmosphere” (1989), cover
the effects of the effective sound-speed gradient and reflecting ground. Plovsing and Kragh,
*Nord2000 Comprehensive Outdoor Sound Propagation Model, Part 2* (2001), §§2–4, uses a linear effective
sound-speed profile for curved rays. Margo keeps the first-order paraxial term with both endpoints fixed
and integrates the resolved path length and effective sound speed by midpoint quadrature.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-010-0660-6>.
[Gilbert and White](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.397587).
[Nord2000](https://forcetechnology.com/-/media/force-technology-media/pdf-files/projects/nord2000/nord2000-comprehensive-outdoor-sound-propagation-model---part-2-propagation-in-an-atmosphere-with-re.pdf).

ITU-R P.526-16 (2025), §4.1 and equations (26)–(31), supplies scalar Fresnel knife-edge loss. The solver
uses the dominant terrain edge, replacing wavelength with the acoustic wavelength. An unobstructed
path adds a coherent image source from one local horizontal plane.
<https://www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-P.526-16-202511-I/en>.

NASA/TM-20250003228 (2025), §3 and Fig. 3-1, gives the front, expansion and rear of the far-field civil
aviation N-wave. The helper samples a prescribed symmetric waveform with optional linear rise.
Laakso, Välimäki, Karjalainen and Laine (1996) describe band-limited fractional-delay methods. Playback
uses the Web Audio DelayNode and tests its sample arrival against the same undelayed chain.
<https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20250003228>, <https://doi.org/10.1109/79.482137>,
and <https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/#DelayNode>.

#### Atomic outdoor paths, terrain visibility and native quadrature

ANSI/ISO atmospheric attenuation above states the eight bands as pure-tone centre values. H. E. Bass,
L. C. Sutherland, A. J. Zuckerwar, D. T. Blackstock and D. M. Hester, *Atmospheric absorption of sound: Further
developments* (1995), compares the relaxation mechanisms and saturation expression. The solver keeps the ISO
coefficients. The TypeScript and Rust pinned functions evaluate the same formula. Native SIMD visits successive
octave pairs, and each band keeps its original midpoint sum order. Diffraction legs retain independent length and
delay sums followed by the original two-leg addition. [Bass et al.](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.412989).

Karsten B. Rasmussen, *Model experiments related to outdoor propagation over an earth berm* (1994), Fig. 1
gives the triangular berm, source location and four receiver heights. Figs. 3–6 report measurements relative to
free field. The diagnostic reads a small set of those outcomes and runs the actual terrain and solver from the
geometry without fitting. The still laboratory atmosphere is evaluated at the existing standard temperature,
humidity and pressure because the paper does not specify them. The original 250 Hz error on the highest
receiver exposed a geometric fault. The direct ray clears the crest, but the outgoing leg from the plane’s
specular point crosses it. Both reflection legs now use the same bed visibility test. This handles a blocked
image and leaves wedge reflections and finite ground impedance open. [Rasmussen](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411404).

Zen'iti Maekawa, *Noise reduction by screens* (1968), tests screening loss as a function of detour relative to
wavelength. The real-terrain bell cutaway checks rendering and audible timing with the existing scalar
knife-edge approximation. It uses accepted distances and octave gains with the Web Audio DelayNode.
[Maekawa](https://doi.org/10.1016/0003-682X(68)90020-0), [Web Audio](https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/#DelayNode).

### Webcam hands and body to a skeleton in Input (2026-11-26)

Michael Gleicher, Retargetting Motion to New Characters (SIGGRAPH 1998, https://doi.org/10.1145/280814.280820), and Jean-Sebastien Monzani, Paolo Baerlocher, Ronan Boulic and Daniel Thalmann, Using an Intermediate Skeleton and Inverse Kinematics for Motion Retargeting (Computer Graphics Forum 19(3), 2000, https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8659.00393), for retargeting through an intermediate humanoid: `BodyDriver` maps the landmarks onto VRM humanoid bones (VRM 1.0 humanoid specification, https://github.com/vrm-c/vrm-specification/blob/master/specification/VRMC_vrm-1.0/humanoid.md) and rotates each bone so its rest direction (toward its child, from the skeleton or a calibration T-pose or A-pose) lies along the landmark direction: the shortest-arc quaternion for one direction, the change of orthonormal frame for a direction plus a side direction (hips, chest, hands). Joint limits clamp the turn from the rest rotation relative to the parent (a cone about the rest pose, the joint constraint of Andreas Aristidou and Joan Lasenby, FABRIK: A fast, iterative solver for the Inverse Kinematics problem, Graphical Models 73(5), 2011, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gmod.2011.05.003). Point orders are the Pose Landmarker (Bazarevsky et al., BlazePose, 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10204) and Hand Landmarker (Zhang et al., MediaPipe Hands, 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10214) maps. Smoothing is the one-euro filter on each landmark direction. No detector, model or weights are shipped or fetched; no rival source was read.

### Webcam face to morph targets in Input (2026-11-26)

Apple's ARKit documentation, ARFaceAnchor.BlendShapeLocation (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/arkit/arfaceanchor/blendshapelocation), gives the 52 blendshape names `ARKIT_BLENDSHAPES` lists and their left/right meaning (the subject's side). Tereza Soukupova and Jan Cech, Real-Time Eye Blink Detection using Facial Landmarks (CVWW 2016, https://vision.fe.uni-lj.si/cvww2016/proceedings/papers/05.pdf), give the eye aspect ratio (|p2 - p6| + |p3 - p5|) / (2 |p1 - p4|) that `measureFace` uses for blinks and wide eyes; the jaw, mouth and brow measures are the same kind of scale-free distance ratio (over the face height or the outer-eye distance), measured against a calibrated neutral face. The point indices come from the published Face Landmarker landmark map (https://ai.google.dev/edge/mediapipe/solutions/vision/face_landmarker) and Kartynnik et al. 2019 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06724). The head rotation is the orthonormal frame of the outer eye corners and the forehead-to-chin line, relative to the calibrated face; smoothing is the one-euro filter (Casiez, Roussel and Vogel 2012) per weight and per quaternion component on the hemisphere of the last value. No detector, model or weights are shipped or fetched; no rival source was read.

### Webcam landmarks in Input (2026-11-26)

Gery Casiez, Nicolas Roussel and Daniel Vogel, 1 Euro Filter: A Simple Speed-based Low-pass Filter for Noisy Input in Interactive Systems (CHI 2012, https://doi.org/10.1145/2207676.2208639), for `OneEuroFilter`: a first-order low-pass with smoothing factor 1 / (1 + tau / dt), tau = 1 / (2 pi fc), whose cutoff fc = minCutoff + beta |dx| follows the low-passed speed. Google's public MediaPipe Tasks documentation (Face Landmarker https://ai.google.dev/edge/mediapipe/solutions/vision/face_landmarker, Hand Landmarker https://ai.google.dev/edge/mediapipe/solutions/vision/hand_landmarker, Pose Landmarker https://ai.google.dev/edge/mediapipe/solutions/vision/pose_landmarker) gives the result shapes `fromMediaPipe` reads, with Yury Kartynnik et al., Real-time Facial Surface Geometry from Monocular Video on Mobile GPUs (2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06724), Fan Zhang et al., MediaPipe Hands (2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10214) and Valentin Bazarevsky et al., BlazePose (2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10204) for the point orders. The W3C Media Capture and Streams specification (https://www.w3.org/TR/mediacapture-streams/) and the WICG video.requestVideoFrameCallback draft (https://wicg.github.io/video-rvfc/) give the webcam helper. No detector, model or weights are shipped or fetched; no rival source was read.

### Shadow map viewer in Shadows (2026-11-25)

Lance Williams, Casting Curved Shadows on Curved Surfaces (SIGGRAPH 1978, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/965139.807402), for shadow depth maps; Rouslan Dimitrov, Cascaded Shadow Maps (NVIDIA, 2007, https://developer.download.nvidia.com/SDK/10.5/opengl/src/cascaded_shadow_maps/doc/cascaded_shadow_maps.pdf) and Fan Zhang, Hanqiu Sun, Leilei Xu and Lee Kit Lun, Parallel-Split Shadow Maps for Large-scale Virtual Environments (VRCIA 2006, https://doi.org/10.1145/1128923.1128975), for cascades; Nathan Reed, Depth Precision Visualized (NVIDIA developer blog, 2015, https://developer.nvidia.com/content/depth-precision-visualized), for reversed depth. `ShadowMapViewer` (`@margoengine/shadows/viewer`) loads one texel per pixel of the chosen layer, mirrors reversed depth, turns a perspective value into distance with d = near * far / (far - z (far - near)) and shows (d - near) / (far - near) as grey. The engine's own light matrices (clustered `lightMatrix` and `orthographicShadow`, shadows `fitCascades`) fix which maps are reversed. The viewer's name comes from public documentation only; no rival source was read.

### Light probe and positional audio helpers in Lines (2026-11-25)

Ravi Ramamoorthi and Pat Hanrahan, [An Efficient Representation for Irradiance Environment Maps](https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/envmap/), SIGGRAPH 2001, give the nine real L2 basis constants and the clamped-cosine band factors (pi, 2pi/3, pi/4) that `shIrradiance` evaluates; the coefficient order is the engine's own `Environment.sh` layout. The W3C [Web Audio API](https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/#PannerNode) PannerNode section defines `coneInnerAngle` and `coneOuterAngle` as whole cone angles in degrees about the orientation (360: no cone) and the `refDistance` / `maxDistance` parameters that `PositionalAudioHelper` draws. Helper names come from public documentation only; no rival source was read.

### BVH, octree and raycaster helpers in Lines (2026-11-25)

Timothy L. Kay and James T. Kajiya, Ray Tracing Complex Scenes (SIGGRAPH 1986), and Donald Meagher, Geometric Modeling Using Octree Encoding (Computer Graphics and Image Processing 19, 1982), define the two hierarchies. `BVHHelper` and `OctreeHelper` walk the engine's own node layouts, draw the boxes at one level and the leaves above it, and nothing else. The helper names and the depth slider come from public documentation only; no rival source was read.

### Infinite shader grid in Lines (2026-11-25)

Eric Chan and Frédo Durand, [Fast Prefiltered Lines](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems2/part-iii-high-quality-rendering/chapter-22-fast-prefiltered-lines), GPU Gems 2 chapter 22, 2005, give the antialiased line as a ramp over the distance to the line centre; David Ebert, F. Kenton Musgrave, Darwyn Peachey, Ken Perlin and Steven Worley, Texturing and Modeling: A Procedural Approach, 3rd ed., 2003, chapter 2, fade a procedural pattern out when its period falls below the sampling rate. `InfiniteGrid` (`@margoengine/lines/infinite-grid`) measures the distance to the nearest line in pixels with the screen-space derivative of the world coordinate, ramps one pixel around a line of the asked width, and fades both line sets out once a cell is under two pixels. The visible plane is a quad under the camera sized by the fade distance. drei's `Grid` and its option names (cell and section size, fade distance, follow camera) were taken from its public documentation only; no rival source was read.

### Offline music renders refill at suspend points (audio, KB5029b, 2026-11-25)

Read Paul Adenot and Hongchan Choi (editors), W3C Web Audio API 1.0 (2021, https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/):
OfflineAudioContext.suspend(suspendTime) and resume(), the 128-frame render quantum, one suspend per quantum
(InvalidStateError otherwise), and the rendering loop that processes every node of the graph each quantum. Measured
in Chromium 158 (one hour at 8 kHz, 1,950 one-shot loops): all scheduled up front 34.9 s, a refilled window 0.86 s, one
source 65 ms, identical samples. Design: keep max(8 s, 8 loops) of sources scheduled and refill half a window ahead at a
quantum-aligned suspend point; without suspend(time), or when the app holds that quantum, schedule the whole render. No
other implementation read.

### DOM host for UI widgets (ui, GAP-FILM-DOMUI, 2026-11-25)

Read the specifications: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 (2023, https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/) and the ARIA Authoring Practices
Guide (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/: tabs with automatic activation, listbox with one tab stop, dialog, and
its note that `role="menu"` is for application menus); the WHATWG HTML Living Standard (forms, the `dialog` element with
`showModal` and `cancel`, `inert`); W3C WCAG 2.2 (2023, https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/: 2.1.1, 2.4.7, 2.5.8 with its 24 CSS
px minimum, 4.1.2); W3C CSS Flexible Box Layout Level 1 (https://www.w3.org/TR/css-flexbox-1/) and CSS Grid for stacks
and grids; W3C CSP Level 3 (https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/: CSSOM writes and constructable stylesheets are not inline
styles). Papers compared for keyed patching: Michael L. Fredman, On computing the length of longest increasing
subsequences, Discrete Mathematics 11, 1975, https://doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X(75)90103-X (patience sorting finds the
longest run of children already in order, so only the rest move); Nick ten Veen, Daco Harkes and Eelco Visser, PixieDust,
WWW '18 Companion, 2018, https://doi.org/10.1145/3184558.3185978 (update from known dependencies rather than diffing whole
trees); Aiden Bai and others, Million.js, 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.08409 (the cost of diff plus patch in keyed
virtual DOM). Combined: every widget keeps its element (the widget is the key, so, as in PixieDust, no tree is diffed),
attributes, text and CSS properties are compared with the last written values, and a reordered child list keeps its
longest increasing run in place (Fredman). Rival behaviour from documentation only: lil-gui
(https://lil-gui.georgealways.com/), Tweakpane (https://tweakpane.github.io/docs/), Babylon GUI (canvas only,
https://doc.babylonjs.com/features/featuresDeepDive/gui/gui) and three.js CSS2DRenderer and CSS3DRenderer. No rival or
companion source read or copied. The test pages are original, under the repository licence.

### Short wind waves and open-water reflection (2026-11-24)

Eric Bruneton, Fabrice Neyret and Nicolas Holzschuch, [Real-time Realistic Ocean Lighting using Seamless
Transitions from Geometry to BRDF](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01618.x), 2010, separate
resolved displacement, normal-scale detail and filtered reflection as the projected footprint grows. Fabrice
Veron and W. Kendall Melville, [Experiments on the stability and transition of wind-driven water
surfaces](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/D92FEDDAD93AB36787C4EE22469873E1), 2001, observe rough
patches forming and moving under wind gusts. Eric Heitz, [Understanding the Masking-Shadowing Function
in Microfacet-Based BRDFs](https://jcgt.org/published/0003/02/03/), 2014, explains the directional
loss of visible facets that plain normal mapping omits.

Water projects each screen derivative into the ripple's rotated lattice, then fades that band over its
own footprint. Two additional short gravity-wave bands use the deep-water law `omega = sqrt(g k)`
and a low-frequency travelling phase warp. The shader includes the warp's spatial derivative when
filtering and shading the wave. The scale, strength and direction of the authored bands and the rough
patch field are procedural parameters. They affect normals. Mesh displacement, depth and buoyancy
continue to use the swell trains.

Both environment paths sample an angular lobe in azimuth and elevation. Down-going rays on the open
surface contribute progressively less sky reflection. The soft reduction is capped at 34% as an
approximation of light returned by other facets. This model traces no secondary water hits and uses no
measured lake roughness field. The regional sky lighting and shoreline blend retain their existing
paths. See the [limits](limits.md#short-wind-waves-and-sky-reflection).

### Colour in the stern wake (2026-11-23)

Amanda T. Nylund, Lars Arneborg, Anders Tengberg, Ulf Mallast and Ida-Maja Hassellöv, [In situ observations of turbulent ship wakes and their spatiotemporal extent](https://doi.org/10.5194/os-17-1285-2021), 2021, characterize the trail of mixed water and its relation to the bubble wake. Yingfei Liu and Ruru Deng, [Ship Wakes in Optical Images](https://doi.org/10.1175/JTECH-D-18-0021.1), 2018, identify the surface trail separately from the divergent waves. Morgan F. Gelinas, Henry Bokuniewicz, John G. Rapaglia and Kamazima M. M. Lwiza, [Sediment Resuspension by Ship Wakes in the Venice Lagoon](https://digitalcommons.sacredheart.edu/bio_fac/28/), 2013, measure suspended material associated with ship passages in shallow water.

Margo applies an authored linear reflectance to the near-surface water and foam. The existing stern trail supplies
the amount, width and age envelope. The strongest coloured parcel supplies the reflectance where two trails
overlap. This is a surface appearance model. It does not compute sediment mass, wavelength-dependent transport or
the location or mechanism that released the material.

### Kelvin wake crest phase (2026-11-23)

Fritz Ursell, [On Kelvin's ship-wave pattern](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/volume/840945DCC46FC5078D12D1BB82B7E65D?pageNum=2), 1960, derives the two stationary points and their coalescence. Marc Rabaud and Frédéric Moisy, [Ship Wakes: Kelvin or Mach Angle?](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.110.214503), 2013, give the deep-water dispersion and the angle constraints. Ravindra Pethiyagoda, Timothy J. Moroney, Christopher J. Lustri and Scott W. McCue, [Kelvin wake pattern at small Froude numbers](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2021.193), 2021, distinguish the transverse and diverging branches. Michael V. Berry and Christopher J. Howls, [NIST DLMF §36.13](https://dlmf.nist.gov/36.13), 2010, give an independent caustic formulation.

For aft distance `x > 0` and absolute side distance `y`, the wave vector's longitudinal and lateral projections
have opposite signs. With `T = tan(theta)` and `tau = y / x`, the phase up to sign is
`k_g x sqrt(1 + T²) (1 − tau T)`. Its derivative vanishes at `tau = T / (1 + 2 T²)`. The previous plus
sign paired the existing roots with a phase that is nonstationary at those roots. The CPU and WGSL use the same
corrected projection. The cusp regression evaluates the coalesced phase directly. The amplitude envelope, hull filter,
and near-hull waterline and stern foam are independent of this correction.

### Animated flow paths in Lines (2026-11-22)

Bruno Jobard and Wilfrid Lefer, [Unsteady Flow Visualization by Animating Evenly-Spaced Streamlines](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8659.00395), 2000, show how a cyclic pattern moving along a streamline conveys direction. Greg Turk and David Banks, [Image-Guided Streamline Placement](https://doi.org/10.1145/237170.237285), 1996, describe using line density and visual contrast to make trajectories readable. Jobard and Lefer, [Creating Evenly-Spaced Streamlines of Arbitrary Density](https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~ma/SIGGRAPH02/course23/notes/papers/Jobard.pdf), 1997, discuss regular spacing by distance.

Margo takes an authored 3D polyline, scrolls its existing world-distance dash pattern from absolute time, and places a quieter line under it to keep the route readable. Endpoint opacity is based on local arc length with intermediate samples inside the fades. The implementation uses Margo's existing depth, draw and disposal paths and introduces no field solver.

### Ship wakes at harbor speed (2026-11-21)

Francis Noblesse, Gérard Delhommeau, Michel Guilbaud, Dane Hendrix and Chi Yang, [Simple analytical relations for ship bow waves](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112008000220), 2008, supply the existing speed law and crest location. Ravindra Pethiyagoda, Timothy J. Moroney, Christopher J. Lustri and Scott W. McCue, [Kelvin wake pattern at small Froude numbers](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2021.193), 2021, describe why slow flow need not show a strong diverging wave. Donald C. Wyatt, Thomas C. Fu, Genevieve L. Taylor, Eric J. Terrill, Tao Xing, Shanti Bhushan, Thomas T. O'Shea and Douglas G. Dommermuth, [A Comparison of Full-Scale Experimental Measurements and Computational Predictions of the Transom-Stern Wave of the R/V Athena I](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.1810), 2008, distinguish the near stern elevation and the spatially uneven bubble signature. Their example is at 5.4 m/s.

The minimum modelled bow span `min(0.75 m, 0.065 beam)`, low-speed side-width blend, stern foam's `0.5..2.2 m/s` ramp,
and a shader mask that concentrates thin foam into patches are Margo's rendering approximations. The wider profile retains
the analytic crest location and height. The shoreline contact band, the Kelvin-wave law and the stern age decay keep their
separate inputs. The visual coefficients were checked on calm GPU fixtures and the existing First Wake camera tracks.

### Ship side wash in Water (2026-11-21)

Gabriel D. Weymouth and Dick K. P. Yue, [Physics-Based Learning Models for Ship Hydrodynamics](https://doi.org/10.5957/JOSR.57.1.120005), 2013, compare at-speed waterline elevation along a Wigley hull using tank measurements and potential flow. Douglas G. Dommermuth, Thomas T. O'Shea, Donald C. Wyatt, Mark Sussman, Gabriel D. Weymouth, Dick K. P. Yue, Paul Adams and Randall Hand, [The Numerical Simulation of Ship Waves Using Cartesian-Grid and Volume-of-Fluid Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.1937), 2006, resolve run-up and local breaking from the body boundary. Donald C. Wyatt, Thomas C. Fu, Genevieve L. Taylor, Eric J. Terrill, Tao Xing, Shanti Bhushan, Thomas T. O'Shea and Douglas G. Dommermuth, [A Comparison of Full-Scale Experimental Measurements and Computational Predictions of the Transom-Stern Wave of the R/V Athena I](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.1810), 2008, document whole-vessel effects that extend into the stern wake.

Margo uses a compact approximation alongside the waterplane. The transverse section `(1-q)²(1-4q)` for normalized
distance `q ∈ [0,1]` integrates to zero. Its width is `min(0.30 beam, max(0.17 beam, 2 crest))`. The section reaches at most
45% of the bow height at contact. It ramps in behind the bow crest and decays toward the transom. The profile, width and
coefficients are Margo's. The two full-flow studies establish the role of hull shape and wave breaking, which the reduced
heightfield cannot resolve. The drawdown depth and longitudinal profile are approximations and have not been fit to a specific hull.

### Swept bow crest in Water (2026-11-21)

Francis Noblesse, Gérard Delhommeau, Michel Guilbaud, Dane Hendrix and Chi Yang, [Simple analytical relations for ship bow waves](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112008000220), 2008, give the contact-curve crest height and location used here. Francis Noblesse, Gérard Delhommeau, Hua Liu, De-cheng Wan and Chi Yang, [Ship bow waves](https://dcwan.sjtu.edu.cn/userfiles/2013-4%20Shipbowwaves.pdf), 2013, compare the longitudinal profile and present examples of how the bow wave develops alongside the hull. Clément Caplier, Germain Rousseaux, Damien Calluaud and Laurent David, [Energy distribution in shallow water ship wakes from a spectral analysis of the wave field](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4964923), 2016, measure the hull-bound bow rise separately from the trailing wave system.

Extruding the contact profile transversely produces a horizontal stripe. In Margo's planform approximation the profile starts at its measured along-hull crest location. From the current hull frame, its offset is `2 d² / w` aft at distance `d` outside the waterline and its amplitude fades over width `w = max(crest, min(0.35 beam, sqrt(beam crest)))`. These planform coefficients are Margo's model. The height and breaking foam use the same phase and envelope. Kelvin waves continue to use the path history.


### Stern foam history in Water (2026-11-21)

Yingfei Liu and Ruru Deng, [Ship Wakes in Optical Images](https://doi.org/10.1175/JTECH-D-18-0021.1), 2018, distinguish the bright turbulent region behind a vessel from the Kelvin wave pattern. Vincent G. Johnston and David T. Walker, [Experimentally Observed Features of the Turbulent Near-Wake of a Model Ship](https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/handle/2027.42/116057/39015075172091.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1), 1991, observed a rapidly spreading surface layer and irregular free-surface disturbances aft. Antonio Posa, Riccardo Broglia and Elias Balaras, [The wake flow downstream of a propeller-rudder system](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijheatfluidflow.2020.108765), 2021, characterize turbulence and shear downstream of the propeller and rudder.

The observations support a turbulent surface trail that starts at the stern. A single bow trajectory with a time offset equal to hull length divided by current speed approximates straight, steady motion. Sampling the actual stern trajectory also follows the time and position of a turn or acceleration. Margo records both end positions at each station. It uses a laterally spreading envelope and exponential decay as artistic approximations. CPU and WGSL are authored here from these observations. No other engine's implementation was used.

of `sprayWhorl` and `branchShoots`, the coarse short-spray width) is Margo-written from these sources; no engine's or
tool's source was read. F. Hallé, R. A. A. Oldeman and P. B. Tomlinson, Tropical Trees and Forests: An Architectural
Analysis, Springer 1978 (rhythmic monopodial growth units and tiered branching); M. Fabrika et al., "Crown architecture
and structural development of young Norway spruce trees (Picea abies Karst.): a basis for more realistic growth

(growth units, branching angles 40 to 70 degrees); R. Pokorný and I. Tomášková 2007 (7.0 m at 20 years, for the 0.5 m

### Directional hard shadows on the receiver plane (clustered, KB-SUNSHADOW-OFFSET1, 2026-11-16)

`clusterDirectionalShadow` and the `behind` test of `localShadowPCF` in `packages/clustered/src/shadows.ts`, and the
directional checks in `scripts/clustered-shadow-gpu-check.js`, are Margo-written from the papers of the next section
(Reeves, Salesin and Cook 1987; Isidoro 2006; Dou, Yan, Kerzner, Dai and Wyman 2014; Holbert 2011), plus cascaded shadow
maps after W. Engel, "Cascaded Shadow Maps", ShaderX5, 2006, and R. Dimitrov, "Cascaded Shadow Maps", NVIDIA, 2007, and
the receiver-plane filter for large kernels in C. Schuler, "Multisampling Extension for Gradient Shadow Maps", ShaderX5,
2006. No engine's source was read. Margo's own: leaving out texels whose stored depth lies behind the receiver's plane
by more than its offsets plus one texel (a search for a paper stating it found none; the receiver-plane literature
notes leaks where the receiver is not planar and caps the bias instead), and the edge test that moves the map's grid
through every rounding phase.

### LocalShadows hard edges on the receiver plane (clustered, KB-LOCALSHADOW-OFFSET1, 2026-11-16)

`localShadowPCF` in `packages/clustered/src/shadows.ts` (point, spot and directional hard shadows of `LocalShadows`) and
its checks in `scripts/clustered-shadow-gpu-check.js` are Margo-written from these papers; no engine's source was read.
W. T. Reeves, D. H. Salesin and R. L. Cook, "Rendering Antialiased Shadows with Depth Maps", SIGGRAPH 1987,
Computer Graphics 21(4), https://doi.org/10.1145/37402.37435 (percentage-closer filtering: the 3x3 bilinear taps, here
read as their 4x4 texels with weights (1 - f, 1, 1, f) / 3 per axis). J. R. Isidoro, "Shadow Mapping: GPU-based Tips and
Techniques", ATI Research, Game Developers Conference 2006 (receiver-plane depth bias: the receiver's tangent plane
mapped into the light's projection gives the reference depth at each filter tap; the area and PCSS paths already used
it). H. Dou, Y. Yan, E. Kerzner, Z. Dai and C. Wyman, "Adaptive Depth Bias for Shadow Maps", ACM I3D 2014 and Journal
of Computer Graphics Techniques 3(4), 2014, https://www.aminer.org/pub/53e9a154b7602d9702a430af/adaptive-depth-bias-for-shadow-maps
(the bias taken per shadow texel from where that texel's ray meets the receiver's tangent plane). D. Holbert, "Saying
Goodbye to Shadow Acne", Game Developers Conference 2011 poster (normal offset, scaled by the slope, 1 - N.L: measured
here, it barely shrinks the leak at 58 degrees). Margo's own: lifting only the texels nearer the light, never below the
receiver's own depth; the 1 + `slopeBias` multiple of the plane's rise (default 0, the exact plane; 2 for normal maps
at grazing light); the defaults 1 and 0.25 texels; directional cascades kept on the flat compare and 1.5 texels; the edge test that averages 16 light positions over every rounding phase of
the rasterized edge; the tilted-normal and pebble checks.

### Batch 187: opaque lightmap visibility

Research compared James T. Kajiya, The Rendering Equation (SIGGRAPH, 1986),
https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15462-s13/www/lec_slides/86kajiyaRenderingEquation.pdf,
with Eric Veach, Robust Monte Carlo Methods for Light Transport Simulation (Stanford dissertation, 1997),
https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/veach_thesis/thesis.pdf (geometric visibility and section 2.6 sampling).
Kajiya separates geometric visibility from scattering support: an opaque obstruction must stop a connection regardless
of winding, while the oriented surface's outgoing radiance is only read on its front. Veach's variance discussion
motivated comparing seed averages during diagnosis, without treating finite-sample error as proof of a transport bug.
The actual regression is deterministic back-face leakage. Implementation is Margo-authored, using MeshBVH's existing
double-side and frontFace APIs. No companion code or other renderer source was read. No new asset or demo was added.
Feature comparison used public descriptions only: ProgressiveLightMap documentation (zalo/three.js contributors,
https://threejs.org/docs/pages/ProgressiveLightMap.html, accessed 2026-11-10) describes mesh-wise accumulation each frame;
PlayCanvas contributors' Runtime Lightmaps and Lightmapping Settings (accessed 2026-11-10),
https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/graphics/lighting/runtime-lightmaps/ and
https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/editor/interface/settings/lightmapping/, describe second-UV baking and
one dominant direction for bump response. Existing Batch 54 APIs already supply these requested behaviours.


## Batch 177 job 2: statistical charts and shared CPU mathematics

Research combined B. W. Silverman, 1986, *Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis*, bandwidth 0.9 min(sample SD,IQR/1.34) n^-1/5 as documented by [NIST kernel width](https://itl.nist.gov/div898/software/dataplot/refman1/auxillar/kernwidt.htm); W. S. Cleveland, 1979, *Robust Locally Weighted Regression and Smoothing Scatterplots*, [paper](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~rnugent/PCMI2016/papers/LowessCleveland.pdf), tricube local-linear fitting and bisquare residual weights; D. B. Carr, R. J. Littlefield, W. L. Nicholson and J. S. Littlefield, 1987, *Scatterplot Matrix Techniques for Large N*, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1987.10478445), hexagonal aggregation rather than overplotted samples. Coordinates use our independently derived axial/cube nearest-cell rounding and expose original membership.

Confidence calculations use the [NIST/SEMATECH t distribution](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3664.htm), [least squares](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmd/section4/pmd431.htm) and [LOESS](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmd/section1/pmd144.htm) descriptions. Student-t quantiles invert the regularized incomplete beta with the continued fraction in NIST DLMF [section 8.17](https://dlmf.nist.gov/8.17#v), dynamically bracketed bisection and gamma normalization from NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, [section 5.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11), Stirling/Bernoulli terms after recurrence to x>=16. No library approximation code or coefficients were copied. Linear mean bands use residual df n-2. LOESS uses fixed final robustness weights, smoother rows S, residual df n-2 tr(S)+tr(S^T S), and conditional variance RSS/df times the row squared norm. Its bands are approximate, pointwise mean intervals, without simultaneous/prediction/causal coverage claims. Tukey box summaries use type-7 interpolated quartiles and 1.5-IQR adjacent values. Empirical CDF is right-continuous, Q-Q uses common midpoint probabilities and independently interpolated sample quantiles. Signed stacking uses separate sign accumulators. SVG axes use Margo's existing Heckbert ticks.

The published [Plotly trace reference](https://plotly.com/javascript/reference/), including [box](https://plotly.com/javascript/reference/box/) and [violin](https://plotly.com/javascript/reference/violin/), and [Vega-Lite transforms](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/docs/transform.html) supply the job checklist, without reading their source. Tests prove numerical values independently, conservation of samples/stack totals, error endpoints, all step modes, missing-value breaks and vector output for every requested family. No rival implementation, paper companion source or speed benchmark was read/run. Moderate bounded CPU workloads remain TypeScript; no Rust gain is asserted.

Data: GHCN .dly uses NOAA's [format specification](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/ghcn/daily/readme.txt), quality flags and tenths-C conversion. The NASA archive API returned HTTP 503 on both official hostnames; a pinned data-only public PSCompPars mirror supplies the original archive fields and signed uncertainties, with no notebook or implementation read. The reduction, source SHA-256, snapshot date, credits and output hashes are frozen in examples/assets/sciviz/stats/source.json. CSV decoding follows Y. Shafranovich, 2005, [RFC 4180](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4180), quoted fields and doubled quotes, independently implemented for data preparation only.

## KB3148e: linear-light layers in the exact, peeled, moment and float32 passes (2026-11-12)

Sources read (papers and specifications only, no companion, sample or rival source code): Thomas Porter and Tom Duff,
*Compositing Digital Images*, SIGGRAPH 1984 (the over operator, applied here to decoded values); IEC 61966-2-1:1999
(sRGB transfer); Larry Gritz and Eugene d'Eon, *The Importance of Being Linear*, GPU Gems 3, chapter 24, 2007
(why blend in linear light); Jason C. Yang, Justin Hensley, Holger Grun and Nicolas Thibieroz, *Real-Time Concurrent
Linked List Construction on the GPU*, EGSR 2010 (per-pixel lists, resolved layer by layer); Cass Everitt, *Interactive
Order-Independent Transparency*, 2001 (peeled layers composited far to near); Cedrick Muenstermann, Stefan Krumpen,
Reinhard Klein and Christoph Peters, *Moment-Based Order-Independent Transparency*, I3D 2018; Morgan McGuire and Louis
Bavoil, *Weighted Blended Order-Independent Transparency*, JCGT 2013; Chris Wyman, *Exploring and Expanding the
Continuum of OIT Algorithms*, HPG 2016, https://research.nvidia.com/publication/2016-06_exploring-and-expanding-continuum-oit-algorithms
(collect, then resolve); Marilena Maule, Joao Comba, Rafael Torchelsen and Rui Bastos, *A survey of raster-based
transparency techniques*, Computers and Graphics 35(6), 2011, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cag.2011.07.006; W3C *WebGPU*
and *WGSL* (instance_index counts from firstInstance; colour attachment bytes per sample).

Compared one linear composite of the whole list per pixel (needs the scene depth, which is not bindable, to drop layers
behind opaque surfaces), a ping-pong of two colour targets per layer (the same copy per layer, plus a second target),
and a snapshot per layer index. Chose the snapshot: the hardware depth and sample-mask test per layer stays as it was,
display layers keep their exact hardware blend, and only frames with a linear layer pay. The weighted passes reuse
OIT's KB3148d composite. The alpha sign as the linear flag, the mark channels and the per-index split are Margo's own.

Note on the Bavoil and Myers citation in "Batch 190 job 1" and "job 2" below (checked 2026-11-12 for the bug sweep):
the link is the whitepaper PDF in the `doc` folder of NVIDIA's OpenGL SDK 10 dual depth peeling sample. Those records
state that only that document was read, not the sample's source files beside it; KB3148e does not use it.

## Batch 190 job 2: float32 weighted accumulation

Research combined: Morgan McGuire and Louis Bavoil, *Weighted Blended Order-Independent Transparency*, JCGT 2(2), 2013, [equations 7 to 10 and precision discussion](https://jcgt.org/published/0002/02/09/paper-lowres.pdf); Louis Bavoil and Kevin Myers, *Order Independent Transparency with Dual Depth Peeling*, 2008, [weighted-average and blending discussion](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/SDK/10/opengl/src/dual_depth_peeling/doc/DualDepthPeeling.pdf); W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, *WebGPU*, 2026, [float32-blendable and plain colour format capabilities](https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/#plain-color-formats); Khronos WebGL Working Group, *EXT_float_blend*, 2019, [float32 blend enablement](https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/extensions/EXT_float_blend/). Papers and specifications only, no companion or rival source code.

`oit/precise` keeps the existing OIT weight/coverage equations, replacing four half-float sums with four scalar R32F targets. The format table rules out multisampled RGBA32F, so scalar R32F preserves both 1x and 4x scene coverage. The composite reads/averages the samples before dividing the weighted colour sum by the weight sum, equivalent to the original resolved targets. Revealage remains R16F (RG16F since KB3148e, the second channel marking linear-light layers). Explicit unfilterable bindings avoid requiring float32 filtering. Native devices explicitly request float32-blendable; full WebGL2 devices use the existing public EXT_float_blend capability. Analytic emissive-intensity tests prove bright stacked transport and show the old half-float saturation side by side, with ordinary radiance and MSAA edges compared to OIT. Existing CC0 Khronos GlassVaseFlowers exercises PBR shading. No new external asset, code or benchmark.

## Batch 190 job 1: texture depth peeling

Sources read, without reading companion or rival implementation code:

- Cass Everitt, *Interactive Order-Independent Transparency*, 2001, [depth peeling and depth invariance](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/assets/gamedev/docs/OrderIndependentTransparency.pdf).
- Louis Bavoil and Kevin Myers, *Order Independent Transparency with Dual Depth Peeling*, 2008, [sections Depth Peeling and Depth Comparisons](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/SDK/10/opengl/src/dual_depth_peeling/doc/DualDepthPeeling.pdf).
- Khronos WebGL Working Group, *EXT_color_buffer_float*, 2017, [renderable R32F and RGBA16F](https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/extensions/EXT_color_buffer_float/).
- Babylon.js documentation, *Transparent Rendering*, retrieved 2026-11-10, [public OIT contract](https://doc.babylonjs.com/features/featuresDeepDive/materials/advanced/transparent_rendering): WebGL2/WebGPU, five dual passes by default for ten layers, no refraction, antialiasing listed as unsupported.

Compared front-to-back peeling, dual peeling and the existing linked lists. `oit/peel` combines Everitt's nearest-layer capture with Bavoil/Myers' unbiased 32-bit depth comparisons, reversed for Margo's reversed Z. It uses hardware depth selection and unblended R32F depth output, avoiding float32 blending and fragment storage. Each captured layer is blended far to near with a hardware test against opaque depth. Ten nearest distinct depths by default match the rival's default layer budget; the positive integer budget is adjustable. Unlike dual peeling it redraws once per layer. No timing claim. Native and compatibility pixel checks cover analytic transport, intersecting sheets, reordered registration, opaque occlusion, post and canvas alpha. The existing CC0 Khronos GlassVaseFlowers asset exercises real PBR primitives; its source/licence remain in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md. No external code or new asset was copied.

## Batch 258 job 4: world panels on preview WebGL2

Research compared Kelsey Gilbert (editor), WebGL 2.0 Specification (2026 editor's draft), https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/specs/latest/2.0/ , with Khronos Group, OpenGL ES Shading Language 3.00 specification (2016), https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.0/GLSL_ES_Specification_3.00.pdf . Framebuffers, complete mip chains, sampler bindings, pixel unpack state and matrix/clip conventions define the new backend. No reference implementation was read.

Tanja Kojic, Danish Ali, Robert Greinacher, Sebastian Moller and Jan-Niklas Voigt-Antons, User Experience of Reading in Virtual Reality: Finding Values for Text Distance, Size and Contrast (QoMEX 2020), https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.01545 , motivates retaining the existing UI's pixel ratio and text treatment rather than replacing its readable draw list. Michael Woerister, Harald Steinlechner, Stefan Maierhofer and Robert F. Tobler, Lazy Incremental Computation for Efficient Scene Graph Rendering (HPG 2013 presentation), https://www.highperformancegraphics.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/Steinlechner-LazySG.pdf , informs version-based reuse of rendered panel textures. No comfort, speed or hardware XR certification is claimed.

Original implementation: the optional world-gl entry subclasses the public WorldPanels interface, preserves WorldPanel identity and inherited ray/controller behavior, and reuses its native WebGPU path. Raw GL paints the same UI list to a mipmapped RGBA8 framebuffer and projects a depth-tested, non-depth-writing quad with back-side UV mirroring. A caller-state snapshot isolates the pass, including foreign sampler and pixel unpack buffers. Browser regressions deliberately bind a foreign unpack buffer, row length and sampler before drawing, and verify actual panel pixels plus exact state restoration afterward. Tests also cover cache reuse, depth occlusion, back faces, removal/re-addition and real mouse rays on preview GL, WebGPU and complete compatibility. The new internal painter framebuffer argument and structural draw-list type add no core/stage code.

The fixture is adapted only from Margo's own world-panel tests; its planet name uses NASA public-domain facts, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ . No outside engine, repository file or companion code was copied.

## Verify cache settlement: repeated metadata work

Research reviewed before implementation, using papers' abstracts and the
official API description, with no companion implementation source:

- Tanmay Agrawal, Ashay Shirwadkar, Pratik Gaikar and Kushagra Verma,
  *MetaCache: Efficient Metadata Caching in Linux file system* (2014),
  https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.8239 . Metadata lookup can dominate workloads with
  many small files. Persistent metadata caching would need cross-lane coherence.
- Jingwei Xu, Mingkai Dong, Qiulin Tian, Ziyi Tian, Tong Xin and Haibo Chen,
  *SwitchFS: Asynchronous Metadata Updates for Distributed Filesystems with
  In-Network Coordination* (2024, revised 2025),
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08618 . Compared latency hiding and amortized
  metadata work with preserving synchronous filesystem semantics. This local
  store needs neither distributed coordination nor deferred capacity checks.
- Node.js contributors, *File system*, synchronous API and `fs.statSync`
  documentation (accessed 2026), https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html . Synchronous
  metadata calls block the event loop; changing them to promises alone would
  leave the repeated work in place.
- Microsoft, *DirectoryInfo.EnumerateFileSystemInfos* and *FileInfo.Length*,
  .NET Framework 4.8.1 API documentation (accessed 2026):
  https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.directoryinfo.enumeratefilesysteminfos?view=netframework-4.8.1
  and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.fileinfo.length?view=netframework-4.8.1 .
  Enumeration pre-populates timestamps and length, avoiding individual metadata
  lookups. No implementation source was read or copied.

Own inference and implementation: the observed store was already at its 5 GiB
cap with about 60,000 archives. Size reuse below cap alone would leave repeated
timestamp lookups at cap. Instead reuse metadata supplied by each fresh Windows
directory enumeration via the system .NET runtime. Keep Node's original listing
order, follow links with stat and preserve the portable stat scan. No metadata
survives an eviction call; backward clock changes and shared-store touches are
observed. Keep per-write eviction rather than defer it to the end: later touches
and recreated keys can otherwise change the result. Deterministic fixtures for
128 archives and 12 outputs prove 1,614 versus zero per-file stats under cap,
1,548 versus zero at cap, identical bytes/retention and zero archive-content
reads by eviction. No elapsed speed result is claimed. All code is original.

## Batch 171 job 4 derived-field numerical design

Continued research after the initial audit (6616a9ce1, rebased from 3d3116d56).
No existing velocity Jacobian, curl/Q/lambda-2 filter or symmetric eigensolver exists in sciviz.
Reuse compute.kernel and its disposal, and the existing GpuArray volume/isosurface inputs.
The CPU entry uses float64 arithmetic on a copied float32 snapshot. There is no measured Rust/Wasm
work-count gain for this new CPU loop, so do not add a Wasm binary or claim a timing gain.

Primary-source comparison, scoped mathematical readings, before implementation:

- Jinhee Jeong and Fazle Hussain, *On the identification of a vortex*, 1995,
  https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112095000462, section 4 and equations 5-6.
  Full paper obtained at https://electronicsandbooks.com/edt/manual/Magazine/J/Journal%20of%20Fluid%20Mechanics/1995%20Volume%20285/S0022112095000462.pdf .
  Lambda-2 is the middle eigenvalue of symmetric S^2+Omega^2, not an eigenvalue of the velocity
  gradient or its singular values. Its pressure interpretation assumes incompressibility and omits
  unsteady strain/viscosity. A negative contour is a local indicator, not a proof of a material vortex.
- J. C. R. Hunt, A. A. Wray and P. Moin, *Eddies, Streams, and Convergence Zones in Turbulent Flows*,
  1988, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19890015184/downloads/19890015184.pdf,
  introduction, section 2.1 and scanned page 196 visually read (equations 2.1a/b and 2.2).
  Rotation must dominate strain; pure shear can have vorticity without a vortex core. Pressure was an
  additional original condition, not computed here from velocity alone.
- Pinaki Chakraborty, S. Balachandar and Ronald J. Adrian, *On the relationships between local vortex
  identification schemes*, 2005, section 2.1.1-2.1.2, equations 2.1-2.3,
  https://www.oist.jp/sites/default/files/img/pages/units/fm/chakraborty-pinaki-pubs/vortex_identification_jfm05.pdf .
  Compared the general second invariant with rotation dominance: they differ by divergence^2/2 in
  compressible flow. This API explicitly returns rotation dominance at all points, and does not claim
  pressure minima or a compressible-flow vortex detector. Algebra gives S^2+Omega^2 = sym(J^2).
- Bengt Fornberg, *Generation of Finite Difference Formulas on Arbitrarily Spaced Grids*, 1988,
  https://www.colorado.edu/amath/sites/default/files/attached-files/mathcomp_88_fd_formulas.pdf,
  scanned page 700, equations 3.1-3.4, visually read. Differentiate the local Lagrange polynomial:
  centred (-1/2,0,1/2)/h and boundary (-3/2,2,-1/2)/h stencils. Rewrite boundary weights in terms of
  differences from the endpoint to preserve constant offsets. Two samples give a first-order secant;
  singleton axes give zero, explicitly extending a planar vector field constantly along that axis.
- Joachim Kopp, *Efficient numerical diagonalization of hermitian 3x3 matrices*, 2008,
  https://arxiv.org/pdf/physics/0610206, mathematical sections 2.1/2.3 and 3 reviewed.
  Compared iterative orthogonal rotations with analytical cubic roots and their cancellation near
  degeneracy. Choose largest-pivot Jacobi on a scaled real symmetric 3x3; no eigenvectors needed.
  CPU uses a 1e-14 relative pivot cutoff; GPU 1e-7, bounded to 48 rotations with a checked 1e-6
  residual. Neither Appendix B, companion implementations, nor any other repository source was read.

Synthesis: regular Cartesian physical coordinates, signed inverse spacing rounded once to f32, row-major
J_ij = du_i/dx_j, curl (J_zy-J_yz,J_xz-J_zx,J_yx-J_xy), divergence trace(J), and scaled tensor products.
A centre or required stencil neighbour masked/missing makes all outputs NaN; no lower-order fallback
across masks. All six GPU fields own separate contiguous arrays, allowing scalar volume/iso reuse without
readback of values. Device replacement requires deriving again on the replacement compute context.
Input copies and CPU work yield every 8192 points, exact-reason AbortSignal; GPU status read is cancellable.

Numerical domain: at most 1000000 points, finite f32 velocities (NaN missing), finite normal f32 inverse
spacing on active axes, and conservative stencil envelope D=8*max(maxAbsVelocity,2^-126)*maxAbsInverseSpacing <=1e18.
This keeps stencil/norm/tensor intermediates within f32 range; rescale physical units outside that domain.
With e=2^-23, t=2^-126, I=maxAbsInverseSpacing: gradient difference <= L=32eD+32t*max(1,I);
divergence/curl <=4L, magnitude <=8L; Q <=256eD^2+128t, lambda2 <=1024eD^2+128t.
Bounds include f32 rounding, flush-to-zero, tensor and residual errors (Weyl perturbation for symmetric
matrices), not finite-difference truncation or uncertainty in measured velocities. They are absolute,
scale-aware envelopes; values closer than the bound to zero cannot be classified reliably by sign.
The factor 8 bounds endpoint stencil amplification; first-order output bounds include sums/norms.
Tensor perturbations are bounded by products of those first-order errors, plus f32 arithmetic and
Jacobi residual; the published factors conservatively dominate those terms. Tests must also use
independent tighter analytic oracles so the conservative cross-device bound cannot hide wrong math.
No benchmark, paired wall-clock run, speed assertion or performance claim.

W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, *WebGPU Shading Language*, 2026-10-21,
https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/CRD-WGSL-20261021/, floating-point evaluation/finite-math and bitcast
sections consulted for masked output encoding. WGSL rejects NaN constant expressions and permits
finite-math assumptions on floating operations. Therefore output storage uses u32 bit patterns over
f32 GpuArray buffers: arithmetic results are bitcast to u32, missing values write 0x7fc00000 directly,
without ever constructing or doing arithmetic on a shader NaN. The mask regression runs on both
backends, including missing endpoint neighbours. No source from external shader libraries was read.


Runtime-input review before the coercion repair compared Gavin Bierman, Martin Abadi and Mads
Torgersen, *Understanding TypeScript*, 2014, abstract (https://research.google/pubs/understanding-typescript/),
and Aseem Rastogi, Nikhil Swamy, Cedric Fournet, Gavin Bierman and Panagiotis Vekris, *Safe & Efficient
Gradual Typing for TypeScript*, 2015, abstract
(https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/safe-efficient-gradual-typing-typescript/).
Their static-versus-runtime distinction motivates checking untyped callers at this array boundary,
without importing a compiler or attempting a general runtime type system. ECMA TC39, *ECMAScript
Language Specification*, living draft consulted 2026-11-09, Math.fround/ToNumber,
https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/numbers-and-dates.html#sec-math.fround,
confirms that rounding coerces its operand and can throw on BigInt/Symbol before an API's own guard.
Validate the primitive type before rounding, retaining the existing linked diagnostic. Regression
cases require RangeError plus the sciviz help link for BigInt/Symbol, null optional components/masks
and the earlier malformed numeric inputs, on both CPU and GPU entry paths before allocation.

## Batch 171 critical-point tracer repair and LIC size attribution

Research before repair compared:

- Christoph Garth and Xavier Tricoche, *Topology- and Feature-based Flow Visualization: Methods and
  Applications*, 2005, section 3.1, https://www.cs.purdue.edu/cgvlab/papers/xmt/siam-gdc05.pdf.
  Critical points are asymptotic limit sets; cycles are a different kind of limit set. A normalized field is
  singular at a zero, so cancellation of integration stages must not be published as a physical orbit.
- Tor Nordam and Rodrigo Duran, *Numerical integrators for Lagrangian oceanography*, 2020, sections
  2.1-2.4, https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/13/5935/2020/ . Compared embedded RK error estimates,
  step adaptation and derivative discontinuities from interpolated grids. Local control is not proof of
  global topology or original-data accuracy. Keep physical velocity sampling separate from unit tangents.
- Germund Dahlquist and Ake Bjorck, *Numerical Methods in Scientific Computing*, chapter 13 draft,
  2007 course copy (draft itself undated), section 13.3.3,
  https://user.it.uu.se/~perl/ODE_07/NumODEsbook.pdf . Step doubling gives the RK4 fine-solution
  error estimate (fine - coarse)/(2^4 - 1). Compared with the embedded-pair approach above; retain Margo's
  classical RK4 and accept the two-half-step solution without extrapolating across a singularity.

Synthesis in fields.ts: RK4 step doubling, error estimate <= 1e-6 of current arc step, and stage/endpoint
forward-half-space checks. Refine before publication. Terminate at minSpeed, missing/boundary samples,
or unresolved spatial progress, floor max(1e-6 min(requested step, grid spacing), 32 epsilon
max(abs(position components), requested step)). The angular/progress guard and floor are Margo's explicit
numerical policy, not a claimed theorem from the papers. Shrinking steps permits actual curvature; the
independent small-circle and near-saddle invariants rule out treating every turn as stagnation. No path
trimming, seed filtering, reduced demo step, relaxed cusp test, global cycle removal or hidden exception.
This uses additional field evaluations to correct the solver; no speed claim or timing comparison is made.
The public sampler also checks physical bounds before converting to grid indices, preventing rounding
from accepting a position just beyond a boundary. Zero speed stops even when minSpeed is zero; invalid
integration controls reject rather than entering an unbounded refinement. Regression covers those paths.
Both the unchanged analytical sink and all-NOAA-seed test fail against the preserved old Margo tracer;
all 190 package/site CPU tests pass with the repair. Permanent tests are in check:merge's existing unit glob.
Only papers, public specifications and Margo source/history were read; no companion or rival source.

LIC attribution uses the same current LIC source, bundler settings, external-import rule and gzip method
in both builds. Substituting only Margo's pre-f33472ed6 colormaps.ts/tables.ts yields exactly 10,429 B;
current published-precision tables yield exactly 23,461 B: +13,032 B. This is shared colour data/lookup,
not a measurement change. The five retained modules are LIC/shaders, linked errors, four layer helpers,

clamped palette gives exact admissible base bitsets. Every surviving header
is scored; initial seeds supply bounds only. Equal costs retain the least
header and smallest selector. Independent exhaustive oracles check the
objective and ties; the mask change also preserves 292 captured payloads.

## Batch 171 job 2: line integral convolution

Audit before implementation: the sciviz README and manifest exports offered arrows, streamlines and moving
particles, but no dense convolution. The new optional `/lic` owns its shaders, image, field copy and lifecycle.
Core and stage source are untouched. No engine/tool source or paper companion repository was read.

Research compared before implementation, from papers/descriptions only:

- Brian Cabral and Leith (Casey) Leedom, *Imaging Vector Fields Using Line Integral Convolution*, 1993,
  [paper](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/csci2370/2000/1999/cabral.pdf),
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/166117.166151). Sections 4, 4.1 and 4.2 supply curved bidirectional convolution,
  normalization of truncated kernels, and phase-shifted motion filtering. Static mode uses a box; animation
  uses a Hann envelope times three ripples per full window. Phase does not represent physical time.
- Detlev Stalling and Hans-Christian Hege, *Fast and Resolution Independent Line Integral Convolution*, 1995,
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/218380.218448),
  [paper transcription](https://paperzz.com/doc/8180821/fast-and-resolution-independent-line-integral-convolution).
  Compared separate field/noise/output resolution, arc-length sampling and rolling box sums. We retain
  independent resolution and normalized discrete convolution but use per-texel GPU integration, not a claim
  to the paper's rolling-sum speedup. Midpoint steps are bounded to at most one image texel.
- Lisa Forssell and Scott Cohen, *Using Line Integral Convolution for Flow Visualization: Curvilinear Grids,
  Variable Speed Animation, and Unsteady Flows*, 1995,
  [authors' description](https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/flowvis2/),
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/2945.468406). Separates geometry, direction and magnitude. Our affine slice
  uses an inverse Gram basis; speed is taken after vector interpolation, whereas an explicit scalar is
  interpolated separately. This entry does not implement the paper's unsteady advection.
- Daniel Weiskopf and Thomas Ertl, *A Hybrid Physical/Device-Space Approach for Spatio-Temporally Coherent
  Interactive Texture Advection on Curved Surfaces*, 2004,
  [paper](https://www.visus.uni-stuttgart.de/documentcenter/forschung/visualisierung_und_visual_analytics/gi04-weiskopf.pdf).
  Object-space noise motivates camera coherence. A retained slice-coordinate image supplies that here;
  the paper's arbitrary curved-surface hybrid method is not claimed.
- Robert S. Laramee, Helwig Hauser, Helmut Doleisch, Benjamin Vrolijk, Frits H. Post and Daniel Weiskopf,
  *The State of the Art in Flow Visualization: Dense and Texture-Based Techniques*, 2004,
  [publisher](https://diglib.eg.org/items/2c61423d-1b92-49e2-b998-0425e772888d),
  [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2004.00753.x). The survey distinguishes steady LIC, periodic
  direction cues, arbitrary-surface methods and physical unsteady advection; these are not conflated here.

packing preserves tiny finite directions. The demo reuses the frozen public-domain NOAA data and hashes.
No wall-clock speed claim is introduced.

restoring scalar magnitude separately. The probe now has zero error on both backends; the permanent entries
regression checks the entire mixed image without changing the existing box/circular/mask/phase/pixel bars.
