## Batch 181 job 1: native sciviz surface and rectangle drawing (2026-11-10)

Retired 2026-11-11 (KB1405, Scott's yes): the driver this section researched was removed, so its shaders and sources no longer
ship. The record below stays as the history of what was consulted.

Research-first survey, before implementation, compared these primary papers and standards:

- Frank Losasso and Hugues Hoppe, [Geometry Clipmaps: Terrain Rendering Using Nested Regular Grids](https://hhoppe.com/geomclipmap.pdf), SIGGRAPH 2004, abstract and introduction: regular height grids and retained GPU geometry.
- Arul Asirvatham and Hugues Hoppe, [Terrain Rendering Using GPU-Based Geometry Clipmaps](https://hhoppe.com/proj/gpugcm/), GPU Gems 2, 2005, authors' abstract and hindsight: vertex textures instead of CPU-expanded geometry.
- Malte Clasen and Hans-Christian Hege, [Terrain Rendering Using Spherical Clipmaps](https://doi.org/10.2312/VisSym/EuroVis06/091-098), EuroVis 2006, publisher abstract: texture displacement of static vertices; spherical mapping is unnecessary for a Cartesian scientific grid.
- Khronos WebGL Working Group, [WebGL 2.0 Specification](https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/specs/latest/2.0/), 2017 onward, buffer/vertex-array, pixel-store, texture and state-query rules.
- Robert J. Simpson (editor), Khronos, [The OpenGL ES Shading Language 3.00, revision 6](https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.0/GLSL_ES_Specification_3.00.pdf), 2016, integer texel fetches and derivative functions.

We combine regular-grid vertex generation with exact R32F vertex texture fetches. Unlike the clipmap papers,
this draws every scientific cell with no view-dependent reduction, resampling or invented detail. Central and
one-sided differences, light/colour/contour formulae and triangle ordering are independently transcribed from
Margo's own WGSL. Rectangles use integer packed-colour attributes and instancing, with no CPU expansion.
The engine supplies its native GL camera convention and current depth buffer. State scopes cover drawing and
uploads. No companion code, paper listing, outside engine source or external implementation was read or copied.
No CPU-heavy geometry loop or new Wasm is added. Timings are deferred; deterministic work is recorded in limits.
The optional attacher's AbortSignal follows WHATWG contributors' [DOM Standard, section 3.3](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#using-abortcontroller-and-abortsignal-objects-in-apis), living standard read in 2026: reject with the exact reason, prevent late attachment and remove the listener after the module settles. Import fetching itself is not canceled.

- Pei Cao and Sandy Irani, *Cost-Aware WWW Proxy Caching Algorithms* (1997),
  [sections 2.2 and 4](https://static.usenix.org/publications/library/proceedings/usits97/full_papers/cao/cao_html/cao.html):
  reviewed the LRU, size-sensitive and cost-sensitive replacement alternatives and making room for an incoming object.
- Neal E. Young, *On-Line File Caching* (2002 journal version; 1997 technical report),
  [section 1 and Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0205033): reviewed the total-byte capacity model and admission
  after space is available. Its general replacement policy is broader than this streamer's protected load range.
- Matt Welsh, David Culler and Eric Brewer, *SEDA: An Architecture for Well-Conditioned, Scalable Internet Services*
  (2001), [sections 3.1-3.3](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~prabal/teaching/resources/eecs582/welsh01seda.pdf):
  reviewed stage boundaries, finite queues and backpressure between asynchronous producers and consumers.

The review supports two separate controls: bound starts using ready/loading reservations, then check actual object
bytes at admission because an estimate cannot enforce capacity for variable-size results. Margo retains its existing
closest-first ordering, outside-range LRU eviction and pending results; cost-ranked replacement and dropping results
would change the established contract. The papers supply general reasoning, not a claim of their performance bounds
for Margo. None was read in full; the cited sections were reviewed. Three deterministic regressions exercise stored,
variable-size and packed-worker results, including resumption after a budget increase.

## Draco replacement specification review (batch 133, 2026-11-09)

The [published Draco bitstream specification](https://google.github.io/draco/spec/),
Version 2,2, was read in full, including all five figures, before implementation.
The retrieved HTML SHA-256 is
`beda7f5ff1e7ac3d54b11c22f06e84ff1a58b785e8a1fa74a7af6a80e743f6d0`.
No codec implementation source was opened or used. The required specification-only
plan is retained in the private batch handoff.

This source does not fully specify the requested replacement. Its
[connectivity dispatch](https://google.github.io/draco/spec/#decodeconnectivitydata)
has no point-cloud path. The generic attribute encoding is enumerated without a
payload decoder; [portable attribute decoding](https://google.github.io/draco/spec/#decodeportableattributes)
skips no-prediction payloads, and [integer decoding](https://google.github.io/draco/spec/#sequentialintegerattributedecoder_decodeintegervalues)
has no uncompressed payload read.

Scott's ruling of 2026-11-10 permits missing rules to be inferred by feeding crafted
inputs to the prebuilt decoder and comparing its outputs. The oracle runs outside
this repository; its implementation source and wrapper source remain unread. Every
inferred rule must cite the input, observed output and distinguishing experiment
here and in the private plan before implementation relies on it. An untested
hypothesis is not an inferred rule. The prior requirement to wait for published
errata is superseded. Both prebuilt decoders remain until implementation, complete
external-corpus bit identity, hostile-input, speed and size gates pass. The review
and revised plan alone make no replacement or performance claim.

### Batch 133 black-box inference ledger

The unchanged full decoder Wasm SHA-256 is
`c55a594e8ffd18426d36b27fea9618af3df5e173640a3e56d46f09d76f0574f2`.
Our original harness executes the opaque build in the private oracle directory
outside the worktree and queries only public decode/metadata/array APIs. No codec
source, disassembly or internal state is inspected. The following experiments
establish rules omitted by the published specification, for version 2.2 only:

| Experiment | Distinguishing inputs and observation | Inferred rule and held-out confirmation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E3/E4 | 45 one-triangle files sweep semantics 0..4 and scalar types 1..6, 9..11. Each contains a second float attribute `[11.5,-3.25,17.75]`; every canary and first attribute decodes exactly. | Semantic bytes 0/1/2/3/4 mean POSITION/NORMAL/COLOR/TEX_COORD/GENERIC. Types 1/2/3/4/5/6/9/10/11 mean i8/u8/i16/u16/i32/u32/f32/f64/bool. Generic payloads are unframed, interleaved little-endian scalars with no prediction byte. Six further signed, boundary and fractional cases preserve the following canary. 64-bit integer types remain untested. |
| E5/E6 | NONE (`fe`) followed by `00`, width 1/2/3/4 and unsigned symbols `[4,13,22]` returns `[2,-7,11]` at every width, then the intact canary. Alternative plain signed hypotheses predict different values. | NONE still consumes the compression flag; zero consumes a byte width and that many little-endian bytes per zigzag symbol. Four held-out cases cover the signed minima/maxima of each width, including int32. |
| E14 | Point-cloud headers followed by LE u32 counts 0/1/2/127/128/257 and sequential attribute descriptors return the exact count/values. Varint candidates reject or return a different count. | Sequential point clouds store a fixed LE u32 point count immediately after the header, then the sequential attribute stream. Held-out counts 3 and 129 with three asymmetric components confirm row order. |
| E1/E2 | Four encodings of nine 3-bit symbols distinguish high/low bit order and per-row/whole-stream alignment. Only continuous low-bit-first data returns the intended values and intact canary. | Tagged values consume low bits first without alignment between component groups; align once at the end. Held-out 3/5-bit streams with changing row widths confirm. Six independently emitted raw ANS cases exercise precision 12/18/20 bits and reverse-byte refill, agreeing with the published entropy algorithm. |
| E7 | Two decoder groups with attribute counts 1+1, 1+2 and 1+3 return every distinct attribute. Quantized three-component values use unequal minima `[-13,2,0.125]`. | Each group uses its own attribute count; each minimum belongs to its component. This corrects the specification's last-group-count and minimum-index typos. |
| E11 | Normal NONE payloads with two portable components succeed and preserve a following canary; three-component candidates reject. A 512-point grid at 4/8/12/16 quantization bits distinguishes arithmetic forms, float widths and signed zero. | Portable normals always use two components. The equivalent octahedral unfolding below matches all 1,536 output scalars; 903 held-out points at 2/3/6/10/20/24/30 bits also match exactly. |
| E12 | The specification's two successive quantization multiplies differ from the oracle by one ULP on the value 8 at 8 bits, range 7.25, minimum 0.125. | Compute the float32 scale as `range / ((1 << bits) - 1)`, then float32 `value * scale + minimum`, rounding after multiply and add. Sixteen held-out files at 4/8/12/20 bits and four unequal ranges match all 6,192 scalars. |

E11's arithmetic is derived from the published octahedral geometry and selected
by experiments, not another implementation: round every operation to float32;
set `scale = 2 / ((1 << bits) - 2)`, `y = s * scale - 1`,
`z = t * scale - 1`, `x = (1 - abs(y)) - abs(z)`. When `x < 0`,
use the original y/z to set y to `abs(z) - 1` if y is negative, otherwise
`1 - abs(z)`, and z to `abs(y) - 1` if z is negative, otherwise
`1 - abs(y)`. Normalize using float32 `((x*x + y*y) + z*z)`, float32 square
root, reciprocal and component multiplies. The subtraction order explains the
positive zeros on folds without a special case for any tested input.

Exact crafted inputs and complete public outputs are retained under the worktree's

not complete attribute decoding or a replacement claim. The prebuilt was measured
before this extension. Its targets and the remaining performance gates are in

| Experiment | Distinguishing observation and rule | Confirmation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E8 | A valence E triangle accepts start-face data followed directly by six context counts. Adding the standard symbol buffer makes it reject. Thus valence omits that buffer, contrary to its figure. Initial E and reverse-pop context symbols follow the pseudocode. | Seven E/L/R/C and mixed-fan cases distinguish context 0 from context 1 and preserve exact index order. All 304 external connectivity extracts also agree. |
| E9 | Unconditionally replacing a vertex representative as the printed `MapCornerToVertex` does changes seam point order. Preserve the left boundary representative when a fan closes. For interior closure, walk previous/opposite from previous(a) to b, then the same walk from previous(b) to c. Asymmetric fans distinguish the printed second walk. | All 304 external extracts agree; 16 further closed fans with one/two independently patterned seam streams agree without changing the algorithm. |
| E9 compaction | Four multi-split fans run with zero and one all-false attribute-connectivity stream return different point numbering. With zero streams, fill isolated IDs in split-discovery order from the highest remaining live vertex, skipping isolated tails. With streams, recompute seam points in vertex order. | All eight paired files agree. This also resolves the independent nonmanifold `test_nm.obj.edgebreaker.cl4.2.2.drc` extract. |
| E10 | Two independent attribute groups accept all routing triples before all descriptors; interleaving a triple with its descriptors rejects. Base data ID is 255; a corner group's data ID indexes attribute connectivity. Connectivity streams still expand seam points when the group count is zero. | Eight two-group canary files cover depth-first and prediction-degree traversal; all 304 zero-group connectivity extracts retain the oracle's point/index order. |
| E12 integer extension | A valid wrap range [-1e9,1e9], first entry values [1e9,1e9,-1e9] and a zero fourth parallelogram correction produce -1e9. Widening the predictor before clamping predicts +1e9. Predictor addition/subtraction therefore wraps to int32 before clamping. | An opposite-sign case and three distinct further arithmetic cases preserve the following float canary and match all returned integer values. |

### Batch 133: E9 capped boundaries and E15 KD-tree observations (2026-11-09 continuation)

The 31 retained capped-fan regressions and 182 newly accepted held-out specimens
across versions 1.1/1.2/2.0/2.1/2.2 match after preserving a boundary
representative on its own vertex and giving corners not reached by point
deduplication the observed initial point zero. Malformed caps may join fans
with different vertex identities; acceptance is not a manifold-validity claim.
No old case was removed or relaxed; the connectivity fixture now has 730 cases.

E15 uses only crafted inputs to the opaque decoder public API, plus the
previously pinned standard `pc_kd_color.drc` input. Experiments `kd-frame`,
`kd-buffers`, `kd-bitorder` and `kd-axis` are indexed with input/output SHA-256
in [the inference checkpoint](whitepaper/results/batch-133-inference-checkpoint.json).
An independent Margo Python model matches every coordinate in 345 accepted
crafted cases, and every color byte and quantized/dequantized position byte
in the 7,733-point external seed. These are observations, not a completed
feature or performance claim. The native Rust/Wasm KD implementation now matches
369 retained complete-file cases, including the unmodified external seed.

Observed framing: group descriptors are followed by one compression-level byte,
LEu32 coordinate width and LEu32 point count. Levels 0/1 use raw number bits,
2/3 use one binary ANS decoder, and 4/5/6 use 32 binary ANS bit planes plus
one spare binary decoder. Three LEu32-length raw buffers carry residuals,
axis choices and uneven-half directions, followed by attribute transforms.
Raw words are little endian, read from their most significant bit; number
planes are visited in most-significant-first order starting at plane zero.
Counts above two subdivide the selected axis. The number width is
floor(log2(count)); the stored difference subtracts from floor(count/2).
Direction one assigns that smaller half to the lower box; otherwise to the
upper box. Output visits the upper box first. Counts one/two emit residual
coordinates in cyclic axis order. Levels 0-5 advance the prior axis cyclically
(initial prior axis zero). Level 6 reads four explicit axis bits at counts
at least 64; smaller nodes choose the largest remaining coordinate width,
breaking ties by first dimension. Width exhaustion emits repeated box origins.
The 33rd ANS stream has no observed use yet; do not infer its semantics.
The `kd-types` and `kd-transform` experiments additionally establish signed
i8/i16/i32 minima as per-component unsigned LEB128 zigzag values. Distinct mixed
signed/float canaries show all floating transforms precede all signed minima,
regardless of descriptor order. The decoder preserves integer low bits when
writing the declared scalar width. Unsigned u8/u16/u32 and float32 also match.
The 369 `kd-regression` inputs trim only unused trailing probe bytes and were
independently re-run through the opaque decoder before becoming positive tests.
Native/Wasm compare every exposed native byte and descriptor, reject 49,779
selected complete-file strict prefixes, pass 4,096 KD mutations and 2,000
decode/free cycles without growth. Historical KD, predictor and full feature
coverage remain to establish; mutated version headers do not establish support.

The opaque decoder accepts 112 crafted predictor-2 discovery cases and 135

2.2, depth-first/degree routing, one/two/three components and large corrections.
Predictor 2 has no crease side flags. It averages the available parallelograms
along SwingRight from the entry corner, stopping at boundary or closure, with

vary fan size and disconnected component count independently of prediction.
All 289 complete files match ordered indices, descriptors and native bytes.

[color attachments](https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/#render-pass-color-attachments), Candidate Recommendation
Draft dated 15 September 2026. Implementation and generated color/triangle fixtures are independently written.
No other engine or library source was read. This is a color subresource API, not scene or camera capture.

Margo is written clean room. This page says what that means, how the 2026-10-24 rewrites were done, and where every
lighting and post-processing formula in the engine comes from.

## The rule

Scott's rule (2026-10-24): Margo never uses files from other repositories, whatever their licence. Code is written from public specifications, papers and
descriptions; nobody copies, adapts or reads another engine's or application's source while writing the matching
Margo code. Other engines run only where they live (`../engine-bench`). The one exception is large standard files
every engine uses (sample models, test assets, prebuilt decoders), each recorded in
[THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md](../THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md). The `clean-room` quality gate
([conventions.md](conventions.md#quality-gate)) fails a new mention of another graphics library in `packages/**`
or a new third-party dependency.

Rulings on what counts (Scott, 2026-10-24):

- **Published engine standards are kept, with a citation.** A formula or constant an engine team published for
  others to use, for example Karis 2014's mobile environment BRDF fit and the 0.045 minimum perceptual roughness of
  the Filament design document. Unreal and Unity interop conventions are kept on the same footing.
- **MagicaVoxel parity fits are kept**, recorded as fitted to observed MagicaVoxel output. They were measured from
  the application's renders, never from its code; its renders are not in the repository.
- **Rewritten:** code that followed another engine's source, and library defaults copied with no physical basis.

## Process

Each area went through four steps, with a different agent at each step so no writer saw the old code:

1. **Dirty spec.** An auditor who may read the old Margo code (never another engine's) writes a words-only spec:
   files and line ranges, the public interface callers rely on, the required behaviour, which constants are
   binding (public sources) and which are the writer's to choose, and the tests, proofs and visual baselines that
   touch it. Specs hold no code.
2. **Stub.** The auditor removes the old body (and any built `dist` that held it), leaves a `CLEAN-ROOM:` marker
   and keeps everything outside the range unchanged, so the package still builds.
3. **Clean writer.** A fresh agent reads only the spec, the public sources it names and the tests it lists, and
   writes the body. It chooses its own internal constants and documents each one in a comment.
4. **Tests.** The package tests, proofs (`npm run proofs -- --current`) and visual checks run against the new body;
   any proof whose feature-off output changes is advanced with a note in
   [whitepaper/claims.md](whitepaper/claims.md).

## Rewrites of 2026-10-24

From commits ac465a00..ccb4a164 and their follow-ups, every area the 2026-10-21 audit found close to other engines' or
libraries' code:

- geometry (primitives, curves, extrusion, earcut triangulation, edges, convex hull, subdivision, utilities)
- controls (orbit, trackball, fly, first-person, transform)
- helpers; CSS3D labels; SDF text; eye-dome lighting
- math edge cases; BVH shapecast
- contact shadows; glitch and afterimage
- hashes and noise
- sheen, thin film, transmission, matcap, depth packing
- light falloff, LTC edge integral, cotangent frame
- ACES fit
- LZF, meshopt, EXR PIZ, USD LZ4 and integer coding, JT LZMA
- SVG, outline-font and MTL loaders
- ORCA avoidance and the path funnel (navigation removed; `@margoengine/navmesh/build` replaces it,
  [renames-2026-10-24.md](renames-2026-10-24.md))
- fixtures from other projects replaced by Margo-generated ones; three and Babylon dropped as dev dependencies

The provenance sweep that produced the table below added five more:

- FXAA, rebuilt from Lottes' 2009 whitepaper (it had followed the FXAA 3.11 reference shader)
- the transmission blur level, now derived from the GGX facet tilt and Snell's law
- the 0-15 voxel light-level curve, now equal CIE L* steps
- the Phong `refractionRatio` default (0.98 to air-to-glass 1/1.5) and the `rgbShift` amount default (0.005 to 0.002)

The FBX importer's Phong exponent to roughness mapping was also corrected to match materials and the exporters
(row EX2).

## Where each formula comes from

Every row of the four provenance tables (groups pbr, env, post and shadow-voxel; ids as in those tables), grouped by
the package of its first site. The source is a public paper, specification or standard; "Margo-own" with the design
it follows; "published engine standard" with its document; or "fitted to observed MagicaVoxel output". Most sites
carry the same citation as a one-line comment in the code.

No source of another CAD kernel is read |

J. Jackson, "Boundary representation modelling with local tolerances", Proceedings of the Third ACM Symposium on Solid Modeling and Applications (SMA '95), 247-254, 1995, doi:10.1145/218013.218067 (section 3: a tolerant vertex is a sphere, a tolerant edge a tube, entities intersect when within the sum of their tolerances, the curves of a face need not meet end to end but must end inside the vertex sphere, and where the tubes of two edges meet, each part must meet a common vertex); M. Segal, "Using tolerances to guarantee valid polyhedral modeling results", SIGGRAPH 1990, Computer Graphics 24(4), 105-114, doi:10.1145/97880.97891 (abstract and method: tolerances kept per entity rather than one epsilon, so topological decisions stay consistent); ISO 10303-43, uncertainty_measure_with_unit and global_uncertainty_assigned_context (one distance for the whole representation, the only tolerance a STEP file states; local tolerances are measured on import, BR10). No source of another CAD kernel is read |

### physics

The own solver's kernel (`packages/physics/kernel`, Rust, no dependencies). Nothing here comes from the source of Rapier, parry, Box2D, Jolt, Bullet, PhysX or any paper's companion repository; none was opened.

| id | formula | file | source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PK1 | Bit-equal floats: every operator rounds to nearest, ties to even; NaN payloads are the one freedom, so no NaN may reach the state; no fused or relaxed operation is used | physics/kernel/src/math.rs, lib.rs | **Read:** the WebAssembly specification, *Execution: Numerics*, section Floating-Point Operations. The rule that follows from it (only + - * / sqrt, compares and integers) is the plan's |
| PK2 | Semi-implicit Euler: `v += h (g + F / m)`, then `x += h v` with the new velocity, so the velocity a body reports is the one that moved it | physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs | **Read:** Catto, "Iterative Dynamics with Temporal Coherence", GDC 2005, eqs. 1, 2, 36, 37, in full; Catto, "Numerical Methods", GDC 2015, in full. The rule that a force reaches every substep and an impulse lands once is Margo's, from its ragdoll findings |
| PK3 | A step split into n substeps, each one velocity update and one pose update; smaller steps beat more iterations for the same work | physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs | **Read:** Macklin, Storey, Lu, Terdiman, Chentanez, Jeschke, Müller, "Small Steps in Physics Simulation", SCA 2019, in full |
| PK4 | Gyroscopic term `I w' + w x I w = 0` in the principal frame, one implicit-midpoint step by Newton's method. The midpoint keeps kinetic energy and the size of angular momentum because both are quadratic in w. A step may not raise the energy | physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs | **Read:** Catto, "Numerical Methods", GDC 2015, for working in the body frame and Newton's method on the implicit step; Hairer, Geometric Numerical Integration lecture notes, week 2, in full (https://www.unige.ch/~hairer/poly_geoint/week2.pdf), for implicit midpoint keeping quadratic invariants. The rest of those notes was not read. The scale-back to the starting energy is Margo's |
| PK5 | Damping as implicit Euler of `v' = -c v`: the factor `1 / (1 + c h)` stays in (0, 1] for every c and h | physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs | Own derivation, one line from the definition of implicit Euler |
| PK6 | Rotation by the exact exponential of `h w`: Maclaurin series of `sin(a/2)/a` and `cos(a/2)` in `a^2`, turns over a radian halved and squared back; its inverse from the series of `asin(s)/s` and the half-angle rule | physics/kernel/src/math.rs | Own derivation from the Maclaurin series, plus and times only, so bit-equal everywhere. The plan named a first-order quaternion update; it was replaced because its turn is not `h w`, so the reported velocity would not be the one that moved the body, which is what the ragdoll findings asked for |
| PK7 | Bodies and colliders in free lists, last freed first, each row with a generation: which row a call gets depends only on the calls before it | physics/kernel/src/world.rs | Margo's own, for replay; the plan names the free list |
| PK8 | Mass of a box `8abc rho`, a ball `4/3 pi r^3 rho`, a capsule as a cylinder plus two hemispheres. Moments: `m (b^2 + c^2) / 3` for a box, `2/5 m r^2` for a ball. For the capsule, the cylinder's `m r^2 / 2` along it and `m (r^2 / 4 + l^2 / 12)` across it; a hemisphere's centroid `3r/8` from its flat face, moved by the parallel axis theorem, gives `m (2/5 r^2 + a^2 + 3/4 a r)` across | physics/kernel/src/mass.rs | Own derivation from the integrals that define mass and moment of inertia, checked against a numeric integral of each solid in tests/bodies.rs |
| PK9 | Principal axes by cyclic Jacobi rotations, using `sqrt` and division only, each plane rotation joined to the frame as a quaternion by its half angle, so the frame stays a proper rotation and the result is bit-equal everywhere | physics/kernel/src/mass.rs | Own derivation from the definition of a Jacobi rotation, the textbook method for a symmetric matrix. No source was copied |
| PK10 | Sweep and prune: one sorted list of box ends per axis, kept from step to step, so sorting is a short walk; an overlap starts or stops only where a min end and a max end change places. Boxes are written first and each crossing asks the final boxes, so the result does not depend on the order ends walk in. Fat boxes extended by a small margin, so a pair is found before contact | physics/kernel/src/broad.rs | **Read:** Cohen, Lin, Manocha, Ponamgi, "I-COLLIDE: An Interactive and Exact Collision Detection System for Large-Scale Environments", I3D 1995, in full (sections 4.2 and 6.3 for this row). Baraff's 1992 thesis, the plan's other source for sort and sweep, was not read: Cornell eCommons holds it (TR 92-1275) as a scan of 220 page images with no text layer, and no tool here could read it. The final-box rule, the pair rows, and the batched join (a stable merge sort, one merge, one sweep with new and old boxes in two open lists) are Margo's |
| PK11 | A step's motion predicted from velocity and the whole step's time, and collision detection once per frame reused by every substep | physics/kernel/src/broad.rs | **Read:** Macklin et al. 2019, section 4.2. The bound `a dt^2` over substeps and the chord bound for a turn are own derivations |
| PK12 | Pair lookup by open addressing with linear probing and backward-shift deletion, pair rows held on two linked lists | physics/kernel/src/broad.rs | Textbook data structures, written from their definitions. No source was copied |
| PK13 | Islands are contact groups: connected components of the contact graph. Locks along a path of joints by block Cholesky of a block tridiagonal J M^-1 J^T, in doubles, the sparsity Baraff 1996 uses; bias of the whole error, then a velocity projection on rows from the new pose, the two stages of RATTLE. Motors and springs as soft rows in implicit form, stiffness and damping per unit of effective mass in the acceleration model. Hinge alignment by a1 x a2, angle read along the axis, unwrapped by a tally; shortest arc to a joint's axis. Own, from derivation and measurement: the pushing pass, the one rule that keeps a rigid row with a warm start stable. Take one mode of J M^-1 J^T that a pass shrinks by g, with share s, error e, y = h J v and p = h a lambda the memory. Remembering every impulse gives p' = y' - y, so as g nears 1 the substep's matrix nears a Jordan block of three, e from y from p, and the only feedback is the error, of size (1 - g) s. Then mu^3 = -(1 - g) s, two of whose roots have a positive real part: the mode grows at any share, as a triple integrator does under position feedback alone. Measured on the 8 by 8 grid: speed triples each 10 steps from step 30, gap 1.5 m, 100 m/s; with 8 passes in place of 2 the same matrix gives 1e-5 m, so the singular matrix is not the cause; without warm starting 8e-4 m. Keeping the bias out of the memory removes the feedback path from the error to the memory, and the model's spectral radius falls under 1 for every g and s tried; measured 1.8e-4 m at 8 by 8 and 9.5e-4 m at 30 by 30. Soft rows have a way out of their own, as gamma lifts the slowest mode. Limits are rigid up to their edge and soft past it, the contact's Soft Step row (Catto 2011 form, per unit of effective mass), measured: with a rigid push a limb on a floor past its cone moved at 0.40 m/s for good, with the soft one it sleeps. A limit's row is the Schur complement of its joint's own locks, t M^-1 t^T - c^T K^-1 c with c = J M^-1 t^T, and it reads the speed those locks leave, own derivation; without it a rod came off its stop at a quarter of its speed, since the locks take back most of each impulse on the free body and the warm start remembers what the passes did not settle. A rope and a spring: a joint's first axis made the line between the anchors, reading their distance, with a limit row or a motor row in the force model; Muller et al. 2020 Eq 25 for the maximum distance, Catto 2011 for the spring. A spherical motor: three motor rows on the rotation vector left to the target, the target being frame A moved onto the rotation asked for; Tan, Liu and Turk 2011 ask the same of a PD servo, the control force from the next state, (M + Kd dt)^-1 in their Eq 11, of which this row's gamma is the scalar form, and their stability condition Kd >= Kp dt does not bind here, as the row is implicit in position too. Their M is the joint-space inertia, which a limit's Schur complement stands for here; a motor's free-body row lands within 0.0006 rad of the closed form as measured, because the passes converge on the row's fixed point, so motors stayed as they were. A cone: swing and twist split of the frame turn, q = swing twist (Dobrowolski 2015), twist 2 atan2(q.x, q.w) with its rate (a1 + a2) . w / (2 (x^2 + w^2)) from differentiating that angle, swing as an ellipse of the rotation vector's Y and Z parts, the row along the gradient measuring the first-order distance past the edge, own derivation. The share of 0.2 for paths that meet by Gauss-Seidel is a measured choice with room: 0.05 to 0.7 all hold a 30 by 30 grid. Rows that depend on each other: K = J M^-1 J^T is not formed; with F F^T = M^-1 per body (the roots of the inverse masses, the Cholesky factor of the inverse inertia), K = A^T A for A = F^T J^T, and Householder QR of A with column pivoting gives R, K's Cholesky factor with complete pivoting (Higham 1990, section 5.2, his (5.2.2)), solved as R^T y = b, R x = y (Higham 2008). Along a path A is block banded, so it is factored front by front: a joint's front is what the joint before left free on the body they share, compressed by a QR of those rows' parts on that body to at most six, and the six rows of its other body; its pivot is the column with the most of its own squared length left, complete pivoting on the matrix scaled to a unit diagonal, as linear and turning rows share no unit; the stop is Higham 1990's test (4.3) at his suggested n u, n the rows of the path, u f32's epsilon, as the rows are f32. The reflection's sign is the one that does not cancel. Why not K: eliminating it joint by joint puts W^T E W into each Schur complement (his Lemma 2.1, W = K11^-1 K12), and with no pivoting across joints W has any size; measured on joint web seed 1, a 13-row path on 12 freedoms with a 43 m spherical joint, the last pivot read 4e-7 of its size where the f32 rows give exactly 0 in rationals (so not the f32 inputs), 4.8e6 rad/s; seed 18 before it, 10 rows on 6 freedoms, Schur noise 1e-7, 3.8e8 m/s. The front by front order and the compression are our own arrangement of banded QR; the stop at n u in place of u alone is Higham's suggestion, and it also drops rows within about sqrt(n u) radians of depending. A push near such a pose: Buss and Kim 2005's bound gamma = min(1, N / M) gamma_max, from their section 4, with N what a path asks, M the fastest any body would go at its centre plus its arm, on the rise in a body's turn and in its centre over its arm. Where the code differs: they work per singular vector and bound the change itself, this cuts the whole path, as a path solve has no decomposition, and takes gamma_max 0.2 for their pi / 4, measured (taut chain 39 m/s at pi / 4; the chain of fifty first cut at 0.1). A first version bounded speed alone, at N, and it acted on 99 percent of a plain pendulum's substeps, cutting pushes to 0.37: the counters showed it, `a_small_gap_closes_in_one_push` holds that. A cut on the push alone left a limit's kick standing' answer to it cut, 1,000 times the energy, seen as a NaN at step 2,690 of one seed, so the cut reads the rise and not the gain. The bias cap is their ClampMag, its turning term their D_max,i = d_i + D_max, and r w h covers the r (h w)^2 / 2 a turn opens up to a turn of 2 radians. The warm start's line search is our own, the exact minimum of f(a) = a m^T J v + a^2 m^T K m / 2, with m^T K m read off as what the memory did to its own rows; a load that is right has its minimum at 1. An always-on search broke a light link and a chain on limits, so it runs only past one push's energy, a threshold set by measurement. | physics/kernel/src/joints.rs | **Read:** Baraff, "Linear-Time Dynamics using Lagrange Multipliers", SIGGRAPH 1996, in full, as extracted text; Hairer, Geometric Numerical Integration notes, section V.5 only, for RATTLE (Andersen 1983, not read itself); Catto, "Soft Constraints", GDC 2011, in full; Muller et al. 2020, in full, their Eq 20, Eq 21 and Algorithm 3; Dobrowolski, "Swing-twist decomposition in Clifford algebra", 2015, in full, Proposition 2 for the shortest arc and the split a cone uses; Wang, Servin and Berglund, "Warm starting the projected Gauss-Seidel algorithm for granular matter simulation", 2015, in full. | PK50 | Substep levels per island and tipping stiffness (`physics/kernel/src/tilt.rs`). Own derivation. A patch of soft contact springs resists a turn about its middle with k_theta = omega^2 sum m_i d_i^2; a body b tilted by psi_b lowers its centre and what it holds up by G_bb psi_b^2 / 2, G_bb = g (m_b (centre - base) + held (top - base)), diagonal in absolute tilts. Along a support path psi_b is the sum of the interface turns under it, so by Cauchy-Schwarz psi_b^2 <= C_b sum k_i dpsi_i^2 with C_b the path's compliance (in parallel over several supports, a conductance), and gravity's energy is at most sum_i k_i dpsi_i^2 A_i with A_i = sum of G_bb C_b over the bodies interface i holds up: if every A_i < 1 nothing tips, a discrete Hardy inequality. The step holds every A_i at 0.5 by raising an interface's stiffness, from masses and contact shape only, never from last step's impulses (a load-following stiffness rocked the pile, measured). The bodies are layered along gravity, lowest first, a tie by row. Where an interface would need more than a quarter of the substep rate, the island steps at level k, world substeps times 2^k, the least k that suffices, up to the 7,680 Hz tick (`@margoengine/math/clock`). The turn bound: a turn t between the rows' pose and the relaxing pass's changes the world inverse inertia by at most 2 \|R - I\| \|W\| = 4 sin(t / 2) \|W\|, and the pass cannot take back more than it gave while that stays under \|W\|: t <= 2 asin(1 / 4) = 0.5054 rad, with 0.5 (holds) and 0.6 (gains 19 percent) measured as the check. Mirtich, "Impulse-based Dynamic Simulation of Rigid Body Systems", PhD thesis, UC Berkeley, 1996 (conservative advancement, impacts in time order); E. Catto, "Continuous Collision", GDC 2013 (time-of-impact sub-stepping); M. Macklin, K. Storey, M. Lu, P. Terdiman, N. Chentanez, S. Jeschke and M. Mueller, "Small Steps in Physics Simulation", SCA 2019; M. Mueller, M. Macklin, N. Chentanez, S. Jeschke and T.-Y. Kim, "Detailed Rigid Body Simulation with Extended Position Based Dynamics", SCA 2020 (pairs found once a step, contacts each substep); B. Smith, D. Kaufman, E. Vouga, R. Tamstorf and E. Grinspun, "Reflections on Simultaneous Impact", SIGGRAPH 2012 (why one solve of several points differs from impacts in order). The bound, the spin rule and the per-island pieces are ours. Written from the papers; no code read |
| PK68 | Locks closed at the end pose (KB2161: `shed_locks`, `project_locks`, `newton_right`, `lock_speeds`, `damp_taut`, `note_springs` in `physics/kernel/src/joints.rs`; the substep level in `tilt.rs`, 2026-11-28). After the passes, every path's locks are closed at the pose the substep reaches by Gauss-Newton on the path's Newton matrix N = J W G^T, J the rows at the iterate, W the inverse masses and G the discrete gradient of the locks over the substep, so a step closes its share of each gap to first order however far the rows have turned; each iterate is cut back by halves while it widens its path's widest gap, up to eight times. N is factored by Householder QR with column pivoting, each column judged against its own size; where it has fewer freedoms than rows, the rows are taken in the path's order while a pivot holds a tenth of its column (threshold partial pivoting), otherwise the steadiest, and the rows whose pivot is rounding are dropped. Plain elimination in the path's order kept pivots near 1.4e-3 of their diagonal on web seed 40 and gained 7.3e7 J there; with the threshold test all 60 web seeds gain 0 J. The speeds follow the midpoint rule: twice the projection's shift over h, and the loads (gravity, a body's force and torque, a tree's implicit springs, locked part only, and on the free axes the whole change the substep made) move the poses by h^2 a / 2 in place of symplectic Euler's h^2 a. Own, from derivation and measurement: the springs as loads. Left out, the locked part was gravity's alone, taken link by link against each link's own joints, a wider span than the chain's locks hold together, and the rest moved the free axes by h^2 g / 2 each substep: a cantilever of 8 implicit springs at 4 substeps stood 0.355 % low, 0.0008 % with them. A taut lock of all three sliding axes damps the free motion where its geometric stiffness outruns a substep: on each diagonal of the body's stiffness in the arm's frame, where h^2 k passes 4 alpha m (alpha = 1, m that axis's mass), the damping b = (h^2 k - 4 alpha m) / 2h joins the inertia as h b, and the spin becomes (1 + W h B)^-1 w. The bound h^2 k / m < 4 is Andrews, Teichmann and Kry's (section 4.1, as in PK24); the damping's form, keyed to that bound per axis, is own. An island's substep level also counts the spin across each joint with locks, and a lock's reach counts the turn of a kinematic or fixed end only, both own, by measurement on the level chain and the web seeds. Each iterate moves each body once, by the sum of its joints' moves over the path in doubles (`move_path`), and a cut takes back each body's half of its own sum: the Gauss-Newton step as its linear model gives it, one increment a body on the rotation group as in Bruls, Cardona and Arnold's Lie group integrator; turned joint by joint, a chain of 100 hinged links turned 11 rad an iterate and flew apart. The paths that meet at branch bodies are joined by union-find (`group_trees`), and a group with no loop among its moving bodies (joints between two moving bodies one fewer than those bodies) is one Newton solve, the whole tree exactly, as Baraff solves any acyclic joint graph; the step's share (`push_share`) reads each body's gain summed over every joint that holds it. A group with a loop (rings, grids) is not projected: its passes keep their share of the gap as before the projection, as its loose paths' steps fought to a stand their dependent rows cannot pass. Coordinates couplings read their error from the poses, a rigid one is put back on its row after the forward kinematics by turning the coupled link with its subtree about its joint (`project_coords` in `couplings.rs`), and the rigid couplings' impulses come out of the start speeds the midpoint move reads before the locks shed (`shed_couplings`). The locked part of the midpoint move's turn is taken back before the poses move by one exact linear step of each exact path on the rows the substep began with, P d with P = W J^T (J W J^T)^-1 J (`take_back_locked`, KB-PHYS-LOCKTURN1), and what the locks gave for it is solved at the pose reached on the projection's own matrix J W G^T and counted as their impulse and shift (`credit_take_back`): a mass-orthogonal projection onto the constraints' tangent space as Bayo and Ledesma's, its multipliers on the rows of the step's start as SHAKE's and RATTLE's, taken before the free move and given after it as Hairer's symmetric projection perturbs and projects. Own, from derivation and measurement: the summed move, the tree test by counts, the loops left to the passes, the summed gains, and the take-back of the turn alone (a lock's rows turn with its bodies and do not move with their centres) solved again at the pose reached. | physics/kernel/src/joints.rs, physics/kernel/src/tilt.rs, physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs | **Read:** as PK24 and PK58. **Cited for the method, not read here in full:** Gonzalez, "Time integration and discrete Hamiltonian systems", Journal of Nonlinear Science 6, 1996, and "Mechanical systems subject to holonomic constraints: differential-algebraic formulations and conservative integration", Physica D 132, 1999 (the discrete gradient and the Newton matrix it is solved with); Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2nd ed., Springer 2006, chapter 3 (backtracking); Golub and Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 4th ed., 2013, Algorithm 5.4.1 (QR with column pivoting); Duff, Erisman and Reid, Direct Methods for Sparse Matrices, 2nd ed., Oxford 2017, section 7.8 (the threshold test, u = 0.1); Nocedal and Wright 2006, chapter 10 (Gauss-Newton), https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-40065-5; Bruls, Cardona and Arnold, "Lie group generalized-alpha time integration of constrained flexible multibody systems", Mechanism and Machine Theory 48, 2012, https://orbi.uliege.be/handle/2268/119869; Baraff, "Linear-time dynamics using Lagrange multipliers", SIGGRAPH 1996, https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~baraff/papers/sig96.pdf; Tarjan, "Efficiency of a good but not linear set union algorithm", Journal of the ACM 22, 1975, https://doi.org/10.1145/321879.321884. Ryckaert, Ciccotti and Berendsen, "Numerical integration of the cartesian equations of motion of a system with constraints: molecular dynamics of n-alkanes", Journal of Computational Physics 23, 1977, https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(77)90098-5 (SHAKE); Andersen, "RATTLE: a 'velocity' version of the SHAKE algorithm for molecular dynamics calculations", Journal of Computational Physics 52, 1983, https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(83)90014-1; Hairer, "Symmetric projection methods for differential equations on manifolds", BIT Numerical Mathematics 40, 2000, https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022344502818; Bayo and Ledesma, "Augmented Lagrangian and mass-orthogonal projection methods for constrained multibody dynamics", Nonlinear Dynamics 9, 1996, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01833296. Compared and not used: Tournier, Nesme, Gilles and Faure 2015, Stable constrained dynamics, https://hal-lirmm.ccsd.cnrs.fr/hal-01157835v2; Andrews, Teichmann and Kry 2017, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13122; Goldenthal et al. 2007, Efficient simulation of inextensible cloth, https://doi.org/10.1145/1276377.1276438; Betsch and Leyendecker 2006, The discrete null space method II, https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1639. No companion code was opened. No engine source |

Not re-read this batch: the same term `Material.lightMap` already uses (materials features.ts) |

The batch 168 irradiance measurement drives Cycles inside Blender 5.3.0 Beta as a black box (`C:\blender\blender.exe`,
`MARGO_BLENDER` overrides the path). The bake is the diffuse direct and indirect passes with the surface color left
out, as the Blender manual describes those passes (https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/cycles/baking.html
and https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/layers/passes.html). The renderer source was not opened. The box
is the published Cornell data (https://bowers.cornell.edu/computer-graphics/data): corners, the white, green and red
reflectance tables, and the emission knots at 400, 500, 600 and 700 nm. RGB is a band average of that table, not a
CIE match. Faces that are not parallelograms are snapped with `p2 = p1 + p3 - p0` on both sides.

| P-38 | Decal culling: frustum planes as sums and differences of the view-projection rows, bounding sphere against each plane, and a conservative screen-span bound r (\|row0.xyz\| + \|x\| \|row3.xyz\|) / (w - r \|row3.xyz\|) | post/src/decals.ts | Plane extraction after Gribb and Hartmann, "Fast Extraction of Viewing Frustum Planes from the World-View-Projection Matrix", 2001 (written from the method as commonly described; the paper was not re-read for this job); the span bound is Margo-own, from the quotient of the projected coordinates, and is checked against sampled spheres in packages/post/test/decals.test.js |
| P-39 | Stochastic rough SSR: GGX visible-normal sampling, orthonormal basis around the normal, per-pixel per-frame random numbers, reprojected history clamped to the neighbourhood mean plus or minus one standard deviation | post/src/ssr.ts | E. Heitz, "Sampling the GGX Distribution of Visible Normals", JCGT 7(4), 2018; T. Duff et al., "Building an Orthonormal Basis, Revisited", JCGT 6(1), 2017; M. Jarzynski and M. Olano, "Hash Functions for GPU Rendering" (pcg3d), JCGT 9(3), 2020; variance clipping after M. Salvi, "An Excursion in Temporal Supersampling", GDC 2016 (written from the method as published; the papers were not re-read for this job). The blend floor and the meeting of the stochastic and mirror paths are Margo-own |
| P-40 | Multi-bounce screen GI: the light at each ray hit read from the previous frame's GI result through the previous camera, one more bounce per frame | post/src/ssgi.ts | Margo-own: the series L = E + T L of the rendering equation (J. Kajiya, "The Rendering Equation", SIGGRAPH 1986) evaluated one term per frame; reprojection is linear algebra |
| P-41 | Anamorphic streaks: bright pass with a soft knee, horizontal chain of sparse 9-tap passes at strides 3^k, additive composite | post/src/anamorphic.ts | Margo-own: the dilated (a trous) filter chain after Holschneider, Kronland-Martinet, Morlet and Tchamitchian, "A real-time algorithm for signal analysis with the help of the wavelet transform", 1989 (method, from memory of the publication, not re-read); weights, sizes and the knee are Margo-own |
| P-42 | Gaussian and box blur: separable horizontal then vertical pass, Gaussian weights exp(-x^2 / (2 sigma^2)) with sigma = radius / 3 normalised over the taps, box weights 1 / (2 radius + 1), edge taps clamped, a region test per pixel | post/src/blur.ts | Margo-own: separability of the 2D Gaussian and box filters is standard signal processing (the 2D kernel is the product of two 1D kernels); sigma = radius / 3 and the region are Margo-own choices; no source was read for this job |
| P-43 | Lens model: radial distortion r(1 + k r^2) scaled so barrel keeps the corners, dirt lit by an eighth-size thresholded glow blurred by a separable Gaussian, a built-in smudge pattern from an integer hash | post/src/lens.ts | Radial distortion after D. C. Brown, "Decentering Distortion of Lenses", Photogrammetric Engineering 32(3), 1966 (the one-term radial model, from memory of the method; the paper was not re-read); the hash is pcg2d after M. Jarzynski and M. Olano, "Hash Functions for GPU Rendering", JCGT 9(3), 2020 (as for P-39); the corner fit, glow and smudge pattern are Margo-own |

The batch 168 timing drives `@mkkellogg/gaussian-splats-3d` 0.4.7 as a black box from its README (https://github.com/mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D): `Viewer` with `selfDrivenMode: false`, then `update` and `render`. The library source was not opened. The photograph and the camera row are the published truck test image `000001` and `cameras.json` from the 3D Gaussian Splatting dataset (Kerbl et al. 2023). The pose is COLMAP's camera frame (https://colmap.github.io/format.html): x right, y down, z forward. Both interpretations of the stored rotation were scored. The shared-memory GPU sort drew nothing in this page, so the timed rival uses the README's CPU sort (`gpuAcceleratedSort` and `sharedMemoryForWorkers` false).

v1.0.1 compared; the USD Glossary at openusd.org (Index, Inherits, Specializes, LIVERPS Strength Ordering). **Observed only, the specification does not settle them:** rules marked in stage.ts, taken from running OpenUSD 26.08 on our own stages and reading its public `GetPrimStack`, `GetPropertyStack` and prim index dump output: specializes arcs order by the depth of the stage prim they first reach (until KB1942c part 6 also: a site an authored arc reaches gives no opinions through an implied arc, and a repeated class site counts once through the later arc); and (KB1942, 2026-11-11, OpenUSD 26.11 from the usd-core wheel run where it lives, public `Usd.Stage` and `Sdf` calls only) within one specializes family the implied copies rank first unless the authored arc sits under a variant or reference whose prim is shallower than the stage prim holding the outermost reference; and (KB1942b, same setup) a class arc implied from an ancestor's inherit keeps that ancestor's own pair, mapped by the arcs above where they can, so a path maps by the longest matching pair and must map back by the same pair or it drops; (KB1942c, same setup, 10 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/fixtures/internal-chain-targets.json`) through a chain of arcs a target maps once by the composed map function, each internal arc carrying the root identity its own pairs shadow: an inner pair goes on through the outer function and an outer pair comes back through the inner one. The specification's Namespace Mappings section describes one arc's mapping, not a chain's; (KB1942c part 2, same setup, 6 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/specializes-specifier.test.js`, read with `Usd.Prim.GetSpecifier()` and the public prim index dump `Usd.Prim.GetPrimIndex().DumpToString()`) a class reached through a specializes arc keeps the prim a class before a weaker `def`, where a class reached by an inherit gives way to it. (KB1942c part 3, same setup, 12 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/implied-class-stops.test.js`, read with `Usd.Prim.GetChildren()` and the public prim index dump) an implied class arc stops at a node of its own stack that already holds its site, and a specializes arc whose site an inherit of the same stack already reaches implies nothing upstream unless its node has another class arc of its own. The specification's Inherits section says an implied arc goes to every upstream layer stack, not where it stops. (KB1942c part 4, same setup, 4 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/carried-class-site.test.js`) a class site that a class arc carried down from the parent prim already holds keeps that arc's place, and an arc placed for the prim on the same site of the same stack gives no opinions; the Strength Ordering section ranks arcs, not two arcs to one site. (KB1942c part 5) a variant set ranks by the depth of the prim that holds it in its own stack, so a set on a class site beats one carried down from its parent: that is the Strength Ordering rule for arcs authored deeper in namespace, checked on 3 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/variant-set-depth.test.js`. (KB1942c part 6, 2026-11-15, OpenUSD 26.11 from the usd-core wheel, public `Usd.Stage`, `Usd.Attribute.Get()`, `Usd.Prim.GetPrimStack()` and `Usd.Prim.GetPrimIndex()` node fields only; 29 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/fixtures/prim-index-queue.json`) a prim index is one list of tasks: references, payloads, inherits and specializes, a higher kind always first and nodes in the order they were queued, then implied class arcs strongest node first, then one variant set at a time; an arc to a root prim is a bare node whose arcs the index follows, one to a deeper prim that prim's index composed alone; the first live node made for a site holds it (a later inherit makes no node, a later specializes an inert placeholder); a specializes arc below the index root leaves an inert placeholder that implies its arc upward and its node goes under the root, ranking from the placeholder. (KB1942c part 7, 2026-11-15, same setup, 15 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/fixtures/ancestral-variants.json`) a specializes node carried down from an ancestor inside a grafted index goes under the root as its site composed alone, so only the class's own sites select its ancestral variants; an implied class arc that stands for an arc carried down from prim A sets its ancestral variants with the selections of A in context, then its own (part 8, 27 stages in all): below the index root, the site that authored the arc into the stack it joins, at the path A maps to there, and the nodes of other stacks in the index of the stage prim A maps to; at the index root, A's own index in that stack when the stack holds the layer that authored the arc, but for the node that stands for the same arc. (Part 9, 7 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/fixtures/specializes-family-grafts.json`) whether a specializes family's implied arcs rank before or after its authored arc (part 10, 9 stages) is decided per implied arc, by the outermost reference or payload around the authored arc up to the node the implied arc hangs from, that node itself counting from the prim that authored it; (part 11, 6 stages in `held-specializes-grafts.json`) a specializes arc authored on a graft's root whose site the index already holds leaves an inert placeholder that implies its arc upward even where an inherit of its stack reaches the site; the Strength Ordering section ranks specializes after all else, not the members of one family against each other; (part 12, 3 stages in `held-class-implied.json`) a grafted index that leaves out a class node because the index it joins holds its site leaves out the class arcs implied from that node too; (part 13, 5 stages in `carried-placeholder-reimplied.json`) a reference carried down to a child prim that gets a class arc of its own there implies the specializes placeholders carried down with it again, and on the index root such an arc takes its site from an implied arc carried down for another arc; (part 14, 4 stages in `ancestral-chain.json`) an implied inherit standing for another implied arc, the chain ending in an arc carried down from an ancestor, reads its class's ancestral selections at the class's parent in the other stacks of the chain; (part 15, 4 stages in `specializes-variant-hop.json`) a specializes arc authored in a variant first implies a placeholder on the node that holds the variant, in the same stack, and within each side of the authored arc the arcs implied further up rank against that placeholder before the stacks' order; (part 16, 3 stages in `reference-namespace-depth.json`) a reference or payload ranks by the depth of its prim in the stack that authors it, the PcpNodeRef class text's namespace depth of the node that introduced it, not by the depth of the stage prim; class arcs keep the stage prim's depth (the same change for them breaks other stress stages); (part 17, 2 stages in `grafted-specializes-late.json`) a specializes arc carried in by a graft (a reference to a prim below a root prim, composed alone) moves under the index root only after the specializes arcs of the index's own nodes, so where both reach one site, an arc of a weaker branch made in this index holds it and implies the family; the Specializes section and the Pcp overview say specializes are weakest and propagate to the root, not which of two arcs to one site goes first; (part 18, 2 stages in `specializes-variant-anchor.json`) an implied specializes arc that hangs from a variant held by a node of the same stack implies a placeholder on that node (OpenUSD's prim index shows it), and the arcs implied above it rank against it as against the authored arc, after the ranking against the authored arc's own placeholder; (part 19, 2 stages in `specializes-root-rank.json`) then each implied arc ranks before the arc implied into the root stack when the node it hangs from has a smaller namespace depth (PcpNodeRef's namespace depth, as OpenUSD's prim index reports it) than the node the root stack's arc stands for, above that node's same-stack variants, and after it otherwise; (part 20, 2 stages in `held-inherit-specializes.json`) an inherit a grafted index leaves out, because the index it joins already holds its site, no longer holds that site for its own prim's specializes arc to it, so that arc leaves an inert placeholder (the prim index dump shows it inert and culled) which implies a specializes arc upward, placed weakest as the Glossary's LIVERPS Strength Ordering entry places specializes, and the implied inherit above then finds the site held; (part 21, 2 stages in `specializes-hang-depth.json`) after those rankings the implied arcs of a family order by the namespace depth of the node each hangs from (PcpNodeRef's namespace depth, as the prim index dump reports it), smaller first, and only on a tie by the strength of the stacks that hold them; (part 22, 2 stages in `implied-origin-order.json`) two implied class arcs on one node, of one kind and namespace depth, rank as the arcs they were implied from do (the prim index dump's origin nodes), an arc implied from deeper in the same stack ranking where the placeholder it passes on the way up would sit; (part 24, 6 stages in `carried-implied-again.json`) at a child prim, the implied inherits carried down from the parent prim below the index root are implied again, strongest carried authored arc first: a carried class arc that implies one of their sites first takes it, and the carried inherit goes with the arcs implied from it; an arc placed for the child prim takes no site from them, and a carried specializes placeholder that made no family at the parent prim takes only the sites of carried inherits made before it (none when its site has no specs at the child or its node authors a specializes arc there); (part 23, 2 stages in `implied-reference-depth.json`) below the index root, sibling class arcs rank by the namespace depth the prim index dump reports for them: an arc authored at its node counts from that node's prim in its own stack, and one implied from an arc under a reference or payload of the same prim counts from that reference's depth; the Inherits section says where an implied arc goes, not when it is withdrawn. The Variants section says selections are evaluated once the arcs that can author them are in, not which index an implied arc's ancestral sets read. Written basis for the parts the documents do say: the Composition chapter's Overview and Outline (an index is built by evaluating arcs), Inherits, Specializes, Variants (selections are evaluated once the arcs that can author them are in), Strength Ordering and Namespace Mappings sections of the AOUSD USD Core Specification v1.1.0 (https://github.com/aousd/specifications-public); Pixar, USD Terms and Concepts, OpenUSD 26.11 (Index, Inherits, Specializes, LIVERPS Strength Ordering, https://openusd.org/release/glossary.html); the Pcp overview text (https://openusd.org/release/api/pcp_page_front.html) and the PcpNodeRef class text (https://openusd.org/release/api/class_pcp_node_ref.html), prose read, no code. One web search for a paper on building a prim index (2026-11-15) found none, only overviews of the strength order; the Rust `openusd` crate a search turns up is code and was not opened. The specification's Specifiers section (AOUSD USD Core Specification v1.1.0, Composition chapter) and the USD Glossary entries Def, Class and Over (openusd.org) say a `def` or `class` beats an `over`, not how a class and a `def` from two class arcs combine. **Observed (KB1942c part 31, 2026-11-25, usd-core 26.11 run as a black box on our own stages, 4 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/fixtures/implied-specializes-claims.json`, read with `Usd.Prim.GetPrimIndex().DumpToString()` and marked prim stacks):** an implied specializes chain leaves a placeholder where an implied inherit carried down from the parent prim waits on the site under another node, keeps going upward, and takes the site of an implied inherit carried onto the index root when its arc is the stronger; the carried inherit under another node keeps its place; an inherit implied at the prim takes no root site from a carried one, and nor does the first hop of a carried placeholder with no specs. (KB1942c part 32, 2026-11-26, usd-core 26.11 run as a black box on our own stages, 5 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/fixtures/implied-path-selection.json`, reduced from stage 139 of seed 7 and stage 9 of seed 1942 with a black-box reducer and varied by hand) an implied class arc that stands for another implied arc takes its class parent's selection from a stronger class arc off the chain that already went into a variant at the path read, in its place in strength order among the authored selections; a weaker class arc gives none, and an implied arc that stands for an authored arc takes none this way. One hypothesis tried on the way, that a selection made earlier in the same stack is reused first, was rejected by those runs. (KB1942c parts 33 to 36, 2026-11-26, usd-core 26.11 run as a black box on our own stages, stages reduced from 38, 31 and 18 of seed 7 and 8 and 33 of seed 1942 with a black-box reducer and varied by hand, read with marked prim stacks and `Usd.Prim.GetPrimIndex().DumpToString()`; 17 stages in `packages/usdz/tests/fixtures/authoring-layer-selection.json`, `grafted-implied-variants.json`, `variant-specializes-carried.json` and `grafted-variant-arcs-late.json`) an implied class arc on the index root reads the authoring prim's index in its stack when that stack holds the layer that authored the arc, a sublayer of the arc's stack too (part 33; the hypothesis that it reads the class's own selection in the arc's stack was rejected by those runs); an implied specializes arc carried down inside a grafted index keeps only the ancestral variants its site selects composed alone (part 34); an implied specializes arc that a variant of the prim implies to a site held by an implied specializes arc carried down onto the index root leaves an inert placeholder and an inert node under the root, and the carried arc goes (part 35; not so for an arc on the prim itself, one to another site, or an inherit); in a site composed alone for an arc the variants carried down from its ancestors are chosen again, after every other task, so a specializes arc of the site holds a class site before an inherit in such a variant (part 36). The Variants and Specializes sections of the specification and the Glossary's LIVERPS Strength Ordering entry give the order of arcs, not these. Research for these parts (2026-11-26): two web searches found no paper on prim index construction; the NVIDIA Learn OpenUSD pages on LIVERPS (https://docs.nvidia.com/learn-openusd/latest/creating-composition-arcs/strength-ordering/what-is-liverps.html) restate the order only; N. Porcino, Elements of Compositional Stability in USD (2026-02-28, https://nickporcino.com/papers/encapsulation/) was found after these rules were built and tested on the black box; its appendix walks through OpenUSD's own source, so only a short summary of it was read and nothing was taken from it; the Rust `openusd` crate the searches turn up is code and was not opened. **History, not hidden:** OpenUSD's source was never opened. Job 1 of batch 44 was debugged using remembered OpenUSD internals as hypotheses (inert implied nodes, origin-based arc order), then confirmed by black-box runs. Memory is not a source, so both were taken out on 2026-11-07 and the code rebuilt from the documents above. The sample implementations in aousd/core-spec-supplemental-public are code and were not read. A web search for the specification returned snippets of a third-party USD project's roadmap; they were not opened or used. |

## Extruded 3D text: `@margoengine/text/extrude`

Written and repaired clean room from the specifications and papers below. No other engine or font-library source
was read, adapted or copied. Only the two standard font assets and their licence were downloaded (see
[third-party notices](../THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md)). The outside CAD repository's package/API boundaries were inspected;
its CAD APIs do not own this optional font decoder or text mesher, and no kernel code/dependency is added here.

| Area | Source and implementation |
| --- | --- |
| Bounded SFNT, cmap, TrueType outlines and composite transforms | [Microsoft OpenType](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/), especially [cmap](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/cmap) and [glyf](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/glyf). Component attachment uses raw point indices before implied points and curve flattening. Scaled/unscaled offsets follow the component flags; the default unscaled offset matches the Microsoft/Apple recommended default. |
| CFF INDEX/DICT/charset and Type 2 | Adobe [Technical Note 5176](https://adobe-type-tools.github.io/font-tech-notes/pdfs/5176.CFF.pdf) and [Technical Note 5177](https://adobe-type-tools.github.io/font-tech-notes/pdfs/5177.Type2.pdf). The interpreter shares its stack, width state, hints and transient storage across calls; masks consume bytes, all curve/flex families are explicit, and recursion/operand bounds are enforced. Appendix B/C numerical StandardEncoding/charset data comes from 5176. Deprecated endchar composites resolve by SID; nested composites are forbidden by 5177 Appendix C. FontMatrix is applied once after decoding raw coordinates. |
| Polygon filling and triangulation | Nonzero winding is computed on split contour edges; only edges separating zero/nonzero faces survive, oriented with fill on the left. Our arrangement splitting, relative coordinate welding and stitching are derived here from line intersection and winding-number definitions. [Eberly, Triangulation by Ear Clipping](https://www.geometrictools.com/Documentation/TriangulationByEarClipping.pdf), sections 2-5: duplicate bridge endpoints, mutually visible hole connections and ear removal. Visibility here is tested against every edge and the local interior cone, rather than a nearest-vertex guess. Incomplete clipping throws, and cap area is verified. |
| Bevel extrusion | Parallel-edge offset intersections give miter displacements; sine/cosine profiles give rounded rims, one segment a chamfer. Caps consume the exact terminal wall rings; wall normals come from their cross products and are normalized. Offset-ring crossings, reversed edges and collapses are rejected. |
| Independent outline evidence | Our `generate-outline-reference.py` uses the public Windows [GetGlyphOutlineW](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-getglyphoutlinew), [TTPOLYGONHEADER](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/ns-wingdi-ttpolygonheader) and [TTPOLYCURVE](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/ns-wingdi-ttpolycurve) contracts, checks the selected face's head bytes, and freezes unhinted absolute cubic controls. Our separate de Casteljau traversal compares both directions with the analytic chord-error bound max second derivative / (8 n squared), plus 16.16 control quantization. No decoder logic is shared with production. |

## GPU pass timing: `@margoengine/stats` (`GPUProfiler`)

Written from the specification and API documentation below; no other profiler's code was read.

| Area | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Which pass timestamps are time going backwards | W3C WebGPU, section 20.4 "Timestamp Query" (Candidate Recommendation Draft, read 2026-11-08): "Timestamp values are implementation-defined. Applications must handle arbitrary timestamp results, and should not be written in such a way that unexpected timestamps cause an application failure." Its note: the device "may reset the timestamp counter occasionally", giving "negative deltas", and "these data points can safely be discarded". Nothing in the section orders one pass's timestamps against another's, so a pass that starts before the pass recorded ahead of it is accepted when the two overlap; an end before its own start, or a pass that ends before the previous pass starts, is discarded as a reset |
| Why passes overlap on Apple GPUs | Apple Metal documentation, "Sampling GPU data into counter sample buffers" (read 2026-11-08): Apple silicon samples "at the stage boundary"; the counters are sampled "when the GPU starts or finishes a stage", and only a sample with a barrier "waits for the GPU to complete all the previous commands in the buffer before sampling". How Chrome maps WebGPU timestamps onto these samples was not read (no browser source) |

Dubinski, "A parallel tree code", New Astronomy 1, 133-147, 1996 (arXiv astro-ph/9603097), section 2.2 read in full: Barnes's 1994 opening test d > l / theta + delta, delta the offset of the centre of mass from the cell's geometric centre, and Salmon and Warren's 1994 finding (J. WGS 84 constants a = 6378137 m and 1/f = 298.257223563 from NIMA TR8350.2, 3rd edition. Tile numbering (2^z by 2^z squares of the Web Mercator world, x from 180 W, y from the north) derived here from the Mercator formulas; no tile code read. |

## Voxel files: `@margoengine/voxel-edit/formats`

VF1 to VF6: file layouts written from each format's public description; no reader or writer of another project was read.

VF7 to VF12 (`.gox` and `.vxm`, 2026-11-08) have no public specification, so they were written in a two-person clean
room that Scott approved on 2026-11-08. A spec writer read Goxel (GPL-3.0) `src/formats/gox.c` and the files it calls at
commit 33be5c8, vengi (MIT) `GoxFormat` and `VXMFormat` at commit 3471178, and one blog post that restates Goxel's header
comment, decoded eight vengi test files (CC BY-SA 3.0), and wrote a prose specification with byte tables and no code.
The implementer read only that specification: no Goxel, vengi or VoxEdit code, and no web search for code. The sample
files were used in a local check only and are not in this repository.

## Smooth voxel meshes: `@margoengine/voxel-edit/smooth`

Written from the paper below; no Surface Nets code of another project was read.

| id | formula | file | source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SN1 | one point per net cell the surface crosses, at the mean of its edge crossings; one quad per filled-to-air sample pair; relaxation toward neighbours kept inside the cell | voxel-edit/src/smooth.ts | Sarah Gibson, "Constrained Elastic Surface Nets", MERL TR-99-24 / MICCAI 1998 |
| SN2 | normals from the density difference across a net cell; a separable box blur by running sums | voxel-edit/src/smooth.ts | Margo-own, central differences and the standard running sum box filter |

## Mesh to voxels: `@margoengine/voxel-edit/voxelize`

Written from the papers below; no voxelizer of another project was read.

| id | formula | file | source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VZ1 | triangle against box by separating axes: three box normals, the triangle normal, nine edge crosses | voxel-edit/src/voxelize.ts | Tomas Akenine-Moller, "Fast 3D Triangle-Box Overlap Testing", Journal of Graphics Tools, 2001 |
| VZ2 | solid by crossing parity along x rows through cell centres, the hit point from barycentric coordinates | voxel-edit/src/voxelize.ts | Moller and Trumbore, "Fast, Minimum Storage Ray/Triangle Intersection", Journal of Graphics Tools, 1997 |
| VZ3 | shared edges on a ray: each edge read in one fixed vertex order and owning its low end, so a closed mesh crosses evenly | voxel-edit/src/voxelize.ts | Margo-own, the half-open crossing rule for point in polygon |
| VZ4 | palette: cut the box of widest channel range at its weighted median, then box means | voxel-edit/src/voxelize.ts | Paul Heckbert, "Color Image Quantization for Frame Buffer Display", SIGGRAPH 1982 |
