### Mixed triangle and voxel tracing (batch 99 job 7)

Research began across all packages, including the existing CPU triangle-query APIs. They do not supply mixed GPU light transport. No external implementation was read or copied. The optional mesh entry owns a feature-local Rust spatial-median BVH, SIMD coordinate validation and WGSL intersections; core and stage import none of it.

- Woop, Benthin and Wald, [Watertight Ray/Triangle Intersection](https://jcgt.org/published/0002/01/05/paper.pdf), JCGT 2013: ray-space translation, shear and projected edge predicates. Margo retains Float32 transformed coordinates; it does not claim the paper's double-precision coordinate fallback.
- Shewchuk, [Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~jrs/papers/robustr.pdf), 1997: uncertainty filters and exact recomputation of uncertain predicate signs. Margo's own fallback forms two 24-by-24-bit products with 16-bit integer limbs, aligns and subtracts them before one final floating-point rounding. This is not a port of the paper's expansion-arithmetic software.
- Karras, [Maximizing Parallelism in the Construction of BVHs, Octrees, and k-d Trees](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/parallelforall/wp-content/uploads/2012/11/karras2012hpg_paper.pdf), 2012: hierarchy construction trade-offs informed the survey. This static builder uses balanced spatial medians, not a Morton/radix construction or a parallel-build claim.
- Kajiya, [The Rendering Equation](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs667/2004sp/readings/kajiya86.pdf), 1986: surfaces in one transport integral. Both geometry types reuse Margo's existing BSDFs, path sampling, light visibility and volume integration.

Generated triangles, scalar packing references and arithmetic/GPU fixtures are authored here. No outside model or decoder was added. Shared edges are tested on native WebGPU and WebGL2 compatibility; the full Float32 geometry domain is not an exact-arithmetic claim.

Review 99 glass repair research compares Eric Veach and Leonidas J. Guibas,
[Optimally Combining Sampling Techniques for Monte Carlo Rendering](https://www.graphics.stanford.edu/papers/combine/),
1995 (sampling support and weights summing to one), Bruce Walter, Stephen R. Marschner,
Hongsong Li and Kenneth E. Torrance,
[Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~srm/publications/EGSR07-btdf.pdf),
2007 (Snell transport and refractive Jacobians), and Wenzel Jakob and Steve Marschner,
[Manifold Exploration: A Markov Chain Monte Carlo Technique for Rendering Scenes with Difficult Specular Transport](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/manifolds-sg12/manifolds-sg12.pdf),
2012 (general specular chains require a geometry-aware proposal). Margo keeps its existing
box-specific light sampler and assigns full path weight to interior triangle-glass chains
it cannot construct. A triangle marker never enters voxel instance lookup. The furnace oracle
is analytic equilibrium, not another tracer. No companion code or outside repository was read.

The separate Review 99 root-glass repair uses Veach and Guibas (1995) above to
keep the candidate sum and the path-side MIS partition consistent when inverse
Snell solutions coincide. Walter et al. (2007) explains the index-matched limit:
different interface normals can yield the same transmitted direction. Instead
of adding an IOR-specific exception, Margo uses its existing direction-equality
predicate and the already computed box-exit face as one canonical representative
of the unchanged direction. The root GPU suite tests the analytic furnace at IOR
1, 1.000001, 1.0001 and 1.5. No sampler PDF, tolerance or furnace bound changes.

## Batch 65 job 6: Road network graph

A broad search of road linkage, shortest-path papers and traffic travel-time models preceded implementation. No foreign source was read or used. Existing Margo APIs hold the heavy algorithms; this entry orchestrates them, without a new CPU-heavy solver or measured Wasm gain.

### Batch 160 transformed native volume absorption

- Khronos Group, KHR_materials_volume specification (ratified 2021), Properties, Refraction and Attenuation: https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_volume/README.md . Mesh thickness and attenuation distance use different coordinate spaces; the medium is homogeneous. Only normative prose/formulas read, no Sample Viewer source.
- Bruce Walter, Stephen R. Marschner, Hongsong Li, Kenneth E. Torrance, Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces (EGSR 2007), section 4.2: https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~srm/publications/EGSR07-btdf.pdf . Snell refraction controls the direction within a smooth local interface; rough-surface lobe transport remains distinct from the slab approximation.
- Matt Pharr, Wenzel Jakob, Greg Humphreys, Physically Based Rendering, fourth edition (2023), section 11.2 Transmittance: https://www.pbr-book.org/4ed/Volume_Scattering/Transmittance . Homogeneous beam transmittance is Beer attenuation integrated over actual path length; concatenated segments multiply.

Synthesis: the staged native slab repair refracts a world-space unit ray at the surface, takes its inverse linear transform into mesh space, and divides mesh thickness by its projected rate along the local slab normal. This gives a world-length ratio for the existing Beer tint. It corrects transformed thickness without claiming that a slab reproduces Cycles multiple scattering, rough refraction or arbitrary boundary intersections. Analytic scale/shear/mirror/angle regressions and the unchanged complete-model pixel budgets must pass. No code from any source was read or copied. The complete-model AMD proofs below retain the frozen reference budgets.


### Batch 160 watchdog research (2026-11-09)

Read standards and research prose only; no companion code.

- Microsoft, WDDM support for timeout detection and recovery (current documentation, read 2026-11-09), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/display/timeout-detection-and-recovery . A TDR means GPU task completion or preemption failed within the scheduler deadline; event 0x141 alone does not distinguish expensive valid work from an invalid access or driver fault.
- Microsoft, DXGI_COMPUTE_PREEMPTION_GRANULARITY (2022), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/dxgi1_2/ne-dxgi1_2-dxgi_compute_preemption_granularity . - Samuli Laine, Tero Karras, Timo Aila, Megakernels Considered Harmful: Wavefront Path Tracing on GPUs (HPG 2013), https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/pubs/2013-07_Megakernels-Considered-Harmful/laine2013hpg_paper.pdf . Separating divergent shading stages reduces register pressure and divergence, but is a larger restructuring than a capture submission bug repair and needs independent output proof. Do not treat this paper as evidence that a particular row bound fixes TDR.
- Matt Pharr, Wenzel Jakob, Greg Humphreys, Physically Based Rendering, fourth edition (2023), section 15.1 prose, https://www.pbr-book.org/4ed/Wavefront_Rendering_on_GPUs/Mapping_Path_Tracing_to_the_GPU . Synthesis for the pending watchdog job: preserve all pixels, samples and partial-sum order. The earlier <=65536-path row-band draft still lost AMD and is unvalidated. Must investigate command-buffer/packet boundaries and shader termination/access invariants; do not claim that awaiting onSubmittedWorkDone ensures a preemptible OS packet. Scott defers speed measurements. No new GPU diagnostic was run by this continuation.

### Review 99 spectral correction (2026-11-09)

Research compared Alexander Wilkie, Sehera Nawaz, Marc Droske, Andrea Weidlich and Johannes Hanika,
[Hero Wavelength Spectral Sampling](https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.12419), 2014, section 3 (path generation
and combined wavelength density), with Ayoung Kim and Atanas Gotchev,
[Spectral Rendering: From Input to Rendering Process](https://doi.org/10.2352/EI.2024.36.10.IPAS-251),
2024 (sampling, reconstruction and wavelength-dependent transport), and Eric Veach,
[Robust Monte Carlo Methods for Light Transport Simulation](https://aperture.stanford.edu/papers/veach_thesis/),
1997 (density-corrected transport and refractive radiance). Only descriptions, papers and existing
Margo sources were read; no companion implementation or external engine source was used.

Synthesis: this RGB-coefficient renderer can integrate wavelength-independent path contributions
exactly without a random wavelength estimator. Keep a single spatial path and its RGB contributions
until dispersion first makes path generation wavelength-dependent. Then use the existing positive
mixture density (25% uniform plus 75% truncated logistic) and the analytic observer weight divided
by that density. A chromatic lens requires this selection at the sensor; glass must reuse it.
This is a deferred single-hero estimator, not Wilkie's full multi-wavelength spectral MIS, and claims
no packet convergence advantage. It removes three identical nondispersive replays deterministically;
there is no timing experiment. Existing eta-squared factors and alpha's geometric integral are kept.

  (2022 revision), https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/extensions/EXT_color_buffer_half_float/ .
  WebGL2 half-float colour attachments include R16F, RG16F and RGBA16F, not RGB16F.
- Mark Callow and the Khronos WebGL Working Group, EXT_color_buffer_float (2017),
  https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/extensions/EXT_color_buffer_float/ .
  The full extension adds 32-bit float and packed HDR targets; its FLOAT readback
  rule cannot be used for a physical UNORM target.
- Jon Leech and Benj Lipchak (editors), OpenGL ES 3.0.6 (2019),
  https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.0/es_spec_3.0.pdf , sections 2.1.2
  through 2.1.6, 3.8, 4.1.7 and 4.3.2: storage encodings, upload types, blending
  and readback conversions. Fixed-point conversion permits adjacent integers;
  the LDR blend oracle therefore uses independent raw GL on the same hardware.
- Kelsey Gilbert (editor), WebGL 2.0 (2026 editor draft),
  https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/specs/latest/2.0/ ; and the W3C GPU for the Web
  Working Group, WebGPU (2026), https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/ , texture formats
  and copies. Logical copy layouts remain separate from physical GL storage.
- Erik Reinhard, Michael Stark, Peter Shirley and James Ferwerda, Photographic Tone
  Reproduction for Digital Images (2002), abstract/introduction,
  https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~lizhang/courses/cs766-2007f/projects/hdr/Reinhard2002PTR.pdf .
  Tone reproduction is an image operation, not a replacement for arbitrary data
  texture values. The tier substitution does not add an implicit tone mapper.
- Greg Ward, High Dynamic Range Imaging (2001), abstract,
  https://library.imaging.org/cic/articles/9/1/art00003 ; Peter Kornerup,
  Jean-Michel Muller and Adrien Panhaleux, Floating-Point Arithmetic on
  Round-to-Nearest Representations (2012), abstract,
  https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.3914 . Compared range preservation and explicit rounding;
  no alternate number representation or paper algorithm was implemented.

Synthesis: change render/storage targets in one device policy, preserve sample-only
float data, convert uploads using the requested byte layout, and carry float readback
bits through core GL integer targets rather than depending on renderable RGBA32F.
Only owned WGSL/GLSL emitter outputs receive LDR store quantization; blend inputs
are left unrounded. A raw GL control of the 0.5 additive blend returns byte 127 on
this machine, exactly matching the layer; the initial analytic upper-neighbour
assumption (128) was invalid. No legacy assertion, tolerance or workload changed.
The current device checks use original analytic fixtures, not a new asset demo.
No rival implementation, paper companion code or external repository file was read.
No speed measurement or Wasm gain is claimed. Package-wide and physical-browser
parity remain outstanding; these device checks do not establish full job completion.

Creation cancellation follow-up (2026-11-09): compared the WHATWG contributors,
DOM Standard (2026 living standard), https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#aborting-ongoing-activities,
with the W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, WebGPU (2026),
https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/#dom-gpu-requestadapter. DOM requires an abortable
promise API to reject with the caller's abort reason. Native requestAdapter has
no cancellation parameter, so the caller's wait is cancelled without changing
that native operation. Compared the existing range/precision approach against
Paul E. Debevec and Jitendra Malik, Recovering High Dynamic Range Radiance Maps
from Photographs (SIGGRAPH 1997), https://www.pauldebevec.com/Research/HDR/debevec-siggraph97.pdf:
scene radiance is not interchangeable with a clamped display value. No implicit
tone mapping is added. The cancellation helper retains no global operation owner;
installation checks the current owner again after awaiting the native probe.
Controlled promises test late native completion, two simultaneous installers,
per-caller cancellation and listener release without wall-clock assertions. No
companion code, rival implementation or external repository file was read.

Lower-tier post precision follow-up (2026-11-09): compared Louis Bavoil, Miguel
Sainz and Rouslan Dimitrov, Image-Space Horizon-Based Ambient Occlusion (2008),
https://rdimitrov.twistedsanity.net/HBAO_SIGGRAPH08.pdf (author-hosted paper),
and Louis Bavoil and Miguel Sainz, Image-Space Horizon-Based Ambient Occlusion
(SIGGRAPH 2008 presentation),
https://developer.download.nvidia.com/presentations/2008/SIGGRAPH/HBAO_SIG08b.pdf,
with Erik Reinhard, Michael Stark, Peter Shirley and James Ferwerda,
Photographic Tone Reproduction for Digital Images (2002),
https://www-old.cs.utah.edu/docs/techreports/2002/pdf/UUCS-02-001.pdf.
Screen-space occlusion depends on geometric depth and orientation; HDR display
mapping depends on radiance before mapping. UNORM substitution cannot preserve
signed geometry buffers or radiance above one. The device still offers LDR
targets, but the owning PostStack, Bloom and SSAO initialization paths refuse
them where their measured outputs exceed the existing parity rule. The shared
requirement helper carries no renderer dependency. No paper algorithm changed,
no rival source or companion code was read, and no tolerance was relaxed.

### Batch 56 compatibility capture investigation

Research compared Jon Leech and Benj Lipchak (editors), OpenGL ES 3.0.6
(Khronos, 2019), sections 2.1.2 (binary16), 4.1.9 (dithering), 4.3.2
(multisample resolve) and appendix A.3 (invariance),
https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.0/es_spec_3.0.pdf ; Robert J.
Simpson (editor), The OpenGL ES Shading Language 3.00, revision 6 (2016),

https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.0/GLSL_ES_Specification_3.00.pdf ;
and the Khronos WebGL Working Group, WebGL 2.0 Specification (current revision

The scientific comparison is Sanjif Shanmugavelu, Mathieu Taillefumier,
Christopher Culver, Oscar Hernandez, Mark Coletti and Ada Sedova,
Impacts of floating-point non-associativity on reproducibility for HPC and deep
learning applications (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05148 . Its reduction
results motivate examining arithmetic order; they do not attribute this raster
failure to a parallel reduction or permit changing an exact assertion.

Our diagnostic inference: 2^-12 is also one binary16 ULP in the interval
[0.25, 0.5); the maximum difference alone cannot identify the format or cause.
The compatibility capture uses RGBA16F, reads FLOAT and encodes binary16 on
the CPU. The standards distinguish that conversion from implementation-defined
multisample resolution and varying interpolation. The investigated glass uses
zero roughness, so its capture does not run the optional reflection blur chain.
Diagnostics retain the original assertion while recording raw component values,
GL draws, resolve operations and readbacks. No mismatching component has yet
been reproduced. No foreign implementation or companion code was read or used.

Follow-up research compared Frederik Dermot Pustelnik, Xhani Marvin Sass and
Jean-Pierre Seifert, Whispering Pixels: Exploiting Uninitialized Register Accesses
in Modern GPUs (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08881 , with John Jacobson,
Martin Burtscher and Ganesh Gopalakrishnan, HiRace: Accurate and Fast Source-Level
Race Checking of GPU Programs (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04701 . The former
distinguishes register initialization from application synchronization; the
latter motivates observing access histories rather than declaring a race from
intermittency alone. Neither establishes the cause of Margo's mismatch.
The WebGL 2 specification's getBufferSubData contract requires sequential
accesses to remain consistent and the operation to finish earlier writes.
Our clean-room diagnostic therefore compares two readbacks of the same image,
raw FLOAT components before binary16 encoding, and buffer-upload bytes.
The reproduced 24-component difference precedes encoding, while repeated
reads and upload bytes agree. This evidence narrows the investigation to
rendering/resolve state; the original exact-zero assertion remains intact.
No companion implementation or other repository's source was read.

### Batch 56 review repairs: HDR direction, view state and temporal cameras

The optional staging/ground entry uses the real first-band basis published by
[Peter-Pike Sloan, Stupid Spherical Harmonics Tricks (GDC 2008)](https://www.ppsloan.org/publications/StupidSH36.pdf),
with Margo's established coefficient order Y, Z, X. Sloan's own
[2012 explanation of dominant direction from RGB SH](https://sourceforge.net/p/gdalgorithms/mailman/message/28778859/)
confirms luminance weighting followed by extraction of the linear coefficient vector;
our positive real basis determines its signs and component order. Taking RGB luminance of that
band gives a vector proportional to the radiance first moment. Its normalized
vector is our dominant-light approximation; this is not a claim that a moment
recovers every light or the brightest texel. The inverse of the environment's
lookup rotation rotates that vector into world space. No image processing loop
is added: only three RGB dot products and constant-size matrix arithmetic.

Directional ray/plane projection is derived from
[Jim Blinn, Me and My (Fake) Shadow (IEEE CG&A, January 1988)](https://www.jimblinn.com/publications/):
for receiver point C, unit normal N, light direction L and caster P,
Q = P - L * dot(N, P-C) / dot(N,L). Dot Q-C with the receiver tangents and
scale to clip coordinates. Retaining caster height as depth clips geometry to
the configured slab. Existing Margo caster/blur/receiver code is reused. The
SH rule and the projection were written from the mathematical descriptions;
no other renderer's implementation was inspected or copied.

W3C WebGPU viewport/scissor rules govern each scene-target pass. Local caster,
blur, history, cube-face and LUT passes explicitly declare their local view
state; the verify unit suite audits every environment/staging render-pass start.
TAA's temporary camera wrapper carries its source under a shared symbol so
separately bundled optional entries agree on identity. Staging supplies the
unjittered projection only during its own integrator interval, then restores
raster jitter before temporal resolve. These changes do not modify core.

https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0212003; Daan Leijen, *Structured Asynchrony with Algebraic

and Ecma International, *ECMAScript 2026 Language Specification* (2026),
https://262.ecma-international.org/17.0/. Confinement motivates retaining and

temporary active scene is not a resource owner, and explicit disposal motivates
terminal, idempotent cleanup. These are design inferences for the engine's
synchronous protocol, not formal proofs. No companion code or other repository
implementation was read.

Animator removed by active name; its factories registered through the active
scene and direct updates checked that temporary namespace. The optional package
now resolves sceneOf(this), attaches factories to the registered Animation's
scene (model root scene when Animation has no registration), and checks playback
dependencies in its own scene. Five of fourteen real-engine cases fail on the
parent. Repaired package and class-wide guard pass 198 checks, zero skips.
All eight real-GPU owner cases pass (242 model pixels each), the complete game
browser passes, and all fifteen runtime README examples pass. The final package
and guard run passes 213 checks. Core and stage are untouched.

### Batch 273 signed polygon offset clamp repair

Compared W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, WebGPU, editors Kai Ninomiya,
Brandon Jones and Jim Blandy (2026), https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/#depth-bias;
Eric Lengyel and Tobias Hector, EXT_polygon_offset_clamp revision 4 (2016),
https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/extensions/EXT/EXT_polygon_offset_clamp.txt;
and Khronos WebGL Working Group, EXT_polygon_offset_clamp revision 3 (2023),
https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/extensions/EXT_polygon_offset_clamp/.
Also compared Hang Dou, Yajie Yan, Ethan Kerzner, Zeng Dai and Chris Wyman,
Adaptive Depth Bias for Shadow Maps (2014),
https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/08/paper-lowres.pdf. The paper explains why
bias magnitude changes visibility. The standards give the exact signed bound
and reset behavior; hardware polygon offset preserves rasterizer slope/precision
semantics better than injecting an approximate fragment depth. The repair uses
that extension and explicitly refuses nonzero clamp when absent. No paper
companion code or rival implementation was read or used.

or other repository implementation was read.

examples pass. Core, stage and the hunter capture repair are untouched.

The corrected GPU fixture draws its neighbor and overlay in the same frame;
WebGPU swapchain textures do not retain undrawn pixels from an earlier task.
The actual parent bundle still changes 4608 out-of-scissor components in this
controlled fixture, while the repair changes zero and fills exactly 512 red

### Batch 133 E20: distinct glTF predictor behavior

Only Margo-crafted inputs and the two opaque shipped public APIs were used. Sixty
complete controls vary components 1/2/3/7, three correction patterns and five
open/split/closed shapes. Separate NONE, difference, parallelogram and multi
payloads distinguish four candidates. Every glTF method-2 output equals full
difference prediction, and none equals the other candidates. The existing
expanded fixtures supply 128 independent divergent cases; all now match the
proper entry flavor. A 214-case native/Wasm fixture retains both opaque outputs.
Probe/output hashes are in [the gate record](whitepaper/results/batch-133-gates.json).
No implementation source, wrapper text, disassembly or remembered internals were
used. The private ABI uses one Wasm and an explicit full/glTF flavor, not per-file
special cases. Public TypeScript integration remains open.

The tagged-bit optimization is direct arithmetic equivalence of the published
LSB-first payload rule: assemble at most five consecutive bytes in a u64, shift
by the cursor alignment, mask to width and advance once. Independent per-bit
reference checks cover input lengths, all alignments, widths 0..33, errors and
the next bit after success/failure. It introduces no new inferred format rule.

### Batch 133 E16: predictive EdgeBreaker traversal

Only Margo-crafted inputs and the opaque full public API supplied the omitted
rules. A 630-candidate framing sweep isolates the standard symbol stream, start
faces and seams followed by a little-endian u32 word and a binary prediction
stream. The word is consumed; its broader semantic role remains unproved.
Symbol/fallback controls establish prediction eligibility after C and R only;
E, L and S clear it. On a successful prediction bit, the new active corner's
next vertex degree at least six selects C, otherwise R. A failed bit consumes
the next standard symbol. Across 1,176 independently reconstructed controls,
this vertex and threshold have zero disagreements; the other tested vertices
and thresholds disagree. The degree model follows the published connectivity
rules and Margo's existing E8/E9 corrections.

The held-out campaign emits 2,160 complete files across six explicitly framed
versions, 60 shapes, successful and failed predictions, split merges, separate
components and raw vertex/corner canaries. All match the full prebuilt in
ordered indices, descriptors and every exposed scalar byte. The glTF prebuilt
rejects all 2,160, so no glTF predictive-output match is claimed. Native and
Wasm fixtures, strict prefixes, mutations and repeated frees retain the rule.
Hashes and exact scope are in [the continuation evidence](whitepaper/results/batch-133-resume8.json).
No implementation, wrapper listing, disassembly or remembered internals supplied
any rule. Seam-free fan search removal is an arithmetic/work equivalence of
Margo's existing mapping, with an independent closed-tetrahedron step count;
it adds no format inference or claimed overall speed gain.

### Batch 133 E41: normals outside the stored octahedron (2026-11-27)

Method: as E26 to E40, Margo-crafted inputs through the public calls of the
vendored full decoder (Wasm SHA-256
`c55a594e8ffd18426d36b27fea9618af3df5e173640a3e56d46f09d76f0574f2`), compared
bit for bit. No codec or wrapper source, disassembly or remembered internals
were used, and no new publication was needed: the octahedral map is E11's.

Observation: on point `(9, 9)` at 2 bits the decoder returns the vector the
published unfolding gives for the zigzag-decoded values `(-5, -5)`, so nothing
refuses a value outside `0..=max`. A sweep of 5,440 files (quantization 0 to 33,
symbol widths 1 to 4 bytes, 296,960 normals) then showed that quantizations
outside 2 to 30 are rejected and that the earlier E11 form of the negative
hemisphere differs in rounding on 98,357 normals once values are far outside.
Of eight f32 operation orders, one matches all 296,960: with
`x = 1 - |y| - |z|` and `over = max(-x, 0)`, each of `y` and `z` moves by
`+over` when it is negative and `-over` otherwise, before normalization. The
inputs are unchanged for values inside the octahedron (the retained E11 to E40
fixtures). The kept inputs and outputs are
`packages/decoders/native/draco/tests/fixtures/octahedron.bin` (186 cases: 116
unpredicted, 70 predicted mesh layouts of E35 to E39 with the stored
quantization narrowed under the transform maximum; SHA-256
`2319e6ae2c8ed242ec430f9dff73cc0c5e026d1ff0d561177f3e5ea3aec2c37c`), checked by
`tests/layouts.rs`; the module before this rule fails 176 of them. The emitter
was a session script and is not retained.

| E44 header split count | The symbol loop refuses only more created vertices than the header's vertex and split counts together. The split count may be lower than the S symbols made, or than the split events, and at most the symbol count. | Vertex and split grids on split meshes; 60,000 combined header mutations leave the differences listed in docs/known-bugs.md. |
| E45 KD level 6 ended axis | A node of 64 or more points reads an explicit axis. When that axis has no bits left, the node ends: all its points are the node's base and no remaining bits are read for them. | Remaining-bit changes leave the output unchanged; random level 6 streams. |
| E46 KD stream ends | A value that would pass the end of the number (levels 0 and 1), axis or half stream reads zero. The remaining-bits stream refuses it. Each stream was made lenient alone to find this. | 90,000 random streams at levels 0 to 6. |
| E47 KD stream sizes | A raw KD stream whose size is not a non-zero multiple of four bytes is rejected. | Every size from 0 to above the length of one seed's three raw streams; the 90,000 streams of E46, half with ragged sizes. |

E43 to E47 correct Margo refusing inputs the opaque decoder accepts. E45 also
corrects other output from Margo, and E47 inputs Margo accepted that the opaque
decoder rejects. The kept inputs and outputs are, in
`packages/decoders/native/draco/tests/fixtures/`: `normal-wide.bin` (290
accepted cases, SHA-256
`5f7a31ef72cee5929da43b210434f45826d36a2c208d85fba17d3333c47d367e`),
`header-counts.bin` (279 cases, 138 accepted, SHA-256
`78205ee63b20cc271b82fc5e7902b051b7c120cbf79680155c5dae6fbfcea543`) and
`kd-streams.bin` (134 cases, 80 accepted, SHA-256
`bada0a5c9f64f18978d20d72a77236c018776825a2190262f3ebac34e48862be`), checked by
`tests/layouts.rs`.

### Batch 133 E48 and E49: header flags and metadata names (2026-11-27)

Method as E42 to E47. 60,000 inputs took retained streams of every version,
set random header flags and inserted built or damaged metadata blocks.

| Experiment | Distinguishing observation and rule | Confirmation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E48 header flags | Flag bits other than 32768 never changed the output or acceptance. Before version 1.3 the metadata bit is ignored too: an inserted block is read as geometry. From 1.3 the bit selects the metadata block. | Versions 1.0 to 2.3, meshes and point clouds. |
| E49 child names | A metadata node with two child nodes of the same name is rejected, at any depth, in attribute or file metadata. Repeated entry keys, attribute ids, an empty key or child name and a child named like an entry are accepted. | Targeted blocks for each case, then the same 60,000 inputs. |

What the 60,000 inputs still differ on is Margo's own decode limits (counts the
prebuilt accepts above them) and the damaged streams listed in
docs/known-bugs.md. The kept inputs and outputs are
`packages/decoders/native/draco/tests/fixtures/metadata-header.bin` (101 cases,
46 accepted, SHA-256
`f35817367e3af51b793baf59699946b58774f1cfaaa6a7dba758453baa61089d`), checked by
`tests/layouts.rs`.

### Batch 133 E50 to E57: damaged streams (2026-11-27)

Method: as E26 to E40, Margo-crafted inputs through the public calls of the
opaque full decoder; its source was not read. Inputs are hand-built version 2.0
and 2.1 EdgeBreaker streams without attribute decoders (every symbol sequence
and start-face choice up to eight symbols, then hundreds of thousands of seeded
random ones with seams, split events and shortened bit streams), crafted
sequential meshes and point clouds, and the differing inputs of the E44 and
E48/E49 probes. Each rule is a hypothesis that was kept only when acceptance,
point count and indices matched on the whole probe.

| # | Rule | Probe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E50 start faces | A mesh has at most one start face for every three symbols: faces - symbols <= symbols / 3, rounded down. | Repeated components of one to four symbols with every start-face count. |
| E51 vertices merged by splits | Without attribute seams, each merged vertex id, in merge order, is filled by the last vertex that still has a representative corner. That vertex's corners are renamed by walking its fan from the representative, left and then, for an open fan, right of it; a walk meeting a corner that does not name it rejects the stream. A merged vertex keeps no representative, even when the split face names it as its third vertex. | Short sequences exhaustively; random ones. |
| E52 split events | There may be more events than split symbols or symbols, up to the face count. An event whose symbol is passed (a C or S symbol, which reads none) rejects the stream at the next L, R or E symbol; an event never reached is ignored, so is a split target never used, and a later write to one target replaces it. | One to twelve events over three and six symbols; 300,000 random streams. |
| E53 sequential points | A sequential mesh with more than three points per face is rejected. | Face and point grids, versions 1.0 to 2.2. |
| E54 connectivity byte | Zero selects entropy-coded indices, every other value raw ones. The opaque decoder also returns indices at or past the point count; Margo refuses those (docs/limits.md). | Bytes 0, 1, 2, 9, 64 and 255; indices from 0 to 600. |
| E55 empty decoders | An attributes decoder holding no attribute rejects the stream, in every method; a stream with no decoder is accepted. | Versions 1.0 to 2.3. |
| E56 clouds without decoders | A KD cloud with no attributes decoder is its point count at every version, with no attributes. | Versions 1.0 to 2.3. |
| E57 bit readers | The raw symbol bits and the pre-2.2 start-face bits are not bounded by their blob's size: reads continue through the input and give zero past its end. | 200,000 streams with either blob cut short. |

### Batch 133 E58 and E59: several KD decoders and repeated ids (2026-11-27)

Method: as E26 to E40, public calls of the opaque full decoder only; its source
was not read. Retained one-decoder KD clouds of equal point count were joined
(4,000 seeded joins of two to four, then crafted variants: up to 255 decoders,
signed minima, empty decoders, short and mismatched trees). Repeated ids were
hand-built sequential clouds and meshes; the opaque glTF build was checked on
the meshes. Each rule was kept only when acceptance and every output byte
matched.

| # | Rule | Probe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E58 several KD decoders | In a version 2.3 KD cloud every decoder's attribute list (count and descriptors) comes first, then for each decoder in the same order its tree and its own transforms. Each tree states the header's point count. Attributes come out in decoder order. | All 4,000 joins accepted by the opaque decoder equal the single clouds' attributes in order. |
| E59 repeated ids | Attribute unique ids may repeat, within a decoder and across decoders, in sequential and KD streams; every attribute is kept in file order and a lookup by id returns the first. | Versions 1.1 and 2.0 to 2.3. |

### Batch 133 E60 and E61: version 1.3 and the normalized byte (2026-11-27)

Method: as E26 to E40, public calls of the opaque full decoder only; its source
was not read. A grid of count, id and point-count widths over hand-built 1.2
and 1.3 clouds, then 250 retained 1.0 to 1.2 streams rewritten as 1.3, kept
only where the opaque decoder gave the original output. Every descriptor byte
value was tried at 1.1, 2.0 and 2.3. The varint id from 1.3 agrees with the
published specification's attribute descriptor table.

| # | Rule | Probe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E60 version 1.3 | Version 1.3 streams, point clouds and meshes, use the 1.2 layout except that an attribute's unique id is a varint, not two bytes. | All 250 rewritten streams match; 1.2 streams only relabelled are rejected by both. |
| E61 normalized byte | Any nonzero normalized byte means true, at every version. A semantic above 4 rejects the stream. | All 256 values of both bytes. |

### Batch 133 E62: vertices no traversal reaches (2026-11-27)

Method: as E26 to E40, public calls of the opaque full decoder only; its source
was not read. Retained EdgeBreaker meshes had their header face and symbol
counts lowered by up to three, with the split count kept or zeroed. Two
hypotheses were compared: the first entry for the output only, and for the
predictors too. The first differed on 24 streams; the second matched every
stream both accept (10,243).

| # | Rule | Probe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E62 unreached vertices | A vertex that no attribute traversal reaches takes entry zero, both for its output value and where a predictor looks it up. | Lowered header counts, versions 1.1 to 2.2. |

### Batch 133 E63 to E66: attribute decoder header and predictor bytes (2026-11-27)

Method: as E26 to E40, public calls of the opaque full decoder only, and of the
opaque glTF build for E66 and the 2.2 cases; neither source was read. On
retained seamed meshes of versions 1.0 to 2.2 every value of each decoder
header, predictor and transform byte was tried, and values with equal complete
output were grouped. Seam bytes were then mutated (about 70,000 accepted
streams match).

| # | Rule | Probe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E63 decoder header | A connectivity id with its high bit set means the plain connectivity, like 255. Any nonzero decoder type means per corner. A per-corner decoder with the degree traversal is rejected. | All 256 values of each byte. |
| E64 transforms | Transform bytes -1, 0, 1, 2 and 3 exist and others reject. Normals use 2 and 3, other values 1; any other pairing leaves the attribute without prediction or prediction data (E40 is one case). | All 256 values. |
| E65 methods | An unknown method is the difference predictor, as is every method but the geometric one on normals. The geometric predictor on other values is rejected. | All 256 values. |
| E67 normal prediction mode 0 | Before 2.2, predictor 6 mode 0 predicts from the entry corner's triangle normal added once for every triangle the swing around the vertex visits (so a sum of k copies, which wraps where the prebuilt's 32-bit arithmetic does). Found black box: on a hand-built face the prediction flipped sign at exactly 2^31/4, 2^31/3 and 2^31/2 of the cross component for vertices with 4, 3 and 2 triangles. Margo decodes while every component of the sum fits int32 and answers `Unsupported` past it, where no tested width model matched every vertex. | normal-mode0.bin, 178 cases: 162 outputs equal, 16 refused; probe of 24,000 mode 0 streams with positions of 2^4 to 2^32 range: no decoded stream differs. |
| E66 glTF predictor 3 | From version 2.0 the glTF build reads predictor 3 as the difference predictor (the full build rejects it). | The 2.2 cases of the fixture. |

### Batch 273 round 9: array-layer capacity and device negotiation

Sources researched before this repair: W3C GPU for the Web Working Group,
*WebGPU* (Candidate Recommendation Draft, 15 September 2026), optional
capabilities, supported limits and requestDevice/new-device algorithms,
https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/ ; Khronos WebGL Working Group, *WebGL 2.0

https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.2/es_spec_3.2.pdf .
The distinction is capability versus negotiated default: GL's backed capacity
is the adapter limit; 256 is the unrequested WebGPU device default, not an
adapter ceiling. The device receives at least that default and any supported
larger request. Core already asks for the adapter's full layer capacity.

Scientific method comparison uses Donaldson, *Metamorphic Testing of Android
Graphics Drivers* (2019), and Donaldson, Evrard and Thomson, *Putting Randomized
Compiler Testing into Production* (2020), linked in the preceding baseline
record. Apply their setup-validation principle to independent adapter/device
states: regression tests cover 256/2048/4096 backed layers, default and explicit
requests, immutable adapter/device limits, refusal and recovery. Native and
compatibility bevel cases retain layers 256/2047 and all image assertions.
Only the standards' relevant limit sections and the papers' scopes recorded
above were read. No companion code or other engine implementation was used.

  abstract and the introduction of their expanded *A Model for Smooth Viewing
  and Navigation of Large 2D Information Spaces* (2004),

  This is not their optimal 2D navigation path algorithm.

  (W3C Working Draft, 2023), https://www.w3.org/TR/web-animations-1/ . Compared
  explicit timeline progress, easing and cancellation lifecycle. Margo uses an
  engine delta clock and resolves cancellation false, rather than DOM animation
  cancellation's rejected finished promise.

  https://yomotsu.github.io/camera-controls/classes/CameraControls.html . Public

  was opened. No rival code, files, dependency or asset was adopted.

Combined design: quintic endpoint easing, angular/quaternion orientation,
logarithmic distance/zoom, target translation, analytic camera-frame box-corner
and sphere-tangent fitting. Symmetric quintic evaluation avoids rounding above
one near the final sample; the regression samples 30 and 60 fps through opposite
views. Input clears existing inertia through protected package hooks and cancels
before applying a new gesture. Synthetic boxes and sphere samples are correctness
fixtures, not downloaded demo assets. No new public asset demo or speed claim.

- Yalong Yang, Bernhard Jenny, Tim Dwyer, Kim Marriott, Haohui Chen and Maxime Cordeil, *Maps and Globes in Virtual Reality* (2018), Computer Graphics Forum, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13431 and author abstract https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.02088 . Public descriptions of globe rotation, hit-based tilt, zoom, altitude limits and input toggles are the row's web-library reference. Source links were not opened.

Combined clean-room design: scale a camera ray by the reference radii, solve its quadratic with the cancellation-resistant root pair, transport geodetic normals by Rodrigues rotation and translate the hit exactly onto the anchor. Zoom is a similarity about the picked point. Tilt rotates the full camera frame about the hit with a local-horizon limit; radial altitude clamps and altitude-dependent clip planes cover orbit/street scales. Floating-origin rebases translate a live grab and recompute the local reference centre. This is not a terrain collision system or a reproduction of a rival controller.

## Batch 252 job 1: walkability queries

Only papers and published API descriptions were consulted, no implementation or companion source.

Combined design: clip an XZ segment against convex polygon half-planes, then follow only connected ground portals at the exit parameter. Explore tied vertex exits so a zero-length polygon crossing is valid. Report the exact edge and outward normal. Local movement searches portals intersecting the disk with the requested segment as diameter and selects the closest point on the reachable polygons. Unlike the reference contract's unprojected move result, Margo projects onto the polygon plane. Filters, blocked polygons, partial tile portals and live rebuilds share the existing mesh graph. Synthetic corridors, ramps and floors are analytic test fixtures; no downloaded asset or new public demo. The outside CAD package's package layout was inspected; these ground graph queries belong to navmesh, not the outside CAD package.

## Batch 252 job 3: sampling and wall distance

Sources compared before implementation: Greg Turk, *Generating Random Points in Triangles* (1990), in Andrew S. Glassner (ed.), *Graphics Gems*, pp. 24-28, publisher table of contents https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780080507538/graphics-gems; Robert Osada, Thomas Funkhouser, Bernard Chazelle and David Dobkin, *Shape Distributions* (2002), ACM TOG 21(4), https://pixl.cs.princeton.edu/pubs/Osada_2002_SD/ (surface-area sampling and square-root barycentrics); I. E. Sutherland and G. W. Hodgman, *Reentrant Polygon Clipping* (1974), https://doi.org/10.1145/360767.360802 (radius bounding-square clipping); Mikko Mononen and Recast Navigation contributors, *dtNavMeshQuery API reference* (2009-present), https://recastnav.com/classdtNavMeshQuery.html (area-weighted random queries, circle neighborhood and wall-segment contracts). Only descriptions/papers were consulted; no rival or companion code read.

Combined design: weight convex fan triangles by true 3D surface area, choose a cumulative-area interval, then sample square-root barycentrics using the existing independent seeded math stream. Radius sampling first limits the connected ground graph to portals touching the circle, clips proposal polygons to its bounding square, and rejects points outside the exact disk, preserving uniform density with a finite proposal bound. Wall queries subtract unions of traversable portal intervals from each polygon edge before taking the closest segment point. This is essential for partial tile portals and area filters. Synthetic distribution, ramp and tiled-floor fixtures only; no new asset demo, timing assertion or speed claim.

and mean-of-max use midpoint sampling; max-average uses set representatives.

singleton and true sampled mean-of-max outputs. No copied code, downloaded asset
demo, timing claim or assertion of truth-preserving logical deduction.

## Batch 252 job 4: worker SIMD rasterization

Sources compared before implementation: I. E. Sutherland and G. W. Hodgman, *Reentrant Polygon Clipping* (1974), https://doi.org/10.1145/360767.360802; Michael Schwarz and Hans-Peter Seidel, *Fast Parallel Surface and Solid Voxelization on GPUs* (2010), https://michael-schwarz.com/research/publ/files/vox-siga10.pdf; W3C WebAssembly Working Group, *WebAssembly Core Specification*, SIMD numeric operations (2025/current 2.0 edition), https://www.w3.org/TR/wasm-core-2/; WHATWG, *HTML Standard: Web workers* (living standard, accessed 2026-11-10), https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html. Compared clipping against conservative overlap voxelization: retain Margo's exact clipping semantics and span order rather than adopting a different coverage rule. Standard f64x2 sub/mul/add preserves scalar lane operation order without relaxed SIMD or fused arithmetic. No companion or rival code was read.

Combined design: one feature-local Rust crate and one SIMD Wasm asset, loaded lazily by ./wasm through new URL. Each build owns a CPU worker, transfers copied input and kernel bytes once, rasterizes and merges spans in Rust with fixed stack clipping buffers, then uses the same TypeScript polygon pipeline as ./build and ./tiles. Triangle classification stays in JS to preserve Math.hypot/slope thresholds exactly. Whole-mesh and tiled results travel through the existing checked binary codec; tiled results retain source geometry for ordinary runtime updates. Abort and timeout terminate the worker during execution. Source and binary hashes enforce a matching committed kernel. Deterministic proof compares the identical candidate/intersection counts and the per-intersection XY vector pair against the scalar reference, with byte-identical polygons. No wall-clock speed claim, benchmark or GPU work.

## Batch 215: tween promises and cancellation (2026-11-10)

Research compared before implementation, without companion code:
- Tian Zhao and Yonglun Li, *A Concurrency Model for JavaScript with Cooperative Cancellation* (SLE 2021), https://boyang.cs.uwm.edu/publication/sle2021.pdf . Cancellation must terminate future writes; a promise alone does not do that.
- Daan Leijen, *Structured Asynchrony with Algebraic Effects* (2017), https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/asynceffects-msr-tr-2017-21.pdf . Compared scoped lifecycle ownership and cleanup against detached callbacks.
- Brian Birtles et al., *Web Animations* (W3C, 2023), https://www.w3.org/TR/web-animations-1/ . Completion and cancellation are separate outcomes; settled promises do not resolve to their thenable animation.
- WHATWG contributors, *DOM Standard*, AbortSignal (living standard, accessed 2026-11-10), https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#abortsignal . Preserve the exact reason and remove abort listeners at settlement.
- GSAP authors, *Timeline.then()* (accessed 2026-11-10), https://gsap.com/docs/v3/GSAP/Timeline/then()/ ; Motion authors, *animate* (accessed 2026-11-10), https://motion.dev/docs/animate . Compared public completion/control behaviour only, no source.

Combined design: optional owners with explicit caller clocks, per-operation completion and cancellation, listener cleanup on every terminal path, group snapshots and replay promises. Tests cover scalar/array/path/custom, repeats, callbacks, pause, replay, exact abort reasons, replacement, invalid input and disposal. These establish the requested completion/AbortSignal row; no claim about all unrelated GSAP/Motion functionality. No external model/data asset is used: examples animate numeric values.

Async cancellation regression (batch 215): cancellation during onRepeat now prevents the same track from writing again or completing. AsyncTimeline gates remaining callbacks and completion after cancellation. The Web Animations cancellation model and the cooperative-cancellation paper above motivate stopping future effects, not just rejecting a promise. Regression: packages/tween/test/async.test.js.

## Batch 252 job 5: cylinder and rotated-box carving

Sources compared before implementation: Paul Heckbert, *Concave Polygon Scan Conversion* (1990), Graphics Gems pp. 87-91, https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/concave-polygon-scan-conversion; Juan Pineda, *A Parallel Algorithm for Polygon Rasterization* (1988), https://people.csail.mit.edu/ericchan/bib/pdf/p17-pineda.pdf; Mikko Mononen and Recast Navigation contributors, *dtTileCache API reference* (2009-present), https://recastnav.com/classdtTileCache.html. Compared scanline spans, exact edge predicates and the web rival's upright cylinder/Y-rotated-box contracts. Only published descriptions/papers were read, no companion or rival implementation.

Combined design: the optional ObstacleNavMesh subclass maps each shape onto exact center-sampled horizontal runs of the existing voxel lattice, then delegates carving, vertical limits, erosion, tile invalidation and bounded rebuilds to ./tiles. A cylinder uses its circle predicate; a rotated box uses inverse right-handed Y coordinates. Each row's accepted integer interval is found by monotone predicate searches, avoiding ill-conditioned division by nearly zero trigonometric coefficients at quarter turns. A one-cell candidate ring covers bounding-box rounding, while the original predicate alone selects the final cells. No tolerance is relaxed and there is no scan over every footprint cell. Groups keep one public id across moves and removal; input validation completes before mutation. The test's independent brute cell masks produce byte-identical tile meshes, including exact quarter-turn regressions. Analytic fixtures only; no public asset demo or speed claim.

## Batch 171 job 6: atmosphere in a geographic frame

Research compared before implementation, without opening any companion implementation:
- Sebastien Hillaire (2020), *A Scalable and Production Ready Sky and Atmosphere Rendering Technique*, EGSR, https://sebh.github.io/publications/egsr2020.pdf, mathematical sections 3-5. Reuse sky's transmittance and multiple-scattering tables and analytic segment integration of the transport equation. Aerial perspective is applied at each data fragment, including transparent flow, rather than at opaque ground depth.
- Eric Bruneton (2016), *A Qualitative and Quantitative Evaluation of 8 Clear Sky Models*, https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.04336, sections 3-4 and discussion. Separate appearance/numerical model approximations from measurement accuracy; no spectral or weather accuracy claim.
- Eric Bruneton and Fabrice Neyret (2008), *Precomputed Atmospheric Scattering*, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2008.01245.x, abstract/design comparison only; its model or companion code is not implemented here.
- IOGP (2019), *Geomatics Guidance Note 7 part 2*, section 4.1.1, https://www.iogp.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/373-07-02.pdf. Combine the existing WGS84 geographic-to-geocentric conversion with meridional/prime-vertical curvature radii to convert east/north m/s into angular rates at grid samples; up remains metres/second. Geometry uses real geodetic metre heights and retains masks.
- Ibrahim Reda and Afshin Andreas (2004, revised report 2008), *Solar Position Algorithm for Solar Radiation Applications*, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.solener.2003.12.003 and https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy08osti/34302.pdf. Published example is an independent solar orientation fixture, not a claim to implement SPA. Existing sky/astro supplies Meeus solar coordinates and apparent Greenwich sidereal time; use geocentric right ascension/declination so a Greenwich observer's parallax does not become a global direction.
- US Naval Observatory, *Computing Approximate Solar Coordinates*, https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/sun_approx, accessed 2026-11-10. Compared ecliptic/equatorial conversion and the distinction between geocentric and observer-based directions. No source-code link opened.
- NOAA PSL, *NCEP-NCAR Reanalysis 1* and *FAQ*, https://psl.noaa.gov/data/gridded/data.ncep.reanalysis.html and https://psl.noaa.gov/data/help/faq.html. Sigma 0.995 is local pressure fraction, not height; the real-data demo explicitly labels all chosen drawing heights.

Combined design: a new sky/planet entry owns the existing Hillaire model in arbitrary planet coordinates. New sciviz/atmosphere composes the existing geo globe with per-fragment solar surface light and aerial perspective. Existing entries receive only a type-only optional appearance interface, so importing the root or flow alone never imports sky. Wind RK4 and trail history remain on the GPU; only a one-time input unit conversion and draw projection are new.
The medium stretches WGS84's polar coordinate by 1/(1-f) to an exact spherical ground for the existing spherical model. Singular values prove distance distortion at most 1/(1-f)-1 < 0.3365 percent. This does not change data geometry or silently reinterpret NOAA pressure levels. The tile mesh's chordal ground fragments use the reference ground radius for surface transport, keeping the atmosphere out of underground chords. No speed measurement, foreign implementation file, new core/stage code or physics change.


## Batch 252 job 6: borderSize padding

Sources compared before implementation: Mikko Mononen and Recast Navigation contributors, *rcConfig API reference* (2009-present), https://recastnav.com/structrcConfig.html (non-navigable heightfield border and voxel units); Gunilla Borgefors, *Distance Transformations in Digital Images* (1986), Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image Processing 34(3), pp. 344-371, https://people.cmm.minesparis.psl.eu/users/marcoteg/cv/publi_pdf/MM_refs/1986_Borgefors_distance.pdf (distance propagation and boundary context); I. E. Sutherland and G. W. Hodgman, *Reentrant Polygon Clipping* (1974), https://doi.org/10.1145/360767.360802 (lattice-aligned clipping retained with shifted cell indices). Compared the published border contract with the existing filter/erosion dependency radius; no implementation source was read.

Combined design: ceil(borderSize) empty cells pad each side of the whole-level grid without shifting its world-space lattice. Tile context is max(ceil(borderSize),ceil(walkableRadius)+2); filtering sees the requested context, then the existing keep rectangle crops output to the tile. The 16,000,000-cell limit counts padding for both build kinds before allocation or tile assignment. The regression directly checks allocated raster columns, empty borders, preserved polygons, cropped tile bounds, seam paths, obstacle rebuilds and worker parity. No GPU, timing measurement or new asset demo.

Sources compared: Christian Nachbar, Franz Zotter, Etienne Deleflie and Alois Sontacchi, AMBIX: A Suggested Ambisonics Format (2011), https://ambisonics.iem.at/proceedings-of-the-ambisonics-symposium-2011/ambix-a-suggested-ambisonics-format; Jens Ahrens, Binaural Audio Rendering in the Spherical Harmonic Domain: A Summary of the Mathematics and Its Pitfalls (2022), https://arxiv.org/html/2202.04393v2; Thomas McKenzie, Damian T. Combined explicit ACN/SN3D normalization, incidence axes, weighted spherical quadrature and native HRTF convolution. ## Batch 257 job 1: worker RPC and task pool

Research compared Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat, MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters (OSDI 2004), https://research.google/pubs/mapreduce-simplified-data-processing-on-large-clusters/ ; Michael Isard, Mihai Budiu, Yuan Yu, Andrew Birrell and Dennis Fetterly, Dryad: Distributed Data-Parallel Programs from Sequential Building Blocks (EuroSys 2007), https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2007/03/eurosys07.pdf ; WHATWG contributors, HTML Living Standard (2026), https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/web-messaging.html#message-ports and https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/structured-data.html#safe-passing-of-structured-data ; WHATWG contributors, DOM Standard (2026), https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#abortsignal . Public rival API reference only: Comlink authors, API documentation (2026), https://github.com/GoogleChromeLabs/comlink/blob/main/README.md . No rival source or companion code read or used.

Combined design inference: sequential task handlers, explicitly transferred messages, namespaced promise responses, fixed concurrency and FIFO waiting. Distributed retries and graph scheduling are unnecessary for a browser worker pool and can repeat side effects; failures reject, never replay. Typed variadic method calls cover the requested RPC row, including promise and synchronous handlers, own-method lookup, receiver binding, input/output transfer, remote errors, independent clients, endpoint failure and disposal. Cancellation reaches each handler's appended context signal. A cancelled caller rejects immediately but its pool slot stays occupied until the handler settles. Deadline expiry closes the pool and terminates owned workers rather than allowing overlapping work. Defaults: two workers, 1024 queued calls, 30000 ms total call deadline. Raw RpcClient endpoints remain caller-owned. This is orchestration, not a CPU-heavy codec or geometry loop; no Rust/Wasm or speed claim. Numeric/buffer correctness fixtures require no external asset; no demo added.

Evidence: packages/worker/tests/rpc.test.js uses real Node workers and MessageChannels. packages/worker/tests/rpc-types.ts verifies method, argument, result and handler-context types. The existing real-GPU browser check also executes a browser worker pool and proves transfer round trips. Core and stage source are unchanged.

## XR smooth movement and stereo comfort (batch 268 job 3)

SmoothLocomotion in the optional xr/locomotion entry combines standard thumbstick axes, radial dead zones, planar movement and smooth yaw with existing teleport and snap turn. Translation is capped diagonally and independent of head height. Movement drives an exponential fade of a soft angular opening, computed from each eye projection and viewport. Both XR rendering routes invoke eye overlays before submission. Session end and AbortSignal remove listeners and release overlay resources. This is a rendering treatment, without a clinical efficacy claim or optical-flow adaptation.

Fernandes and Steven Feiner, *Combating VR Sickness through Subtle Dynamic Field-of-View Modification* (IEEE 3DUI, 2016), https://www.cs.columbia.edu/2016/combating-vr-sickness/images/combating-vr-sickness.pdf; Fei Wu and Evan Suma Rosenberg, *Adaptive Field-of-view Restriction: Limiting Optical Flow to Mitigate Cybersickness in Virtual Reality* (VRST, 2022), https://doi.org/10.1145/3562939.3565611 (primary institutional abstract: https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/adaptive-field-of-view-restriction-limiting-optical-flow-to-mitig/); W3C Immersive Web Working Group, *WebXR Device API* (2026), https://www.w3.org/TR/webxr/ (offset reference spaces); W3C Immersive Web Working Group, *WebXR Gamepads Module Level 1* (2026), https://www.w3.org/TR/webxr-gamepads-module-1/ (xr-standard thumbstick axes). Compared Thomas Porter and Tom Duff, Compositing Digital Images (1984), https://doi.org/10.1145/800031.808606 (coverage as a fourth channel); Simon Fraser, Dean Jackson and Edward O'Connor (editors), CSS Transforms Module Level 2 (2021), https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transforms-2/ (homogeneous matrices and flattening); W3C FX Task Force, Compositing and Blending Level 1 (2024), https://www.w3.org/TR/compositing-1/; and Khronos WebGL Working Group, WebGL 2.0 Specification (living standard), https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/specs/latest/2.0/. ## Batch 245 job 5: per-sprite blending (2026-11-10)
Research first: Thomas Porter and Tom Duff, *Compositing Digital Images* (1984), https://keithp.com/~keithp/porterduff/p253-porter.pdf ; Chris Harrelson (editor; former editors Rik Cabanier and Nikos Andronikos), *Compositing and Blending Level 1* (2024), https://www.w3.org/TR/compositing-1/ ; PixiJS team, *Scene Objects: Blend Modes* and *Performance Tips: BlendModes* (accessed 2026-11-10), https://pixijs.com/8.x/guides/components/scene-objects and https://pixijs.com/8.x/guides/concepts/performance-tips . Only papers, standards and public behaviour descriptions read; no rival source or asset copied.

Combined design: preserve z/y/add order, group adjacent equal operators, and retain the normal sprite layer's atlas pages, filtering, masks and lifecycle through protected pipeline/draw hooks. Normal/add/screen use premultiplied fixed-function blending. Multiply needs the uncovered source term on transparent backdrops: let P=Cs*As and D=1-As+P. First add P/D*(1-Ab) to RGB without changing alpha, then multiply existing RGB by D and perform source-over alpha. Zero D uses zero contribution. The two passes are interleaved per sprite, not per whole group, so overlapping multiply sprites retain their order. Intermediate RGBA8 rounding contributes at most one output byte versus the ideal single-sprite equation. No quality is dropped to save optional bytes. Synthetic pixels only; no public asset demo or speed claim. GPU proof is required before landing (blend-check.mjs, both backends).

### Signed normalized compute storage uploads (lane T)

The CPU compute route already quantizes normalized stores, but its publication path attached native SNORM textures to framebuffers. Compared framebuffer drawing with native signed-byte uploads using three primary standards: W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, Alan Baker, Mehmet Oguz Derin and David Neto (2026), *WebGPU Shading Language*, texel formats, https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#texel-formats; Khronos Group, Jon Leech and Benj Lipchak (2019), *OpenGL ES 3.0.6*, sections 2.1.5 and 3.8.3, https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.0/es_spec_3.0.pdf; Khronos Group, Kelsey Gilbert (2026), *WebGL 2.0 Specification*, texture uploads and typed BYTE arrays, https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/specs/latest/2.0/. These distinguish sampleable SNORM storage from color-renderable attachments. Native byte storage avoids a float backing representation and its extra view/copy conversions. No companion code or other repository source was read or copied.

The owning compute runtime encodes clamped channels to signed 8-bit bytes with nearest rounding at scale 127, uploads only contiguous written spans, and reuses writeTexture for mip/layer ownership synchronization. Untouched native bytes remain untouched. The independent browser regression compares exact bytes for all 256 signed input codes, clamping and fractional values across r8/rg8/rgba8, 2D/array/3D, and mip/layer views. The old runtime fails this regression with incomplete framebuffer errors.

## Batch 225 job 2: analytic curve queries

Patrikalakis, Takashi Maekawa and Wonjoon Cho, Shape Interrogation for Computer Aided Design and Manufacturing (2009 hyperbook), sections 1.3.4, 1.3.5 and 4, https://web.mit.edu/hyperbook/Patrikalakis-Maekawa-Cho/ ; Danny Hermes, Geometric Curve Intersection (2024 documentation, algorithm prose only), https://bezier.readthedocs.io/en/2024.6.20/algorithms/geometric-curve-intersection.html . ## Batch 225 job 3: signed offsets and reversal
Compared Rida T. Farouki and C. Andrew Neff, Analytic properties of plane offset curves (1990), https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8396(90)90023-K ; Nicholas M. Patrikalakis, Takashi Maekawa and Wonjoon Cho, Shape Interrogation for Computer Aided Design and Manufacturing (2009 hyperbook), sections 11.2.1 and 11.2.4, https://web.mit.edu/hyperbook/Patrikalakis-Maekawa-Cho/node219.html and https://web.mit.edu/hyperbook/Patrikalakis-Maekawa-Cho/node222.html ; and the same authors' Bernstein subdivision description, section 1.3.5, https://web.mit.edu/hyperbook/Patrikalakis-Maekawa-Cho/node13.html . General exact offsets are not cubic polynomials; control-polygon translation alone has uncontrolled error. Combined design: exact signed normal evaluation and analytic offset derivative, adaptive endpoint-Hermite cubics, then independent interval verification of the residual cubic against the normalized quadratic derivative hull. Verification bounds every parameter interval, rather than accepting the fit samples alone. Splitting the source and residual together tightens the enclosure. This is our own interval construction, not the specific higher-degree interval-Bezier algorithm discussed in the survey. Rounded arithmetic uses an explicit scale-dependent allowance, not formal directed rounding. Non-G1 joins get explicit bevel pieces; zero-width source ranges identify them, and their geometry is outside the local offset error claim. Curvature-induced local loops are retained, as in a raw parallel curve; no topology-changing trim is implied. Reversal reverses exact cubic controls and piece order. No rival source, companion implementation, demo or third-party asset added. Polynomial fixtures exercise signed distance, alternate planes, dense between-sample error, closed seams, corner joins, every existing cubic kind, source ownership and explicit singular/work-limit errors.

Compared Ingo Wald, On fast Construction of SAH-based Bounding Volume Hierarchies (2007), https://publications.sci.utah.edu/publications/wald07/fastbuild.pdf (streamed binning and independent recursive tasks); Tero Karras and Timo Aila, Fast Parallel Construction of High-Quality Bounding Volume Hierarchies (2013), https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/pubs/2013-07_Fast-Parallel-Construction/karras2013hpg_paper.pdf (quality costs of replacing SAH with linear hierarchies); and WHATWG contributors, HTML Living Standard, Web workers (2026), https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html (nested module workers, transferable results and termination). Combine a shallow SAH frontier with bounded independent SAH subtree jobs, then relocate packed child and triangle offsets in one coordinator worker. Retain the same split rule, initial subtree face order and remaining global depth budget, rather than substitute a different topology. Existing TypeScript construction is reused, not rebuilt as a new numeric kernel; no Rust/Wasm gain is asserted or measured during the speed deferral.

## Batch 249 job 4: binary world snapshots and deltas
Sources compared: David G. Korn and Kiem-Phong Vo, Engineering a Differencing and Compression Data Format (USENIX 2002), https://www.usenix.org/conference/2002-usenix-annual-technical-conference/engineering-differencing-and-compression-data; David Korn, Joshua MacDonald, Jeffrey Mogul and Kiem-Phong Vo, RFC 3284 (2002), https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3284; Glenn Fiedler, Snapshot Compression (2015), https://gafferongames.com/post/snapshot_compression/; WHATWG contributors, HTML structured data (2026), https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/structured-data.html and Compression Standard (2026), https://compression.spec.whatwg.org/; TC39 contributors, Uint8Array to/from base64 (2025), https://tc39.es/proposal-arraybuffer-base64/spec/; bitECS contributors, Serialization (2026 API documentation), https://bitecs.dev/docs/serialization. Combined design: versioned identity graph, explicit typed bytes, native bounded deflate streams, selected component membership plus all live entity ids, and baseline/target SHA-256 fingerprints on deltas. Native 256-character block comparisons skip unchanged snapshot text; changed blocks or a full replacement are compressed once. This is a private version-1 format, not VCDIFF or an implementation copied from any source. Baselines must be acknowledged by the transport as Fiedler describes. Native JSON, base64 and compression own the heavy codec loops; no measured Wasm gain exists and no speed claim is made.
WorldSerializer validates schema, membership, references, sizes and capacity before changing entities, with bounded abortable stream operations. Restore returns remote-to-local ids and never resurrects a stale handle. Surviving entities retain unselected components; missing entities are destroyed. Component defaults now run only for omitted object fields, so a fully supplied restore cannot invoke an unrelated factory. Numeric add observers see complete restored values. Portable JS graphs preserve cycles, shared references/buffers, Map, Set, Date, RegExp, sparse arrays, undefined, bigint and special numbers in reference fields. App codecs cover opaque/executable resources without source evaluation. No rival or companion source read, no external demo assets and no rendering changes.
Evidence: packages/ecs/test/serialize.test.js proves binary round trips, real deflate corruption rejection, generational replacement, empty entities, tags, partial selection, default factory behavior, sparse binary deltas and reverse deltas, cancellation, expansion bounds, schema failures and capacity preflight. Numeric component fields obey the existing finite-number contract, while reference-field numeric values retain specials. Work-count proof is byte count for a single changed block with identical reconstructed snapshot bytes, not a timing bar.

## Batch 249 job 5: worker-parallel shared ECS systems
Research compared Arthur J. Bernstein, Analysis of Programs for Parallel Processing (1966), https://doi.org/10.1109/PGEC.1966.264565 (read/write independence); A. B. Kahn, Topological sorting of large networks (1962), https://doi.org/10.1145/368996.369025 (acyclic dependency order); WHATWG contributors, HTML Workers (2026), https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html; ECMA International, SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics (2026), https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/structured-data.html; and Last Olive Games, Becsy Systems/Queries/Components (2026 public documentation), https://lastolivegames.github.io/becsy/guide/architecture/systems, https://lastolivegames.github.io/becsy/guide/architecture/queries and https://lastolivegames.github.io/becsy/guide/architecture/components. Combined design: explicit dependency layers, stable ordering for hazards, and concurrent worker dispatch only when write buffers are disjoint from other reads/writes. Accesses are compared by physical shared-buffer identity, so aliased registration names cannot race. This is orchestration, not an engine numerical loop; user systems remain independent modules. No rival source or companion code read, no external demo data and no speed claim.
SharedWorld allocates shared numeric fields/membership; SharedComponent maintains generation-checked shared sparse rows before observers run. Main-thread structural operations reject during dispatch. ParallelSchedule owns bounded workers, exposes only declared components, preserves asynchronous module completion, joins termination on abort/failure, never replays a system, and notifies change trackers once per physical written component after success. A failed host termination keeps structural storage locked rather than release memory a live worker may still use. Defaults: two workers, 30000 ms per system, default module export, no explicit order or accesses. Browser isolation is required; Node embedders provide an endpoint factory. Public APIs support typed stores and asynchronous disposal.
Evidence: packages/ecs/test/parallel.test.js uses real Node workers, a separate atomic rendezvous to prove independent systems overlap without timing assertions, different dense layouts, conflict graphs, shared aliases, structural guards, abort, module errors, worker exit, deadline and failed-host cleanup. packages/ecs/test/parallel-browser.test.js loads the actual packaged worker in an isolated browser, observes shared writes, and rejects the unisolated surface. That browser fixture disables GPU and performs no GPU rendering/compute; it is a CPU correctness test and uses no GPU. packages/ecs/test/objects-types.ts verifies public type composition. No speed budget changed.
Worker disposal reentry regression: compared ECMA International, Promise.prototype.then and promise jobs (2026 living specification), https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/control-abstraction-objects.html#sec-promise.prototype.then, and TC39, Explicit Resource Management (2026 specification), https://tc39.es/proposal-explicit-resource-management/. Publish the one stop promise before invoking host termination callbacks, using a promise job for cleanup. A deterministic custom endpoint previously terminated twice when its termination callback reentered stop; parallel.test.js now requires one termination and the identical promise. No error is suppressed or retried.

## Batch 208 job 3: browser and service worker cache proof
Compared Monica Chintala and Yoshisato Yanagisawa (editors), *Service Workers* (W3C draft, 2026), https://www.w3.org/TR/service-workers/ (fetch events, message lifetime, registration replacement and persistent storage); Scott Haseley (editor), *Cooperative Scheduling of Background Tasks* (2025), https://www.w3.org/TR/requestidlecallback/ (window idle scheduling and timeout fallback); and Wang, Lin, Zhong and Chishtie, *How Far Can Client-Only Solutions Go for Mobile Browser Speed?* (2011), https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.3691 (caching and prefetching as distinct mechanisms). ## Review 99 full-scene mesh build checkpoint

Research compared before implementation:
- Ingo Wald, On Fast Construction of SAH-based Bounding Volume Hierarchies,
  2007, section 3, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~wald/Publications/2007/ParallelBVHBuild/fastbuild.pdf .
- Timo Aila, Tero Karras and Samuli Laine, On Quality Metrics of Bounding Volume
  Hierarchies, 2013, sections 1-2, https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/pubs/2013-09_On-Quality-Metrics/aila2013hpg_paper.pdf .
- Thiago Ize, Robust BVH Ray Traversal, 2013 (2015 correction), sections 1-2,
  https://jcgt.org/published/0002/02/02/paper.pdf .
- Jonathan Richard Shewchuk, Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and
  Fast Robust Geometric Predicates, 1997, sections 2.3-2.4,
  https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~jrs/papers/robustr.pdf .

Wald supplies centroid binning with full primitive bounds. The builder uses
16 bins on all axes and the area-times-count objective; coincident centroids
and a 32-level SAH prefix fall back to balanced median partitions to bound
Wasm recursion. Aila et al. show why SAH alone establishes no throughput claim.
Ize distinguishes geometry bounds from traversal arithmetic; existing outward
rounding and GPU slab handling stay intact. Single-precision products fit
exactly in Float64; error-free addition retains the six signed area products
without a tolerance, so only exact zero-area inputs are removed. Independent
BigInt decisions cover 512 Float32 cases. The retained original triplet ordinal
is separate from packed triangle index. No companion code or foreign engine
source was read. Private kernel APIs were inspected first; no serializable
offline BLAS builder fits this packet, so the feature-local crate remains owner.

already decoded arrays, with format parsing retained by the consumer. The

wrapping and nearest texels. Validation rejects malformed attributes before

Johannes Guenther, Solomon Boulos, Thiago Ize, Warren Hunt, Steven G. Parker
and Peter Shirley, State of the Art in Ray Tracing Animated Scenes, 2007,
sections 3.2.2 and 4.3, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~wald/Publications/2009/STAR09/star09.pdf .

## Review 99 composition timeout diagnosis

Compared W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, WebGPU, 2026,
sections 3.2.2, 9 and 10, https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/ ;
Lewis Crawford and Michael O'Boyle, A Cross-platform Evaluation of Graphics
Shader Compiler Optimization, ISPASS 2018,
https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/56917122/A_Cross_platform_Evaluation_of_Graphics_Shader_Compiler_Optimization.pdf ;
and Yong He, Theresa Foley and Kayvon Fatahalian, A System for Rapid Exploration
of Shader Optimization Choices, SIGGRAPH 2016,
https://graphics.cs.cmu.edu/projects/spire/he16_spire.pdf .
The specification distinguishes module, pipeline, queue and mapping promises,
with no general ordering guarantee. Crawford and O'Boyle motivate treating
compiler behavior as platform dependent; He et al. discuss architectural shader
choices rather than a universal compiler workaround. Neither paper identifies
this native failure. Caching hints, shader restructuring and the separate
WebGL2 wavefront investigation therefore cannot be claimed as a repair here.
The clean-room test supervisor tracks these operations separately on the host,
preserves the failing phase and kills its own child tree within the existing
time limit. This is diagnostics and timeout correctness, not a speed experiment.
No foreign engine, paper companion implementation or browser compiler source
was read. The native compiler root remains unresolved in known-bugs.

https://llvm.org/pubs/2008-06-Reiter-Thesis.pdf ; Khronos Group, glTF 2.0
Specification (2017, maintained specification), transformations and triangle
winding, https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html .
Wald/Reiter motivate shared object-space hierarchies beneath a world-space
instance hierarchy; glTF supplies affine placement and reflected outside
orientation conventions. Keep Margo's existing bounded binned SAH and exact
Woop/Benthin/Wald predicate, with no foreign implementation. Transform rays
without normalizing their directions, preserving t. Derive normal transforms
from the inverse transpose. Transform all eight corners in Float64, enclose
Float32 arithmetic by gamma(7), round outwards, then build the TLAS with the
same Rust SAH builder. Per-tracer exact SIMD word comparison invalidates changed
geometry, indices, attributes or palette ids; no hash/revision assumptions.
The SIMD equality loop compares four u32 words per vector group plus a scalar
tail, proven against changes in every lane/tail. This is a work description,
not an overall speed claim (copies and validation are still performed).
Outside indexed-mesh and scene-picking contracts were rechecked; there is no
serialized GPU BLAS API to consume. No outside CAD code, parser or dependency
was added. Mathematical descriptions/standards only; no companion source used.
