The implementation combines instanced vertex reads, independent column normalisation, a small axis-order/flip buffer, a shared keyed mask, per-axis intersection, matrix rectangle brushes, selected-row diagonal histograms, and exact integer density counts. The full matrix uses one canvas/device, not a context per cell. Data reuse: the existing public NASA Exoplanet Archive 80-row snapshot and its source/licence/hash record in examples/assets/sciviz/stats/source.json. Axes show period, radius and period uncertainty, retaining missing observations. The direct NASA TAP download failed with a connection reset, so the existing attributed snapshot is reused without another download or another repository's code.

GPU proof: 2,000,000 physical rows repeat the real observations. One 24,000,000-byte column snapshot drives 4,000,003 line instances (all row segments plus axes), with no endpoint expansion or sampling. Every pixel of a 6,000,000-vote density raster equals the independently computed weighted base-observation reference. Native density uses GPU atomics; compatibility geometry uses the GPU, while its density kernel uses the existing CPU compute tier in 245 bounded chunks. Timing is deferred.

The package-script fixture-root repair follows Node.js contributors, *Process: process.chdir* and *ECMAScript modules: URLs* (2026), https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#processchdirdirectory and https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html#urls . # Batch 180 job 2: vector geography (2026-11-10)

Sources combined clean room: Howard Butler, Martin Daly, Allan Doyle, Sean Gillies, Stefan Hagen and Tim Schaub, The GeoJSON Format, RFC 7946 (2016), https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7946; Mike Bostock and Calvin Metcalf, The TopoJSON Format Specification (2013), https://github.com/topojson/topojson-specification/blob/master/README.md; Vladimir Agafonkin et al., Mapbox Vector Tile Specification 2.1 (2016), https://mapbox.github.io/vector-tile-spec/; David Eberly, Triangulation by Ear Clipping (2002, revised 2024), https://www.geometrictools.com/Documentation/TriangulationByEarClipping.pdf; John P. Snyder, Map Projections: A Working Manual (1987), USGS PP1395, https://pubs.usgs.gov/pp/1395/report.pdf; Daniel Carr, Richard Littlefield, W. Nicholson and J. Littlefield, Scatterplot Matrix Techniques for Large N (1987), https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1987.10478445. Great-circle equations: Eric W. Weisstein, Great Circle, MathWorld (accessed 2026-11-10), https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GreatCircle.html.

GeoJSON straight longitude/latitude segments are unwrapped before the existing owning-package ear clipper, then triangles/segments are clipped into periodic flat-map strips. Polar rings close through a pole. Longest-edge subdivision limits angular spans before WGS84 ellipsoid projection; normals support fragment horizon rejection. Great circles instead use a unit-vector tangent basis, with deterministic antipodal orientation and a metre-valued arch. Square flooring and axial hex cube rounding operate after projection, retaining exact source membership. Existing clean-room loaders/geo supplies GeoJSON, MVT protobuf and polygon holes; sciviz adds a lazy shared-arc TopoJSON decoder. Stable equivalent Mercator northing asinh(tan(latitude)) avoids cancellation at the equator and below machine epsilon in the older log-tan formula. Regression tests assert both signs and exact zero without rounding or changed tolerances.

Behavioural reference documents read, no implementation source: deck.gl GeoJsonLayer https://deck.gl/docs/api-reference/layers/geojson-layer and GreatCircleLayer https://deck.gl/docs/api-reference/geo-layers/great-circle-layer, accessed 2026-11-10. The requested row is covered by mixed point/line/polygon rendering, hole triangulation, TopoJSON shared boundaries, MVT tile/layer decoding, typed-key joins, safe-text labels with decluttering/horizon tests, spherical arcs and projected hex/square aggregations on planes and globe. No claim of matching unrelated icon atlases, extrusions or GPU aggregation is made. No rival package or companion code was read or imported. No timing result or unproven Wasm speed claim.

Real data: unmodified Natural Earth 110m country archive and Census 2024 1:20m cartographic state boundary archive derived from TIGER, public domain. Source URLs, terms, archive hashes and derived-field processing are in examples/assets/sciviz/geo-vector/source.json and prepare.mjs. The demo joins POP_EST and ALAND by their original administrative keys; labels/bins use computed interior anchors. The displayed geometric arc does not assert an observed traffic connection.

Boundary validation combines the TopoJSON integer/transform contract and GeoJSON nesting model above with David Goldberg, What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic (1991), https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html, and ECMA International, ECMAScript Language Specification, Number.isSafeInteger (2026), https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-number.issafeinteger. Delta sums reject lost integer precision, arc/bin calculations reject overflow rather than returning invalid geographic values, and preparation checks collection depth before unwrapping even hand-built GeoResult objects. Regression fixtures exercise these boundaries. Derived JSON/GeoJSON bytes are pinned to LF on Windows and validated against the asset source record.

## Review 2: live Blender Ping-Pong (2026-11-10)

Compared Blender Foundation, Math Node, Blender 5.4 Manual (2026), https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/5.4/render/shader_nodes/utilities/math/math.html (indexed description specifies bouncing from zero to Scale); Eric W. Weisstein, Triangle Wave, MathWorld (2026), https://mathworld.wolfram.com/TriangleWave.html ; and John C. Hart, Procedural Solid Texturing, SIGGRAPH Real-Time Shading Languages course (2002), https://redirect.cs.umbc.edu/~olano/s2002c36/ch06.pdf . The triangle-wave reference supplies periodic phase and reflection; the manual supplies the named operator contract; the course describes procedural evaluation on the GPU rather than baking. A floor-based period of twice the absolute scale, reflected about the scale, gives zero at even half-periods and the scale at odd half-periods. Zero scale remains zero through the existing guarded wrap. No external engine implementation or companion code was read.

Ground truth: Blender 5.3.0 Beta ecaf39c37b28, public evaluated Geometry Nodes API, 140 cases spanning signed inputs and positive/negative/zero scales. Reproduce with packages/blender/tests/pingpong-reference.py; frozen outputs are packages/blender/tests/fixtures/pingpong-truth.json. The GPU regression failed before the fix at Ping-Pong(-32,0.5), rendering 0.5 instead of zero. The old shader wrapped around a centered range, reversing phase; its original test repeated that formula and used low-sensitivity pixel encoding. Independent reference values now test every sample at a larger pixel separation with the existing one-byte tolerance. No benchmark or speed claim.

Research combined WHATWG, HTML Server-Sent Events (living standard, 2026), https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html (UTF-8/BOM, CR/LF/CRLF lines, comments, multiline data, event/id/retry fields, unfinished-event discard and HTTP 204 stop); WHATWG, WebSockets (2026), https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (browser connection and close semantics); I. Fette and A. Melnikov (2011), The WebSocket Protocol, RFC 6455, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455 (the independent local test server's handshake/frames); WHATWG Fetch (2026), https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/ and DOM AbortSignal (2026), https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#interface-abortsignal (cancel owned requests, readers, interval waits and asynchronous parsing). J. Heer and G. G. Robertson (2007), Animated Transitions in Statistical Data Graphics, https://idl.uw.edu/papers/animated-transitions, motivated continuous, stable transitions between data windows. The time recurrence is independently derived: end(t+dt) = target + (end(t)-target) exp(-dt/tau), with expm1 for the weight and a stable difference form when representable. Its semigroup and clock behavior are tested without wall-clock speed assertions.

Design comparison: queued WebSocket messages need an explicit capacity because the browser WebSocket API has no inbound backpressure; overflow rejects rather than silently dropping observations. Fetch SSE/polling naturally wait for consumer demand. Polling never overlaps requests; all sources surface HTTP/parse/connection failures and do not hide reconnection/retry loops. A native Figure replacement is built before publication, preserving the original layer object, styling, visibility and pick references. A tiny internal weak mapping handshake lets the existing optional chart controller retain original coordinates and secondary/broken mappings while data stream. No optional chart feature enters core or stage. No rival, companion or external implementation code read.

The example freezes an unmodified USGS all_day GeoJSON response and sorts only finite time/magnitude observations in the consuming demo. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program public-domain attribution, original generated time, count and SHA-256 are in examples/assets/sciviz/stream/source.json. Protocol tests use independently written local HTTP/SSE and RFC 6455 fixtures, not external source code.

## List 3 batch 66 job 5: underwater view (2026-11-10)

Extinction follows the Bouguer-Lambert-Beer law; the single-scattering phase function is L. G. Henyey and J. L. Greenstein, Diffuse radiation in the Galaxy, Astrophysical Journal 93 (1941) 70-83; Fresnel transmission uses C. Schlick, An Inexpensive BRDF Model for Physically-based Rendering, Computer Graphics Forum 13(3) (1994); refraction is Snell's law; shaft focusing uses the conservation of flux in a ray bundle (irradiance inversely proportional to the bundle's cross-section, M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, section 3.1) applied to the Jacobian of the refracted ray map. Absorption defaults reuse Water's existing values of the order of R. M. Pope and E. S. Fry (1997), already cited. These were written from those published formulas; none of the papers was re-read in this session, and C. D. Mobley, Light and Water (1994), on ocean scattering coefficients, could not be read. No engine source was read.

### Batch 234 job 3 continuation: dielectric underside and continuous traces (2026-11-10)

Compared Morgan McGuire and Michael Mara, Efficient GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing, JCGT 3(4), 2014, https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/paper.pdf (abstract and algorithm properties, sections 1.1 and 1.2, not the implementation listing or companion code); Bruce Walter, Stephen R. Marschner, Hongsong Li and Kenneth E. Torrance, Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces, EGSR 2007, https://doi.org/10.2312/egwr/egsr07/195-206 (publication abstract and refraction framing); Matt Pharr, Wenzel Jakob and Greg Humphreys, Physically Based Rendering, fourth edition, Specular Reflection and Transmission, 2023, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/Reflection_Models/Specular_Reflection_and_Transmission (physical principles, Snell/Fresnel equations and total internal reflection; no implementation copied); and Tiago Sousa, Generic Refraction Simulation, GPU Gems 2 chapter 19, 2005, https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems2/part-ii-shading-lighting-and-shadows/chapter-19-generic-refraction-simulation (capture ownership/foreground-contamination discussion, no sample code).

The combination is exact dielectric interface transport plus frustum-clipped traversal through the projected ray's actual grid-edge crossings. Original local depth-plane reconstruction and per-texel intersection validation replace the rejected distance-based march and binary depth-discontinuity crossings. Analytic tests exposed missed short corner intervals and independently reconstructed plane cracks at float32 texel boundaries; visit every crossed cell and use a relative arithmetic envelope. Snapshot current opaque depth before FFT writes its interface, preventing first-frame self-hits. The GPU shader helper is shared with an independent world-space plane oracle (1,026 rays); full rendered Water/FFT images use a separate double-precision Snell/Fresnel oracle. All fixtures are original mathematics. The preview uses existing NOAA/NDBC 46042 public-domain wind data (test/data/README.md). No rival source, companion code or foreign files were read or copied.

Public web-library behaviour checked: Orillusion authors, Water Rendering - WaterRenderer, retrieved 2026-11-10, https://www.orillusion.com/en/guide/water/Readme.html, describes Snell's window about 48.6 degrees from vertical and reflection of submerged geometry outside it. At IOR 1.333 Margo's analytic critical angle is asin(1/1.333), and the GPU oracle independently proves both sides, transmitted sky/environment and visible opaque scene tracing. The row's other components were built by ee255b572. Hidden/off-screen geometry and a full-scene path-traced result are not claimed.

## Review 3 P1: stationary smoothing endpoint (2026-11-10)

Compared Ecma International, ECMAScript 2027 Language Specification draft (2026), Number::exponentiate, https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/ecmascript-data-types-and-values.html#sec-numeric-types-number-exponentiate ; Matt Pharr, Wenzel Jakob and Greg Humphreys, Physically Based Rendering, fourth edition (2023), Managing Rounding Error, https://www.pbr-book.org/4ed/Shapes/Managing_Rounding_Error ; and MIT 6.310 teaching staff, First Order Difference Equations (2026), https://introcontrol.mit.edu/fall26/prelabs/prelab3/propc_deriveq . The recurrence supplies the retained-error power and stationary endpoint; the numeric references explain overflow and the specified NaN for a unit base with an infinite exponent. Evaluate the equivalent weight as -expm1(log1p(-lerp) * delta * 60), with a zero-delta endpoint. Multiplying by the log decay before 60 prevents premature frame-count overflow; log1p retains tiny positive lerp values that 1-lerp rounds away, and expm1 avoids cancellation in the closed fraction. The standard also specifies both operations and their zero/infinite endpoints: https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/numbers-and-dates.html#sec-math.log1p and https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/numbers-and-dates.html#sec-math.expm1 . The finite nonnegative time domain is unchanged without a cap or new API. Independent CPU assertions cover scalar/per-axis zero, unit and fractional smoothing, zero/subnormal/frame/near-maximum/maximum finite deltas, and a 1e-20 smoothing fraction across 1e20/60 seconds with independently expected [63,126] pixels. The regression fails on the original implementation. No external implementation or companion source was read.

## Batch 132 audit: splines sources not recorded before

- Kochanek-Bartels tangents (`kind: 'kochanek-bartels'`, packages/splines/src/index.ts): D. H. U. Kochanek and R. H.
  Bartels, "Interpolating splines with local tension, continuity, and bias control", SIGGRAPH 1984,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/800031.808575 . Not read in full (ACM paywall); the code's source and destination tangent
  weights (1 - t)(1 +- b)(1 +- c) / 2 were checked against the published form as it is widely restated.
- Uniform cubic B-spline basis ((1 - u)^3, 3u^3 - 6u^2 + 4, -3u^3 + 3u^2 + 3u + 1, u^3, over 6): textbook, checked by
  partition of unity and C2 joins.
- Rotation-minimising frames (packages/splines/src/frames.ts): W. Wang, B. Juttler, D. Zheng and Y. Liu, "Computation
  of rotation minimizing frames", ACM TOG 27(1), 2008, https://doi.org/10.1145/1330511.1330513 . Not read in full (the
  publisher copy is paywalled, the Microsoft Research page has only the abstract, the HKU copy is gone); the two
  reflections (v1 = x(i+1) - x(i), then v2 = t(i+1) - t(i) reflected) match the algorithm as restated in the abstract
  and in later citing work. The closed-loop twist spread evenly over the samples is Margo's own.
- Curve fitting (packages/splines/src/fit.ts): least-squares cubic with fixed end tangent directions, Newton
  reparameterisation and a split at the worst point, as in P. J. Schneider, "An algorithm for automatically fitting
  digitized curves", Graphics Gems (1990). Not read in full (book).
- Exact closest point (packages/splines/src/closest.ts, batch 132 fix): the stationary points of the squared distance to
  a cubic Bezier piece are the roots of the quintic (B(u) - q) . B'(u), written in Bernstein form by the product rule
  for Bernstein polynomials and isolated by de Casteljau subdivision, bounded by the sign changes of the coefficients
  (variation diminishing), as in Patrikalakis, Maekawa and Cho, Shape Interrogation (hyperbook, sections 1.3.4 and 4,
  already cited for batch 225); pieces whose control-point box lies farther than the best distance are skipped by the
  convex hull property. Margo's own design otherwise; no rival or companion code read.

The independent model combines WGS72 un-Kozai recovery, J2/J3/J4 gravity, atmospheric/perigee adjustments, full drag polynomials, two rotated third-body bases, piecewise resonance eccentricity/inclination functions, 720-minute Taylor integration from epoch on each seek, perturbed-inclination Lyddane corrections and TEME reconstruction. Only papers, standards and public behaviour descriptions were consulted; no companion or rival implementation was read or copied.
Roberts motivates shared state with explicit coordination boundaries; Chen et al. motivates independently captioned comparative cells. The implementation selects several figures, as permitted by the job, and uses existing engine frame callbacks plus controls events to copy complete camera pose or selected physical ranges, stamping recipients to prevent echoes. Date origins and log mappings transfer through each scale's inverse/forward functions, using existing plot-space limits internally. There is no prototype patching or core/stage change. FigureLayout owns its DOM and engines; ComparativeGrid instantiates one immutable PipelineJSON with a shared operator registry for every time/parameter cell, with independent caches and explicit release. Figure creation and comparison failures clean up owned resources and preserve unrelated DOM.
Teem's physical spacing and the reslice-cursor behaviour reference motivate a nearest-sample physical crosshair: three true orthographic 2D slice figures and the matching three planes inside a 3D volume. Every output sample retains its original voxel index and endpoint orientation. Crosshair coordinates clamp and snap to original sample centres, updates are serialised, unpublished planes are cleaned on cancellation, and crosshairs appear in all four figures through the existing optional annotation entry. Equal physical distances occupy equal screen distances; resize retains zoom and centre. The slice loop copies only three requested planes; no CPU throughput claim or Rust/Wasm gain was measured.
Full requested row coverage is in views.test.js and views-browser.mjs: bidirectional camera and selected-axis range links, echo prevention, physical date origins, time and parameter comparison cells, transactional failure/disposal, exact descending/anisotropic slice values and IDs, real NOAA daily wind cells, actual linked drag, OpenNeuro T1 crosshairs/planes, isotropic projection and resize, and cancelled queued work on both rendering backends. Existing OpenNeuro ds000030 (CC0, 2 mm sampled spacing) and NOAA Reanalysis 1 (public domain) assets and provenance records are reused. Comparative speeds are derived only from observed east/north samples; the 15 m/s parameter masks samples, and does not fabricate observations. No neurological registration, oblique reslicing, clinical, memory-sharing or timing claim.

Golub and Randall J. LeVeque, "Algorithms for Computing the Sample Variance: Analysis and Recommendations" (1983), https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1983.10483115 (paper https://math.pku.edu.cn/teachers/litj/notes/numer_anal/AmerStat_37_242_Chan_Variance.pdf ); NIST DLMF editorial team, "Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, 3.3 Interpolation" (2010 onward), https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.3 ; Brian Eaton, Jonathan Gregory, Bob Drach, Karl Taylor, Steve Hankin et al., "NetCDF Climate and Forecast Metadata Conventions 1.12" (2024), https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14275599 , section 4.4; Kitware / ParaView contributors, "Loading Data: Handling temporal file series" (6.2 documentation, read 2026-11-10), https://docs.paraview.org/en/latest/UsersGuide/dataIngestion.html ; Plotly contributors, "Time Series in JavaScript" (read 2026-11-10), https://plotly.com/javascript/time-series/ . Only papers, mathematical definitions, the published file format and public behaviour docs were read; no rival repository code was inspected, copied or adapted.

Welford supplies the online centered recurrence; Chan/Golub/LeVeque motivates shifting before accumulation to avoid cancellation on large-offset small-variance fields, instead of naive sum-of-squares subtraction or a second reader pass. NIST's degree-one interpolation supplies exact adjacent-key weights. CF supplies fixed duration units and explicit reference origins; calendar decoding remains separate. ParaView supplies numbered-file grouping and .series JSON version 1.0. Plotly's public date-series behaviour informs gap-preserving charts using existing Figure primitives, with a relative origin to preserve float32 detail. Mathematical reductions are checked against independent two-pass reference calculations, including real data; chart raster and resource behaviour is checked on both backends. This covers the requested temporal row without depending on another engine. Native curves, spatial probes and restoration reuse their owning packages rather than introducing rendering code here.

Data research: Stephan Rasp et al., "WeatherBench 2: A Benchmark for the Next Generation of Data-Driven Global Weather Models" (2024), https://doi.org/10.1029/2023MS004019 ; Hans Hersbach et al., "The ERA5 global reanalysis" (2020), https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.3803 . The previously prepared WeatherBench2 2m-temperature subset retains actual six-hour samples and the original float32 values in CDF2. NOAA daily wind is repacked from the repository's pinned NetCDF without a new download. Producer licence links, exact selections, transformations and hashes are in examples/assets/sciviz/temporal/source.json. scripts/prepare-sciviz-temporal.mjs regenerates the NOAA series and manifest locally. No synthetic climate observations are used.

Entry: 0 -> 3,901 B gzip, ceiling 4,157 B. One small optional entry keeps the source contract, file-series bridge and time units coherent; a split would add loader/API coordination. Spatial probing stays behind import('@margoengine/sciviz/probe'). Core + stage stays 24,209 B. No timing measurement, speed claim or new Wasm kernel: these streaming reductions have no measured Wasm/SIMD gain.

Only papers and public descriptions were consulted, not their implementations.

Execution uses one private feature-local Rust/Wasm instance per model, loaded by new URL only when loadOnnx is called. Tensor handles own immutable shared storage with copy-on-write output mutation. A graph's last-use references and nested execution frames retain live tensors, captured values, loop state and scans, then release intermediates deterministically. Returned host tensors copy their data and remain valid after model disposal. The test corpus includes unchanged Model Zoo MNIST-12 input/output data, exact int64 above 2^53, scalar broadcast SIMD and odd tails, memory growth, retained outputs, instance isolation, function reference attributes, external ranges, sparse coordinates, branch capture, Loop/Scan direction/state, sequence/optional values, cancellation and repeated runs. No speed claim or full-catalogue completion claim is made by this record.

Additional job 5 schema references: ONNX contributors, RNN/LSTM/GRU and Resize schemas (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__RNN.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__LSTM.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__GRU.html and https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__Resize.html . These supply i,o,f,c and z,r,h gate layouts, i,o,f peepholes, both GRU reset placements, direction/layout/state/length conventions, coordinate transforms, nearest tie modes, cubic convolution and widened antialias filters. Separable interpolation retains f64 intermediates and converts to the declared output type once; nearest copies raw typed elements. The research already cited for job 4 supplies recurrent and cubic-interpolation background. Rust contributors, slice::sort_by and f64::total_cmp API contracts (2026), https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html#method.sort_by and https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html#method.total_cmp , require a total comparator even with NaNs. TopK therefore places NaNs above finite values, keeps equal-value index ties stable and tests mixed NaN/finite input; this is a deterministic choice for the schema's otherwise unspecified NaN ordering. No Rust sorting implementation was read. Empty EyeLike outputs return before traversing metadata rows, covered by a two-billion-row zero-width regression with zero element work.

Model-local function validation caches each immutable definition's validated nesting height. This follows the typed graph-lowering separation in Jin et al. (2020) and the ONNX IR's model-local function identity/opset rules cited above. Shared call DAGs are not expanded into trees during validation. The regression checks exactly 25 validated definitions for a depth-24 double-call DAG, a smaller graph's exact integer64 output, and rejection of a cached definition reused beyond nesting depth 64. Inference counts expanded node invocations, including function wrappers and loop bodies, against maxNodes (default 1000000, caller adjustable); the work-limit regression aborts at its explicit count and proves temporary disposal. These are deterministic correctness/work-count checks, with no wall-clock assertion or speed claim.

The same DAG reasoning applies to typed input/output containers: Identity handles sequence and optional values, cyclic input containers reject with guidance, and shared nested sequences are uploaded, type-checked, traversed for retention and snapshotted once per shared object/type. The regression retains a 16-level double-reference sequence graph, exact int64 leaf values and shared output identity, and rejects a cyclic container without live storage. Typed empty/erased sequences retain their declared element dtype, so a later insertion cannot change it. Input types of nested Loop/Scan body graphs are checked as well as their outputs. These are ONNX IR/type/Identity semantics from the specifications cited above, implemented without another runtime's source.

ONNX contributors, ReduceMean and ReduceL2 schemas (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__ReduceMean.html and https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__ReduceL2.html , were checked against the integer64 boundary cases from the conformance strategy above. Integer ReduceMean now sums in signed/unsigned 128-bit storage and divides exactly before returning the declared integer type: the tensor element cap proves the intermediate sum fits, while neither f64 rounding above 2^53 nor a 64-bit sum overflow can corrupt an otherwise representable mean. Native and Wasm model tests cover repeated 9007199254740993, signed extrema and unsigned extrema. Empty-set integer mean remains undefined by ONNX; the current typed result is zero. Composite reduction cast/version conformance remains part of the unfinished importer catalogue review.

- John K. Salmon, Mark A. Moraes, Ron O. Dror and David E. Shaw, Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1, 2, 3 (2011), https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/john-salmon/parallel-random.pdf ; George E. P. Box and Mervin E. Muller, A Note on the Generation of Random Normal Deviates (1958), https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177706645 . Philox4x32-10 supplies counter-based streams, Box-Muller supplies normal variates. The native test checks the paper's zero-key/counter vector. Each expanded lexical function/graph call site owns a persistent stream; repeated runs and loop iterations advance that stream, while sessions isolate storage and state. ONNX does not prescribe a seeded bit sequence across runtimes. Multinomial uses stabilized log-probability weights; Dropout applies inverse keep-probability scaling only in training. Specifications: ONNX contributors, RandomUniform, RandomNormal, Bernoulli, Multinomial and Dropout schemas (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__RandomUniform.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__RandomNormal.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__Bernoulli.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__Multinomial.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__Dropout.html . Small output types round once; uniforms exclude their upper endpoint after narrowing, including a zero upper bound.
- Guy E. Blelloch, Prefix Sums and Their Applications (1990), https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs.cmu.edu/project/scandal/public/papers/CMU-CS-90-190.html ; Nicholas J. Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, second edition, chapter 9 (2002), https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9780898718027.ch9 . The associative scan formulation supplies reverse/exclusive cumulative products; partial pivoting supplies batched determinants. Jonathan T. Barron, Continuously Differentiable Exponential Linear Units (2017), https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.07483 ; Prajit Ramachandran, Barret Zoph and Quoc V. Le, Searching for Activation Functions (2017), https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05941 . These supply Celu and Swish, combined with ONNX's typed scalar/shape rules for Shrink and SwiGLU. Unique uses stable lexicographic ordering over whole axis slices, then restores first occurrence order for sorted=0; int64 comparisons never pass through f64. Source schemas: ONNX contributors (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__Unique.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__Det.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__CumProd.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__CenterCropPad.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__ReverseSequence.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__BitCast.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__SwiGLU.html .
- Max Jaderberg, Karen Simonyan, Andrew Zisserman and Koray Kavukcuoglu, Spatial Transformer Networks (2015), https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02025 ; Kaiming He, Georgia Gkioxari, Piotr Dollar and Ross Girshick, Mask R-CNN (2017), https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06870 ; Alexander Neubeck and Luc Van Gool, Efficient Non-Maximum Suppression (2006), https://homes.esat.kuleuven.be/~konijn/publications/2006/eth_biwi_00446.pdf . Grid interpolation and affine homogeneous coordinates come from spatial transformers, unquantized ROI bins from Mask R-CNN. The NMS paper addresses image-local maxima, so it is background, not the box-IoU algorithm: ONNX's specification defines score-ordered box suppression, stable ties and strict greater-than IoU. Compared schemas: ONNX contributors (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__GridSample.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__AffineGrid.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__RoiAlign.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__NonMaxSuppression.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__MaxRoiPool.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__Col2Im.html . All grid dimensions and interpolation taps are retained; Col2Im sums overlapping blocks, without changing the work to imitate another runtime's speed.
- Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio and Aaron Courville, Deep Learning (2016), https://www.deeplearningbook.org/ , numerical computation and maximum-likelihood chapters; ONNX contributors, NegativeLogLikelihoodLoss and SoftmaxCrossEntropyLoss schemas (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__NegativeLogLikelihoodLoss.html and https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__SoftmaxCrossEntropyLoss.html . Max-shifted log-softmax avoids overflow; ignored labels contribute neither loss nor normalization weight. Tests retain the channel axis for arbitrary spatial targets and the optional log-probability output.
- Leo I. Bluestein, A Linear Filtering Approach to the Computation of the Discrete Fourier Transform (1970), https://doi.org/10.1109/TAU.1970.1162132 ; Fredric J. Harris, On the Use of Windows for Harmonic Analysis with the Discrete Fourier Transform (1978), https://web.mit.edu/xiphmont/Public/windows.pdf ; S. S. Stevens, Jens Volkmann and Edwin B. Newman, A Scale for the Measurement of the Psychological Magnitude Pitch (1937), https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1915893 . Radix-two FFT plus Bluestein avoids quadratic prime transforms; the native test independently evaluates the defining DFT sum at prime/composite lengths and checks inverse normalization. ONNX defines the Mel formula and triangle spacing, periodic/symmetric window conventions, optional lengths, padding/truncation, component dimensions, arbitrary DFT axis, one-sided forward and real inverse, and STFT frame/window layout. Source schemas: ONNX contributors (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__DFT.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__STFT.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__HannWindow.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__HammingWindow.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__BlackmanWindow.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__MelWeightMatrix.html . No speed measurement or wall-clock assertion was run.
- ONNX contributors, StringConcat, StringSplit, StringNormalizer, SequenceMap and ai.onnx.ml operator schemas (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__StringConcat.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__StringSplit.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__StringNormalizer.html , https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__SequenceMap.html and https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/ . Rust handles UTF-8 concatenation and bounded splitting; platform locale casing handles StringNormalizer, including Turkish, with default en-US and C/POSIX mapped to that locale. SequenceMap executes the complete lexical body per element. ML preprocessing follows exact integer/category keys, tensor-valued label attributes and last-key wins; map operators preserve typed scalar values and int64 keys. The model input's map value declaration types an empty dictionary. Dictionary vectorization uses the schema's [1,C] output convention. All code is original; schema function bodies were read only as normative specifications, not copied. No companion or rival implementation source was read.

These are build notes for an incomplete importer, not an ONNX/ONNX Runtime parity or completion claim. Remaining operators and conformance cases must be built and tested before job 5 can land.

Further batch 274 job 5 conformance evidence (2026-11-10): 96 pinned, original analytic cases agree with unmodified ONNX Runtime 1.31.1 CPUExecutionProvider, ONNX 1.23.2 and NumPy 2.5.4; graph optimizations are disabled and both runtime thread counts are one. The external runtime lives in ../../Tools/margo-oracles/onnx-batch274 from the checkout (the workstation's tools folder), outside this repository. Only its public Python API was invoked; no implementation file was opened, copied or adapted. Two additional requested comparisons (float64 Det and int64 Binarizer) are unavailable in that provider and have independent analytic regressions instead. This is coverage evidence for these cases, not full importer parity. The same pinned references run in Node and Chromium without that runtime installed. Source and versions are in packages/compute/tests/fixtures/onnx/operators-reference.json; original fixture generator, external runner and recorder are packages/compute/scripts/onnx-oracle-{cases.mjs,record.mjs} and onnx-oracle.py.

The comparison exposed and now covers three specification details: StringSplit removes trailing whitespace from its unsplit whitespace suffix; RoiAlign mode=max takes the maximum weighted corner contributions as in ONNX's published mode-max conformance data (not the average mode's sum); MelWeightMatrix first quantizes inverse-Mel boundaries to frequency bins and uses the published example's bins+2 interval convention. Small and wider matrices both test coincident boundaries and fractional ramps. Spectral window scalar coefficients use f32 constants (Blackman from alpha=0.16) before promotion, matching the tested runtime's construction. Relevant published examples are on the StringSplit, RoiAlign and MelWeightMatrix schema pages cited above. No tests or numerical tolerances were weakened.

LinearClassifier and LinearRegressor use the ONNX contributors' ai.onnx.ml schemas (2026), https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx_aionnxml_LinearClassifier.html and https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx_aionnxml_LinearRegressor.html . Eight full-score-vector cases cover NONE, LOGISTIC, SOFTMAX and SOFTMAX_ZERO against the external runtime. Binary class state, exact integer labels, multiple targets and omitted intercepts also have analytic tests. Michael J. Wichura, The Percentage Points of the Normal Distribution, Algorithm AS 241 (1988), https://doi.org/10.2307/2347330 , was compared with NIST DLMF, sections 7.9, 7.17 and 8.9 (2026), https://dlmf.nist.gov/7.9 , https://dlmf.nist.gov/7.17 and https://dlmf.nist.gov/8.9 . Unlike the paper's rational approximation, Margo independently inverts the smaller normal tail by bounded bisection using the existing incomplete-gamma continued fraction, avoiding 1-CDF cancellation. Native tests cover p=0.2, 0.975, 1e-20 and 1e-40 to 2e-13 absolute z error. Accepted numerical difference under review before final job completion: the external runtime's PROBIT at float32 p=0.2 is about -0.8417561, while Margo returns the correctly rounded value near -0.8416212; single-target regression also applies the declared LOGISTIC/SOFTMAX transforms rather than the external provider's raw-score shortcut. The native exact-quantile and single-target analytic tests prove the intended mathematical behavior. This is not a blanket equivalence claim.

Map keys are validated and normalized before upload, with number/bigint aliases rejected as duplicate keys and declared signed/unsigned 32/64-bit bounds enforced. BitCast retains raw bool bits within the graph; owned host Tensor<bool> snapshots canonicalize truth values to 0/1. The regression observes both the logical bool snapshot and a subsequent in-graph BitCast back to the original uint8 bytes. The protobuf/IR specifications cited above own these representation and map-type boundaries.

The empty-product review also covers Col2Im, AffineGrid, ROI outputs and FeatureVectorizer: zero elements terminate before traversal of metadata rows or interpolation grids. The regression passes a billion-row, zero-width batch through Col2Im and FeatureVectorizer and checks exact empty shapes, without a timing assertion. This is the same row-major tensor product invariant from the ONNX IR and the work-count reasoning already cited above; no benchmark or reduced nonempty workload was introduced.

## Batch 175 job 5: GPU graph layout

Clean-room TypeScript and WGSL, without companion or rival source code. Research compared:

- Thomas M. J. Fruchterman and Edward M. Reingold, 1991, "Graph Drawing by Force-directed Placement", https://doi.org/10.1002/spe.4380211102. Retain the existing CPU reference; use its weighted attraction, repulsion and quench/simmer on the GPU.
- Josh Barnes and Piet Hut, 1986, "A hierarchical O(N log N) force-calculation algorithm", https://doi.org/10.1038/324446a0. A complete Morton grid tree supplies actual occupied bounding boxes, mass-weighted centres, exact leaf interactions and a stackless traversal. Cells containing the target always open; the opening test includes the centre-of-mass offset. Bitonic compare-exchange sorting is device-side on both backends, avoiding the compute package's CPU compatibility radix route.
- Mathieu Jacomy, Tommaso Venturini, Sebastien Heymann and Mathieu Bastian, 2014, "ForceAtlas2, a Continuous Graph Layout Algorithm for Handy Network Visualization Designed for the Gephi Software", https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0098679. Combine degree-plus-one masses, weighted attraction, optional LinLog/dissuade-hubs/strong gravity/radius overlap prevention, and swinging/traction global and local speed control. GPU reductions keep the adaptive controller on the device. The CPU all-pairs reference independently evaluates these equations.
- Danny Holten and Jarke J. van Wijk, 2009, "Force-Directed Edge Bundling for Graph Visualization", https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01450.x. Combine symmetric angle, scale, position and visibility compatibility, fixed endpoints, compatible electrostatic attraction, springs and arc-length resampling. Reversed directions reverse subdivision correspondence. Degenerate edges have zero compatibility.
- Peng Mi, Maoyuan Sun, Moeti Masiane and Chris North, 2016, "Interactive Graph Layout of a Million Nodes", https://doi.org/10.3390/informatics3040023. Motivates GPU-resident hierarchy/layout/drawing and explicit million-node work evidence; Margo uses a spatial hierarchy rather than their topological clustering.

Rival behaviour reviewed from public documentation only: Cosmograph configuration and concept, https://cosmograph.app/docs-lib/api/internal/interfaces/GraphConfigInterface/ and https://next.cosmograph.app/docs/concept/. This job covers GPU many-body layout, directed styled edges and label suppression at scale; it adds named FR/FA2 references and FDEB. No relative speed claim. Labels use priority-ordered four-anchor placement with a spatial hash, retaining only disjoint in-viewport rectangles. Pixel tests cover changing widths, colours, arrows and bundled paths.

OpenAlex citation metadata and relationships are CC0. The 80 original query results retain original work IDs, titles, years and outgoing referenced-work IDs. The demo uses their induced citation subgraph; the million-node correctness proof explicitly repeats that topology, not a million distinct publications. Query, retrieval time and SHA-256 live next to the fixture. Reproduce with packages/sciviz/scripts/fetch-graph-gpu-data.mjs; a fresh query can change, so tests use the pinned snapshot.

WGSL arithmetic and buffer alignment follow W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, WebGPU Shading Language, Candidate Recommendation Draft 6 November 2026 (editors Alan Baker, Mehmet Oguz Derin and David Neto), https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/CRD-WGSL-20261106/#arithmetic-expr. The straight-edge regression covers unsigned zero subtraction: clamp the point count before subtracting, so each unbundled instance retains its own edge index.

Research compared Brian Eaton, Jonathan Gregory, Bob Drach, Karl Taylor, Steve Hankin et al., NetCDF Climate and Forecast (CF) Metadata Conventions 1.12 (2024), https://cfconventions.org/Data/cf-conventions/cf-conventions-1.12/cf-conventions.html , sections 3-5, 6.1, 7.1, 8.1 and appendices D/F; John P. Snyder, Map Projections: A Working Manual (1987), USGS PP1395, https://doi.org/10.3133/pp1395 , mathematical pages 100-109, 161-162 and 251-252; and John P. Snyder and Philip M. Voxland, An Album of Map Projections (1989), USGS PP1453, https://doi.org/10.3133/pp1453 , Robinson definition and table on pp. 222-223 (public USGS paper mirror https://www.imaginary.org/sites/default/files/an_album_of_map_projections.pdf ). Scanned mathematical pages were rendered and read, not companion programs.
Also compared Philip W. Jones, First- and Second-Order Conservative Remapping Schemes for Grids in Spherical Coordinates (1999), https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1999)127%3C2204:FASOCR%3E2.0.CO;2 , area-overlap weighting and the distinction between conserving cell integrals and interpolating point values; F. N. Fritsch and J. Butland, A Method for Constructing Local Monotone Piecewise Cubic Interpolants (1984), https://doi.org/10.1137/0905021 , local monotone cubic construction; and P. J. Rasch and D. L. Williamson, On Shape-Preserving Interpolation and Semi-Lagrangian Transport (1990), https://doi.org/10.1137/0911039 , bibliographic/abstract comparison of shape preservation. No claim of reproducing the latter's full transport method. Our map display uses bounded bilinear weights and strict/renormalized masks; the separate first-order conservative rectilinear remap uses exact longitude times sine-latitude overlap areas and returns coverage. The Robinson table is interpolated by local harmonic-slope cubic Hermite segments, with an inverse of the same segments. Its original published table does not prescribe a unique between-knot interpolant; no fitted coefficients were borrowed.
CF owns lazy coordinate metadata over the existing NetCDF decoder, arbitrary data-axis transposition, scalar and auxiliary coordinates, unit conversions, model-calendar arithmetic and vertical formula broadcasting. Named dimensions prevent silent first-time/first-level selection. Geographic auxiliary coordinates take priority over projected x/y. The new projection entry owns ellipsoidal conics, polar stereographic and Mercator plus spherical world projections, inverse-domain masking and central-meridian wrapping. Core and stage are untouched. These are bounded analytical transforms and display remaps, not a new iterative dense solver or a performance claim; no timing proof was run in the build phase.
Black-box comparisons: PROJ 9.8.1 via pyproj 3.8.0 was invoked only as an installed numerical tool; no implementation source was read. The owner-generated numerical fixture packages/sciviz/tests/fixtures/climate-projection-reference.json records the actual version and all 392 coordinates. Ellipsoidal and spherical conics, both polar aspects and Mollweide agree within 1e-6 metres at the fixture points. Robinson defining knots agree within 1.2 metres (PROJ's coefficient precision differs); off-knot forward/inverse consistency and spherical area Jacobians are tested separately. No external implementation files were copied. Incidental search snippets from projection repositories were not used.
Rival documentation read 2026-11-10: deck.gl BitmapLayer https://deck.gl/docs/api-reference/layers/bitmap-layer (geographic bounds/corners and image resampling); CesiumJS ImageryLayer https://cesium.com/learn/cesiumjs/ref-doc/ImageryLayer.html (imagery presentation); PROJ projection behavior https://proj.org/en/stable/operations/projections/robin.html . Requested CF/calendars/vertical/regrid and five named projections are all implemented; the graphics raster layers alone do not interpret CF metadata. No speed or universal CF-validator claim. Tests are cf.test.js, projections.test.js and cf-browser.mjs.
Real ERA5 and IPSL CMIP6 tas/sftlf fields, coordinates, scalar labels and monthly time bounds are retained in examples/assets/sciviz/climate/. ERA5 indices 89124:89132 are 2020-01-02 00:00 through 2020-01-03 18:00, six-hourly; CMIP6 is 12 monthly samples of 1850. ERA5 CC BY 4.0 (Copernicus catalogue https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/reanalysis-era5-single-levels?tab=overview, distributed via WeatherBench 2) and the IPSL producer's CC BY 4.0 relicense https://cmc.ipsl.fr/online-resources/ were checked. Ten deprecated legacy-tree ML5 exports are refused by that external provider and retain analytic Margo checks, alongside the two existing unavailable provider kernels. The newer TreeEnsemble ML5 path is directly compared in both float32 and float64. Chromium runs all pinned cases and analytic cases without an external runtime. ## Batch 176 job 5: tensor fields
Written clean room from papers and public numerical-library APIs, never companion code. James Demmel and Kresimir Veselic (1992), *Jacobi's Method is More Accurate than QR*, https://doi.org/10.1137/0613074 ; Joachim Kopp (2008), *Efficient numerical diagonalization of hermitian 3x3 matrices*, https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0610206 . Comparing iterative rotations with analytic roots favoured scaled largest-pivot Jacobi for stability. Gordon Kindlmann (2004), *Superquadric Tensor Glyphs*, https://doi.org/10.2312/VisSym/VisSym04/147-154 and https://cgl.ethz.ch/teaching/scivis_common/Literature/kindlmann04.pdf (equations 2 and 7) supply trace-normalized linear/planar shape metrics, axis selection and sharpness. The implementation retains exact analytic quarter-turn zeros before signed fractional powers; this preserves sharp glyph symmetry despite finite-precision trigonometry. Signed tensors use their absolute spectral geometry while retaining signed eigenvalues in the result.
Peter J. Basser, James Mattiello and Denis Le Bihan (1994), *Estimation of the effective self-diffusion tensor from the NMR spin echo*, https://doi.org/10.1006/jmrb.1994.1037 supplies ordinary log-linear least squares; the implementation fits all seven parameters including baseline using one shared, twice-reorthogonalized QR decomposition. Susumu Mori, Barbara J. Crain, Vadappuram P. Chacko and Peter C. M. van Zijl (1999), *Three-dimensional tracking of axonal projections in the brain by magnetic resonance imaging*, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9989633/ and Mori et al. (1999), *3D Reconstruction of Axonal Fibers from Diffusion Tensor Imaging using Fiber Assignment by Continuous Tracking (FACT)*, https://archive.ismrm.org/1999/0320.html motivate deterministic voxel-boundary traversal. Chamberlin, Rosendo Valero, Christopher J. Cramer and Donald G. Truhlar, *Consistent van der Waals Radii for the Whole Main Group* (2009), https://doi.org/10.1021/jp8111556. Research first compared Nystad, Lassen, Pomianowski, Ellis and Olson (2012),
*Adaptive Scalable Texture Compression*, sections 4 and 5,
https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15869-f11/www/readings/nystad12_astc.pdf;
Wang, Bovik, Sheikh and Simoncelli (2004), *Image Quality Assessment: From Error
Visibility to Structural Similarity*, equations 13-17,
https://ece.uwaterloo.ca/~z70wang/publications/ssim.pdf; and Chou, Lookabaugh and
Gray (1989), *Entropy-Constrained Vector Quantization*, sections II-III,
https://web.stanford.edu/class/ee398a/handouts/papers/Chou%20-%20EC%20VQ.pdf.
Griffin and Olano (2015), *Evaluating Texture Compression Masking Effects using
Objective Image Quality Assessment Metrics*, NIST abstract only,
https://www.nist.gov/publications/evaluating-texture-compression-masking-effects-using-objective-image-quality-assessment,
distinguishes texture metrics from rendered masking; this job retains Scott's
texture bars. These sources were read only in the stated sections, not in full.

The unconditioned data row passed both bars but exceeded its byte budget. Finer
RDO alone still failed. A Node built-in Zstandard black-box probe demonstrated
lossless rate headroom; no implementation was inspected. The implementation
combines the merge construction described in David A. Huffman (1952), *A Method
for the Construction of Minimum-Redundancy Codes*, publication scan metadata,
https://compression.ru/download/articles/huff/huffman_1952_minimum-redundancy-codes.pdf,
with Yann Collet and Murray Kucherawy (2021), *RFC 8878: Zstandard Compression and
the application/zstd Media Type*, sections 3.1.1.3.1, 4.1.1 and 4.2, read in full,
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8878.html. No companion source was read. The
bounded eleven-bit tree smooths rare frequency counts when needed; FSE weight
descriptions and reverse streams follow the normative RFC. The existing Margo
Zstandard decoder supplied independent in-repository interoperability checks.
No RDO objective, fitting code, corpus or quality assertion changed in round 10.

### Cache eviction removal totals (2026-11-10)

Compared Steve Becker (editor), W3C, *Indexed Database API 3.0* (2026 working draft), transaction lifecycle and asynchronously executing requests, https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/WD-IndexedDB-3-20261030/, with Roy Fielding, Mark Nottingham and Julian Reschke, *RFC 9111: HTTP Caching* (2022), section 4.1, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-4.1. Vary selects distinct stored representations; IndexedDB executes requests in placement order and accepts further requests in success callbacks. The removal batch accumulates each distinct key's contribution before one totals write, with no per-key reads of stale totals. No external implementation or companion code was read or copied.

### Zero-to-transmission lifecycle (lane Q, 2026-11-10)

Compared The Khronos Group, *KHR_animation_pointer* (2024, [specification](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_animation_pointer/README.md)); The Khronos Group, *KHR_materials_transmission* (2020, [specification](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_transmission/README.md)); The Khronos Group, *KHR_materials_volume* (2021, [specification](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_volume/README.md)); and Matt Pharr, Wenzel Jakob and Greg Humphreys, *Physically Based Rendering*, fourth edition, section 11.2 (2023, [Transmittance](https://www.pbr-book.org/4ed/Volume_Scattering/Transmittance)). Read specifications and the textbook only, no companion or engine source.

Animation capability follows the authored extension, rather than the initial scalar value. The transmission percentage and the medium's optical depth are separate state: zero transmission is opaque while the medium remains available for later samples. The parser reserves attenuation, optical depth and volume only for a physical transmission extension. Pointer writes create tint on positive transmission and remove it at zero; capture registration is inactive until tint is present. No core/stage or optional import boundary changes.

### Asset-cache delayed hit bookkeeping (2026-11-10)

Compared Steve Becker (editor), W3C, *Indexed Database API 3.0* (2026 working draft), transaction lifecycle and scheduling, https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/WD-IndexedDB-3-20261030/, with Roy Fielding, Mark Nottingham and Julian Reschke, *RFC 9111: HTTP Caching* (2022), section 4.3.4, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-4.3.4. The read and conditional update stay within one transaction; 304 freshness is applied only while the stored validators match the validated snapshot. Last use updates the current record, preserving all its other metadata, and cannot recreate a removed record. No external implementation or companion code was read or copied.

## Text bidi numbers (batch 132 audit, lane I, 2026-11-10)

Read in full for this fix: Unicode Standard Annex #9, *Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm*, revision 52, https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr9/ (rules P2, W1 to W7, N0 to N2, I1 and I2, table 4 of bidirectional character types). `packages/text/src/layout.ts` now types European digits EN, Arabic-Indic digits and number signs AN, the separators ES and CS, terminators ET and Arabic-script letters AL from the first code point of a cluster, with the code point lists written from the annex's type descriptions and the Unicode character names (no bidi data file or other implementation read), then applies W2 to W7, N1 with numbers acting as R, and I1 and I2. Explicit embeddings, isolates and overrides (X1 to X10) are not implemented, and N0 stays the simplified bracket rule recorded before. tests/text.test.js holds the annex's own list example and four more cases.

## Shared owner/lifetime model (check:owners)

Research compared ownership confinement, explicit behavioral test models,
browser listener semantics and GPU device/resource lifetimes before writing the
shared harness. Sources: Anindya Banerjee and David A. Naumann,
"Ownership Confinement Ensures Representation Independence for Object-Oriented
Programs" (2002), https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0212003; Bernhard Rumpe,
"Model-Based Testing of Object-Oriented Systems" (2003; arXiv deposit 2014),
https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.6603; WHATWG contributors, "DOM Standard" (2026),
https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-event-listener; W3C GPU for the Web Working
Group, "WebGPU" (2026; editors Kai Ninomiya, Brandon Jones and Jim Blandy),
https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/CRD-webgpu-20260915/.

Confinement motivates instance identity and independent owner domains; it does
not prescribe this test implementation. Rumpe's explicit test models motivate
reusing the same transition sequences with package-specific construction. DOM
defines listener identity by type, callback and capture, including once and
AbortSignal removal. WebGPU requires same-device objects and defines explicit
destruction, device loss and per-pass viewport/scissor defaults. The engineering
combination is an external observer plus independent CPU and real-GPU adapters,
not a formal proof of ownership. The observer's injected-defect tests verify
that its assertions are effective; historical Margo sources verify that the
check rejects defects which previously escaped the gate. Only papers and
standards were read; no companion code or other repository source was used.

2026-11-10 continuation: an async fixture factory now keeps its owner until its promise settles
(`LifetimeObserver.hold`), so constructors, buffers and listeners it makes after its first await are attributed to it;
before, they ran with no owner and a leak there passed (`tests/owner-lifetime.test.js`, "async factory work after an
await is owned", fails on the old harness). This is the confinement reading above applied to asynchronous construction:
the owner domain is the whole factory, not its first synchronous slice. No new source was read.

KB0477 (2026-11-11), ImageBitmap copies on the WebGL2 layer: compared W3C, WebGPU (2026 retrieval), sections on
GPUCopyExternalImageSourceInfo (origin from the top-left of the unflipped source, flipY copies the region bottom row
first) and GPUCopyExternalImageDestInfo (premultipliedAlpha; the copy converts from the source's alpha state),
https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/ ; Khronos Group, WebGL 1.0 specification section 5.14.8 (2026 retrieval: an ImageBitmap
is uploaded as held, the unpack flip and alpha flags are ignored, and canvas premultiplication loses precision),
https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/specs/latest/1.0/ ; WHATWG HTML, ImageBitmap and createImageBitmap premultiplyAlpha
'default' left to the user agent (2026), https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/imagebitmap-and-animations.html ;
Thomas Porter and Tom Duff, Compositing Digital Images (1984), https://doi.org/10.1145/964965.808606 , and Alvy Ray
Smith, Image Compositing Fundamentals, Microsoft Technical Memo 4 (1995), http://alvyray.com/Memos/CG/Microsoft/4_comp.pdf ,
for premultiplied colour and its inverse (divide by a non-zero alpha); IEC 61966-2-1:1999 for the sRGB decode. Design
from these: upload the region as held and as a premultiplied canvas copy, decide the alpha state on the GPU from any
texel where they differ, convert in f32 in a draw. No foreign source read.

## KB3240: glTF metal/dielectric diffuse weight (2026-11-12)

Source: Khronos Group, *glTF 2.0 Specification*, version 2.0.1, Appendix B "BRDF
Implementation" (metal_brdf, dielectric_brdf and material = mix(dielectric_brdf,
metal_brdf, metallic)), https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html, read from
its AsciiDoc source https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/Specification.adoc.
Compared with Christophe Schlick, *An Inexpensive BRDF Model for Physically-based
Rendering* (Computer Graphics Forum 13(3), 1994), https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8659.1330233,
for the Fresnel term the mix interpolates. Expanding the mix: the specular parts sum to
Schlick at f0 = mix(0.04, base, metallic) exactly, while the diffuse keeps (1 - metallic)
times 1 minus the dielectric Fresnel; weighting it by 1 minus the mixed Fresnel is not
an identity. The Sample Viewer was used only as a black-box picture; its source was not
read. No other engine's code was read.

## KB3240b: the same diffuse weight outside gltf/pbr (2026-11-12)

Sources as KB3240 above (glTF 2.0 Appendix B, Schlick 1994), and for the coloured F0 Khronos Group,
*KHR_materials_specular* (https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_specular/README.md),
whose dielectric Fresnel mix weighs the layer under it by 1 minus the largest channel of the Fresnel. Since the F90 is
one number, that largest channel is mix(max channel of F0, F90, (1 - vh)^5). Applied to clustered's shared per-light
BRDF and to the VAT, imposter, material decal, voxel and WebGL2 preview direct lights. No other engine's code was read.

frames flipped against a reference, colour aware, viewing distance in pixels per degree, one error map, no learned
weights. Implemented from the paper's text only (CSF Gaussians b 0.0047, 0.0053, two for blue-yellow; YyCxCz from
T. J. Flohr et al., Model-based color image quantization, SPIE 1913 (1993), https://doi.org/10.1117/12.152701; Hunt
adjustment; HyAB from S. Abasi, M. Amani Tehran and M. D. Fairchild, Distance metrics for very large color
differences, Color Research and Application 45(2) (2020), https://doi.org/10.1002/col.22451; power 0.7 and the 0.4 /
0.95 compression; edge and point features at sigma 0.5 x 0.082 degrees, power 0.5). The paper's companion code was not
read; the feature input is the achromatic channel scaled to 0..1, which is Y over the white's.

HDR-FLIP (`hdrFlip`, 2026-11-27): P. Andersson, J. Nilsson, P. Shirley and T. Akenine-Moller, Visualizing Errors in
Rendered High Dynamic Range Images, Eurographics 2021 Short Papers, https://doi.org/10.2312/egs.20211015 (the PDF read,
HDRFLIP-paper.pdf in the asset library, 105,227,498 B, SHA-256
69590f0a22152a4b136e883686ae6cb1ac23b0df76f2274d183403af747297a4, downloaded with Scott's approval; text extracted
with pdftotext). Every constant comes from the paper's text: exposure compensation 2^c I (section 2.1); tone curves as
the rational form of Equation 1, the positive root of Equation 2 and c = log2(x_p / I) of Equation 3; target 0.85 with
I = the reference's largest luminance for the start and its median for the stop; N = max(2, ceil(stop - start))
exposures spread evenly over [start, stop] (the ceiling read against Figures 1 and 4: 11.9 stops gives 12 columns,
17.5 gives N = 18), tone mapped and clamped to [0, 1]; the per-pixel maximum of LDR-FLIP over them (Equation 4) and an
exposure map of the exposure that gave it; ACES as the default tone mapper and 67 pixels per degree. The ACES curve is
K. Narkowicz, ACES Filmic Tone Mapping Curve (2016), with the 0.6 pre-scale `acesNarkowicz` in packages/shared/aces.js
already uses; Reinhard is E. Reinhard, M. Stark, P. Shirley and J. Ferwerda, Photographic Tone Reproduction for Digital
Images, ACM TOG 21(3) (2002), https://doi.org/10.1145/566654.566575, L / (1 + L). Read as ours where the paper is
silent: luminance is CIE Y of linear Rec.709 (the same matrix as FLIP's), the median of an even count is the mean of
the two middle values, the tone mapped values enter LDR-FLIP as linear light (the sRGB decode is skipped, which equals
encoding then decoding without 8-bit rounding), and a black reference, negative or non-finite light are refused rather
than guessed at. Compared before building: HDR-VDP-2 (Mantiuk et al. 2011, above; the paper reports its poor
localisation), SMAPE, relMSE and RMAE (statistics on the HDR values, which the paper shows miss errors seen at some
exposures), and the mPSNR of J. Munkberg, P. Clarberg, J. Hasselgren and T. Akenine-Moller, High Dynamic Range Texture
Compression for Graphics Hardware, ACM TOG 25(3) (2006), https://doi.org/10.1145/1141911.1141944 (MSE averaged over
exposures). The companion code (NVlabs/flip) was not read.

Per-check sources: noise, J. Immerkaer, Fast Noise Variance Estimation, CVIU 64(2) (1996),
https://doi.org/10.1006/cviu.1996.0060; isolated pixels, H. Hwang and R. A. Haddad, Adaptive median filters: new
algorithms and results, IEEE TIP 4(4) (1995), https://doi.org/10.1109/83.370679 (order statistics of the neighbours);
banding, P. Tandon, M. Afonso, J. Sole and L. Krasula, CAMBI: Contrast-aware Multiscale Banding Index, PCS (2021),
https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.00079 and Z. Tu, J. Lin, Y. Wang, B. Adsumilli and A. C. Bovik, BBAND index, ICASSP
(2020), https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.11891 (both look for small steps between flat areas; Margo counts flat runs split
by a step that skips a code, which is the histogram gap of an 8-bit gradient); blocks, Z. Wang, A. C. Bovik and B. L.
Evans, Blind measurement of blocking artifacts in images, ICIP (2000), https://doi.org/10.1109/ICIP.2000.899622 and Z.
Wang, H. R. Sheikh and A. C. Bovik, No-reference perceptual quality assessment of JPEG compressed images, ICIP (2002),
https://doi.org/10.1109/ICIP.2002.1038064 (a step signal at a known period; Margo tests the phase per tile and period
so one object's edges are no pattern); edge hardness, P. Marziliano, F. Dufaux, S. Winkler and T. Ebrahimi, A
no-reference perceptual blur metric, ICIP (2002), https://doi.org/10.1109/ICIP.2002.1038902 (edge width between
extrema); light discs, A. Rosenfeld and J. L. Pfaltz, Sequential operations in digital picture processing, JACM
13(4) (1966), https://doi.org/10.1145/321356.321357 (connected components); flicker, B. Guthier, S. Kopf, M. Eble and
W. Effelsberg, Flicker reduction in tone mapped high dynamic range video, SPIE 7866 (2011),
https://doi.org/10.1117/12.872449 and G. Eilertsen, R. Wanat, R. K. Mantiuk and J. Unger, Evaluation of tone mapping
operators for HDR-video, CGF 32(7) (2013), https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.12198 (frame mean brightness against its
neighbours); luma, ITU-R BT.709-6 (2015), https://www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-BT.709; sRGB, IEC 61966-2-1 (1999). The horizon
is the vanishing line of horizontal planes, the cross product of the images of two horizontal directions (R. Hartley
and A. Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry, 2nd ed. (2004), section 8.6). No other engine's or tool's code was read; the
contact sheet font is Margo's own 5 x 7 bitmap.

## Shot master encode checks: CIEDE2000, the MP4 colr box, the proxy detail measure (tools/shot, 2026-11-14)

Written from the papers and standards, no code read: G. Sharma, W. Wu and E. N. Dalal, "The CIEDE2000 color-difference
formula: implementation notes, supplementary test data, and mathematical observations", Color Research and Application
30(1), 2005 (https://doi.org/10.1002/col.20070), for the formula and the test pairs in tests/shot-encode.test.js;
CIE 15:2004 for CIELAB; IEC 61966-2-1:1999 for sRGB to XYZ; ITU-R BT.709-6 for the Y'CbCr matrix and limited range;
ISO/IEC 14496-12 (box structure, the visual sample entry), ISO/IEC 14496-15 (avc1) and ISO/IEC 23091-2 (the nclx
code points) for tools/shot/mp4.mjs. The proxy check's fine-detail share projects the copy's luma Laplacian on the
original's (a least-squares gain of the high band), chosen over the ratio of Laplacian energies because blocking and
ringing raise a re-encode's energy (measured: 1.08 to 1.27 kept at 8 Mbps on a spark field by energy, 0.91 to 0.96 by
projection). ffmpeg is driven by its documented options only. No other engine's code was read.

Written from the papers, no code read (the companion code of the papers was not opened): O. James, E. von Tunzelmann,
P. Franklin and K. S. Thorne, "Gravitational lensing by spinning black holes in astrophysics, and in the movie
Interstellar", CQG 32, 065001 (2015), https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03808 (geodesic equations A.15, camera frame A.9 to
A.12, ray bundles and point stars); J. M. Bardeen, W. H. Press and S. A. Teukolsky, ApJ 178, 347 (1972),
https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1972ApJ...178..347B (horizon, ISCO, photon orbit, circular orbits); D. N. Page and
K. S. Thorne, ApJ 191, 499 (1974), https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1974ApJ...191..499P (disk flux, eq. 15n);
J.-P. Luminet, A&A 75, 228 (1979), https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1979A&A....75..228L (observed flux g^4 F);
K. Asada and M. Nakamura, ApJL 745, L28 (2012), https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ApJ...745L..28A (parabolic
jet); M. L. Lind and R. D. Blandford, ApJ 295, 358 (1985), https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1985ApJ...295..358L
(beaming D^(2 + alpha)); H. Igehy, "Tracing ray differentials", SIGGRAPH 1999,
https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/trd/ (pixel footprint); A. Norton, A. P. Rockwood and P. T. Skolmoski,
"Clamping", SIGGRAPH 1982, https://doi.org/10.1145/965145.801274 (octave fade); F. Neyret, "Advected textures", SCA
2003, https://hal.inria.fr/inria-00537472 (two crossfaded phases); B. Kang, O. Moon, C. Hong, H. Lee, B. Cho and Y.
Kim, J. Korean Physical Society 41, 865 (2002) (Planckian locus fits). Compared and combined: James et al.'s ray
bundles over plain point sampling (dashed stars) and over a sky texture blur (no magnification); Neyret's two phases
over a single advected phase (unbounded winding) and over a static disk (no shear). The negated-division fault was
found with a minimal WGSL repro written here; WGSL's atan2 definition and accuracy are from the W3C WGSL
specification. No other engine's or renderer's code was read.

Sources: Khronos Group, *KHR_materials_sheen* extension specification (ratified), sections "Sheen distribution",
"Sheen visibility" and "Sheen layering: Albedo-scaling technique" (punctual form min(1 - max3(sheenColor) E(VdotN),
1 - max3(sheenColor) E(LdotN)) and its simplified VdotN form), https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_sheen;
A. Estevez and C. Kulla, "Production Friendly Microfacet Sheen BRDF", Sony Pictures Imageworks technical report, 2017
(Charlie distribution, cited for the distribution already in use and for the open visibility row); Khronos Group,
*glTF 2.0 Specification*, version 2.0.1, Appendix B "BRDF Implementation" (the dielectric diffuse weight used by
