## Blast thermal: weather/eruption BlastCloud (2026-11-24)

Written from the papers' text and equations only; no other engine's or tool's code was read. Sources: B. R. Morton,
G. I. Taylor and J. S. Turner, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 234, 1-23, 1956, https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1956.0011 (the
instantaneous source's entrainment equations and the B^(1/4) N^(-1/2) height scale); R. S. Scorer, J. Fluid Mech. 2,
583-594, 1957, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112057000397 (thermal spread b / z near 0.25, rise as (B t^2)^(1/4)); J. S.
Turner, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 239, 61-75, 1957, https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1957.0023 (the buoyant vortex ring as the
cap); M. P. Escudier and T. Maxworthy, J. Fluid Mech. 61, 541-552, 1973, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112073000856
(added mass); J. S. Turner, Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 1, 29-44, 1969, https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.fl.01.010169.000333
(review); S. Glasstone and P. J. Dolan, The Effects of Nuclear Weapons, 3rd ed., 1977, ch. 2 (buried bursts: the
earth column, dust cloud and base surge, described only); W. E. Baker et al., Explosion Hazards and Evaluation,
Elsevier, 1983 (cube-root scaling and the TNT heat of detonation). Model choices, stated in the source: the initial
radius tnt^(1/3) m, `heatShare` 0.4, the cap's ring proportions and the base surge's growth. Tests check the laws:
b - b0 = alpha z and z^2 growing at 2 B / ((1 + k) alpha^3) in uniform air, the stopping height doubling for 16 times
the buoyancy or a quarter of N, and the ICAO N^2.

Second pass (2026-11-24, judged on film frames against the Halifax 1917 and Sailor Hat photographs). Added sources,
read as text: F. P. Ricou and D. B. Spalding, J. Fluid Mech. 11, 21-32, 1961, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112061000834,
and B. R. Morton, Symp. (Int.) Combust. 10, 973-982, 1965, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0082-0784(65)80240-5 (entrainment
of a light flow scaled by (rho / rho_a)^(1/2)); Escudier and Maxworthy 1973 again (a light thermal's momentum is its own
small mass plus the added mass); T. B. Benjamin, J. Fluid Mech. 31, 209-248, 1968,
https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112068000133, and M. Ungarish, An Introduction to Gravity Currents and Intrusions, CRC
Press, 2009 (an intrusion's front at Fr N h, giving the umbrella R^3 = R_s^3 (1 + 4 Fr N t) for a fixed volume, Fr 0.5
a model choice); P. D. Kaye and P. F. Linden, J. Fluid Mech. 502, 41-63, 2004 (coalescing plumes, used for merging
caps once their spheres overlap); A. Bouthors and F. Neyret, "Modeling clouds shape", Eurographics 2004 short papers,
and F. Neyret, Eurographics Workshop on Animation and Simulation 1997, 113-124 (the cauliflower surface as a hierarchy
of blobs on their parents' outward side at about half the size; here 1 + 5 + 15 puffs a tree). Measured data the tests
hold the model to: Glasstone and Dolan 1977, table 2.12 (the 1 Mt cloud top at 2, 4 and 6 miles after 0.3, 0.7 and
1.1 minutes, read as text from the archive.org transcription; the model, with 0.65 of the yield as heat, is 10 to
20 percent low), and the Halifax cloud's peak of 3,600 m for about 2.9 kt (Ruffman and Howell, Ground Zero, 1994,
p. 323, read through its citation, not the book; the model gives 3,465 m at `heatShare` 0.4). Model choices: the
hot start at `fireTemperature` 2,000 K, the lightest cloud 0.05 of the air's density, the oblate cap of half height
0.75 b keeping the thermal's top, the merge ramp, the tree's sizes (children 0.42 to 0.58 of the parent, 0.78 and
0.62 of its radius out), the glow's share by height and level, and the stem's widths.

Third pass (2026-11-24, lane D). Added sources, read as text: J. Akhavan, The Chemistry of Explosives, 3rd ed., RSC,
2011 (TNT's oxygen balance of -74 percent, so its detonation leaves free carbon: the soot grey-black default colours);
C. L. Mader, Numerical Modeling of Explosives and Propellants, 3rd ed., CRC Press, 2008 (Chapman-Jouguet temperatures
of 3,000 to 4,000 K for military explosives; `fireballTemperature` 3,000 K a model choice at the low end); Planck's law
in its Wien limit and the Stefan-Boltzmann law (textbook physics: the fire's glow at 555 nm against that of its first
temperature, and power ~ area T^4, so the fire's shrinking outline carries part of its power drop and its temperature
only the rest); R. Swinbank and R. J. Purser, "Fibonacci grids", Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 132, 1769-1793, 2006,
https://doi.org/10.1256/qj.05.227, and A. Gonzalez, "Measurement of areas on a sphere using Fibonacci and
latitude-longitude lattices", Math. Geosci. 42, 49-64, 2010, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11004-009-9257-x (the cap's trees
on a golden-angle spiral of even area); L. G. Mastin, "A simple calculator of ballistic trajectories for blocks ejected
during volcanic eruptions", USGS Open-File Report 01-45, 2001 (ballistic paths slowed by drag, for the jets; the linear
drag of time constant 1.5 s is a model choice). Model choices: trees of three levels (a fourth spent 30 of 51 puffs on
the smallest lobes and left a quarter of the cap's face open), blobs at 0.78 of the cap's radii, the first lobes in a
jittered ring 55 degrees off the blob's normal, and the jets' quarter share of the stem's puffs while they show.

## Explosion crater: terrain/ground-change 'crater' event (2026-11-24)

Written from the sources' text only; no other engine's or tool's code was read. S. Glasstone and P. J. Dolan, The
Effects of Nuclear Weapons, 3rd ed., US DoD and ERDA, 1977, ch. 2 and 6 (a buried burst lifts a mound that vents, then
leaves an apparent crater with a lip and ejecta); T. R. McGetchin, M. Settle and J. W. Head, "Radial thickness
variation in impact crater ejecta", Earth Planet. Sci. Lett. 20, 226-236, 1973,
https://doi.org/10.1016/0012-821X(73)90162-3 (the blanket thinning as (r / R)^-3). The dome's rise is a surface
thrown up at sqrt(2 g H) and slowed by gravity, h = H (1 - (1 - t / T)^2), T = sqrt(2 H / g). Model choices: the
dome's shape (1 - (r / 1.3 R)^2)^2, the paraboloid bowl, the crater's growth under constant deceleration from half
its radius, the lip ramp over the last 15 percent of the radius and the blanket's cut at 5 R. Tests: test/crater.test.js.

## Water planar capture edges (2026-11-24)

The reflection on an open water surface showed the edge of a finite camera capture.
Morgan McGuire and Michael Mara, *Efficient GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing* (2014),
[paper](https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/), describe the coverage limits of a finite viewport.
Xiaolong Wu, Yanning Xu and Lu Wang, *Stereo-consistent Screen Space Reflection* (2024),
[paper](https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.15159), section 4.2, use fading at the viewport edge to prevent abrupt
changes. Mikkel Gjøl and Mikkel Svendsen, *The Rendering of Inside* (2016),
[GDC presentation](https://media.gdcvault.com/gdc2016/Presentations/Gjoel_Svendsen_Rendering_of_Inside.pdf),
also fade screen-space reflections to an environment fallback. Margo's optional Water adapter applies
that principle to the UV of a planar reflection: use the larger of the filter footprint and the maximum
wave shift as a transition width on each axis and apply the cubic
[WGSL smoothstep](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#smoothstep-builtin). This calculation was written from the
descriptions without consulting implementation code.

## Soft bodies: particles, distance constraints and contacts (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-24)

Written clean room from the papers below and Rapier's published Soft-bodies user guide page (the guide only; no Rapier or other engine source was read). The solver is compliant distance constraints in the mass-independent softness form, many small steps of few iterations, position-level contacts with bounded Coulomb friction, and a contact correction shared with a rigid body by inverse mass and inertia.

- M. Macklin, M. Müller and N. Chentanez, "XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics", Motion in Games, 2016. https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/publications/XPBD.pdf
- M. Macklin, K. Storey, M. Lu, P. Terdiman, N. Chentanez, S. Jeschke and M. Müller, "Small Steps in Physics Simulation", SCA 2019. https://mmacklin.com/smallsteps.pdf
- M. Macklin, M. Müller, N. Chentanez and T.-Y. Kim, "Unified Particle Physics for Real-Time Applications", ACM TOG 33(4), 2014 (friction as a bounded displacement, and the share of a contact correction between particle and body).
- M. Müller, B. Heidelberger, M. Hennix and J. Ratcliff, "Position Based Dynamics", J. Visual Communication and Image Representation 18(2), 2007.
- Catenary check: the closed form of a hanging chain, length = 2a sinh(span / 2a), height = a cosh(x / a) (any mechanics text).

### Tethers: long range attachments (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-27)

Written clean room from the paper below: no engine's source and no companion code was read. Each free particle is tied to its nearest pinned particle by the shortest path through the body's structural and shear edges (Dijkstra over the rest lengths, run again after a tear, a pin change or a change of the tether stretch; bend edges are left out, as they span a tear), and once per pass, after the edges, a particle farther from its pin than that geodesic times the stretch is put back on the sphere around the pin. The paper's unilateral projection is kept as written: a particle inside its sphere is not moved, so a slack cloth moves bit for bit as it would untied.

- T.-Y. Kim, N. Chentanez and M. Müller-Fischer, "Long Range Attachments: A Method to Simulate Inextensible Clothing in Computer Games", ACM SIGGRAPH/Eurographics Symposium on Computer Animation, 2012. https://doi.org/10.2312/SCA/SCA12/305-310
- E. W. Dijkstra, "A note on two problems in connexion with graphs", Numerische Mathematik 1, 1959 (the geodesic distances).

### Skinned cloth: motion constraints and linear blend skinning (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-27)

Written clean room from the papers and the public glTF specification below; no engine's source and no companion code was read. Each skinned particle has a point on the character's skin (the skinned mesh's vertex, from the skeleton by linear blend skinning), a max distance from it and a backstop behind the skin's plane there. The point moves at a steady speed over the step, carried a piece at a time in the kernel. Once per pass and once after the exact thread solve, a particle outside its sphere is projected onto it, and a particle behind the backstop onto that plane (one-sided position constraints). A max distance of 0 makes the particle a pin with a target, so it rides the skin exactly and anchors the tethers. Rivals' public documentation was read for the feature list only (max distance and backstop, or surface penetration, per vertex).

- M. Müller, B. Heidelberger, M. Hennix and J. Ratcliff, "Position Based Dynamics", J. Visual Communication and Image Representation 18(2), 2007 (one-sided constraint projection). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvcir.2007.01.005
- T.-Y. Kim, N. Chentanez and M. Müller-Fischer, "Long Range Attachments", SCA 2012 (character clothing tied to skinned anchors). https://doi.org/10.2312/SCA/SCA12/305-310
- T. Jakobsen, "Advanced Character Physics", Game Developers Conference 2001 (projection of particles onto limits).
- N. Magnenat-Thalmann, R. Laperrière and D. Thalmann, "Joint-dependent local deformations for hand animation and object grasping", Graphics Interface 1988 (linear blend skinning).
- Khronos Group, glTF 2.0 Specification, section 3.7.3, Skins (joint matrices, JOINTS_0 and WEIGHTS_0). https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html

### Cloth faces in the air: attached lift, stall and separated flow (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-27)

Written clean room from the papers below; no engine's source and no companion code was read. Each face of a cloth is a thin plate meeting the air at an angle. In attached flow its normal force coefficient is Polhamus's, K_p sin a cos a + K_v sin^2 a, with K_p Helmbold's lift slope for a wing of the body's aspect ratio and K_v pi (Polhamus's slender limit); the flow separates where that reaches the square plate's normal force C_N90, past which the coefficient is Lindenburg's fit to flat-plate data, C_N90 sin a / (0.56 + 0.44 sin a); skin friction acts along the face. The normal coefficient per sin a is finite edge-on, so each load is linear in the face's speed through the air with the rest frozen, taken implicitly over the step. Measured validation: the lift slope and the angle of the most lift against low-aspect-ratio flat plates in a wind tunnel (Torres and Mueller 2004, read from their figures as tabulated in the Energies paper below).

- E. C. Polhamus, "A Concept of the Vortex Lift of Sharp-Edge Delta Wings Based on a Leading-Edge-Suction Analogy", NASA TN D-3767, 1966. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19670003842
- H. B. Helmbold, "Der unverwundene Ellipsenflügel als tragende Fläche", Jahrbuch der Deutschen Luftfahrtforschung, 1942 (the low-aspect-ratio lift slope 2 pi AR / (2 + sqrt(AR^2 + 4))).
- C. Lindenburg, "Investigation into Rotor Blade Aerodynamics", ECN-C--03-025, Energy research Centre of the Netherlands, 2003 (the separated flat plate's normal force).
- S. F. Hoerner, *Fluid-Dynamic Drag*, 1965 (the square plate's 1.17).
- G. E. Torres and T. J. Mueller, "Low-Aspect-Ratio Wing Aerodynamics at Low Reynolds Numbers", AIAA Journal 42(5), 865-873, 2004. https://doi.org/10.2514/1.439
- Energies 8(4), 2438, 2015, table 1, which tabulates Torres and Mueller's angle of the most lift and K_p for aspect ratios 0.5, 0.75 and 1 from their figures 6 and 10. https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1073/8/4/2438
- F. Keckeisen, S. Kimmerle et al., "Modelling Effects of Wind Fields in Cloth Animations", WSCG 2004 (wind on cloth triangles).

### Soft-world snapshots (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-27)

Written clean room; no engine's source was read. A soft world runs in its own Wasm instance, so its whole state is its linear memory (the kernel's columns, counts and allocator) plus the JavaScript state of the world and its bodies; a snapshot copies both, and a restore writes the memory back (grown to size first) and puts the same body objects back, retiring any made since. The rigid world's snapshot carries its clock so time-driven loads replay. Determinism between steps is what makes this a replay rather than an approximation, as in rollback netcode.

- G. Fiedler, "Deterministic Lockstep", Gaffer On Games, 2014. https://gafferongames.com/post/deterministic_lockstep/
- T. Cannon, GGPO rollback networking SDK, documentation (save, load and advance of the whole game state). https://www.ggpo.net/

### Adaptive tearing of sheets (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-27)

Written clean room from the papers below; no engine's source and no companion code was read. After each step every face of an adaptive sheet has its deformation gradient taken against the rest triangle its three edges' rest lengths give, and its greatest principal stretch from the right Cauchy-Green tensor. Faces past the tear strain are cut, most stretched first, a capped number a step: from a crack tip, then a boundary corner, then any corner, along the line in the face's plane perpendicular to the greatest stretch, to the opposite side, where a vertex is inserted (its rest distances by Stewart's theorem) and both faces on that side are split so the mesh stays conforming; a cut within a fifth of a side of a corner runs along the side instead (no slivers). Edges crossing the cut are dropped. Then every vertex whose ring of faces the crack's sides divide is copied, one copy for each part, mass shared by the parts' areas, so the crack opens behind its tip and stays joined at it.

- T. Pfaff, R. Narain, J. M. de Joya and J. F. O'Brien, "Adaptive Tearing and Cracking of Thin Sheets", ACM Transactions on Graphics 33(4), SIGGRAPH 2014. https://doi.org/10.1145/2601097.2601132
- J. F. O'Brien and J. K. Hodgins, "Graphical Modeling and Animation of Brittle Fracture", SIGGRAPH 1999 (the crack across an element perpendicular to its greatest principal stress).
- N. Molino, Z. Bao and R. Fedkiw, "A Virtual Node Algorithm for Changing Mesh Topology During Simulation", SIGGRAPH 2004 (copies of a vertex for each side of a crack).
- M. Stewart, *Some General Theorems of Considerable Use in the Higher Parts of Mathematics*, 1746 (a cevian's length from the sides).

### Vertex block descent for cloth (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-27)

Written clean room from the paper below; its companion code was not read. A cloth on the vertex-block solver has its edges as springs; each pass visits the particles in order and takes one Newton step on the particle's own three coordinates of the incremental potential (inertia m/(2h^2)|x - y|^2 plus the springs at it), the spring Hessian projected to stay positive when squeezed, damping stiffness-proportional at each edge's own frequency, and the first guess from the paper's adaptive initialisation (gravity scaled by the particle's last acceleration along it, clamped to 0..1), whose previous velocity is a column of the soft world. A thread's measured strain limit is projected after the passes (Provot 1995). Since 2026-11-28 (KB-SOFT-VBDBEND1) each block step is backtracked (halved until it lowers the block's own potential: inertia, springs, measured bending and the damping's Rayleigh potential), the passes start from the point of the segment from the previous place to the first guess with the least incremental potential (so a piece never ends above where it began, the minimizing-movement energy estimate of implicit Euler), and a piece sweeps the blocks at least 8 times, alternating direction (symmetric Gauss-Seidel).

- A. H. Chen, Z. Liu, Y. Yang and C. Yuksel, "Vertex Block Descent", ACM Transactions on Graphics 43(4), SIGGRAPH 2024. https://doi.org/10.1145/3658179
- J. Nocedal and S. J. Wright, *Numerical Optimization*, 2nd ed., Springer 2006, section 3.1 (backtracking line search).
- M. Ortiz and L. Stainier, "The variational formulation of viscoplastic constitutive updates", Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 171, 1999. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0045-7825(98)00219-9 (the incremental potential of an implicit step and its energy estimate).
- C. Kane, J. E. Marsden, M. Ortiz and M. West, "Variational integrators and the Newmark algorithm for conservative and dissipative mechanical systems", International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering 49, 2000. https://doi.org/10.1002/1097-0207(20001210)49:10<1295::AID-NME993>3.0.CO;2-W
- X. Provot, "Deformation Constraints in a Mass-Spring Model to Describe Rigid Cloth Behavior", Graphics Interface 1995 (strain limiting).
- H. M. Irvine, *Cable Structures*, 1981 (the elastic cable sag the test meets).

### Shape matching (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-24)

- M. Müller, B. Heidelberger, M. Teschner and M. Gross, "Meshless Deformations Based on Shape Matching", ACM TOG 24(3), 2005.
- M. Müller, J. Bender, N. Chentanez and M. Macklin, "A Robust Method to Extract the Rotational Part of Deformations", MIG 2016. The rotation step uses the quaternion Cayley form (a rotation about w by 2 atan(|w| / 2)) in place of the paper's exact exponential, so the step path calls no trigonometric function. The constraint is the XPBD form of the same paper family as the edges (Macklin et al. 2016).

## Soft bodies: tetrahedral cells, plasticity, tearing and clusters (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-24)

Written clean room from the papers below and Rapier's published Soft-bodies user guide page (the guide only; no Rapier or other engine source was read, nor any companion code of a paper). The elasticity is constraints on the deformation gradient solved by XPBD in small steps, plastic flow is a multiplicative split folded into each cell's rest shape, tearing removes a cell, and clusters are shape matching held as an implicit spring. The polar decomposition is a fixed number of scaled Newton steps, so a step is bit for bit the same everywhere.

- M. Macklin and M. Müller, "A Constraint-based Formulation of Stable Neo-Hookean Elasticity", Motion, Interaction and Games, 2021. https://mmacklin.com/neohookean.pdf

- M. Müller and M. Gross, "Interactive Virtual Materials", Graphics Interface 2004 (co-rotated elasticity).

### Volume preservation (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-24)

One scalar constraint on the volume a closed triangle surface encloses, V = sum of x_a . (x_b x x_c) / 6 over its triangles, whose gradient at a vertex is the sum of the cross products of the other two vertices of each triangle around it over 6, held to a target by the XPBD correction (Macklin, Mueller and Chentanez 2016). The balloon constraint is that of M. Mueller, B. Heidelberger, M. Hennix and J. Ratcliff, "Position Based Dynamics", J. Visual Communication and Image Representation 18(2), 2007, section 4.4, with the divergence-theorem volume of a closed mesh (any computational geometry text).

### Soft contact with rigid bodies (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-24, KB-SOFT-LIGHT1)

A cloth meets a rigid body at its particles (the swept particle probe) and at its faces (the rigid kernel's face query, `kernel/src/face.rs`: conservative advancement on the GJK distance of a moving triangle to each convex piece, then the triangle's contact manifold), each contact found once a step with what the collider's surface is there: a face (told by where the shape's support moves as the direction turns about the normal) or the radius of curvature of a round place, corner or edge. The soft kernel holds each through the step's pieces as a position constraint shared by generalized inverse masses, a face by its plane turning with the body and a round place from its centre of curvature, so the push on the body and on the cloth lie on one line; the body's turn in a piece is a normalised quaternion and its inertia turns with it; the contacts the position pass pushed on are then made inelastic with Coulomb friction. The rigid body takes the push as an impulse at the start of its step and a force over it, solved from the rigid kernel's semi-implicit Euler substeps so a free body ends where the soft step took it (own derivation), and its spin as the change the soft step gave it. Written from:

- M. Mueller, B. Heidelberger, M. Hennix and J. Ratcliff, "Position Based Dynamics", J. Visual Communication and Image Representation 18(2), 2007, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvcir.2007.01.005 (positions are corrected and the velocities follow from them; section 4.4, the point and triangle constraint with a thickness).
- M. Mueller, M. Macklin, N. Chentanez, S. Jeschke and T.-Y. Kim, "Detailed Rigid Body Simulation with Extended Position Based Dynamics", SCA 2020, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14105 (equations 2 to 4, the generalized inverse mass at a point; equations 8 and 9, the rotation update made unit again; section 3.4, the velocity a pose change implies; sections 3.5 and 3.6, a contact keeps its points on each body and the velocity pass runs over the contacts the position pass made).
- R. Bridson, R. Fedkiw and J. Anderson, "Robust Treatment of Collisions, Contact and Friction for Cloth Animation", SIGGRAPH 2002, https://doi.org/10.1145/566654.566623 (cloth as triangles with a thickness; point and triangle proximity).
- E. Shinar, C. Schroeder and R. Fedkiw, "Two-way Coupling of Rigid and Deformable Bodies", SCA 2008, https://www.cs.ucr.edu/~shinar/papers/2008_rigid_deformable.pdf (the reaction at a point of a deformable surface shared among the nodes that carry it).
- B. Mirtich, "Impulse-based Dynamic Simulation of Rigid Body Systems", PhD thesis, UC Berkeley, 1996 (conservative advancement, the bound the face query halves the step by).
- G. van den Bergen, "Collision Detection in Interactive 3D Environments", Morgan Kaufmann, 2004 (GJK distance, already the kernel's).
- M. do Carmo, "Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces", 1976, section 3.2 (curvature of a surface along a normal section, the sphere that fits a surface at a point); J. Kerr and B. Roth, "Analysis of Multifingered Hands", International Journal of Robotics Research 4(4), 1986 (rolling contact described by the contact's centre of curvature).
- C. Ericson, "Real-Time Collision Detection", Morgan Kaufmann, 2005, section 3.4 (barycentric coordinates of a point of a triangle).
- E. Catto, "Fast and Simple Physics using Sequential Impulses", GDC 2006, https://box2d.org/files/ErinCatto_SequentialImpulses_GDC2006.pdf (read for the first fix of KB-SOFT-LIGHT1, 0a4570d8e, which handed the push to the body as a pose change apart from its velocity, as a split impulse hands a pseudo-velocity; that hand-off is replaced by the impulse and force above, which carry the same change as motion).

### Drawing a soft body (`@margoengine/gltf/soft-mesh`, 2026-11-24)

Vertex normals as the sum of the unnormalised face normals of the triangles around a vertex, each face weighted by its area (the standard smooth-shading normal of any computer graphics text), and tangents with their handedness from the UV gradients of each triangle, made orthogonal to the normal by Gram-Schmidt:

- E. Lengyel, "Computing Tangent Space Basis Vectors for an Arbitrary Mesh", Terathon Software, 2001, https://terathon.com/blog/tangent-space.html (read for the formula; no code was copied).

The rivals were read as feature names only: the cloth example of three.js and the soft-body mesh update of Babylon.js (copy the particle positions into a mesh each frame, recompute its normals).

### Anisotropic cloth (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-24)

A woven sheet's threads have springs of their own, each an XPBD distance constraint (Macklin et al. 2016) with its own natural frequency and damping ratio: the warp along the builder's `du`, the weft along `dv`, the diagonals of each cell as shear, and bend edges two along; the stretch and the shear are separate terms of an orthotropic sheet as in D. Baraff and A. Witkin, "Large Steps in Cloth Simulation", SIGGRAPH 1998, and B. Thomaszewski, S. Wacker and W. Strasser, "A consistent bending model for cloth simulation with corotational subdivision finite elements", SCA 2006 (for the bend); H. Wang, J. F. O'Brien and R. Ramamoorthi, "Data-driven elastic models for cloth: modeling and measurement", ACM TOG 30(4), 2011, for the anisotropic stretch measured on real cloth.

### Two-way contacts between soft particles and rigid bodies (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-24)

A touched rigid body is a participant of the soft step's contact constraints: each contact moves the particle by its share of the correction and the body by the rest, by its generalized inverse mass at the contact point (translation and a small turn about its centre), and the next contact of the piece meets the body where that left it (Gauss-Seidel over a body's contacts); the body's velocity is its pose change over the piece, and the host gives the real body the same as a force over the step. After the positions, the relative speeds of the contacts are solved inelastically with Coulomb friction, the tangential direction's own inverse mass included. Sources: M. Mueller, M. Macklin, N. Chentanez, S. Jeschke and T.-Y. Kim, "Detailed Rigid Body Simulation with Extended Position Based Dynamics", Computer Graphics Forum (SCA) 39(8), 2020 (positional corrections with the generalized inverse mass, applied per constraint; the velocity solve after the positions); M. Macklin, M. Mueller, N. Chentanez and T.-Y. Kim, "Unified Particle Physics for Real-Time Applications", ACM TOG 33(4), 2014 (the share of a contact between a particle and a body, friction as a bounded displacement).

### Character controllers: moving ground, contact listener, push limits and the dynamic character (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-24)

The kinematic controller carries the character with the body it stands on by that body's velocity at the foot (the linear velocity plus the spin crossed with the arm from the centre of mass, first order in the step) and turns it about `up` by the spin's share along `up`; the push on a dynamic body is the reduced mass of the pair times the closing speed (the character's wish into the body less the body's own speed along the normal), capped by a strength times the step and refused over a mass ratio; a contact listener sees each obstacle as it is met. Own derivation from rigid-body kinematics; the shape of the options (platform velocity, inner body, contact listener, maximum strength, mass) follows what Jolt's published `CharacterVirtual` documentation lists, read as the published page, no source. The dynamic character keeps a rigid body upright with the stable proportional-derivative controller of S. Tan, K. Liu and G. Turk, "Stable Proportional-Derivative Controllers", IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications 31(4), 2011: the position term taken at the end of the step and the velocity term implicit, so `v' = (v - h k x) / (1 + 2 h zeta w + h^2 k)` for any stiffness `k = w^2` and step `h` (derived from the paper's equations, no companion code). The walking is a velocity controller whose change per step is limited (the grip), over the velocity of the ground under it, and a force cancelling gravity's share along the ground holds it on a slope for the whole step (a velocity to cancel it would be worn away by gravity within the step: measured as a creep of 0.5 mm a step before the force).

### Integration parameters of the own solver (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-24)

Where friction is solved (`frictionInBiasPass`), the number of relaxing passes (`internalStabilizationIterations`), the friction model, the continuous-collision floor, tolerance and advance count, quarantine and the collision-only step follow what Rapier's published documentation says of `IntegrationParameters` (`friction_in_bias_pass`, `num_internal_stabilization_iterations`, `friction_model`, `min_ccd_dt`, `max_ccd_substeps`), `FrictionModel`, `CollisionPipeline`, `PhysicsPipeline::quarantine` and `Counters` (docs.rs rapier3d 0.36.1, read as published pages; no source). The simplified friction model is one constraint at the mean of a manifold's points in a circular cone of the friction coefficient times the summed normal impulse, with a twist about the normal limited by the coefficient times each point's normal impulse times its distance from the mean: the limit surface of a friction patch, P. Goyal, A. Ruina and J. Papadopoulos, "Planar Sliding with Dry Friction, Part 1: Limit Surface and Moment Function", Wear 143(2), 1991, and Coulomb's cone as in D. Stewart, "Rigid-Body Dynamics with Friction and Impact", SIAM Review 42(1), 2000. The time floor of the sweep stops it at the time it has reached, which conservative advancement (Mirtich 1996; Catto 2013) keeps before any touch. The finer solver timers are sums over the substeps of the stretches of the step the solver already has.

### Sleeping a body the solver is still moving (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-24, KB-PHYS-SLEEP-PUSH1)

A body that a joint or a contact pulls home by moving its pose, with no velocity left, is not at rest, so the sleep timer is held at zero while the pose it moved through in a step carries kinetic energy per unit of mass above the body's threshold. Written clean room from:

- K. Erleben, "Stable, Robust, and Versatile Multibody Dynamics Animation", PhD thesis, University of Copenhagen, 2005, section 6.5 (a body is ready to sleep when its kinetic energy per unit of mass stays under a threshold for a time, and an island sleeps when all its bodies are ready).
- E. Catto, "Soft Constraints", GDC 2011, https://box2d.org/files/ErinCatto_SoftConstraints_GDC2011.pdf, and "Solver2D", https://box2d.org/posts/2024/02/solver2d/ (a soft step corrects position in a biased pass and takes the velocity of that correction out in a relax pass, which is why velocity alone shows a body being pulled home as still).

No published source states the pose-displacement criterion itself; it is this engine's own rule, and a search (Box2D's and Bullet's sleep descriptions, island-sleeping notes) found none that does. The rule is held by `next-sleep-pushed.test.js`.

Soft contact equilibrium (`next-parameters.test.js`): the resting give of a soft contact is g over omega squared, derived from the update of Catto 2011 (the product of the mass-scale to impulse-scale ratio and the bias rate is h omega squared whatever the damping ratio). Open difference at a damping ratio of 10: KB-PHYS-SOFTGIVE1.
Where friction is solved (`frictionInBiasPass`), the number of relaxing passes (`internalStabilizationIterations`), the friction model, the continuous-collision floor, tolerance and advance count, quarantine and the collision-only step follow what Rapier's published documentation says of `IntegrationParameters` (`friction_in_bias_pass`, `num_internal_stabilization_iterations`, `friction_model`, `min_ccd_dt`, `max_ccd_substeps`), `FrictionModel`, `CollisionPipeline`, `PhysicsPipeline::quarantine` and `Counters` (docs.rs rapier3d 0.36.1, read as published pages; no source). The simplified friction model is one constraint at the mean of a manifold's points in a circular cone of the friction coefficient times the summed normal impulse, with a twist about the normal limited by the coefficient times each point's normal impulse times its distance from the mean: the limit surface of a friction patch, P. Goyal, A. Ruina and J. Papadopoulos, "Planar Sliding with Dry Friction, Part 1: Limit Surface and Moment Function", Wear 143(2), 1991, and Coulomb's cone as in D. Stewart, "Rigid-Body Dynamics with Friction and Impact", SIAM Review 42(1), 2000. The time floor of the sweep stops it at the time it has reached, which conservative advancement (Mirtich 1996; Catto 2013) keeps before any touch. The finer solver timers are sums over the substeps of the stretches of the step the solver already has. The tree broad phase is a dynamic tree of the fat boxes: J. van den Bergen, "Efficient Collision Detection of Complex Deformable Models using AABB Trees", Journal of Graphics Tools 2(4), 1997; the insertion cost of A. Goldsmith and J. Salmon, "Automatic Creation of Object Hierarchies for Ray Tracing", IEEE CG&A 7(5), 1987, as E. Catto, "Dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchies", GDC 2019, sets it out; the binned build is I. Wald, "On fast Construction of SAH-based Bounding Volume Hierarchies", IEEE Symposium on Interactive Ray Tracing, 2007; the clustered build is D. Meister and J. Bittner, "Parallel Locally-Ordered Clustering for Bounding Volume Hierarchy Construction", IEEE TVCG 24(3), 2018; the rotations are of D. Kopta, T. Ize, J. Spjut, E. Brunvand, A. Davis and A. Kensler, "Fast, Effective BVH Updates for Animated Scenes", I3D 2012 (papers read, no companion code). Contact recycling and clustering follow the descriptions in Rapier's `IntegrationParameters` documentation (a pair that moved less than a distance keeps its points; manifolds of near normals are one cluster of at most four points); the choice of the four points (the deepest, the farthest from it, then the two that spread them) is the contact reduction of D. Gregorius, "Robust Contact Creation for Physics Simulations", GDC 2015.

### Couplings of two joints' coordinates (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-24, J-26)

A row on four bodies, the two links and their parents, whose speed is the first coordinate's rate plus `ratio` times the second's: a hinge's rate is its axis dotted with the child's turn less the parent's, a slider's the axis dotted with the child's centre velocity in the parent's frame, v_c - v_p - w_p x (x_c - x_p). Its effective inverse mass is J M^-1 J^T, found as the speed a unit impulse along the row gives it, which is exact where the two sides share a parent (the sum of each side's own is not). A row between the coordinates of joints is the form of Baraff, "Linear-Time Dynamics using Lagrange Multipliers", SIGGRAPH 1996, solved with the sequential impulses and the soft form of Catto, "Soft Constraints", GDC 2011, as the other couplings are. Held by `next-dof-coupling.test.js`.
### Vehicle tyres, drivetrain and shape-cast wheels (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-24)

`pacejkaTyre` is the sine form of the Magic Formula as published in H. B. Pacejka and E. Bakker, "The Magic Formula Tyre Model", Vehicle System Dynamics 21 (supplement), 1992, and H. B. Pacejka, "Tyre and Vehicle Dynamics", 3rd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann 2012, chapter 4 (the coefficients are textbook-typical dry-asphalt values chosen so the longitudinal force peaks near a slip ratio of 0.14 and the lateral near a slip angle of 8 degrees, not a fitted tyre); the two forces are held in the ellipse of their peaks, the friction ellipse of the same chapter. `brushTyre` is the brush model of Pacejka 2012 section 3.3 and J. Svendenius, "Tire Modeling and Friction Estimation", PhD thesis, Lund University 2007: `F = mu Fz (1 - (1 - theta s)^3)` with `theta = 2 c a^2 / (3 mu Fz)` along the combined slip. Wheel spin dynamics, the slip ratio `(omega R - v) / |v|` and the slip angle are the SAE definitions of Pacejka's book; the tyre force of a step is the one that agrees with the slip the step leaves (an implicit step, found by bisection), an own derivation. The `Drivetrain` follows G. Rill, "Road Vehicle Dynamics", CRC Press 2011, chapters 2 and 3 (engine torque curve, clutch, gearbox, differentials) and W. F. Milliken and D. L. Milliken, "Race Car Vehicle Dynamics", SAE 1995, on differentials; the torque a locked or limited-slip differential moves is the one that brings its sides to one speed within the step, an own derivation. Anti-roll bars are a spring on the difference of two wheels' compression (Milliken and Milliken). A shape-cast wheel sweeps a cylinder of the wheel's size along the suspension with the world's shape cast.

The tracked vehicle follows J. Y. Wong, "Theory of Ground Vehicles", 4th ed., Wiley 2008, chapter 3 (the shear stress of a track on the ground rising as `1 - exp(-j / K)` with the shear displacement, here with the slip speed in its place, and the lateral resistance of skid steering): each road wheel casts a ray, carries a share of the hull on a spring and pushes the ground along the slip of its belt against it. The motorcycle's rider steers into the fall as in R. S. Sharp, "The Stability and Control of Motorcycles", Journal of Mechanical Engineering Science 13(5), 1971, and K. J. Astrom, R. E. Klein and A. Lennartsson, "Bicycle Dynamics and Control", IEEE Control Systems Magazine 25(4), 2005; the lean of a steady turn is `atan(a / g)`, the balance of the weight and the sideways acceleration, and the gains are tuned on the model, not taken from a paper.

### Block solve of a manifold's normal rows (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-24, B-08)

The exact solve of a contact manifold's normal rows follows D. Baraff, "Fast Contact Force Computation for Nonpenetrating Rigid Bodies", SIGGRAPH 1994 (principal pivoting on the contact linear complementarity problem), E. Catto, "Iterative Dynamics with Temporal Coherence" and "Solving Rigid Body Contacts", GDC 2005 and 2006 (the two-point block solve by trying each assignment of points to free or at zero), E. Catto, "Solver2D" (2024, the soft step this solver uses), R. W. Cottle, J.-S. Pang and R. E. Stone, "The Linear Complementarity Problem", Academic Press 1992, chapter 4 (a positive definite matrix gives a unique solution), K. Erleben, "Numerical Methods for Linear Complementarity Problems in Physics-Based Animation", SIGGRAPH 2013 course notes, and R. Smith's Open Dynamics Engine documentation of the constraint force mixing term (the diagonal added to make a rank-deficient matrix definite). No code of any of them was read. The size of the diagonal shift, the square root of f32 rounding of each point's own stiffness (about 3.5e-4), is the shift that makes a rank-three matrix of four coplanar points positive definite for a Cholesky factorisation that must be done in f32 (N. J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms", 2nd ed., SIAM 2002, section 10.3, on the Cholesky factorisation of semidefinite matrices and shifts): a shift of rounding itself is lost in the factorisation, one of order one moves the answer, and the geometric mean of the two does neither. Its effect is measured, not assumed: a box on four points splits its load within 2 percent and rests where the sweeps leave it to 0.1 mm (`kernel/tests/block_solver.rs`). The enumeration finds the answer of every manifold of a 210-box pile, a 12-row pyramid, a single box and the ten thousand steps of the replay scene (`no_manifold_of_the_standard_scenes_is_left_to_the_sweeps`, `the_block_solver_leaves_no_manifold_of_the_scene_to_the_sweeps`), so the fall-back to the sweeps is a counted event that has not fired.

## ASCII post effect (2026-11-24)

`@margoengine/post/ascii`. Feature names were compared with the public API documentation of three.js AsciiEffect (https://threejs.org/docs/pages/AsciiEffect.html: character set, resolution, colour, block, invert, text output) and pmndrs postprocessing ASCIIEffect (characters, font, font size, cell size, colour, inverted); no source of either was read.

Research compared:
- Xuemiao Xu, Linling Zhang and Tien-Tsin Wong, *Structure-based ASCII Art* (SIGGRAPH 2010, ACM TOG 29(4)), https://doi.org/10.1145/1778765.1778789. Matches glyph shapes to image lines with an alignment-insensitive metric while deforming the picture; an offline optimisation, not used.
- Xuemiao Xu, Linyuan Zhong, Minshan Xie, Xueting Liu, Jing Qin and Tien-Tsin Wong, *ASCII Art Synthesis from Natural Photographs* (IEEE TVCG 23(8), 2017), https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2016.2569084. Offline selection and optimisation, not used.
- Moonjun Chung and Taesoo Kwon, *Fast Text Placement Scheme for ASCII Art Synthesis* (IEEE Access 10, 2022), https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2022.3167567. Orientation features and placement over seconds per picture, not used.
- Josef Bigun and Gosta H. Granlund, *Optimal Orientation Detection of Linear Symmetry* (ICCV 1987, pp. 433-438); the construction as restated by Bigun and Fernando Alonso-Fernandez, *Note on the Construction of Structure Tensor* (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23137. Used: the 2 x 2 tensor of gradient products summed over a cell gives the dominant orientation, half atan2(2 Jxy, Jxx - Jyy), and its coherence sqrt((Jxx - Jyy)^2 + 4 Jxy^2) / (Jxx + Jyy).

Built: tone ramp selection per cell, with the tensor choosing among four edge characters in one fragment pass, which is real time at the cost of shape matching. The threshold is the squared central difference a straight step of the given contrast leaves in a cell, about t^2 (width + height) / 4. The coherence limit 0.5, the default ramp (ordered by the ink count of the built-in glyphs, checked by test) and every default are Margo's. The 95 bitmap glyphs of `packages/post/src/ascii-glyphs.ts` were drawn by hand for Margo, not taken from any font.

### Island by island solving (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-24, B-05)

Solving each island of bodies through all its substeps, as apart from the other islands, follows D. Baraff, "Dynamic Simulation of Non-Penetrating Rigid Bodies", PhD thesis, Cornell University, 1992 (a world is split into islands of bodies joined by contacts and joints, which share no unknown), and, for solving independent groups of constraints in parallel, R. Tonge, F. Benevolenski and A. Voroshilov, "Mass Splitting for Jitter-Free Parallel Rigid Body Simulation", ACM Transactions on Graphics 31(4), SIGGRAPH 2012. A kinematic body's pose at each substep is its pose at the start of the step advanced with the arithmetic of the integrator, so it needs no source. No code of any of them was read.

### Mesh path tracer BLEND alpha (`@margoengine/voxel-pathtracer/mesh-pbr`, 2026-11-25)

Built from the papers and specification below; no path tracer source (three-gpu-pathtracer included, feature list only) was read.

- Khronos Group, *glTF 2.0 Specification*, section 3.9.4 "Alpha Coverage", https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#alpha-coverage (BLEND alpha is coverage; MASK uses alphaCutoff).
- E. Enderton, E. Sintorn, P. Shirley and D. Luebke, "Stochastic Transparency", I3D 2010, https://doi.org/10.1145/1730804.1730817 (coverage as the probability that a surface stops a sample; order independent and unbiased in expectation).
- C. Wyman and M. McGuire, "Hashed Alpha Testing", I3D 2017, https://doi.org/10.1145/3023368.3023370 (a hash of the surface point instead of a fresh random number, so one surface point takes one decision).
- M. Pharr, W. Jakob and G. Humphreys, *Physically Based Rendering*, 4th ed., 2023, section 7.1.1 "Geometric Primitives", https://pbr-book.org/4ed/Primitives_and_Intersection_Acceleration/Primitive_Interface_and_Geometric_Primitives (stochastic alpha inside intersection, from a hash of the ray, so every ray kind shares the rule).
- S. Woop, C. Benthin and I. Wald, "Watertight Ray/Triangle Intersection", JCGT 2(1), 2013, https://jcgt.org/published/0002/01/05/ (why a ray through a shared edge meets both triangles, and so why the decision is keyed on the hit distance, not the triangle).
- E. Veach, *Robust Monte Carlo Methods for Light Transport Simulation*, PhD thesis, Stanford, 1997, chapter 9 (the light-point emission is the coverage expectation, so the existing power-heuristic weights stay valid).

Combined: Pharr et al.'s in-traversal test with Wyman and McGuire's point keying, the point being the hit distance rounded to 13 mantissa bits, hashed with the ray's current random state, which is read but not advanced.

### Counter-based random numbers (`kernel-common`, 2026-11-25, K02)

`kernel-common/src/random.rs` is Philox 4x32 with ten rounds as specified in J. K. Salmon, M. A. Moraes, R. O. Dror and D. E. Shaw, "Parallel random numbers: as easy as 1, 2, 3", Proceedings of SC 2011, section 3.3 and Table 2 (the multipliers 0xD2511F53 and 0xCD9E8D57, the key increments 0x9E3779B9 and 0xBB67AE85, the round structure), written from the paper. Its three known-answer vectors (counter and key of zeros, of ones, and of the digits of pi) are the vectors published for the generator, and the implementation reproduces all three; the code of the authors' library was not read. The streams of (seed, solver, tick, element, stream) are this crate's own layout of the counter and key: key [seed, solver number] (two whole 32-bit words; the solver number is the full FNV-1a hash of its id, so a hundred solvers meet in about one world in 900,000, where 16 bits met in about one in twelve), counter [element, stream, tick low word, tick high word] (changed 2026-11-25; the world's seed is one 32-bit word and a larger one is refused). The integer range draw is the multiply-shift of D. Lemire, "Fast random integer generation in an interval", ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation 29(1), 2019, without the rejection step, so the number of draws never depends on the numbers drawn.

### Deterministic radix sort (`kernel-common`, 2026-11-25, K03)

`kernel-common/src/sort.rs` is the least significant digit radix sort the graph colouring already used, moved out so every solver shares it and run over all eight bytes of a `key << 32 | id` entry, so that the order is the entries' order as numbers (key, then id) whatever order they arrive in. The method is the counting sort of H. H. Seward, "Information sorting in the application of electronic digital computers to business operations", MIT Report R-232, 1954, applied a byte at a time as in T. Cormen, C. Leiserson, R. Rivest and C. Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms", chapter 8. The colouring's order is unchanged (its entries arrive in id order).

### Snapshot, restore and state hash of the framework's solvers (`@margoengine/physics/world`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/world/snapshot.ts` takes, restores and hashes the regions each solver names as its state and its extra
history (docs/physics-framework.md, section 8), in canonical order (solvers by id, regions as listed), with no memory
offsets in the stream. The hash is two lanes of MurmurHash3's 32-bit function with different seeds, written from the
algorithm's published description: A. Appleby, "MurmurHash3", 2011, public domain, https://github.com/aappleby/smhasher/wiki/MurmurHash3
(the description page; no source file of it was read). It is checked against the function's published vectors ("" seed 0:
0, "hello" seed 0: 0x248bfa47, "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" seed 0: 0x2e4ff723), fed whole and in
three-byte pieces. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/world-snapshot.test.js`.
### The field registry of the physics framework (`@margoengine/physics/world`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/world/fields.ts` and `memory.ts` keep every field that crosses a solver boundary (docs/physics-framework.md,
section 4): one writer, readers and contributors, values at the coupling tick with the previous one mirrored in the world's
memory, and contributions summed by contributor id then element. The access model is the "privileges" of task-based runtimes and
render graphs: M. Bauer, S. Treichler, E. Slaughter and A. Aiken, "Legion: Expressing Locality and Independence with Logical
Regions", SC 2012, https://doi.org/10.1109/SC.2012.71, and Y. O'Donnell, "FrameGraph: Extensible Rendering Architecture in
Frostbite", GDC 2017; fields shared by coupled models as in D. Gaston, C. Newman, G. Hansen and D. Lebrun-Grandie, "MOOSE: A
parallel computational framework for coupled systems of nonlinear equations", Nuclear Engineering and Design 239(10), 2009,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nucengdes.2009.05.021, and C. Hill, C. DeLuca, V. Balaji, M. Suarez and A. da Silva, "The
Architecture of the Earth System Modeling Framework", Computing in Science and Engineering 6(1), 2004,
https://doi.org/10.1109/MCISE.2004.1255817 (all known through the framework's survey, not read in full here). The order-fixed sum
is the canonical order of the framework's section 7; the mirrors, the meta region and the f64 contribution regions are this
package's own arrangement. Transfers are named after the methods that will fill them (Jiang et al. 2015, APIC; Jones 1999 and
Ullrich and Taylor 2015, conservative remapping; Farhat, Lesoinne and Le Tallec 1998), none implemented yet. Proof:
`packages/physics/tests/world-fields.test.js`.
### Counter-based random numbers of the physics framework (`@margoengine/physics/world`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/math/src/random.ts` (`@margoengine/math/random`, until 2026-11-25 in `packages/physics/src/world/random.ts`, which re-exports it) is Philox4x32-10, the TypeScript twin of the engine's one counter-based generator
(docs/physics-framework.md, section 7; `kernel-common/src/random.rs`, K02), with its key (the seed and the solver's number, each a whole 32-bit word) and counter
(element, stream, the tick's two words) laid out alike (changed 2026-11-25 from a 64-bit seed and a solver folded to 16 bits, which
met in about one world in twelve at a hundred solvers); `kernel-common/tests/random-vectors.txt` pins both
languages to the same words (`random_twin.rs` and `world-random.test.js`). Written from J. K. Salmon, M. A. Moraes, R. O. Dror and D. E. Shaw, "Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1, 2, 3",
SC 2011, https://www.thesalmons.org/john/random123/papers/random123sc11.pdf, read in full (section 4.3: the Philox S-box, the
Philox-4x32 multipliers 0xD2511F53 and 0xCD9E8D57, the Weyl key increments and the round counts; the paper's companion code
was not read). Checked against the published Philox4x32-10 answers for the all-zero, all-ones and pi-digit counters and keys.
A solver's number is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of its id's UTF-8 bytes (G. Fowler, L. C. Noll and K.-P. Vo; D. Eastlake, T.
Hansen, G. Fowler, K.-P. Vo and L. Noll, "The FNV Non-Cryptographic Hash Algorithm", IETF Internet-Draft,
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-eastlake-fnv/), checked against its published values for "", "a" and "foobar", and
used whole (32 bits; it was xor-folded to 16 bits before the layout change). Proof: `packages/physics/tests/world-random.test.js`.
### The physics world: clock, coupling order, rate levels and origin cells (`@margoengine/physics/world`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/world/world.ts` and `graph.ts` run the framework's solvers on one clock and one memory
(docs/physics-framework.md, sections 2 and 5): a base tick grid at the finest dyadic rate, frames mapped to ticks in exact
integers, solvers ordered by their coupling graph, rate levels chosen from state at 1/60 s boundaries, and integer origin
cells, with the world's own state in regions of the shared memory so the snapshot and hash of the framework take it along.
Written from:

- R. Tarjan, "Depth-First Search and Linear Graph Algorithms", SIAM Journal on Computing 1(2), 1972,
  https://doi.org/10.1137/0201010 (strongly connected components; written here without recursion).
- A. B. Kahn, "Topological Sorting of Large Networks", Communications of the ACM 5(11), 1962,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/368996.369025 (the order of the coupling groups; ties broken by solver id).
- C. W. Gear and D. R. Wells, "Multirate Linear Multistep Methods", BIT 24, 1984, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01934907, and W.
  H. Neal and T. Belytschko, "Explicit-Explicit Subcycling with Non-Integer Time Step Ratios for Structural Dynamic Systems",
  Computers and Structures 31(6), 1989 (solvers at different rates meeting on shared ticks; known through the framework's
  survey, not read in full here).
- C. A. Felippa, K. C. Park and C. Farhat, "Partitioned analysis of coupled mechanical systems", Computer Methods in Applied
  Mechanics and Engineering 190, 2001, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0045-7825(00)00391-1 (the staggered exchange; known through
  the framework's survey, not read in full here).
- C. Thorne, "Using a Floating Origin to Improve Fidelity and Performance of Large, Distributed Virtual Worlds",
  International Conference on Cyberworlds, 2005, https://doi.org/10.1109/CW.2005.15 (positions kept relative to a moving
  origin; known through the framework's survey, not read in full here). The integer cell and the exact cell shift are this

### Wakes (`WakeSolver`, `@margoengine/physics/sea`, 2026-11-25, SEA-04)

`packages/physics/src/sea/wake.ts` is written from:

- J. Tessendorf, "Simulating Ocean Water", course notes, 1999-2004, read pages 3-4 to 3-15: the linearised potential flow
  with the pressure kept in the Bernoulli equation (eq. 14), the surface's vertical velocity as an operator on the surface
  potential (eqs. 19 and 21), and iWave's operator g sqrt(-grad^2) and its finite-depth form with tanh (eqs. 50 to 52).
  iWave's own numerical kernel is in Tessendorf's "Interactive Water Surfaces" (Game Programming Gems 4, 2004), which was
  not read; the operator is applied here where it is exact instead, by the shared FFT, and each mode's step is the exact
  solution of the two linear equations derived here (in the file's header).
- M. Rabaud and F. Moisy, "Ship wakes: Kelvin or Mach angle?", Physical Review Letters 110, 214503 (2013), arXiv:1304.2653,
  read (arXiv v1): the wake's angle of largest amplitude is Kelvin's asin(1/3) for Froude numbers up to
  sqrt(3 / (4 pi)) = 0.49 and narrows above it (their eqs. 3a, 3b and 4). The test of the Kelvin wedge runs at 0.37.

#### SEA-04 finite screen and circular cylinder

The production finite wake is checked against the Penney–Price thin-screen solution in the
two-Fresnel-term form of Takayama and Kamiyama, and the MacCamy–Fuchs cylinder solution.
The screen test compares complex elevation on both sides and launches a separate incident-only
packet. The cylinder fixture uses the outgoing Hankel modes with coefficients
`-J′ₙ(ka)/H′ₙ(ka)`. The spatial probes are fixed between grids and the open-water controls
use the same input and sample times. No parameters come from the reference elevations.
[Penney and Price, 1952](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1952.0003)
[Takayama and Kamiyama, 1977](https://www.pari.go.jp/en/1977/09/1977090160301.html)
[MacCamy and Fuchs, 1954](https://usace.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/api/collection/p266001coll1/id/7401/download)

#### SEA-04 uniform current, capillary restoring force and weak viscosity

Each mode has vertical potential gradient `K = k tanh(k D)`, restoring coefficient
`G = g + sigma k² / rho` and intrinsic frequency `sqrt(K G)`. Scott's 1981 tank study gives
this dispersion relation and reports separately measured wavelengths, period, depth and
surface tension. The uniform flow shifts the frequency by `k dot U`, following the
intrinsic-frequency treatment of Bretherton and Garrett. The small-viscosity surface terms
in Dias, Dyachenko and Zakharov give equal diagonal damping `2 nu k²` in height and potential.
The specified viscosity applies those surface terms over finite depth, with a slip bed.
[Scott, 1981](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112081002024)
[Bretherton and Garrett, 1968](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112068002181)
[Dias, Dyachenko and Zakharov, 2008](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.3352)

The optional step holds pressure fixed in the world over the tick. It integrates the pressure
impulse exactly in each eigenbranch using the continuous limit of `(exp(z) - 1) / z`, where
`z = dt (-2 nu k² - i (k dot U ± sqrt(K G)))`. The zero mode keeps the separate displaced
volume ledger. The samples report the potential's velocity perturbation. Horizontal advection
omits each unresolved even-grid Nyquist derivative to preserve real Fourier symmetry.
`sea-wake-modes.test.js` covers resonant held pressure by independent Simpson integration,
oblique wave phase and attenuation, and exact rerun and seek. At the seven measured
100–200 ms periods that Scott groups together, the separately predicted wavelengths give
1.30% relative RMS versus 22.36% for gravity alone. The wavelength precision was 0.4%.
Scott reports faster observed propagation in these short-period tests, possibly from tank drift.
No measured wavelength was used to choose the model inputs.

#### SEA-04 bathymetry, rain impulses and native transforms

The finite volume query reports the first solid depth in each wet surface column. A stepped
tank verifies the long-wave free-surface reflection and transmission coefficients from continuity
of height and depth-integrated flow. With speeds `c = sqrt(g D)`, these are
`(c1 - c2)/(c1 + c2)` and `2 c1/(c1 + c2)`, respectively.
The test separates the incident and reflected waves at upstream gauges and confirms that the
flow below the shallow bed is dry. [Lamb, Hydrodynamics, 1932](https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/toc/344665/9780521458689_toc_001.pdf)

A supplied rain drop adds its sphere volume and normal momentum to the local wave solver.
The raised-cosine pressure profile has the same integrated impulse at a grid centre and between
cells. Schreck et al. and Le Méhauté model small-drop gravity–capillary waves by linear momentum
forcing. The adapter uses the solver's existing spatial quadrature and holds the impulse over
one physical tick. For a supplied contact the ATMO-04 equivalent drop preserves per-impact
liquid volume and kinetic energy from the measured flux contracts. The production test compares
against a direct Fourier sum and time integration.
[Le Méhauté, 1988](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112088003301)
[Schreck, Hafner and Wojtan, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1145/3306346.3323002)

The native transform uses a Stockham mixed-radix plan with pinned twiddles and the same
sum order as the TypeScript implementation. Each complex product uses two f64x2 products
and one f64x2 sum. Integer twiddle indices are prepared once per plan. The private-memory
plan copies one spatial and one spectral buffer per transform, in either direction.
The production coupling and depth outputs reproduce the same bytes across both backends,
and the same asset draws on WebGPU and WebGL2.
[Stockham, 1966](https://doi.org/10.1145/1464182.1464209)
[WebAssembly SIMD specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/2025/CRD-wasm-core-2-20250616/)

#### SEA-04 breaking crest readback

The local wake estimates the crest along the strongest negative curvature direction, then
compares fitted crest positions from the last two accepted wave surfaces. It recovers
the water velocity from the accepted potential at that subcell crest. Both speeds use
the same water-relative frame. The fixed onset ratio is 0.85 from Barthélemy and
Derakhti. The estimator declines near-isotropic, unresolved or pressure-forced
stencils. The foam consumer represents each reported crest sample by its grid cell's
nominal surface area, limited by the receiving foam cell. This publishes local active and
residual coverage and feeds the existing spray reader. The wake remains linear and
the field does not resolve overturning, bubble entrainment or breaker energy loss.
[Barthélemy et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2018.93)
[Derakhti et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JC015886)

Saket's Table 1 supplies independent measured particle and crest velocities with separate
observed breaker labels. Applying the fixed criterion to those inputs rejects all 13
recurrent cases and flags 8 of 13 nominal marginal breakers. The other five lie within
the reported ±0.020 uncertainty on the ratio. The manufactured oblique wave and live
wake-to-foam test separately measure estimator convergence and verify exact replay.
[Saket et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04354)

#### SEA-04 moving pressure amplitude

Havelock's 1908 deep-water pressure impulse solution, sections 12–13 and equations 67–69,
gives a radial Green function. A moving finite pressure field superposes the impulse at each
held midpoint. The test computes a direct periodic modal sum and an independent open-water
Hankel integral for the raised-cosine footprint. Spatial and periodic-image effects are
measured from those two references. Radial integration by parts bounds the tail separately
from the finite quadrature. The production gauge signal matches the periodic sum to
1.08e−15 m and the open reference to 98.44 µm against an independent 149.40 µm budget.
[Havelock, 1908](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1908.0097)

#### SEA-04 pressure on a prescribed mean hull

The finite wake closes the mean hull cells and places the small-motion flux
`n dot (V + Ω cross r)` at every wetted face. This is the boundary condition
linearized about the mean wetted surface in Cummins's equation 34. Face normals
and their moment arms supply the transpose pressure map. The pressure impulse is
computed from the accepted bulk-potential difference. The midpoint boundary work
and the extra boundary term in Green's identity use the same signed flux, so the
measured work is coupled to the actual potential. The oscillating piston and
heave fixtures check this balance, exposed velocity, physical pressure, signed
volume and exact seek. A fixed or oscillating mask is distinct from a translating
hull that changes the wetted geometry.
[Cummins, The Impulse Response Function and Ship Motions, 1962](https://dome.mit.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/4a239966-bc09-4811-8917-d152923c167f/content)

`bakeWakeHullMask` pairs triangle crossings along each cell-center ray and uses even–odd fill
for solids and enclosed cavities. The projected edge sign is evaluated in a canonical direction
with half-open ties so both triangles agree on every shared diagonal. A box and a polygonal
cylinder supply independent volume bounds. Reindexing, seam copies and live pressure replay
exercise the same public bake as imported and procedural hulls.
[Nooruddin and Turk, Simplification and Repair of Polygonal Models Using Volumetric Techniques, 2003, §3.2](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~turk/my_papers/volumetric_simp.pdf)
[Woop, Benthin and Wald, Watertight Ray/Triangle Intersection, 2013](https://jcgt.org/published/0002/01/05/)

### The sea's surface and water (`@margoengine/physics/sea`, 2026-11-25, SEA-02)

`packages/physics/src/sea/surface.ts` is written from:

- J. Tessendorf, "Simulating Ocean Water", course notes, 1999-2004 (coursenotes2004.pdf, Clemson University), read pages
  3-1 to 3-12: the linearised potential flow (eqs. 11 to 21: u = grad phi, Laplace's equation inside the water, d phi /
  dt = -g h on the surface, and the linearised Bernoulli equation, eq. 14), the dispersion relations for deep water and
  over a bottom D deep (eqs. 31 and 32), the surface as a sum of waves (eq. 30) and its slope (eq. 37).
- The depth profile is derived here from those equations, not taken from another source: each wave's potential solves eq.
  18 (d^2/dy^2 = k^2) with no flow through a flat bottom, so it goes as cosh(k (y + D)); eq. 20 fixes its size, and its
  gradient with eq. 32 gives u = A omega cosh(k (y + D)) / sinh(k D) cos(theta) along k and w = A omega sinh(k (y + D)) /
  sinh(k D) sin(theta); eq. 14 gives the pressure rho g (A cosh(k (y + D)) / cosh(k D) cos(theta) - y). The tests check
  each against these closed forms, the surface moving with the water (w = dh/dt) and the water not compressing.
- The wavenumbers and band widths are the wave solver's own (`wavenumber`, `bandWidth` of `@margoengine/physics/waves`), so
  the sea and its spectrum agree on every wave.

### The world's region allocator (`Arena` in `@margoengine/physics/world`, 2026-11-26)

`allocate`, `free` and `resize` in `packages/physics/src/world/memory.ts` are written from the papers below; no allocator's
code was read.

- P. R. Wilson, M. S. Johnstone, M. Neely and D. Boles, "Dynamic Storage Allocation: A Survey and Critical Review",
  International Workshop on Memory Management, LNCS 986, 1995, https://www.cs.hmc.edu/~oneill/gc-library/Wilson-Alloc-Survey-1995.pdf,
  read for the policies (first fit, address-ordered first fit, best fit) and for immediate coalescing of freed neighbours.
- M. S. Johnstone and P. R. Wilson, "The Memory Fragmentation Problem: Solved?", ISMM 1998,
  https://sfkaplan.people.amherst.edu/courses/2016/fall/COSC-461/documents/Johnstone-Memory-fragmentation-problem.pdf,
  read: in their traces address-ordered first fit and best fit are the two policies with the least fragmentation. Own
  choices: a sorted list of free blocks (the arena holds few regions, so no tree), 8-byte granularity, a block reaching the
  top lowering the top, and resize in place where the block grows into the top or into the free block after it.

### Solver modules on one memory (`@margoengine/physics/world`, `scripts/physics-modules.mjs`, 2026-11-25)

The module table, the build check and the loader (`packages/physics/src/world/memory.ts`) are written from the linker's and
the standard's documentation and from what the builds were measured to contain; no engine's code was read.

- LLVM Project, "WebAssembly lld port" (lld documentation), https://lld.llvm.org/WebAssembly.html, read: `--global-base`
  ("Address at which to place global data"), `--stack-first` (the stack at the start of linear memory, not after the data),
  `--import-memory`, `--max-memory`, `--export`. `--shared-memory` and `-z stack-size` are not on that page; their effect
  here is what the builds were measured to contain (`inspectModule` in the script: a shared memory import with the declared
  maximum, data from the slot's base to `__data_end`, a stack pointer at 0 with a stack size of 0).
- WebAssembly Community Group, "Threading proposal for WebAssembly" (proposals/threads/Overview.md),
  https://github.com/WebAssembly/threads/blob/main/proposals/threads/Overview.md, read: a linear memory marked shared is
  shared between the agents of a cluster and must declare a maximum; a `WebAssembly.Memory` posted to a worker is
  instantiated there as the module's memory, and one agent's writes are seen by the others. The page says data segments are
  copied again on each instantiation; the shared builds here hold one passive segment that the module copies once at start,
  and `tests/world-modules.test.js` checks that no later instance or step rewrites a module's window.

### The coupling scheduler and its harness (`@margoengine/physics/world`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/world/scheduler.ts` and the world's `couple()` give a coupling group one of five schemes
(docs/physics-framework.md, section 5); `packages/physics/tests/coupling/harness.js` and `scripts/check-coupling.mjs` are the
guard of section 10. Written from:

- H. F. Walker and P. Ni, "Anderson Acceleration for Fixed-Point Iterations", SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 49(4), 2011,
  https://doi.org/10.1137/10078356X, read in full (the unconstrained least-squares form, m_k = min(m, k), solved here by
  modified Gram-Schmidt QR with dependent columns given no weight).
- U. Langer and H. Yang, "Partitioned solution algorithms for fluid-structure interaction problems with hyperelastic models",
  arXiv:1312.5561, 2013, read in full (eqs. 52-53: Aitken's dynamic relaxation as Kuttler and Wall give it). U. Kuttler and W.
  A. Wall, "Fixed-point fluid-structure interaction solvers with dynamic relaxation", Computational Mechanics 43, 2008, could not be read here; the formula is taken from Langer and Yang.
- P. Causin, J.-F. Gerbeau and F. Nobile, "Added-mass effect in the design of partitioned algorithms for fluid-structure
  problems", Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 194, 2005, could
  not be read here; the staggered amplification factor -m_a / m_s used by `staggeringStable` was derived here for a rigid
  body in a fluid that reacts with -m_a times its acceleration, which is the paper's known result for this model.
- G. Strang, "On the Construction and Comparison of Difference Schemes", SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 5(3), 1968,
  https://doi.org/10.1137/0705041 (the symmetric splitting A(dt/2) B(dt) A(dt/2)).
- C. Farhat, K. G. van der Zee and P. Geuzaine, "Provably second-order time-accurate loosely-coupled solution algorithms for
  transient nonlinear computational aeroelasticity", Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 195, 2006 (the predicted interface state; known through the framework's survey).
- C. Batty, F. Bertails and R. Bridson, "A Fast Variational Framework for Accurate Solid-Fluid Coupling", ACM Transactions on
  Graphics 26(3), 2007, and A. Robinson-Mosher, C. Schroeder and R. Fedkiw, "A
  symmetric positive definite formulation for monolithic fluid structure interaction", Journal of Computational Physics
  230(4), 2011 (bodies inside the pressure solve; known through the survey).
- J. Degroote, K.-J. Bathe and J. Vierendeels, "Performance of a new partitioned procedure versus a monolithic procedure in
  fluid-structure interaction", Computers and Structures 87, 2009 (iterated
  coupling against a monolithic solve; known through the survey).

The scheme loop (Jacobi runs of a group over saved registry regions, the predicted extrapolation to each step's end, the
implicit-pressure re-import) is this framework's own arrangement. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/world-scheduler.test.js`,
`packages/physics/tests/coupling/framework.test.js` and `tests/check-coupling.test.js`.
### Pinned elementary functions and fixed-order sums (`kernel-common`, 2026-11-25, K01)

`kernel-common/src/pinned.rs` has `exp`, `ln`, `sin`, `cos`, `pow` and a fixed-partition sum over f64, built only from + - * / and integer operations, so every build gives the same bits. The methods are the textbook ones: argument reduction by the leading and trailing parts of ln 2 and of pi / 2 (W. J. Cody and W. Waite, "Software Manual for the Elementary Functions", Prentice-Hall, 1980; the parts are split here with exact arithmetic from the decimal digits of pi and ln 2, not copied) and Taylor series on the reduced interval (J.-M. Muller, "Elementary Functions: Algorithms and Implementation", 3rd ed., Birkhauser, 2016, chapters 4 and 11); `pow` carries ln x and the product y ln x as pairs of doubles (TwoSum, T. J. Dekker's split product, "A floating-point technique for extending the available precision", Numerische Mathematik 18, 1971; Muller 2016, section 4.3). The sum adds blocks of 256 in order and the blocks' sums by a balanced tree over their indices, the fixed-partition idea of J. Demmel and H. D. Nguyen, "Parallel reproducible summation", IEEE Transactions on Computers 64(7), 2015. Accuracy is held against the host's functions by `kernel-common/tests/pinned.rs`: within 2 ulp for exp, ln, sin and cos, within 4 ulp for pow.

### Uniform-grid neighbour search (`kernel-common`, 2026-11-25, K04)

`kernel-common/src/neighbours.rs` bins points into cells of one size with a counting sort and lets a query visit the cells around a point in a fixed order, the points of a cell by id: the linked-cell method of R. W. Hockney and J. W. Eastwood, "Computer Simulation Using Particles", McGraw-Hill, 1981, chapter 8, with binning by counting sort as described in S. Green, "Particle Simulation using CUDA", NVIDIA white paper, 2010. No hash table is used, so no table size or insertion order decides the sequence of candidates.

Sparse storage (added 2026-11-25 for large fluid domains): a point set whose bounding box would need more than 2^26 cells, or more than five cells a point (the memory cost of the dense counters against the sorted keys, derived in the module's `Storage` comment), keeps only the occupied cells: the points sorted by a 96-bit cell key (three 32-bit coordinates, z most significant) with a stable least-significant-digit radix sort (H. H. Seward, 1954, as the existing sort of `sort.rs`; T. Cormen, C. Leiserson, R. Rivest and C. Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms", chapter 8), and a query finds a cell by binary search over the sorted keys. The compact, sorted-cell layout follows M. Ihmsen, N. Akinci, M. Becker and M. Teschner, "A parallel SPH implementation on multi-core CPUs", Computer Graphics Forum 30(1), 99-112, 2011 (the paper, not any implementation of it); their hash table is not used. Sorted keys are the order a query visits cells in, so sparse and dense storage give the same candidates in the same order (a test). A set wider than 2^32 - 1 cells along an axis is refused: a grid counts its cells along an axis in 32 bits, which no f32 point set reaches at a cell its coordinates can resolve.

### Crowd walls as ORCA constraints (navmesh, 2026-11-25)

`packages/navmesh/src/orca.ts` (`wallLine`, the hard rows of `leastViolation`, `accelerate`) and the wall gathering of
`packages/navmesh/src/crowd.ts`, written from the paper alone; no crowd library or engine source was read:

- J. van den Berg, S. J. Guy, M. Lin and D. Manocha, "Reciprocal n-Body Collision Avoidance", Robotics Research (ISRR
  2009), Springer Tracts in Advanced Robotics 70, 2011, pp. 3-19, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-19457-3_1 (read in
  full). Used: section 5.4, equation 11: the velocity obstacle of a line-segment obstacle; the optimisation velocity 0
  for obstacles, so a permitted velocity always exists; full responsibility; a shorter time horizon for obstacles than
  for agents; obstacle constraints are not relaxed when the linear program of section 5.1 is infeasible, which is the
  hard rows of section 5.2's three-dimensional program here.
- D. Helbing and P. Molnar, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Physical Review E 51(5), 4282-4286, 1995,
  https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.51.4282. Compared: a wall acts on a pedestrian from the nearest point of the wall,
  as the half-plane does here; its repulsive potential is not used (a force cannot keep a fast agent off a wall it
  approaches within one step, a hard constraint can).

Margo's own: the walls are the navmesh border, the edges (or parts of edges at tile seams) that no portal to allowed
ground opens, gathered through portals within the distance the agent can close in the wall horizon; the wall horizon
is the agent's time to stop from top speed, `maxSpeed / maxAcceleration` (at least one step), the shortest at which the
braking the half-plane asks for stays within the acceleration limit; the border bounds the agent's centre (radius 0),
since the mesh is eroded by the agent radius; only walls whose nearest point to the agent lies inside them give a
half-plane, because the half-plane of a wall's end, a corner of the border, brakes an agent walking at it, and every
route corner lies on such a corner; the acceleration limit is applied by solving the same linear program in a disc of
radius `maxAcceleration * dt` round the current velocity with the walls kept, and gives way to the walls when they need
more. Proof: `packages/navmesh/test/crowd-walls.test.js` (a Z bend at full speed, a diagonal corridor head on and in a
group: no frame stopped by a wall, no velocity reversals).

### Crowd route corners passed by straight view (navmesh, 2026-11-25)

The corner rule of `packages/navmesh/src/crowd.ts` (`straight`), from the paper alone:

- I. Karamouzas, R. Geraerts and M. Overmars, "Indicative Routes for Path Planning and Crowd Simulation", Foundations of
  Digital Games (FDG) 2009, pp. 113-120, https://webspace.science.uu.nl/~gerae101/pdf/fdg09.pdf (read: sections 4.2 and 4.3). Used:
  the attraction point is the furthest point of the route the character can still reach through the free space round
  it, always ahead of it, so it is never pulled back to a point of the route it has passed.

Margo's own: the route stays the funnel's corners; a corner is passed once it is within reach this frame (as before) or
once the corner after it can be walked to in a straight line on ground the agent may use, tested by following the
segment through the polygons it crosses, each left through a portal; the start of an off-mesh link is still passed
only by reaching it. Proof: `packages/navmesh/test/crowd-corners.test.js` (three agents following each other round the
two corners of a diagonal corridor: no turning back on the spot, no loop).

### Crowd arrival at a target others cover (navmesh, 2026-11-25)

The `joins` rule of `packages/navmesh/src/crowd.ts` and the detour that leaves a standing agent on the target alone.
Sources compared, papers only:

- C. W. Reynolds, "Steering Behaviors For Autonomous Characters", Game Developers Conference 1999,
  https://www.red3d.com/cwr/steer/gdc99/ (read: arrival and path following). Used: the arrival ramp the crowd already
  had (speed falling over `slowDownDistance`); it stops only at the target, so it cannot by itself end at a target
  someone else stands on.
- D. Helbing and P. Molnar, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Physical Review E 51(5), 4282-4286, 1995,
  https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.51.4282. Compared: a destination attracts and other people repel; at a destination
  people already stand on, the two balance short of it and the pedestrian stays pressed against them, which is what an
  arrival test that asks only for the target never ends.
- I. Karamouzas, B. Skinner and S. J. Guy, "Universal Power Law Governing Pedestrian Interactions", Physical Review
  Letters 113, 238701, 2014, https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.238701. Compared: interaction by time to
  collision, which spaces people out but likewise has no notion of a goal that is taken.
- J. van den Berg, S. J. Guy, M. Lin and D. Manocha (2011, above). Compared: ORCA keeps agents apart but leaves an agent
  whose preferred velocity points at a covered target pressing forever.

Margo's own: an agent on its last leg arrives where it meets the group at its target: when it touches (within
`arrivalDistance`) an agent that covers the target (within the two radii of it) and stands still or walks nearer it
(the lower id on a tie), or one that arrived for the same place (its own target within the two radii); or when it is
held back within its own radius more of one of them and its step took it no nearer the target. The detour, which steers
