round standing agents in the way, leaves alone a standing agent that covers the target: the agent joins it instead of
going round it and back. Proof: `packages/navmesh/test/crowd-arrival.test.js` (eight agents to seats 0.5 m apart, nine
agents from three sides to one point, two agents to one point beside a diagonal wall: all arrive, none turns on the
spot or circles, and all end apart).

### Walkers pushed back step back (humans `walkCrowd`, navmesh `preferredVelocity`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/humans/src/crowd.ts` (the heading and phase of an agent pushed back) and `CrowdAgent.preferredVelocity` in
`packages/navmesh/src/crowd.ts`. Sources, abstracts read:

- G. Arechavaleta, J.-P. Laumond, H. Hicheur and A. Berthoz, "On the nonholonomic nature of human locomotion",
  Autonomous Robots 25(1-2), 25-35, 2008, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10514-007-9075-2. Used: in goal-directed walking the
  trunk steers like a wheeled vehicle's front wheel, so a walker faces the way it walks to its goal.
- K. Mombaur, J.-P. Laumond and E. Yoshida, "An Optimal Control-Based Formulation to Determine Natural Locomotor Paths
  for Humanoid Robots", Advanced Robotics 24, 515-535, 2010. Used: human locomotion has holonomic modes (steps sideways
  and back) beside the nonholonomic forward walk.

Margo's own: the heading follows the velocity as before, except while the velocity points against the preferred
velocity (the crowd pushes the agent back): then the heading keeps to the preferred direction and the walk cycle runs
backward by the ground covered. Proof: `packages/humans/test/crowd.test.js` "people sent to packed seats or to one
meeting point never turn on the spot".

### The standard atmosphere as one shared entry (`@margoengine/math/atmosphere`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/math/src/atmosphere.ts` holds the standard atmosphere `weather/src/eruption.ts` had, moved so the physics wind
force, the weather and the framework's wind contract share one implementation (docs/physics-solvers.md, K03); weather
re-exports it. Written from International Organization for Standardization, ISO 2533:1975, "Standard Atmosphere", and
International Civil Aviation Organization, Doc 7488, "Manual of the ICAO Standard Atmosphere", 3rd edition, 1993 (the same
model: layer lapse rates, sea-level 288.15 K and 101,325 Pa, the gas constant 287.05287 J/(kg K), g = 9.80665 m/s^2, and the
tabulated values the test checks, -1 km to 47 km). Below sea level the first layer continues, as ISO 2533 tabulates to
-2 km (before the move it held sea-level values there). Proof: `packages/math/test/atmosphere.test.js`. Since 2026-11-25 the
canonical implementation is `packages/physics/kernel-common/src/atmosphere.rs`, the same operations on the pinned `exp` and
`pow` (K01); `kernel-common/tests/atmosphere_twin.rs` writes and checks `atmosphere-vectors.txt` (218 heights from -2 km to
50 km, shifted sea levels and tropopauses, and the ISO 2533 table), and the TypeScript reproduces every row bit for bit.

## Seams between meshes (2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/kernel/src/mesh.rs` (`Held`, `on_open_edges`): a contact of a round shape or a box with an open edge of a
triangle is dropped when the shape, a few slops smaller, stays on one side of the triangle's plane through the step. The argument is
plain geometry (a flat triangle lies in its plane, so a shape strictly on one side of it cannot touch it) with the ghost-collision
problem as Catto states it in "Ghost Collisions" (box2d.org, 2020) and the speculative contact it comes from in Catto, "Solver2D"
(2024); the cast I tried first, van den Bergen, "Ray casting against general convex objects with application to continuous
collision detection", Journal of Graphics Tools 9(3), 2004, was dropped because its termination is relative to the size of the
triangle. Proof: `kernel/tests/mesh.rs`, `tests/next-mesh-seam.test.js`.


### Pinned maths in TypeScript, the twin of K01 (`@margoengine/math/pinned`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/math/src/pinned.ts` is kernel-common's `pinned.rs` (K01) written again in TypeScript step for step: the same
reduction constants, the same series to the same terms, the same order of every operation, truncation where the Rust casts,
and the exponent and mantissa read from the bits, so the results are the same doubles (JavaScript never fuses a multiply and
an add, and Rust does not contract them unasked). The methods are those the Rust cites: W. J. Cody and W. Waite, "Software
Manual for the Elementary Functions", Prentice-Hall, 1980; J.-M. Muller, "Elementary Functions: Algorithms and
Implementation", 3rd ed., Birkhauser, 2016; T. J. Dekker, "A floating-point technique for extending the available
precision", Numerische Mathematik 18, 1971; J. Demmel and H. D. Nguyen, "Parallel reproducible summation", IEEE Transactions
on Computers 64(7), 2015. `hypot` is the square root of the sum of squares, which IEEE 754 rounds correctly everywhere.
`kernel-common/tests/pinned_twin.rs` writes `pinned-vectors.txt` from the Rust (2,844 vectors over each function's range) and
checks it; `packages/math/test/pinned.test.js` reproduces every one bit for bit.
### Above-water refraction depth (2026-11-21)
- Tiago Sousa, [Generic Refraction Simulation](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems2/part-ii-shading-lighting-and-shadows/chapter-19-generic-refraction-simulation), 2005. Validate a sample in the displaced scene image to avoid foreground silhouette bleed.
- Morgan McGuire and Michael Mara, [Efficient GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing](https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/), 2014. Compare projected ray depth to the framebuffer and bound the ray search.
- Chris Wyman, [An Approximate Image-Space Approach for Interactive Refraction](https://cwyman.org/papers/sig05_approxISRefr.pdf), 2005. Follow the direction changed by the refractive interface to find the color received by the eye.
Margo intersects a homogeneous ray with each candidate depth plane and
checks the resulting texel. The wide-step crossing search supplies fallback
seeds where a depth discontinuity defeats the first estimate. It uses the
existing Water snapshots, depth convention and Snell normal. The shader and
regression were written from these descriptions and analytic geometry.

### Grazing refraction onto a shallow bed (2026-11-26, KB-WATER-SEABEDMAZE1)
- Morgan McGuire and Michael Mara, [Efficient GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing](https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/), JCGT 3(4), 2014. A ray step counts as a hit when the depth buffer's surface lies within a thickness of the ray's own depth; the march stops at the screen's edge.
- Yasin Uludag, "Hi-Z Screen-Space Cone-Traced Reflections", GPU Pro 5, 2014. Bracket the crossing coarsely, then refine it by binary search between the last point in front and the first behind.
- Bart Wronski, [The future of screen space reflections](https://bartwronski.com/2014/01/25/the-future-of-screen-space-reflections/), 2014. Rays that leave the frame have no data past its edge; renderers clamp or fade there rather than draw a fixed colour.
The texel reprojection kept from 2026-11-21 is a fixed-point iteration; on a
bed whose view-depth changes faster across the screen than the ray's does it
diverges. Margo now accepts the bisected crossing with a thickness of 5 cm or
2% of the distance, and takes the last on-screen texel for a ray that leaves
the frame in front of the scene. Written from these descriptions.

### Short-crested surf and dry-sand ripples (2026-11-26, KB-WATER-SURFBANDS1, KB-TERRAIN-SANDWET1)
- C. Baker, M. Moulton, M. L. Palmsten, K. Brodie, E. Nuss and C. C. Chickadel, [Remotely sensed short-crested breaking waves in a laboratory directional wave basin](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coastaleng.2023.104327), Coastal Engineering 183, 2023. Breaking crests get shorter and their ends more numerous as directional spread grows; refracting-wave theory overestimates their length.
- O. M. Phillips, [Spectral and statistical properties of the equilibrium range in wind-generated gravity waves](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112085002221), JFM 156, 1985; J. M. Kleiss and W. K. Melville, [Observations of wave breaking kinematics in fetch-limited seas](https://doi.org/10.1175/2010JPO4383.1), JPO 40(12), 2010. Breaking is a length of crest per area, not whole crests.
- P. J. Haller and P. A. Catalan, [Remote sensing of wave roller lengths in the laboratory](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008JC005185), JGR 114, 2009. The roller's extent as seen in imagery.
- M. Jarzynski and M. Olano, [Hash Functions for GPU Rendering](https://jcgt.org/published/0009/03/02/), JCGT 9(3), 2020. The PCG hash under the section noise.
- S. L. Namikas and D. J. Sherman, "A review of the effects of surface moisture content on aeolian sand transport", Desert Aeolian Processes, 1995; G. F. S. Wiggs, A. J. Baird and R. J. Atherton, [The dynamic effects of moisture on the entrainment and transport of sand by wind](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geomorph.2003.09.002), Geomorphology 59, 2004. Moisture raises the wind's threshold, so wet sand keeps no fresh wind ripples.
Margo swings the breaker index along each crest with value noise laid along
the deep mean direction and the lead component's phase, scaled from the
spread as Baker et al. describe; the constants are chosen against the s18
still. Written from these descriptions.

### White water as a lit bubble layer (2026-11-26, KB-WATER-WHITEWATERLIGHT1)
- C. H. Whitlock, D. S. Bartlett and E. A. Gurganus, [Sea foam reflectance and influence on optimum wavelength for remote sensing of ocean aerosols](https://doi.org/10.1029/GL009i006p00719), GRL 9(6), 1982. Foam reflectance from 0.55 to 2.8 um, about one half in the visible.
- P. Koepke, [Effective reflectance of oceanic whitecaps](https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.23.001816), Applied Optics 23(11), 1984. Fresh whitecaps reflect about 0.55, thinning and fading as they age; the area-averaged effective value is 0.22.
- R. Frouin, M. Schwindling and P.-Y. Deschamps, [Spectral reflectance of sea foam in the visible and near-infrared: in situ measurements and remote sensing implications](https://doi.org/10.1029/96JC00629), JGR 101(C6), 1996. Surf-zone foam from the Scripps pier: flat through the visible, falling toward the red and much lower in the near infrared (40% less at 0.85 um than at 0.44 um).
- A. A. Kokhanovsky, [Spectral reflectance of whitecaps](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003JC002177), JGR 109, C05021, 2004. Foam as a densely packed, weakly absorbing layer of bubbles: a deep layer reflects nearly all visible light, diffusely; absorption by water sets the spectrum.
- H. M. Dierssen, [Hyperspectral measurements, parameterizations, and atmospheric correction of whitecaps and foam from visible to shortwave infrared for ocean color remote sensing](https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2019.00014), Frontiers in Earth Science 7, 2019. Whitecaps average about 0.4 in the visible, lower where the layer is thin.
- P. Kubelka and F. Munk, "Ein Beitrag zur Optik der Farbanstriche", Zeitschrift fur technische Physik 12, 1931. Two-stream reflectance of a scattering layer of finite depth over a substrate.
Margo's foamLight takes the deep-layer reflectance from Kokhanovsky and the
Frouin spectrum (0.84, 0.86, 0.87) for dense foam and thins it by the
Kubelka-Munk layer over black water, the foam amount as optical depth (8 at
full foam), under the fragment's cover blend; it lights the foam by the sky's
cosine-weighted radiance on a lumpy normal plus the sun's N.L. The lump sizes
and slopes, the depth and the hollows' openness (0.95, down to 0.75) are chosen
against the s18 still, whitecaps.browser.mjs's look and whitecap-coverage's
count. Written from these descriptions.

### Gravity-capillary detail and the sea's reactive mask (2026-11-26, KB-WATER-NEARDETAIL1, KB-WATER-TAASMEAR1)
- T. Elfouhaily, B. Chapron, K. Katsaros and D. Vandemark, [A unified directional spectrum for long and short wind-driven waves](https://doi.org/10.1029/97JC00467), JGR 102(C7), 1997. The short-wave curvature spectrum B_h = 0.5 a_m (c_m / c) exp(-(k / k_m - 1)^2 / 4), k_m 370 rad/m, c_m 0.23 m/s, a_m = 0.01 (1 + ln(u* / c_m)) below c_m and 0.01 (1 + 3 ln(u* / c_m)) above.
- J. Wu, [Wind-stress coefficients over sea surface from breeze to hurricane](https://doi.org/10.1029/JC087iC12p09704), JGR 87(C12), 1982. The drag coefficient (0.8 + 0.065 U10) 1e-3 that gives the friction velocity.
- H. Lamb, *Hydrodynamics*, 6th ed., 1932, sec. 267. The phase speed of capillary-gravity waves, c^2 = g / k + (T / rho) k.
- C. Cox and W. Munk, [Measurement of the roughness of the sea surface from photographs of the sun's glitter](https://doi.org/10.1364/JOSA.44.000838), JOSA 44(11), 1954. The total mean square slope 0.003 + 0.00512 U the octaves draw part of.
- E. Bruneton, F. Neyret and N. Holzschuch, [Real-time realistic ocean lighting using seamless transitions from geometry to BRDF](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01618.x), Computer Graphics Forum 29(2), 2010. Slope variance a pixel resolves is drawn as normals; the rest widens the reflectance lobe, so the sea looks the same at every distance.
- B. Karis, "High Quality Temporal Supersampling", SIGGRAPH 2014 Advances in Real-Time Rendering. TAA history is valid only for what the motion vectors follow; a surface whose look moves otherwise needs its history distrusted.
Margo's shortOctave draws five octaves of gradient noise (k 25 to 340 rad/m, a cell 2 pi 0.6 / k long, crests 1.8
cells long), each scaled to B_h(k) ln 2 of mean square slope at the friction velocity of a 16 x chop m/s wind, drifting
at Lamb's phase speed and faded by the pixel footprint like the ripple layers; the resolved share comes off the glint
lobe's Cox and Munk remainder. The reactive mask is the fastest train's deep-water phase speed times the frame's delta
over the pixel footprint, through smoothstep(0.25, 1). The octave ratios and turns, the 16 m/s per unit of chop and the
mask's quarter-pixel knee are Margo choices. Water publishes the mask on the pass context and TAA reads every published
mask with no wiring, taking the maximum of several, the way an upscaler's reactive mask gathers every effect that moves
without motion vectors into one texture (AMD, "FidelityFX Super Resolution 2", GPUOpen documentation, 2022,
https://gpuopen.com/fidelityfx-superresolution-2/, the reactive and transparency-and-composition masks; Karis, "High
Quality Temporal Supersampling", SIGGRAPH 2014 Advances in Real-Time Rendering, for history rejection by such a mask).
Written from these descriptions.

## A buried voxel cell and the nearer side (2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/kernel/src/voxel.rs` (`nearer_hidden_side`): when the ghost rule would snap a contact to an exposed face the
normal leans away from, the snap is dropped if it makes the contact deeper than it was, as a point inside a box leaves through the
nearer side. Plain geometry on top of the ghost rule of Catto, "Ghost Collisions" (box2d.org, 2020); no other source. Proof:
`kernel/tests/voxel.rs`.

## The terrain bed field (2026-11-25, PA-37)

`packages/physics/src/earth/` and `packages/math/src/fields/bed.ts`: a regular grid of elevations sampled on the kernel's own
triangulation (barycentric interpolation of a triangle, its normal from the two edge slopes), with each vertex's share of the
triangulated volume worked out as a triangle's area times the mean of its corner heights; elementary geometry, no source.
The bed's layout and triangle split are the kernel's height field's (already recorded). Proof: `tests/earth-bed.test.js` and
`tests/coupling/earth-bed.test.js`.

### The FFT of the physics framework, Rust and TypeScript twins (K17, `@margoengine/math/fft`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/kernel-common/src/fft.rs` and `packages/math/src/fft.ts` are one mixed-radix FFT written twice with the same
operations in the same order: decimation in frequency in the autosort (Stockham) form, any length with prime factors 2, 3
and 5, twiddles w^j = exp(-2 pi i j / n) computed once from the pinned sin and cos (K01) and stored; transforms along x, y
and z for grids, and a real 2D transform through the complex one with the half spectrum kept (Hermitian symmetry restores
the rest). Written from J. W. Cooley and J. W. Tukey, "An algorithm for the machine calculation of complex Fourier series",
Mathematics of Computation 19(90), 1965; T. G. Stockham, "High-speed convolution and correlation", AFIPS Spring Joint
Computer Conference, 1966; and C. Van Loan, "Computational Frameworks for the Fast Fourier Transform", SIAM, 1992 (sections 1.7
and 2.3; the stage formula is derived in the files' headers). The real transform does the full complex one (the packing
of two real halves into one complex sequence, Van Loan section 4.4, is a speed item for later). `kernel-common/tests/fft_twin.rs`
writes and checks `fft-vectors.txt` (37 cases) and checks the transform against a direct DFT and by round trips;
`packages/math/test/fft.test.js` reproduces every case bit for bit.

### The framework's wind: log-law boundary layer and Mann turbulence (ATMO-01, ATMO-02, `@margoengine/weather/boundary-layer` and `/turbulence`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/weather/src/turbulence.ts` (`MannBox`) synthesises Mann's uniform-shear spectral tensor on a periodic box and
`packages/weather/src/boundary-layer.ts` (`BoundaryLayerWind`) adds the log-law mean wind and the standard atmosphere, as the
framework's `Wind`. Written from:

- B. Keith, U. Khristenko and B. Wohlmuth, "Learning the structure of wind: A data-driven nonlocal turbulence model for the
  atmospheric boundary layer", Physics of Fluids 33, 2021, arXiv:2107.11046, read in full: the von Karman energy spectrum,
  the isotropic spectral tensor, the rapid-distortion solution (the matrix D, zeta1 to zeta3, C1 and C2) and the IEC eddy
  lifetime with its hypergeometric function, eqs. 4-5 and 12-17 (its neural eddy lifetime is not used).
- M. Faccioni, D. Kiehn and P. Vrancken, "Generating high-fidelity wind fields from the wind speed correlation tensor", Wind
  Energy Science 11, 2093-2101, 2026, https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-11-2093-2026, read in full: the discrete Fourier synthesis
  C* C = (2 pi)^m / V Phi (eqs. 3-5) and the finite box's loss of the largest eddies (section 4).
- R. B. Stull, "An Introduction to Boundary Layer Meteorology", Kluwer, 1988 (section 9.7: the neutral log law and sigma_u
  about 2.5 u*), and G. I. Taylor, "The spectrum of turbulence", Proceedings of the Royal Society A 164, 1938 (frozen
  turbulence): textbook results, known through these references.
- IEC 61400-1 (length scale 0.8 times 42 m and shear 3.9 for the defaults): known through Keith et al.; the standard was not
  read.

The factor G = D G0, G0 = sqrt(E / (4 pi)) / k0^2 [k0]x, the Nyquist and mean bins left empty, the scaling of the box to a
standard deviation, Pfaff's transformation of the hypergeometric function to a series that converges for every argument,
and an atan from + - * / only are this package's own arrangement. Proof: `packages/weather/tests/turbulence.test.js` (isotropy,
the IEC ratios 0.68 and 0.51, u'w' < 0, divergence below 1e-12, determinism) and `tests/boundary-layer.test.js`.

ATMO-02 checked the original tensor and lifetime against Jakob Mann, [The spatial structure of neutral atmospheric
surface-layer turbulence](https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/the-spatial-structure-of-neutral-atmospheric-surface-lay/),
*Journal of Fluid Mechanics* 273 (1994), eqs. 2.16–2.17, 3.3 and 3.13–3.17. In the available
[Models in Micrometeorology](https://backend.orbit.dtu.dk/ws/portalfiles/portal/254755257/Mann1994PhD.pdf)
(Risø-R-727(EN), 1994), Part IB §1.3 and eqs. 1.7, 1.11–1.12 describe the large-box Gaussian Fourier
construction. It became [Wind field simulation](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0266-8920(97)00036-2) (1998).
The continuous limit of eqs. 3.15–3.17 at zero along-wind wavenumber and nonzero across-wind
wavenumber is `zeta1 = -beta`; the original branch dropped this shear. Evaluating the angle difference
before dividing by the small along-wind wavenumber avoids cancellation. The FFT uses the Stockham
work order already established for K17. The added f64x2 path keeps the arithmetic order of the
scalar Weather FFT, while component plans run independently on the caller and optional helpers.

The placed gust uses the longitudinal envelope of the discrete gust in FAA,
[Dynamic Gust Loads](https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_25_341-1.pdf)
(2014), §6.2.1 and 14 CFR 25.341(a)(2), with the length set to twice the gradient distance.
The direction, amplitude vector, advection speed and optional vertical taper are author inputs.
The envelope is the square of the sine of pi times penetration divided by length, algebraically
equal to the one-cosine law while preserving the small onset near the leading edge.
The vertical taper uses the same envelope on the optional height span.

Rieska Mawarni Putri et al., [Turbulence in a coastal environment: the case of Vindeby](https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-7-1693-2022)
(2022), Fig. 11 provides independent near-neutral co-coherence markers at 12, 27 and 39 m vertical separation.
`packages/weather/scripts/atmo02-vindeby-measured.mjs` uses four fixed seeds, with the pre-existing 33.6 m length
scale and 3.9 shear. The measured ordinate is excluded from the model inputs. The refined grid's along-wind,
across-wind and vertical co-coherence RMSEs are 0.242, 0.293 and 0.409. At `kΔz = 0.31576` across 39 m the
vertical prediction is 0.695, versus 0.156 measured. Each of the 12 refined vertical predictions exceeds its
observation. The diagnostic reports model seed uncertainty and observed high-wavenumber scatter separately.
The paper gives no per-marker confidence interval. Ground blocking and stability-dependent coherence
remain open.

ATMO-01 integrates the surface-layer momentum gradient from the roughness length. A. J. Dyer
and B. B. Hicks, [Flux-gradient relationships in the constant flux layer](https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.49709641012)
(1970), give the unstable factor `(1-16 z/L)^(-1/4)`. A. J. Dyer,
[A review of flux-profile relationships](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00240838) (1974), gives
the stable factor `1+5 z/L`. Charles A. Paulson, [The mathematical representation of wind speed and
temperature profiles in the unstable atmospheric surface layer](https://www2.mmm.ucar.edu/wrf/users/physics/phys_refs/SURFACE_LAYER/MM5_part1.pdf)
(1970), derives the logarithm and arctangent antiderivative. The Weather and native entries
use the same pinned arithmetic. The independent Weather control directly integrates the gradient
in log-height coordinates and retains its composite Simpson error bound.

The finite-height Mann box uses Taylor advection at the local layer mean speed. Hunt and
Graham, [Free-stream turbulence near plane boundaries](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112078000130)
(1978), show the decrease in normal fluctuations near a plane boundary. The authored taper
enforces zero disturbance at roughness and box top and uses the last represented vertical
plane through the top taper. It is a finite box boundary rule. The original spectral box
remains available on its own. Shearing and tapering the sample are not a solenoidal projection.

Christopher J. Cox et al., [Met City meteorological and surface flux measurements, MOSAiC](https://doi.org/10.18739/A2PV6B83F)
(2023, CC0), provide the sensor heights, wind and flux data. The separate prior roughness
comes from P. Ola G. Persson et al., [Measurements near the Atmospheric Surface Flux Group tower at SHEBA](https://doi.org/10.1029/2000JC000705)
(2002). Only the low sonic measurement, local stability and externally reported roughness enter
the speed-anchored wind calculation. A second comparison uses separately recorded low-sonic
eddy-covariance friction velocity for the gradient, with both upper wind readings withheld in
each comparison. Recorded misses remain in `atmo01-mosaic-measured.mjs`.

### The framework's precipitation: rain, snow, graupel and hail (ATMO-04, `@margoengine/weather/precipitation`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/weather/src/precipitation.ts` (`PrecipitationField`, the fall-speed functions) is the framework's `Precipitation`
(`packages/math/src/fields/precipitation.ts`). Written from:

- K. Loftus and R. D. Wordsworth, "The physics of falling raindrops in diverse planetary atmospheres", JGR Planets 126,
  2021, arXiv:2102.09570, read (sections 2.1, 2.2 and 3.4): Green's shape balance (eq. 2), the Clift and Gauvin drag law
  with Loth's shape factor (eqs. 6 and 7), the terminal speed of an oblate drop (eq. 8) and the Rayleigh-Taylor size limit
  (eq. 21). Green (1975), Clift and Gauvin (1970), Loth (2008) and Komabayasi et al. (1964) are known through it.
- A. Heymsfield and R. Wright, "Graupel and hail terminal velocities: does a 'supercritical' Reynolds number apply?",
  J. Atmos. Sci. 71, 2014, read in full: the Best number (eq. 5), the Re-X fit (eq. 6), the graupel density law (eq. 3),
  hail's 0.9 g/cm^3 (after List et al. 1970) and the power laws used as checks (eqs. 7 and 8).
- A. J. Heymsfield and C. D. Westbrook, "Advances in the estimation of ice particle fall speeds using laboratory and field
  measurements", J. Atmos. Sci. 67, 2010: not readable here; its modified Best number X* = X Ar^1/2 with delta0 = 8.0 and
  C0 = 0.35 is taken from S. Vazquez-Martin, T. Kuhn and S. Eliasson, "Mass of different snow crystal shapes derived from
  fall speed measurements", ACP 21, 2021 (read, section 3.1), and M. W. McCorquodale and C. D. Westbrook, "TRAIL part 2"
  (read, section 2.2.1), which both restate it.
- A. Seifert and F. Jakub, "On the geometry of aggregate snowflakes", Tellus A (read in part): the asymptotic area ratio of
  large aggregates, about 0.33 of the circumscribing ellipse, and its aspect ratio 0.74.
- Brown and Francis (1995), m = 0.0185 D^1.9 (SI): not read; known through Hogan et al. (2006, J. Appl. Meteor. Climatol.)
  and Heymsfield et al. (2010, J. Atmos. Sci.), which cite it as matching observations in the mean.
- Marshall and Palmer (1948): N0 = 8000 per m^3 per mm and Lambda = 4.1 R^-0.21 per mm, as restated by T. J. Garrett et al.,
  "Analytical solutions for precipitation size distributions at steady state", arXiv:1901.02163 (read).
- K. S. Jennings, T. S. Winchell, B. Livneh and N. P. Molotch, "Spatial variation of the rain-snow temperature threshold
  across the Northern Hemisphere", Nature Communications 9, 1148, 2018 (read): the 1.0 C mean threshold. A. Dai,
  "Temperature and pressure dependence of the rain-snow phase transition over land and ocean", GRL 35, 2008: the land slope
  of about 0.7 per K, from its abstract.
- Gunn and Kinzer (1949), the measured raindrop speeds the tests check against, known through Loftus and Wordsworth.
- IAPWS, "Revised release on surface tension of ordinary water substance", 2014, and the U.S. Standard Atmosphere (1976)
  Sutherland constants: standards, known from their published formulas.

Snow that carries the mass flux and the number flux of the drops it melts into (one slope found by bisection), the rain
intercept set so the drops carry exactly the rate, the drift of a shaft by the median drop's fall time and the wind at the
middle of its fall, and the 64-point Gauss-Legendre integrals in units of the slope are this package's own arrangement.
Proof: `packages/weather/tests/precipitation.test.js`.

### The framework's clouds: moist convection with warm rain (ATMO-03, `@margoengine/physics/clouds`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/clouds/convection.ts` (`CloudSolver`, a framework solver). Written from:

- M. J. Harris, W. V. Baxter, T. Scheuermann and A. Lastra, "Simulation of cloud dynamics on graphics hardware", Graphics
  Hardware 2003, read in full: the incompressible equations of motion (eqs. 1 and 2), potential temperature and the Exner
  function (eq. 3), the buoyancy of the virtual potential temperature less the hydrometeors (eq. 4), the saturation mixing
  ratio (eq. 6, after Rogers and Yau 1989), water continuity and latent heating (eqs. 7 and 8, L = 2.501e6 J/kg), the
  stable-fluids solution (semi-Lagrangian advection and a pressure projection, after Stam 1999), and vorticity
  confinement (after Fedkiw, Stam and Jensen 2001).
- S. Hittmeir et al., "A discontinuous Galerkin approach for atmospheric flows with implicit condensation",
  arXiv:2305.13847, read (section 2): the COSMO closure of Kessler's warm rain, autoconversion (eq. 5b),
  accretion (eq. 5c), rain evaporation (eq. 5a) and the Marshall-Palmer rain fall speed (section 2.1). Kessler (1969) and
  Kessler (1995, Atmospheric Research 38) were not readable here (a scan).
- T. Hadrich et al., "Thunderscapes: simulating the dynamics of mesoscale convective systems", arXiv:2412.00703, read
  (section 4): Kessler's autoconversion threshold of 1e-3 (eq. 9), and the cold-phase blend not yet used.
- S. Arabas et al., "libcloudph++ 0.2", arXiv:1310.1905, read (sections 3.1 to 3.1.4): the single-moment scheme's
  structure, the autoconversion threshold range 1e-4 to 1e-3 kg/kg, and the heat capacities.

The staggered (MAC) grid, the midpoint back-trace, Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients with
the wall's constant null space taken out, the two-pass linearised saturation adjustment, column sedimentation in
substeps of at most a cell, the surface fluxes made patchy by the framework's counter-based random numbers, environment
air at the upwind side, and the cloud's own clock (`timeScale`, `interval`) are this package's own arrangement. Proof:
`packages/physics/tests/clouds.test.js` and `tests/coupling/clouds.test.js`.

ATMO-03's resolved cloud upgrade uses:

- F. H. Harlow and J. E. Welch, “Numerical Calculation of Time-Dependent Viscous Incompressible Flow of Fluid with
  Free Surface” (1965), MAC difference operators. A. J. Chorin, “Numerical solution of the Navier–Stokes
  equations” (1968), equation 20 gives the compatible pressure Laplacian. The corrected velocity subtracts the
  discrete gradient with one power of inverse cell width. [Harlow and Welch](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1761178) ·
  [Chorin](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1968-0242392-2)
- M. R. Hestenes and E. Stiefel, “Methods of conjugate gradients for solving linear systems” (1952), section 3. Native
  Rust SIMD evaluates the structured matrix product in the same order as scalar, with one contiguous block of X
  rows per worker. An ordered canonical reduction and independently recomputed residual set the convergence rule.
  [Hestenes and Stiefel](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.049.044)
- J. E. Hansen and L. D. Travis, “Light Scattering in Planetary Atmospheres” (1974), and A. Slingo, “A GCM Parameterization
  for the Shortwave Radiative Properties of Water Clouds” (1989). Visible cloud extinction uses the large-drop
  limit of extinction efficiency two and the droplet population’s liquid mass to area ratio.
  [Hansen and Travis](https://pubs.giss.nasa.gov/abs/ha09500o.html) ·
  [Slingo](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469%281989%29046%3C1419%3AAGPFTS%3E2.0.CO%3B2)

### Aerodynamic loads from shape (AERO-01, `WindForce` in `@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/aero.ts` cuts each collider's surface into panels and `fields.ts` loads them: on each windward panel the
flat-plate normal force C_N90 sin(a) q A along its inward normal, and skin friction C_f q A along the tangential relative air,
summed about the centre of mass. The laws are the textbook ones of S. F. Hoerner, "Fluid-Dynamic Drag", 1965 (chapters 2 and 3:
skin friction and the flat plate's 1.17), and "Fluid-Dynamic Lift", 1975 (chapter 21, the plate's normal force after
Flachsbart), as tabulated in J. Katz and A. Plotkin, "Low-Speed Aerodynamics", 2nd ed., Cambridge, 2001; none was read here.
M. Padilla, A. Segall and O. Sorkine-Hornung, "Rigid Body Dynamics in Ambient Fluids", arXiv:2601.13971, 2026, was read in
full: its surface-slip dynamic pressure gives a smooth body's drag and Magnus lift but no force on a flat face square to the
flow (a box would take none), so it was not used for these mostly flat-faced bodies; its added mass and separation angle are
follow-ups. The icosphere, strip and box tessellations are this package's own. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/aero.test.js`.

AERO-01 checked the split against Sighard F. Hoerner, [Fluid-Dynamic Drag](https://home.hvl.no/ansatte/gste/ftp/MarinLab_files/Litteratur/Hoerner_1965_Fluid-dynamic_drag.pdf)
(1965), ch. II pp. 2-1 and 2-4 onward for tangential skin drag and ch. III pp. 3-12 to 3-16 for normal and oblique plate
loads. The local sine law and coefficients remain approximations for panel traction. The rigid kernel evaluates
bounds at a body pose that cancels the collider's relative position and rotation. The approximation preserves the local
bounds' centre. The Wasm path sums forces in panel order to preserve the centre-of-mass torque. Workers divide the 13
finite-difference probes of the implicit load.

Elmar Achenbach, [Experiments on the flow past spheres at very high Reynolds numbers](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112072000874)
(1972), §3 and Fig. 4 provide independent drag measurements for a 200 mm polished sphere. `aero01-sphere-measured.mjs`
scores the original hollow strain-gauge symbols reproduced in Guillaume Dupeux et al. (2011), Fig. 4c. The readout
uses three source pixels (0.00935 Cd) and the text endpoint uses a 0.005 rounding allowance. The condition inputs
use recorded geometry and air conditions matched by Reynolds number because per-marker tunnel settings are
unavailable. Total measurement uncertainty remains unavailable. Subcritical predictions run 48–61% high. All eleven
plateau and recovery observations miss. [Dupeux et al., Football curves](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfluidstructs.2011.03.022).

The AVIARY-5 test authors new folded panels in Margo and uses 80 g/m² stock to set paper mass from area. A native
rope joint bears each crane. The shape refers to a museum object. [Smithsonian Colorful Origami Crane](https://www.si.edu/object/colorful-origami-crane%3Aacm_2011.0004.0081).

### The surf zone (SEA-05, `@margoengine/physics/surf`, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/surf/index.ts` (`SurfSolver`), with the forcing field, the `sea` and `periodic` sides and the wave-stirred
friction it adds to `packages/physics/src/hydro`. Written from papers and public manuals only (no code of XBeach, SWAN, Delft3D
or any model was opened):

- D. Roelvink, A. Reniers, A. van Dongeren, J. van Thiel de Vries, R. McCall and J. Lescinski, "Modelling storm impacts on
  beaches, dunes and barrier islands", Coastal Engineering 56, 1133-1152, 2009, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coastaleng.2009.08.006
  (the paper unreachable; the model as the public XBeach manual documents it, read): the wave action balance with refraction
  (eqs. 1 to 4), Roelvink's breaking (eq. 12, defaults gamma 0.55, alpha 1, n 10), the roller balance with D_r = 2 beta g E_r / c
  (eqs. 38 to 43), the GLM momentum with bed friction on the Eulerian velocity and the Stokes drift (eqs. 46 to 48), the
  wave-stirred bed shear with 1.16 u_rms (after Ruessink et al. 2001), the directional sector about the mean direction.
- The Delft3D-FLOW manual (public), appendix B, read: the roller's radiation stress 2 E_r (cos^2, sin cos, sin^2), the convention
  under which the roller's momentum, mass flux 2 E_r / c and dissipation agree for Svendsen's (1984) roller; the roller here is
  carried at c, as XBeach's eq. 38 writes it.
- M. S. Longuet-Higgins and R. W. Stewart, "Radiation stresses in water waves", Deep-Sea Res. 11, 1964, and A. J. Bowen, D. L.
  Inman and V. P. Simmons, "Wave 'set-down' and set-up", J. Geophys. Res. 73, 1968, as P. J. Visser (1977) restates and
  tabulates them (read): the radiation stress, the set-down -(1/8) k H^2 / sinh(2 k h), the set-up slope (3 gamma^2 / 8) / (1 +
  3 gamma^2 / 8) of the beach's.
- J. A. Battjes and M. J. F. Stive, "Calibration and verification of a dissipation model for random breaking waves", J.
  Geophys. Res. 90(C5), 1985 (ICCE 1984 version read): random-wave breaking and its gamma.
- M. S. Longuet-Higgins (1970), longshore currents, as Fleming and Swart (1982) restate it (read): the shallow-water driving
  -dS_xy/dx and its balance with the bed.
- H. F. Stockdon, R. A. Holman, P. A. Howd and A. H. Sallenger, "Empirical parameterization of setup, swash, and runup", Coastal
  Engineering 53, 2006 (via its restatements): the field set-up the limits compare with.
- The Riemann invariants u +- 2 sqrt(g h) of the shallow-water equations for the open sea side: a textbook result (and
  `flood.ts`'s Flather boundary).

Added the same day:
- Wave-current interaction: the absolute frequency omega = sigma + k . u kept and the action E / sigma carried at c_g + u,
  with the currents' refraction terms (the XBeach manual, eqs. 5 to 10; F. P. Bretherton and C. J. R. Garrett, "Wavetrains in
  inhomogeneous moving media", Proc. R. Soc. A 302, 1968, known through it).
- The bound long wave at the offshore side, zeta_b = (2n - 1/2)(E - mean E) / (rho (c_g^2 - g h)) and u_b = c_g zeta_b / h (M.
  S. Longuet-Higgins and R. W. Stewart, J. Fluid Mech. 13, 1962, as the Delft3D manual's eqs. B.66 and B.67 state it), fed
  through the open sea's incoming Riemann invariant.
- The incident swash S_inc = 0.75 beta_f sqrt(H0 L0) and R2 = 1.1 (<eta> + sqrt(S_inc^2 + S_IG^2) / 2) of Stockdon et al.
  (2006), the infragravity part from the shoreline record.

The wave groups as the envelope of 48 equal-variance components drawn from the incoming sea by energy on the counter-based
random numbers, the open-sea side by the invariants, the periodic sides with one face's flux taken by both ends, the stress
force by central differences with a dry neighbour holding the cell's own stress, the run-up and wet-sand record, and the
coupling through an accumulated field are this package's own arrangement. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/surf.test.js` and
`tests/coupling/surf.test.js`.


### Loads in the water (SEA-12, `@margoengine/physics/loads`, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/loads/` (`LoadSolver`, `QuayWall`, the Morison coefficients, the ellipsoid added masses and the quay
formulas). Written from standards, papers and public reports only (no code of any offshore, riser or CFD program was opened):

- DNV-RP-C205, "Environmental conditions and environmental loads", Det Norske Veritas, October 2010 (sections 3.3.3, 3.4.4,
  6.1 to 6.13, 9.1 and 9.2, appendices D, E and F, read; the figures' formulas checked on page images): Morison's equation in
  its relative-velocity form and for small 3D bodies, C_DS by roughness, the wake amplification psi(KC) below KC 12 (above it
  only a figure: here psi falls from its value at 12 toward 1 as 12 / KC), C_A by KC, Eames's tangential drag (as 6.3.1.3
  gives it), the 2D and 3D added-mass and drag tables, Lamb's ellipsoid integrals (table D-2), Strouhal's frequency and
  lock-in, the standing wave at a wall and sea water's constants.
- F. A. Morrison, "An Introduction to Fluid Mechanics", Cambridge University Press, 2013, the sphere's drag correlation (eq.
  1, read).
- M. L. Facchinetti, E. de Langre and F. Biolley, "Vortex-induced travelling waves along a cable", Eur. J. Mech. B/Fluids 23,
  199-208, 2004 (sections 2 and eq. 5, read): the van der Pol wake, q = 2 C_L / C_L0, C_L0 0.3, A / eps 40 and the lift
  magnification, written here as the root of K^3 - K = (A / eps) y0 / 2 (the two cube roots of eq. 5 multiply to 1/3 and their
  cubes sum to that). The companion paper verifies eps 0.3 and A 12 for the wake equation described below.
- USACE Coastal Engineering Manual, EM 1110-2-1100, tables VI-5-52 and VI-5-53 (read), and Y. Goda, "New wave pressure
  formulae for composite breakwaters", Proc. 14th ICCE, 1974 (eqs. 1 to 8, read): Sainflou's and Goda's wall pressures.
- F. Tukker, TU Delft MSc thesis, 2021 (sections 2.2 and 2.3, page images read), restating PIANC report 180 (2015): a bow
  thruster's efflux 1.17 (P / (rho D^2))^0.33 and the Dutch method's bed velocity at a quay (Blokland 1996).
- C. Caspersen et al., 2010 (abstract read), and Kjendlie et al., 2009 (through it): a swimmer's added mass about a quarter of
  its mass.
- O. Breivik, A. A. Allen, C. Maisondieu and J. C. Roth, "Wind-induced drift of objects at sea: the leeway field method",
  Applied Ocean Research 33, 2011 (read): measured leeways the windage default is held to.

The equivalent ellipsoid of a mesh (its second moments by signed tetrahedra, semi-axes sqrt(5 I / V)) supplies its
drag and added mass axes. The strip-theory drag of a spinning body, the
added mass held as M (M + A)^-1 (F + W) - W with members' added mass in the same tensor, the water's acceleration as a centred
difference of the pure sample, and the quay wall's doubling by 1 + R at its face are this package's own arrangement. Proof:
`packages/physics/tests/loads.test.js` and `tests/coupling/loads.test.js`.

Rigid member vibration uses the material midpoint's accepted linear and angular velocity to drive the existing wake
oscillator. The dimensional source is (12 / D) times its acceleration along the lift direction, and the sectional
lift is ρ U² D C_L0 q / 4. Here U is the mean incident normal stream relative to the member along that stream.
The coherent load acts at the clipped wetted interval centre. The branch keeps the existing Morison drag and
added inertia, with the wake as a separate force. [Facchinetti, de Langre and Biolley (2004), Eqs. 5, 9 and 14](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfluidstructs.2003.12.004).

The held-out prescribed-motion test uses the 2005 Carberry experiment with A/D = 0.25, Re = 4410 and f_e/f_0 = 1.15.
The dominant peak comes from a separate strain-gauge force transducer. The motor sets only the prescribed
displacement. The simulated vortex-force signal matches the observed frequency at both world rates. The free
shedding control uses the same prescribed motion and gives a frequency ratio of 1.03338.
The independent case differs from the earlier Re = 2300, A/D = 0.5 series. Its measured vortex-force phase is
−78°. A force comparison needs a shared definition of the viscous and apparent-mass contributions.
[Carberry, Sheridan and Rockwell (2005), §2 and Fig. 17(c)](https://flair.monash.edu/publications/pdfs/Carberry_etal_JFM2005.pdf).

Facchinetti's Figure 9 already includes Khalak and Williamson's peak amplitudes. The independent Usta and Duranay
free-vibration cases give A/D of 0.9375, 0.7877 and 0.6861 at currents of 0.338, 0.390 and 0.442 m/s. The
unchanged Facchinetti structural equations give 0.152, 0.126 and 0.101 for those inputs. Their higher blockage
and low mass ratio place those cases in a regime where wake-branch selection and the force applied in each
part of the cycle matter. [Khalak and Williamson (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jfls.1999.0236) ·
[Usta and Duranay (2021), Tables 2, 4, 6 and 8](https://www.jafmonline.net/article_1102_c667d53acd899a97a85de0c201ba99be.pdf).

For hydrostatics, spheres and ellipsoids use an analytic cap. A closed mesh or box reuses
SEA-08 wetted triangle clipping and [D. A. Dunavant's degree-four triangle quadrature (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1620210612).
The plane uses the local sea height at the shape centre. Hydrostatic pressure is linear on each wet triangle.
About the rigid centre of mass, the pressure moment is quadratic. The integrals give displaced volume and its
righting moment by the divergence theorem. Unit-specific-weight pressure keeps the volume meaningful at zero
gravity, and relative coordinates keep sea-level translation out of the quadrature. [Tsutomu Hori, *Position of
Center of Buoyancy of a Vessel*, Part 6 (2021)](https://doi.org/10.18949/jinnavi.215.0_69)

For an ellipsoid with shape matrix `A` and upward direction `n`, let `H = |Aᵀn|` and let `h` be the normalized
height of the submerged cap. Integrating the unit sphere's discs gives volume fraction `h²(3−h)/4` and axial
centroid distance `3(2−h)²/[4(3−h)]` from the centre toward the cap. Mapping the centroid back gives the
offset along `−A Aᵀn/H`. The tests compare both mesh and box to finite-angle trapezoid pressure moments
and the small-heel `GM = KB + I_waterplane / V − KG` limit. An inclined ellipsoid separately checks
the affine half-cap moment.

In [Tsutomu and Manami Hori, *Theoretical Hydrostatics of Floating Bodies* (2023), §4.6, Fig. 4.6](https://vixra.org/pdf/2307.0154v2.pdf),
a 30 × 11.5 × 10 cm prism settles at a photographed 27.5°. The reported 18.09 N weight and the reported
relative density 0.458 imply different displacement in nominal fresh water. The solver runs both inputs,
from 12° and 39° releases, and settles at 26.91° and 26.68°, respectively. Neither input comes from the
held-out angle. The upper edge spans about 187 pixels in a 2× page raster. One pixel of coordinate reading
uncertainty at each end and the printed rounding give a 0.92° comparison band. These are static heel
results. The added body damping is used to reach equilibrium and does not validate measured roll decay.

The surface-pressure option uses the same wet shell quadrature for the incident Froude–Krylov wrench and
separately integrates unit depth for displaced volume. The centre velocity derivative accounts for added
mass and any independently supplied flow. The exact tests use a submerged
box under a quadratic pressure and a dry-centred box cut by a plane. See J. M. J. Journée and W. W. Massie,
[*Offshore Hydromechanics* (2001), §6.3](https://ocw.tudelft.nl/wp-content/uploads/OffshoreHydromechanics_Journee_Massie.pdf),
and [Dunavant (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1620210612).

For a harmonic member load, the flow now samples one quarter and one half period from the current phase.
The half-cycle average is the mean. The largest eigenvalue of the Gram matrix of the two normal harmonic
vectors gives the squared peak in their ellipse. This keeps (KC=U_mT/D) consistent through the cycle,
as defined in [G. H. Keulegan and L. H. Carpenter (1958), *Forces on cylinders and plates in an oscillating fluid*](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.060.043).
Two Gauss points integrate the linearly clipped wet interval.

The optional smooth-cylinder model uses Turgut Sarpkaya,
[*Vortex shedding and resistance in harmonic flow about smooth and rough circular cylinders at high Reynolds numbers* (1976), report NPS-59SL76021](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3c/Vortex_shedding_and_resistance_in_harmonic_flow_about_smooth_and_rough_circular_cylinders_at_high_Reynolds_numbers_%28IA_vortexsheddingre00sarp%29.pdf).
Appendix A, pp. 158 and 163 supply the two calibration cylinders (β = 3123 and 5260). The
member integration applies the interpolated `C_M` and `C_D` at the requested dimensionless flow conditions.
The full β = 4480 diameter series is withheld from the fit. Its ten
runs inside the untapered KC range on p. 160 serve as comparisons for the solver's projected force coefficients
and its peak versus the load cell. The coefficient bands follow the calibration span and run-to-run repeatability.
The peak comparison also includes the original Morison residual from Eq. (16). Mean absolute errors in the ten
runs are 0.092 for `C_M` and 0.063 for `C_D`, with a maximum peak `C_F` error of 0.374. DNV gives
0.039 and 0.214 mean coefficient errors, respectively, on the same runs. DNV remains the default.
The independent Keulegan–Carpenter Table 3 runs reach β = 3,000, or below 3,076 allowing for half
the printed precision in both inputs. The land-based oscillation data fall below the Sarpkaya calibration
band, and DNV §6.7.2.1 gives its oscillatory correction for supercritical flow. All 57 runs use the DNV
fallback and show 0.429 and 0.379 mean absolute errors in inertia and drag. These are scope diagnostics.

Optional rotational inertia uses the velocity potential for a rotating ellipsoid. Integrate the outer potential
in Lamb's Art. 112 Eq. (6) against the normal velocity to get the fluid kinetic energy. The denominator has
`2(b²−c²)+(b²+c²)(β₀−γ₀)`, also printed in Bateman's report. The two axisymmetric cases in the NACA
Report 323 Table VI agree to half its last printed digit. The held torque uses the inverse-inertia tensor
published by the rigid body. Solving in wrench space keeps the system defined for constrained rigid axes.
[H. Lamb, *Hydrodynamics*, Art. 112](https://scispace.com/pdf/hydrodynamics-by-horace-lamb-14s3kx3ak5.pdf) ·
[H. Bateman, NACA Report 164, p. 163](https://web.stanford.edu/~cantwell/AA200_Course_Material/AA200_References/Jones_Classical_Aerodynamic_Theory.pdf)

The supplied passive radiation modes approximate the zero-forward-speed Cummins kernel in principal motions.
Each exponential stores the history of its velocity. Over one step, an exponential with decay time `τ`
contributes its old memory times `exp(−dt/τ)` and its end-of-step velocity times `τ (1−exp(−dt/τ))`.
Eliminating the new velocity from the wrench transfers a nonnegative term to the effective mass or inertia.
The kit stores the preceding wet amplitude and recomputes history from the actual rigid velocity on the next step.
The exact two-state implicit system tests the velocity history and hash after restore. The reference coefficients
are caller-provided for the body and draft. [W. E. Cummins, *The Impulse Response Function and Ship Motions* (1962), Eq. 61](https://dome.mit.edu/handle/1721.3/49049)

The civil woody-debris first-contact model combines wood and support normal compliance in series. A compressing
elastic contact reaches its peak at a quarter of the reduced-mass oscillator period. The rigid-port adapter uses
the point mobility of both bodies, then applies a single normal impulse with opposite linear and angular reactions.
Haehnel and Daly's 2.4 MN/m estimate is the envelope of their Series 1, 3 and 4. At the measured momentum and
speed of the held-out concrete-facing Series 6, the model predicts 30.42 kN. The upper measured replicate is
30.31 kN and the reading uncertainty is 0.37 kN. The test also compares Series 8 near-central impacts. The
force prediction covers the upper-envelope contact, with individual Series 6 replicates from 28.74 to 30.31 kN.
[R. B. Haehnel and S. F. Daly, *Maximum Impact Force of Woody Debris on Floodplain Structures*, ERDC/CRREL TR-02-2, Figs. 13–14](https://archive.org/details/DTIC_ADA398916)

The taut line is the massless, near-neutral limit of the elastic mooring element. The axial force is
`EA max(L-L₀, 0) / L₀`. Solve it against both attachments' rigid point mobilities, and stage equal and
opposite impulses at the two points. A fixed pile retains its reaction as a reported force. The test checks
slack engagement, the peak of the exact axial oscillator within its discrete damping bound at 60 and 240 Hz,
and linear and angular momentum through replay. The straight line covers short taut tethers.
[Hall (2024), *Generalized Quasi-Static Mooring System Modeling*, §2.1](https://doi.org/10.3390/en17133155) ·
[Hall and Goupee (2015), *Validation of a lumped-mass mooring line model*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oceaneng.2015.05.035)

Compact bodies use actual projected areas and the orientation-dependent Hölzer–Sommerfeld coefficient.
For the 16 held-out Khan cube points at Reynolds numbers around 500–1500, the RMS coefficient error is
0.1459. The fixed-unity former law gives 0.3002. The maximum error of the shape law is 0.3215 around
Reynolds number 510. The test records the published measurement uncertainty and digitization error.
The wind sample lies at the projected centroid of the clipped area. Analytic box and tilted ellipse
sections and a projected triangle union test the geometric calculation and the wind's lever arm.
[A. Hölzer and M. Sommerfeld (2008), *New simple correlation formula for the drag coefficient of non-spherical particles*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2007.08.021) ·
[M. A. Khan et al. (2018), Fig. 15](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.expthermflusci.2017.12.013)

Spin torque follows Jeffery's creeping-flow ellipsoid resistance with Dennis, Singh and Ingham's
numerical and asymptotic rotating-sphere correction. For nonspherical bodies the finite-Re correction
uses the transverse geometric-mean radius. The solver computes translations, wind torque and water
spin torque separately. [G. B. Jeffery (1922), Eq. 36](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1922.0078) ·
[S. C. R. Dennis, S. N. Singh and D. B. Ingham (1980), Tables 2–3 and Eqs. 50–55](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112080001656)

The native optional batch preserves the order of double-precision operations in the TypeScript
reference. It packs 32 f64 words per rigid row in the world arena and uses two-lane SIMD for each
dot product while preserving the reference reduction order. Plain and shared imports each tested
321 mixed rows bit for bit. The live-world test measures one call for 24 bodies, checks every wrench
and trajectory against the TypeScript variant and replays the same snapshot hash. Field queries
convert any separate origins through integer cell differences, with a live test at cell indices up to 2²⁹.

The shallow-water coupling distinguishes immersed drag from impermeable blockage. The immersed drag
stages matched body and water impulses using the same wet-cell weights and the body and water point
mobilities in the implicit quadratic slip equation. Mass remains in the water cells. Body-local principal
areas are projected along slip. The exposed box-face sum and the ellipsoid cofactor norm follow directly
from the corresponding projected triangles and transformed unit-sphere area. The obstruction
integrates each face opening in time and length. It integrates its moving wall pressure and lever arm
over the same time interval. The resulting conservative flux balance gives the fluid's geometric
storage and the rigid reaction in the same tick. The guided rigid test feeds the changed body velocity
back into the next accepted obstruction step. The pressure wall uses Causon, Ingram and Mingham,
Sections 3.2–3.2.1. [Causon et al. (2001), *A Cartesian cut cell method for shallow water flows with moving boundaries*](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0309-1708(01)00010-0) ·
[Sanders, Schubert and Gallegos (2008), *Integral formulation of shallow-water equations with anisotropic porosity*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2008.08.009)

In Causon et al. §3.4, equations 34–38 sum the conserved quantities of a disappearing cell and a fluid
neighbour. For one obstacle bounded by the area of a grid cell, a two-cell aggregate always has at least
one cell's worth of water storage. Both Runge–Kutta stages integrate mass and discharge with the same
pair and swept geometry before dividing by the aggregate's new open area. The common internal
face term cancels, and the wall pressure still contributes one paired impulse to water and rigid.

Projected drag at a shoreline uses the finite-volume water state after wetting, drying, and bed friction.
The implicit impulse uses final cell masses and the same normalized weights for slip and spreading.
The geometric lever arm is the weighted centre of the accepted water slices. The rigid receipt takes its
impulse and moment from the actual signed changes in f64 discharge at those slices. This applies the
force and first-moment identities in [C. S. Peskin (2002), *The immersed boundary method*, §5,
equations 5.1–5.8](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0962492902000077) at the accepted centre of immersion.
The same force law and reduced mobility as the fixed-wet exchange dissipate the isolated pair's
kinetic energy. The manufactured shoreline test compares the post-flux momentum to independent
ordinary HYDRO transport. The split sends each deposited impulse into the next transport step.
On a periodic axis the stencil wraps storage indices and uses the adjacent geometric images for the
moment arms. The two weights of a one-cell periodic axis combine before evaluating inverse water
mass, and their weighted first moment gives the query coordinate. This preserves the normalization
and first-moment identities of Peskin §5 across the seam. A transverse counterflow and an asymmetric
wet stencil check the force, rigid response and replay against independent formulas.

The same shallow-water impulse model loads clipped paddle blades at their actual lever arms and wading
profiles at their centres of pressure. The rigid shaft receives torque from the immersed blade, and a
driven motor returns momentum to the water. The test uses actual revolute and shallow-water solvers.
The wading solver applies buoyancy to the legged body and returns the coupled horizontal force to the
water. The support-force test proves reduced ground load and supplies the pressure balance.
[R. Labbé et al. (2019), *Physics of rowing oars*, Eq. 4](https://doi.org/10.1088/1367-2630/ab4226) ·
[M. I. V. Orselli and M. Duarte (2011), *Joint forces and torques when walking in shallow water*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbiomech.2011.01.017)

The swim transport records passive linear drag after the native body and fin solve. It evaluates the exposed
strip mobility against the accepted velocity and returns that drag separately from actuator, contact, gravity,
buoyancy and added-fluid momentum. The live receiver uses wet weights and opposite horizontal impulse, with
44-frame rigid/swimmer/water closure through the public body-drag adapter and independent disabled-return
controls. A separate hull and debris fixture tests the two directions through the live shallow-water
port with no external impulse writer. The actuator receiver distributes the signed tail and pectoral
reactions from the separately published wake field. The active two-way test checks both impulses and
a 40-frame closed momentum ledger after disabling each return in turn. The rotated strip test checks
the traction decomposition. [Peskin (2002), *The immersed boundary method*, §5](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0962492902000077) The damping coefficient of a compact body is now evaluated from the starting slip
and applied at the end-of-step velocity. The stiff lightweight case checks the analytic speed and steady loss
of kinetic energy.

For floating hulls, `radiationProfile` fits nonnegative band-pass terms to the physical damping of the existing
strip theory or finite-depth panel reference at the solved draft. Each resonator uses `x′ = q` and
`q′ = v − ω²x − γq`. Its stored energy is `r(q² + ω²x²)/2`. Backward Euler's energy balance separates
physical damping and numerical loss. The box case's largest normalized RMS fit error is 3.36%. A triangular
holdout from Vugts Report 194 Table 5.1 and Fig. 6.5 has a 0.30 m draft and a normalized forced-heave crest
of 0.57–0.60. The geometry-only profile computes 0.299987 m and 0.597699. The measured damping is held out
of the reference solve and of the fit. [J. H. Vugts (1968), *The hydrodynamic coefficients for swaying, heaving and rolling cylinders in a free surface*](https://doi.org/10.3233/ISP-1968-1516702) ·
[T. Pérez and T. I. Fossen (2008), *Time- vs. Frequency-domain Identification of Parametric Radiation Force Models*](https://doi.org/10.4173/mic.2008.1.1)

The full panel profile fits the complex impedance `B(ω) + iω(A(ω) − A∞)` in all six body motions, using
signed rank-one directions and positive residues. The same direction projects rigid velocity into each
mode and distributes its force and torque about the rigid centre of mass. The outer products preserve
reciprocity and let the backward-Euler hold account for stored energy and dissipation. Poles outside the
sampled range represent reactive tails without adding artificial reference observations. The finite-depth
panel fixture reports 0.7842% normalized RMS and 5.4741% maximum reference-fit error and −194.278 kg·m
sway–roll cross inertia at infinite frequency. Those errors are against the panel solve. The separate
width-confined Vugts B/T=2 rectangular tank holdout compares six signed sway–roll inertia ordinates. The
maximum absolute discrepancy is 0.0060. The predicted damping crest is −0.129833 at normalized
frequency 0.865. The two reciprocal experiments give −0.142 and −0.184. Their difference supplies the
observed comparison bound. The tank fixture qualifies the width-confined strip response. The live
rigid fixture verifies simultaneous forces and torques and passive memory through dry and rewet intervals.
[Vugts (1968), Report 194, §§5.1, 5.7 and the rectangular-section sway–roll plots](https://doi.org/10.3233/ISP-1968-1516702)

Full frequency-dependent matrix coupling is used by the specialist solvers as well. The loads profile
reuses Margo's clean-room panel solve and offers a principal-motion reference for lower cost.
[OrcaFlex vessel added mass and damping](https://www.orcina.com/webhelp/OrcaFlex/Content/html/Vesseltypes%2CStiffness%2Caddedmassanddamping.htm) ·
[HydroDyn modeling considerations](https://openfast.readthedocs.io/en/dev/source/user/hydrodyn/modeling_considerations.html)

### Ships under way (SEA-09, `@margoengine/physics/ship`, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/ship/` (`ShipSolver`, `Manoeuvring`, `Propeller`, `raceVelocity`, `holtropMennen`, `ittc1957`, `squat`,
`icorels`, `huuska`, `rudderLiftSlope`, `thrusterThrust`), with the `wash` of a `FoamSolver` ship in
`packages/physics/src/foam/index.ts`. Written from papers and public documentation only (no code of any manoeuvring simulator,
ship-design tool, CFD code or companion code was opened):

- H. Yasukawa and Y. Yoshimura, "Introduction of MMG standard method for ship maneuvering predictions", J. Mar. Sci.
  Technol. 20, 37-52, 2015, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00773-014-0293-y (open access, read with its tables 1 to 5): the
  equations of motion about the midship (eq. 4), the hull's polynomials (eq. 7), the propeller's thrust and wake (eqs. 8 to
  16), the rudder's normal force with Fujii's f_alpha and the inflow of eq. 25 (appendix A), and the KVLCC2 particulars,
  derivatives, interaction constants and simulated turning and zig-zag results the tests hold. The propeller's place x'_P
  = -0.48 is from the SIMMAN 2008 particulars as remembered (not in the paper's tables).
- J. Holtrop and G. G. J. Mennen, "An approximate power prediction method", International Shipbuilding Progress 29, 1982, and
  J. Holtrop, "A statistical re-analysis of resistance and propulsion data", ISP 31, 1984 (read): the resistance set, the
  wake fraction, thrust deduction, eta_R and Keller's blade area, and the worked example the test reproduces (the wetted area
  of the appendages counts in c8 and R_A, as the printed figures need).
- ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-02-03-01.4, "1978 ITTC Performance Prediction Method" (read): the ITTC-1957 line.
- A. Haeusler, A. Saccon, A. Pascoal, J. Hauser and A. Aguiar, four-quadrant propeller modelling, 2015 (read), after Healey et
  al. 1995: c_L = c_Lmax sin 2 alpha, c_D = c_Dmax (1 - cos 2 alpha) / 2. Here its pitch angle and two constants are fitted to
  the open-water quadratic (bollard thrust, its slope and its zero), the engine's own arrangement.
- G. A. Hamill and C. Kee, "Predicting axial velocity profiles within a diffusing marine propeller jet", Ocean Engineering
  124, 2016, and G. A. Hamill and J. A. McGarvey, 1996 (read): the efflux 1.59 n D sqrt(C_t) of Blaauw and van de Kaa (1978),
  the zone of flow establishment to 3.25 D (Stewart 1992) with Berger et al.'s ring profile, eq. 7 and eq. 20 for the
  maximum speeds and Fuehrer and Roemisch's exp(-22.2 (r / X)^2).
- S. Serban and V. Panaitescu, 2016 review of squat formulas (read, with its worked canal case): ICORELS, Huuska and Guliev,
  Hooft's form of Tuck's law (E. O. Tuck, J. Fluid Mech. 26, 1966, through it).
- The tunnel thruster's momentum bound T = (4 rho A)^(1/3) P^(2/3) is derived from the momentum balance of a jet that does not
  contract; its figure of merit 0.55 (installed thrusters give 0.45 to 0.65) and the speed-loss curve's shape (a minimum near
  half the thrust at a speed of 0.4 of the jet's, Karlikov and Sholomovich as a TU Delft thesis restates them) are
  calibrations, recorded in docs/limits.md.

Added on 2026-11-26 (`ship/empirical.ts`, `ship/race.ts`):
- K. Kijima, T. Katsuno, Y. Nakiri and Y. Furukawa, "On the manoeuvring performance of a ship with the parameter of loading
  condition", J. Soc. Naval Architects of Japan 168, 141-148, 1990, https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjasnaoe1968/1990/168/1990_168_141/_article
  (eqs. 1 to 15 and table 1, read): the regression set, its database's ranges and the wake 0.5 C_B - 0.05. Restatements with
  sign errors were found and not used (Y'rr in Lotovskyi et al. 2025; Y'vrr's +0.11 in Taimuri et al. 2020).
- Y. Yoshimura and Y. Masumoto, "Hydrodynamic database and manoeuvring prediction method with medium high-speed merchant ships
  and fishing vessels", J. JASNAOE 14, 63-73, 2011, https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjasnaoe/14/0/14_0_63/_article
  (eqs. 4.1 to 4.7, read): cubic, surge and trim terms and the rudder interaction set; N'brr with the sign of their figure 3.2.
- R. Lotovskyi et al., 2025 (read), for X'vr's conversion and the hull-swap error spread; Taimuri et al., 2020 (read), restating
  Clarke, Gedling and Hine (1983) and Brix (1993) added masses, Clarke's yaw term taken as -0.33 B/L, which KVLCC2's captive
  J'z supports; Kim and Kim (2020) (read) for MARIN's free-running KVLCC2 turning.
- J. Pennings, "Dynamics of vortex cavitation", PhD thesis, TU Delft, 2016 (read): its propeller's circulation, the vortex
  models and pressure, the cavity's radius, its wing case; P. Kumar and K. Mahesh, "Large eddy simulation of propeller wake
  instabilities", J. Fluid Mech. 814, 361-396, 2017 (read): tip vortices unstable from 0.8 D and gone by 1.5 D, the far wake a
  swirling column; A. Amini et al., "On the physical mechanism of tip vortex cavitation hysteresis", Exp. Fluids 60, 2019 (read):
  inception at 1.7 and desinence near 4.0 in air-saturated water; W. H. Lam et al. (2010, 2012, abstracts read): peak swirl 76
  to 82 percent of peak axial at efflux, a band check.
The swirl's free-vortex profile with a viscous hub core, the tip vortices' nearest-core field, their fade between 0.8 and 1.5
D, the rudder jet's turn as a rotation of the race about the rudder, the hysteresis's desinence scaled by the gas saturation
and the aeration rate as the cavities' volume carried at the disc speed are this package's own arrangement.

The rigid body held to the MMG equations (eq. 3's forces on its own mass, its yaw inertia from the bodies port), squat as a
sea drawn down along the hull for the HullSolver to float on, the race's induced speed as its far wake less its inflow, the
quay's pull from a one-dimensional continuity estimate of the gap flow, the hull's draught as wake sources and the race's
boil where its jet's e-folding radius reaches the shaft's depth are this package's own arrangement. Proof:
`packages/physics/tests/ship.test.js`, `tests/coupling/ship.test.js` and the race's boil in `tests/foam.test.js`.

### Tides, storm surge and currents (SEA-07, `@margoengine/physics/surge`, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/surge/index.ts` (`SurgeSolver`, `tidalLevel`, `TIDAL_CONSTITUENTS`, `inverseBarometer`), with the
`surfaceWaterPotential` field, the Coriolis rotation and the time scale it adds to `packages/physics/src/hydro`. Written
from papers, reports and public documentation only (no code of ADCIRC, SLOSH, Delft3D, FVCOM, ROMS, TPXO or any tide model
was opened):

- R. A. Luettich and J. J. Westerink, "Formulation and numerical implementation of the 2D/3D ADCIRC finite element model
  version 44.XX", 2004, https://adcirc.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2255/2018/11/adcirc_theory_2004_12_08.pdf (eqs. 2.2 to 2.6,
  read): the depth-integrated momentum with -g H d/dx (zeta + P_s / (g rho_0) - alpha eta), the tide, the air's pressure and
  the free surface as one gradient. Here the gradient enters as a potential added to the bed of the hydrostatic
  reconstruction (E. Audusse, F. Bouchut, M.-O. Bristeau, R. Klein and B. Perthame, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 25, 2050-2065, 2004,
  known through the shallow water's own record), so water at rest under it is balanced as over a bed.
- C. P. Jelesnianski, J. Chen and W. A. Shaffer, "SLOSH: Sea, Lake, and Overland Surges from Hurricanes", NOAA Technical
  Report NWS 48, 1992, https://www.weather.gov/media/mdl/SLOSH_TR48.pdf (sections 1 to 4, read): the hydrostatic
  (inverse-barometer) height, prescribed at an open deep sea; its surface stress coefficient C_D rho_a / rho_w = 3e-6.
- M. A. Donelan, B. K. Haus, N. Reul, W. J. Plant, M. Stiassnie, H. C. Graber, O. B. Brown and E. S. Saltzman, "On the
  limiting aerodynamic roughness of the ocean in very strong winds", Geophys. Res. Lett. 31, L18306, 2004,
  https://doi.org/10.1029/2004GL019460 (read): the drag coefficient saturating at 2.5e-3 above 33 m/s; M. D. Powell, P. J.
  Vickery and T. A. Reinhold, Nature 422, 2003 (as Donelan et al. state it): about 2.6e-3 near 35 m/s. J. R. Garratt, Mon. Wea.
  Rev. 105, 1977 (the shallow water's existing law, as restated).
- R. H. Stewart, "Introduction to Physical Oceanography", chapter 17.4 (read): the degree-2 tide-generating potential, its
  species, the equilibrium tide and Apel's (1987) constituent periods. The potential itself comes from the celestial solver
  (SPACE-02, `tidalDrive`).
- IERS Conventions 2010, G. Petit and B. Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note 36 (as secondary sources quote it): k_2 = 0.30102
  and h_2 = 0.6078, so the Love numbers' reduction 1 + k_2 - h_2 = 0.693.
- D. J. Schwab, "Hydrodynamic modeling in the Great Lakes from 1950 to 1990 and prospects for the 1990s", 1992,
  https://www.glerl.noaa.gov/pubs/fulltext/1992/19920019.pdf (read): wind set-up proportional to fetch, U^2 and 1/depth; lake
  tides of a few centimetres.
- D. B. Rao and D. J. Schwab, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 281, 1976 (as its abstract states): Lake Superior's fundamental seiche
  of 7.86 h. Merian's period 2L / sqrt(g h) (via the USACE Coastal Engineering Manual's restatement).
- D. A. Williams, K. J. Horsburgh, D. M. Schultz and C. W. Hughes, "Proudman resonance with tides, bathymetry and variable
  atmospheric forcings", Natural Hazards 102, 1239-1263, 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-020-03896-y (pp. 1 to 4, read):
  the forced wave 1 / (1 - Fr^2) times the inverse barometer and its linear growth at Fr = 1 (eqs. 2 and 3). The test holds
  the growth to the exact linear solution from rest, derived here: for eta_tt - c^2 eta_xx = c^2 P_xx with P = -B f(x - c t),
  eta = (c t / 2) B f'(xi) + (B / 4) f(xi) - (B / 4) f(x + c t), xi = x - c t (a particular solution t G(xi) with
  G = -(c / 2) P', and the free waves that start it from rest).
- T. R. Hultquist, M. R. Dutter and D. J. Schwab, "Reexamination of the 9-10 November 1975 'Edmund Fitzgerald' storm using
  today's technology", BAMS 87, 607-622, 2006 (through NWS Marquette's and secondary accounts): the 982 hPa low over the lake and
  winds of 50 to 60 knots.
- The Kelvin wave, the inertial circle, Merian's seiche and the quarter-wave co-oscillating tide are textbook results (A. E.
  Gill, "Atmosphere-Ocean Dynamics", 1982, known from memory, and G. I. Taylor 1922 as restated), held by the tests.

The Coriolis force as an exact rotation of the momentum by f dt after each substep, the potential's mean over the wet water
taken off (so a closed lake keeps its mean level and only differences move water), the cells' Earth-fixed positions on the
tangent plane brought back to the sphere, the tanh ramp and the water's time scale (its own inputs on its time, other solvers' fields on the world's, as the spectral
sea's `timeScale` already does) are this package's own arrangement. The quarter-wave tide is measured by harmonic analysis
of the M2 constituent (least squares at the tide's frequency over whole periods, as tide gauges are reduced), since a
frictionless channel keeps the seiche its start rang. The water's time scale is checked by a derived bound: two-stage
Runge-Kutta turns a mode of frequency w by w dt + (w dt)^3 / 6 a step (the argument of 1 + i w dt - (w dt)^2 / 2), and a
simple long wave travelling at sqrt(g h) (1 + 3 eta / (2 h)) grows a second harmonic of 3 a^2 k c t / (4 h), the
Riemann simple wave expanded to first order (A. E. Gill, "Atmosphere-Ocean Dynamics", known from memory). The world's
refusal of a field read at another time scale than its writer's is this package's own arrangement. Proof:
`packages/physics/tests/surge.test.js` and `tests/coupling/surge.test.js`.

### Nonlinear and rogue waves (SEA-03, `@margoengine/physics/rogue`, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/rogue/index.ts` (`NonlinearSea`, `seaStatistics`, `pairKernels`, `heightChance`, `crestChance`,
`expectedMaximum`, `kurtosisFactor`). Written from papers and public documentation only (no code of WAVEWATCH III, the ECMWF
wave model, any HOS or NLS solver or any wave library was opened; no companion code of the papers below):

- J. F. Dalzell, "A note on finite depth second-order wave-wave interactions", Applied Ocean Research 21(3), 105-111, 1999,
  https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0141118799000085, as T. A. A. Adcock and S. Draper restate it in "The second order
  contribution to wave crest amplitude: random simulations and NewWave", Proc. 25th ISOPE, 2015, ISOPE-I-15-515 (appendix,
  read): the sum and difference kernels B+ and B- with alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon and zeta. The pair counting (each
  unordered pair once, a component with itself at half weight, its own difference term 0) is set by the tests: Stokes's (1/2) k
  a^2 cos 2 psi deep and its finite-depth form, Longuet-Higgins's (k1 + k2)/2 and -|k1 - k2|/2, and, for close frequencies in
  finite water, Longuet-Higgins and Stewart's (1962) bound long wave -(2n - 1/2) g / (g h - c_g^2) (0.05 percent apart).
- A. Alberello, A. Chabchoub, O. Gramstad, A. V. Babanin and A. Toffoli, "Non-Gaussian properties of second-order wave orbital
  velocity", Coastal Engineering 110, 42-49, 2016, arXiv:1510.01535 (read): the second-order potential (its velocities are not
  used here, see the limits) and the self-difference term set to 0.
- ECMWF, IFS Documentation Cy50r1, Part VII: ECMWF Wave Model, chapter 8, "Extreme wave forecasting", 2025,
  https://www.ecmwf.int/sites/default/files/elibrary/062026/81737-ifs-documentation-cy50r1-part-7-ecmwf-wave-model.pdf (read,
  sections 8.1 to 8.3.7): C4 = <eta^4> / (3 <eta^2>^2) - 1; eps = k_bar sqrt(m0) with 0.89 omega_bar = omega(k_bar), omega_bar =
  m0 / m_-1; delta_omega = 1 / (Q_p sqrt(pi)) with Goda's peakedness over E > 0.4 E_p; delta_theta = sqrt(2 (1 - R1)) over the
  peak band; nu = sqrt(m0 m2 / m1^2 - 1); the deep-water BFI^2 = 2 eps^2 / delta_omega^2 and R = delta_theta^2 / (2 nu^2); the
  dynamic kurtosis J(R) BFI^2 with J's fit (Gamma 0.9, alpha = 4 sqrt 3 / pi, beta = 1/3 + 2 sqrt 3 / pi, delta = 2 sqrt 3 / pi
  - 4/3, J(R) = -J(1/R) / R above 1); the height exceedance e^(-2 H^2) (1 + C4 2 H^2 (H^2 - 1)) of N. Mori and P. A. E. M.
  Janssen, "On kurtosis and occurrence probability of freak waves", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 36, 1471-1483, 2006 (as restated).
- P. A. E. M. Janssen, "Nonlinear four-wave interactions and freak waves", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 33, 863-884, 2003 (as the IFS
  documentation restates it): the Benjamin-Feir index and the bound kurtosis 6 eps^2 of a narrow deep sea.
- M. A. Tayfun and F. Fedele, "Wave-height distributions and nonlinear effects", Ocean Engineering 34, 1631-1649, 2007 (read,
  key equations), and F. Fedele, C. Lugni and A. Chawla, "The sinking of the El Faro: predicting real world rogue waves during
  Hurricane Joaquin", Sci. Rep. 7, 2017, arXiv:1703.08161 (read, eqs. 13 to 19): the crest exceedance exp(-8 xi0^2) (1 + Lambda xi0^2
  (4 xi0^2 - 1)), xi = xi0 + 2 mu xi0^2, mu = lambda_3 / 3, Lambda about 8 lambda_40 / 3 = 8 C4, and the narrowband bound
  kurtosis lambda_40 = 2 lambda_3^2.
- M. A. Tayfun, "Narrow-band nonlinear sea waves", J. Geophys. Res. 85, 1548-1552, 1980 (as restated): the narrow deep sea's
  skewness 3 k sigma, which the tests hold the kernel sum to.
- P. S. Tromans, A. R. Anaturk and P. Hagemeijer, "A new model for the kinematics of large ocean waves", Proc. 1st ISOPE,
  1991 (as Adcock and Draper restate it, eq. 4): NewWave, the autocovariance shape of an extreme crest. Its constrained form in
  a random sea, eta + (A - eta(0)) rho + (0 - eta'(0)) rho' / lambda_2, after P. H. Taylor, P. Jonathan and L. A. Harland, J.
  Offshore Mech. Arct. Eng. 119, 1997 (not read; known only from memory), so it is derived here from the conditions it meets
  (the crest's height and a still surface there) and the tests hold those conditions.
- M. Christou and K. Ewans, "Field measurements of rogue water waves", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 44, 2317-2335, 2014 (as restated): a
  rogue is a height above 2 H_s or a crest above 1.25 H_s.
- J. D. Wheeler, "Method for calculating forces produced by irregular waves", J. Petroleum Technology 22, 359-367, 1970 (as
  the offshore literature restates it): stretching linear kinematics to the instantaneous surface.

Added the same day, runs of high waves (the three sisters, `packages/physics/src/rogue/groups.ts`):
- A. Kimura, "Statistical properties of random wave groups", Proc. 17th ICCE, 1980, https://doi.org/10.9753/icce.v17.175
  (eqs. 5 to 19, tables 1 and 2, read): the two-dimensional Rayleigh law of successive heights, the correlation of eq. 7, p22,
  the mean run and runs of j waves.
- J. A. Battjes and G. Ph. van Vledder, "Verification of Kimura's theory for wave group statistics", Proc. 19th ICCE, 1984,
  https://doi.org/10.9753/icce.v19.43 (eqs. 3 to 5, read): kappa from the spectrum at T_m02, biased toward short groups.
- G. Ph. van Vledder, "Statistics of wave group parameters", Proc. 23rd ICCE, 1992 (eqs. 2.8, 4.3, 4.4 and 9.6 to 9.8, read):
  the corrected correlation of successive heights.
- F. Fedele, "Stochastic wave groups in weakly nonlinear random waves", 2008 (sections 1 to 4, read), restating Lindgren
  (1970) and Boccotti: the expected group about a large crest from the autocovariance.
The elliptic integrals by the arithmetic-geometric mean, Marcum's Q by Simpson's rule over the scaled Rice density, p22 as
the integral of Rice's law over the high first heights, and three sisters as three constrained crests a group spacing apart
are this package's own arrangement. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/sisters.test.js`.

The equal-variance draw (stratified quantiles of the frequency marginal, the direction from the bin's distribution), the
joint solve of several events' crest and slope constraints, the secant correction of each linear crest for the second order's
rise, the events' space-time window with amplitudes that vary over it, the rate of drawn rogues (one wave per zero-crossing
wavelength squared per zero-crossing period times the crest chance with the full kurtosis less that with the bound kurtosis),
the skewness as the kernels' sum over the spectrum's bins and the pressure's second-order rise taken as hydrostatic are this
package's own arrangement. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/rogue.test.js`.
### Accepted whitewater grid and native transport (SEA-13)

Bram van Leer, *Towards the ultimate conservative difference scheme IV. A new approach to numerical
convection* (1977), §§2 and 5 equations 14–16 and 66 derive the upwind linear face reconstruction and
monotonized centered slope. For matching signs the scalar slope is the signed minimum of the centered
and twice the two one-sided differences. The SIMD lanes compute the existing coverage and its weighted
decay independently. Each directional sweep joins before the orthogonal one starts. The candidate solver
state publishes after the worst face and final derived coverage are checked. [Van Leer](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(77)90095-X).
