Adrian Callaghan, Gerrit de Leeuw, Leo Cohen and Colin D. O’Dowd, *Relationship of oceanic whitecap coverage
to wind speed and wind history* (2008), measured North Atlantic whitecaps with a ship camera. The author
archive supplies total observed coverage, collocated retrospective neutral wind and wave age. The diagnostic
uses a fixed wind-only spin-up and selects low, middle and high input winds within three wave-age groups.
The measured coverage and the authors’ fitted curve are held out. The image-threshold sensitivity of
Callaghan and White (2009), §3f, is a component of uncertainty. The paper archive lacks complete per-row
uncertainty and realized spectra. [2008 experiment](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008GL036165),
[figure data](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.25460128.v1), [image processing](https://doi.org/10.1175/2008JTECHO634.1).

Grant B. Deane and M. Dale Stokes, *Scale dependence of bubble creation mechanisms in breaking waves*
(2002), identify distinct size spectra above and below the Hinze scale. Edgar L. Andreas, *A New Sea Spray
Generation Function for Wind Speeds up to 32 m s⁻¹* (1998), treats spume separately from spray by bubble
bursting. These motivate the remaining air entrainment and spray work. This surface transport preserves
the existing spectral foam and plume models. [Deane and Stokes](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature00967),
[Andreas](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485%281998%29028%3C2175%3AANSSGF%3E2.0.CO%3B2).

### Whitecaps, foam and spray (SEA-13, `@margoengine/physics/foam`, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/foam/breaking.ts` (breaking statistics of a spectrum), `foam/spray.ts` (spray source functions) and
`foam/index.ts` (`FoamSolver`, a framework solver). Written from papers only (no code of any model was opened):

- F. Leckler, F. Ardhuin, J.-F. Filipot and A. Mironov, "Dissipation source terms and whitecap statistics", Ocean Modelling
  70, 62-74, 2013, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocemod.2013.03.007, author draft read:
  - the directional saturation with cos^2 over +-80 degrees (eq. 2; the C_g / 2 pi factor of Ardhuin et al. 2010 eq. 12 is a
    misprint, their footnote 3);
  - the breaking probability 28.4 (sqrt(B') - sqrt(B_r))^2 (eq. 4) and the crest length Lambda = P_b / (2 pi^2) (eq. 5);
  - the whitecap coverage W = kappa integral of lambda Lambda, kappa = 0.30 for ST4, tuned to Monahan and Woolf (1989) and
    WindSat (eqs. 14 and 15).
- F. Ardhuin et al., J. Phys. Oceanogr. 40, 2010 (arXiv:0907.4240, read): eqs. 12 to 17, B_r = 0.0009 and its depth
  correction (eq. 15).
- N. Reul and B. Chapron, "A model of sea-foam thickness distribution for passive microwave remote sensing applications", J.
  Geophys. Res. 108(C10), 3321, 2003, https://doi.org/10.1029/2003JC001887, read:
  - a breaker's active stage of 0.8 T (Phillips et al. 2001) and foam persistence of about 5 T (eq. 21 with a = 0.8 and 5:
    the active share 0.16);
  - the bubbles' surface lifetime, 3.85 s in salt water and 2.54 s in fresh (Monahan and Zietlow 1969);
  - Duncan's (1981) breaking crest of about 0.3 of a wavelength.
- P. Callaghan, G. de Leeuw, L. Cohen and C. O'Dowd, Geophys. Res. Lett. 35, L23609, 2008, read: their whitecap fits; and
  Callaghan, Deane, Stokes and Ward, J. Geophys. Res. 117, C09015, 2012 (abstract): foam decay times of 1.4 to 4.8 s, longer
  for larger patches.
- F. Ardhuin, L. Marie, N. Rascle, P. Forget and A. Roland, "Observation and estimation of Lagrangian, Stokes and Eulerian
  currents induced by wind and waves at the sea surface", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 39, 2009, arXiv:0810.3537 (abstract): a
  quasi-Eulerian wind drift of 0.4 to 0.8 percent of U10.
- S. Leibovich, "The form and dynamics of Langmuir circulations", Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 15, 391-427, 1983, read: windrows
  along the wind within minutes of a wind above 3 m/s, surface sweep speeds of about 1 percent of U10.
- J. Reed and J. H. Milgram, "Ship wakes and their radar images", Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 34, 469-502, 2002, read:
  - the stern's violent bubbly zone, about two beams long;
  - the wake's width growing as x^(1/5);
  - the turbulence 0.05 / (x / L + 0.07)^(4/5) (Hoekstra and Ligtelijn 1991, their eq. 26).
- D. R. Trevorrow, S. Vagle and D. M. Farmer, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 95, 1994 (abstract): bubble wakes acoustically strong for
  about 7.5 minutes at 10 knots.
- G. de Leeuw et al., "Production flux of sea spray aerosol", Rev. Geophys. 49, RG2001, 2011, read: the appendix's Gong (2003)
  and Monahan, Spiel and Davidson (1986) functions, the whitecap method, r80 = r0 / 2.
- Y. Troitskaya et al., "The 'bag breakup' spume droplet generation mechanism at high winds", Sci. Rep. 7, 1614, 2017, read:
  the bag-breakup event rate (eq. 1).

This package's own arrangement:
- Breakers as Poisson events at the rate Lambda / (L_b tau*), with whiteness d and persistence tau_e chosen so the average
  coverage is Leckler's W with Reul and Chapron's active share; for d up to 1, d tau_e = 0.2377 T, so storm breakers leave
  dense foam that lasts longer.
- The active patch's depth along the wave, 0.048 of a wavelength, the active share of W.
- Breakers born beyond the grid by a sweep so the edges balance.
- The flux-form, MC-limited transport of the foam's whiteness with its rate-weighted share.
- Independent overlap 1 - (1 - a)(1 - b) for foam laid on foam.
- The windrows as a sinusoidal surface convergence spun up exponentially.
- The bow waves' foam arms at Kelvin's angle with a Froude-number ramp from 0.15 to 0.4.
- Wake foam's 150 s persistence (the 7.5 minutes taken as three e-foldings).

Validation:
- On ST4's developed seas the coverage is 1.41, 0.98, 0.74 and 0.56 of Monahan and Woolf at 7, 10, 13 and 16 m/s (Leckler et
  al. note the model follows Monahan and Woolf below 15 m/s and grows about linearly above, as satellites see).
- The event model covers 1.03 of Leckler's W at 10 m/s, 0.167 of it active.
- The surface Stokes drift of a narrow swell is sigma k a^2 to 1e-9.
- Foam is conserved as it is carried, to 1e-6.
- Known: ST4 counts too many short breakers against Melville and Matusov's (2002) Lambda(c) (Leckler et al.), which the
  coverage, weighted by lambda, barely feels.

Proof: `packages/physics/tests/foam.test.js` and `tests/coupling/foam.test.js`.

### Rivers, floods and dam breaks: conservative shallow water (HYDRO-01, `@margoengine/physics/hydro`, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/hydro/shallow.ts` (the finite-volume kernel, K14) and `hydro/index.ts` (`ShallowWaterSolver`, a
framework solver). The scheme is the one `@margoengine/water/flood` already runs, from its CPU reference
(packages/water/test/flood-reference.js, Margo's own code, whose header records the papers it was written from: Chen and
Noelle 2017; Audusse et al. 2004; Harten, Lax and van Leer 1983; Kurganov and Petrova 2007; Borges, Carmona, Costa and Don
2008; Jiang and Shu 1996; Castro, Costa and Don 2011; Shu and Osher 1988; Chertock, Cui, Kurganov and Wu 2015), carried
onto the framework's f64 state and the terrain bed. Read again for this solver (papers only; no code of any library, engine
or paper's companion was opened, SWASHES' and FullSWOF's included):

- A. Kurganov and G. Petrova, "A second-order well-balanced positivity preserving central-upwind scheme for the Saint-Venant
  system", Commun. Math. Sci. 5(1) 133-160, 2007, https://doi.org/10.4310/CMS.2007.v5.n1.a6, read in full: the one-sided
  speeds and the desingularised velocity (eq. 2.17) the flux uses, and the Courant bound of its positivity theorem.
- E. Audusse, F. Bouchut, M.-O. Bristeau, R. Klein and B. Perthame, "A fast and stable well-balanced scheme with hydrostatic
  reconstruction for shallow water flows", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 25(6) 2050-2065, 2004,
  https://doi.org/10.1137/S1064827503431090, read in full: the reconstruction (eqs. 2.9 to 2.16 and 3.1 to 3.9), its lake
  at rest with dry cells and its positivity (Theorem 2.1, Proposition 2.2), and the centred bed source of second order.
- A. Bollermann, G. Chen, A. Kurganov and S. Noelle, "A well-balanced reconstruction of wet/dry fronts for the shallow water
  equations", J. Sci. Comput. 56(2) 267-290, 2013, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10915-012-9677-5, read in full; and Bollermann,
  Noelle and Lukacova-Medvid'ova 2011 on the draining time in 2D: why a central-upwind scheme with a corner bed needs tiny
  steps at shorelines, which the cell-centred hydrostatic reconstruction here does not (its step is the Courant bound's).
- A. Chertock, S. Cui, A. Kurganov and T. Wu, "Well-balanced positivity preserving central-upwind scheme for the shallow water
  system with friction terms", Int. J. Numer. Methods Fluids 78(6) 355-383, 2015, https://doi.org/10.1002/fld.4023, read
  (sections 1 to 3), and V. Michel-Dansac, C. Berthon, S. Clain and F. Foucher, "A two-dimensional high-order well-balanced
  scheme for the shallow water equations with topography and Manning friction", Comput. Fluids 230, 2021, arXiv:2004.04484
  (eqs. 2.27 to 2.37): the friction update q / (1 + dt g n^2 |u| / h^(4/3)) is the exact solution of the friction ODE at a
  frozen depth (their eq. 2.29), so it slows the flow, never turns it back, and goes to 0 with the depth.
- E. D. Schubert and B. F. Sanders, "Building treatments for urban flood inundation models and implications for predictive
  skill and modeling efficiency", Adv. Water Resour. 41, 2012, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2012.02.012 (as
  `flood.ts` records it): buildings as raised bed (the building-block method).
- O. Delestre et al., "SWASHES: a compilation of shallow water analytic solutions for hydraulic and environmental studies",
  arXiv:1110.0288, read: the closed forms of Ritter's and Stoker's dam breaks, Thacker's planar bowl (4.2.2) and the lake at
  rest the tests hold the solver to (the originals of Ritter 1892, Stoker 1957 and Thacker 1981 were not read). Manning's
  normal depth h = (q n / sqrt(S))^(3/5) and the default n = 0.03 of a clean, straight natural channel: Chow, "Open-Channel
  Hydraulics", 1959, known through these.
- Garratt's drag coefficient C_D = (0.75 + 0.067 U10) 1e-3 (J. R. Garratt 1977), as `flood.ts` records it.

The cell's bed as the mean of the terrain's two triangles over it, the open side that carries the bed's slope on past the
edge (with the minmod slope in the ghosts beside it, so a river leaves at its normal depth; a flat ghost bed backed a
river up, 60 percent too deep near its outlet), the adaptive substeps that end exactly on each tick, the volume ledger of
inflow, rain and sides weighed as the Runge-Kutta stages weigh them, and `water.flow` are this package's own arrangement.
Proof: `packages/physics/tests/hydro.test.js` and `tests/coupling/hydro.test.js`.

### Tracers and slicks in water (SEA-15, `@margoengine/physics/tracers`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/tracers.ts` (`TracerSolver`, a framework solver). Written from:

- R. I. Ferguson and M. Church, "A simple universal equation for grain settling velocity", J. Sediment. Res. 74, 2004: not
  readable here; its equation w = R g D^2 / (C1 nu + sqrt(0.75 C2 R g D^3)), C1 = 18 and the turbulent-drag range of C2
  (0.4 to 1.2) as restated by A. Metelkin and B. Vowinckel, arXiv:2410.12477 (read, section 2.1, eqs. 2 and 3).
- The wind drift factor of floating oil, a constant share of the wind (3 percent the traditional value): Liu, Li and Mu,
  Frontiers in Marine Science 2023 (abstract read), and the 0 to 5 percent range tested in arXiv:2409.20096 (abstract read).
- The random walk of diffusion, a step of sqrt(2 K dt) times a standard normal number giving a variance 2 K t (the
  diffusion equation's solution), and the Box-Muller transform: textbook results.

The particle columns in world memory, the source's carried remainder, the exact mass ledger, the reflecting surface and
the absorbing bed, the floating state, and the concentration grid with mass-weighted colour are this package's own
arrangement. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/tracers.test.js` and `tests/coupling/tracers.test.js`.

For the ray's bed jet (BB-7), D. J. Phares, G. T. Smedley, and R. C. Flagan, “The wall shear stress
produced by the normal impingement of a jet on a flat surface” (2000), describes the off-centre wall
jet and wall-stress dependence on jet height. Read §§2–3 and the submerged-jet evidence in §5.
<https://doi.org/10.1017/S002211200000121X>. L. C. van Rijn, “Sediment Transport, Part II:
Suspended Load Transport” (1984), uses the excess bed shear term relative to the critical stress.
<https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9429(1984)110:11(1613)>.

The default onset follows R. L. Soulsby and R. J. S. Whitehouse, “Threshold of sediment motion in coastal
environments” (1997), reproduced as Eq. 3 in the [USACE sediment reference](https://www.hec.usace.army.mil/confluence/rasdocs/d2sd/ras2dsedtr/6.5/model-description/critical-thresholds-for-transport-and-erosion)
and in the [HR Wallingford STEP paper](https://eprints.hrwallingford.com/id/eprint/771/1/HRPP491-STEP_Model.pdf).
The default dry mass flux is L. C. van Rijn, [“Sediment Pick-Up Functions” (1984)](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9429(1984)110:10(1494)),
as given in Eq. 1 of L. C. van Rijn, R. Bisschop, and C. van Rhee, [“Modified Sediment Pick-Up Function” (2019)](https://www.leovanrijn-sediment.com/papers/Pickup2019.pdf).
For positive relative excess shear, the flux per bed area is `0.00033 ρ_s sqrt((s−1) g d) D_*^0.3 excess^1.5`,
where `s = ρ_s/ρ_w` and `D_* = d [((s−1) g)/ν²]^(1/3)`. The cited 1984 data cover low-flow noncohesive sand
of roughly 100 to 1,500 μm. The 40 μm silt setting extrapolates the relation to noncohesive silt.

For clean, densely packed sand, van Rijn, Bisschop and van Rhee (2019), Eq. 5, adds a damping factor `1/Θ`
above grain Shields number `Θ=1`. The optional damping uses the same measured diameter and grain density as the
threshold, with no changes below `Θ=1`. [“High-Velocity Erosion of Sand,” O. A. Heijmeijer, A. J. Nobel, G. Keetels,
and C. van Rhee (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)HY.1943-7900.0001949) supplies the independent BOKA
flume wall stresses and bed retreat rates (Tables 2–3, Fig. 11). A live TerrainBed with 125 µm Geba sand gets the
four measured stresses through the wash sampler. Quartz density and the central test porosity of 0.43 convert loss
of dry mass to retreat speed. The initial clean-water check compares pickup with net retreat while deposition is
negligible in the model. None of the BOKA retreat rates set an input or a fitted constant. The RMS log retreat error
falls from 1.734 to 0.734, with the largest shortfall a factor of 2.81. This is a stress-to-pickup test, with no claim
to reproduce the flume's evolving flow or a ray's wake.

The radial model reconstructs a uniform nozzle speed from normal impulse per step and nozzle area. It uses
Phares et al.'s Eq. 2.31 and the theoretical circular jet curves in Fig. 5b (clearance/diameter 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8),
with the exact fully developed maximum from Eq. 2.33. Linear interpolation of the plotted curve nodes supplies
the impingement-region shear. Beyond its peak, the Poreh et al. wall-jet law (Phares Eq. 2.37) limits the shear.
The last tabulated core value carries through the default join if the outer law is still above it.
Two-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature integrates the mass flux in squared radius,
with 32 core and 16 outer annuli. Four stratified parcels sample the mass-weighted radial distribution.
The downstream stress test reads four submerged electrochemical observations of Alekseenko and Markovich
(1994) from Phares Fig. 10 (H/D = 2, Re = 42,600), with both log axes bounded by the marker sizes.
Those observations were separate from the Poreh law's calibration and the Fig. 5b theoretical samples.

The swimmer's wake uses the framework `Port.cell` convention. The tracer converts the position into its own cell
before it reads water depth or terrain. The test repeats a native fin stroke with different cell coordinates and
compares the same suspended mass, parcel positions, terrain elevations and replay.
Cargo from hull openings uses the same coordinate conversion. A separate live flooding test compares the released
pellets and fines in shifted and unshifted tracer cells with a roundoff bound derived from the number of steps.

For an inclined bed the fin wake intersects the tangent plane of the source's terrain triangle. Clearance and
delivered impulse are normal components. The rotation taking the world up vector to the oriented bed normal
maps both annulus axes into that plane, retaining their area. Duff et al.,
[“Building an Orthonormal Basis, Revisited” (2017)](https://jcgt.org/published/0006/01/01/), compares
stable basis constructions. The upward terrain normal keeps `1 + normalY` away from cancellation. The radial
pressure closure remains Phares's normal-incidence law. S. Beltaos's
[“Oblique Impingement of Circular Turbulent Jets” (1976)](https://www.iahr.org/library/infor?pid=7059)
describes the directional shear outside that assumption. A rigid rotation of the live swimmer and planar bed
preserves the lifted dry mass and rotates each emitted footprint coordinate.

The tracer allocates the pick-up request to the terrain triangle's three vertex control volumes by barycentric
weight. Each contribution stops at its own mobile stock. The parcel receives the sum of accepted contributions,
and each accepted contribution lowers the bed by its packed volume divided by the corresponding vertex area. A two-cell wash drains
one corner and then removes half of its adjacent shared vertex's stock. The test measures both vertex changes,
the 5.30 kg lifted, zero bedrock rejection and exact replay.

The optional developing wall layer uses Phares et al. Eq. 2.12 and Fig. 4 for the free-stream half width and
velocity plateau. Using the plateau as constant edge speed, it integrates their axisymmetric Falkner momentum
layer (Eqs. 2.34–2.36 with the inverse one-sixth shear dependence) analytically. The zero-gradient
Pohlhausen quartic gives the upstream momentum thickness from the laminar shear via Eq. 2.27. The closure starts
three half widths out, where the plotted inviscid speed reaches its plateau, and applies when the turbulent
shear rises. One annulus ends at that radius. Poreh's Eq. 2.37 limits the outer transition. Fig. 10 supplies 14
separate wall-shear observations at H/D 2 and 4. All inputs and constants come from theory and velocity data.
The sampled RMS log stress error is 0.097 compared with 0.127 for the default. Strong adverse pressure gradients,
transition timing within a fin stroke, and the short-gap jet remain outside this closure.

Van Rijn's Part II Eq. 37 uses a suspension reference plane at half the bedform height, or at the equivalent
roughness height if bedform measurements are unavailable, with a minimum of 1% of local water depth. The
tracer uses that plane to represent where lifted parcels enter suspension. The visual fixture takes half of
the 35 mm ripple height reported in J. Fredsøe, K. H. Andersen, and B. M. Sumer, [“Wave plus current over a
ripple-covered bed” (1999)](https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/wave-plus-current-over-a-ripple-covered-bed/).
The ripple height is a physical input for the fixed-camera fixture. An independent ray-plume profile remains open.

For clearances shorter than a diameter, or explicitly prescribed footprint shear, the reduced model spreads
the wake radius by 0.1 m per metre of travel and uses 5% of incident normal momentum flux. These jet constants
are modelling choices. An explicitly prescribed linear erosion option is available for a specified bed.
They settle by the SEA-15 grain law. In the render fixture, their optical cross section is twice the
projected geometric area in the large-particle limit (van de Hulst, *Light Scattering by Small
Particles*, 1957, extinction paradox). The mass, source placement, and replay assertions use the
same packed wake from the live swimmer. Manufactured stresses verify onset, dry mass flux and grain
size dependence through the live ray path. Independent dry mass pickup measurements remain to be checked.

For the cargo plume (EF-11), the [U.S. Coast Guard Marine Board report](https://www.dco.uscg.mil/Portals/9/DCO%20Documents/5p/CG-5PC/INV/docs/boards/edmundfitz.pdf)
describes Great Lakes taconite pellets of about one-half inch in diameter. The
[NTSB report MAR-78-3 (1978)](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/MAR7803.pdf) gives the
3/8 to 5/8 inch diameter range. The tested 12 mm pellet is a representative input. The fixture's mixture and
individual grain density are prescribed, and its test checks mass conservation, differential settling and replay.
The release carries a separate mass remainder by material from the same port record and uses Ferguson and Church
settling after release. The cargo reports supply size context. A comparison against measured plume evolution remains open.

The tracer sea binding uses the shared `SeaSurface` query for elevation and surface velocity, and `SeaSurface.water`
for submerged flow. It translates from the tracer origin to the sea origin before sampling. The floating parcels
follow the material surface as in G. B. Airy's [*Tides and Waves* (1845)](https://books.google.com/books/about/Tides_and_Waves.html?id=41dSAAAAcAAJ).
Submerged parcels reflect when the step crosses the moving
surface. The coupling test advances a slick and submerged dye over a single travelling Fourier mode in a different
origin cell, checks both paths at every step and replays the snapshot. This is an exact coupling check; the motion
comes from the live SEA-02 solver.

The sand plume and bed share an optional volume exchange (BB-7) using the sediment continuity relation in
C. Paola and V. R. Voller, [“A Generalized Exner Equation for Sediment Mass Balance” (2005)](https://doi.org/10.1029/2004JF000274).
Each lifted parcel debits the bed by its dry mass divided by grain density times solid fraction. On impact its mass
adds the same packed volume at the landing position. The same three triangle weights route the mass and the f64 vertex
heights, with each vertex's tributary area converting volume to height. The configured active-layer inventory bounds
pickup at each vertex. `coupling/swim.test.js` verifies the transient loss, final balance and exact replay against
the real `TerrainBed` ledgers. The rendered fixture draws the bed heights and verifies negative and positive relief.
Independent lifted-mass measurements and playback of the original BB-7 shot remain open.

Finite surface releases use J. A. Fay, [“Physical Processes in the Spread of Oil on a Water Surface” (1971)](https://iosc.kglmeridian.com/downloadpdf/view/journals/iosc/1971/1/article-p463.xml),
Tables I and II. The three axisymmetric radii use Fay's 1.14, 1.45 and 2.30 constants with age powers 1/2, 1/4 and
3/4. The gravity envelope takes the smaller of its inertial and viscous radii. Positive net interfacial tension
dominates where its radius exceeds that envelope. This continuous join is Margo's approximation for the regime
transitions. Antipodal equal-area parcels give the initial patch; each step expands about its transported centroid
and applies the usual surface advection and diffusion. The closed-form check uses all three regimes and exact
mass and snapshot replay. Independent field validation of oil extent remains open.

V. Maderich, I. Brovchenko and K. T. Jung, [“Oil spreading in instantaneous and continuous spills on rotating
earth” (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10652-012-9239-2), Eqs. 27 and 30, give axisymmetric gravity-viscous
radius laws with 1.06 for a fixed volume and 0.816 for a constant inflow. During feed the radius grows as `t^(7/12)`.
At shutoff we start the fixed-volume law from the release radius using equivalent age `(0.816/1.06)^4 T`.
The Fay inertial cap uses the cumulative released volume. The represented source feeds one mixed moving patch,
so rotation, thickness stratification, separate parcel ages and stationary sources in shear are outside this model.
The six open-circle radius points in Brönner et al., Fig. 4, are held out. The MGO experiment feeds 4 L over 120 s.
The model uses the published 846 kg/m³ oil density and nominal seawater properties. The comparison covers 30–240 s
and gives 0.134 m RMS error versus 1.081 m when the same final volume is released instantly by Fay's law. The
largest relative error is 13.2%. Radii are read to centimetres from the optically reconstructed equivalent extent.

The waxy film uses U. Brönner, Ø. Johansen, F. Leirvik, T. Nordam, and K. R. Sørheim,
[“Spreading of waxy oils on calm water” (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marpolbul.2018.02.021),
equations A7–A8. The shear yield stress supplies the stopping thickness through the paper's factor of √3.
We use the fixed-volume Nihoul profile recounted in that appendix, `h/h₀=√(1−(r/R)²)`, with area mean `2h₀/3`.
The coefficient in the viscous force balance follows the zero-yield Fay radius. The implementation does not fit
Brönner's tank results. With fixed volume, multiply A8 by `3R^(8/3)` to obtain an equation for `R⁴`, with rate given
by the zero-yield Fay `R⁴` rate times `max(1−(R/R∞)²,0)^(2/3)`. Inverting its separable integral avoids a singular
initial radius. The early inertial envelope is Fay's. Antipodal parcels use the radial mass quantile of the profile.
Independent terminal radius estimates from Brönner's tank use optical thickness contours and ultrasound. The solver
inputs are the separate oscillatory rheometer stress, oil density, 4 L final volume and nominal seawater properties.
At the paper's 180 s sampling time, the nine reported terminal radii give an RMS log error of 1.056 for unyielded
Fay spreading and 0.480 for the waxy film law. The worst error is a factor of 3.59 for the single 30% blend run,
which fractured. The coherent-film law omits breakup. The radius comparison uses the fixed final volume after the
tank's 120 s feed ends, with replicates grouped by their experiment IDs in the text above Table 2.

Oil evaporation follows W. Stiver and D. Mackay, [“Evaporation rate of spills of hydrocarbons and petroleum mixtures” (1984)](https://doi.org/10.1021/es00129a006).
The [Environment Canada catalogue (1990), §3.1](https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2020/eccc/en84/En84-183-1990-eng.pdf)
gives the working equation `F = ln(1 + C θ exp(A − B T₀/T))/C`, with `A = 6.3`, `B = 10.3`,
`C = B T_G/T` and exposure `θ = ∫kA(t)dt/V₀`. D. Mackay, I. A. Buist, R. Mascarenhas and S. Paterson,
[“Oil Spill Processes and Models” (1980), chapter 3](https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2020/eccc/en40/En40-980-1980-eng.pdf),
uses the initial volume in its exposure normalization. This implementation integrates each active Fay radius
squared over its exact age interval. It uses a constant surface temperature and transfer coefficient and the initial
oil density, so the explicit volume fraction is also the mass fraction. Evaporation removes mass from the floating
parcels and records it as vapour in snapshot state. M. Fingas's [pan experiments (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-3894(97)00051-4)
find that many crude oils are weakly sensitive to wind. The transfer coefficient is explicit, and independent measured
validation of the expanding-slick evaporation model remains open. The early, intermediate and late analytical cases
compare against independent quadrature at 30 and 60 world steps per second.

For a fixed exposure area, `referenceThickness = V₀/A` makes the exposure `θ = kt / referenceThickness`.
W. Stiver and D. Mackay's [Environment Canada report EE-49 (1983), Eqs. 3, 7 and 13 and Figs. 9 and 12](https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2024/eccc/en40/En40-249-49-eng.pdf)
defines the same dimensionless exposure for tray evaporation and saturated gas stripping. A straight-line fit to the
12 Norman Wells atmospheric distillation circles in Fig. 9 gives an intercept of 380.03 K and slope of 463.83 K
per unit distilled fraction. The largest fit residual is 3.26 K. Allowing 1 K for plot reading gives 4.3 K for
the distillation input. The comparison uses the seven 0 °C measured circles in Fig. 12. Equation 18 was fitted
to the 22 °C rate data, and the solid prediction line in Fig. 12 supplies no reference values. The world clock
maps 1,000 exposure units to a second. The test propagates the distillation error, 0.001 fraction and 75
exposure units for plot reading, and half a tick through Eq. 13. The peak discrepancy is 0.45 percentage points.
This covers fixed exposure, with a constant-density conversion from volume to mass. An independent measurement
of evaporation from a freely expanding slick remains open.

Water-in-oil emulsification applies the wind-dependent exponential uptake from M. Reed et al.,
[“Revision of the OCS Oil-Weathering Model, Phases II and III,” MMS 2005-020, Eqs. 21–23 and 28](https://www.boem.gov/sites/default/files/boem-newsroom/Library/Publications/2005/2005_020.pdf).
Each step samples the horizontal wind at ten metres above the slick. It normalizes `(1 + U)²` by 121 and
updates water fraction with the prescribed field half time. The code stores water volume separately from oil
parcel mass. Evaporation removes only oil. Dispersing oil releases the same share of the emulsion water
back to the surrounding sea. Resurfacing contributes oil to the parent slick. Oil-only film thickness can
gate uptake because the minimum effective thickness varied by oil in P. S. Daling et al.,
[“Norwegian Testing of Emulsion Properties at Sea” (2003), §5](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1353-2561(03)00016-1).
Mixture density uses additive component volumes. Dynamic viscosity uses Mooney's law with the salt-water
coefficient 0.654 from [D. Mackay et al., “Oil Spill Processes and Models” (1980), §4.4 and Fig. 4.4](https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2020/eccc/en40/En40-980-1980-eng.pdf).

The Troll benchmark uses the independent Table 5.5 laboratory saturation of 75%. It converts the
`2 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹` coefficient from M. Reed, E. Gundlach and T. Kana,
[“A Coastal Zone Oil Spill Model” (1989), Eq. 24](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0269-8579(89)80019-X)
to a field half time at 10 m/s. The coefficient predates the 1995 Charlie oil samples. Table 5.3 supplies
the measured wind history. All Table 5.1 water measurements
from the field are separate. Four points from 7.3 to 33.5 h give a water fraction RMS difference of
2.13 percentage points versus their 2.38-point temporal sample standard deviation. The largest whole-run
error is 36.74 points at 1 h. This checks late water uptake. Early uptake kinetics, change of oil-only
viscosity and spreading under coalescence remain open. The model reports mixture thickness and uses the
existing Fay footprint.

Reversible oil dissolution uses the interfacial concentration difference in Henrik Rye,
[*A Multicomponent Oil Spill Model for Dissolved Aromatic Concentrations* (1995), Eq. 4](https://iosc.kglmeridian.com/downloadpdf/view/journals/iosc/1995/1/article-p49.xml)
and Jonas Gros et al., [*First Day of an Oil Spill on the Open Sea* (2014), Eq. 2](https://doi.org/10.1021/es502437e).
The two well-mixed reservoirs exchange a constituent at `k A (M_o/(K V_o) − M_w/V_w)`. Oil and
water volumes and the equilibrium partition ratio are constant. The dissolved pool can also lose
mass at a supplied first-order rate. This is the dilute, constant-biomass limit of the Monod
model in [Vilcáez, Li and Hubbard, *A New Model for the Biodegradation Kinetics of Oil Droplets* (2013), Eq. 4–5](https://doi.org/10.1186/1467-4866-14-4).
The finite update solves the two-compartment system exactly for constant area. With a changing
footprint it uses the interval mean Fay area. The no-decay case integrates that area exactly.
The ledger has separate dissolved and biodegraded inventories and restores them on seek.

The holdout uses Lulwa Nasser Ali, [*The Dissolution and Photodegradation of Kuwait Crude Oil in Seawater* (1994), §2.4.2 and Table 3.12](https://doi.org/10.24382/3595).
The starting oil composition, water volume, stir time and area describe the experiment.
The partition ratio comes from the dilute liquid solubility from
[Rojo-Nieto, Smith, Perales and Mayer (2012), Table 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aquatox.2012.04.006),
and the 210 g/mol average for a separate Kuwaiti export assay, reported by
[M. R. Riazi, *Oil Spill Occurrence, Simulation, and Behavior* (2021), Table 7.1](https://www.routledge.com/oil-spill-occurrence-simulation-and-behavior/riazi/p/book/9780367742560).
The transfer velocity uses the midpoint of the separate Brent crude experiments in
[Ghoshal, Pasion and Alshafie (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1021/es034832j),
with the range transcribed by [Liu, Maier, Grathwohl and Haderlein (2012), Table 2](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)EE.1943-7870.0000528).
The simulation gives 67.60 µg of naphthalene at 24 h against Ali's 75.70 µg GC-MS measurement
(10.7% low). The comparison threshold uses twice the independent 7% seawater solubility
coefficient of variation. The solubility assay was at 20 °C and the Kuwait preparation was at
25 °C. The endpoint tests one constituent close to equilibrium. Compound-specific exchange
kinetics, measured biodegradation, open-water plume transport, air transfer, and dissolving
droplets remain open.

Depth-dependent vertical diffusion uses André W. Visser, [“Using random walk models to simulate the vertical distribution of particles in a turbulent water column” (1997)](https://doi.org/10.3354/meps158275), equation 6.
The random step includes the diffusivity-gradient drift and evaluates its variance at half that drift. A manufactured
linear profile verifies the first two moments and the midpoint using a uniform control with the same random input.
For CMO Experiment 4, the midpoint of the independent microstructure uncertainty interval supplies the local
diffusivity near 17 m. The simulated variance implies 1.61 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s, within the 1.4–2.2 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s interval
inferred from Rhodamine fluorescence. The still-water test preserves `K·t` while accelerating the 97-hour interval.
This comparison covers local broadening. The measured layer migration also depended on solar heating.
[Oakey and Greenan (2004), Table 2](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003JC002193),
[Ledwell, Duda, Sundermeyer and Seim (2004), Figure 14](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003JC002194).

Wave-averaged Stokes transport uses the directional moments of a fixed wave spectrum. The kernel sums the
finite-depth Kenyon profile in each frequency band, using two decaying exponentials for its hyperbolic depth factor.
In deep water this becomes `a²ωk exp(−2kd)` for a wave of amplitude `a`, wavenumber `k` and a parcel at depth `d`
below still water. The tracer adds this mean transport to a supplied Eulerian current while the sea
can still provide the instantaneous elevation. The test compares a crossed pair of waves against the analytical
profile at the surface and two depths, and checks exact replay in finite and deep water. Independent measurements
of wave-induced mean flow in the field remain open. [Breivik, Janssen and Bidlot, “Approximate Stokes Drift Profiles in Deep Water” (2014), equations 1 and 4](https://doi.org/10.1175/JPO-D-14-0020.1).

L. Melito, N. Soori, M. Postacchini, B. Khorbatly, H. Kalisch and M. Brocchini,
[“Long-Wave Modulation of Stokes Drift and Mass Transport in Short Waves” (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s42286-026-00154-9),
§3.1 supplies the measured 0.025 m wave height, 1 s period and 0.12 m depth for the shallow-platform check.
§3.4 and Fig. 7 supply the held-out Stokes component from fitted Lagrangian and Eulerian velocities tracked below
the surface. We read the red marker centres in three six-wave blocks at 50, 60, 75, 90 and 100 mm depth. The plot
axis separates 5 mm/s by approximately 48 px. The test admits a two-pixel reading margin around the blocks'
envelope. The 15 points share one wave configuration and give a 0.82 mm/s RMS discrepancy. The benchmark covers
weakly nonlinear monochromatic drift over a shallow platform, without a field return-flow or breaking-wave claim.

The optional horizontal mixing law evolves the radial variance `q` of each release as `dq/dt = 4K_ref (3√q/L_ref)^b`.
The solver integrates this ordinary differential equation exactly, then splits each variance increment equally
between the two horizontal axes. This applies the Richardson scale dependence to an isotropic cloud moment. Each
parcel's snapshot stores its age in steps. The Cape Kennedy check fits a four-thirds law to the 38 black squares in
Poje et al. Figure 6. Their geometric mean coefficient gives apparent diffusivity 37.6 m²/s at scale 30 km. With cubic
variance growth, the instantaneous diffusivity is three times the apparent value. All nine dye extents from releases
3–6 in Okubo's Table 1 are reserved for comparison. The model improves the RMS log extent error from 1.996 to 0.537
against constant diffusivity at the same reference value. The largest residual is a factor of 2.34 in extent. This is
a cross-site comparison of horizontal extent. The model leaves coherent eddies and anisotropic shear to the flow field.
[Poje et al., “Submesoscale dispersion in the vicinity of the Deepwater Horizon spill” (2014), Figure 6](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1402452111),
[Akira Okubo, “Oceanic diffusion diagrams” (1971), Table 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/0011-7471(71)90046-5).

Breaking waves transfer slick oil into suspended droplets using the Delft Hydraulics flume relations. The
model integrates `C E^0.57 F d^0.7` across the diameter bounds and the active Fay area-time, with `E` the
energy lost per breaking area, `F` the turnover rate, and `C` the oil-specific coefficient. It integrates mass and
number in logarithmic bins, places droplets within the `1.5 H_b` intrusion layer, and uses buoyant settling velocity
with the sign reversed to return oil to the parent slick. The water, slick and vapour terms conserve total released
oil. The tests check the analytic flux and size moments, resurfacing and rejection of an invalid breaker sample
before mass moves. Li's separate untreated-oil experiments report a number slope near −2.1 with a break near
800 µm. The Delvigne law uses −2.3 over the configured range. The absolute entrained mass, intrusion depth
and high-diameter transition still need measured validation. [Delvigne, van der Stel and Sweeney, “Measurement of Vertical Turbulent Dispersion and Diffusion of Oil Droplets and Oiled Particles” (1987), ES.3 and ES.5–ES.7](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-I-1c4b61dc1fa26f8aee85455a627f47e3/pdf/GOVPUB-I-1c4b61dc1fa26f8aee85455a627f47e3.pdf),
[Delvigne and Sweeney, “Natural dispersion of oil” (1988)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0269-8579(88)80003-0),
[Li et al., “Size Distribution and Dispersion of Droplets Generated by Impingement of Breaking Waves on Oil Slicks” (2017), §3.3.3](https://doi.org/10.1002/2017JC013193).

Propeller and thruster wash maps resolved velocity inside a rough-wall logarithmic layer to bed stress using
`u* = 0.4 U_t/ln(z/z₀)` and `τ = ρ u*²`. The scene supplies the hydraulic roughness and the sampling distance
along each bed triangle's normal. The sample's tangential velocity drives stress, and the projected grid area
is divided by the normal's vertical component before integrating the van Rijn pickup flux. `ShipSolver.water`
drives the coupled propeller test on real TerrainBed. Switching off the screw gives zero erosion, and a
second-origin sloping bed checks both the area and the velocity projection. Measurements in confined propeller
jets show that boundary-layer structure and stress fluctuate with clearance. Absolute field pickup mass and the
log-layer assumption at very small clearances remain open. [R. A. Soulsby, “Dynamics of Marine Sands” (1997)](https://www.icevirtuallibrary.com/doi/book/10.1680/doms.25844),
[Liao, Wang and Wang, “In situ measurement of sediment resuspension caused by propeller wash” (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.flowmeasinst.2014.10.008),
[Toni Llull, “Ship propeller induced scour of non-cohesive sediment in low bed-clearance conditions” (2021), §2.3.3](https://upcommons.upc.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/14f411e3-4c77-41f1-aeac-86a82213a315/content).

M. L. Albertson, Y. B. Dai, R. A. Jensen and H. Rouse's “Diffusion of Submerged Jets” (1950) gives the
developed round-jet centreline law `U_c/U_0=6.2D/x` and describes the Gaussian radial profile. We use
`b=max(D/2,x/12.4)` and `U=U₀(D/2)/b exp(−r²/(2b²))`. The width floor represents the core and keeps
the section integral `∫ρU² dA=ρπ(D/2)²U₀²` constant. The actual thruster command scales the nozzle
momentum before the existing hull-speed loss. Discharge follows the rigid body's active outlet and its
pose is snapshot state. This is a free jet. It leaves out jet bending, quay confinement and wall attachment.
The independent LDA turbulent-jet fit from L. P. Xia and K. M. Lam (2009), Tables 1 and 3, gives a centreline
ratio of 0.275 at 20 diameters. The tunnel model gives 0.310, 12.7% high. That comparison covers established
free-jet flow. The separate bed-transport test uses the native field and checks dry mass and snapshot replay.
[Albertson et al.](https://doi.org/10.1061/TACEAT.0006302) [Xia and Lam](https://hub.hku.hk/handle/10722/137242).

Cohesive tracers use Winterwerp's aggregate and breakup balance. Setting fractal dimension 2, breakup exponent
`p = 1` and shear exponent `q = 1/2` in Eq. 1 yields `D′ = D²[k_A c G − k_B G^1.5(D − D_p)]/2`. Freezing
the positive mobility `D²` gives an exponential relaxation toward the local equilibrium for that step. The
size is saved per parcel. The dry mass stays constant and the excess density decreases as `D_p/D`. Settling
uses Eq. 9 with unit shape factors and the Schiller–Naumann drag correction. The test integrates an independent
implicit solution to verify the settling path and first-order convergence. A second case checks breakup under
shear and exact replay. Measured aggregate-size and velocity distributions remain open. The fixed fractal
dimension and spherical drag approximate the effects of permeability and mixed primary sizes documented in
recent flume and field experiments. [Winterwerp, “A simple model for turbulence induced flocculation of cohesive sediment” (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1080/00221689809498621),
[Winterwerp, Manning, Martens, de Mulder and Vanlede, “A heuristic formula for turbulence-induced flocculation of cohesive sediment” (2006), equations 1 and 9](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecss.2006.02.003),
[Nghiem et al., “Testing floc settling velocity models in rivers and freshwater wetlands” (2024)](https://doi.org/10.5194/esurf-12-1267-2024).

The Wax Lake Delta check uses the four sites with camera tracks in Figure 6. The CaltechDATA release supplies
`primaryparticle_sizedistn.csv` independently of the floc camera. We use `frac_num` as the number weight in
the second moment of `diameter.center`, take its square root, then take the median across samples at each profile.
This is Eq. 5 for a fractal dimension of two and zero weighting dimension. `floccam.csv` supplies a geometric
mean optical diameter and a separate geometric mean displacement speed per profile. The 222 positive speeds
are retained across the four profiles. Supplied optical diameter holds aggregate size fixed so the comparison
isolates drag and buoyancy. The RMS log error of the four speed means goes from 4.681 for individual primary
grains to 0.854 for the aggregates. In the fall profile, the settled aggregate moves at 0.166 mm/s in the model
versus 0.830 mm/s tracked. The benchmark leaves growth, permeability and high-organic composition unconstrained.
[Nghiem et al., source data](https://doi.org/10.22002/w4ave-nrg52).

The optional shear-limited closure reads R. Kuprenas, D. Tran and K. Strom,
[“A Shear-Limited Flocculation Model for Dynamically Predicting Average Floc Size” (2018), Eqs. 1 and 9](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018JC014154).
For two-dimensional fractal mass scaling, it multiplies the Winterwerp breakup term by
`(ρν² (D/η)²/F_y)^(1.5 D/η)`, with `η = √(ν/G)` and `ν` the kinematic viscosity.
The step freezes the positive `D²` mobility and solves the new breakup term implicitly. For
`r = D/η` and `c = ρν²/F_y`, the correction has minimum `exp(−3/(e √c))`. This bounds the
root above. The logarithmic derivative of `(D − D_p) (c r²)^(1.5 r)` is positive when
`c > 9/e⁴`, using the minimum of `r (ln(c r²) + 2)` at `r = e⁻²/√c`. The method bisects
that bracket with logarithms to represent high shear without overflowing the breakup term.

The lab comparison transforms the paper's Set A coefficients `k′_A = 0.45`, `k′_B = 1.16 × 10⁻⁶`
and `D_p = 5 µm` to the solver's SI form. Set A's 50 mg/L time series and 50-to-400 mg/L equilibrium
spread supplied the published calibration. All three separate Set B time series from D. Tran, R. Kuprenas
and K. Strom, [“How do changes in suspended sediment concentration alone influence the size of mud flocs under steady turbulent shearing?” (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csr.2018.02.008),
are reserved for comparison. The solver runs at 50 s⁻¹ with 60 lab minutes of 400 mg/L and the programmed
drop to 50 mg/L over 50, 100 or 200 lab minutes. Each of five phase centres per trial uses the eleven
adjacent one-minute observations of volume-median size. The inputs use the nominal concentration program.
The result's 6.58 µm RMS error is below the observed pooled temporal scatter of 6.84 µm. The largest
mean error is 12.22 µm at the end of the 200-minute ramp. The original equation with the same coefficients
gives 1,696.70 µm RMS error. Size is recovered from the last step's particle displacement with the separate
drag balance. The bench checks kinetics under prescribed conditions. Field settling and permeability
are separate and the Wax Lake Delta fall profile discrepancy remains.
[Tran et al., time-series measurement tables 15–17](https://github.com/FlocData/Data-2018-TranEtal/tree/master/01%20Time%20Series%20Data).

### The sea's waves: a spectral wave model (SEA-01, `@margoengine/physics/waves`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/waves/spectral.ts` (`WaveSolver`, a framework solver) and the contract `WaveSpectrumField`
(`packages/math/src/fields/waves.ts`). Written from:

- The SWAN Scientific and Technical Documentation (swanmodel.sourceforge.io/online_doc/swantech, read 2026-11-25, nodes 11,
  12, 14 to 19, 43, 47 and 48), which states the third-generation source terms of WAM (WAMDI Group 1988) and SWAN (Booij,
  Ris and Holthuijsen 1999): the energy and action balance (eqs. 2.17 and 2.19) and dispersion; wind input (eqs. 2.33 to
  2.38: Cavaleri and Malanotte-Rizzoli 1981 with Tolman's filter, Komen et al. 1984, the drag fit of eq. 2.36); whitecapping
  (eqs. 2.44 to 2.49, Komen et al. with delta = 1, SWAN's default since 40.91A); the discrete interaction approximation
  (Hasselmann et al. 1985, eqs. 2.76 to 2.80); JONSWAP bottom friction (eq. 2.60); Battjes and Janssen breaking (eqs. 2.65
  to 2.69); the action limiter of Hersbach and Janssen (eq. 3.42). The linear-growth filter's exponent, clipped in the page,
  is read as exp(-(sigma / sigma*_PM)^-4) from the fragment that shows.
- The JONSWAP relations (Hasselmann et al. 1973): alpha = 0.076 chi^-0.22 and omega_p = 22 (g / U) chi^(-1/3), as restated
  in arXiv:2606.28165 and arXiv:2608.27105 (search abstracts read), with gamma = 3.3 and sigma = 0.07 and 0.09; the energy
  growth g^2 E / U^4 = 1.6e-7 chi the tests compare against is the same paper's, known through these.
- The Pierson-Moskowitz fully developed sea, H_s = 0.21 U^2 / g and f_p = 0.13 g / U (in the wind at 19.5 m; 0.241 in U10, see the ST4 record below for the bound the tests now use), and the dispersion
  relation sigma^2 = g k tanh(k d): textbook results.

First-order upwind fluxes in space in substeps of half a cell, refraction in direction from the depth's gradient, the
quadruplets' partners spread over their four neighbouring bins so action and energy are both kept, the semi-implicit
source step (decay implicit, growth and transfer explicit), the breaking fraction by bisection, periodic edges, the
JONSWAP builder's cos^2 spread, and the arctangent from arithmetic are this package's own arrangement. Proof:
`packages/physics/tests/waves.test.js` and `tests/coupling/waves.test.js`.

#### ST4 physics, third-order propagation and the calibration of the sheltering (KB-SEA-GROWTH1, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/waves/st4.ts` (the default `physics: 'st4'`) and the propagation of `spectral.ts`. Written from:

- The WAVEWATCH III user manual, version 5.16 (The WAVEWATCH III Development Group, NOAA/NWS/NCEP/MMAB Technical Note 329,
  2016), read 2026-11-25 as public documentation (the model's code was not read): section 2.3.9, eqs. 2.99 to 2.105 (Janssen's
  input with the wave-supported stress and its f^-5 tail), section 2.3.10, eqs. 2.110 to 2.124 (sheltering, swell
  dissipation, saturation and cumulative breaking), tables 2.6 and 2.7 (the TEST405, TEST451 and TEST471 constants), and
  section 3.4, eqs. 3.12 to 3.23 (the ULTIMATE QUICKEST scheme of Leonard 1979 and 1991, known through it).
- F. Ardhuin, W. E. Rogers, A. V. Babanin, J.-F. Filipot, R. Magne, A. Roland, A. van der Westhuysen, P. Queffeulou, J.-M.
  Lefevre, L. Aouf and F. Collard, "Semi-empirical dissipation source functions for ocean waves. Part I: definition,
  calibration and validation", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 40, 1917-1941, 2010 (arXiv:0907.4240), read in part (eqs. 8 to 25 and the
  parameter discussion): the cross-check of every term above, and the sign of C_cu.
- P. A. E. M. Janssen, "Quasi-linear theory of wind-wave generation applied to wave forecasting", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 21,
  1991, and O. S. Madsen, Y.-K. Poon and H. C. Graber, "Spectral wave attenuation by bottom friction: theory", Proc. 21st
  ICCE, 1988: known through the manual and the SWAN documentation (eq. 2.63) respectively.
- The growth data: H. K. Kahma and C. J. Calkoen, "Reconciling discrepancies in the observed growth of wind-generated
  waves", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 22, 1992, through the composite fetch law g^2 E / U^4 = 5.2e-7 chi^0.9 and omega_p U / g =
  13.7 chi^-0.27 as P. A. Hwang, "Duration- and fetch-limited growth functions of wind-generated waves parameterized with
  three different scaling wind velocities", J. Geophys. Res. 111, C02005, 2006, tabulates it; JONSWAP and Pierson-Moskowitz
  as in the SEA-01 record above.

Published constants, taken as they stand (TEST471): alpha_0 0.0095, beta_max 1.43, z_alpha 0.006, kappa 0.4, the wind
height 10 m, z0_max 1.002, s1 0.66, s2 -0.018, s3 0.022, Re_c 1.5e5 (times 4 / H_s), s5 1.2, s7 3.6e5, r_z 0.04, C_ds -2.2e-5,
B_r 0.0009, the +-80 degree saturation sector, delta_d 0.3, C_cu -0.40344, r_cu 0.5, the cutoff 2.5 f_m and the quadruplets'
C_nl4 2.5e7. One constant was calibrated:

- **The sheltering s_u.** The manual gives 0.3 for TEST471 and 1 for TEST471 before March 2012 and for TEST500 (table 2.6 and
  its caption). Data fitted: Kahma and Calkoen's stable fetch law in friction-velocity scaling, e* = g^2 E / u*^4 = 2.1e-3
  chi*^0.79, chi* = g x / u*^2, valid for chi* 3e4 to 4e6, as Liu et al. (2019) restate it from Komen et al. (1994) and use it
  to test ST4 (their figure 2: ST4 with the DIA within 4 percent rms in e*). U10 = 10 and 20 m/s, every cell past the first
  five (their protocol) inside the valid range, on 192 cells over chi = g x / U^2 of 0 to 12,000. Method: compare the
  published values 0.3 and 1, minimising the rms of ln(e* / law). Result: 1 fits best, rms 0.108 (10 m/s) and 0.046 (20
  m/s), against 0.125 and 0.099 at 0.3, whose drag is also higher (C_D 2.53e-3 against 2.25e-3 at 20 m/s). z0_max 0.002
  against 1.002 changed nothing to three figures. Both values lie in the published range; above 1 was not tried.
- **The first calibration (2026-11-25) was on an unresolved grid.** It fitted s_u on Kahma and Calkoen's composite in U10
  scaling on 48 cells over chi 0 to 12,000 and found a fetch law flatter than measured, chi^0.66 (KB-SEA-GROWTH1). The cause
  was the grid, not the physics. The slope was the same, 0.62 to 0.66, for every source-term change tried: swell
  dissipation off; cumulative breaking off; C_nl4 3e7; B_r 0.0008; TEST471 as published. It was also the same with a 30 s
  source step, 48 frequencies, 36 directions or a 48 h warm-up. It steepened with the cells alone: 0.63 at 48, 0.69 at 96,
  0.74 at 192 (0.80 in friction-velocity scaling against the law's 0.79). Liu et al. (2019) and Tolman and Chalikov (1996)
  nest three grids for this reason and drop the first five points. The drag hardly changes along the fetch (C_D 1.52e-3 to
  1.49e-3 at 10 m/s), so a sea-state-dependent drag does not cause the slope.
- **Validation, on data not fitted:**
  - At 30 m/s on the resolved grid: rms 0.038 and a slope of 0.76 in friction-velocity scaling.
  - In U10 scaling at 10 m/s: the height within 14 percent of Hwang's fetch law, e = 6.19e-7 chi^0.81 (Hwang and Fan 2017,
    restating Hwang 2006), and of JONSWAP's, e = 1.6e-7 chi, over chi 1,000 to 10,000. Kahma and Calkoen's composite,
    5.2e-7 chi^0.9, is the highest of the published laws at long fetch (Hwang's, Young and Verhagen's deep-water law and
    JONSWAP's lie 23 to 48 percent below it at chi 1e4).
  - Full development, unlimited fetch, run to g t / U10 = 2.5e5 (KB-SEA-FULLDEV1): 0.221, 0.281 and 0.355 U10^2 / g at
    10, 20 and 30 m/s against J. H. G. M. Alves, M. L. Banner and I. R. Young, "Revisiting the Pierson-Moskowitz asymptotic
    limits for fully developed wind waves", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 33, 1301-1323, 2003, https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(2003)033<1301:RTPALF>2.0.CO;2,
    read in full: e = (4.02 +- 0.62) 1e-3, H_s = 0.254 U10^2 / g, f_p = 0.123 g / U10, no trend with wind over 9.5 to 21.6 m/s.
    Pierson and Moskowitz's 0.21 is in U19.5 (U19.5 = 1.077 U10, so 0.241 in U10); the old bound compared it with U10.
    The rise with wind (1.27 from 10 to 20 m/s against the data's 1.02) is ST4's u* scaling: pure u* scaling gives 1.30 to
    1.45, Rogers, Babanin and Wang (2012, J. Atmos. Oceanic Technol. 29, read) note the KHH family scales with u*, Ardhuin
    et al. (2010) that ST4 has no true full development, and Liu et al. (2019) that ST4 with the DIA reaches e* = 1.00e3
    (0.266 U10^2 / g) at 20 m/s. The roughness cap (0.0015, 0.002 or none) moves the 30 m/s sea by under 2 percent.
  - A 300 s source step lowers the short-fetch end: the action limiter, a fixed amount of action a step, then shapes the
    growth. ST4 was tuned at steps where it rarely acts.
- Sources for this record, read 2026-11-26 (papers and public documentation, no code):
  - Q. Liu, W. E. Rogers, A. V. Babanin, I. R. Young, L. Romero, S. Zieger, F. Qiao and C. Guan, "Observation-based source
    terms in the third-generation wave model WAVEWATCH III: updates and verification", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 49, 489-517,
    2019, https://doi.org/10.1175/JPO-D-18-0137.1, section 3a and figure 2.
  - P. A. Hwang and Y. Fan, "Low-frequency mean square slopes and dominant wave spectral properties: toward tropical
    cyclone remote sensing", J. Phys. Oceanogr. 47, 2017, eqs. 1 and 2, restating Hwang (2006).
  - I. R. Young and L. A. Verhagen, "Fetch limited spectral evolution in finite depth water", Proc. 25th ICCE, 1996.
  - V. E. Zakharov, S. I. Badulin, P. A. Hwang and G. Caulliez, "Universality of sea wave growth and its physical roots",
    J. Fluid Mech. 780, 2015, arXiv:1411.7235: the spread of measured fetch exponents, 0.7 to 1.1.
  - Tolman and Chalikov (1996) known through Liu et al.; Komen et al. (1994) through Liu et al.; Kahma and Calkoen (1992)
    through both.

The mean frequency from the action's p = 0.5 moment for the cutoff, the Madsen friction factor solved by bisection with
its 0.3 cap below a_b / K_N = 1.57, the precomputed per-cell tables of the saturation's cos^2 sector and of the cumulative
term's weights, the friction velocity iterated to 1e-7 on U10 = (u* / kappa) ln(z_u / z_1), the face value taken at the
upstream two cells and the downstream one with first order beside land, an open edge or a short stencil, and the axis order
alternating per substep are this package's own arrangement. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/waves.test.js`, "a gale of 20 m/s grows the sea along its fetch as Kahma and Calkoen
measured, in friction-velocity scaling (KB-SEA-GROWTH1)", the friction-velocity test, and the 10 m/s JONSWAP test with
both physics.

### Flight: wings, rotors and lifting gas (AERO-03, `WingForce`, `RotorForce` and `LiftingGas` in `@margoengine/physics/flight`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/flight.ts`, on the vortex-lattice core `packages/physics/src/lattice.ts` that `SailForce` (AERO-02)
now shares. Written from:

- Maximilian Ranneberg, *Direct Wing Design and Inverse Airfoil Identification with the Nonlinear Weissinger Method* (2015), §2.1 gives the finite segment in equation 2 and the semi-infinite limit in the following derivation used by the lattice. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.04983).
- Y. Su, Fan, Onoue, Vejdani and Breuer, "An improved aerodynamic model for quasi-steady simulations of animal flight at
  moderate Reynolds numbers", arXiv:2302.09602, read in full: the flat wing's lift and drag coefficients (eqs. 10 and 11)
  and the blade-element forces at the quarter chord (eqs. 3 and 4). Dickinson, Lehmann and Sane (1999) are known through it.
- The Wikipedia article "Blade element momentum theory", read 2026-11-25: the actuator disk's thrust and wake, and the blade
  element's forces in the inflow angle.
- The Wikipedia article "Lifting-line theory", read 2026-11-25: the elliptic wing's induced drag C_L^2 / (pi AR), the bound
  the tests hold the lattice to, and the finite wing's lift slope.
- Helmbold's lift slope 2 pi AR / (2 + sqrt(AR^2 + 4)), as the AERO-02 tests already use it.
- S. F. Hoerner's flat-plate normal force and skin friction (through Katz and Plotkin, as AERO-01 records), here as the
  separated law of a fixed wing and the profile drag 2 x 0.004.

The flapping wing's own velocity by a central difference of its shape, the mirrored pair as one lattice, the momentum
term written with the mass flow's magnitude so one bisection finds each annulus's induced velocity in hover, climb and
descent, the arctangent from arithmetic (`angleOf`), the load held as a force through the step, and the linearly implicit
load (a finite-difference Jacobian of the force and torque in the body's velocity and spin, then the backward Euler step of
the load and gravity) are this package's own arrangement. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/flight.test.js`.

The separated-wing equations of Yunxing Su, Xiaozhou Fan, Kyohei Onoue, Hamid Vejdani and Kenneth Breuer (2026)
give the complete quasi-steady drag coefficient. Profile drag was previously added again after the separated law.
The stalled panel now takes its separated load and carries zero attached-flow horseshoe circulation. Attached panels
retain the vortex-lattice force and profile drag over their own area. The distinction between attached circulation
and empirical separated section loads follows Thomas Ozoroski's discussion of viscous corrections to the linear
lattice (2015). The existing abrupt stall remains a reduced model. The analytic 25° plate and mixed-flow tests
check the two force paths. The original light flapping-wing regression checks stable integration.
[Su et al.](https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.70142) [Ozoroski, NASA/CR–2015–218969](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20160000765)

#### Body-centered loads and native wing lattice (AERO-03 four-point pass)

Ludwig Prandtl, *Applications of Modern Hydrodynamics to Aeronautics*, NACA TR-116, §§11–14, sets out
the bound and trailing vortex account. Ranneberg’s finite segment and semi-infinite leg formulas are
evaluated two target rows at a time. Each target still sums sources in the original order. The caller
runs partial-pivot elimination in the original index order. SIMD updates disjoint columns of a row.
Rust runs on private optional Wasm scratch. Workers join before accepted wing diagnostics and rigid forces
are published. Torque arms and lattice geometry are formed about the local centre of mass, then only the
wind query is relocated between signed cells. [Prandtl, NACA TR-116](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19930091180).

F. X. Caradonna and C. Tung, *Experimental and Analytical Studies of a Model Helicopter Rotor in Hover* (1981),
§2 and figures 1 and 3–6 supply geometry, operating inputs and independent integrated thrust coefficients.
The runtime diagnostic holds out the thrust results and reports the overprediction and the anomalous literal
figure value separately. The existing axial annulus balance is the combined momentum and blade-element form
described in the rotor theory literature. It omits tip-vortex and compressible effects. [Caradonna and Tung, NASA TM-81232](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19820004169), [NASA combined momentum and blade-element analysis](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19900004033/downloads/19900004033.pdf).

Jia-chi Wu and Zoran Popović, *Realistic Modeling of Bird Flight Animations* (2003), uses forces and joint
motion to produce flight from authored wingbeats. Michael H. Dickinson, Fritz-Olaf Lehmann and Sanjay P. Sane,
*Wing Rotation and the Aerodynamic Basis of Insect Flight* (1999), separates translational and rotational effects.
Colin J. Pennycuick, *Modelling the Flying Bird* (2008), separates gliding performance from powered flight.
The Aviary cutaway compares a held wing with one downstroke using the existing quasi-steady law. It does not
claim unsteady motion or measured insect-force agreement. [Wu and Popović](https://doi.org/10.1145/1201775.882360),
[Dickinson, Lehmann and Sane](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/k0ywt-79d59), [Pennycuick](https://shop.elsevier.com/books/modelling-the-flying-bird/pennycuick/978-0-12-374299-5).

#### The air's loads in a world (`AirSolver` of `@margoengine/physics/flight`, `air-hold.ts`, 2026-11-25)

No outside source: the framework's own `bodyForces` contract (docs/physics-framework.md, section 4) and the rigid solver's
rule of taking off exactly what the f32 columns took, which the soft solver's fix KB-SOFT-FORCERESIDUE1 set down. One hold per
Physics sums every air load on a body in f64 in the order the loads were made, adds the sum to the columns once (as the rigid
solver adds a summed port) and takes the columns' difference off after the step; in a world the `AirSolver` writes the same
sums into `bodyForces` and gives the loads the world's tick as their clock. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/world-air-solver.test.js`
and `tests/coupling/air.test.js`.

### Sails and flags, a vortex lattice on the cloth (AERO-02, `SailForce` in `@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/sail.ts` solves a vortex lattice on a cloth's grid every step. Written from M. Klein and others, "Direct
Wing Design and Inverse Airfoil Identification with the Nonlinear Weissinger Method", arXiv:1501.04983, 2015, read in full
(the horseshoe path: bound on the quarter chord, legs along the chord, then downstream; Biot-Savart's closed form for a
straight segment and its limit for a leg to infinity, eqs. 1-4; Kutta-Joukowski), and the article "Vortex lattice method"
in Wikipedia, read 2026-11-25 (collocation at three-quarter chord, the influence matrix, the flow-tangency condition and the
force per horseshoe, after J. Katz and A. Plotkin, "Low-Speed Aerodynamics", 2001, not read here). The check against H. B.
Helmbold's low-aspect-ratio lift slope, 2 pi AR / (2 + sqrt(AR^2 + 4)) (1942, known through the textbooks), is the test's.
Stalled cells take the flat-plate law of AERO-01. The cloth grid as lattice, the mean apparent wind as wake direction, the
segment core and the fixed-order elimination are this package's own. The load leans on the cloth's own speed through the air, so each corner takes it damped implicitly, F dt / (1 + K dt) (backward Euler on that aerodynamic damping, K the slope of its panels' loads against their normal speed over its mass: the lattice's own, from the diagonal of the inverse of its influence matrix, or the flat plate's); given explicitly, a sail of real sailcloth weight flew apart within ten steps. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/sail.test.js`.

## Reflection cone: rough planar and screen-space reflections with contact hardening (2026-11-25)

Gap row "Blurred / rough planar and screen-space reflections" (docs/rival-parity-gaps.md). Code: packages/shared/reflection-cone.js (CPU and WGSL), used by environment's Reflector, Refractor and PBRReflector (`contactHardening`), water's WaterReflection (`contactHardening`) and post's SSR composite.

Research, read for this job: Brian Karis, *Real Shading in Unreal Engine 4*, SIGGRAPH 2013 course notes, https://cdn2.unrealengine.com/Resources/files/2013SiggraphPresentationsNotes-26915738.pdf (GGX with Disney's alpha = roughness^2); Bruce Walter, Stephen R. Marschner, Hongsong Li and Kenneth E. Torrance, *Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces*, EGSR 2007, https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~srm/publications/EGSR07-btdf.pdf (Phong exponent alpha_p = 2 alpha_b^-2 - 2 makes Phong and Beckmann close; GGX alpha is used as the Beckmann width, an approximation). From the published descriptions, not re-read in full: Yasin Uludag, *Hi-Z Screen-Space Cone-Traced Reflections*, in W. Engel (ed.), GPU Pro 5, CRC Press, 2014, https://www.routledge.com/product/isbn/9781482208634 (the reflected lobe as a cone whose footprint picks a mip of a blurred colour chain; the chapter's own energy constant was not used); Tomasz Stachowiak and Yasin Uludag, *Stochastic Screen-Space Reflections*, SIGGRAPH 2015 Advances in Real-Time Rendering, https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/stochastic-screenspace-reflections/51840375 (importance-sampled rough SSR; Margo's `stochastic` path already takes the sampled form, P-39); Morgan McGuire and Michael Mara, *Efficient GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing*, JCGT 3(4), 2014, https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/ (the march, unchanged, P-16). Public rival docs compared: drei's MeshReflectorMaterial (https://drei.docs.pmnd.rs/shaders/mesh-reflector-material, depth-driven blur). No rival or companion source was read.

Derivation (Margo's): the share of a cos^n lobe inside angle t is 1 - cos^(n+1) t, so the half-vector cone holding 3/4 of it has cos^(n+1) t = 1/4; the mirror ray turns by twice the normal's turn, so the reflected cone is 2t, capped at 1.4 rad. With x = 2 ln(1/4) alpha^2 / (2 - alpha^2) = ln cos^2 t, tan t = sqrt(-expm1(x) / e^x), with -expm1 by its series for |x| < 0.01 in WGSL so smooth surfaces keep a cone. At distance s along the ray the cone covers a disc of diameter 2 s tan(2t); the level read is log2 of that diameter in level-0 texels, clamped to the chain. The 3/4 share, the 2x and the cap are Margo's choices. Planar distance: the capture's view ray through the surface point continues past the plane as the reflected (or, for Refractor, transmitted) ray, so s solves depth(p + s d) = captured depth with d from the cross product of the capture matrix's x and y clip planes through p (any projection, the oblique near plane included). The depth is the nearest of the 2x2 texels a bilinear lookup reads, so a silhouette's level follows the object and does not flip with rounding (found on the WebGL2 layer, where nearest-texel picks differed from WebGPU's by a few pixels per row). Texels per world unit: row 1 of the matrix times half the image height over the hit's clip w. SSR: the same level from distance(p, hit) at the hit's clip w, which replaced log2(screen length x roughness^2 x 2). Water: the cone's roughness is (2 variance)^(1/4) from the in-pixel normal variance (alpha^2 = 2 sigma^2, after Toksvig, *Mipmapping Normal Maps*, JGT 10(3), 2005, already cited by water), at least the `roughness` option.

Proofs: packages/environment/tests/reflection-cone.test.js (CPU, against the closed form), packages/environment/tests/contact-hardening-browser.mjs, packages/water/test/reflector-cone.browser.mjs, packages/post/test/ssr-cone-browser.mjs (real frames, WebGPU and the WebGL2 compatibility layer; the SSR one fails on the old on-screen-length level).

### KB5339e: Cycles' noise by baking, not by reimplementing its hash (2026-11-25)

Problem: the live Noise node shows another stochastic pattern than Cycles for the same settings. A procedural noise is fixed by its lattice hash and gradient set (K. Perlin, An image synthesizer, SIGGRAPH 1985, https://doi.org/10.1145/325334.325247; K. Perlin, Improving noise, SIGGRAPH 2002, https://doi.org/10.1145/566654.566636; survey: A. Lagae et al., A Survey of Procedural Noise Functions, Computer Graphics Forum 29(8), 2010, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2010.01827.x). Hashes of this kind are designed so that their outputs look unrelated (M. Jarzynski and M. Olano, Hash Functions for GPU Rendering, Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques 9(3), 2020, https://jcgt.org/published/0009/03/02/), so this one is not fitted from samples, and Blender's source is not read. Coordinator's ruling: record the accepted difference and offer Cycles' own result as texels.

Method: the add-on's existing Cycles bake through Blender's documented Python API (`bpy.ops.object.bake`, https://docs.blender.org/api/current/bpy.ops.object.html#bpy.ops.object.bake). `bake_noise` selects the materials with a Noise Texture on a path to the active output, node groups included. Result: 0 differing texels from an independent Cycles emission bake. Regression: `tools/blender-addon/tests/blender_bake_noise.py`, run by `npm run modern:test:blender`.
### Cloth as measured fabric, solved exactly (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-25, KB-SOFT-LOOPSTRETCH1)

`packages/physics/soft-kernel/src/rigid.rs` holds a woven sheet's threads, the links to bodies and the contacts with bodies
in one solve. Each Newton step solves for the rows' multipliers with MPRGP on the Jacobi-scaled system (Z. Dostal and J.
Schoberl, "Minimizing quadratic functions subject to bound constraints with the rate of convergence and finite
termination", Comput. Optim. Appl. 30, 2005: the proportioning test, the expansion step of length 1 / ||A||, here the
Gershgorin bound). The step then goes as far as an Armijo line search on the sum of squared violations allows (J. Nocedal
and S. J. Wright, *Numerical Optimization*, 2nd ed., 2006, section 3.1), until every row is within its tolerance. That
tolerance is 0.1 percent strain for a sheet's threads (R. Goldenthal, D. Harmon, R. Fattal, M. Bercovier and E. Grinspun,
"Efficient simulation of inextensible cloth", SIGGRAPH 2007, Algorithm 1 and figures 4-5).

- **Bodies.** Bodies are six-degree-of-freedom unknowns with their world inverse inertia (T. Shinar, C. Schroeder and R.
  Fedkiw, "Two-way coupling of rigid and deformable bodies", SCA 2008).
- **Compliant threads.** A thread is a compliant row, with alpha-tilde = 1 / (k h^2) (M. Macklin, M. Mueller and N.
  Chentanez, "XPBD", MIG 2016). Past its measured strain it is held rigid (X. Provot, "Deformation constraints in a
  mass-spring model to describe rigid cloth behavior", Graphics Interface 1995).
- **Redundant rows.** A row a body's rigidity already holds is left out (J. Tournier, M. Nesme, B. Gilles and F. Faure,
  "Stable constrained dynamics", SIGGRAPH 2015, section 2).
- **Friction.** Friction is its own box-bounded solve after the normal one (D. M. Kaufman, S. Sueda, D. L. James and D. K.
  Pai, "Staggered projections for frictional contact in multibody systems", SIGGRAPH Asia 2008).
- **Row damping.** A row with no compliance of its own is damped by a share of its own diagonal: K. Levenberg, Q. Appl.
  Math. 2(2), 1944; D. W. Marquardt, J. SIAM 11(2), 1963, damping scaled by the diagonal.
  - A contact's row keeps sqrt(f32 epsilon), a regularized contact (C. Lacoursiere, "Ghosts and machines", PhD thesis,
    Umea 2007, chapter 5), because two contacts that ask for what no motion gives keep asking. The size is the one the rigid
    kernel's block solve uses, with the same reasoning (N. J. Higham, *Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms*,
    2002, section 10.3).
  - An edge's or a link's damping is the worst violation squared, up to that, so it fades as the rows close (N. Yamashita
    and M. Fukushima, Computing Suppl. 15, 2001; J. Fan and Y. Yuan, Computing 74, 2005: Levenberg-Marquardt with a damping
    of the residual squared keeps quadratic convergence without a nonsingular Jacobian). A fixed damping left every
    piece's last step a tolerance short, and a slack-only rope drifted on the speed that gave.
  - Without the damping, redundant rows left the system singular: a flat triangle mesh's rigid edges hold its interior
    twice over in its plane, and a light box is pinched between two sides. The multipliers ran off along the motion that
    cancels itself, and rounding of the f32 directions turned them into large motions: a kicked mesh flew apart in five
    steps, and a 1 g box was thrown off a sheet at 10 m/s.
  - On a system with one answer, a damped step lands on the same bits as an undamped one, and over many steps the two
    differ no more than a one-ulp nudge of one coordinate makes them differ (`soft-kernel/tests/threads.rs`).
- **MPRGP with two bounds.** A row with no room between its bounds is never freed, and the proportioning step stops at
  each freed row's far bound, as the conjugate gradient step does (Dostal and Schoberl 2005 state the method for bounds on
  one side). A friction row of a contact with no push, bounded at zero both ways, was otherwise freed and spun the body it
  touched.

The fabric data are from E. Luible's thesis, *Study of mechanical properties in the simulation of 3D garments*, Universite
de Geneve, 2008, doi 10.13097/archive-ouverte/unige:688, Annex C, the KES-F tables. The presets use samples 2 (shirt
cotton, 120 g/m^2), 5 (wool gabardine), 8 (silk), 10 (jute plain weave, for canvas) and 29 (polyester plain weave, for
sailcloth). The conversions are this package's own:

- **Shear stiffness.** G in gf/cm/degree times 56.187 gives N/m per radian. A diagonal of length L across a cell of sides a
  and b gets G L^2 / (2 a b).
- **Tensile stiffness.** The linear spring that stores the measured tensile energy WT up to the strain EMT, 2 WT / EMT^2,
  times 0.980665 for N/m.
- **Damping from hysteresis.** Shear damping is 2HG / (pi G 0.5 degrees), and thread damping is (1 - RT) / (4 pi). Both use
  L. S. Jacobsen's equivalent viscous damping ("Steady forced vibration as influenced by damping", Trans. ASME 52, 1930),
  known through the vibration textbooks and not read here.

Spread across sources, recorded in the README and in `docs/limits.md`:

- **Cotton broadcloth.** Seo and Tamura (Sen'i Seihin Shohi Kagaku 58(8), 2017, doi 10.11419/senshoshi.58.8_686) measured
  G = 3.50/3.57, against Luible's shirting at 0.367/0.321: ten times apart.
- **Wool gabardine.** G = 2.93/2.67 there, against Luible's 0.588/0.545.
- **Silk habutae.** Miura, Tsukada and Sakaguchi (J. Silk Sci. Tech. Jpn 18, 2010, doi 10.11417/silk.18.45) measured
  G = 0.51, and Nakajima and Miura (JARQ 47(2), 2013, doi 10.6090/jarq.47.175) G = 0.11.
- **Canvas and sailcloth.** No published KES-F table of either was found, so those presets are the nearest measured
  fabrics and say so.

The air on a cloth's faces is a flat plate's drag, coefficient 1.17 (S. F. Hoerner, *Fluid-Dynamic Drag*, 1965, chapter
3, the value `WindForce` uses). Each face's drag is integrated in closed form over the step, u / (1 + k |u| dt), so a
light face in a strong wind cannot overshoot. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/soft.test.js` (the sag of a cotton strip
against an elastic cable's, d = L (3 rho_A g L / (64 K))^(1/3); the inextensible sheet at 0.1 percent; ATTACHKICK1; the
two drape cases) and `soft-kernel/tests/threads.rs`.

### Mesh instance motion blur in the path tracer (FG-17 piece 4a, 2026-11-25)

`packages/voxel-pathtracer/src/mesh-instances.ts`, `mesh-shader.ts`, `motion.ts` and `mesh-kernel/src/lib.rs`. A
moving triangle instance is seen by each path at the path's own time in the shutter, the time-averaged picture of
distributed ray tracing (Robert L. Cook, Thomas Porter and Loren Carpenter, "Distributed Ray Tracing", SIGGRAPH 1984,
https://doi.org/10.1145/964965.808590). Its TLAS leaf holds the box swept over the whole interval, the one-box-per-node
form of a motion BVH (Sven Woop, Attila T. Afra and Carsten Benthin, "STBVH: A Spatial-Temporal BVH for Efficient
Multi-Segment Motion Blur", HPG 2017, https://doi.org/10.1145/3105762.3105779, section 2 on bounding a linear motion
by the union of its key-frame boxes; the per-node two-box form of their paper is for piece 4b). The rotation blend is the
existing voxel 'trs' path (shortest-arc slerp, Ken Shoemake, "Animating Rotation with Quaternion Curves", SIGGRAPH 1985,
https://doi.org/10.1145/325165.325242). Written from these papers; no renderer's code was read.

### Moving and deforming mesh emitters in the path tracer (FG-17-EMITTERS, 2026-11-26)

`packages/voxel-pathtracer/mesh-kernel/src/lib.rs` (`light_packet`) and `src/mesh-light-shader.ts`. Emissive triangles
on a moving or deforming mesh are sampled by next-event estimation at the path's own time, the one time per path of
distributed ray tracing (Robert L. Cook, Thomas Porter and Loren Carpenter, "Distributed Ray Tracing", SIGGRAPH 1984,
https://doi.org/10.1145/964965.808590), so the light point, its occluders and its shadow ray share one instant. The
pick is by world area times power and the point uniform on the triangle by the square-root barycentric map, with the
area-measure pdf turned into solid angle at the shading point (Peter Shirley, Changyaw Wang and Kurt Zimmerman, "Monte
Carlo Techniques for Direct Lighting Calculations", ACM TOG 15(1), 1996, https://doi.org/10.1145/226150.226151). The
area at the path's time comes from the cofactor identity for a transformed cross product, so no second inverse is
built. Light samples and path hits are combined by the power heuristic with one pdf formula on both sides (Eric Veach
and Leonidas J. Guibas, "Optimally Combining Sampling Techniques for Monte Carlo Rendering", SIGGRAPH 1995,
https://doi.org/10.1145/218380.218498; Eric Veach, "Robust Monte Carlo Methods for Light Transport Simulation", PhD
thesis, Stanford, 1997, https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/veach_thesis/). The moving point's shadow ray stops short
by a bound scaled to its coordinates (Carsten Wachter and Nikolaus Binder, "A Fast and Robust Method for Avoiding
Self-Intersection", Ray Tracing Gems, 2019, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4842-4427-2_6). The GPU test's oracle is
Lambert's polygon irradiance formula as given by Daniel R. Baum, Holly E. Rushmeier and James M. Winget, "Improving
Radiosity Solutions Through the Use of Analytically Determined Form-Factors", SIGGRAPH 1989,
https://doi.org/10.1145/74333.74367. Read and set aside: a light tree with swept bounds and cones (Alejandro Conty
Estevez and Christopher Kulla, "Importance Sampling of Many Lights with Adaptive Tree Splitting", HPG 2018,
https://doi.org/10.1145/3233305; Pierre Moreau, Matt Pharr and Petrik Clarberg, "Dynamic Many-Light Sampling for
Real-Time Ray Tracing", HPG 2019, https://doi.org/10.2312/hpg.20191191) and spherical-triangle sampling (James Arvo,
"Stratified Sampling of Spherical Triangles", SIGGRAPH 1995, https://doi.org/10.1145/218380.218500): each would change
the still path's samples. Written from these papers; no renderer's code was read.
### A hull on the sea: wetted-surface loads (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-25)
