`packages/physics/src/seakeeping/wetted.ts` integrates the water's pressure over the part of a hull mesh under the sea's
surface. It was written from these, read for this job (a research summary, papers only, no code):

- J. Kerner, "Water interaction model for boats in video games", Game Developer, 2015 (parts 1 and 2, text only): cut each
  triangle by its vertices' heights over the surface, one wet corner leaving a triangle and two a quadrilateral in two.
- G. Giorgi, S. Sirigu, M. Bonfanti, G. Bracco and G. Mattiazzo, "Fast nonlinear Froude-Krylov force calculation for
  prismatic floating platforms", J. Ocean Eng. Mar. Energy, 2021, doi 10.1007/s40722-021-00212-z (introduction and
  formulation): the nonlinear Froude-Krylov load as the incident pressure over the instantaneous wetted surface, with
  Wheeler stretching as the cheap choice that leaves the pressure 0 at the surface.
- D. A. Dunavant, "High degree efficient symmetrical Gaussian quadrature rules for the triangle", IJNME 21(6), 1985, doi
  10.1002/nme.1620210612 (the published degree-four six-point rule).
- J. M. J. Journee and W. W. Massie, *Offshore Hydromechanics*, TU Delft, 2001, chapters 6 to 8: the heave natural period
  2 pi sqrt((m + a) / (rho g A_wp)) the coupling test checks (without the added mass a, which is not built yet).

The secant refinement of each cut (two fixed steps), the moment about the centre of mass, and the framework solver
(`HullSolver`, through `bodyForces`) are this package's own. The wall-sided righting arm,
GZ = sin(phi) (GM + BM tan^2(phi) / 2), is the textbook stability result. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/seakeeping.test.js`
(a box's buoyancy to f64 rounding, the righting arm to 1e-9, the linear Froude-Krylov heave load of a box in a small wave)
and `tests/coupling/seakeeping.test.js`. The research summary is kept with the solver's notes, and covers what comes next
(Cummins radiation in state-space form from strip-theory coefficients, diffraction, drift, green water).

### GPU scene tree for real-time ray tracing (FG-17 piece 6a, 2026-11-25)

`packages/bvh/src/gpu-scene.ts` and `src/gpu-pack.ts`. Two-level hierarchy, a top tree over placed bottom trees with
rays moved into each instance's space (Ingo Wald, Carsten Benthin and Philipp Slusallek, "Distributed Interactive Ray
Tracing of Dynamic Scenes", IEEE PVG 2003, https://doi.org/10.1109/PVGS.2003.1249040). Top build by binned SAH with
16 bins on centroids (Ingo Wald, "On fast Construction of SAH-based Bounding Volume Hierarchies", IEEE RT 2007,
https://doi.org/10.1109/RT.2007.4342588). Refit with a rebuild once the SAH cost passes a ratio of the built cost, as
the CPU SceneBVH does. The ray/triangle test is the watertight one already cited for `bvh/gpu` (Woop, Benthin and Wald,
JCGT 2013, https://jcgt.org/published/0002/01/05/), fed object-space rays with unnormalized directions so distances stay
world lengths. Compared and not used yet: stackless traversal by parent pointers (Michal Hapala, Tomas Davidovic, Ingo
Wald, Vlastimil Havran and Philipp Slusallek, "Efficient Stack-less BVH Traversal for Ray Tracing", SCCG 2011,
https://dcgi.fel.cvut.cz/~havran/ARTICLES/sccg2011.pdf) and constant-time backtracking (Nikolaus Binder and Alexander
Keller, "Efficient Stackless Hierarchy Traversal on GPUs with Backtracking in Constant Time", HPG 2016,
https://research.nvidia.com/publication/2016-06_efficient-stackless-hierarchy-traversal-gpus-backtracking-constant-time),
kept for the compatibility layer if its stack walk proves slow. Written from these papers; no engine's code was read.

### Ray-traced reflections behind screen-space reflections (FG-17 piece 6b, 2026-11-25)

`packages/post/src/rt-reflections.ts` and the `traced` hook in `src/ssr.ts`. Hybrid order, screen-space march first and
a ray through the scene where it fails (Colin Barre-Brisebois, Henrik Halen, Graham Wihlidal, Andrew Lauritzen, Jasper
Bekkers, Tomasz Stachowiak and Johan Andersson, "Hybrid Rendering for Real-Time Ray Tracing", Ray Tracing Gems ch. 25,
2019, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4842-4427-2_25; Tomasz Stachowiak, "Stochastic Screen-Space Reflections", SIGGRAPH
2015 Advances in Real-Time Rendering course). The share split uses SSR's existing fades as the screen's coverage. Rough
rays keep SSR's VNDF sampling (Eric Heitz, "Sampling the GGX Distribution of Visible Normals", JCGT 7(4), 2018,
https://jcgt.org/published/0007/04/01/); compared and not used: spherical-cap VNDF sampling (Jonathan Dupuy and Anis
Benyoub, "Sampling Visible GGX Normals with Spherical Caps", CGF 2023, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14867), equal in
distribution, kept for a later speed pass. Hit shading is core's own glTF 2.0 Appendix B BRDF text; traversal is
`sceneBvhWGSL` of piece 6a. Written from these papers; no engine's code was read.

### Ray-traced bounce light behind screen-space GI (FG-17 piece 6c, 2026-11-25)

`packages/post/src/rt-gi.ts`, `src/rt-shade.ts` and the `traced` hook in `src/ssgi.ts`. The same hybrid order as piece
6b, screen first and the scene where the screen has no hit (Barre-Brisebois et al., "Hybrid Rendering for Real-Time Ray
Tracing", Ray Tracing Gems ch. 25, 2019, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4842-4427-2_25), applied to SSGI's
cosine-weighted rays (Matt Pharr, Wenzel Jakob and Greg Humphreys, "Physically Based Rendering", 3rd ed., 13.6.3,
2016). Compared and not used yet: reservoir reuse of bounce paths (Yaobin Ouyang, Shiqiu Liu, Markus Kettunen, Matt
Pharr and Jacopo Pantaleoni, "ReSTIR GI: Path Resampling for Real-Time Path Tracing", CGF 40(8), HPG 2021,
https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14378), and a variance-guided denoise (Christoph Schied, Anton Kaplanyan, Chris Wyman et
al., "Spatiotemporal Variance-Guided Filtering", HPG 2017, https://doi.org/10.1145/3105762.3105770), both left for a
later piece as SSGI's blur already filters the sum; probe volumes (Zander Majercik, Jean-Philippe Guertin, Derek
Nowrouzezahrai and Morgan McGuire, "Dynamic Diffuse Global Illumination with Ray-Traced Irradiance Fields", JCGT 8(2),
2019, https://jcgt.org/published/0008/02/01/) answer a different question (world-space caches) and are not part of
this piece. Hit shading is core's own BRDF text, shared with piece 6b. Written from these papers; no engine's code was
read.

### Traced effects on limited devices, and Hi-Z at the compatibility level (FG-17 piece 6d, 2026-11-26)

`packages/post/src/rt-shade.ts` (`TracedLight.active`) and `src/hiz.ts` (`createHiZ`, `encodeHiZ`), used by SSR, SSGI,
`RTReflections` and `RTGI`. Written from specifications: the WebGPU specification (W3C, https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/,
the `maxStorageBuffersInFragmentStage` limit and `featureLevel: 'compatibility'`), the WebGPU compatibility mode
proposal (GPU for the Web Community Group, https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/blob/main/proposals/compatibility-mode.md,
its default of 4 fragment-stage storage buffers and its rule of one view of a texture per draw or dispatch), and the
OpenGL ES 3.1 specification (Khronos, 2014, its minimum implementation limits: `MAX_FRAGMENT_SHADER_STORAGE_BLOCKS` 0,
https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.1/es_spec_3.1.pdf). The fallback order, the traced pass when the device
can bind the scene and the screen-space pass otherwise, is the hybrid order of Barre-Brisebois et al. (piece 6b). The
per-level Hi-Z textures keep the pyramid of Y. Uludag (GPU Pro 5, 2014) and M. McGuire and M. Mara (JCGT 3(4), 2014)
unchanged; only where each level is written moves. No engine's code was read.

### Deforming mesh motion blur in the path tracer (FG-17 piece 4b, 2026-11-25)

`packages/voxel-pathtracer/src/mesh-instances.ts`, `mesh-build.ts`, `mesh-shader.ts`, `sequence.ts` and
`mesh-kernel/src/lib.rs`. Each vertex of a deforming mesh moves on a straight line over the shutter and each path sees
the mesh at its own time (Cook, Porter and Carpenter 1984, as above). The BVH topology is built once over boxes holding
both shutter ends, and each node keeps a box at each end that a ray blends at its time: the linear blend of boxes
bounding each end's vertices bounds the blended vertices (Woop, Afra and Benthin, STBVH, HPG 2017, section 2, as above;
Leonhard Grunschloss, Martin Stich, Sehera Nawaz and Alexander Keller, "MSBVH: An Efficient Acceleration Data Structure
for Ray Traced Motion Blur", HPG 2011, https://doi.org/10.1145/2018323.2018334, on per-node key-frame boxes interpolated
at ray time). Both the boxes and the corners are blended by the same expression a(1 - t) + bt, which is monotone in
each input under rounding, so the blended box still holds the blended corners in float. The shared-edge predicate is the
existing watertight ray-triangle test (Sven Woop, Carsten Benthin and Ingo Wald, "Watertight Ray/Triangle
Intersection", JCGT 2013, https://jcgt.org/published/0002/01/05/), fed the blended corners, which neighbouring
triangles compute identically. Written from these papers; no renderer's code was read.
### A hull's added mass from its sections (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/seakeeping/strips.ts` cuts the hull into stations, maps each section under the waterline to its Lewis
form and integrates the sections' added mass at infinite frequency over the hull. Written from J. M. J. Journee and
W. W. Massie, *Offshore Hydromechanics*, TU Delft, 2001, Part 2:
- the Lewis form (eqs. 7.88-7.95), its range and the clamp of the area coefficient to it;
- the book's container section (B 25.40 m, D 9.00 m: M 12.2400, a1 0.1511, a3 -0.1136), which the test checks;
- the strip integrals of the zero-speed coefficients (eq. 8.25: A33, A35 and A55 from the sections' heave added mass, and
  sway and yaw in the same way).

The heave and sway coefficients at infinite frequency, (rho pi B^2/8)((1+a1)^2 + 3 a3^2)/(1+a1+a3)^2 and
(rho pi T^2/2)((1-a1)^2 + 3 a3^2)/(1-a1+a3)^2, are Lewis's (F. M. Lewis, "The inertia of the water surrounding a vibrating
ship", SNAME Trans. 37, 1929; known through the literature, not read here). The tests hold them to the exact limits of
a half circle and of flat plates on and through the surface: half the unbounded body's rho pi R^2 and rho pi a^2, the
potential being 0 on the free surface at high frequency.

The added mass enters through the held load M (M + A)^-1 (F + W) - W. That fold is this package's own: a held force cannot
carry -A a explicitly (unstable once A is about M), as the research summary notes after Kerner 2015, whose game model drops
the added mass for that reason. The sections are taken from the mesh under the mean waterline in the body's frame each
step, also this package's own. Proof: `packages/physics/tests/seakeeping.test.js` and `tests/coupling/seakeeping.test.js`
(a box heaves at 2 pi sqrt((m + a)/(rho g A_wp)) with its added mass, and at the bare period without).

### A hull's radiation: Ursell-Tasai sections and Cummins' memory (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/seakeeping/radiation.ts` solves a heaving section's two-dimensional radiation problem, and
`memory.ts` turns the hull's damping into the force it remembers. Written from J. M. J. Journee and W. W. Massie,
*Offshore Hydromechanics*, TU Delft, 2001, Part 2, read for this job:
- the potentials and stream functions of the progressive waves and the multipoles (eqs. 7.71-7.79), and Tasai's Lewis form
  of them (eqs. 7.103-7.112);
- the body condition, the pressure and the heave force;
- Cummins' equation and the retardation function (section 6.4; W. E. Cummins, "The impulse response function and ship
  motions", Schiffstechnik 9, 1962, known through the book).

These are this package's own, each checked:
- **Least squares over the contour.** The book states only that the body condition determines the unknowns.
- **The closed form of the waves' integral**, -e^{ikz} E1(ikz). It was checked against direct quadrature of the book's
  integrals before use. E1 is by its power series (Abramowitz and Stegun, *Handbook of Mathematical Functions*, 1964, eq.
  5.1.11), and the complex angle by Newton steps on the pinned sine and cosine.
- **The energy check.** The damping from the pressure must equal rho g^2 Abar^2 / w^3, the energy the waves carry away.
  The high- and low-frequency limits of the half circle (a -> 1; b -> 8 / pi) follow from the free-surface condition and
  the waves' amplitude ratio.
- **The direct convolution**, in place of Perez and Fossen's state-space fit (MIC 29(1), 2008, doi 10.4173/mic.2008.1.1),
  which a later change may add as a speed-up.
- **The load at the step's middle**, the pose carried half a step on. Held from the step's start, a restoring force has
  the update determinant 1 + (w dt)^2 / 2, a negative damping; at the middle it is 1.
- **Every other load on the body**, estimated from its last two steps for the added-mass solve.

Published Ursell curves (Ursell 1949, Vugts 1968) could not be read online. In their place the solver is held to:
- its own energy check;
- the exact limits;
- the frequency-domain answer of a driven box (`packages/physics/tests/coupling/seakeeping.test.js`, within 3 percent at 60
  steps a second; measured 0.6, 1.5 and 2.1).

No constant here is calibrated: every coefficient comes from the equations above, and the tests' bounds are their stated
numerical errors.

### A hull's sway and roll radiation (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-25)

`lateralSection` in `packages/physics/src/seakeeping/radiation.ts` solves a section swaying and rolling, and `memory.ts`
adds the sway, roll and yaw pairs. Written from the same book (Journee and Massie 2001, Part 2): the antisymmetric
multipoles and wave of Tasai's Lewis form, the stream function's body condition in sway and roll, and the sway, roll and
sway-roll coefficients. Two printed signs are not followed; each printed form, the correction and its proof:
- **The sway body condition (eq. 7.66).** Printed: Psi0 = -x' r0 cos(theta) + C on the circle (heave: -y' r0 sin(theta);
  roll: -beta' r0^2 / 2). Used: Psi0 = +x' y0 + C (on the circle +x' r0 cos(theta)). Proof by re-derivation: heave and
  sway are both rigid translations, so their stream functions take one orientation of the contour; with n ds = (dy, -dx)
  a translation U along x gives dPsi = U dy, Psi = +U y0, and one V along y gives Psi = -V x0. On the book's circle
  (x0 = r0 sin(theta), y0 = r0 cos(theta)) the printed heave, -y' x0, is that orientation and the printed sway, -x' y0, is
  the other: they cannot both hold, and the sway alone disagrees (the printed roll, a rotation in the same orientation,
  agrees with the heave). Integrating the book's own differential form (eq. 7.65) on that circle gives +x' r0 cos(theta)
  too. Checked in the code by rigid kinematics: a roll about an axis p below the origin is the roll about the origin plus
  the translation the roll gives the origin, so a44(p) = a44(0) + 2 p a24(0) + p^2 a22 and the same for the damping;
  measured on a box section (B 2 m, T 0.5 m) at 2 and 4 rad/s and p = 0.25 and -0.5 m, within 0.1 percent with the sign
  used, and off by 6 percent to 8 times with the printed one (the roll about p, which the printed roll condition gives and which is not in question, holds the translation as +p y0). Energy and reciprocity cannot tell the two apart (the printed
  sign turns both couplings together).
- **The antisymmetric multipoles' stream function (eq. 7.108, and 7.76 on the circle).** Printed: psi_A = +cos((2m+1)
  theta) - xi sum (...) cos((2m+2n) theta), with phi_A = sin((2m+1) theta) - xi sum (...) sin((2m+2n) theta). Used: psi_A
  = -cos((2m+1) theta) + xi sum (...) cos((2m+2n) theta), phi_A as printed. Proof by Cauchy-Riemann in the book's own
  convention: its heave pair (eq. 7.107), phi = e^(-2m alpha) cos(2m theta) with psi = +e^(-2m alpha) sin(2m theta), is
  phi - i psi = e^(-2m zeta) (zeta = alpha + i theta); the sway potential sin((2m+1) theta) e^(-(2m+1) alpha) is the real
  part of i e^(-(2m+1) zeta), whose -imaginary part is -cos((2m+1) theta) e^(-(2m+1) alpha). Physical check: with the
  printed sign the damping from the pressure is 0.85 to 1.83 of the energy the waves carry away and the couplings are not
  reciprocal (a24 / a42 from -0.20 to 0.43); with the sign used, 1.000 within 0.2 percent and reciprocal within 0.2
  percent (the same box section, 2 to 6 rad/s).

These are this package's own, each checked:
- **The roll about the centre of mass**, by the stream function's body condition -(x^2 + (y - pivot)^2) / 2, so the
  couplings need no shift afterward. Checked: a half circle rolling about its centre moves no water (its coefficients are
  0), and the coupling is reciprocal.
- **The added mass at infinite frequency** in sway and roll, by a straight line in 1 / xi through xi = 64 and 128. A
  section's coefficients approach their limits as 1 / xi; a half circle's sway limit is 0.405 of rho pi R^2 / 2, as the
  free surface reverses the mirrored double body's motion. The rigid-lid value, which an earlier version of the solver used
  at infinite frequency, is the zero-frequency limit; it is kept as `swayAddedMassRigidLid`.
- **The frequency table to xi = 48**, where the heave table stopped at 12: sway and roll damping fall off slowly, and the
  tail matters (measured on the driven box: 3.7 percent off with the table to 12, 2.3 with it to 48).
- **The yaw pairs** from the sections' sway, -int b22 x and int b22 x^2, in the body's axes.

Proof: `packages/physics/tests/seakeeping.test.js` (energy, reciprocity, the half circle) and
`tests/coupling/seakeeping.test.js` (a box driven sideways sways and rolls within 3 percent of the coupled frequency-domain
equations at 60 steps a second, measured 0.3 to 1.1; 0.05 to 0.9 at 240). No constant is calibrated.

### FIRE-06 heat conduction and phase change (`@margoengine/physics/thermal`, 2026-11-25)

- H. S. Carslaw and J. C. Jaeger, [*Conduction of Heat in Solids*](https://books.google.com/books?id=ySRRAAAAMAAJ), 2nd ed., 1959. The insulated-slab cosine mode gives an analytic decay benchmark.
- V. R. Voller and C. Prakash, [A fixed grid numerical modelling methodology for convection-diffusion mushy region phase-change problems](https://doi.org/10.1016/0017-9310(87)90317-6), 1987. The fixed grid and enthalpy variable retain latent heat without tracking a moving mesh.
- B. J. Kaaks, M. Rohde, J. L. Kloosterman and D. Lathouwers, [An energy-conservative DG-FEM approach for solid–liquid phase change](https://doi.org/10.1080/10407790.2023.2211231), 2023. Equation (2) gives the isothermal enthalpy inversion, and section 5.1 gives the Stefan interface balance used for the front test.

Used a Cartesian finite-volume discretization of the conduction term. Two half-cell resistances in series give one shared face conductance, so each interior flux leaves one cell and enters its neighbour. Each tick integrates cell enthalpy in joules and inverts it to temperature and liquid fraction. Forward Euler uses a half-unit bound on the row sum of conductances divided by the minimum sensible heat capacity. The first test bounds Fourier-mode error by the spatial eigenvalue error and the time-step logarithm remainder. The phase test sets the initially unconverted side to the melting temperature, so the two-sided Stefan balance reduces to its one-phase similarity solution.

The [NASA Passive Thermal Control Engineering Guidebook](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20220006584/downloads/NASAPassiveThermalGuidebookv5%201Public.pdf), revision 5.1, 2024, describes radiative heat transfer between a grey surface and its surroundings. The constant is the [2022 CODATA Stefan–Boltzmann constant](https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?sigma). Exchange at the face equals Fourier conduction across the half cell, with convection and net longwave emission evaluated at the face temperature. The power bracket runs from zero to the smaller of the unimpeded surface exchange and half-cell conduction. Its 53 halvings match the f64 significand.

N. Tubini, S. Gruber and R. Rigon, [A method for solving heat transfer with phase change in ice or soil that allows for large time steps while guaranteeing energy conservation](https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-15-2541-2021), 2021, equations (12) and (16), gives the new-time flux balance. We use that balance with harmonic face conductance and a piecewise-linear sensible/latent enthalpy graph. R. Barrett et al., [Templates for the Solution of Linear Systems, §2.2.1](https://netlib.org/linalg/html_templates/node12.html), SIAM, 1994, gives the Jacobi diagonal split. Here each diagonal independently inverts `H(T) + dt*G*T` across the latent interval. For a radiating face, moving its half-cell conductance to the diagonal adds `g*T_surface` to the right-hand side. The grey-face balance makes the surface temperature monotone and 1-Lipschitz in the cell temperature for nonnegative K. With `dt*G/C_min <= 2`, the simultaneous temperature update contracts in the maximum norm by at most 2/3. After convergence the solver updates enthalpy with paired face fluxes evaluated at the converged temperature to preserve energy. The backward Euler tests exercise the exact discrete diffusion eigenmode, phase plateau and a grey face evaluated at the new temperature.

R. Abeyaratne, [Continuum Mechanics](https://web.mit.edu/abeyaratne/Volumes/RCA_Vol_II.pdf), 2012, equation (11.22), gives the thermoelastic compliance relation. With traction-free sides, fixed ends, and a constant expansion coefficient, it reduces to axial stress equal to minus Young's modulus times the expansion coefficient and temperature rise. A restrained-bar stand-in reads the published temperature and verifies that coupling against a prescribed heat flux.

J. B. Mason, [Analysis of Thermally Induced Structural Vibrations by Finite Element Techniques](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19690011648), 1968, sections on static thermoelasticity and discrete elements, gives the initial-strain load and its assembly at nodes. The thermal grid uses six affine tetrahedra per cell, with conforming faces between cells. The volume and displacement gradients are constant within each tetrahedron. The isotropic elastic stress uses the deviatoric strain and the volumetric strain less three times the free thermal expansion. Exterior tractions default to zero, and specified displacements are enforced at individual nodal components.

M. R. Hestenes and E. Stiefel, [Methods of Conjugate Gradients for Solving Linear Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.049.044), 1952, §3, gives the conjugate-gradient iteration used for the symmetric free-node system. The implementation applies its element stiffnesses directly to the vectors, uses a diagonal preconditioner, and checks the residual from the resulting displacements. A minimal set of coordinate constraints removes any rigid translations and rotations left by the user's restraints. The solve publishes each cell's mean Cauchy stress and the nodal forces at the user's restraints.

M. Raffel, [Background-oriented schlieren (BOS) techniques](https://elib.dlr.de/95959/1/Raffel_2015.pdf), 2015, Eqs. 1–3, gives the Gladstone–Dale density relation and small-angle deflection from the transverse gradient of refractive index. P. E. Ciddor, [Refractive index of air: new equations for the visible and near infrared](https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.35.001566), 1996, Eqs. 5–8, gives the reference air refractivity. The temperature-volume path uses fixed local pressure and ideal gas density to convert kelvin to relative refractivity. It intersects each camera ray with the grid, clips by the opaque depth, and integrates the trilinear field's gradient and distance weighting in two Gauss points per traversed interval. That integrand is at most cubic within a voxel.

The kiln test reads the temperature registry port and passes each value into the existing Planck-spectrum emitter. Colour conversion uses the [CIE 1931 standard colorimetric observer](https://www.cie.co.at/datatable/cie-1931-colour-matching-functions-2-degree-observer), CIE 2019. The turbofan test uses a fixed pressure gas stand-in after applying heat. The expected temperature and the density ratio follow conservation of enthalpy and the ideal gas law. [NASA Glenn Burner Thermodynamics](https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/airplane/burnth.html) and [NASA Glenn Equation of State](https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/equation-of-state/).

The Rust stencil, SIMD enthalpy inversion, TypeScript bridge and shader implementation were written from the published methods. No companion code was used.

### A hull's diffraction: the relative motion principle (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/seakeeping/solver.ts` (`diffract`) and `memory.ts` (`DiffractionStrip`, `DiffractionForm`) load each
section with the waves' diffraction. Written from J. M. J. Journee and W. W. Massie, *Offshore Hydromechanics*, TU Delft,
2001 (https://ocw.tudelft.nl/wp-content/uploads/Part_2.pdf), read for this job:
- the relative motion principle (section 6.3.3, eq. 6.62, and section 8.3, eqs. 8.17-8.20): the wave load on a
  restrained section is its potential mass times the water's equivalent acceleration plus its potential damping times the
  water's equivalent velocity, plus the Froude-Krylov load;
- the equivalent motions from the Froude-Krylov load (eqs. 8.38-8.45): in heave the water's motion at the depth T3* of
  the section's mean wave pressure, whose long-wave limit (eqs. 8.42-8.44) is the section's area over its breadth;
- the strip integrals for heave and pitch (eqs. 8.47-8.48), and for sway, roll and yaw in the same way.

These are this package's own:
- **The time domain.** The potential mass and damping at the waves' frequency become the section's added mass at infinite
  frequency times the water's acceleration plus its radiation kernel convolved with the water's velocity over the
  memory (Cummins), as for the hull's own motion, so a sea of many frequencies takes each its own coefficients.
- **The sway's depth.** The section's centroid, where the water's mean horizontal motion over the section is in long
  waves (the sway Froude-Krylov force over the section's area).
- **The accelerations** as central differences of the sea's velocities over the step.
- **The roll** from the sections' sway-roll coupling about the centre of mass.

Proof: `packages/physics/tests/coupling/seakeeping.test.js`. In head seas a box heaves within 1 percent of eq. 8.47's
frequency-domain answer at 2.5, 3 and 3.5 rad/s (a box section's mean-pressure depth is exactly its draft in head seas),
82 to 267 percent off without the diffraction. Held in beam seas, its sway force and roll moment are within 1.5 percent of
the Froude-Krylov load plus (i w a(w) + b(w)) U, 50 to 390 percent off without. No constant is calibrated.

### A hull's wave drift: two-dimensional scattering and the far field (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-26)

`scatterSection` in `packages/physics/src/seakeeping/radiation.ts` gives a section's reflected and transmitted waves and the
wave's load on it, and `solver.ts` (`driftOf`, `driftLoad`) turns them into the hull's drift. Read for this job: J. M. J.
Journee and W. W. Massie, *Offshore Hydromechanics*, TU Delft, 2001 (https://ocw.tudelft.nl/wp-content/uploads/Part_2.pdf
and Part_3.pdf): the mean wave load on a wall (section 6.4.1, eqs. 6.86-6.106, 1/2 rho g a^2 for full reflection), the
second-order wave forces by direct pressure integration (section 9.3.1, eq. 9.67, Pinkster), and the low-frequency drift
by its spectrum (section 9.3.6). The far-field drift 1/2 rho g a^2 |R|^2 per metre is the momentum flux balance of the
incident, reflected and transmitted waves (deep-water momentum flux 1/4 rho g a^2, with |R|^2 + |T|^2 = 1), as Maruo
(1960) gives it; Newman's approximation of the slow drift (J. N. Newman, "Second-order, slowly-varying forces on vessels
in irregular waves", 1974) is known through the book.

These are this package's own, derived and checked:
- **The scattering from the radiation solution.** The held section's scattered flow is the same multipoles and outgoing
  wave as the radiation's, with the incident wave's stream function cancelled on the contour, split into its even part
  (heave's basis) and its odd part (sway's), each wave's two components unknowns of the least squares. The series' wave
  functions are the physical flow only on the side x > 0 (on the other they take the opposite parity, a branch of the
  logarithm), so the far field is read there and continued even or odd by hand. Checked: |R|^2 + |T|^2 = 1 within 1e-4
  for a box and a half circle from long waves (R -> 0) to short (R -> 1).
- **The motions' phase.** The incident potential raises the surface a quarter period after it, so a motion given against
  the elevation enters the stream function times i. Checked: in long waves a section heaving with the surface sends out
  the wave that cancels its scattering (to 0.1 percent), and with the other phase does not.
- **The held section's loads** from the pressure of the incident and scattered flow over the contour, their sign and
  phase fixed by energy: a free section moved by them and its own radiation keeps |R|^2 + |T|^2 = 1 within 1e-3 at every
  frequency, which none of the other fifteen combinations of sign and quarter period does.
- **The drift the solver applies** is the far field (the hull's true motions, from those loads) less the mean its
  Froude-Krylov pressure over the moving wetted surface gives in the motions the solver's own loads produce (their time
  average by `wettedLoads`), so the time domain's mean is the far field. Checked
  (`packages/physics/tests/coupling/seakeeping.test.js`): a moored box's mean drift within 3 percent of the wall's force
  of the far field at 3 and 8.7 rad/s, and the wall's in short waves.
- **Newman's approximation in O(N)**: Re[(sum a_i D_i e^(i theta_i))(sum a_j e^(-i theta_j))], the difference frequencies
  with the mean of the two waves' coefficients, so a coefficient of either sign is taken.
- **Oblique waves** by their share across the hull squared. That scaling is assumed, not derived.

### A hull's green water: shallow water on its deck (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/seakeeping/deck.ts` (`deckOf`, `stepDeck`) moves the water on a hull's deck, and `solver.ts`
(`deckLoad`) couples it to the hull and the sea. Written from:
- S. Zhang and A. M. Reed, "Green water effect on ship motions and loads via dam breaking model", 39th IWWWFB, 2024
  (https://sites.dundee.ac.uk/iwwwfb2024/wp-content/uploads/sites/197/2024/04/IWWWFB39_57.pdf): the shallow-water
  equations in the deck's frame, gravity replaced by the frame's effective acceleration, the deck's pressure hydrostatic,
  the sea coming aboard as a dam that breaks;
- J. J. Stoker, *Water Waves*, 1957, known through the paper and the literature: Ritter's dam break on a dry bed;
- E. Audusse, F. Bouchut, M.-O. Bristeau, R. Klein and B. Perthame, "A fast and stable well-balanced scheme with hydrostatic
  reconstruction for shallow water flows", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 25(6), 2004: the hydrostatic reconstruction;
- E. F. Toro, *Shock-Capturing Methods for Free-Surface Shallow Flows*, Wiley, 2001, known through the literature:
  Rusanov's flux and boundary conditions by Riemann invariants.

These are this package's own, each checked (`packages/physics/tests/seakeeping.test.js` and
`tests/coupling/seakeeping.test.js`):
- **A two-dimensional deck grid**, where the paper solves one-dimensional strips along the waves.
- **Every edge takes the sea in or lets the water go**, by the characteristic state between the deck's water and the sea,
  clamped to critical flow from upstream where it would be supercritical. Over a dry edge from still sea that is
  Ritter's state at the dam (4/9 of the height, 2/3 of sqrt(g h)): measured equal to (8/27) sqrt(g) h^1.5 within 1e-4.
  Into the air it is critical depth at the brink. Rusanov's flux at the dry edge instead passed 1.4 times that.
- **The deck from the mesh**, the highest upward face over each cell above the still waterline.
- **The deck's faces taken out of the Froude-Krylov integration** while the deck water counts their sea: a box held
  with its deck under still water takes the whole submerged box's buoyancy within 1e-4.
- **The `deckInflow` and `deckClaims` fields**, so a liquid solver on the deck takes the water that comes aboard and
  owns its load once.

Also checked: Ritter's dam break within 1.8, 1.1 and 0.7 percent at 200, 400 and 800 cells, mass kept to 1e-9, and a lake
on a sloped, half-dry deck at rest to rounding. No constant is calibrated.

### The motor joint and extra substeps per island (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-26)

Built from texts only; no other code was read. Box2D's motor joint and Rapier's `additional_solver_iterations` were matched
by their public documentation.

- E. Catto, "Soft Constraints" and "Modeling and Solving Constraints", GDC 2011 (box2d.org publications), and the Box2D v3
  documentation of the motor joint: a joint that drives a relative pose with its accumulated linear and angular impulses
  each clamped to a maximum force and torque as vectors.
- E. Catto, "Solver2D" (box2d.org blog, 2024), soft step: the substep a constraint is solved at; an island at more
  substeps solves the same rows at a shorter length.
- Margo's own: the vector cut after the per-axis motor rows, pushed back along each row; the island's count as the world's
  substeps plus the most its bodies ask, with warm starts and break loads read at that count and the adaptive level on top.
- Checked against: gravity sag of the per-kilogram spring, the capped speed on a slant, a moving anchor; an island with
  extra substeps equal bit for bit to a world stepped at that count.

### Physics worlds in netcode: rollback, snapshot diffs and server bodies (`@margoengine/netcode/physics`, 2026-11-26)

Built from texts only; no other code was read.

- The GGPO documentation (ggpo.net) and G. Fiedler, "Deterministic Lockstep", Gaffer On Games, 2014: peers step the same
  deterministic simulation, a wrong guess of an input is undone by loading the state before it and stepping again.
- G. Fiedler, "Snapshot Compression", Gaffer On Games, 2015: a state sent as its difference from a baseline both ends hold.
- G. Fiedler, "Snapshot Interpolation", Gaffer On Games, 2014: a client plays a server's bodies back between the states it
  has, a little behind (the existing `SnapshotBuffer`).
- Margo's own: the physics world as its own rollback state through its snapshot, loaded before and saved after each step;
  the diff as runs of unchanged 32-bit words and XORed changed ones, with varint counts.
- Checked against: every confirmed frame of two peers under latency, jitter and loss equal to the world stepped offline;
  a diff undone exactly; a thrown ball's interpolated path against its stepped one.

### Joint armature, the augmented mass and each coordinate's inverse inertia (`@margoengine/physics` multibodies, 2026-11-26)

Built from texts only; no other code was read. Rapier's augmented mass and MuJoCo's armature were matched by name from their
public documentation.

- R. Featherstone, Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms, Springer, 2008, section 9.7: a motor's rotor reflected through its gear
  as an inertia on the joint coordinate, added to the joint-space inertia's diagonal (and to the articulated-body
  algorithm's D = S^T I^A S).
- E. Todorov, T. Erez and Y. Tassa, "MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control", IROS 2012, and the MuJoCo modelling
  documentation: armature as that added diagonal inertia, which also steadies stiff joints.
- D. Baraff and A. Witkin, "Large steps in cloth simulation", SIGGRAPH 1998, eq. 18: a spring and damper taken implicitly
  over a step h add h c + h^2 k to the matrix the step solves against, which is what the augmented mass matrix reads.
- Margo's own: the rotor in the kernel's velocity projection, held to the speed it had when the step began (read before the
  step lands its impulses) through the cost 1/2 a (qd - rotor)^2, and carried on by each projection.
- Checked against: a compound pendulum's period with the rotor's inertia, tau / (I + a) for a torque and an impulse, the
  implicit damper's decay, and the inverse of the mass matrix.

### PID and PD controllers with split axes, caps and anti-windup (`@margoengine/physics` pid.ts, 2026-11-26)

Built from texts only; no other code was read. Rapier's `PidController`, `PdController`, `PdErrors` and axes mask were
matched by name from its public API pages.

- K. J. Astrom and R. M. Murray, Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers, Princeton, 2008
  (https://fbswiki.org), ch. 10 (the parallel PID law, the derivative on the measured speed, feedforward of the
  reference's speed) and sec. 5.3 (a second-order step response: overshoot exp(-pi zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2)) and peak
  time pi / (wn sqrt(1 - zeta^2))).
- K. J. Astrom and T. Hagglund, Advanced PID Control, ISA, 2006, sec. 3.5: integrator windup under actuator
  saturation, and conditional integration (stop integrating while the output is saturated) against it.
- A. Visioli, "Modified anti-windup scheme for PID controllers", IEE Proc. Control Theory Appl. 150 (1), 2003: the
  conditional-integration and back-calculation schemes compared; conditional integration chosen here because it adds
  no gain to tune.
- Margo's own: the command as an acceleration landed as mass (or world inertia) times acceleration times the step, so
  the loop is the unit-mass loop for every body; a cap on the length of the command vector, which keeps its direction;
  the angular error as twice the vector part of the short turn.
- Checked against: the second-order step response's overshoot and peak time, a ramp's zero lag with the reference's
  speed fed forward and kd v / kp without it, and a capped move against the same PID capped outside it (which winds up).

### Soft bodies in water: Morison's loads on ropes and cloth (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, SOFT-01, 2026-11-27)

Built from texts only; no other code was read.

- J. R. Morison, M. P. O'Brien, J. W. Johnson and S. A. Schaaf, "The force exerted by surface waves on piles", Petroleum
  Transactions AIME 189, 1950: the load on a body in an oscillating flow as an inertia term (the water's acceleration on
  the displaced volume and on the added mass) plus a quadratic drag on the relative velocity.
- S. F. Hoerner, Fluid-Dynamic Drag, 1965: a circular cylinder's drag across the flow below the drag crisis, 1.2, and a
  flat plate's normal force, 1.17 (already the cloth's air drag).
- Added mass: a circular cylinder's across the flow is its displaced volume's (C_a = 1, potential flow); a disk's normal
  to itself (8/3) rho a^3 (H. Lamb, Hydrodynamics, 6th ed., 1932, section 108), taken for the whole sheet and shared by
  area.
- Margo's own: the carried water taken implicitly, by setting a submerged particle's inverse mass to 1 / (m + m_a) and
  its gravity to m g / (m + m_a) less the buoyancy, the steady accelerations applied in each substep with gravity's (a
  jump at the step's start drifted a neutral rope); a segment's volume as each end particle's shared among its segments.
- Checked against: neutral buoyancy, a rope's and a tarp's terminal speeds, a pendulum's period in water, and a neutral
  rope riding an oscillating current.

### A damaged hull's bubble plume and its boil (`@margoengine/physics/foam` plume.ts, SEA-10 to SEA-13, 2026-11-26)

Built from papers only; no other code was read.

- The plume: the integral round plume of Morton, Taylor and Turner ("Turbulent gravitational convection from maintained
  and instantaneous sources", Proc. R. Soc. A 234, 1956), top-hat, with the bubbles' buoyancy g Q_g / (u + u_s) of the
  gas in a metre of plume (McDougall 1978; Milgram, "Mean flow in round bubble plumes", J. Fluid Mech. 133, 1983), as
  Dissanayake, Gros and Socolofsky review it ("Integral models for bubble, droplet, and multiphase plume dynamics in
  stratification and crossflow", Environ. Fluid Mech. 18, 2018): entrainment 0.055, Socolofsky, Bhaumik and Seol's
  best fit for the inner plume of a bubble plume (2008), and the inner plume's start at a Froude number of 1.6; the
  slip of millimetre air bubbles, 0.23 m/s (Wuest, Brooks and Imboden 1992, restated by Einarsrud and Brevik, "Kinetic
  energy approach to dissolving axisymmetric multiphase plumes", arXiv:0804.2789).
- The boil: Fannelop and Sjoen's surface flow ("Hydrodynamics of underwater blowouts", AIAA 1980) as Milgram and
  Burgess restate and test it ("Measurements of the surface flow above round bubble plumes", Applied Ocean Research 6,
  1984, eqs. 1-8): a Gaussian radial current that keeps its momentum flux and entrains beta V a unit area, started at
  twice the plume's radius with the plume's mass and momentum fluxes; beta 0.061, their mean over four conditions.
  V(r) and h(r) were derived here from the stated conservation laws (the printed equations are illegible in the scan);
  they match its form.
- Checked against: Morton, Taylor and Turner's exact far field of a pure plume (b = 6 alpha z / 5, u = (3 F / (4 pi
  beta^2))^(1/3) z^(-1/3)) and the surface flow's own conservation of momentum and entrainment.

### A hull's flooding: compartments, Bernoulli's openings, Boyle's air and the cargo that leaves (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-10, 2026-11-26)

Built from papers and public procedures only; no other engine's or tool's code was read.

- Progressive flooding as a hydraulic network: compartments joined by openings, water through each by Bernoulli's
  equation with a discharge coefficient, the floodwater's surface level and the floating position quasi-static or
  dynamic, the air compressed by Boyle's law. Sources: P. Ruponen, "Progressive flooding of a damaged passenger ship",
  doctoral thesis, Helsinki University of Technology, 2007 (its pressure-correction method; known through its abstract
  and Dankowski's account); H. Dankowski, "A fast and explicit method for simulating flooding and sinkage scenarios of
  ships", doctoral thesis, TU Hamburg-Harburg, 2013 (doi:10.15480/882.1125); H. Dankowski and S. Kruger, "Dynamic
  extension of a numerical flooding simulation in the time-domain", STAB 2015, Glasgow
  (https://www.shipstab.org/files/Proceedings/STAB/STAB2015/Papers/7.2-3-Dankowski.pdf), eqs. 1-4: the pressure
  height difference dz = (pa - pb) / (rho g) + (ua^2 - ub^2) / (2 g) + za - zb, u = sqrt(2 g dz), the flux the
  integral of u over the opening times Cd, large openings split into elementary parts, Boyle's law for trapped air, and
  the floodwater's masses updating the mass matrix at each step of the motion's integration.
- The discharge coefficient: the contraction of a jet through a sharp-edged slot, pi / (pi + 2) = 0.611, by
  Kirchhoff's free-streamline theory (G. Kirchhoff, "Zur Theorie freier Flussigkeitsstrahlen", J. reine angew. Math.
  70, 1869; R. von Mises, "Berechnung von Ausfluss- und Ueberfallzahlen", Z. VDI 61, 1917).
- Permeability: SOLAS chapter II-1, regulation 7-3 (0.95 for spaces in general, 0.85 machinery, 0.60 to 0.70 cargo).
- Margo's own: the opening's strips integrated exactly (the pressure difference is linear in height between the two
  water levels, so the mean of its square root over a strip is (2/3) (g1^(3/2) - g0^(3/2)) / (g1 - g0)); the time step
  as backward Euler on the compartments' volumes, then on their air's pressures, each by nonlinear Gauss-Seidel with a
  bracketed root (bisection, then the Illinois method), which keeps every level between its neighbours' where the
  explicit step's derivative of sqrt(dh) is unbounded; a full compartment's pressure as its own unknown, so water
  passes through it; the floodwater as point masses in the hull's added-mass solve.
- Cargo out of a breach: W. A. Beverloo, H. A. Leniger and J. van de Velde, "The flow of granular solids through
  orifices", Chem. Eng. Sci. 15, 1961 (W = C rho_b sqrt(g) (D - k d)^(5/2), C = 0.58, k = 1.5); T. J. Wilson,
  C. R. Pfeifer, N. Mesyngier and D. J. Durian, "Granular discharge rate for submerged hoppers", Papers in Physics 6,
  060009, 2014 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2812; under water W = C rho_g v_t (D - k d)^2 with v_t a grain's terminal
  speed, their Fig. 2's line 0.67 (D/d - 2.4) through the 0.3 to 3 mm glass beads, so C = 0.67^2); the terminal speed by
  R. I. Ferguson and M. Church, "A simple universal equation for grain settling velocity", J. Sediment. Res. 74, 2004
  (the tracers' own `settlingVelocity`).
- Checked against: Torricelli's draining law, the weir's flow, Boyle's law with hydrostatics, and the lost-buoyancy
  equilibrium of a holed barge (computed independently from the hull's and the tank's volumes under the sea).
- A sinking hull's form drag: Newton's impact law (I. Newton, *Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, 1687, book
  II, proposition 34: the pressure of a stream on a surface as the square of its speed normal to it), with the drag
  coefficient of a cube face-on, 1.05 (S. F. Hoerner, *Fluid-Dynamic Drag*, 1965, chapter 3; a disk 1.17, a sphere
  0.47); integrated over the same wet pieces as the Froude-Krylov pressure.

### A hull's slamming: Wagner's wetted width and the momentum of the water (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-11, 2026-11-26)

`packages/physics/src/seakeeping/slamming.ts` (`slamStations`, `slamSlope`) tabulates each station's added mass against
its depth of entry, and `solver.ts` (`slamLoad`) applies the impact. Written from:
- T. von Karman, "The impact on seaplane floats during landing", NACA TN 321, 1929: the force as the rate of the momentum
  the water takes up, d(m V)/dt;
- H. Wagner, "Uber Stoss- und Gleitvorgange an der Oberflache von Flussigkeiten", ZAMM 12, 1932, known through the
  literature: the wetted half-breadth with the water's pile-up, from the mean of the section's height over c sin(theta)
  equal to the depth (pi / 2 the still-water cut for a wedge), and the flat plate's added mass rho pi c^2 / 2;
- R. Zhao, O. Faltinsen and J. Aarsnes, "Water entry of arbitrary two-dimensional sections with and without flow
  separation", 21st Symposium on Naval Hydrodynamics, 1996 (https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/5870/chapter/29): the
  comparison of Wagner, von Karman and the exact similarity solution (Wagner high at larger deadrise), and flow
  separation at knuckles.

These are this package's own:
- **The sections' profiles from the mesh**: the half-breadth at a ladder of heights, Wagner's condition solved for c at
  each by bisection over a 32-point mean.
- **The impact (dm/dh) V^2 applied only while a section enters**, with V its depth's rate over the step (kept as state).
- **No impact past the section's full breadth**: the flow leaves the hull.

Checked (`packages/physics/tests/seakeeping.test.js`, `tests/coupling/seakeeping.test.js`): the wetted width and the slope
against Wagner's wedge within 0.1 and 0.2 percent; a 30 degree wedge entering at a steady speed takes Wagner's force within
0.02 percent until the chine is wet, and none past it. No constant is calibrated. Measured forces were not available to
read (the drop tests' forces are in figures only), so the check is against Wagner's theory and the known bias of it is
recorded in docs/limits.md.

### A hull's viscous roll damping (`@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-25)

`packages/physics/src/seakeeping/viscous.ts` gives each section's eddy-making and skin-friction roll damping, and the
solver applies them. Written from ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-02-07-04.5, "Estimation of Roll Damping", revision 02,
2024 (https://www.ittc.info/media/11942/75-02-07-045.pdf), section 4.2.1, read for this job:
- the component sum and the equivalent linearisation (eqs. 22-26);
- the eddy-making component at zero speed (eqs. 42-44, after Ikeda, Himeno and Tanaka 1978, Ikeda et al. 1977, with
  Katayama et al. 2022's form), and the bilge radius from the area coefficient (eq. 57);
- Kato's skin friction (eqs. 37-39, Kato 1957).

These are this package's own:
- **The eddy component in time**, as the quadratic moment -1/2 rho d^4 C_R p |p| that eq. 42 defines C_R by, not its
  linearisation at an amplitude.
- **The friction section by section**, with the girth and its mean distance from the roll axis integrated on the Lewis
  contour, in place of Kato's whole-ship regressions, and taken at the hull's natural roll frequency (the restoring moment
  from the wetted surface heeled each way, over the roll inertia with its added inertia at infinite frequency).
- **The implicit damping**: -c p / (1 + dt c / I), backward Euler on the damping alone.
- **The axis held at most 0.95 d deep**, the formula's range.

Held-out roll decay uses the one-degree-of-freedom apparatus of [Kwang Hyo Jung, Kuang-An Chang and Hyo Jae Jo,
2006, *Viscous Effect on the Roll Motion of a Rectangular Structure*](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9399(2006)132:2(190)).
[Jung’s dissertation, 2004, chapter VI, §§6.1 and 6.3](https://hdl.handle.net/1969.1/2249) gives the hinge
and its constraints. [Jung, Suh and Chun, 2007, §2 and Figure 2](https://kci.go.kr/kciportal/ci/sereArticleSearch/ciSereArtiView.kci?sereArticleSearchBean.artiId=ART001064432)
distinguish the 0.05 m draft from the acrylic box’s 0.10 m total height with 0.90 m span and 0.30 m beam.
The reported 0.236 kg m² dry inertia and 0.519 N m s
equivalent damping apply to the entire box. Geometry fixes GM at 0.125 m. The 60 Hz solver gives extinction
slope 0.35051 versus 0.33271 measured and period 0.89340 s versus 0.930 s. At 240 Hz these become
0.34851 and 0.89470 s. The tank depth was 0.90 m (kh ≈ 4.2). The strip calculation uses deep water. The
separate unconstrained control loses roll more slowly with sway enabled. No outcome sets a parameter.

The load point in the step is this package's own: a restoring load -k x taken at x + theta v dt, held through a rigid
step of s symplectic-Euler substeps, has the update's determinant 1 + (w dt)^2 (1 - theta - (s + 1) / (2 s)), so
theta = (s - 1) / (2 s) neither feeds nor drains the motion; the radiation force is carried there linearly.

## N-body and orbital dynamics (SPACE-01)

- Ernst Hairer, Christian Lubich and Gerhard Wanner, [Geometric Numerical Integration](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-30666-8)
  (2006), and their [Acta Numerica Störmer–Verlet paper](https://www.math.mcgill.ca/gantumur/docs/down/gniverlet.pdf)
  (2003), §§1–3. The kernel computes each unordered Newton pair once and applies equal and opposite forces.
  Two half velocity kicks use acceleration at either end of the position drift. Haruo Yoshida,
  [Construction of higher order symplectic integrators](https://doi.org/10.1016/0375-9601(90)90092-3) (1990),
  equations 4.4–4.6, composes three such steps. Their time factors are `1 / (2 - 2^(1/3))` for the outer
  steps and `-2^(1/3) / (2 - 2^(1/3))` for the middle step. Gravity uses fixed-order SIMD in the orbital
  plane and scalar arithmetic in z, with the CODATA 2022 value of G from [NIST](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2022.pdf).
- Jack Wisdom and Matthew Holman, [Symplectic maps for the N-body problem](https://web.mit.edu/wisdom/www/nbodymap.pdf)
  (1991), demonstrate Kepler splitting for a dominant central mass. Hanno Rein and David Spiegel,
  [IAS15](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.4779) (2015), §2, use adaptive high-order quadrature for close encounters.
  The engine's general Cartesian layout uses the position-dependent symmetric split so no central hierarchy
  is required. It exposes fixed subdivisions. An ideal bound orbit uses the eccentric anomaly bracket
  `M ± e` and rotates the standard perifocal position and velocity into the requested inertial plane.
- NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, [Fundamentals of Orbital Mechanics](https://spsweb.fltops.jpl.nasa.gov/portaldataops/mpg/MPG_Docs/MPG%20Book/Release/Chapter7-OrbitalMechanics.pdf),
  Chapter 7 on conics, zonal gravity and drag. The orbit model differentiates the J2 term of the axial potential
  and reacts the correction on its source body. Atmospheric drag uses the stated `-ρ Cd A |v| v / 2` force
  with atmosphere-relative velocity. At fixed density its relative velocity has the exact rational decay
  `1 / (1 + ρ Cd A |v| dt / (2m))`. A half drag step on each side of conservative transport keeps air resistance
  dissipative through the positive-duration part of the update. David Vallado, Paul Crawford, Richard Hujsak and
  T. S. Kelso, [Revisiting Spacetrack Report #3](https://celestrak.org/publications/AIAA/2006-6753/) (2006),
  establishes the independent SGP4 mean-element path which remains in `sciviz/geo`.
- J. M. Bardeen, W. H. Press and S. A. Teukolsky, [Rotating Black Holes](https://www.osti.gov/biblio/4585183)
  (1972), give circular angular velocity `1 / (r^(3/2) + a)` in geometric units. J. E. Pringle,
  [Accretion Discs in Astrophysics](https://courses.physics.ucsd.edu/2020/Winter/physics116/Pringle_%20Accretion%20Disks.pdf)
  (1981), describes advective radial transport in a thin disk. The emitter model holds a prescribed radial
  velocity over a texture phase. With radius varying linearly, the zero-spin integral of angular velocity
  rationalizes to `2 t / (√r0 √r1 (√r0 + √r1))`. For spinning disks the renderer applies two-point
  Gauss–Legendre to the Kerr angular velocity along that path. Doppler hue follows the existing observer
  redshift, and local emission modulates beaming brightness as the texture moves through the flow.

- David Tommasini and Daniele Olivieri, [Two fast and accurate routines for solving the elliptic Kepler
  equation for all values of the eccentricity and mean anomaly](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202141423)
  (2022), identify the loss of accuracy near eccentricity one and mean anomaly zero. The bracketed
  solver evaluates `(1-e)E + e(E-sin E) - M` with the Taylor residual close to zero and uses the
  half-angle identity for the associated radius and velocity denominator. The independent test starts
  from an eccentric anomaly and derives the mean anomaly, position and velocity with their series.
- Ryan S. Park, William M. Folkner, James G. Williams and Dale H. Boggs, [The JPL Planetary and
  Lunar Ephemerides DE440 and DE441](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/doc/Park.2021.AJ.DE440.pdf) (2021),
  equation 27. Normalize extreme displacement components, then evaluate the inverse-square force
  with its original direction. This keeps the source mass from amplifying an underflowing intermediate.
  The ordinary SIMD force and integration retain their summation order. Workers partition acceleration
  rows, with the serial J2 correction applied in its original order before the next kick.
- Alain Chenciner, [Central configurations](https://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Central_configurations)
  (2007), triangular relative equilibrium. Three unequal masses in a rotating equilateral formation
  have common angular frequency `sqrt(G sum(m) / side³)`. This gives the orbit and barycentre reference
  for the live field cutaway.

The binary test checks fourth-order step refinement and barycentre symmetry. Other tests check a quadrupole
orbit, exact constant-density drag, inclined Kepler states, the disk phase, and equal hashes after restore
and across shared and plain SIMD builds. The shader tests exercise the Event Horizon observations against
real pixel readback at a fixed camera in addition to the CPU orbit checks.

The close-encounter comparison uses Victor Szebehely and C. Frederick Peters, [Complete Solution of
a General Problem of Three Bodies](https://doi.org/10.1086/110355) (1967), Table I and its defined initial
coordinates. The separate lunar comparison uses Nicholas Colmenares, James B. R. Battat, Daniel P.
Gonzales, Thomas W. Murphy Jr. and Sanchit Sabhlok's [APOLLO archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7818557)
(2023, CC BY 4.0). It takes the first grade A or B Apollo 15 point on each observed October 2020 UTC date.
Park et al. Table 3 lists Apache Point observations only through 2017. The withheld return times
are never inputs. The fixture lists hashes for the source archive and NASA NAIF centre and orientation
kernels. Both the N-body and DE440 comparisons use the same two-leg geometric observable. This is a
diagnostic against held-out measurement rather than a complete lunar ranging data reduction.

## Underwater acoustics (SOUND-03)

- Finn B. Jensen, William A. Kuperman, Michael B. Porter and Henrik Schmidt, [Computational Ocean Acoustics](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-8678-8),
  2nd ed. (2011), [Ray Methods](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-8678-8_3). For a range-independent medium
  with depth positive down, a ray's horizontal slowness `p = cos(angle) / c` is constant. At fixed speed
  gradient `g`, the vertical direction cosine `u = sin(angle)` obeys `du/dt = -g * (1 - u²)`. The implemented
  hyperbolic-tangent addition formula integrates this relation in time. In each layer the path is the circular
  arc with signed radius `1 / (p * g)`, or a straight segment for a uniform layer. Solving the same relation
  for the known speed at the next interface identifies its crossing time. Each subinterval keeps its own
  gradient, and a reflection changes only the vertical direction and the signed pressure coefficient.
- Michael B. Porter and Homer P. Bucker, [Gaussian beam tracing for computing ocean acoustic fields](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.395269)
  (1987), equations 5–13 and §IV. The [authors' scan](https://www.hlsresearch.com/personnel/porter/papers/JASA/gbt%20bw%20with%20errata.pdf)
  gives the complex beam curvature `P/Q` and the waist where amplitude falls to 1/e. The authors' follow-up,
  [Applications of Gaussian beam tracing to two- and three-dimensional problems in ocean acoustics](https://hlsresearch.com/personnel/porter/papers/GBT%203D%20grey.pdf)
  (1989), defines the paraxial equations `dQ/ds = c P` and `dP/ds = -c_nn Q / c²` in equation 5. Within a linear layer
  `c_nn` vanishes and the central arc gives the integral of `c² dt` exactly. At an interface the normal
  derivative integrates a slope discontinuity into a real kick to `P/Q` while preserving width. Reflecting a
  flat boundary is equivalent to unfolding the ray against a mirrored profile. We advance the argument of
  `Q` along its drift segment to keep the phase continuous. The pressure is normalized against the assigned
  launch pressure for a single beam in the propagation plane.
- Timothy G. Leighton, [Fundamentals of underwater acoustics and ultrasound](https://resource.isvr.soton.ac.uk/staff/pubs/PubPDFs/Pub2488.pdf)
  (1998), section on acoustic rays in piecewise-linear profiles. Equations 7.10–7.11 independently give the circular
  path through a linear gradient. The code uses a time form of that same arc so a step crosses interfaces
  without assuming a prescribed range or depth increment.

The uniform column follows the image-ray construction in Jensen et al. (2011). For a fast crossing ray we
apply a triangular depth fold to the full straight path, reflect the final vertical direction by parity and
apply the pressure factors over each boundary's count by integer exponentiation. The uniform beam has
constant `P`, so the total drift is the sum of the identical subinterval integrals (Porter and Bucker,
1987). For an extreme beam size, factoring out positive scales from `Q` preserves the argument of
its normalized cross and dot products. Ordinary arithmetic keeps its original order.
The native implementation ports this same model using Margo's pinned math. SIMD advances range
and depth together, handles the complex beam drift and checks pairs of candidate rays. Workers
own consecutive ray ranges and never share a mutable ray row. The published state is independent
of the number of partitions. Work counters come from resolved events and executed drifts, with
their integer range verified before publication.

The field timing comparison uses independent geometry and measured water speed from Table I and the
excess arrival times from Table II of Mandar Chitre, [A high-frequency warm shallow water acoustic communications
channel model and measurements](https://arl.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/publications/Chitre2007b.pdf) (2007).
It omits the reflection, material and motion parameters fitted by that paper. The tank comparison uses
the geometry, nominal sound speed and independent measured delays of Ruben Viegas, Friedrich Zabel and
Antonio Silva, [In-Lab Demonstration of an Underwater Acoustic Spiral Source](https://doi.org/10.3390/s23104931)
(2023), §3, Figures 6 and 8. The script records misses in both regimes without fitting solver parameters.

Tests compare the uniform beam width, attenuation and phase, the analytic circular arc and turning point,
the change in wavefront curvature at a knot, and repeated flat-boundary reflections with closed solutions.
The coupling test verifies the recorded delay and complex pressure against the live registry reader and exact
snapshot and frame-rate repeatability.

## Ice thermodynamics (ICE-05)

- Josef Stefan, [Über die Theorie der Eisbildung](https://www.zobodat.at/pdf/SBAWW_98_2a_0965-0983.pdf),
  presented 1889 and [published in Annalen der Physik](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.18912780206) (1891).
  For a vertical quasi-steady ice column, the outgoing conductive flux is conductivity times the difference
  between the freezing point and the boundary temperature divided by the ice thickness. Fusion converts
  that flux into the change in solid ice thickness. Integrating the bare column gives square-root growth in time.
- Gary A. Maykut and Norbert Untersteiner, [Some results from a time-dependent thermodynamic model of sea ice](https://doi.org/10.1029/JC076i006p01550)
  (1971), Fig. 1 and the governing boundary heat balances. Albert J. Semtner Jr.,
  [A Model for the Thermodynamic Growth of Sea Ice in Numerical Investigations of Climate](https://frouingroup.ucsd.edu/Most_recent_figs/Refs/semtner-1976.pdf)
  (1976), Appendix. Their zero-layer approximation treats the two layers as thermal resistances in series.
  Multiplying the snow thermal resistance by the ice conductivity gives an effective ice thickness
  `s = kIce * snowThickness / kSnow`. The closed update adds
  `2 * kIce * (Tfreeze - Tboundary) * dt / (density * latentHeat)` to `(thickness + s)^2` while growing.
  Above the freezing point the separate surface balance uses the boundary sensible flux
  `h * (Tboundary - Tfreeze)`. Divide by density and latent heat for the ablation depth per second,
  and end at zero solid. Basal and registered heating consume the energy delivered by each source.
- N. P. Fofonoff and R. C. Millard Jr., [Algorithms for Computation of Fundamental Properties of Seawater](https://www.jodc.go.jp/info/ioc_doc120810/UNESCO_tech/059832eb.pdf)
  (UNESCO, 1983), freezing point chapter. The tested surface value uses the atmospheric-pressure polynomial with
  PSS-78 salinity. Fresh water uses 273.15 K. In between 0 and the lower measured salinity 4, the expression smoothly
  approaches the fresh-water endpoint.
- Daniel M. Murphy and Thomas Koop, [Review of the vapour pressures of ice and supercooled water for atmospheric applications](https://doi.org/10.1256/qj.04.94)
  (2005), Eq. 7. The ice saturation pressure uses that equation in kelvin and pascals. Dividing vapour pressure by
  the gas constant of water vapour and the local gas temperature gives density. A steady film of specified mass
  conductance transfers mass in proportion to the density difference across it. The surface deposition or sublimation
  mass is converted to porous frost thickness with the specified bulk density.
- Lasse Makkonen, [A Model of Icicle Growth](https://doi.org/10.3189/S0022143000009072) (1988), equations and
  discussion for ice growth on the sides and at the tip. Margo integrates each area as one axisymmetric cylinder.
  Heat removed sets the amount frozen and the remaining supply reaches the tip. Cylindrical volume then gives
  the new radius and length. The converse heat input melts both surfaces. Excess feed drains.
- US Army Corps of Engineers, [Mechanical and Electrical Design for Lock and Dam Operating Equipment](https://www.publications.usace.army.mil/Portals/76/Publications/EngineerManuals/EM%201110-2-2610_FINAL_18Mar2025.pdf)
  (2025), section on mechanical ice control, and IAPWS, [Revised Release on the Equation of State 2006 for H₂O Ice Ih](https://www.teos-10.org/pubs/IAPWS-06-Revised_2009.pdf)
  (2009). Near-freezing density and fusion energy use conventional rounded values. After the solid is exhausted,
  externally supplied heat warms the meltwater to 373.15 K using a constant liquid-water heat capacity before it
  pays the latent heat of vaporisation. Available mass bounds the resulting steam.

`tests/ice.test.js` checks the independent slab solution, the UNESCO S = 35 table value, vapour-film mass,
and side/tip mass conservation. `tests/coupling/ice.test.js` exchanges layout-1 fields, closes the mass and energy
budgets, then compares exact hashes across display rates, snapshot/restore and seek.

## Celestial ephemeris and rotation (SPACE-02)

The optional physics/celestial entry uses the world tick and independent TT, UT1 and TDB epoch offsets. An Earth-fixed position is obtained by an IAU 2006 celestial-pole rotation, ERA and optional measured polar motion. The solar and tidal field ports depend on little fixed-size f64 regions with documented layouts. For a complete planetary SPK file, position and velocity are evaluated from its actual polynomial records, and the Sun and Moon's apparent directions include one-way light time and stellar aberration.

- Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, 2nd ed. (1998), ch. 22 and 47, [publisher entry](https://www.astrobooks.com/browseproducts/Astronomical-Algorithms-2nd-Edition-%28Hardback%29-%5BJean-Meeus---1998%5D.HTML). The four nutation terms and the lunar longitude, latitude and range use the scientific coefficients already in Margo's sky package, evaluated with pinned transcendental functions. The lunar series originates in M. Chapront-Touzé and J. Chapront, [The Lunar Ephemeris ELP 2000](https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1983A%26A...124...50C) (1983).
- E. M. Standish, [Keplerian Elements for Approximate Positions of the Major Planets](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/planets/approx_pos.html), Table 1. The bundled planet orbit elements apply over 1800–2050, with Earth's position corrected from the Earth–Moon barycentre by the Moon's mass share.
- P. Bretagnon and G. Francou, [Planetary theories in rectangular and spherical variables, VSOP 87 solutions](https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1988A%26A...202..309B) (1988). Its six series representations and truncation convention were compared with the direct modern JPL ephemeris. The high-accuracy path evaluates the user-supplied JPL state polynomials since a JPL file also provides the Moon and uses a common reference frame.
- R. Park, W. Folkner, J. Williams and D. Boggs, [The JPL Planetary and Lunar Ephemerides DE440 and DE441](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/doc/Park.2021.AJ.DE440.pdf) (2021), NASA NAIF's [DAF record specification](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/toolkit_docs/FORTRAN/req/daf.html) and [SPK required reading](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/toolkit_docs/IDL/req/spk.html), and F. W. J. Olver et al., [NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions §3.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.11), Clenshaw coefficients and recurrence. The derivative of the position recurrence gives type 2 velocity. Type 3 supplies separate velocity series. No ephemeris file is bundled.
- G. Petit and B. Luzum (eds.), [IERS Conventions (2010), ch. 5](https://iers-conventions.obspm.fr/content/chapter5/icc5.pdf), and P. Wallace and N. Capitaine, [Precession–nutation procedures consistent with IAU 2006 resolutions](https://syrte.obspm.fr/iau2006/aa06_459.IAU06prec.pdf) (2006), equations 4, 7–9 and worked example A.16. The optional polar coordinates let callers refine the terrestrial frame, and the solver uses the dominant periodic term of [IERS table 5.2d](https://iers-conventions.obspm.fr/content/chapter5/additional_info/tab5.2d.txt).
- F. Espenak and J. Meeus, [Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses](https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/SEpubs/5MCSE.html) (2006) and [Five Millennium Canon of Lunar Eclipses](https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/SEpubs/5MCLE.html) (2009). Topocentric solar disc overlap uses geometric angular radii and a WGS 84 site. The lunar shadow enlargement is Danjon's, lunar canon equations 1-5 and 1-6. Tests classify the published 2017 and 2024 total solar and 2022 total lunar events.
- National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, [World Geodetic System 1984](https://earth-info.nga.mil/?action=wgs84&dir=wgs84), International Astronomical Union, [2015 Resolution B3](https://www.iau.org/static/resolutions/IAU2015_English.pdf) and [JPL solar system dynamics constants](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/astro_par.html). Geodetic axes use the ellipsoid's prime-vertical radius of curvature. The IAU nominal solar irradiance follows inverse-square range and the local projected area. Gravity uses a rationalized point-mass Newton potential with the constant and linear terms removed, preserving the small tide signal and an analytic Earth-fixed gradient.
- K. Anderson and M. Mikofski, [Slope-Aware Backtracking for Single-Axis Trackers](https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy20osti/76626.pdf) (2020), equations 4, 5, 14–16 and 32. Tests reproduce SOLARFIELD-2 and SOLARFIELD-3 with individual row slope/bias, wind stow and the independent closed-form projected aperture.

The finite-precision check used JPL's official DE440s BSP (32,726,016 bytes, SHA-256 c1c7feeab882263fc493a9d5a5b2ddd71b54826cdf65d8d17a76126b260a49f2) and [Horizons vector queries](https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/doc/horizons.html) as an independent oracle. Query target 10, 301, 5 or 7, centre 500@399, ICRF, FRAME, VEC_CORR=NONE, KM-S, and TLIST of 2451545.0, 2457987.25 and 2460409.25 TDB. The twelve positions agree with Horizons DE441 within 2 m, and the component velocities within 0.00001 m/s. This is a sample comparison between ephemerides. Checked-in synthetic data exercises both byte orders and SPK representations, the common centre, time boundaries, and malformed input. The world harness tests live consumption of both fields and bit-identical results across frame rates and after restore.
### Land-surface energy and water balance (ATMO-09, `@margoengine/weather/surface-energy`, 2026-11-25)

- J. L. Monteith, [Evaporation and environment](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/5321565/), 1965, introduced the
  canopy resistance in series with aerodynamic resistance. The original scan is catalogued by Rothamsted. The resistance
  equation and the definition of its two terms were verified in Allen et al., [Crop Evapotranspiration, FAO-56,
  Chapter 2](https://www.fao.org/4/x0490e/x0490e06.htm), 1998, equations 1–4. The patch solves for its surface
  temperature directly, so it keeps the nonlinear surface saturation deficit. It uses the equation for saturation
  pressure from [Chapter 3](https://www.fao.org/4/x0490e/x0490e07.htm), Eq. 11, and the 2.45 MJ/kg water vaporization
  convention used for reference evapotranspiration. The daily grass-reference coefficients do not enter the solver.
- G. E. Liston and K. Elder, [A Distributed Snow-Evolution Modeling System (SnowModel)](https://www.fs.usda.gov/rm/pubs_other/rmrs_2006_liston_g001.pdf),
  2006, §2(b), Eq. 1, gives the surface terms and holds the snow surface at its melting temperature while the energy
  surplus melts available snow. The patch uses 333.7 kJ/kg for melting and puts snowmelt in the liquid store.
- K. W. Oleson et al. and the Community Terrestrial Systems Model team,
  [CLM5 Technical Note, Momentum, Sensible Heat, and Latent Heat Fluxes](https://escomp.github.io/CTSM/release-clm5.0/tech_note/Fluxes/CLM50_Tech_Note_Fluxes.html),
  2018, §§2.5.2 and 2.5.5, gives the bulk resistance fluxes in specific humidity and the exact conversion
  `q = 0.622 e / (p - 0.378 e)`. The model holds one air density and heat capacity fixed for a step.
- L. S. Bradshaw, J. E. Deeming, R. E. Burgan and J. D. Cohen,
  [The 1978 National Fire-Danger Rating System, Technical Documentation](https://www.fs.usda.gov/rm/pubs_int/int_gtr169.pdf),
  1983, Eq. 25, gives the exponential timelag relaxation. The targets reuse Margo's implementation of J. D. Cohen
  and J. E. Deeming, [The National Fire-Danger Rating System, Basic Equations](https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/27298),
  1985.

Backward Euler adds a positive heat-capacity slope to the monotone outgoing energy balance at each patch.
A bracketed solve conserves storage and boundary fluxes to f64 roundoff. The water budget limits evaporation
to available liquid, caps snow fusion at the remaining snow mass and sends liquid overflow to runoff.
Patches have no lateral cross terms, so the optional Rust kernel evaluates two residuals at a time with f64x2
and finishes the independent brackets in canonical patch order. The scalar tail uses the same equations.
The TypeScript path needs no batch assets. The tests compare the linear result to its closed
form, check both budgets, exercise rain and dew, and verify that the material darkens as the RITS-10 ground wets.
The implementation uses the publications and Margo's existing interfaces.

- S. Morin, Y. Lejeune, B. Lesaffre, J.-M. Panel, D. Poncet, P. David and J. Sudul, *An 18-yr,
  hourly resolution dataset of meteorological observations at the Col de Porte site* (2012).
  Incoming irradiance, ambient air and deep soil temperature drive the comparison. The previous
  snow water equivalent, albedo and starting temperature initialize each run. Three later radiometric
  temperatures per run remain held out. The retrieval convention in §2.3.4 supplies an emissivity-1
  sensitivity case alongside the default 0.97. Neither uses the later observations as inputs.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-4-13-2012)
  [Dataset](https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.774249)
- S. A. Twomey, C. F. Bohren and J. L. Mergenthaler, *Reflectance and albedo differences between wet
  and dry surfaces* (1986), explains the optical effect of wetting. The technical cutaway feeds
  the existing `wetColor` and `wetRoughness` material functions with the solver's accepted wetness.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.25.000431)


### Point-mass steering (PA-83, LIFE-04)

Craig W. Reynolds, [Steering Behaviors for Autonomous Characters](https://www.red3d.com/cwr/papers/1999/gdc99steer.pdf), GDC 1999,
uses capped steering force divided by inertial mass. The NASA Glenn [Drag Equation](https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/drag-equation/)
gives force magnitude `rho Cd A |u|² / 2` for velocity relative to the medium. The drag-only update integrates
`du/dt = -k |u| u` by preserving direction and replacing the speed `s` with `s / (1 + k s dt)`.
The lateral acceleration cap follows normal acceleration `s² / R` along a curve, applied in the medium frame.
Katz et al., [Inferring the structure and dynamics of interactions in schooling fish](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3219116/),
PNAS 108(46), 2011, measured distinct longitudinal and lateral reactions. These tests check longitudinal force divided
by mass, independently limited lateral acceleration, and the exact drag-only speed law.


### Collective animal motion (LIFE-04, `@margoengine/physics/schooling`)

- Craig W. Reynolds, [Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model](https://www-graphics.stanford.edu/courses/cs448-01-spring/papers/reynolds.pdf)
  (SIGGRAPH 1987). Local collision avoidance, velocity matching, and flock centering produce motion without a scripted
  group trajectory. Reynolds (1999), cited above, also motivates steering away from a future threat position. Here
  closest approach uses both bodies' velocities. For separation vector `r` and relative velocity `v`, minimize
  `|r + vt|²` by clamping `−(r·v)/(v·v)` to the prediction interval.
- Iain D. Couzin, Jens Krause, Richard James, Graeme D. Ruxton, and Nigel R. Franks,
  [Collective Memory and Spatial Sorting in Animal Groups](https://case.edu/affil/sigmaxi/documents/collectiveMemoryAndSpatialSortingInAnimalGroups_CouzinKrauseJamesRuxtonFranks.pdf)
  (Journal of Theoretical Biology, 2002, equations 1–3). Priority repulsion uses the negative sum of unit displacement
  vectors. In the visible middle zone orientation uses unit neighbour velocities and in the outer zone attraction
  uses unit displacements. Each nonzero zone direction is normalized before equal-weight blending. Their angular
  turn cap serves the same purpose as the solver's velocity-dependent physical normal-acceleration constraint.
- Michele Ballerini et al., [Interaction ruling animal collective behavior depends on topological rather than metric distance](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2234121/)
  (PNAS, 2008). Their measured starling interaction range was approximately six to seven neighbours, and the paper
  distinguishes the cited two-dimensional fish estimates. The solver exposes the number of eligible neighbours
  and uses a configurable physical sensing radius. With no count specified, all visible in-zone peers contribute.
- Federal Aviation Administration, [Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge](https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/2022-03/pilot_handbook.pdf)
  (FAA-H-8083-25B, Figure 5-34). In the level-turn controller fixture, the vertical component of lift balances
  weight and the horizontal component supplies centripetal acceleration. Their component ratio is `a/g`.


### GPU flocking (LIFE-04, `@margoengine/vfx/flocking`, 2026-11-27)

Written from the papers and documents below, read as text. No engine source was read, three.js's GPU birds examples
included: the README's three.js note describes those examples from their public descriptions. Taken over from a
Gemini draft on Scott's order; every shader and step was rewritten or checked line by line against these sources.

- Craig W. Reynolds, [Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model](https://doi.org/10.1145/37402.37406)
  (SIGGRAPH 1987): separation (collision avoidance), alignment (velocity matching) and cohesion (flock centering),
  each from the neighbours a boid perceives.
- Craig W. Reynolds, [Steering Behaviors For Autonomous Characters](https://www.red3d.com/cwr/steer/gdc99/) (Game
  Developers Conference 1999): steering as a desired velocity at maximum speed minus the current velocity, truncated to
  a maximum force; flee from a predator; containment. Each rule here asks that way and the sum is capped by `maxForce`.
- Iain D. Couzin, Jens Krause, Richard James, Graeme D. Ruxton and Nigel R. Franks,
  [Collective Memory and Spatial Sorting in Animal Groups](https://doi.org/10.1006/jtbi.2002.3065) (Journal of
  Theoretical Biology 218, 2002): a blind volume behind the animal (`visionAngle`) and a bounded turning rate (here a
  cap on the acceleration across the heading, `maxTurnAccel`).
- Michele Ballerini et al., [Interaction ruling animal collective behavior depends on topological rather than metric distance](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0711437105)
  (PNAS 105, 2008): real flocks steer by a bounded number of neighbours. `maxNeighbors` bounds the count, but takes the
  neighbours in grid order, not the nearest (the physics `SchoolSolver` takes the nearest; `docs/limits.md`).
- Matthias Teschner, Bruno Heidelberger, Matthias Müller, Danat Pomeranets and Markus Gross,
