  [Optimized Spatial Hashing for Collision Detection of Deformable Objects](https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/publications/tetraederCollision.pdf)
  (VMV 2003): the cell hash, three large primes XORed and masked to a power-of-two table.
- Simon Green, [Particle Simulation using CUDA](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/assets/cuda/files/particles.pdf)
  (NVIDIA, 2010), and Rama C. Hoetzlein, Fast Fixed-Radius Nearest Neighbors: Interactive Million-Particle Fluids (GPU
  Technology Conference 2014): a uniform grid one interaction radius wide, a count per cell, a prefix sum into cell
  starts, a scatter into cell order, and a search of the 3 x 3 x 3 cells around each particle.
- Guy E. Blelloch, Prefix Sums and Their Applications (CMU-CS-90-190, 1990): the work-efficient up-sweep and
  down-sweep exclusive scan of each 256-bucket block and of the block sums.
- Mark Jarzynski and Marc Olano, [Hash Functions for GPU Rendering](https://jcgt.org/published/0009/03/02/) (JCGT 9(3),
  2020), on M. E. O'Neill's PCG (2014): the per-boid tint hash.

Margo's own: the rank pass after the atomic scatter (each boid counts the lower indices in its bucket, so a bucket lists
its boids in index order and the step is deterministic on one GPU and driver), counting a bucket once when two of the 27
cells share it, the CPU twin in the same order with the cell index in f32, splitting a long `dt` into equal steps of at
most 0.05 s, the predator push strength (1 + 2 u^2), the containment and obstacle pushes, the banking and flap-phase
animation, and the built-in bird and fish meshes.

### GPU particle liquid (FLUID-02 and FLUID-03, parity bar P13, `GPULiquid` in `@margoengine/water/liquid`, 2026-11-27)

Written from the papers below, read as text. No engine source was read, three.js's `webgpu_compute_particles_fluid`
included: the README's three.js note describes that example from its public description (an MLS-MPM liquid in
compute shaders), and no companion code of any paper was opened.

- Yuanming Hu, Yu Fang, Ziheng Ge, Ziyin Qu, Yixin Zhu, Andre Pradhana and Chenfanfu Jiang,
  [A Moving Least Squares Material Point Method with Displacement Discontinuity and Two-Way Rigid Body Coupling](https://doi.org/10.1145/3197517.3201293)
  (ACM TOG 37(4), SIGGRAPH 2018): MLS-MPM, the particle's stress folded into its affine momentum with
  D_p^-1 = diag(4 / h^2) for quadratic B-splines, so a step is one scatter, a grid update and one gather.
- Chenfanfu Jiang, Craig Schroeder, Andrew Selle, Joseph Teran and Alexey Stomakhin,
  [The Affine Particle-in-Cell Method](https://doi.org/10.1145/2766996) (ACM TOG 34(4), SIGGRAPH 2015): the affine
  matrix C = sum w v (D^-1 d)^T carried by each particle, which keeps linear and angular momentum through the transfers.
- Michael Steffen, Robert M. Kirby and Martin Berzins,
  [Analysis and reduction of quadrature errors in the material point method](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.2360)
  (IJNME 76, 2008): the quadratic B-spline weights 0.5 (1.5 - f)^2, 0.75 - (f - 1)^2, 0.5 (f - 0.5)^2 and their
  partition of unity and linear completeness, which the momentum checks rely on.
- J. J. Monaghan, [Simulating Free Surface Flows with SPH](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcph.1994.1034) (J. Comput. Phys.
  110, 1994), and Markus Becker and Matthias Teschner,
  [Weakly compressible SPH for free surface flows](https://doi.org/10.2312/SCA/SCA07/209-217) (SCA 2007): the Tait
  equation p = B ((rho / rho0)^7 - 1) with B = rho0 c^2 / 7, no tension below rest density, and the trade between the
  speed of sound and compression (hydrostatic r(d) = (1 + 6 g d / c^2)^(1/6), the closed form the limits compare with).
- Alexey Stomakhin, Craig Schroeder, Lawrence Chai, Joseph Teran and Andrew Selle,
  [A Material Point Method for Snow Simulation](https://doi.org/10.1145/2461912.2461948) (ACM TOG 32(4), 2013): rigid
  colliders as level sets applied on the grid, the relative velocity's normal part removed when it points into the body
  and the tangential part reduced by Coulomb friction.
- Nadir Akinci, Markus Ihmsen, Gizem Akinci, Barbara Solenthaler and Matthias Teschner,
  [Versatile Rigid-Fluid Coupling for Incompressible SPH](https://doi.org/10.1145/2185520.2185558) (ACM TOG 31(4),
  2012), and P. W. Randles and L. D. Libersky,
  [Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics: Some recent improvements and applications](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0045-7825(96)01090-0)
  (CMAME 139, 1996): a boundary that counts in the density as liquid at rest, and mirror (ghost) particles across a
  wall. Here the container's walls lie on grid nodes and the grid's mass is mirrored across them, and a collider's
  inside counts as liquid at rest by the B-spline's share of each node behind its surface.
- Ming Gao, Xinlei Wang, Kui Wu, Andre Pradhana, Eftychios Sifakis, Cem Yuksel and Chenfanfu Jiang,
  [GPU Optimization of Material Point Methods](https://doi.org/10.1145/3272127.3275044) (ACM TOG 37(6), 2018):
  particle-to-grid scatter with atomics on the GPU.
- Mark Jarzynski and Marc Olano, [Hash Functions for GPU Rendering](https://jcgt.org/published/0009/03/02/) (JCGT 9(3),
  2020): the PCG hash of the start lattice's jitter.
- Christer Ericson, Real-Time Collision Detection (Morgan Kaufmann, 2005), section 5.1.5, "Closest point on triangle to
  point": the Voronoi-region test behind `bakeLiquidMesh`'s distance to each triangle.
- Alec Jacobson, Ladislav Kavan and Olga Sorkine-Hornung,
  [Robust Inside-Outside Segmentation using Generalized Winding Numbers](https://doi.org/10.1145/2461912.2461916) (ACM
  TOG 32(4), SIGGRAPH 2013): the sign of the mesh field from the winding number, which holds for meshes with small holes
  and either winding; and A. Van Oosterom and J. Strackee,
  [The Solid Angle of a Plane Triangle](https://doi.org/10.1109/TBME.1983.325207) (IEEE TBME 30(2), 1983): the closed
  form tan(Omega / 2) = det[a b c] / (|a||b||c| + (a.b)|c| + (a.c)|b| + (b.c)|a|) of each triangle's share.
- Sarah F. Frisken, Ronald N. Perry, Alyn P. Rockwood and Thouis R. Jones,
  [Adaptively Sampled Distance Fields](https://doi.org/10.1145/344779.344899) (SIGGRAPH 2000): a sampled distance field
  read by trilinear interpolation, with its normal from the field's gradient, as a collider's level set; the capsule
  and plane distances are the closed forms (segment distance less the radius, and n . (x - p)).
- H. Vogel, [A better way to construct the sunflower head](https://doi.org/10.1016/0025-5564(79)90080-4) (Mathematical
  Biosciences 44, 1979): points k = 0.. at radius R sqrt((k + 1/2) / N) and the golden angle apart cover a disc evenly,
  which places an emitter's particles over its nozzle without a lattice.
- The accurate profile (2026-11-27), compared before it was built. Alexandre Joel Chorin,
  [Numerical Solution of the Navier-Stokes Equations](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1968-0242392-2) (Math. Comp.
  22(104), 1968): the projection, an intermediate velocity without the pressure and then the pressure that makes it
  divergence-free. Fan Zhang, Xiong Zhang, Kam Yim Sze, Yanping Lian and Yan Liu,
  [Incompressible material point method for free surface flow](https://repository.hku.hk/handle/10722/242215) (J.
  Comput. Phys. 330, 2017; a summary of the paper, whose host did not resolve here): the same split in MPM, reported better
  than weakly compressible MPM on a dam break and on drops. Shyamini Kularathna and Kenichi Soga,
  [Implicit formulation of material point method for analysis of incompressible materials](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2016.10.013)
  (CMAME 313, 2017; a summary of the abstract): the non-incremental projection is stable in MPM and removes the explicit scheme's pressure
  oscillations and small steps. Markus Ihmsen, Jens Cornelis, Barbara Solenthaler, Christopher Horvath and Matthias
  Teschner, [Implicit Incompressible SPH](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2013.105) (IEEE TVCG 20(3), 2014; a summary of
  the paper and its introduction): a stiff equation of state restricts the time step severely, and an implicit pressure
  solve handles large steps at density deviations down to 0.01 percent, which is why the accurate profile steps at the
  flow's speed rather than the speed of sound. Yongning Zhu
  and Robert Bridson, [Animating Sand as a Fluid](https://doi.org/10.1145/1073204.1073298) (ACM TOG 24(3), 2005): particles
  carrying velocity through a grid whose pressure solve keeps it incompressible, a cell liquid when particles fill it.
  Christopher Batty, Florence Bertails and Robert Bridson,
  [A Fast Variational Framework for Accurate Solid-Fluid Coupling](https://doi.org/10.1145/1276377.1276502) (ACM TOG
  26(3), 2007): the projection as the least-kinetic-energy divergence-free velocity, which here is weighted by the nodes'
  lumped masses (W = rest density over the node's mass), holds a solid's normal velocity at its nodes and keeps the
  system symmetric. Robert Bridson, *Fluid Simulation for Computer Graphics* (2nd ed., CRC Press, 2015): the liquid's
  velocity extrapolated past its surface before the particles read it. Tassilo Kugelstadt, Andreas Longva, Nils Thuerey
  and Jan Bender, [Implicit Density Projection for Volume Conserving Liquids](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2019.2947437)
  (IEEE TVCG, 2021; a summary of the abstract): a divergence-free solve sees density changes only as a rate, so volume
  errors from steps and solver tolerance accumulate unseen; they track the density on the particles and put its deviation
  into the pressure solve. Here the deviation is the cells' density over rest (the node weights, walls mirrored) as a
  target divergence of half the excess a substep in the same solve, two-sided where no neighbour is air. M. R. Hestenes and E. Stiefel (1952, above in this file): the conjugate gradient
  solve, Jacobi-preconditioned, its sums in a fixed tree so it repeats bit for bit. The trilinear-velocity,
  constant-pressure pair (the Q1-P0 element of finite elements) has checkerboard pressure modes; the projected velocity,
  the least-kinetic-energy divergence-free field, is unique whatever the pressure's null modes, and the conjugate
  gradient solve converges on its consistent right-hand side. No companion code of any of them was read.
- The dam-break checks (2026-11-27, `gpu-liquid-dambreak.test.js`). J. C. Martin and W. J. Moyce,
  [An Experimental Study of the Collapse of Liquid Columns on a Rigid Horizontal Plane](https://www.math.ntu.edu.tw/~shyue/orch08/benchmarks/lowmach/broken-dam/91519.pdf)
  (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 244, 1952): read from the scanned pages as images, every run of tables 1 to 3 (Z against
  T = n t sqrt(g / a), each run set to one T at Z = 1.44), section 3's 300 frames a second and section 4's reason for
  the normalisation; the test copies each run it uses at each station. L. Lobovsky, E. Botia-Vera, F. Castellana,
  J. Mas-Soler and A. Souto-Iglesias, [Experimental investigation of dynamic pressure loads during dam
  break](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.0115) (J. Fluids Struct. 48, 2014): the tank, the gate 0.6 m from its end, the front's
  mean speed after t* = 1 at 300 and 600 mm (Table 1, with the other measured dam breaks it gathers) and the sensors'
  size and heights (Fig. 3, Table 2).
- W. Daniel Hillis and Guy L. Steele, [Data Parallel Algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1145/7902.7903) (CACM 29(12),
  1986), and Guy E. Blelloch, [Prefix Sums and Their Applications](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~guyb/papers/Ble93.pdf) (CMU
  technical report, 1990): the inclusive scan inside a workgroup and the per-block counts scanned once more, so the drains'
  compaction keeps the particles in order and repeats exactly.
- Barbara Solenthaler and Renato Pajarola,
  [Density Contrast SPH Interfaces](https://doi.org/10.2312/SCA/SCA08/211-218) (SCA 2008): with liquids of different
  densities the density is taken from the particles' number density and each particle's pressure from its own rest
  density, which keeps the interface sharp; here the grid sums the particles' weight (the number density) apart from their
  mass, and each liquid's Tait pressure scales with its density.
- J. U. Brackbill, D. B. Kothe and C. Zemach,
  [A Continuum Method for Modeling Surface Tension](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(92)90240-Y) (J. Comput. Phys. 100,
  1992): surface tension as the volume force sigma kappa grad c of a smoothed colour c (here the density over rest
  density on the grid), the acceleration f / rho, and the explicit step limit dt < sqrt(rho h^3 / (2 pi sigma)) that
  bounds `surfaceTension`. B. Lafaurie, C. Nardone, R. Scardovelli, S. Zaleski and G. Zanetti,
  [Modelling Merging and Fragmentation in Multiphase Flows with SURFER](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcph.1994.1123) (J.
  Comput. Phys. 113, 1994): the same force in conservative form, the divergence of the capillary tensor
  sigma (|grad c| I - grad c grad c^T / |grad c|), which needs no unit normal where |grad c| is small. A first version
  scattered that tensor as a particle stress (MLS-MPM's stress path); it gained energy at the surface, where particles
  under rest density carry no pressure to resist the tension (the tensile instability of particle methods, J. W.
  Swegle, D. L. Hicks and S. W. Attaway, [Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics Stability
  Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcph.1995.1010), J. Comput. Phys. 116, 1995), so the force is taken on the grid.
- Nadir Akinci, Gizem Akinci and Matthias Teschner,
  [Versatile Surface Tension and Adhesion for SPH Fluids](https://doi.org/10.1145/2508363.2508395) (ACM TOG 32(6),
  2013): adhesion as a pull of the liquid towards the boundary with a kernel of the distance. Theirs is zero next to the
  boundary so SPH particles are not drawn into the boundary's particles; here the boundary is a constraint on the grid,
  so the pull is full within a cell and fades to zero at two (a cubic Hermite step).
- The smooth walls (2026-11-28, `walls`). B. E. Launder and D. B. Spalding, [The numerical computation of turbulent
  flows](https://doi.org/10.1016/0045-7825(74)90029-2) (Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Eng. 3, 1974): the wall function,
  the log law u / u* = ln(E y u* / nu) / kappa with kappa = 0.4187 and E = 9.793 for a smooth wall, the viscous sublayer
  u+ = y+ below it, met at y+ = 11.225, the wall's shear rho u*^2 taken from the speed at the first grid point because a
  grid cell is far thicker than the boundary layer. S. B. Pope, Turbulent Flows (Cambridge, 2000), chapter 7: the
  sublayer and log-law regions and why the larger u* of the two holds. D. Sulsky, Z. Chen and H. L. Schreyer,
  [A particle method for history-dependent materials](https://doi.org/10.1016/0045-7825(94)90112-0) (Comput. Methods
  Appl. Mech. Eng. 118, 1994): a traction t on the boundary enters MPM as the nodal force f_i = integral of N_i t dA,
  here with the quadratic B-spline's values at the wall (1/8, 3/4, 1/8) and its integral over the container's extent.
  Margo's own: the speed the node on the wall reads lies at the B-spline weights' mean distance from the wall (13/32 of
  a cell) in the linear sublayer and at their geometric mean (exp(9/8 ln 3 - ln 2 - 11/6) = 0.2751) under the log law;
  each node's friction never reverses its motion along the wall.
- Hu et al. 2018 (above), section 6: two-way rigid coupling by giving the body the opposite of the momentum the grid
  takes at its boundary. `link` does this between frames: the collider follows the body's pose and velocity, and the
  summed impulse and moment (about the collider's centre) go to the body through its own `applyImpulse` and
  `applyTorqueImpulse`, read and cleared on the GPU in one submit so each impulse is applied once.
- The surface is `ParticleLiquid`'s, from van der Laan, Green and Sainz (I3D 2009) and Truong and Yuksel (I3D 2018),
  cited in `docs/water-liquid.md`.

Margo's own: the fixed-point integer sums (2^16 for mass and momentum, 2^10 for the collider impulses) that make the GPU
step the same on every run, the grid density with the walls mirrored and the colliders covered, the walls placed on
nodes by giving each axis a whole number of cells, the per-node speed limit of one cell a substep, the pointer as a
stirring stick that blends node velocities towards its own, counting both the grid's and the particles' collider pushes
as the body's impulse, the substep from a Courant number of 0.4 on the speed of sound, and the CPU twin in the same
order.

### Bubbles (`BubbleSolver`, `@margoengine/physics/bubbles`, 2026-11-26, FW-4)

Written from papers and a thesis read as text (no code, no companion repositories):

- S. A. Thorpe (1982) and R. F. Keeling (1993), as L. Deike and W. K. Melville, "Gas transfer by breaking waves",
  Geophys. Res. Lett. 45, 10482-10492, 2018, https://doi.org/10.1029/2018GL078758, print it: the rise of a bubble
  whose surface is rigid with surfactants (the check: their formula's values).
- A. M. Castro, "Polydispersed bubbly flow model for ship hydrodynamics with application to Athena R/V", PhD thesis,
  University of Iowa, 2011: the dissolution model (Sherwood numbers of Levich and Whitaker, Henry's law at the wall,
  kappa = 2e-9 m^2/s, H = 2.38e-7 kg/(m^3 Pa)) and its time scales at the Athena's stern (the check); the
  entrainment depth phi_ent = 0.1 m.
- G. B. Deane and M. D. Stokes, "Scale dependence of bubble creation mechanisms in breaking waves", Nature 418,
  839-844, 2002, as E. Moraga, P. Carrica, D. Drew and R. Lahey, "The modeling of air entrainment processes for surface
  ships", Mecanica Computacional XXIV, 2549-2560, 2005, use it: the size spectrum the air enters as; where a ship takes
  air in.
- P. Carrica, F. Bonetto and D. Drew (1997) and E. Paterson et al. (1997), as Castro gives them: 10 percent void at
  the injection.
- T. D. Anguelova and P. Huq, J. Mar. Sci. Eng. 5, 41, 2017: bubbles 2.5 to 4.2 mm across rise at 25 to 29 cm/s (why
  the radii stop at 1 mm).

Calibrated: the entrainment strength. The cited models all tune a source strength (S0 in Moraga et al. and Castro);
here it is the 10 percent injection void of Carrica et al. and Paterson et al. over Castro's 0.1 m, not yet checked
against a measured ship wake (only abstracts of those measurements were found).

### Grid-particle liquids (`FlipSolver`, `DeckWaterSolver`, `@margoengine/physics/flip`, 2026-11-26, FLUID-03)

Written from papers and notes read as text (no code, no companion repositories):

- C. Jiang, C. Schroeder, A. Selle, J. Teran and A. Stomakhin, "The affine particle-in-cell method", ACM Trans. Graph.
  34(4), 51, 2015, and the J. Comput. Phys. version, arXiv 1603.06188: the MAC-grid transfers (a vector c_a a face axis,
  trilinear weights, the gradient of the weight in place of D_p^-1) and their conservation of linear and angular
  momentum.
- Y. Zhu and R. Bridson, "Animating sand as a fluid", ACM Trans. Graph. 24(3), 2005: eight particles a cell, the
  surface from the particles (k(s) = max(0, (1 - s^2)^3), R twice the spacing), velocity carried into the air. Their
  particles are jittered in the octants; Margo's sit at the octants' centres, because jittered seeds set still water
  moving (measured, 6 mm/s at cells of 5 cm).
- R. Bridson and M. Muller-Fischer, "Fluid simulation", SIGGRAPH 2007 course notes, and R. Bridson, Fluid Simulation for
  Computer Graphics, 2nd ed., 2015: the MAC grid, the pressure system, MIC(0) with tau = 0.97 and its sigma = 0.25 guard;
  solid walls that take only the normal velocity, the velocity extrapolated into them, so the inviscid liquid slips
  along a solid box as along the grid's own sides.
- F. Gibou, R. Fedkiw, L.-T. Cheng and M. Kang, J. Comput. Phys. 176, 205-227, 2002 (as the course notes give it): the
  ghost-fluid free surface, theta = phi_i / (phi_i - phi_j), held at 0.01 or more.
- T. Kugelstadt, A. Longva, N. Thuerey and J. Bender, "Implicit density projection for volume conserving liquids", IEEE
  TVCG 27(4), 2021, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2019.2947437 (Algorithm 1, eqs. 10 to 12, section 3.2): the particles'
  density on the grid (trilinear, rest density at eight particles a cell), held at 1 or more beside the air and to 0.5
  to 1.5, the solids sampled as water at rest; a second pressure solve with the density's deviation as its source,
  whose gradient moves the particles, their velocities unchanged.
- H. Goldstein, C. Poole and J. Safko, Classical Mechanics, 3rd ed., 2002, section 4.10: the rotating frame's
  d'Alembert, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis accelerations, for the box riding a hull.
- M. Roberts, "The unreasonable effectiveness of quasirandom sequences", 2018 (the R2 sequence of the plastic number):
  the inflow's particle places along a bulwark.
- G. I. Taylor, "The dynamics of thin sheets of fluid. III. Disintegration of fluid sheets", Proc. R. Soc. A 253,
  313-321, 1959, and F. E. C. Culick, "Comments on a ruptured soap film", J. Appl. Phys. 31, 1128-1129, 1960: a sheet's
  rim retracts at sqrt(2 sigma / (rho e)), the estimate of what surface tension would take off a lab breaker's jet tip
  (KB-FLIP-CREST1).
- G. B. Deane and M. D. Stokes, "Scale dependence of bubble creation mechanisms in breaking waves", Nature 418,
  839-844, 2002: the cavity a plunging jet closes breaks up into the bubbles of a breaker (the box's `aeration()`, the air
  it closes over).
- M. Lobovsky, E. Botia-Vera, F. Castellana, J. Mas-Soler and A. Souto-Iglesias, "Experimental investigation of dynamic
  pressure loads during dam break", J. Fluids Struct. 48, 407-434, 2014, arXiv 1308.0115, Tables 1 and 2: the tank,
  the front's mean speed after t* = 1 and the far wall's peak pressures (the 3-D check, `check-dambreak3d.mjs`).
- J. C. Martin and W. J. Moyce, "An experimental study of the collapse of liquid columns on a rigid horizontal plane",
  Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 244, 312-324, 1952, table 2 (the check).

- N. Chentanez, M. Muller and T.-Y. Kim, "Coupling 3D Eulerian, heightfield and particle methods for interactive
  simulation of large scale liquid phenomena", SCA 2014, https://doi.org/10.2312/sca.20141117: a liquid region held to a
  larger water model in a band at its border, blending towards it over a few cells (the `sea` option's band).
- The dispersively focused wave packet of M. S. Longuet-Higgins (1976) and R. J. Rapp and W. K. Melville (Phil. Trans.
  R. Soc. A 331, 1990), as Erinin et al. describe it (both read only through that description): components of equal
  spacing in frequency converging at one place and time; the crest test gives them equal steepness a k, summing to S.
- D. Erinin, X. Liu, Q. Wang and J. H. Duncan, "Plunging breakers - Part 1", J. Fluid Mech., 2023, arXiv 2210.01925:
  N = 32 components, N dw / w = 0.77, f0 = 1.15 Hz; crest speed at jet formation 1.511 to 1.536 m/s, jet tip at impact
  1.904 to 2.010 m/s, 1.24 to 1.33 times the crest speed (the check).
- X. Barthelemy et al., "On a unified breaking onset threshold for gravity waves in deep and intermediate depth water",
  J. Fluid Mech., 2018, arXiv 1508.06002: breaking sets in where the crest's water speed passes 0.85 of the crest's
  speed (why the crest test asks for the jet to outrun the crest).

No constant is calibrated. The surface's particle radius (half a cell) and the extrapolation depth (two faces) are
Zhu and Bridson's choices.

### Water entry and exit (`EntrySolver`, `@margoengine/physics/entry`, 2026-11-26, SEA-14)

Written from papers read as text (no code, no companion repositories):

- H. Wagner, "Uber Stoss- und Gleitvorgange an der Oberflache von Flussigkeiten", ZAMM 12, 193-215, 1932, in the
  axisymmetric form T. Hulin, L. Tassin and A. Korobkin, "Gravity effects in water impact models", J. Fluid Mech. 944,
  A9, 2022, https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2022.448, give (eq. 3.3, after Korobkin and Scolan 2006): the wetted radius.
- A. A. Korobkin, "Analytical models of water impact", Eur. J. Appl. Math. 15, 821-838, 2004, the modified Logvinovich
  model, in the form of Hulin et al. eqs. 2.17 to 2.19 (after Tassin et al. 2013): the slam's pressure.
- A. Shiffman and D. C. Spencer, AMP Report 42.1R, 1945, as J. T. Antolik, J. L. Belden, N. B. Speirs and D. M. Harris,
  "Slamming forces during water entry of a simple harmonic oscillator", J. Fluid Mech. 976, 2023, arXiv 2304.08672,
  measure it (rigid spheres at 2 to 6 m/s), and N. B. Speirs, Z. Pan, J. Belden and T. T. Truscott, J. Fluid Mech. 863,
  2019, arXiv 1806.11453: the peak C of about 1 at 10 to 20 percent of the radius (the check).
- G. Birkhoff et al., "Ricochet off water", AMP Memo 42.4M, 1944, as W. Johnson and S. R. Reid, J. Mech. Eng. Sci. 17,
  71-81, 1975, and I. M. Hutchings, Int. J. Mech. Sci. 18, 243-248, 1976: the impact pressure 1/2 rho (U . n)^2 and the
  critical angle 18 degrees / sqrt(sigma) (the check).
- C. Duez, C. Ybert, C. Clanet and L. Bocquet, "Making a splash with water repellency", Nature Physics 3, 180-183, 2007,
  arXiv cond-mat/0701093: the cavity threshold.
- V. Duclaux et al., J. Fluid Mech. 591, 1-19, 2007, and J. M. Aristoff, T. T. Truscott, A. H. Techet and J. W. M. Bush,
  "The water entry of decelerating spheres", Phys. Fluids 22, 032102, 2010, https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3309454: the
  cavity's walls, d^2(R^2)/dt^2 = -2 g z from R0 at sqrt(alpha) U, alpha = cot^2(theta_c - pi/2), theta_c 160 degrees;
  the pinch (eq. 14 to 19). Their eq. 15 drops the R0^2 term of the collapse time (their limit alpha U^2 F / z >> 1); the
  solver keeps it, so its pinch is up to some 7 percent later than their closed form where that ratio is near 3.
- J. M. Aristoff and J. W. M. Bush, "Water entry of small hydrophobic spheres", J. Fluid Mech. 619, 45-78, 2009: the
  sheet's retraction speed sqrt(2 gamma / (rho delta)) and its measured thickness of about 0.2 mm.
- S. Gekle and J. M. Gordillo, "Generation and breakup of Worthington jets after cavity collapse. Part 1", J. Fluid
  Mech. 663, 293-330, 2010, arXiv 0907.5154: the jet's speed (their golf ball, 20 m/s from 2.03 m/s).
- H. Lamb, Hydrodynamics, 6th ed., 1932, section 373: the prolate spheroid's added-mass coefficients.
- S. F. Hoerner, Fluid-Dynamic Drag, 1965, ch. 6: streamlined bodies' drag; the ITTC 1957 friction line.
- P. Ward and E. Asphaug, "Asteroid impact tsunami: a probabilistic hazard assessment", Icarus 145, 64-78, 2000, as C.
  Kharif and E. Pelinovsky, C. R. Physique 6, 361-366, 2005, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crhy.2004.12.016: a transient
  cavity's water in a rim out to sqrt(2) of its radius (the wake's sources).
- R. Gunn and G. D. Kinzer, J. Meteorol. 6, 243-248, 1949: drops' terminal speeds (the splashes' heights).
- J. A. Segre et al., "Energetic and physical limitations on the breaching performance of large whales", eLife 9,
  e51760, 2020, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.51760: humpbacks leave the water at 6.1 +- 1.8 m/s pitched 56 +- 13 degrees
  (the breach's test).

Published and calibrated constants:

| Constant | Value | Source | How it was set |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| alpha (cavity opening) | 0.1325 | Aristoff et al. 2010, theta_c about 160 degrees | Published |
| xi (wetting threshold) | 0.1 | Duez et al. 2007 | Published |
| Jet speed / entry speed | 9.85 | Gekle and Gordillo 2010, golf ball | Calibrated on that one sphere; their disc threw 12.3 times (20 percent above). No other measurement found to validate it on; uncertainty some 25 percent. |
| Sheet thickness | 0.2 mm | Aristoff and Bush 2009 | Published, one case |

#### Native section geometry and independent impulse checks (SEA-14, 2026-11-28)

The native profiler implements the projected cut-section area used to recover the axisymmetric shape in
the Wagner condition. Each plane clips the original triangles, sums signed fan projections in input
order, and supplies its area to the existing radius calculation. Rust preprojects vertex positions
and packs two independent planes per f64x2 operation. No horizontal SIMD reduction changes the sum order.
The penetration and pressure still use eqs. 3.2–3.3 and 2.17–2.19 from
[Hulin, Tassin and Korobkin, 2022, *Gravity effects in two-dimensional and axisymmetric water impact models*](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2022.448).
The crown threshold uses the local liquid density in the sheet retraction speed from
[Aristoff and Bush, 2009, *Water entry of small hydrophobic spheres*](https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2012/09/aristoff-splash.pdf).

`node packages/physics/scripts/sea14-entry-measured.mjs` uses the published geometry, density ratio,
entry speed and sample rate of the plain 50 mm sphere, Figure 3(c) and §3 in
[Speirs, Belden, Pan, Holekamp, Badlissi, Jones and Truscott, 2019, *The water entry of a sphere in a jet*](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2018.931).
No measured outcome tunes the solver. Its impulse from contact to descending half-peak is 0.04520 of
entry momentum versus 0.067 ± 0.003 measured. The 1 kHz aperture-phase diagnostic gives 0.03750–0.04414.
A separate coarse read from the authors’ published figure puts descending half-peak at 4.3 ± 1 ms versus
1.98 ms modelled. Integrating the model to a fixed 4.3 ms gives 0.07260, so the short modelled pulse
matters to the impulse discrepancy. Mesh and step refinement and an analytic sphere profile did not
close the gap.

The same script can take the authors’ pinned CSV for the nominal 4 m/s, 22.23 mm hemispherical nose
from Figure 3(b) of [Antolik, Belden, Speirs and Harris, 2023, *Slamming forces during water entry of a simple harmonic oscillator*](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2023.820).
It checks the digest before reading the external replicate means and standard deviations. At one nose
radius divided by nominal speed the model integrates 0.01823 of initial body momentum versus 0.01560
measured (+16.8%). No data are embedded in the package and the measurements are separate from the model.

## Rooted plants in wind and water (`@margoengine/physics/vegetation`, BIO-01)

`vegetation/model.ts` and `vegetation-kernel/src/lib.rs` were written from the following sources without companion
code. The dry beam uses a two-term Rayleigh–Ritz projection with tip-normalized, uniform clamped-free shapes.
Taper, a hollow section and a distributed crown enter the mass and stiffness integrals.

- Sascha Eisenträger, Santosh Kapuria, Mayank Jain and Junqi Zhang,
  *On the numerical properties of high-order spectral (Euler-Bernoulli) beam elements*, 2023,
  [doi:10.1002/zamm.202200422](https://doi.org/10.1002/zamm.202200422), §3.3.2.2 and Eqs. 63–65. For a uniform
  beam, `cos(beta) cosh(beta) = -1` defines the roots and `omega = beta^2 sqrt(E I / (rho A)) / H^2`.
- Jos Stam, *Stochastic Dynamics: Simulating the Effects of Turbulence on Flexible Structures*, 1997,
  [doi:10.1111/1467-8659.00152](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8659.00152), §2 and Appendix A. Modal mass,
  stiffness and damping use projection of a distributed load. Ralf Habel, Alexander Kusternig and Michael Wimmer,
  *Physically Guided Animation of Trees*, 2009, [doi:10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01391.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01391.x),
  §3, motivates reducing tapered-plant dynamics to a few modes.
- Frank W. J. Olver et al., NIST *Digital Library of Mathematical Functions*, [§3.5(v)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.5.v).
  Gauss–Legendre weights integrate dry inertia and curvature with 16 nodes. Stem and crown drag, inertia and
  buoyancy each use three force stations.
- J. R. Morison, M. P. O’Brien, J. W. Johnson and S. A. Schaaf, *The Force Exerted by Surface Waves on Piles*, 1950,
  [Eq. 4](https://onemine.org/documents/offshore-operation-the-force-exerted-by-surface-waves-on-piles), derives the
  quadratic drag and acceleration load on a fixed cylinder. Mitul Luhar and Heidi Nepf, *Wave-induced dynamics of
  flexible blades*, 2016, [Eqs. 2–6](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.01237), give the moving-plant form. Relative
  transverse velocity sets drag, `rho V a_fluid` is the pressure-gradient term, and `rho Ca V` multiplies relative
  acceleration. Bring the plant's share of that acceleration to its mass matrix. Density times displaced volume
  minus tissue mass gives the applied buoyancy after multiplication by gravity. Its tension or compression above
  each section contributes geometric stiffness through the product of the two shape slopes. The wet test field uses
  the depth decay of Airy's deep-water orbital velocity in J. M. J. Journee and W. W. Massie,
  [*Offshore Hydromechanics*, §5.3](https://ocw.tudelft.nl/courses/offshore-hydromechanics/).
- Heli Peltola, Seppo Kellomäki, Hannu Väisänen and Veli-Pekka Ikonen, *A mechanistic model for assessing the risk
  of wind and snow damage to single trees and stands of Scots pine, Norway spruce, and birch*, 1999,
  [doi:10.1139/x99-029](https://doi.org/10.1139/x99-029). Compare the maximum outer fibre stress `E R kappa`
  and the moment `E I kappa` at the root with distinct rupture and anchorage thresholds.
  Barry Gardiner, Heli Peltola and Seppo Kellomäki compare the separate resistance criteria against field data in
  *Comparison of two models for predicting the critical wind speeds required to damage coniferous trees*, 2000.
  [doi:10.1016/S0304-3800(00)00220-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-3800(00)00220-9).
- Ernst Hairer, Christian Lubich and Gerhard Wanner, *Geometric Numerical Integration*, 2006,
  [doi:10.1007/3-540-30666-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-30666-8). Implicit midpoint preserves the quadratic
  energy of an undamped beam. Its free oscillator phase is `2 atan(omega dt/2)`. The inequality
  `0 <= x-atan(x) <= x^3/3` gives less than 1% relative phase error per step when `omega dt <= sqrt(0.12)`.
  Freezing the nonnegative drag coefficient over each solve keeps the drag term dissipative in still fluid.
- Emmanuel de Langre, *Effects of Wind on Plants*, 2008, [doi:10.1146/annurev.fluid.40.111406.102135](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.fluid.40.111406.102135),
  reviews plant-load coupling. Charlotte Py, Emmanuel de Langre and Bruno Moulia, *A frequency lock-in mechanism in the
  interaction between wind and crop canopies*, 2006, [doi:10.1017/S0022112006002667](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112006002667),
  describes feedback absent from a prescribed field. Frédérick Gosselin, Emmanuel de Langre and Bruno Machado-Almeida,
  *Drag reduction of flexible plates by reconfiguration*, 2010,
  [doi:10.1017/S0022112009993673](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112009993673), measures geometry-dependent reconfiguration.
  The solver uses small deflections and its configured projected area.

The coupling test `packages/physics/tests/coupling/vegetation.test.js` checks two uniform-beam frequencies, midpoint
energy and phase, a travelling gust, an attenuating Airy wave, rupture and uprooting, and bit-identical replay.

The worker extension splits independent modal integrations. Each participant writes only candidate rows. The
caller checks an ordered receipt before accepting the unchanged midpoint equations. The native discriminant
must be finite before a negative-roundoff clamp, so a failed worker cannot publish a fabricated frequency.

H. Spatz, F. Brüchert and J. Pfisterer, “Multiple resonance damping or how do trees escape dangerously large
oscillations?” (2007), provides independent paired stem and intact-tree ringdowns and static elastic measurements.
M. Luhar and H. M. Nepf, “Wave-induced dynamics of flexible blades” (2016), provides flume forcing, geometry and
elastic stiffness separately from the measured tip excursions. Equivalent cross-section and waveform assumptions
are reported in the diagnostic scripts and limits. [Tree experiment](https://doi.org/10.3732/ajb.94.10.1603) ·
[Blade experiment](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfluidstructs.2015.11.007)

Scatter reads those same modal coordinates in the colour, depth and shadow vertex stages. For a horizontal
offset `d(y)`, (x',y',z') = (x+d_x(y),y,z+d_z(y)); the inverse-transpose Jacobian changes only the normal's
y component, to `n_y - dot(n_xz, slope)`. See Alan H. Barr, *Global and local deformations of solid primitives*,
1984, [doi:10.1145/964965.808573](https://doi.org/10.1145/964965.808573), §3. Tests render a displaced crown,
its planted root, and a tiled counterpart on WebGPU and the WebGL2 compatibility layer.

### Rainfall runoff, infiltration and channel routing (HYDRO-02, 2026-11-25)

- W. H. Green and G. A. Ampt, [Studies on Soil Physics, Part I](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-agricultural-science/article/abs/studies-on-soil-phyics/6EE03D61E70FCEFD6EAE4D59BFCC1FF9),
  1911, pp. 1–24, establishes the sharp wetting-front conductivity and capillary relation. The publisher extract was
  checked against the modern expression and integrated form in the
  [USACE Green-Ampt technical reference](https://www.hec.usace.army.mil/confluence/rasdocs/ras1dtechref/latest/overview-of-optional-capabilities/modeling-precipitation-and-infiltration/green-ampt).
  R. G. Mein and C. L. Larson, [Modeling infiltration during a steady rain](https://doi.org/10.1029/WR009i002p00384),
  1973, separates rainfall-limited infiltration from the ponded step. S.-T. Chu,
  [Infiltration during an unsteady rain](https://doi.org/10.1029/WR014i003p00461), 1978, retains infiltration from before
  ponding. The ponded flux is `Ks(1 + A/F)`, with `A` equal to suction head times moisture deficit. For a tick with
  constant rain `r > Ks`, the threshold is `F = Ks A/(r-Ks)`. Solving the integrated law inside the available-water
  interval preserves both continuity at ponding and the water budget.
- K. J. Beven and M. J. Kirkby, [A Physically Based, Variable Contributing Area Model of Basin Hydrology](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/02626667909491834),
  1979, Eqs. 4–9, relates saturation to `ln(a/tan β)` and mean water storage. The solver applies the
  resulting local deficit as a further cap on infiltration. Each grid cell keeps independent soil water and uses
  a linear store for downward recharge.
- M. J. Lighthill and G. B. Whitham, [On Kinematic Waves I. Flood Movement in Long Rivers](https://courses.physics.ucsd.edu/2018/Fall/physics218a/Whitham_Lighthill_Kinematic%20Waves%201.pdf),
  1955, Eqs. 1–6 and §§2, 4, gives the conservation equation and the one-directional rating-law characteristics.
  The wide Manning section has rating `Q = w sqrt(S) h^(5/3)/n`. Positive characteristics give the upstream
  face discharge and backward Euler balances that face flux with cell storage. The implicit system is triangular
  in drainage order. The substitution `h = u³` gives a monotone equation in `u³` and `u⁵`. The exact routed volume
  is debited upstream and credited downstream.
- R. E. Horton, [Erosional development of streams and their drainage basins](https://pdodds.w3.uvm.edu/research/papers/others/1945/horton1945a.pdf),
  1945, discusses infiltration excess and drainage structure. L. B. Leopold and T. Maddock Jr.,
  [The hydraulic geometry of stream channels and some physiographic implications](https://doi.org/10.3133/pp252),
  1953, describes observed relationships between discharge and channel hydraulics. BiomeView estimates mean flows
  from contributing area times annual precipitation less actual evapotranspiration. It inverts the existing
  Fu-Budyko moisture-index function for the local climate estimate. A live view can take the routed discharge.

The numerical implementation uses the repository's pinned scalar arithmetic and a SIMD pass for rain and melt.
The work memory and prognostic quantities belong to the world arena. Tests exercise ponding, steady Manning flow,
wetness-index saturation, volume closure, flood spread, and deterministic replay. The implementation uses the
publications and this repository's field contracts.

- Roger E. Smith, [Comment on Modeling Infiltration During a Steady Rain by Mein and Larson](https://www.tucson.ars.ag.gov/unit/publications/PDFfiles/170.pdf), 1973, equations 6 and 8. The native step retains the preponding and ponded balance and uses overflow-safe equivalents for extreme ratios. The monotone numerical roots and ordered water sums must give finite candidate state before publication.
- W. Ahrens, James Demmel and Hong Diep Nguyen, [Algorithms for Efficient Reproducible Floating Point Summation](https://doi.org/10.1145/3389360), 2020. Floating-point addition depends on evaluation order. The runoff worker partitions write per-cell receipts, then the caller folds the volumes in the original cell order. The ordered topographic means and kinematic drainage graph keep their existing operations.
- Reed M. Maxwell et al., [Surface-subsurface model intercomparison](https://doi.org/10.1002/2013WR013725), 2014. Its tilted V catchment motivates the staged test geometry and rain/recession sequence. The camera test is for routing and renderer direction with authored inputs.

### Aquatic locomotion (LIFE-03, `@margoengine/physics/life`)

- Jesús Sánchez-Rodríguez, Christophe Raufaste and Médéric Argentina, “Scaling the tail beat frequency and
  swimming speed in underwater undulatory swimming” (2023). Equation 4 relates length and the fast frequency
  envelope. Figure 1 reports the fit `f₀ = 22 Hz, Lc = 0.4 m, κ = 4`. The code solves the monotone
  polynomial in a scaled bracket even for very long bodies. [Primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41368-6)
- Sparks et al. (2024), Table 1 still, free-stream trout trials. The diagnostic drives the measured waveform
  from rest with no target velocity. Webb et al. (1984) gives independent same-species morphology for estimated
  geometry. [Sparks et al.](https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.247873) · [Webb et al.](https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.109.1.77)

- M. J. Lighthill, [Note on the swimming of slender fish](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112060001110) (1960),
  equations 6–7 and 13–16. Read the trailing-edge momentum and power integrals. For a sinusoidal travelling
  wave of angular frequency ω and wavenumber k with zero trailing envelope slope, mean thrust is
  m′a²(ω²−k²U²)/4 and through-flow power is m′Ua²ω(ω−kU)/2, where m′ = πρs²/4 and s is the full span.
  The operating efficiency is (1+kU/ω)/2 when both flux and useful work are positive. At startup the
  cycle-mean thrust is extrapolated to zero through-flow. A stopped tail applies no active load.
- M. S. Triantafyllou, G. S. Triantafyllou and D. K. P. Yue,
  [Hydrodynamics of Fishlike Swimming](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.fluid.32.1.33) (2000), publisher
  abstract on unsteady foil and vortex wake effects. D. Floryan, T. Van Buren, C. W. Rowley and A. J. Smits,
  [Scaling the propulsive performance of heaving and pitching foils](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2017.302)
  (2017), sections 2 and 7 for the role of amplitude and reduced frequency. G. K. Taylor, R. L. Nudds and
  A. L. R. Thomas, [Flying and swimming animals cruise at a Strouhal number tuned for high power efficiency](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02000)
  (2003), for the measured 0.2–0.4 range used in one cruise fixture. The simulation reports St = 2af/U
  across its domain. It leaves species-dependent gait and speed to the supplied parameters.
- X. Tu and D. Terzopoulos, [Artificial Fishes: Physics, Locomotion, Perception, Behavior](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~turk/bio_sim/articles/fish_terzopoulos.pdf)
  (1994), sections 2.2–2.4 for local body and fin control. R. W. Blake,
  [The mechanics of labriform locomotion I. Labriform locomotion in the angelfish](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=fd622a360d0729f55e096ee056a307ceb6341662&repid=rep1&type=pdf)
  (1979), equation 6 for quadratic blade drag. A feathered recovery leaves a half-wave cos² active and the
  cycle integral of that factor is 1/4. P. Domenici and R. W. Blake,
  [The kinematics and performance of fish fast-start swimming](https://www.mbl.ku.dk/JFSteffensen/FHL/Reviewjeb1997.pdf)
  (1997), for body-scaled but species-specific curvature and manoeuvres.
- T. I. Fossen and O. E. Fjellstad, [Nonlinear modelling of marine vehicles in 6 degrees of freedom](https://www.fossen.biz/publications/1995%20Fossen%20and%20Fjellstad%20JMMS.pdf)
  (1995), for Kirchhoff momentum transport and separation of rigid and relative-fluid inertia.
  [MIT 13.021 hydrodynamics supplement](https://web.mit.edu/13.021/13021_2003/suppnotes/supp03.pdf)
  (2003), for potential-flow added mass of elliptic cross sections. Integrating an ellipsoid's strips gives
  transverse geometric mass factors 2πLr²/3, geometric pitch/yaw factors πL³r²/30 and the rolling factor
  πL(rx²−ry²)²/15. Each is multiplied by local wet density. J. R. Morison, M. P. O'Brien, J. W. Johnson and
  S. A. Schaaf, [The force exerted by surface waves on piles](https://onemine.org/documents/offshore-operation-the-force-exerted-by-surface-waves-on-piles)
  (1950), equation 4 for undisturbed fluid inertia plus added mass and drag. Material acceleration comes from
  the velocity difference along a first-order fluid trajectory. A local wave tangent cuts the ellipsoid at
  normalized level d. Integrating disk sections gives submerged fraction (2+d)(1+d)²/4 for −1 < d < 1.
- [ITTC Resistance Test, 7.5-02-02-01](https://www.ittc.info/media/11780/75-02-02-01.pdf), ITTC-1957
  correlation line 0.075/(log10(Re)−2)², paired with the Blasius flat-plate coefficient 1.328/√Re
  from [NACA TN 4318](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19930085111/downloads/19930085111.pdf), figure 5.
  Use the smoothstep blend over the configurable transition range [Re₀, 2Re₀]. Drag is linearly implicit
  with the previous speed in its coefficient. A coast with constant quadratic coefficient therefore steps
  the straight-line solution exactly at every tick.
- D. Floryan, T. Van Buren and A. J. Smits, [Forces and energetics of intermittent swimming](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00971)
  (2017), verified the use of an active/recovery duty cycle. D. Weihs,
  [Dynamics of dolphin porpoising revisited](https://academic.oup.com/icb/article-pdf/42/5/1071/1878017/i1540-7063-042-05-1071.pdf)
  (2002), describes the submerged burst, glide and aerial phases and sensitivity to the entry/exit process.
  Preserve ballistic motion while dry. The simulation resolves partial displacement with tangent-plane
  immersion. Unsteady wave breaking and entry splash feedback require separate fluid solvers.

The spine's smoothstep amplitude envelope has zero trailing slope. A front-loaded quadratic correction
cancels the mass-weighted transverse motion of the ellipsoid's spine without changing the tail displacement
or tail slope. Its coefficient is obtained by integrating the envelope against an elliptical cross section.
The kernel uses Rust SIMD for vector products and square roots, a unit-quaternion midpoint rotation and
world-owned f64 rows. Wasm exports the exact opposite of the propulsive and fin impulses to the wake port.
The kernel and bindings were written from the cited equations. The sampling and memory contract come from
Margo Engine's own field and solver specifications.

## Falling plates, winged seeds and hail (AERO-05)

- Anders Andersen, Umberto Pesavento and Z. Jane Wang, *Analysis of transitions between fluttering,
  tumbling and steady descent of falling cards* (2005), [doi:10.1017/S0022112005005847](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112005005847).
  Equations 3.1–3.9 give the elliptical plate's mass, added mass and moment of inertia, buoyant
  weight, Kirchhoff cross terms, translational and rotational circulation, drag and dissipative pitch
  moment. Transform the equations to the fixed flight plane. Its acceleration has the difference
  of the two added masses in the rotating-basis terms. The defaults are the paper's §5.2 coefficients
  for its Figure 3 sweep. Along the span a separate drag term acts on the cross-sectional area.
- Anders Andersen, Umberto Pesavento and Z. Jane Wang, *Unsteady aerodynamics of fluttering and
  tumbling plates* (2005), [doi:10.1017/S002211200500594X](https://doi.org/10.1017/S002211200500594X).
  Its measurements motivate a circulation term proportional to angular velocity. Andrew Belmonte,
  Hagai Eisenberg and Elisha Moses, *From Flutter to Tumble: Inertial Drag and Froude Similarity
  in Falling Paper* (1998), [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.81.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.81.345),
  gives a separate falling-paper experiment. The observed transition depends on the geometry and
  setup. The solver advances the equations for every plate throughout its fall.
- David Lentink, William B. Dickson, Johan L. van Leeuwen and Michael H. Dickinson, *Leading-Edge
  Vortices Elevate Lift of Autorotating Plant Seeds* (2009),
  [doi:10.1126/science.1174196](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1174196), observed the attached
  vortex of rotating seeds. Djamel Rezgui, Ignacio Hernández Arroyo and Raf Theunissen,
  *Model for Sectional Leading-Edge Vortex Lift for the Prediction of Rotating Samara Seeds
  Performance* (2020), [doi:10.1017/aer.2020.25](https://doi.org/10.1017/aer.2020.25), Eqs. 7, 11–18
  and 20–23 and Table 1, supply the velocity triangles, polar, literature coefficients, elemental
  thrust and torque. Project body motion onto each strip's tangent and the spin axis. The signed
  extension of the polar uses absolute sine and cosine inside the normal coefficient and a signed
  `sin(alpha) cos(alpha)` multiplier. Its pressure drag cancels the cosine in `CL tan(alpha)`.
  The kernel sums the strip forces and axial moments and advances the body's velocity and spin.
  Jonathan McConnell and Tuhin Das, *Reduced Order Modeling of an Autorotating Samara for
  Steady-State and Dynamic Analysis* (2022), [doi:10.1016/j.ifacol.2022.11.163](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ifacol.2022.11.163),
  discusses time integration of blade torques and lift and the effect of degrees of freedom removed.
- Victor Manuel Ortega-Jimenez, Noah Suk-Won Kim and Robert Dudley, *Superb autorotator: rapid decelerations
  in impulsively launched samaras* (2019), [doi:10.1098/rsif.2018.0456](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2018.0456),
  reports separate natural free-drop morphology, speed, spin and cone statistics in Table 1.
  Only the five natural hand drops inform the comparison. Published speed, spin and cone are held out.
- Gary K. Nave Jr. et al., *Wind Dispersal of Natural and Biomimetic Maple Samaras* (2021),
  [doi:10.3390/biomimetics6020023](https://doi.org/10.3390/biomimetics6020023), Table 1 gives the
  independent Norway maple still-air cohort. Mean measured mass, length, wing loading and centre of mass
  determine the input rectangle and its axis. The measured lab speed and spin are held out. Both cohorts
  retain the Rezgui polar and the production blade pitch. No external models, source code or video are bundled.
- Frank W. J. Olver et al., NIST DLMF [§3.5(v)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.5.v) gives Gauss–Legendre
  quadrature. Three nodes exactly integrate the cubic radius moment in the opposed-blade
  test. Ernst Hairer, Syvert P. Nørsett and Gerhard Wanner, *Solving Ordinary Differential
  Equations I*, 2nd ed. (1993), [doi:10.1007/978-3-540-78862-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-78862-1),
  describes explicit Runge–Kutta methods and extrapolation. RK4 step doubling uses a local
  error estimate of the full/half step difference divided by 15. Both accepted half steps advance
  the state. World and inner subdivisions are dyadic.
- Wouter Terra, Andrea Sciacchitano and Fulvio Scarano,
  *Aerodynamic drag of a transiting sphere by large-scale tomographic-PIV* (2017),
  [doi:10.1007/s00348-017-2331-0](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00348-017-2331-0), report `Cd=0.47` for
  their sphere at `Re≈10,000`. It is a rounded-grain default. Andrew Heymsfield and Robert Wright,
  *Graupel and Hail Terminal Velocities: Does a “Supercritical” Reynolds Number Apply?* (2014),
  [doi:10.1175/JAS-D-14-0034.1](https://doi.org/10.1175/JAS-D-14-0034.1), Eqs. 5 and 6,
  supply precipitation's local air and size law. Equating quadratic drag to buoyant weight
  at that terminal speed gives `Cd = 4 D (rhoIce - rhoAir) g / (3 rhoAir Vt²)`.
- Gino van den Bergen, *Ray Casting against General Convex Objects with Application to Continuous
  Collision Detection* (2004), [author presentation references](https://media.gdcvault.com/gdc2012/slides/Programming%20Track/Vincent_ROBERT_Track_ADifferentApproach.pdf), gives the conservative advancement underlying the rigid scene's
  sweep. A contact against fixed geometry reverses the inward normal component by the
  restitution coefficient, leaving the tangent component unchanged. Rigid geometry is queried
  through an adapter. The solver also accepts a pure swept-sphere boundary for analytic tests.
- W3C GPU Working Group, [*WebGPU Shading Language*, storage buffers](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#storage-address-space).
  The Hail vertex shader reads two f32 vectors per rendered stone. Their pose comes from the world
  clock. The existing ribbon lighting and depth tests apply at the actual position.

The solver and its tests were written from equations and specifications. The APW flutter/tumble
pair, exact grain and plate solutions, cubic blade moment, rigid wall and platform contacts,
frame-rate and snapshot equality, and physical hail GPU replay are exercised by focused fixtures.

### Sediment transport and channel morphodynamics (HYDRO-03, 2026-11-25)

- E. Meyer-Peter and R. Müller, [Formulas for Bed-Load Transport](https://repository.tudelft.nl/record/uuid:4fda9b61-be28-4703-ab06-43cdc2a21bd7),
  1948, measures solid flux above a critical Shields stress. M. Wong and G. Parker,
  [Reanalysis and Correction of Bed-Load Relation of Meyer-Peter and Müller Using Their Own Database](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9429(2006)132:11(1159)),
  2006, Eq. 24, supplies the plane-bed correction. Its dimensionless capacity is
  `3.97 max(0, Shields − 0.0495)^(3/2)`, scaled by the square root of submerged gravity times median grain diameter
  cubed. Bed shear follows the same Manning drag used by shallow water. All transferred bed material comes from
  the mobile layer whose mass is tallied separately.
- L. van Rijn, [Sediment Transport, Part II. Suspended Load Transport](https://www.leovanrijn-sediment.com/papers/P2-1984b.pdf),
  1984, Eqs. 1–3, 11–13, 19a and 38, supplies the dimensionless grain size, transport stage, three clear-water settling
  regimes, Rouse profile and near-bed concentration. The solver holds the concentration below the reference level
  at its reference value and uses eight-point Gauss-Legendre panels above it. Its depth-mean load relaxes to that
  profile over one settling time, with a formation-specific representative suspended diameter. The relaxation
  uses an exponential over the tick, and finite-volume advection uses donor concentration and a shared face
  water flux. A donor limiter preserves nonnegative sediment carried through each face.
- C. Paola and V. Voller, [A Generalized Exner Equation for Sediment Mass Balance](https://doi.org/10.1029/2004JF000274),
  2005, derives solid storage over the bed. In a bed with constant porosity, deposited solid volume divided by
  the local solid fraction and the triangulated vertex area gives elevation gain. Losses take the opposite
  sign. Each face uses the same transferred volume on both sides. The open-boundary ledger plus water-column and
  bed inventories closes the solid mass balance.
- S. Ikeda, G. Parker and K. Sawai, [Bend Theory of River Meanders. Part 1. Linear Development](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/abs/bend-theory-of-river-meanders-part-1-linear-development/EAE7F1CD6803CC4F4F61148CB4FE96B3),
  1981, §§2–3, Eqs. 11–13, relates bank erosion and deposition to the tangential velocity perturbation at a bank.
  The bordered cell supplies the near-bank velocity. The connected wet band transverse to the interface
  supplies the depth-weighted tangential mean. Its sign defines downstream. The two-sided transfer changes
  storage by equal and opposite amounts; optional root pressure reduces the mobilised area and raises
  the Shields threshold. Gary Parker's [Universal Bank Erosion Coefficient for Meandering Rivers](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9429(1989)115:6(744))
  (1989) examines the local relation and how bank materials set the erodibility. The engine resolves
  finite Cartesian sections and uses the caller's bank coefficient.
- Hasan Eslami et al., [Investigating the celerity of propagation for small perturbations and dispersive sediment aggradation under a supercritical flow](https://esurf.copernicus.org/articles/13/437/2025/)
  (2025), §4.1 and the [CC BY 4.0 measurement workbook](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14883164). The separate
  diagnostic prescribes rectangular normal flow from measured water discharge, imposed slope, flume width and
  Manning roughness from preliminary tests. The eleven independently measured solid capacities stay outside
  the solver inputs. The diagnostic uses the separately measured grain properties and untuned Wong–Parker
  coefficient, and reports the discrepancies and the limits of the comparison.

The SIMD module reads the framework's water field and the solver contributes to TerrainBed's existing vertex
accumulator. Water follows that bed. The same concentration enters the renderer's existing absorption and
back-scattering law by way of a float texture. Tests reproduce van Rijn's three settling regimes, an analytic
Rouse profile, Wong–Parker transport, quiescent delta deposition, a two-sided bank transfer and rooted control,
solid mass balance, the coupled bed and water response, snapshots and backend-equivalent optical results.
The solver uses the papers and the repository's existing coupling infrastructure.

### Pedestrian contact and crowd motion (LIFE-05)

- D. Helbing, I. Farkas and T. Vicsek, [Simulating dynamical features of escape panic](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0009448)
  (2000), equations 1–3. Desired-motion acceleration is (v* − v)/τ. For contact overlap δ,
  normal stiffness contributes kδ and sliding friction acts against relative tangential speed
  with coefficient κδ. Static walls use the same compression and sliding relations.
  The documented default stiffness and friction are the paper's illustrated material values.
- I. Karamouzas, B. Skinner and S. J. Guy, [Universal power law governing pedestrian interactions](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.238701)
  (2014), equations 2–3. Energy is k exp(−t/τ₀)/t² and the force is its negative gradient
  with respect to separation. If a = v·v, b = r·v and c = r·r − R² for combined contact radius R,
  the first forward root is c/(√(b²−ac)−b). Its spatial gradient is
  (r+vt)/√(b²−ac). Apply the measured inverse-square energy law before overlap with an
  explicit response-time offset for short times. The authors estimate an unscreened decay
  near 3 s and report shorter observed horizons in the denser scenes.
- R. Narain, A. Golas, S. Curtis and M. C. Lin, [Aggregate dynamics for dense crowd simulation](https://doi.org/10.1145/1618452.1618468)
  (2009), equations 7–9 and 13–18. Compression activates a response when predicted packing would
  exceed the density bound. This implementation uses a local one-sided speed reduction as a
  compressible approximation. The discrete normal and friction impulses give the per-body
  contact force. The normalized compact density weight in two dimensions is
  4(1−r²/h²)³/(πh²) for r<h, obtained by integrating the cubic radially over a disk.
- J. van den Berg, S. J. Guy, M. Lin and D. Manocha, [Reciprocal n-body Collision Avoidance](https://gamma.cs.unc.edu/ORCA/publications/ORCA.pdf)
  (2011), equation 5 and section 5.4. A relative correction u gives two permitted half-planes.
  The original equal shares minimize equal squared corrections. Minimizing their mass-weighted
  squared magnitudes subject to δv₁−δv₂=u gives fractions m₂/(m₁+m₂) and m₁/(m₁+m₂).
  A wall or a scripted obstacle gives the moving person full responsibility.
- W. H. Warren and S. Whang, [Visual guidance of walking through apertures](https://doi.org/10.1037/0096-1523.13.3.371)
  (1987), observed shoulder rotation when the clearance becomes small relative to body width.
  The solver determines the minimum orientation needed from the projected support of an
  ellipse with the supplied shoulder width and fore-aft depth. A finite turn rate updates the heading.
  A. Seyfried, O. Passon, B. Steffen, M. Boltes, T. Rupprecht and W. Klingsch,
  [New Insights into Pedestrian Flow Through Bottlenecks](https://doi.org/10.1287/trsc.1090.0263)
  (2009), table 2 and sections 3–4, measured stop, release and staggered passage in different
  door widths. A six-walker fixture verifies staggered passage and release with available clearance.

- U. Weidmann, [Transporttechnik der Fussgänger](https://doi.org/10.3929/ethz-b-000242008)
  (1993), chapter 4, is the source for the ordinary free pace of 1.34 m/s and the reference
  packing density of 5.4 people/m². The crowd's locally compressible law uses those scales.

For a pair of masses use inverse effective mass μ = 1/m₁+1/m₂. With undamped closing velocity v
along the outward normal, the backward-Euler spring impulse is
dt·k·max(0,δ−dt·v)/(1+μ·k·dt²). The sliding update divides the tangential relative
speed by 1+μ·dt·κ·δ′, where δ′ is the remaining compression after solving the normal.
A pair receives opposite impulses. The Rust kernel uses world-owned row storage, sorted neighbor
cells, normalized elliptical projection and SIMD products, floors and square roots. Shape contact
uses the two support radii along the line separating body centres. No companion code was used.

### Landscape evolution (HYDRO-04)

- Jean Braun and Sean D. Willett, [A very efficient O(n), implicit and parallel method to solve the stream power equation governing fluvial incision and landscape evolution](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geomorph.2012.10.008), 2013,
  use a backward difference in time and solve downstream elevations first. Guillaume Cordonnier, Jean Braun,
  Marie-Paule Cani, Bedřich Beneš, Éric Galin, Adrien Peytavie and Eric Guérin, [Large Scale Terrain Generation from Tectonic Uplift and Fluvial Erosion](https://cs.purdue.edu/homes/bbenes/papers/Cordonier16CGF.pdf), 2016, equation 2,
  show the closed-form update with uplift for the linear slope case. With weights \(w_{ij}\) over receivers and
  physical edge lengths \(d_{ij}\), the mesh uses \(a_{ij}=\Delta t K Q_i^m w_{ij}/d_{ij}\) and solves
  \(h_i'=(h_i+\Delta t U_i+\sum a_{ij}h_j')/(1+\sum a_{ij})\). Shields thresholds and the sediment balance are
  applied as separate physical constraints.
- Thomas G. Freeman, [Calculating catchment area with divergent flow based on a regular grid](https://doi.org/10.1016/0098-3004(91)90048-I), 1991,
  apportions discharge to descending neighbours by the 1.1 power of the slope. Shashank Kumar Anand, Milad
  Hooshyar and Amilcare Porporato, [Linear layout of multiple flow-direction networks for landscape-evolution simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.03176),
  2020, section 4, give the downstream-first ordering by receiver count for a directed acyclic terrain graph.
  Hugo Schott, Axel Paris, Lucie Fournier, Eric Guérin and Éric Galin, [Large-scale Terrain Authoring through Interactive Erosion Simulation](https://doi.org/10.1145/3592787),
  2023, section 4.1, add local rainfall before passing runoff down the slope. Their steepest receiver and parallel
  approximation were compared with the exact multidirectional graph. The graph here distributes the actual local
  rainfall in m³/s using the bed's triangle support areas. It processes donors before receivers for routing.
- Philippe Davy and Dimitri Lague, [Fluvial erosion/transport equation of landscape evolution models revisited](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008JF001146),
  2009, equations 3–8, balance erosion and deposition with a travel length. A constant length within a reach gives
  exponential survival over that reach. Miguel Wong and Gary Parker, [Reanalysis and Correction of Bed-Load Relation of Meyer-Peter and Müller Using Their Own Database](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9429(2006)132:11(1159)),
  2006, give dimensionless transport \(3.97(\theta-\theta_c)_+^{3/2}\) with \(\theta_c=0.0495\). This caps
  the volume sent downstream per class, from local Shields stress, wetted width and geological time. Incoming
  material above capacity deposits in the loose layer. The layer keeps its transported fractions on subsequent steps.
- Guillaume Cordonnier, Éric Galin, James Gain, Bedřich Beneš, Eric Guérin, Adrien Peytavie and Marie-Paule Cani,
  [Authoring Landscapes by Combining Ecosystem and Terrain Erosion Simulation](https://people.cs.uct.ac.za/~jgain/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/cordonnier2017.pdf),
  2017, separate vegetation's root stabilisation and climate-driven weathering from runoff. Bedřich Beneš and Rafael
  Forsbach, [Layered Data Representation for Visual Simulation of Terrain Erosion](https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/sccg/2001/12150080/12OmNxvwoYe),
  2001, transfer loose material above a repose slope. Joshua Roering, James Kirchner and William Dietrich,
  [Evidence for nonlinear, diffusive sediment transport on hillslopes and implications for landscape morphology](https://doi.org/10.1029/1998WR900090),
  1999, equations 1–2, give the small-slope diffusion law and its conservation equation. This solver combines
  linear creep and a second flux proportional to the excess above repose. For each face, its two elevation values
  have a conserved weighted mean and an exactly solvable exponential height difference. If the difference crosses
  repose, the rest of the step continues with creep alone. The symmetric face sweeps compose those fluxes.
- Tien H. Wu, William P. McKinnell III and Douglas N. Swanston, [Strength of tree roots and landslides on Prince of Wales Island, Alaska](https://doi.org/10.1139/t79-003),
  1979, treat roots as an added shear strength. The solver adds supplied root pressure to the mechanical thresholds.
  For rooted loose soil the small-slope overburden closure increases the repose slope by root stress divided by
  the soil's weight per support area.
- Xing Mei, Philippe Decaudin and Bao-Gang Hu, [Fast Hydraulic Erosion Simulation and Visualization on GPU](https://www-evasion.imag.fr/Publications/2007/MDH07/FastErosion_PG07.pdf),
  2007, and Ondřej Šťava, Bedřich Beneš, Matthew Brisbin and Jaroslav Křivánek, [Interactive Terrain Modeling Using Hydraulic Erosion](https://dcgi.fel.cvut.cz/publications/2008/stava-sca-erosion/),
  2008, evolve a resolved water column and use its velocity to transfer bed material. Here discharge is a
  catchment average and the world can receive time-averaged stress from HYDRO-03. The hydraulic event path
  remains the shallow-water and sediment solvers.

The Rust and TypeScript implementation follows the equations and this repository's terrain and registry contracts.
The coupling tests cover the implicit result, exact face diffusion, rainfall and sediment balances, the linked
sediment shear field, the rigid heightfield and deterministic playback.

## Utility post passes: Kawase and dual-filter blur, 1D LUT, colour average, depth downsampling (2026-11-25)

`@margoengine/post/kawase-blur`, `lut1d`, `color-average` and `depth-downsample`. Feature names and options were compared
with the public API documentation pages of pmndrs postprocessing (KawaseBlurPass, KawaseBlurMaterial, KernelSize,
MipmapBlurPass, LUT1DEffect, ColorAverageEffect, DepthDownsamplingPass,
https://pmndrs.github.io/postprocessing/public/docs/); no source of it was read.

Research compared:
- Masaki Kawase, *Frame Buffer Postprocessing Effects in DOUBLE-S.T.E.A.L (Wreckless)*, GDC 2003. Used: four bilinear
  taps k + 0.5 texels out per pass. The preset offset lists are Margo's, chosen by the variance each pass adds,
  (k^2 + (k + 1)^2) / 2 per axis, to match a Gaussian of sigma = kernel width / 6 (checked by a unit test).
- Marius Bjorge, *Bandwidth-Efficient Rendering*, SIGGRAPH 2015 course "Moving Mobile Graphics". Used: the dual filter
  (five-tap halving, eight-tap doubling).
- Jorge Jimenez, *Next Generation Post Processing in Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare*, SIGGRAPH 2014 (13-tap pyramid;
  Margo's Bloom already uses it; heavier than a plain blur needs).
- Filip Strugar, *An Investigation of Fast Real-Time GPU-Based Image Blur Algorithms*, Intel, 2014 (compares Gaussian,
  Kawase and compute blurs by quality and cost).
- Jeremy Selan, *Using Lookup Tables to Accelerate Color Transformations*, GPU Gems 2, 2005, chapter 24,
  https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems2/part-iii-high-quality-rendering/chapter-24-using-lookup-tables-accelerate-color
  and Adobe, *Cube LUT Specification* 1.0, 2013 (the 1D table text format).
- Rafael Gonzalez and Richard Woods, *Digital Image Processing*, ch. 6 (intensity as the channel mean).
- Ned Greene, Michael Kass and Gavin Miller, *Hierarchical Z-Buffer Visibility*, SIGGRAPH 1993,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/166117.166147 (conservative depth reductions); Louis Bavoil and Johan Andersson, *Stable SSAO
  in Battlefield 3 with Selective Temporal Filtering*, GDC 2012 (alternating min and max); Johannes Kopf, Michael Cohen,
  Dani Lischinski and Matt Uyttendaele, *Joint Bilateral Upsampling*, SIGGRAPH 2007,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/1276377.1276497 (what a low-resolution depth guides). The median choice of the representative
  mode is Margo's: the median is one of the samples, unchanged by the nonlinear depth encoding, and lies on the surface
  covering most of the footprint.

## Render graph (2026-11-26)

`@margoengine/post/render-graph` `RenderGraph`. Feature names were compared with the public documentation pages of
Babylon.js Frame Graph and Node Render Graph (https://doc.babylonjs.com, "Frame Graph" section); no source of it was
read. The JSON shape, slot types, `name@previous` history reads, effect tasks over the PostStack protocol and the
error codes are Margo's.

Research compared:
- Yuriy O'Donnell, *FrameGraph: Extensible Rendering Architecture in Frostbite*, GDC 2017,
  https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1024612/FrameGraph-Extensible-Rendering-Architecture-in (setup, compile and execute
  phases; transient resources declared by passes and aliased by lifetime).
- Graham Wihlidal, *Halcyon: Rapid Innovation using Modern Graphics*, Reboot Develop 2019 (a render graph with
  automatic resource transitions and transient aliasing).
- Arthur B. Kahn, *Topological Sorting of Large Networks*, CACM 5(11), 1962, https://doi.org/10.1145/368996.369025
  (the build order and cycle detection).
- Massimiliano Poletto and Vivek Sarkar, *Linear Scan Register Allocation*, ACM TOPLAS 21(5), 1999,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/330249.330250 (lifetimes assigned in order to a free list of physical slots, as transient
  textures are here).

## Trail texture (2026-11-26)

`@margoengine/post/trail` `TrailTexture`. Feature names and options were compared with the public documentation of
drei's `useTrailTexture` (https://drei.docs.pmnd.rs/misc/use-trail-texture) and its live examples; no source of it was
read. The texture identity kept across frames (fade into a second target, copy back), the half-radius stamp spacing,
the frame-speed weight and the cut to black below 1/1024 are Margo's.

Research compared:
- Thomas Porter and Tom Duff, *Compositing Digital Images*, SIGGRAPH 1984, https://doi.org/10.1145/800031.808606
  (stamps composited over the trail).
- Rafael Gonzalez and Richard Woods, *Digital Image Processing*, 4th ed., 2018, ch. 3 (screen, additive and lighten
  combinations of intensities).
- Robert G. Brown, *Smoothing, Forecasting and Prediction of Discrete Time Series*, 1963 (exponential smoothing of the
  pointer samples).
- Turner Whitted, *Anti-Aliased Line Drawing Using Brush Extrusion*, SIGGRAPH 1983, and Steve Strassmann, *Hairy
  Brushes*, SIGGRAPH 1986 (a stroke as a brush footprint swept along the path; sampling it closer than its radius leaves
  no gaps).

## Mesh blending (2026-11-26)

`@margoengine/post/mesh-blend` `MeshBlend`. Built from published prose descriptions only; no engine's or plugin's
shader or source was read. The feature list (per-mesh tag and radius, depth-slope rejection) follows the gap row and
public feature descriptions of screen-space mesh blenders. The tag pass that also writes untagged core surfaces (so
only a pixel whose centre holds no visible core surface borrows a neighbour's tag, which settles the 1x tag pass
against the stack's nearest-sample resolved depth), the golden-angle spiral search refined by bisection, the
meet-in-the-middle depth test with each side's slope carried half the seam span, and the float16-exact split key are
Margo's.

Research compared:
- Jack Tollenaar, *Mesh Seam Smoothing/Blending* (project write-up, undated),
  https://sites.google.com/view/jack-tollenaar/mesh-seam-smoothing-blending: per-object ids in a separate target, a
  post pass that finds the nearest id change within a radius scaled by depth, samples the colour mirrored across the
  seam and mixes 50% at the seam down to 0% at the radius, with a depth comparison so overlapping but untouching
  objects do not blend. Margo takes the id target, the mirror and the falloff from this description.
- Andrew Hamilton and Kenneth Brown, *Photogrammetry and Star Wars Battlefront*, GDC 2016,
  https://gdcvault.com/play/1022981/Photogrammetry-and-Star-Wars-Battlefront (natural meshes blended into the
  environment as an art-pipeline goal; no screen-space method described).
- Jeremy Moore, *Terrain Rendering in Far Cry 5*, GDC 2018, https://gdcvault.com/play/1025480/Terrain-Rendering-in-Far-Cry
  (terrain data sampled by objects: object-space blending, the per-object alternative, which needs the terrain's
  material on every object).
- Tristan Lorach, *Soft Particles*, NVIDIA whitepaper, 2007,
  https://developer.download.nvidia.com/whitepapers/2007/SDK10/SoftParticles_hi.pdf (a smooth fade over a depth
  difference instead of a binary depth test; the smooth falloff and the depth-difference fade).
- Carlo Tomasi and Roberto Manduchi, *Bilateral Filtering for Gray and Color Images*, ICCV 1998,
  https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV.1998.710815 (a range term that stops a filter crossing a depth edge: the rejection).
- Lance Williams, *Casting Curved Shadows on Curved Surfaces*, SIGGRAPH 1978, https://doi.org/10.1145/965139.807402,
  and Hang Dou et al., *Adaptive Depth Bias for Shadow Maps*, JCGT 3(4), 2014, https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/08/
  (a depth comparison widened by the local depth slope: each side's slope carries its depth to the seam).
- Helmut Vogel, *A better way to construct the sunflower head*, Mathematical Biosciences 44, 1979,
  https://doi.org/10.1016/0025-5564(79)90080-4 (the golden-angle spiral: even disc coverage with no directional
  spokes, which eight fixed search directions left at mesh corners).

## Spatial upscaler (2026-11-26)

`@margoengine/post/upscale` `SpatialUpscale` (gap row: single-frame spatial upscaler). Built from AMD's published
descriptions of FidelityFX Super Resolution 1 only: the talk text and slides, and the GPUOpen product and manual pages.
No shader source of AMD's, of any port, or of any engine was read. Read for the method:
- Timothy Lottes and Kleber Garcia, *Improved Spatial Upscaling through FidelityFX Super Resolution for Real-Time Game
  Engines*, SIGGRAPH 2021 Advances in Real-Time Rendering course,
  https://advances.realtimerendering.com/s2021/Unity%20AMD%20FSR%20-%20SIGGRAPH%202021.pdf (the 12-tap window around
  the 2x2 quad, a luma of r + 2g + b, central-difference direction, feature length from gradient reversal on three
  texels per axis, analysis interpolated bilinearly, kernel rotated and scaled 1 to sqrt 2 on one axis and 1 to 2 on
  the other, a base times an adaptive window from radius sqrt 2 to 2, clamp to the 2x2 quad's range; perceptual input).
- AMD, *AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution 1 (FSR 1)*, GPUOpen, https://gpuopen.com/fidelityfx-superresolution/ (quality
  modes 1.3x, 1.5x, 1.7x and 2x per axis; EASU then RCAS).
- AMD, *FidelityFX Super Resolution 1.2 (FSR1)*, GPUOpen manual,
  https://gpuopen.com/manuals/fidelityfx_sdk/techniques/super-resolution-spatial/ (input in 0..1 and perceptual, after
  anti-aliasing and tone mapping, before grain and UI).
- AMD, *FidelityFX Contrast Adaptive Sharpening (CAS)*, GPUOpen, https://gpuopen.com/fidelityfx-cas/ (sharpening scaled
  by local contrast; RCAS described as solving for the most sharpening possible before clipping).

Margo's own: the kernel polynomial (1 - s)(1 - s / 4) (zeros at one and two texels) times (1 - s / r^2)^2, the feature
length as the square of |right - left| / max(left, right) taking the larger axis, which axis gets which scaling (across
the gradient 1 to 1 / max(|dx|, |dy|), along the edge 1 to 2), the sharpen bound derived from the five taps' range
(w >= -min / (4 max) and w >= -(1 - max) / (4 (1 - min)), floored at -0.2), the linear-frame sRGB round trip, and the
pass placement (orders -75 to 45). Nothing of AMD's constants beyond the published ranges is used.

Research compared:
- Claude E. Duchon, *Lanczos Filtering in One and Two Dimensions*, Journal of Applied Meteorology 18(8), 1979,
  https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0450(1979)018<1016:LFIOAT>2.0.CO;2 (the two-lobe windowed sinc the kernel follows).
- Don P. Mitchell and Arun N. Netravali, *Reconstruction Filters in Computer-Graphics*, SIGGRAPH 1988,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/54852.378514 (the blur against ringing trade-off of negative lobes).
- Ken Turkowski, *Filters for Common Resampling Tasks*, Graphics Gems, 1990 (Lanczos-2 against bilinear and cubic in
  resampling).
- Xin Li and Michael T. Orchard, *New Edge-Directed Interpolation*, IEEE Transactions on Image Processing 10(10),
  2001, https://doi.org/10.1109/83.951537 (interpolating along edges rather than across them).
- Lei Zhang and Xiaolin Wu, *An Edge-Guided Image Interpolation Algorithm via Directional Filtering and Data Fusion*,
  IEEE Transactions on Image Processing 15(8), 2006, https://doi.org/10.1109/TIP.2006.877407 (direction-weighted
  estimates fused per pixel).
- Andrea Polesel, Giovanni Ramponi and V. John Mathews, *Image Enhancement via Adaptive Unsharp Masking*, IEEE
  Transactions on Image Processing 9(3), 2000, https://doi.org/10.1109/83.826787 (sharpening that adapts to local
  contrast to avoid noise and overshoot).
The CPU test (packages/post/test/upscale.test.js) compares against bilinear: on a step, the edge-adaptive output beside
the edge stays at least 0.02 nearer each side's own value.

## Contact and modal sound (SOUND-04)

- Kees van den Doel and Dinesh K. Pai, [*The Sounds of Physical Shapes*](https://www.persianney.com/kvdoelcsubc/publications/sound-shapes.pdf)
  (1998), derives material- and geometry-dependent frequencies and damping by separating linear vibration modes.
  A force excites each mode through its projection on the mode shape. The runtime uses modal data measured or
  authored for its tracks.
- Kees van den Doel, Paul G. Kry and Dinesh K. Pai, [*FoleyAutomatic: Physically-based Sound Effects for
  Interactive Simulation and Animation*](https://persianney.com/kvdoelcsubc/publications/foleyautomatic.pdf)
  (2001), §§2, 4.2 and 4.3. Equation 1 is the sum of damped sine impulses. The complex state
  `z = q + i y` advances by multiplication with `exp((-d - i omega) dt)`. An impulse of magnitude `J`
  adds `i gain J`. Integrating this exponential over a sample gives the exact affine update for a
  held force. The scoped test compares every output sample against the direct analytic integral.
  Sliding uses Coulomb power `mu F_n v_slip`, so its force amplitude scales with the square root of
  power. Contact speed plays a seed-phased spatial profile. A longer-wavelength rolling profile
  accounts for the smaller slopes felt by a rolling patch. The four spatial bands and their weights
