  are an authored profile and the taper near Nyquist is an audio sampling choice.
- Changxi Zheng and Doug L. James, [*Rigid-Body Fracture Sound with Precomputed Soundbanks*](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/FractureSound/files/fractureSound_comp.pdf)
  (2010), §3.3, uses released strain energy to excite the modes of debris. In its scalar special case
  with one mass starting from rest, `J² / (2 m) = eta E`. Joint fracture provides a real event source
  for this path until a brittle-fracture producer supplies finer crack and debris loads.

The implementation uses separately built plain and shared SIMD Wasm against the world arena. Hardware
sine, cosine and exponential setup use the pinned math entry. Track phases, modal state, input ticks,
integer sample carry and PCM history survive a snapshot.

The linear stream-power implicit row can be divided by its largest magnitude without changing the solution. The scaled path retains this equivalent form when ordinary coefficient or receiver-slope arithmetic cannot be represented. Candidate elevation deltas and the loose sediment and export sums must remain finite. The Braun-Willett steady profile and Roering et al. equations 1-2 supply independent analytic controls for an uplifted channel and hillslope smoothening. The independent local vertex pass can use the shared workers before the sorted receiver graph. Budget addition and sediment accumulation use canonical order to keep the serial rounding path.

### Drainage fog and its live medium (ATMO-08)

- P. C. Manins and B. L. Sawford (1979), [A Model of Katabatic Winds](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/atsc/36/4/1520-0469_1979_036_0619_amokw_2_0_co_2.xml).
  The shallow hydraulic layer has drag, entrainment and buoyant forcing from the cold layer's density excess.
  The implementation carries depth, momentum, moist enthalpy and total water. It computes reduced gravity from
  the ambient and layer virtual temperatures and applies it along the gradient of the layer top. The shear
  entrainment flux is `E0 |u - uAmbient| / (1 + Ri)` with `Ri = gReduced depth / |u - uAmbient|²`. This is its
  regularized neutral-to-stable closure. It carries ambient momentum, water and heat with entrained air.
- P. G. Duynkerke (1991), [Radiation Fog: A Comparison of Model Simulation with Detailed Observations](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/mwre/119/2/1520-0493_1991_119_0324_rfacom_2_0_co_2.xml).
  The observed processes used here are longwave cooling, turbulent transport, fog condensation and droplet
  settling. A grey-layer boundary applies `emissivity * sigma * (skyT⁴ - airT⁴)`. Surface sensible and latent
  exchanges are separate inputs. Stokes settling passes `2 rhoWater g r² / (9 muAir)` through an implicit depth
  update and credits the settled mass to the ground.
- D. Bolton (1980), [The Computation of Equivalent Potential Temperature](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/mwre/108/7/1520-0493_1980_108_1046_tcoept_2_0_co_2.xml).
  Equation 10 is `eSat = 611.2 exp(17.67 T_C / (T_C + 243.5))` in Pa, and the vapour mixing ratio is
  `0.622 e / (p - e)`. Solve equilibrium by keeping `qVapour + qLiquid` and
  `1005 (T - 273.15) + 2500000 qVapour` fixed during phase change. The native solver calls the project's pinned
  exponential for both modes. Its column light extinction follows geometric optics with efficiency 2, giving
  `3 rhoDryAir qLiquid / (2 rhoWater radius)` for dispersed spherical droplets.
- J. Stam (1999), [Stable Fluids](https://doi.org/10.1145/311535.311548), and Y. Dobashi, K. Kaneda,
  H. Yamashita, T. Okita and T. Nishimoto (2000), [A Simple, Efficient Method for Realistic Animation of Clouds](https://doi.org/10.1145/344779.344795).
  The PA-34 research calls for density to evolve in the flow in place of rigid procedural scrolling. This fog
  solver uses a conservative donor-cell flux for depth and the transported fields, with a face sill at the higher
  bed elevation. Environment interpolates the resulting extinction in X and Z before froxel accumulation.

G. L. Stephens, [Radiation Profiles in Extended Water Clouds. II: Parameterization Schemes](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469%281978%29035%3C2123%3ARPIEWC%3E2.0.CO%3B2)
(1978), gives effective emissivity as a function of liquid-water path. The
[Meteorological Research Institute's 2001 atmospheric model report](https://www.mri-jma.go.jp/Publish/Technical/DATA/VOL_42/42_047.pdf)
reproduces the exponential law and the upward broadband coefficient of 0.130 m²/g. The solver uses
130 m²/kg for a single grey layer. It multiplies dry transmissivity `1 − emissivity` by
`exp(−130 ρ h qLiquid)`. The path uses the resolved pre-entrainment liquid and depth.
Explicit grey mode retains the fixed emissivity. E. G. Wærsted et al.,
[Radiation in fog](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-17-10811-2017) (2017), give independent context for the
importance of liquid-water optical thickness, ambient humidity and overlying cloud. The coefficient is fixed independently of those events.

M. Mazoyer, F. Burnet and C. Denjean, [Experimental study on the evolution of droplet size distribution during the fog life cycle](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-22-11305-2022)
(2022), Fig. 7 gives optical microphysics measured separately from visibility. The diagnostic uses droplet
diameter and liquid water at 2.5 m from particle probes and tests the 4 m diffusometer visibility at fixed
times in F9 and F32 as the held-out output. T. Elias et al.,
[Particulate contribution to extinction of visible radiation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.atmosres.2009.01.006)
(2009), report a 10–25% instrument uncertainty. The diagnostic adds the conservative 25% bound to figure
readout, and reports microphysics readout separately. The input and comparison sensors differ in height.
The five F32 failures keep independent optical accuracy open. Aerosol activation, stratification and
independent valley-flow validation still require evidence.

### Layered snowpack and dense avalanche obstacles (ICE-01)

- P. Bartelt and M. Lehning (2002), [A physical SNOWPACK model for the Swiss avalanche warning, Part I](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-232X%2802%2900074-5).
  Equations 45–48 couple sensible heat and water/ice mass through fusion. The solver integrates layer enthalpy
  relative to melting ice, with `333700 J/kg` of latent heat and equal and opposite conduction between adjacent
  layers. Its scalar backward-Euler interface solve keeps mass and energy balanced through the melting plateau.
- M. Lehning, P. Bartelt, R. L. Brown, C. Fierz and P. Satyawali (2002), [Part II, Snow microstructure](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-232X%2802%2900073-3).
  Equation 36 gives the fresh-snow effective viscosity `0.007 rho^(4.75 - T_C / 40)`. This implementation uses
  that bulk relation until the caller provides a measured viscosity for an older or crusted layer. Mid-layer
  overburden compresses the volume, limited by the volume of the ice itself. Part III describes the operational
  surface forcing and settling balance. [Part III, meteorological forcing](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-232X%2802%2900072-1).
- N. R. Hedstrom and J. W. Pomeroy (1998), [Measurements and modelling of snow interception in the boreal forest](https://research-groups.usask.ca/hydrology/documents/pubs/papers/hedstrom_pomeroy_1998.pdf).
  Their new-snow density relation is `67.92 + 51.25 exp(T_C / 2.59)` kg/m³, evaluated at a freezing temperature
  or below. This closure sets the layer's added volume from its snowfall mass.
- M. Sturm, J. Holmgren, M. König and K. Morris (1997), [The thermal conductivity of seasonal snow](https://doi.org/10.3189/S0022143000002781).
  The linear and quadratic branches use density in g/cm³, with the switch at 0.156. From 0.60 to solid ice the
  implementation interpolates to 2.2 W/(m K). A volume-weighted contribution from retained water uses 0.56 W/(m K).
- S. C. Colbeck (1974), [The capillary effects on water percolation in homogeneous snow](https://doi.org/10.3189/S002214300002339X).
  The default retained water fills 7% of the pore volume. Excess falls to the next layer, where it can refreeze,
  or leaves as runoff if there is no next layer. This is a gravity storage balance with immediate drainage.
- M. Lehning, H. Löwe, M. Ryser and N. Raderschall (2008), [Inhomogeneous precipitation distribution and snow transport in steep terrain](https://doi.org/10.1029/2007WR006545).
  Their comparison separates wind redistribution at short scales from preferential precipitation at ridge scale.
  Here the Pomeroy and Gray (1990) Equation 11 exposed-snow flux is passed conservatively to adjacent downwind
  columns. The lee sides with smaller transport capacity accumulate the deficit. Surface snowfall is an independent
  forcing. [Pomeroy and Gray, Saltation of snow](https://doi.org/10.1029/WR026i007p01583).
- H. Yu, G. Li, B. Walter, M. Lehning, J. Zhang and N. Huang (2023), [Wind conditions for snow cornice formation in a wind tunnel](https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-17-639-2023).
  Equation 9 relates the caught mass per unit ridge width to incident mass flux. This implementation tags that
  fraction of the crossing mass at a steep lee break. With rectangular cross-section it converts the mass to
  overhang length using density and thickness. The default accretion window from one to two threshold speeds
  follows their observed range. Above that range the tagged overhang snow is exposed to scouring.
- J. Schweizer, J. B. Jamieson and M. Schneebeli (2003), [Snow avalanche formation](https://doi.org/10.1029/2002RG000123).
  The local stability diagnostic compares the overburden's slope-parallel stress to the interface cohesion and
  friction from its normal stress. Measured strengths are inputs. Root support adds an interface stress.
- M. Teich, J.-T. Fischer, T. Feistl, P. Bebi, M. Christen and A. Grêt-Regamey (2014), [Computational snow avalanche simulation in forested terrain](https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-14-2233-2014).
  Their depth-averaged momentum balance shows that obstacles matter to runout. The dense-flow implementation
  applies distributed quadratic resistance using H. M. Nepf (1999), [Drag, turbulence, and diffusion in flow through emergent vegetation](https://doi.org/10.1029/1998WR900069),
  with user-supplied `Cd * frontalArea / 2` per unit volume. Impermeable cells reflect the normal velocity in the
  neighboring ghost state and exchange zero mass.

### Aeolian transport and blowing snow (EARTH-07)

- G. Sauermann, K. Kroy and H. J. Herrmann (2001), [Continuum saltation model for sand dunes](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.64.031305).
  Equations 32–36 supply the partition of wind stress between air and grains and the saturated moving column.
  Equations 46–47 give spatial saturation. With fixed mean grain speed `u`, the time-domain terms are
  `mSat = 2 alpha (tau - tauImpact) / g` and `growth = u / lSat`, with
  `lSat = 2 alpha u² tauImpact / (g gamma (tau - tauImpact))`. This implementation uses their simplified-model
  `alpha = 0.35`, `gamma = 0.2` and `Cd = 3` to set the drag relaxation length `4 rhoGrain d / (3 Cd rhoAir)`.
  It solves the resulting reaction by backward Euler, computes face transport from the updated areal mass,
  and derives the advection substeps from the face-crossing speed. Equation 43 transports the equal and opposite
  bed change. Direct fluid entrainment seeds one grain per square metre per `sqrt(d/g)` above the fluid threshold,
  a mesh-area-independent seed for the simplified model's zero-mass equilibrium.
- B. T. Werner (1995), [Eolian dunes: Computer simulations and attractor interpretation](https://doi.org/10.1130/0091-7613(1995)023%3C1107:EDCSAA%3E2.3.CO;2).
  The model illustrates saltation plus downhill transfer at repose. Here an implicit pair transfer apportions
  the slope correction using both vertices' bed areas and bounds it by the donor's mobile mass.
- P. S. Jackson and J. C. R. Hunt (1975), [Turbulent wind flow over a low hill](https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.49710143015),
  and K. Kroy, G. Sauermann and H. J. Herrmann (2002), [Minimal model for aeolian sand dunes](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.66.031302).
  Use the low-hill stress correction proportional to `H[dh/ds] + B dh/ds` along the wind. The discrete symmetric
  sum uses the caller's integration reach and the active bed extent. Its coefficient defaults are exposed for input
  conditions. A negative predicted surface stress is replaced by zero.
- J. F. Kok, E. J. R. Parteli, T. I. Michaels and D. Bou Karam (2012), [The physics of wind-blown sand and dust](https://doi.org/10.1088/0034-4885/75/10/106901).
  Section 2.2 and Table 2.3 distinguish the fluid and impact thresholds on Earth. The default impact velocity
  is 0.8 times the Bagnold fluid velocity. Equation 4.14 gives vertical dust emission as efficiency per metre
  times the horizontal saltation flux. The default 0.001/m lies within the reported range and scales with exposure.
- J. W. Pomeroy and D. M. Gray (1990), [Saltation of snow](https://doi.org/10.1029/WR026i007p01583).
  Equation 11 gives `Q = 0.68 rho uImpact (uStar² - uVegetation² - uImpact²) / (g uStar)` when positive.
  The exposure controls the share of stress acting on snow, so `uStar² - uVegetation² = exposure uStar²`.
  The paper's fixed grain-speed closure uses `2.8 uImpact`. Dividing the flux by that speed gives the equilibrium
  moving column in the same conservative finite-volume solver. Snow's default threshold is 0.2 m/s.
- R. S. Anderson (1987), [A theoretical model for aeolian impact ripples](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-3091.1987.tb00814.x).
  Equations 7–8 give the slope-dependent impact rate `max(0, 1 + cot(angle) dh/ds)` and Equation 14 distributes
  the ejected grains over short downwind hops. The solver integrates exponential hop probability over each grid
  interval and transfers mass in conservative pairs. The ejection coefficient uses one effective splash grain per
  mean saltation hop, with the 0.3 m representative saltation length from Kok et al., Table 2.3. Supply the mean
  short-hop length explicitly to resolve changes in the ripple regime.

The Rust implementation and the renderer integration were written from these equations and descriptions. The
renderer samples moving mass and grain velocity at the emitter and maps the mass to opacity as `m / (m + referenceMass)`.
This opacity function is a visualization setting. Terrain and transported mass are advanced on the physics clock.

- M. Creyssels, P. Dupont, A. Ould El Moctar, A. Valance, I. Cantat, J. T. Jenkins, J. M. Pasini and
  K. R. Rasmussen (2009), [Saltating particles in a turbulent boundary layer: experiment and theory](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112008005491).
  Section 2 and Table 1 give independently measured wind shear and grain diameter and density as inputs.
  The outlet collector weighings are the holdout. The comparison retains the defaults for impact threshold,
  grain speed and splash. The unreported inlet feed is represented by sampling a settled, homogeneous patch
  of the working section. The test propagates the reported 5% wind and collector uncertainties separately.

The worker implementation partitions independent terrain slopes, air stress, local grain exchange and
publishable diagnostics. Rust f64x2 vectors evaluate disjoint wind and grain speed pairs and adapters keep the
unpaired tail. Source reactions preserve the positive backward-Euler root, and the face, splash-hop and
avalanching writes stay in the original order to preserve their donor limits. Empty Hilbert-sum samples past
both grid edges are zero. Skipping that suffix leaves the low-hill stress unchanged.

### Groundwater and springs (HYDRO-06)

- Lorenzo A. Richards, [Capillary conduction of liquids through porous mediums](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1745010),
  1931, derives the conductivity law with hydraulic potential and storage. Integrating horizontal saturated Darcy
  flow over the wetted thickness gives the unconfined aquifer flux. Vertical drainage through the active soil is
  supplied by the HYDRO-02 recharge field.
- David E. Rupp and John S. Selker, [On the use of the Boussinesq equation for interpreting recession hydrographs
  from sloping aquifers](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006WR005080), 2006, equations 3–4, apply that integration and
  continuity with drainable porosity. On a level, homogeneous aquifer at steady state, integrating
  \(q=-K h\,dh/dx\) shows that saturated thickness squared varies linearly between fixed heads. The face
  discretisation reproduces the result because \((h_i+h_j)(h_i-h_j)=h_i^2-h_j^2\).
- Arlen W. Harbaugh, [MODFLOW-2005, The U.S. Geological Survey Modular Ground-Water Model: The Ground-Water Flow
  Process](https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/tm6A16), 2005, chapters 2, 5 and 6, assembles positive face conductance,
  harmonic resistance between differing porous materials and specific-yield storage. The horizontal face in this
  solver uses the harmonic conductivity and the mean saturated thickness above the shared bottom. A fixed boundary
  is half a cell away. The spring law uses Harbaugh's equations 6–11A/B with outward sign,
  \(Q=C\max(0,H-H_\mathrm{spring})\). Its active set is solved with backward Euler.
- Magnus R. Hestenes and Eduard Stiefel, [Methods of Conjugate Gradients for Solving Linear Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.049.044),
  1952, give the residual and conjugate direction recurrences for a symmetric positive system. The solver uses the
  storage-plus-conductance diagonal for preconditioning and checks the residual of the assembled equation. Face
  volumes are used in equal and opposite pairs to update storage. A donor-volume limit maintains nonnegative
  storage during rapid wetting. Surface overflow is left with the outlet as explicit seepage.

The aquifer keeps water thickness relative to its bottom, so small inputs survive large coordinate elevations.
Tests reconstruct the fixed-head solution, a two-cell material contact, a draining spring, and the water-volume
exchange with the existing runoff and shallow-water solvers. The implementation uses the papers and the repository's
field contracts. Native participants assemble only disjoint face weights, initial storage and spring-activity
rows. The conjugate-gradient order, unilateral drain updates and equal-and-opposite face-volume recovery stay
fixed in the caller. Adrien Guérin, Olivier Devauchelle and Éric Lajeunesse, [Response of a laboratory aquifer
to rainfall](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2014.590), 2014, measure conductivity with a Darcy column and packing
porosity by mass. Their separate rainfall and discharge records let the diagnostic hold out the outlet samples
of the 1 mm and 4 mm glass-bead tanks. The 1 mm run uses the paper's absolute clock. The 4 mm panels use
elapsed time from outlet onset, so they test the rise shape and do not establish rain-to-outlet travel time.
The solver uses imposed recharge directly, with initial drainable storage set to zero. The groundwater
and surface-water transect in Thomas C. Winter, Judson W. Harvey, O. Lehn Franke and William M. Alley,
[Ground water and surface water: A single resource](https://doi.org/10.3133/cir1139), 1998, informed the
authored cutaway. The cutaway uses the Harbaugh drain law for the accepted transfer and has its own
idealized terrain and time scale.

### Confined Darcy flow and Hele-Shaw cells (HYDRO-06 groundwater entry, for HYDRO-07)

- Henry Darcy, *Les fontaines publiques de la ville de Dijon*, 1856 (print), gives the linear seepage law.
- H. S. Hele-Shaw, [The flow of water](https://doi.org/10.1038/058033a0), 1898, and G. K. Batchelor,
  [An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511800955), 1967, section 4.8: the gap-averaged
  velocity between plates a gap b apart is -b²/(12 μ) ∇p, a potential flow, so the cell takes transmissivity
  b³/(12 μ) on the pressure.
- Arlen W. Harbaugh, [MODFLOW-2005](https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/tm6A16), 2005, chapter 2: block-centred
  finite volumes, harmonic face conductances and a specified-head side half a cell from the centre.
- Hestenes and Stiefel 1952 (cited above) for the Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients.

Tests check plane Poiseuille flow in a channel, resistances in series, a quadratic potential under harmonic faces,
conservation and a closed stream function around an obstacle, and a well, all against closed forms.

### Pipe flow, hydraulic structures and machines (HYDRO-07)

- Water: G. S. Kell, [Density, thermal expansivity, and compressibility of liquid water from 0° to 150 °C](https://doi.org/10.1021/je60064a005),
  1975; J. Kestin, M. Sokolov and W. A. Wakeham, [Viscosity of liquid water in the range -8 °C to 150 °C](https://srd.nist.gov/jpcrdreprint/1.555581.pdf),
  1978 (the cubic correlation about 1.0016 mPa s at 20 °C); A. L. Buck, [New equations for computing vapor pressure
  and enhancement factor](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0450(1981)020%3C1527:NEFCVP%3E2.0.CO;2), 1981.
- Friction: C. F. Colebrook, [Turbulent flow in pipes, with particular reference to the transition region between the
  smooth and rough pipe laws](https://doi.org/10.1680/ijoti.1939.13150), 1939 (solved by Newton on 1/√f);
  S. E. Haaland, [Simple and explicit formulas for the friction factor in turbulent pipe flow](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3240948),
  1983; S. W. Churchill, *Friction-factor equation spans all fluid-flow regimes*, Chemical Engineering 84(24), 1977
  (print), the default because it is smooth across laminar, transitional and turbulent flow.
- Pipes, orifices and meters: F. M. White, *Fluid Mechanics*, 7th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2011 (print), sections 3.5,
  6.6 to 6.9 and 6.12, for the energy equation, minor losses and the sharp orifice; ISO 5167-4:2003, *Venturi tubes*
  (standard), for the machined discharge coefficient 0.995. The two-basin equalisation integrates
  dD/dt = -Cd a √(2gD) (1/A1 + 1/A2) in closed form (√D falls linearly).
- Water hammer: N. Joukowsky, *Über den hydraulischen Stoss in Wasserleitungsröhren*, 1898 (trans. O. Simin, Proc.
  AWWA 24, 1904), for ρ a Δv; E. B. Wylie and V. L. Streeter, *Fluid Transients in Systems*, Prentice Hall, 1993
  (print), chapters 1 and 2, for the elastic wave speed with its three restraint cases and the lumped compliance
  C = A L / (ρ a²).
- Hydraulic ram: G. O. Lungudi, S. Cohen, S. Nasraoui, C. Dupont, S. G. Salinas-Rodriguez, M. Kennedy and D. Ferras,
  [Numerical and experimental analyses of hydraulic rams](https://doi.org/10.1080/00221686.2024.2401899), 2024, for the
  cycle's phases (acceleration, waste closure, delivery, recoil); the d'Aubuisson (1840) and Rankine (1872)
  efficiencies as stated in the hydraulics texts.
- Networks: E. Todini and S. Pilati, *A gradient algorithm for the analysis of pipe networks*, in Computer
  Applications in Water Supply, vol. 1, Research Studies Press, 1988 (print): Newton on link flows and junction heads
  with the flows eliminated, one symmetric positive-definite system per step.
- Open channels: J.-B. Belanger, 1828 (print), the momentum balance across a jump; V. T. Chow, *Open-Channel
  Hydraulics*, McGraw-Hill, 1959 (print), chapters 3, 6 and 15; W. H. Hager, R. Bremen and N. Kawagoshi,
  [Classical hydraulic jump: length of roller](https://doi.org/10.1080/00221689009499048), 1990,
  L_r / y1 = 160 tanh(F1 / 20) - 12.
- Machines: S. L. Dixon and C. A. Hall, *Fluid Mechanics and Thermodynamics of Turbomachinery*, 7th ed.,
  Butterworth-Heinemann, 2014 (print), chapter 10, and White 2011, section 11.6, for the Pelton momentum theory
  (peak efficiency Cv²(1 + k cos β)/2 at half the jet speed). The hinged bellows volume is derived here: the ruled
  solid between two boards hinged on one edge holds A g (1 + cos θ)/2 + M sin θ for outline area A and first moment M.

No other engine's or library's code was read. Tests compare against an independent Colebrook iteration,
Hagen-Poiseuille, a Runge-Kutta run of the basins, Bernoulli and continuity, the 10.1 m vapour limit, Joukowsky,
the ram's own water balance and step convergence, momentum across a jump with Chow's tabled ratio, the wide-channel
Manning depth, the momentum-theory Pelton optimum, quadrature of the bellows, and a three-reservoir bisection.

## Glacier and ice-sheet flow (ICE-02)

- Ralf Greve and Heinz Blatter, [Dynamics of Ice Sheets and Glaciers](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-03415-2),
  2009, chapters 4, 5 and 7. Grounded, no-slip shallow ice with Glen exponent 3 yields the depth-integrated
  flux q = −(2/5) A (ρᵢg)³ H⁵ |∇s|² ∇s, with thickness H and surface s = bed + H.
- Ed Bueler, Craig S. Lingle, Jed A. Kallen-Brown, Latrice N. Bowman and David N. Covey,
  [Exact time-dependent similarity solutions for isothermal shallow ice sheets](https://www.cs.uaf.edu/~bueler/simice.pdf),
  2005, section 7, compare arithmetic face-thickness (type I) with averaged cell diffusivities.
  Ed Bueler, [Stable finite volume element schemes for the shallow-ice approximation](https://doi.org/10.1017/jog.2015.3),
  2016, separates face fluxes and positive thickness on nonflat bed. The Margo implementation freezes the
  symmetric face diffusivity for each backward-Euler step, solves its five-point linear system with
  Jacobi-preconditioned CG, and limits summed outgoing face transfer to available donor ice.
- C. J. van der Veen, [Fracture mechanics approach to penetration of surface crevasses on glaciers](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-232X(97)00022-0), 1998, compares ice overburden, tensile stress and
  water pressure at the crack tip. The optional glacier uses the closely-spaced, zero-net-stress
  approximation without crack-tip toughness, appropriate for a first-order grid-scale fracture front.
- Douglas I. Benn, Charles R. Warren and Ruth H. Mottram, [Calving processes and the dynamics of calving glaciers](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.earscirev.2007.02.002), 2007, equations (10), (11) and section 4.6. The dry Nye depth
  is 2 (ε̇/A)^(1/3)/(ρᵢg). An already opening crack gains the hydrostatic term (ρw/ρᵢ) times its water
  column. The solver obtains tensile strain by projecting the discrete free-surface velocity gradient
  along local flow. Freeboard is the marine break-off threshold, and the buoyancy ratio follows Archimedes.
- Antoine Pralong and Martin Funk, [Dynamic damage model of crevasse opening and application to glacier calving](https://doi.org/10.1029/2004JB003104), 2005, studied failure of a hanging glacier. Here a dry receiver
  needs an actual drop in bed elevation and a through-column fracture. Grid release evaluates the
  failure threshold, while trajectories or damage below a released column belong to separate solvers.
- John F. O’Callaghan and David M. Mark, [The extraction of drainage networks from digital elevation data](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0734-189X(84)80011-0), 1984. Connect each active surface cell to its steepest of
  eight descending neighbours using metric distances. A topological sweep transmits each liquid volume once.
- Charles F. Raymond, [Flow in a Transverse Section of Athabasca Glacier, Alberta, Canada](https://doi.org/10.3189/S0022143000012995),
  1971. Figure 3a and Table I give independently observed geometry. The measured centre-line depth mean from
  Figure 10a and page 73 is held out. The observed margin shear and varying basal motion motivate resolving
  transverse stress and sliding separately from the isothermal no-slip layer.
- Nathan Maier, Neil Humphrey, Joel Harper and Toby Meierbachtol, [Sliding dominates slow-flowing margin regions,
  Greenland Ice Sheet](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aaw5406), 2019. The input strip uses only the drill
  thickness and surveyed surface slope from Methods. The winter GPS speed and borehole-derived deformation
  from Results are held out. The script uses the no-slip Glen n=3 surface-to-depth-mean ratio of 5/4.
- Ed Bueler and Jed Brown, [Shallow shelf approximation as a sliding law in a thermomechanically coupled
  ice sheet model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008JF001179), 2009, demonstrate coupling membrane stresses to
  a sliding law. The optional glacier retains its no-slip shallow-ice model at this checkpoint.
  No external solver code or measurement files are redistributed.

The tests derive the exact two-column backward-Euler update, the linear-slope Glen velocity, the Nye
depth and its hydrostatic increment, and the closed mass balance. The HYDRO-01 fixture measures the actual
flood inlet volume. A registry-only observer uses the source layout SEA-06 will consume.

### Ground animal locomotion (LIFE-02)

- David L. Hu, Jasmine Nirody, Terri Scott and Michael J. Shelley, [The mechanics of slithering locomotion](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0812533106), 2009, Eq. (2), Eq. (3) and Fig. 1. Use one normalized ground-tangent slip vector for the fore/aft and lateral coefficients. A travelling tangent angle integrates the paper's travelling curvature and supplies an inextensible chain. The discrete midpoint velocities are recentered, and the angular update subtracts the shape angular momentum before integrating yaw. Spring-damper contact load accounts for the bed normal, and `slipSpeed` regularizes tangential slip at zero. The default cloth coefficients come from that experiment. Shape and material settings remain configurable.
- Philip Holmes, Robert J. Full, Daniel Koditschek and John Guckenheimer, [The Dynamics of Legged Locomotion: Models, Analyses, and Challenges](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0036144504445133), 2006, §3 and Fig. 13. A massless spring leg acts on a loaded body only while in compression. Margo adds axial damping, a prescribed stance rest-length extension and actual terrain normals. Swing feet show the kinematic path and carry zero force.
- Marc H. Raibert, Michael Chepponis and H. Benjamin Brown Jr., [Running on four legs as though they were one](https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/pub3/raibert_m_h_1986_1/raibert_m_h_1986_1.pdf), 1986, Eqs. (2)–(6). Touchdown places the foot at predicted half-stance travel plus the velocity error correction. A grounded PD attitude response uses quaternion error. An active foot may generate shear as well as axial load, with each force and moment sharing the Coulomb budget `|F_t| + |M| / (leg length / 2) ≤ μF_n`. The support lever represents the stance footprint in this reduced model. The world integrates the sum of applied reactions and moments without imposing speed or orientation. Zero gains give passive axial spring contacts.
- Claire T. Farley and T. Christine Ko, [Mechanics of locomotion in lizards](https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.200.16.2177), 1997, measured a bouncing trot in two lizard species. Robert J. Full and Michael S. Tu, [Mechanics of six-legged runners](https://polypedal.berkeley.edu/publications/020_Full_TheMechanicsofSixLeggedRunners_JExpBiol_1990.pdf), 1990, Fig. 4, measured alternating insect tripods.
- Joseph C. Spagna, Edgar A. Valdivia and Vivin Mohan, [Gait characteristics of two fast-running spider species](https://www.americanarachnology.org/journal-joa/joa-all-articles/article/download/arac-39-01-84.pdf/), 2011, measured alternating tetrapods. Reinhard Blickhan and Robert J. Full, [Locomotion energetics of the ghost crab: II](https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.130.1.155), 1987, measured lateral running and spring-like whole-body motion.

The Wasm regions use double-precision state, pinned sine and cosine and explicit semi-implicit Euler stepping on the
world's dyadic clock. The fixed-rate bound considers contact-mode stiffness and damping, friction regularization,
stance/swing sampling and controller response. Worker partitions own disjoint animal rows and disjoint contact ranges.
They retain the ordered force and moment accumulation within each animal. The measured-snake diagnostic uses
the paper's separately measured friction and its prescribed shape normalization. Flat speed and incline markers,
including the change of direction on an uphill cloth runway, are held out. No photograph, code or dataset is bundled.
The engine tests verify Eq. (2), spring reaction, the friction-wrench
bound, link closure, frictionless motion, swing loads, alternating footholds, lateral crab motion, and plain/shared
and snapshot replay. The coupling tests compare the published reaction to the actual flat and sloped TerrainBed
fields. The animal templates reproduce the documented coordination patterns and physical loads. The default masses,
geometry and controller gains describe a generic starting point for each gait.

## Material ageing and surface optics (BIO-04)

- Julie Dorsey and Pat Hanrahan, [*Modeling and Rendering of Metallic Patinas*](https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/patina/)
  (1996), §§3–4. Coat and substrate layers are modeled separately. The diffuse finite-layer
  Kubelka–Munk equation follows from the two-flux transport coefficients `K` and `S`, with mode
  `m = sqrt(K(K + 2S))`. We evaluate its exponential form and apply their §4.2
  combining rule `R = R₁ + T₁²R₂/(1 - R₁R₂)`. Zero absorption reduces to
  `R = S d/(1 + S d)` and `T = 1/(1 + S d)`. The test uses the hyperbolic form as its independent reference.
- Jinwei Gu, Chien-I Tu, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Peter Belhumeur, Wojciech Matusik and Shree
  Nayar, [*Time-Varying Surface Appearance: Acquisition, Modeling and Rendering*](https://cave.cs.columbia.edu/old/publications/pdfs/Gu_TOG06.pdf)
  (2006), Eq. 2. Spatial exposure rate alters local age; the special case `Aφ + D`
  supplies the scalar-weathered fraction model for wood and stone. The reflectance palettes
  are authored linear colors. Copper's inner oxide saturates with substrate loss; residual
  consumed copper feeds the exterior carbonate layer. Oxide volume per unit metal volume
  follows molecular mass, stoichiometry and density.
- International Organization for Standardization, [*ISO 9223:2012*](https://www.iso.org/standard/53499.html)
  (2012), §8.2 Eqs. 1 and 3, supplies first-year loss versus annualized RH, temperature, SO₂
  and chloride deposition. [*ISO 9224:2012*](https://www.iso.org/standard/53500.html) (2012), Eqs. 1
  and 3 and Table 2, give the long-term power law and linear continuation from 20 years.
  For a changed annual climate, inverting the new loss curve at the accumulated depth
  preserves the previous penetration. Immersion has a separate time and loss contribution.
- ASTM International, [*G102-23: Standard Practice for Calculation of Corrosion Rates and
  Related Information from Electrochemical Measurements*](https://store.astm.org/standards/g102)
  (2023), uses Faraday's law. In SI the immersion depth rate is `j M/(n F ρ)`.
  Robert E. Melchers, [*Predicting corrosion for life estimation of ocean and coastal steel
  infrastructure*](https://doi.org/10.1002/maco.202314201) (2025), reports a representative
  long-term rate of about 0.06 mm/year in the coastal case near 20 °C. The default current
  is the carbon-steel current equivalent for that case.
- Hannu Viitanen, Tomi Toratti, Lasse Makkonen, Ruut Peuhkuri, Tuomo Ojanen,
  Leena Ruokolainen and Jarmo Räisänen, [*Towards modelling of decay risk of wooden
  materials*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00107-010-0450-x) (2010). The [2011 VTT
  presentation](https://webpages.tuni.fi/nsb2011/sites/www.tut.fi.nsb2011/files/b11_4_viitanen_et_al_durability_of_wood_nsb_2011.pdf)
  shows the exact critical time and mass-loss equations. The model accumulates activation,
  subtracts dry deactivation and integrates irreversible mass loss from the instant activity reaches one.
- S. Muko, K. Sakai and Y. Iwasa, [*Dynamics of marine sessile organisms with space-limited
  growth and recruitment*](https://doi.org/10.1006/jtbi.2001.2298) (2001). Recruitment is proportional
  to available surface and larval abundance. An aggregate group with first-order loss has
  `C' = a(1-C)-bC`, whose fixed-input solution is exact. Recruitment and removal rates are adjustable.
- Frederick W. Lipfert, [*Atmospheric damage to calcareous stones*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-6981(89)90587-8)
  (1989), supplies the clean-rain equilibrium contribution of 18.8 µm recession per metre of rainfall.
  Michael M. Reddy, [*Acid rain damage to carbonate stone*](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/acid-rain-damage-carbonate-stone-a-quantitative-assessment-based-aqueous-geochemistry)
  (1988), and Paul A. Baedecker et al., [*Effects of acidic deposition on the erosion of carbonate stone*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0957-1272(92)90018-N)
  (1992), distinguish clean-rain dissolution, acidity and dry deposition. In the solver's ideal acid
  balance, two excess moles of protons dissolve one mole of CaCO₃, converted to depth by density.

## Iceberg rigid-body dynamics and calving (ICE-03)

- J. C. Burton, J. M. Amundson, D. S. Abbot, A. Boghosian, L. M. Cathles, S. Correa-Legisos, K. N. Darnell,
  N. Guttenberg, D. M. Holland and D. R. MacAyeal,
  [Laboratory investigations of iceberg capsize dynamics, energy dissipation and tsunamigenesis](https://doi.org/10.1029/2011JF002055), 2012. The submerged fraction is ρᵢ/ρw and the
  critical aspect ratio is √(6 α (1 − α)) for α = ρᵢ/ρw (equations 19, 27 and 29).
  The buoyant force and torque here are integrated exactly on the wetted cuboid faces.
  The velocity and orientation evolve continuously, with no imposed quarter turn.
- Till J. W. Wagner, Alon A. Stern, Rebecca W. Dell and Ian Eisenman,
  [On the representation of capsizing in iceberg models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocemod.2017.07.003),
  2017. Their corrected stability sign and small-angle result agree with two-sided torque checks.
  The pressure integral remains applicable after the top face crosses the waterline.
- Till J. W. Wagner, Rebecca W. Dell and Ian Eisenman,
  [An analytical model of iceberg drift](https://doi.org/10.1175/JPO-D-16-0262.1), 2017.
  We retain the opposing water and air drag in a time-dependent body model and distinguish basal
  from sidewall recession following appendix A. This implementation accepts SI recession rates
  and scales their contribution by wetted face area.
- Jerry Tessendorf, [Simulating Ocean Water](https://jtessen.people.clemson.edu/reports/papers_files/coursenotes2002.pdf),
  2001–2004. The existing wake works with the linear pressure and volume input in the modal surface
  calculation. We use equal-and-opposite raised-cosine volume patches to represent a local outward
  displacement without a mean water gain. The patch scale comes from the projected body area.

The exact heave check derives g/(α H) directly from the waterplane stiffness ρw g A and the
body mass ρᵢ A H. It distinguishes the continuous oscillator from the discrete leapfrog phase.
The capsize fixture contrasts a restoring wide box and an unstable narrow box under the same heel.
The real registry chain transfers a calved glacier column to a free-floating iceberg and the signed
wetted-volume change to a WakeSolver, where crest and trough travel away from the source.

## BIO-03 live forest competition and succession

- Daniel B. Botkin, James F. Janak and James R. Wallis, [*Some Ecological Consequences of a Computer Model of Forest Growth*](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2258570), 1972. The individual annual growth and death events motivate the ecosystem clock.
- Stephen W. Pacala et al., [*Forest Models Defined by Field Measurements: Estimation, Error Analysis, and Dynamics*](https://www.sortie-nd.org/research/pubs/Pacala_et_al_1996_Ecol_Monogr_66_1-43.pdf), 1996. Growth, recruitment and mortality use individual, species-dependent light responses. Margo's Q16 crown overlap, logistic crown-radius increment and suppression probability are its previously shipped reduced forms.
- James S. Clark, Miles Silman, Ruth Kern, Eric Macklin and Janneke HilleRisLambers, [*Seed Dispersal Near and Far: Patterns Across Temperate and Tropical Forests*](https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/2094), 1999. Integrating the two-dimensional t kernel over a disk at shape 1 gives radial CDF `1 - 1/(1 + (r/a)²)` with `a = sqrt(u)`. With a uniform upper-tail variate `v`, the inverse is `a sqrt(1/v - 1)`. The offline and live models share the fixed-point inverse sampling and its existing tail bound.
- Guillaume Cordonnier, Éric Galin, James Gain, Bedřich Beneš, Éric Guérin, Adrien Peytavie and Marie-Paule Cani, [*Authoring Landscapes by Combining Ecosystem and Terrain Erosion Simulation*](https://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/bbenes/papers/Cordonnier17ToG.pdf), 2017. Section 4.6 and Figure 13 provide the reference for the bidirectional plant/erosion feedback and disturbance-driven regrowth. Gross resolved incision integrated over a model year is compared with each species' measured scour tolerance.
- L. J. Waldron, [*The Shear Resistance of Root-Permeated Homogeneous and Stratified Soil*](https://doi.org/10.2136/sssaj1977.03615995004100050005x), 1977. The effective additional cohesion in Pa is tensile stress times root area fraction and a geometric/friction factor. The forest takes their measured product beneath a full crown. The patch model weights by projected crown area and bounds representative cover at unity.
- Don Minore, [*Effects of Artificial Flooding on Seedling Survival and Growth of Six Northwestern Tree Species*](https://andrewsforest.oregonstate.edu/pubs/pdf/pub752.pdf), 1968, and John M. Kabrick et al., [*Quantifying Flooding Effects on Hardwood Seedling Survival and Growth for Bottomland Restoration*](https://www.nrs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/jrnl/2012/nrs_2012_kabrick_001.pdf), 2012. The controlled exposure experiments motivate species-specific depth and duration thresholds, which callers set for their site and life stage. The solver counts ticks at or above the chosen depth.
- John E. Wade and E. Wendell Hewson, [*Trees as a Local Climatic Wind Indicator*](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/apme/18/9/1520-0450_1979_018_1182_taalcw_2_0_co_2.xml), 1979, and G. L. Wooldridge, R. C. Musselman, R. A. Sommerfeld, D. G. Fox and B. H. Connell, [*Mean Wind Patterns and Snow Depths in an Alpine–Subalpine Ecosystem as Measured by Damage to Coniferous Trees*](https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/48421.pdf), 1996. Leeward form follows chronic exposed wind. The solver's reduced growth rule averages `U |U|` and sets the direction of new crown area to `leanMax * meanLoad / (referenceSpeed² + |meanLoad|)`. Its existing and new axes are averaged by projected crown areas before and after growth. The saturation and area moment are Margo assumptions, with site calibration separate from the observed wind-deformation relation.

The transition reuses Margo's integer ecosystem. The annual crown search has an original Rust neighbourhood table in
arena memory and gives identical succession with plain and shared Wasm. Measurements for the matching examples and
exact tests are in the package README and whitepaper claims.

### Grounded biped and quadruped gait (LIFE-01)

- R. McNeill Alexander and A. S. Jayes, [A dynamic similarity hypothesis for the gaits of quadrupedal mammals](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-7998.1983.tb04266.x), 1983, supplies relative stride and Froude scaling. Alexander's [author review](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~cga/legs/alexander.pdf), 1984, compares dimensionless duty and stride in quadrupeds and bipeds. With `Fr = v² / (g h)`, use the published `L/h = 2.3 Fr^0.3` curve and integrate cadence `v/L` through speed changes. The simulated support stride also observes `2 × accessible foot travel / duty`, with the single-stance moment bound `r ≤ μ × support lever`.
- Reinhard Blickhan, [The spring-mass model for running and hopping](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9290(89)90224-8), 1989, motivates compressive stance springs and ballistic unloaded phases. Thomas Geijtenbeek, Michiel van de Panne and A. Frank van der Stappen, [Flexible Muscle-Based Locomotion for Bipedal Creatures](https://courses.washington.edu/bioen520/notes/Geijtenbeek_%28Trans_on_Graphics_2013%29.pdf), 2013, Fig. 5 and §4.4, motivate separate stance/swing phases and trunk feedback during stance. The reduced world solver reuses the grounded spring and contact kernel. It applies a finite support couple, with a shear allowance reduced by the moment budget of an offset centre of mass. Torso collision absorbs angular motion through rolling friction.
- Huiling Tan and Alan Wilson, [Grip and limb force limits to turning performance in competition horses](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3107634/), 2011, derives the small-radius traction limit. Use `a_lat = speed × turn rate`, and enforce `a_tan² + a_lat² ≤ (μ g_n)²`. Bank follows the ratio of lateral acceleration to normal gravity. The measured fit `μ = 0.6` is a surface default and can be changed.
- Alberto E. Minetti, Luca P. Ardigò, E. Reinach and F. Saibene, [The relationship between mechanical work and energy expenditure of locomotion in horses](https://www.bio.utexas.edu/faculty/pianka/Horse_Energetics.pdf), 1999, Table 1 and Fig. 8, measured pace-dependent frequency and body motion. Alberto E. Minetti et al., [Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes](https://iris.unibs.it/bitstream/11379/540545/1/Minetti%20JAP%202002.pdf), 2002, supplies measured human evidence for climbing cost. The equine drive uses gravitational work `m g Δh` against a fixed work-per-metre command, without applying human metabolic fit coefficients to a horse.

The engine verifies variable cadence, coupled normal and lateral traction, mean support height from independent hoof
samples, an airborne trot phase, canting and slope work, world-space foot forces and opposing impulse on an actual
rigid platform. Full limb mechanics, rig hand-off and water displacement remain separate couplings.

## Discrete-element pack ice and vessel loads (ICE-04)

- W. D. Hibler III, “A Dynamic Thermodynamic Sea Ice Model” (1979). Its area and thickness distribution
  motivates separate bookkeeping for a remaining level-ice footprint and conserved ice volume. This
  entry represents already fragmented ice at the scale of individual floes.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(1979)009%3C0815:ADTSIM%3E2.0.CO;2)
- Agnieszka Herman, “Molecular-dynamics simulation of clustering processes in sea-ice floes”
  (2011), equations 1–11. Circular area and submerged and exposed edge heights set the linear
  ocean and quadratic air drag. The hard-disc normal impulse is the reduced mass times
  `(1+e)` times closing speed. The air term here uses relative velocity. See also Herman,
  “Discrete-Element bonded-particle Sea Ice model DESIgn, version 1.3a” (2016), section 4,
  for disk contact and Coulomb slip. This solver uses an impulse law for the unbonded floes.
  [Hard-disc paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.0617) · [DESIgn paper](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-9-1219-2016)
- D. Vella and J. S. Wettlaufer, “Explaining the patterns formed by ice floe interactions”
  (2008), equation 12. The simple rafting threshold is `(8/3) exp(π/2)(1−ν²)σ²/(ρwgE)`.
  Its table 1 sea-ice data and section 2.2 thickness range are checked separately.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008JC004781)
- M. A. Hopkins, S. Frankenstein and A. S. Thorndike, “Formation of an aggregate scale in
  Arctic sea ice” (2004). Ridging converts level ice into thick rubble during compression. The
  local remap here takes an annulus with the same radial loss as the contact band and conserves
  its mass on the parent row. Thick ice first pays a fracture-work estimate `σ × edge area × cut`.
  Remaining dissipated work pays `ρi g h` per cubic metre for lifting a raft, or `ρw g h/2`
  per cubic metre for lifting and submerging equal halves of a ridge.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003JC001855)
- Gustav Lindqvist, “A straightforward method for calculation of ice resistance of ships”
  (1989), distinguishes breaking and submerging ice from other hull losses. The local capsule
  contact here transmits its impulse to the live rigid body. It uses the computed discrete contact
  work for fracture and piles rather than adding Lindqvist's empirical continuous level-ice drag.
  [Proceedings](https://iptek.its.ac.id/index.php/ijmeir/article/downloadSuppFile/4042/312)

The one shared contact point defines torque and the Coulomb bound. The SIMD native step rebuilds
a deterministic fixed-load spatial hash, reduces initial relative travel per substep, solves each
local pair once per substep, and uses only world-owned scratch. The same compiled solver works
with or without shared memory. No companion code or external assets were used.

### Ductile crashworthiness (BREAK-03)

- M. M. Kamal, [Analysis and Simulation of Vehicle to Barrier Impact](https://doi.org/10.4271/700414) (1970), uses measured component crush characteristics to drive a barrier test model. The engine takes the member's measured loading curve as input.
- Matthew Huang, [Vehicle Crash Mechanics](https://www.routledge.com/Vehicle-Crash-Mechanics/Huang/p/book/9780429118371) (2002), §4.4.4 and §4.5.1, derives reduced mass and the spring-barrier turning point. Eqs. 4.25(6) and 4.26 yield effective mass `mA mB / (mA + mB)` for central contact and elastic peak stroke `v sqrt(m / k)`.
- Preben Terndrup Pedersen and Shengming Zhang, [On impact mechanics in ship collisions](https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/on-impact-mechanics-in-ship-collisions-2/) (1998), separate the external impulse from structural work. The engine uses that separation for the normal component at a configured berthing station. Zhang's [The Mechanics of Ship Collisions](https://backend.orbit.dtu.dk/ws/files/5436875/Zhang.pdf) (1999), §3.2 and Fig. 3.1, discusses the scope of V. U. Minorsky's [An Analysis of Ship Collisions with Reference to Protection of Nuclear Power Plants](https://doi.org/10.5957/jsr.1959.3.2.1) (1959). The volume correlation sets historical context. The engine uses measured force-displacement response at the station.

For unit normal `n` and contact arm `r`, the point's inverse mass along `n` is `1/m + (r × n) · I⁻¹(r × n)`. Sum both sides and invert to obtain effective mass. The yield curve is `F = Fy + H p` for persistent stroke `p`. Solving `F = k(x − p)` concurrently gives the post-yield tangent `kH/(k+H)`. Integrate each linear branch with `ΔW = F0 Δx + 0.5 k Δx²` and invert at incident relative kinetic energy. The recoverable energy is triangular elastic work plus the loaded backing's elastic work when compacted. The rest is permanent work. Apply the equal and opposite impulse implied by incident and rebound speeds at a single contact point so the angular momenta balance as well. This reduced event model was written from the cited mechanics and equations.

Continuing support uses the compression-only normal condition from David E. Stewart and Jeffrey C. Trinkle,
“An implicit time-stepping scheme for rigid body dynamics with inelastic collisions and Coulomb friction”
(1996). David Baraff and Andrew Witkin, “Large Steps in Cloth Simulation” (1998), Eq. 4 gives the implicit
velocity update. For current compression `d`, inward speed `v`, effective inverse mass `w`, tick `h` and
backing stiffness `k`, critical relative damping is `c = 2 sqrt(k/w)`. Evaluating the spring and dashpot
at `d + h(v − Jw)` and `v − Jw` gives the nonnegative normal impulse
`J = max(0, h[kd + (c+hk)v] / [1 + h(c+hk)w])`. Only positive compression and force produce sustained
support. The same-point impulse is applied to the rigid pair. In the steady-load fixture a tick receives
`J = Fh` and the rigid substeps integrate a velocity ramp with zero mean, so the end velocity is
`Fhw(S−1)/(2S)` for `S` substeps. Substitution gives the tested compression. The proof uses two
actual rigid bodies as well as a fixed support.
[Stewart and Trinkle](https://www.cse.lehigh.edu/~trink/Papers/STicra00.pdf)
[Baraff and Witkin](https://graphics.stanford.edu/courses/cs448b-00-winter/papers/baraff_98.pdf)

Continuous plastic contact uses the one-dimensional return map in Juan C. Simo and Thomas J. R.
Hughes, “Computational Inelasticity” (1998), Chapter 1, together with the backward Euler velocity
step in Baraff and Witkin (1998), Eq. 4. If `d` is the current total stroke, `v` the closing speed,
`w` the effective inverse mass and `h` the remaining tick after initial contact, the end stroke
satisfies `x + h²w F(x) = d + hv`. The material curve is continuous with elastic slope `k`, plastic
loading slope `kH/(k+H)`, and backing slope `kb` after compaction. Evaluate `x + h²w F(x)` at its two
breakpoints to select a branch and solve that affine equation. Apply impulse `hF(x)` at the same
point on both rigid bodies. The material return map computes permanent stroke and work from the
end stroke, including continuing plastic flow through the same contact. The guided live tube check
uses the independent prescribed travel and material properties from Yob et al. and two refinement
levels of the driving sequence at the world's fixed 60 Hz rate.
[Simo and Hughes (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1007/b98904)

Staged station loads use the force-envelope form of Mayville, Johnson, Stringfellow and Tyrell,
*The Development of a Rail Passenger Coach Car Crush Zone* (2003), and the pretest dashed trace
in Jacobsen et al., *Crash Energy Management: One- and Two-Car Passenger Rail Impact Tests*
(2016), Figure 4. The control points give `p = x − F/k` and piecewise-linear `F(x)`. The engine
integrates the full segment for incident work, `F dp` for permanent work, and evaluates the
elastic energy separately. The continuous solver checks that `x + h²wF(x)` increases along each
active segment and that the rigid input is one tick old at the same rate. The FRA experiment
holds out the measured pulse and peak displacement. NHTSA 8035 supplies only the road-car
calibration. Independently measured NHTSA 8104 supplies the comparison outputs.
[Mayville et al.](https://ntlrepository.blob.core.windows.net/lib/47000/47400/47474/rail_cw_2003_2.pdf) · [FRA report](https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/12397) · [NCAP raw channels and reduction](whitepaper/reproduce.md#break-03-independent-ncap-road-car-pulse)

The optional wet channel forms instantaneous mobility from the rigid inertia and the zero-time
water contribution. This takes the added mass term from W. E. Cummins, *The Impulse Response
Function and Ship Motions* (1962), and the circular-cylinder strip limit of J. M. J. Journée and
W. W. Massie, *Offshore Hydromechanics* (2001), §7.3.1. For physical impulse `J` about the rigid
centre, `M (M+A)^−1 J` produces the intended wet velocity jump through the dry integrator.
An exact receipt removes that contribution from the following inferred external load.
[Cummins](https://dome.mit.edu/handle/1721.3/49049) · [Journée and Massie](https://ocw.tudelft.nl/wp-content/uploads/OffshoreHydromechanics_Journee_Massie.pdf) · [Wet contact proofs](whitepaper/reproduce.md#break-03-wet-contact-inertia)

Kristjan Tabri, Jukka Määttänen and Janne Ranta, *Model-scale experiments of
symmetric ship collisions* (2008), supply an independent marine compression
comparison using the staged station model. Only the loading curve and elastic
recovery of trial 103 enter the force law. The material is frozen before applying
the initial conditions and author-calculated instantaneous added inertia for
trials 104 and 105. The test compares separately measured strokes and work.
[Tabri, Määttänen and Ranta](https://aaltodoc.aalto.fi/server/api/core/bitstreams/a6449cf0-7cdb-4a06-8c7f-1363c7d54b26/content) · [Exact fixture and results](whitepaper/reproduce.md#break-03-held-out-model-ship-contacts)

Native shell friction applies the same constrained dissipation objective to the live projected
triangle point. It uses the contact inverse-mass construction of Tobias Preclik, Sebastian Eibl
and Ulrich Rüde, *The Maximum Dissipation Principle in Rigid-Body Dynamics with Purely Inelastic
Impacts* (2018), Eqs. 1–3. In each half-kick the tangent solve uses material-point and sphere
mobility, with the normal Hertz half-impulse setting the Coulomb radius. Node impulses sum
to the opposite rigid impulse. The moment of this impulse is about the same world point for
both bodies, and the sphere's first time moments feed the existing rigid accumulator ports.
[Preclik, Eibl and Rüde](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.00221) · [Independent balance and replay checks](whitepaper/reproduce.md#break-03-distributed-shell-friction)

For simultaneous shell contacts, David E. Johnson and Peter Willemsen,
*Accelerated Haptic Rendering of Polygonal Models through Local Descent*
(2004), use local distance minima to define repulsive contact points.
Miles Macklin and colleagues, *Local Optimization for Robust Signed
Distance Field Collision* (2020), derive per-face minima on a rigid distance
field. The engine specialises this idea to the exact sphere. An edge or vertex
projection is a minimum only while every incident direction has a nonnegative
squared-distance derivative. Barycentric weights from Bridson, Fedkiw and
Anderson, *Robust Treatment of Collisions, Contact and Friction for Cloth
Animation* (2002), distribute the force and friction to the live shell.
[Johnson and Willemsen](https://www-old.cs.utah.edu/gdc/publications/papers/johnson2004.pdf) · [Macklin et al.](https://mmacklin.com/sdfcontact.pdf) · [Bridson, Fedkiw and Anderson](https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/cloth-sig02/)

Pekka Ruponen, *Progressive Flooding of a Damaged Passenger Ship* (2007),
Eq. 3.2, expresses total pressure as air pressure plus hydrostatic head.
M. L. Bucalem and K. J. Bathe, *Finite Element Analysis of Shell Structures*
(1997), Eq. 5, integrate pressure over the current surface along its
normal. The native panel integrates `Nᵢ (pinside − poutside)` against
the current area normal. A waterline clips each affine hydrostatic head.
The clipped integral uses barycentric moments of the linear shape functions
and linear head. SEA-10 supplies the exterior sample and interior water
and air state from the same live opening used in the flooding calculation.
[Ruponen](https://aaltodoc.aalto.fi/server/api/core/bitstreams/745b4f83-7891-4a64-bf68-25f016159491/content) · [Bucalem and Bathe](https://web.mit.edu/kjb/www/Publications_Prior_to_1998/Finite_Element_Analysis_of_Shell_Structures.pdf) · [Exact force and coupling checks](whitepaper/reproduce.md#break-03-hydrostatic-shell-feedback)

Dry friction minimizes the kinetic-energy change `vₜ · q + 0.5 qᵀ W q` with `|q| ≤ μJₙ` after the normal step.
Tobias Preclik, Sebastian Eibl and Ulrich Rüde, “The Maximum Dissipation Principle in Rigid-Body Dynamics
with Purely Inelastic Impacts” (2018), Eqs. 1–3, derive the contact inverse mass and energy objective.
Here the compliant normal reaction sets the fixed friction disk radius. In the tangent plane `W` adds
the two inverse masses and each body's angular response `(r × eᵢ) · I⁻¹(r × eⱼ)`. The zero-slip solution
is `W q = −vₜ`. If that exceeds the disk, choose the unique shift `λ > 0` for which
`(W + λI) q = −vₜ` and `|q| = μJₙ`. The norm decreases monotonically with the shift and is bounded by
`|vₜ|/λ`. Applying the two impulses at the same point transfers momentum while the friction update
dissipates energy. The fixture infers the impulses from the actual motions of unequal rectangular
rigid bodies and derives the effective mass from the box dimensions.
[Preclik, Eibl and Rüde](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.00221)

Tomasz Wierzbicki and Włodzimierz Abramowicz, “On the Crushing Mechanics of Thin-Walled
Structures” (1983), Eq. 7.4 gives `9.56 σ₀ t^(5/3) b^(1/3)` for mean progressive square-tube
folding, with thickness `t` and outside width `b`. The elastic spring starts at `EA/L`, where
`A = 4t(b − t)` is the cross-sectional area. The input flow stress is the mean of tensile proof
and ultimate strengths. Włodzimierz Abramowicz and Norman Jones, “Dynamic Progressive Buckling
of Circular and Square Tubes” (1986) supplies the effective shortening ratio `0.73` for the
reserve before backing engages. This combines the original mean folding law with a separate
finite-stroke limit. It leaves the initial peak, oscillatory folds and global buckling outside the
envelope. At imposed shortening `x`, the trial increase of plastic stroke is
`max(0, x − p − (Fy + Hp)/k) k/(k+H)` truncated at the available stroke. Integrate the flow stress
over that increment for permanent work, and the unloading and backing branches for stored energy.
[Wierzbicki and Abramowicz (1983)](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3167137)
[Abramowicz and Jones (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0734-743X(86)90017-5)

The held-out compression work is from Mohd Yob, Khairul Ismail, M. A. Rojan, Mohd Othman and Ahmad
Ahmad Zaidi, “Quasi Static Axial Compression of Thin
Walled Aluminum Tubes: Analysis of Flow Stress in the Analytical Models” (2016), Table 4 S1–S5.
Tables 1 and 3 separately supply the dimensions and tensile data. The independent test machine's
100 mm travel is the prescribed loading input. Its observed work and mean force never determine a
constant in the solver. The numerical sled uses the same geometry/tensile model and checks work
transfer through the live rigid coupling. [Yob et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.5539/mas.v10n1p34)

Hull openings linked to `crushPatch` use the abrupt change in watertight topology modeled by Pekka
Ruponen, “Progressive Flooding of a Damaged Passenger Ship” (2007), sections 3 and 5.2. The authored
aperture remains sealed through partial damage. After the irreversible structural seal threshold it
feeds the existing SEA-10 hydrostatic-head, air and mass integrator. A horizontal aperture at depth `h`
has dry initial flow `Cᵈ A √(2gh)`. In the coupled fixture, the upper bound assumes a dry, vented
compartment. The lower bound subtracts the largest possible water level rise and Boyle-pressure head
within one tick. The same geometry with partial damage stays shut.
[Ruponen (2007)](https://aaltodoc.aalto.fi/server/api/core/bitstreams/745b4f83-7891-4a64-bf68-25f016159491/content)

Charles S. Smith, “Influence of Local Compressive Failure on Ultimate Longitudinal Strength of
a Ship’s Hull” (1977), treats the section as independent load-shortening elements. Shen Li, Zhiqiang Hu
and Simon Benson, “Progressive Collapse Analysis of Ship Hull Girders Subjected to Extreme Cyclic
Bending” (2020), §2.2,
summarize the curvature increment, element tangent, neutral-axis shift and force balance. For imposed
curvature `κ`, element `i` has strain `ε₀ + κ yᵢ`. At each of its curve breakpoints the derivative of
its section force changes by `Aᵢ (kᵢ⁺ − kᵢ⁻)`. Translate the breakpoints by `−κ yᵢ`, sum those
changes in order and solve the linear force equation on each interval. This gives the stable or
plastically neutral axial roots of the tabulated section. The prior strain identifies the continuation
branch. The signed moment is `Σ yᵢ Aᵢ σᵢ`. The published implementation evaluates the section envelope
at imposed curvature. Deformable shells and cyclic material history remain open.
[Smith (1977)](https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1570291226435916160)
[Li, Hu and Benson (2020)](https://pure.strath.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/118344108/Li_etal_MS_2020_Progressive_collapse_analysis_of_ship_hull_girders.pdf)

J. M. Gordo and C. Guedes Soares, “Experimental Analysis of the Effect of Frame Spacing Variation on the
Ultimate Bending Moment of Box Girders” (2014), §3 supplies the N200 cross-sectional area, second moment
and elastic steel data. Two equal fibers at `±√(I/A)` preserve the area and the second moment for linear
elastic bending. The section predicts 153.6 MN·m² for slope of moment versus curvature. The held-out
relaxed elastic cycles have a 140–160 MN·m² observed band in Fig. 12. The two-fiber reduction is only
for this elastic comparison. The ultimate moments and loading cycles remain separate validation targets.
[Gordo and Guedes Soares (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marstruc.2014.03.003)

Kazuhiro Iijima, Kazuhiro Kimura, Weijun Xu and Masahiko Fujikubo, “Hydroelasto-plasticity
approach to predicting the post-ultimate strength behavior of a ship’s hull girder in waves”
(2011), §2.1, connect the two rigid bodies with reciprocal interface force and a rotational
spring. M. A. Crisfield's “A Consistent Co-Rotational Formulation for Non-Linear,
Three-Dimensional, Beam-Elements” (1990) derives forces and tangents from strain in a
rotating frame. Tassilo Kugelstadt and Elmar Schömer's “Position and Orientation Based
Cosserat Rods” (2016), §5, discretizes Darboux curvature as twice the vector part of relative
rotation divided by segment length. For the selected unit axis `a`, take relative quaternion
`(r,w)`, projected bend `κ = 2(a·r)/L` and angular gradient `g = wa + r×a`.
Work conjugacy with section moment `M` gives the couple `M R_A g` in world axes. The
constant-axial-force moment tangent is
`Σ A E_t y² − (Σ A E_t y)² / Σ A E_t`. The angular update uses its nonnegative directional
tangent to advance the couple over the step. The point spring evaluates the anchor gap, holds
step velocities at the anchors' common midpoint and inverts their combined three-axis
mobility. Both reactions are reciprocal. The tensile limit releases both.
[Iijima et al. (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00773-011-0142-1)
[Crisfield (1990)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0045-7825(90)90106-V)
[Kugelstadt and Schömer (2016)](https://diglib.eg.org/items/eb5dd4ac-529c-4d6b-86ab-454cec714272)

The fracture flag can release a connected compartment opening. Its fixed aperture enters
the existing pressure-head flooding model in the same tick. Hendrik Dankowski's “A Fast
and Explicit Method for Simulating Flooding and Sinkage Scenarios of Ships” (2013) describes
the compartment connection and hydrostatic head. The coupled test bounds the first inflow
using the dry orifice's Bernoulli discharge above and the maximum air and floodwater head
that one step could build below. The control repeats the same fracture with its aperture shut.
[Dankowski (2013)](https://tore.tuhh.de/entities/publication/c9f6ab74-3ae3-4dae-8aa1-ff7bf96a86b2)

Preben T. Pedersen's “Ship grounding and hull-girder strength” (1994) separates the first
contact impulse and the continued frictional response. Bo C. Simonsen's “Ship grounding
on rock—I. Theory” (1997) separates exterior rigid-body motion from local material resistance.
The terrain adapter follows that split and supplies the existing station with the actual
heightfield support normal. John Amanatides and Andrew Woo, “A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm”
(1987), march through grid crossings in order. On a two-dimensional bed, use successive
x/z cell edges and split each interval at its triangle diagonal. Inside the interval,
signed distance to the face is affine, so solving its zero with the surviving permanent
stroke gives the first support. Use the same triangles as the terrain's ordinary collision mesh.
[Pedersen (1994)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0951-8339(94)90008-6)
[Simonsen (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0951-8339(98)00002-1)
[Amanatides and Woo (1987)](https://doi.org/10.2312/egtp.19871000)

Bo Cerup Simonsen and Lars Peder Lauridsen, “Energy absorption and ductile failure in
metal sheets under lateral indentation by a sphere” (2000), Eqs. 1, 8, 12–15 and 18,
formulate the axisymmetric membrane with vertical displacement and conserved volume.
Let `s = sin θ` and `c = cos θ`. The radial strain is `ε = −ln c` and the deformed
thickness is `t c`. Rodney Hill's *The Mathematical Theory of Plasticity* (1950) gives
associated von Mises flow in plane strain. Under zero hoop strain and zero thickness
stress, `σθ = σr/2`, `σeq = √3 σr/2`, and `εeq = 2 ε/√3`. Transforming the
uniaxial Hollomon law into this state multiplies radial stress by `(2/√3)^(1+n)`.
This conversion uses the coupon's parameters directly. The shape solves vertical
equilibrium `r c s ε^n = rC cC sC εC^n` on the outward, low-slope branch and integrates
`tan θ` in logarithmic radius. The spherical-contact radius uses the physical sphere
plus half the sheet thickness. Localization is the first maximum of
`F = 2π C t rC cC sC εC^n (2/√3)^(1+n)`. Work integrates the force–stroke relation.
For render samples, the measured rest plane is held on its outer edge.
[Simonsen and Lauridsen (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0734-743X(00)00024-5)
[Hill (1950)](https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Mathematical_Theory_of_Plasticity.html?hl=en&id=DIDOuwEACAAJ)

The four measured circular specimens are held out from this calculation. Table 1 gives
the stroke and work at localization. Geometry (radius 111.4 mm, thickness 1 mm, tip radii
10, 13, 25 and 50 mm) and separate uniaxial coupon values (497 MPa, exponent 0.19, Table 2)
are the inputs. The predictions are 25.47, 29.49, 41.80 and 57.39 mm versus measured
26.84, 31.20, 41.84 and 60.00 mm. Predicted work is 150.3, 224.3, 605.1 and 1654.7 J
versus measured 159.17, 254.24, 575.20 and 1687.30 J. The lower work on the two smaller
tips remains visible. The regime is quasi-static, axisymmetric, and ends at localization.

The native impulse path uses relative normal speed `v` and inverse mass `w` from
the shared RigidSolver port. Append `min(v²/(2w), Wf − Wprior)` to retained material
work, invert the monotone work integral to obtain the new stroke, then solve
`J = 2ΔW/(v + √(v² − 2wΔW))`. Both bodies receive opposite impulses at the shared
point. An intact dent can carry a lower continuing normal load up to its previous force
without growing. Rupture releases the station and latches its seal loss, which uses
the existing SEA-10 aperture contract. The geometric layer samples the same stored
permanent stroke. The coupled moving pair measures the change in relative kinetic
energy independently of the work ledger.

Manuel Stein, “Loads and Deformations of Buckled Rectangular Plates” (1959), NASA TR R-40, Eqs. 1–3
and Fig. 1, gives the von Kármán plate equations and longitudinal mode selection. Pai C. Hu, Eugene
E. Lundquist and S. B. Batdorf, “Effect of Small Deviations from Flatness on Effective Width and
Buckling of Plates in Compression” (1946), Appendix, uses the stress-free initial curvature in
the nonlinear strain terms. The first-mode displacement is `a sin(αx) sin(βy)`, `α = mπ/L`, `β = π/B`.
The Airy compatibility equation has a forcing proportional to `α²β²(a² − a₀²)(cos 2αx + cos 2βy)`.
Projection of the membrane force onto the first mode gives `σ/E = εcr(1 − a₀/a) + K(a² − a₀²)`,
with `εcr = t²(α² + β²)²/[12(1 − ν²)α²]` and `K = (α⁴ + β⁴)/(16α²)`. The imposed shortening strain
adds the mean geometric term `α²(a² − a₀²)/8`. The positive-amplitude solution is monotone if
there is an initial crest. Its sign follows the authored imperfection. Surface normals use derivatives
with respect to the shortened x and y coordinates, and all four support edges have zero out-of-plane motion.
[Stein (1959)](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19980235521)
[Hu, Lundquist and Batdorf (1946)](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19930081796)

Stein’s Appendix gives a 25.36 in by 4.71 in by 0.072 in plate bay in a knife-edge fixture. The first
three early postbuckling comparison points come from the experimental trace in Fig. 3 before secondary
mode changes. At nondimensional shortenings 1.25, 1.50 and 1.75, the measured loads are approximately
1.13, 1.27 and 1.42. Calculated loads are 1.137, 1.272 and 1.407, with five longitudinal half-waves.
The test uses the held-out measured line and derives the model from the elastic equations. The 0.02
dimensionless load band covers line thickness and rounding when reading the printed axes. The measured trace extends into plasticity
and changes to six, seven and eight half-waves. Those regimes are outside this first-mode model.

The linked plate samples the first mode at the continuous contact's current total stroke. The
unilateral release samples the material return map's permanent stroke. The saved region records
one total stroke per configured plate, so the field is independent of the sample mesh resolution.
This uses the existing station's material curve for reaction and the first-mode geometry for
rendering local shortening. The live fixture pushes and retracts a real RigidSolver carriage.

## Thin liquid films on moving surfaces (FLUID-07)

- Alexander Oron, Stephen H. Davis and S. George Bankoff, “Long-scale evolution of thin liquid
  films” (1997), equations 2.25–2.30. Substrate-normal gravity and surface tension give the
  reduced pressure. Through-depth integration yields pressure mobility
  `(h³/3 + βh²)/μ` and shear mobility `(h²/2 + βh)/μ` for Navier slip length β.
  The normal momentum balance in §II.A gives the hydrostatic wall load `ρ (g · n) h`.
  Integrating the pressure and its first moment over the cells gives the net load and torque
  about the rigid body's centre of mass.
  The rendering geometry uses the graph of substrate height plus film depth. In Eq. 2.112,
  the normal comes from the height derivative. For the planar two-coordinate graph use
  `normalize(n − u ∂H/∂u − v ∂H/∂v)`. Extend the edge cells to the authored boundary.
  The mesh preserves the film clock and does not write into the solver arena.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.69.931) · [Paper](https://www.tmfcr.cz/39/pdf/04-oron.pdf)
- Leonard W. Schwartz and Richard R. Eley, “Simulation of Droplet Motion on Low-Energy and
  Heterogeneous Surfaces” (1998). Add pressure `A (r² − r³)` for the resolved precursor, where
  `r = h*/h` and `A = 2 σ (1 − cos θ) / h*`. Integrating from `h*` to infinity gives the
  wetting energy `σ (1 − cos θ)` per unit area. Oron et al. equation 2.47b gives the pressure
  sign. The linear continuation below `h*` matches the pressure and its slope at the
  precursor. The implicit slope `A/h*` bounds the resulting local energy curvature, while
  the remaining pressure stays in the face right-hand side.
  A patterned backing uses the local angle in each cell's pressure and energy. The cell
  stiffness then enters the symmetric face solve as a diagonal, and the exact face
  preconditioner includes the sum of the two adjacent stiffnesses.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcis.1998.5448)
- A. M. Cazabat and M. A. Cohen Stuart, “Dynamics of wetting: effects of surface roughness”
  (1986), and Peter Ehrhard, “Experiments on isothermal and non-isothermal spreading”
  (1993), Table 2. Their spherical-drop measurements give the complete-wetting,
  capillary-controlled exponent interval 0.094–0.125 for silicone oils on glass.
  The independent solver check uses a fixed one-microlitre shallow cap and the
  zero-gravity limit of the film equations. Multiplying the viscosity and clock by the
  same factor preserves those equations. No measured radii or exponents set the model.
  [Cazabat and Cohen Stuart](https://doi.org/10.1021/j100280a075) · [Ehrhard](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112093003167)
- Herbert E. Huppert, “The propagation of two-dimensional and axisymmetric viscous gravity
  currents over a rigid horizontal surface” (1982), §3 and Table 1(a), run ×. The input is
  the measured 406 mL release and 13.2 cm²/s kinematic viscosity in the 45 mm radius cylinder.
  In the gravity-dominated limit, density cancels between pressure and dynamic viscosity.
  Integrating the late-time profile in equation 2.28 gives a radial mass moment of `3R²/7`.
  The measured radius fit `0.900 (g V³ / (3 ν))^(1/8) t^0.120` is used only to check the
  simulated radii. The release starts from the gate geometry without a similarity profile.
  The gravity-only approximation omits the experimental surface-tension effects near the front.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112082001797)
- Herbert E. Huppert, “Flow and instability of a viscous current down a slope” (1982),
  equations 2 and 7, and “Gravity currents: a personal perspective” (2006), supplementary Movie 1.
  A finite-volume release on a slope has a late profile `h ∝ sqrt(x)` and front distance
  `x_N = (9 A² g sin θ t / (4 ν))^(1/3)`. Its downstream mass centroid is `3x_N/5`.
  The separate simulation starts from a prescribed 5 cm gate and 8 cm² cross section. The movie
  supplies only the ratio of consecutive increments of cubed front distance, which cancels an
  unknown constant image scale, recording speed and start time. No video measurement sets a
  solver input. [Nature](https://doi.org/10.1038/300427a0) · [Supplementary Movie 1](https://doi.org/10.1017/S002211200600930X)
- Gene H. Golub and Charles F. Van Loan, “Matrix Computations”, fourth edition (2013), §4.3.
  A strip's face gradient times its transpose has diagonals `−1, 2, −1`. Its square gives the
  curvature term's five bands. The film pressure solve factors that symmetric positive definite
  band directly, using scratch already owned by the solver. The modal regression checks the same
  discrete equation with three independent Neumann cosine modes.
  [Publisher](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781421407944)
- Eike H. Müller and Robert Scheichl, “Massively parallel solvers for elliptic PDEs in
  numerical weather and climate prediction” (2014), sections 4.2 and 6.2.2, use complete
  grid lines to precondition elliptic coupling. The thin-film face operator uses the
  principal five-band blocks along each grid axis with Cholesky factorization. The
  capillary contribution coupling consecutive faces contains the shared cell's grid
  degree plus two, and their second-neighbour coupling comes from one Laplacian edge.
  The remaining couplings are applied by the full operator at every iteration.
  [Author preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2036)
- Yvan Notay, “Flexible Conjugate Gradients” (2000), section 2, gives explicit
  orthogonalization of the search directions for an approximate preconditioner.
  At high stiffness Margo eliminates the face correction from
  `(I + D K Dᵀ) δx = r`, giving `(I + DᵀD K) δh = Dᵀr`.
  Here `D` is the mobility-weighted gradient and `K` contains the time-scaled height
  stiffness and, when enabled, the contact diagonal. The cell operator is symmetric
  in the `K` inner product. Four Jacobi sweeps use the cell mobility diagonal, and
  conjugate directions are orthogonalized against the previous step.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1137/S1064827599362314)
- James Demmel, Yozo Hida, William Kahan, Xiaoye S. Li, Sonil Mukherjee and E. Jason Riedy,
  “Error Bounds from Extra Precise Iterative Refinement” (2006), Algorithm 1. Only the
  residual-correction identity is used here. The film computes in f64 and evaluates
  the original face operator after each reconstructed correction. Only the true face
  residual can satisfy the original pressure threshold.
  [Author PDF](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~wkahan/itref.pdf)
- Shuo Zhang and Jinchao Xu, “Optimal solvers for fourth-order PDEs discretized on
  unstructured grids” (2014), section 2. Their analysis distinguishes the eigenvalue
  distribution from the worst-case condition number in fourth-order solves. The film
  regression tests the nearly uniform modal case independently of the variable-mobility
  cap. The diagonal preconditioner is retained when the positive mobilities span
  at most a factor of four.
  [Author preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.0632)
- Huamin Wang, Peter J. Mucha and Greg Turk, “Water Drops on Surfaces” (2005), sections 4–6.
  Young's relation supplies the equilibrium angle and Laplace pressure relates curvature to
  pressure. Equation 10 brackets the stationary contact front by the advancing and receding
  contact angles. A deposited drop contributes its volume and subcell footprint through
  conservative finite volumes.
  [Author PDF](https://wanghmin.github.io/publication/wang-2005-wds/Wang-2005-WDS.pdf)
- Giovanni Alberti and Antonio DeSimone, “Quasistatic evolution of sessile drops and contact angle
  hysteresis” (2011), sections 2.6–2.7. The loss per unit change of footprint is
  `σ(cos θ_eq − cos θ_a)` when advancing and `σ(cos θ_r − cos θ_eq)` when receding.
