  The resolved footprint uses `χ(h) = (1 − h*/h)²` above the precursor and zero below.
  The frozen derivative `χ′(h)` converts the two area losses to pressure thresholds.
  This is a smooth-footprint adaptation of the paper's dissipation distance.
  [Author PDF](https://cvgmt.sns.it/media/doc/paper/827/gads2.pdf)
- Stephen Boyd, Neal Parikh, Eric Chu, Borja Peleato and Jonathan Eckstein, “Distributed
  Optimization and Statistical Learning via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers”
  (2011), sections 3.1–3.3. The weighted face flux and cell wet-area rate form the two blocks.
  The face solve includes the tangential body force and air shear. The cell update clips the
  multiplier to the interval between its advancing and receding thresholds. The face and cell
  residuals must both converge. Cell scaling uses the diagonal approximation of the face
  solve's inverse to account for capillary and wetting stiffness.
  [Author PDF](https://stanford.edu/~boyd/papers/pdf/admm_distr_stats.pdf)
  On one-row or one-column strips the cell diagonal from the augmented term changes only the
  nearest face coupling and leaves five bands. The solution without the augmented term sets
  the initial wet-area rate. The augmented factor is reused while its right hand side changes.
  Section 3.4.3's over-relaxation uses 1.6 in the wet-area proximal step and leaves the
  convergence checks on the original rates.
- C. G. L. Furmidge, “Studies at phase interfaces. I. The sliding of liquid drops on solid
  surfaces and a theory for spray retention” (1962). The downslope component of weight balances
  capillary retention. For a spanwise-uniform cap the work of a rigid translation uses unit
  transverse width. Multiplying each advancing and receding area cost by the smooth footprint
  change gives the force per unit width `σ(cos θ_r − cos θ_a)χ(h_peak)`. This brackets the
  numerical onset on two grids.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1016/0095-8522(62)90011-9)
- Joël De Coninck, François Dunlop and Thierry Huillet, “Contact angles of a drop pinned
  on an incline” (2017), equations 15–17. In the small-tilt circular limit, the azimuthal
  integral multiplies Furmidge's diameter by π/4. The level thin film supplies the
  smooth footprint's projected width. The model infers a quasi-static release angle
  from the separately measured angles and volume.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052805)
- Sravanthi Vallabhuneni, “Designing Non-Textured, All-Solid, Slippery Hydrophilic Surfaces”
  (doctoral thesis, 2023), chapter 4. Section 4.4 supplies advancing and receding
  angles of 39° and 36° for water on PEG-coated silicon. The 72 mN/m water case in
  Table 4.3 separately reports the measured 20 μL slide threshold of 3°. Only that
  measured column is used for comparison with the small-tilt force integral.
  [Author thesis](https://repository.lib.ncsu.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/2f887b7a-5e67-4945-9782-8fde454cb016/content)
- L. Zhornitskaya and A. L. Bertozzi, “Positivity-Preserving Numerical Schemes for
  Lubrication-Type Equations” (2000). The fourth-order equation lacks the second-order maximum
  principle. Here each shared face uses one single flux limited by the donor's total outgoing
  water. This is a conservative remap after the implicit pressure solve.
  [Author PDF](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~bertozzi/papers/ZhornitskayaBertozzi.pdf)
- Ross Gunn and Gilbert D. Kinzer, “The Terminal Velocity of Fall for Water Droplets in
  Stagnant Air” (1949). The atmospheric contract supplies both the measured-fall-speed model
  and water-equivalent precipitation. The surface converts the horizontal flux to its
  own area by the ratio of inward relative normal speed to still-air fall speed.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469(1949)006%3C0243:TTVOFF%3E2.0.CO;2)
- Ruiqi Wang, Haijun Jia and Riqiang Duan, “Experimental Observation of Flow Reversal in
  Thin Liquid Film Flow Falling on an Inclined Plate” (2020). Section 2, Table 2 and the
  Reynolds numbers label the independently calibrated inlet and glycerol properties. The
  published PIV/PLIF error bars in Figure 9(a–c) supply the held-out depth check. The
  fixture starts dry and uses the 20° plate and 350 mm probe from the experimental setup.
  [Journal and original figure](https://doi.org/10.3390/coatings10060599)
- M. Fermigier, L. Limat, J. E. Wesfreid, P. Boudinet and C. Quilliet, “Two-dimensional
  patterns in Rayleigh–Taylor instability of a thin layer” (1992).
  Equation 1.3 gives the linear rate `M(ρg q² − σq⁴)` under an inverted plate when gas
  inertia and density are negligible. The film treats the adverse normal gravity explicitly
  and retains implicit curvature. The fastest mode has rate `M(ρg)²/(4σ)`. At that
  wavelength the explicit gravity coefficient is twice the rate, so the native solver
  subdivides to keep the explicit contribution at most one-half per step.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112092001447)
- Etienne Jambon-Puillet, Pier Giuseppe Ledda, François Gallaire and P.-T. Brun,
  “Drops on the Underside of a Slightly Inclined Wet Substrate Move Too Fast to Grow”
  (2021). Supplement S1 gives the suspended film equation with full height-graph
  curvature `div(grad h / sqrt(1 + |grad h|²))`. Freeze the positive face metric in each
  semi-implicit solve and use the same face mobility for the downslope body force and
  pressure gradient. The starting drop comes from the Young–Laplace equation S2 and
  Fig. 2(b). The Fig. 3 measured five-minute amplitude and travel are held-out outputs.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.127.044503)
- Yasuhiko H. Mori, “Harkins–Brown correction factor for drop formation” (1990), equations
  3 and 7. For a wet circular rim of diameter `D`, the ideal volume is `Vp = πDσ/(ρg)`.
  The released volume is `Vp[0.6 + 0.4(1 − D/(1.4 Vp^(1/3)))^2.2]` in the published
  diameter-ratio range. Accumulate volume from the assigned edge cell and publish each
  crossing of this volume as a detached drop. This is a quasistatic, primed-rim model.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1002/aic.690360819)
- Xiaoguang Zhang and Osman A. Basaran, “Dynamics of drop formation from a capillary in
  the presence of an electric field” (1996), Figure 1 without an electric field. Its
  1 mL/min input through a 3.2 mm outer diameter and roughly 3.09 s observed cycle imply
  51.5 μL per cycle. The uncalibrated model releases 50.17 μL per cycle.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112096008300)
- Kenneth V. Beard, “Terminal Velocity and Shape of Cloud and Precipitation Drops Aloft”
  (1976). Use the Davies-number relation for a steady wake and the Bond number and
  physical-property number for a deformed drop with an unsteady wake. Both terminal Reynolds
  relations use volume-equivalent diameter. The maximum modeled diameter is 7 mm.
  Integer products and pinned transcendental functions keep the flight state replayable.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469(1976)033%3C0851:TVASOC%3E2.0.CO;2)
- Pao K. Wang and Hans R. Pruppacher, “Acceleration to Terminal Velocity of Cloud and
  Raindrops” (1977). Invert Beard's relation at the instantaneous Reynolds number to get
  the equivalent terminal drop. Its weight balance gives the drag coefficient. The
  acceleration on the actual drop follows by dividing the resulting drag force by the
  actual mass. The available sphere relation handles the creeping-flow limit, and the
  last deformed-drop coefficient applies above the range of the terminal relation.
  Freeze the rate at a midpoint predictor and integrate velocity and displacement together.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0450(1977)016%3C0275:ATTVOC%3E2.0.CO;2)
- Steven E. Hinkle, Dale F. Heermann and Michael C. Blue, “Falling Water Drop Velocities”
  (1987), Tables 1 and 2. Four independently measured
  diameters at 20 °C and 84.1 kPa give fall speeds at 1, 3 and 5 m. Neither instrument's
  output determines the drag coefficients or initial conditions.
  [USDA paper](https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/30100000/Publications%201989-1980/189%201987%20Hinkle%20-%20Falling%20water%20drop%20velocitie.pdf)
- Lawrence F. Shampine and Skip Thompson, “Event location for ordinary differential equations”
  (2000). Find the first root of the receiver clearance along the continuous frozen-drag
  trajectory. Its normal velocity is monotone, so splitting at its zero also catches a crossing
  that returns to positive clearance within the same step. At contact, project the spherical centre
  onto the receiving plane and publish its volume and inward normal speed in the existing impact layout.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0898-1221(00)00045-6)
- Christer Ericson, *Real-Time Collision Detection* (2005), §§5.5.3–5.5.5. Use a signed
  radius offset to find sphere–plane contact and subtract the receiver's translation
  from both drop and wind velocities. The frozen drag rate and buoyed gravity carry into
  that frame unchanged. The plane translates linearly between registered rigid endpoint
  poses. The receiver transforms the hit back into its UV coordinates and publishes the
  relative inward speed for the normal recoil. Save the prior rigid pose in the flight
  snapshot to replay a sweep including fractional births.
  Section 5.5.6 motivates the rounded collision region of a bounded wet surface. For
  optional edge capture, calculate the closest point on the local rectangle and find
  the zero of squared distance minus sphere radius squared. Its derivative is continuous
  across the face–edge and edge–corner transitions. Bound its curvature using the
  sphere's body-relative speed and acceleration over the interval. Use the closest wet
  point for deposition and the radial contact normal for recoil on the liquid side.
  [Publisher](https://shop.elsevier.com/books/real-time-collision-detection/ericson/978-1-55860-732-3)
- Joan Solà, “Quaternion kinematics for the error-state Kalman filter” (2017), Eq. 203.
  Interpolate the two orientations with the normalized shortest chord and use
  `2 Im(q̇ q*)` to obtain world-frame angular velocity. For the unnormalized chord
  `Q(λ) = q0 + λ Δq`, the numerator `Im(Δq Q*)` is constant and `|Q|²` is bounded below
  by `(1 + |q0 · q1|)/2`. This gives bounds on the normal's first and second derivatives.
  [Author paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.02508)
- Xinyu Zhang, Stéphane Redon, Minkyoung Lee and Young J. Kim, “Continuous collision
  detection for articulated models using Taylor models and temporal culling” (2007),
  §§5–7. Adapt time-interval culling to a drop sphere and one rotating plane. If signed
  clearance curvature is bounded by `M`, its deviation from a secant over width `T` is at
  most `M T²/8`. Subdivide uncertain intervals before solving the first descending root.
  The normal's derivatives depend only on displacement and speed perpendicular to the
  rotation axis. At contact use the relative normal speed and the surface-point offset
  from the rigid centre. The receiving film uses the same normal and offset for its impulse.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1145/1276377.1276396)
- Gianpietro E. Cossali, Aldo Coghe and Marco Marengo, “The impact of a single drop on a wetted
  solid surface” (1997). The optional absorbing receiver represents deposition with conserved liquid
  volume. The experiments distinguish deposition from a separate splash regime.
  [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1007/s003480050073)
- Xiaolong Yu, Yifan Shao, Kwee-Yan Teh and David L. S. Hung, “Force of droplet impact on thin
  liquid films” (2022). The resolved force history depends on film depth and on the short
  impact timescale. The rigid option represents the unresolved, absorbed normal impulse
  `−ρ V U n`. Deposit the droplet in the film and apply this impulse and its moment about
  the body centre through the registered body force port. The wake option owns the other
  route for that pulse. [Journal](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0083437)
- IAPWS, *Release on the Refractive Index of Ordinary Water Substance* (1997), Eq. 1.
  The moving-window browser regression uses water IOR 1.333, the rounded visible index at
  room temperature. The render reads meters of solver depth into the surface mesh and its
  linear thickness map. Centre-difference gradients give the free-surface normals. The
  existing material transmission uses the green channel for thickness, following Khronos,
  *KHR_materials_volume*, and the microfacet refraction model of Bruce Walter, Stephen
  R. Marschner, Hongsong Li and Kenneth E. Torrance (2007). An airborne drop is drawn as
  a sphere at the integrated position and with the volume-equivalent diameter.
  [IAPWS R9-97](https://iapws.org/technical-guidance/release/Rindex) ·
  [Khronos volume](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_volume/README.md) ·
  [Walter et al.](https://doi.org/10.2312/EGWR/EGSR07/195-206)

The clean-room face system uses the cell-to-face gradient G, the lagged diagonal mobility M, and
the symmetric cell pressure operator K. It solves
`[I + Δt sqrt(M) G K Gᵀ sqrt(M)] y = −sqrt(M) G p` by Jacobi PCG before applying the positive
mass remap. A patch mounted on a body uses the published pose, angular velocity and the previous
centre velocity. The impact couples to the wave-pressure field through the incoming normal
momentum divided by step duration and the analytical area of the raised-cosine footprint.

## ATMO-06 environmental airborne particles

- Roland Clift, John R. Grace and Martin E. Weber, *Bubbles, Drops, and Particles* (1978). Spherical drag starts from the Stokes force 3πμd |Δu|. Schiller–Naumann multiplies it by 1 + 0.15 Re^0.687 with Re = ρₐ d |Δu| / μ. The spherical approximation uses Cᴅ = 0.44 above Re = 1,000. Cross-section divided by particle mass is 3/(2ρₚd). [Original volume](https://books.google.com/books?id=n8gRAQAAIAAJ).
- C. N. Davies, *Definitive Equations for the Fluid Resistance of Spheres* (1945). The slip factor 1 + (λ/r)[1.257 + 0.4 exp(−1.1r/λ)] divides the low-Re drag rate. Mean free path follows from gas viscosity, density and molecular mean speed. [Published paper](https://doi.org/10.1088/0959-5309/57/4/301).
- William Sutherland, *The Viscosity of Gases and Molecular Force* (1893). The viscosity ratio is (T/T₀)^(3/2)(T₀ + S)/(T + S) with dry-air coefficients and temperature in kelvins. [Original paper](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786449308620508).
- D. J. Thomson, *Criteria for the Selection of Stochastic Models of Particle Trajectories in Turbulent Flows* (1987). Use the homogeneous Gaussian case. Set a = exp(−Δt/Tᴸ). Each gust component keeps a times its prior value and takes an independent Gaussian increment with standard deviation σ√(1 − a²), sampled by the parcel and tick's Philox keys. [Original paper](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112087001940).
- James Clerk Maxwell, steady diffusion to a sphere (1877), and V. A. Vlasov, *On a Theory of Mass Transfer During the Evaporation of a Spherical Droplet* (2021). The diffusive mass flux is 4πrDᵥ times the difference between the saturated and ambient vapour densities. Combining it with spherical volume gives d(d²)/dt = −8Dᵥ times that density difference divided by liquid density. The Buck CR-1A manual supplies the saturation equation. [Mass-transfer paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijheatmasstransfer.2021.121597) · [Buck Research manual](https://www.hygrometers.com/wp-content/uploads/CR-1A-users-manual-2009-12.pdf).
- M. D. Petters and S. M. Kreidenweis, *A Single Parameter Representation of Hygroscopic Growth and Cloud Condensation Nucleus Activity* (2007). Equation 6 with a flat interface gives the wet-to-dry diameter-cubed ratio 1 + κ RH/(1 − RH). Table 1 gives κ = 1.12 for mean measured sodium chloride growth. Shrinkage stops at equilibrium or at the dry solute when ambient humidity is zero. [Original paper](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-7-1961-2007).
- S. L. Gong, *A Parameterization of Sea-Salt Aerosol Source Function for Sub- and Super-Micron Particles* (2003), and E. L. Andreas, *A New Sea Spray Generation Function* (1998). The existing SEA-13 Gong source is per area of active whitecap. Three midpoint bins integrate the source over 1–20 µm r₈₀. SEA-13's formation convention sets r₀ ≈ 2r₈₀. The number flux times formation volume, density and patch area gives each representative mass-rate band. [Gong](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003GB002079) · [Andreas](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485%281998%29028%3C2175%3AANSSGF%3E2.0.CO%3B2).

The equation for frozen local wind and drag over a step is dv/dt = −β(v − u) + g(1 − ρₐ/ρₚ).
Its analytical velocity and displacement use the exponential decay, its time integral and the
integral of that integral. The Rust kernel computes X and Y together and uses the same arithmetic
order for Z. Field reads precede the native batch. The transported materials are environmental
mineral dust and water droplets.

ATMO-06 applies the frozen parcel integration to disjoint rows. X and Y position and velocity remain paired
in Rust SIMD. Z uses the same arithmetic order. Each thread counts its actual updates. Philox keys, source
emission, bed queries, stable compaction and mass sums stay in fixed caller order. For very slow homogeneous
turbulence, evaluate Thomson's Ornstein–Uhlenbeck variance with its Taylor expansion to avoid cancellation.

R. Gunn and G. D. Kinzer (1949) studied freely falling drops. K. V. Beard and H. R. Pruppacher (1969)
measured drop drag independently in a wind tunnel. The atmospheric settling diagnostic uses these references
without fitting the drag or gas slip coefficients. The separate Kinzer–Gunn (1951) free-fall evaporation
comparison uses the tabulated factors from Smithsonian Table 117 and retains the measured differences.
[Smithsonian tables](https://repository.si.edu/items/5b259e9c-a900-48e0-ad68-07bb46302156) ·
[Beard and Pruppacher](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469%281969%29026%3C1066%3AADOTTV%3E2.0.CO%3B2) ·
[Kinzer and Gunn](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469%281951%29008%3C0071%3ATETATR%3E2.0.CO%3B2)

The spray display uses the large-drop extinction limit described by J. E. Hansen and L. D. Travis (1974),
with visible optical area equal to the drop count times twice its geometric cross-section. Depositing that
area into a spatial volume divides by the integral over the three-standard-deviation spherical Gaussian.
This integral follows by substituting radial distance into the normal density. The renderer compares
the discretized volume to the separate radial integral in `environment/tests/density-volume.test.js`.
[Hansen and Travis](https://pubs.giss.nasa.gov/abs/ha09500o.html)

### Developmental plant growth (BIO-02)

- Przemyslaw Prusinkiewicz and Aristid Lindenmayer, [The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants](https://algorithmicbotany.org/papers/#abop) (1990), chapters 2 and 4. The tree example in Fig. 2.6 uses a parent apex that creates an internode, a continuing apex and a lateral apex on the same production. The module instantiates that production synchronously at season boundaries. Lateral azimuth follows a configurable fixed divergence angle with the golden-angle default.
- Wojciech Pałubicki, Kipp Horel, Steven Longay, Adam Runions, Brendan Lane, Radomír Měch and Przemyslaw Prusinkiewicz, [Self-organizing tree models for image synthesis](https://algorithmicbotany.org/papers/selforg.sig2009.small.pdf) (2009), §§4.1–4.5 and Fig. 8. The source adds penumbra `a b^(-q)` per layer, restores the emitting bud's own shade and distributes vigor in proportion to `λQmain` and `(1−λ)Qlateral`. The engine implements the attenuation as repeated multiplication by a retained fraction. Available source extension is bounded by the plant's measured seasonal maximum and scaled by relative soil water. The new direction is the normalized weighted sum of the current bud heading, a light-seeking direction from the shadow gradient, and the vertical tropism. The area-specialized pipe model sums squared radii at forks and keeps existing wood when support demand falls.
- Sören Pirk, Ondřej Šťava, Julian Kratt, Michel Abdul Massih Said, Boris Neubert, Radomír Měch, Bedřich Beneš and Oliver Deussen, [Plastic Trees](https://graphics.uni-konstanz.de/publikationen/Pirk2012PlasticTreesInteractive/Pirk2012PlasticTreesInteractive.pdf) (2012), §5.3. Tree and obstacle shadows change branch results. Our branch creation follows the prior developmental model and tests new segments against the occupied voxel interior. It avoids re-deforming the existing parent skeleton.

Each solver gets a contiguous topology region whose size follows the productive lifetime, the minimum eligible extension and the maximum seasonal resource. The two layout-compatible native kernels accumulate voxel penumbrae in fixed order and vectorize consecutive x cells. No initial bytes are written into the arena, as verified by a full-memory sentinel in both builds.

## SOUND-02 enclosed and urban acoustic pressure and early paths

- J. B. Allen and D. A. Berkley, *Image Method for Efficiently Simulating Small-Room Acoustics* (1979).
  Equation 10 gives distance divided by sound speed for arrival time and the product of wall pressure coefficients
  divided by 4π times distance for the spherical Green function. Our gains are relative to a direct source at
  one metre, which removes the shared 4π factor. We reflect the point across each finite convex face, reconstruct the
  path backward and reject bounces outside the polygon or segments blocked by another face. [Paper](https://jontalle.web.engr.illinois.edu/Public/Allen-PDFs/PDFs/AllenBerkley79.pdf).
- N. Raghuvanshi and J. Snyder, *Parametric Wave Field Coding for Precomputed Sound Propagation* (2014). Figure 1 and
  the response-parameter discussion motivate separating directional early arrivals from the wave response that
  carries diffracted pressure and late reverberation. The optional entry exposes those two response types directly.
  [Paper](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/ParametricWaveField.pdf).
- B. Hamilton and S. Bilbao, *FDTD Methods for 3-D Room Acoustics Simulation with High-Order Accuracy in Space and Time*
  (2017). The seven-point finite-difference baseline uses two pressure states with a second-order time update.
  A cubic lattice with λ = cΔt/h is stable for λ ≤ 1/√3. The solver chooses enough dyadic steps inside the 60 Hz
  world step to meet that bound. [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASLP.2017.2744799).
- S. Bilbao and B. Hamilton, *Passive Volumetric Time Domain Simulation for Room Acoustics Applications* (2019).
  A dissipative boundary prescribes normal pressure derivative proportional to the negative time derivative.
  For a real normal-incidence pressure reflection R, the normalized admittance is η = (1 − R)/(1 + R).
  Applying the flux per closed face with a centered time derivative gives D = ληNclosed/2 + γΔt.
  The update divides [2p + (D − 1)p_previous + λ² sum(p_neighbor − p)] by 1 + D. Solid cells have no pressure
  and the sum includes only open neighbours. γ is the optional uniform attenuation rate.
  [Paper](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31046344/).
- C. F. Eyring, *Reverberation Time in “Dead” Rooms* (1930). The diffuse mean free path is 4V/S. Multiplying
  energy by the mean survival fraction 1 − α on each wall encounter gives RT60 = 24 ln(10)V/[−cS ln(1 − α)].
  [Paper](https://www.trueaudio.com/array/downloads/CF%20Eyring-Reverb%20Time%20in%20Dead%20Rooms.pdf).
- M. R. Schroeder, *New Method of Measuring Reverberation Time* (1965). We expose the backward sum of squared
  pressure samples divided by its initial total for the measured finite impulse response. The normalization
  peak rescales before squaring to preserve finite near-zero and large pressure values.
  [Paper](https://labrosa.ee.columbia.edu/~dpwe/papers/Schro65-reverb.pdf).

The native pressure update uses SIMD over adjacent cells, immutable boundary coefficients and two pressure regions.
The continuous reflection model, fractional sample projection and audio-node setup are independently testable.

Hamilton and Bilbao (2017), §II.C–D and equations 10–18, describe overwriting the older pressure value at each
voxel because neighbours are read from the current pressure array. Each native participant therefore writes
disjoint cell pairs. The caller joins the partitions, applies the source, reads the receiver and alternates the
arrays before the next sample. The guard and solid lanes keep their existing masks. Bilbao's finite-volume
derivation expresses locally reacting passive wall admittance as a face flux. [Face-flux derivation](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASL.2013.2256897)

- J. Borish, *Extension of the image model to arbitrary polyhedra* (1984). The concert-hall cutaway
  independently unfolds two finite wall reflections and compares bounce locations, incident direction and
  direct and twice-reflected impulse timing with the production path and Web Audio convolver.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.390983)
- F. Brinkmann, L. Aspöck, D. Ackermann, R. Opdam, M. Vorländer and S. Weinzierl, *A benchmark for room acoustical
  simulation. Concept and database* (2021). RS1 rigid-floor geometry and recorded conditions set the
  ten source/receiver cases. The measured outputs are excess reflection delays extracted from the
  original WAVs by locating two arrivals independently of the predicted path. The difference removes
  recorder latency. The comparison never adjusts a model input to match an observed delay.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apacoust.2020.107867)
  [BRAS version 3](https://doi.org/10.14279/depositonce-6726.3)

## Finite-strain viscoplastic flow (FLUID-06)

- Daniel Ram, Theodore Gast, Chenfanfu Jiang, Craig Schroeder, Alexey Stomakhin, Joseph
  Teran and Pirouz Kavehpour, “A Material Point Method for Viscoelastic Fluids, Foams
  and Sponges” (2015). The elastic left Cauchy–Green tensor carries material strain.
  A Newtonian solvent part can dissipate energy independently of plastic flow.
  [Paper](https://mass.math.ucdavis.edu/~jteran/papers/RGJSSTK15.pdf)
- Yonghao Yue, Breannan Smith, Christopher Batty, Changxi Zheng and Eitan Grinspun,
  “Continuum Foam: A Material Point Method for Shear-Dependent Flows” (2015), equations
  2, 12–18. Predict `Finc = I + dt ∇v`, update `J` with its determinant and evolve
  the normalized tensor with `Finc B Fincᵀ`. Volumetric Kirchhoff stress is
  `κ(J²−1)/2`. Reduce the deviator only above yield, then restore the tensor's
  unit determinant. The scalar implicit return is a bracketed solve, with a closed
  form for Bingham flow. The API uses the shear invariant `||s||/√2` so its
  yield parameter is the simple-shear value.
  [Paper](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~yonghao/tog15/yue-mpm-shear-dependent-flow.pdf)
- Chenfanfu Jiang, Craig Schroeder, Andrew Selle, Joseph Teran and Alexey
  Stomakhin, “The Affine Particle-In-Cell Method” (2015), equations 8–12. The
  27-node quadratic basis uses inverse affine covariance `4/dx²`. The
  differentiated basis independently integrates strain. Momentum and strain
  have different units and are transferred separately.
  [Paper](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~jteran/papers/JSSTS15.pdf)
- Xin Huang and Marcelo H. García, “A Herschel–Bulkley model for mud flow down
  a slope” (1998), equation 1.1. The shear rate above yield is
  `((|τ|−τy)/K)^(1/n)`. Its continuous free-surface profile has an unyielded
  plug over a shear layer. This entry carries the three-dimensional strain
  and separate material points needed to resolve both regions.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112098002845)

The world owns the particles, a padded Eulerian grid and the occupied-node list. Contact
projects momentum against a closed box or the live terrain normal. The optional solvent
operator is a symmetric graph diffusion on occupied nodes. Each face weight is scaled by
the shared resident fraction. Solving momentum plus the graph Laplacian by Jacobi PCG
preserves uniform translation and dissipates differences. The inlets carry reference
volume in SI units on the same clock. All of the implementation was written in this
repository from the papers.

- Edward Anderson, [Algorithm 978: Safe Scaling in the Level 1 BLAS](https://doi.org/10.1145/3061665), 2017. The norm scales by its largest component before squaring when the direct norm would overflow or underflow. Ordinary finite states preserve their original operation order. Acoustic and solvent reductions must stay finite before accepting a native step.
- Yunxin Sun, Tamar Shinar and Craig Schroeder, [Effective time step restrictions for explicit MPM simulation](https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14101), 2020, sections 4.2-4.4. Strong affine motion can invalidate a step with a low centre velocity. The candidate requires positive deformation throughout the incremental path.
- Rida T. Farouki, [The Bernstein polynomial basis: a centennial retrospective](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cagd.2012.03.001), 2012. A row norm below one certifies invertibility for the whole step. For larger increments, the native solver encloses the cubic determinant's Bernstein coefficients by outward rounding and subdivides only uncertain intervals. An interval that cannot certify a positive determinant rejects the candidate.
- Chenfanfu Jiang, Craig Schroeder, Andrew Selle, Joseph Teran and Alexey Stomakhin, [The affine particle-in-cell method](https://doi.org/10.1145/2766996), 2015, Section 5, and Xinlei Wang, Yuxing Qiu, Stuart R. Slattery, Yu Fang, Minchen Li, Song-Chun Zhu, Yixin Zhu, Min Tang, Dinesh Manocha and Chenfanfu Jiang, [A Massively Parallel and Scalable Multi-GPU Material Point Method](https://doi.org/10.1145/3386569.3392442), 2020, Sections 3 and 4. Once the grid is updated, each material point gathers independently. Margo assigns disjoint occupied nodes and material points between the shared Wasm workers, then reduces each exit in original order. The scatter and PCG retain their original serial ordering.
- Steve Cochard and Christophe Ancey, [Experimental investigation of the spreading of viscoplastic fluids on inclined planes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnnfm.2008.08.007), 2009. The renderer regression uses the flume arrangement for an authored pulse, with a volume ledger from its authored input. It reads the accepted MPM particles and hands them to the existing screen-space surface. The test exercises film controls and coupling.

## Sealed soft-body gas pressure (SOFT-06)

- Matthias Müller, Bruno Heidelberger, Marcus Hennix and John Ratcliff, [*Position Based Dynamics*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvcir.2007.01.005), 2007, §4.4 equations (13–14). A closed shell has a signed-volume constraint with a gradient that distributes its pressure over the mesh. Use one-sixth of the tetrahedral triple product to obtain cubic metres. On a watertight mesh, the cross-product terms that share each vertex telescope to one-third of the oriented area of each incident triangle.
- Miles Macklin, Matthias Müller, Nuttapong Chentanez and Tae-Yong Kim, [*Unified Particle Physics for Real-Time Applications*](https://mmacklin.com/uppfrta_preprint.pdf), 2014, §8. Stretch and bending constraints form the shell around its volume constraint, and the same contact pipeline handles the shell and rigid bodies.
- Maciej Matyka and Mark Ollila, [*Pressure Model of Soft Body Simulation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0407003), SIGRAD 2003, §2.3 equations (4–5). Isothermal gas stores the constant product `nRT` and has absolute pressure `nRT/V`. The shell feels the difference between its internal pressure and the pressure on the outside.
- Miles Macklin, Matthias Müller and Nuttapong Chentanez, [*XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics*](https://mmacklin.com/xpbd.pdf), 2016, equations (17–18). A change `Δλ` in the position multiplier moves each particle by its inverse mass times `∇V Δλ`. Here `λ = h² (nRT/V − pOutside)` uses the gas law directly. Linearizing volume as `Vnext = V + (Σ w|∇V|²) Δλ` gives a quadratic with one positive root. Computing the positive root using the reciprocal form when the free volume term is negative avoids cancellation at high ambient pressure. The solver recomputes geometry inside the existing native constraint pass. A pinned tetrahedron reduces to an affine volume with a closed-form backward-Euler reference.

Only publications and existing Margo code were consulted.

### Arcade car, vehicle debug lines and the three.js migration note (DYN-04, P5)

`Vehicle.car` lays four ray-cast wheels out from the chassis's box and sets their springs and dampers from ride
targets; `vehicle.debugRender()` draws the vehicle's last step as line segments. Sources:

- Thomas D. Gillespie, *Fundamentals of Vehicle Dynamics*, SAE International, 1992,
  [doi:10.4271/R-114](https://doi.org/10.4271/R-114), chapter 5 (ride): a corner's static deflection fixes its
  natural frequency `f = sqrt(k / m) / 2 pi`, and passenger cars damp their suspension at about 0.2 to 0.4 of
  critical. `Vehicle.car` sets the spring per kilogram from a chosen static sag (`k = g / (n sag)`, `n` wheels) and
  the dampers at 0.3 (compression) and 0.5 (extension) of `2 sqrt(n k) / n`, the critical damping of the chassis
  on `n` such springs.
- William F. Milliken and Douglas L. Milliken, *Race Car Vehicle Dynamics*, SAE International, 1995,
  [doi:10.4271/R-146](https://doi.org/10.4271/R-146), chapters 16 and 22 (ride and wheel rates, dampers): firmer
  rebound than bump damping, the reason for the 0.5 extension and 0.3 compression shares.
- Hans B. Pacejka, *Tyre and Vehicle Dynamics*, 3rd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2012,
  [doi:10.1016/C2010-0-68548-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/C2010-0-68548-8), chapter 4: the Magic Formula's force
  peaks near a slip of 0.1, the point at which the debug lines show a tyre-model wheel as sliding.
- The migration note's description of the three.js `physics_rapier_vehicle_controller` example and Rapier's
  `DynamicRayCastVehicleController` comes from Rapier's public JavaScript API reference
  ([rapier.rs/javascript3d](https://rapier.rs/javascript3d/classes/DynamicRayCastVehicleController.html), method
  names and what each sets) and the running example page
  ([threejs.org/examples](https://threejs.org/examples/#physics_rapier_vehicle_controller)). No source of three.js,
  Rapier or any other engine was read.

The wheel layout (radius from the body's smaller half size, rest length, track and wheelbase shares) is Margo's own
choice for a car that looks and drives right with no tuning, and the debug lines are Margo's own drawing of state the
vehicle already keeps.

### Vehicle road loads and lane pursuit (DYN-04)

- R. Craig Coulter, [Implementation of the Pure Pursuit Path Tracking Algorithm](https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/pub3/coulter_r_craig_1992_1/coulter_r_craig_1992_1.pdf) (1992), §§2.0–3.3, gives curvature `2 x/l²` from the lateral target offset and squared chord. RoadDriver finds the first forward intersection of the look-ahead circle and the lane segments. The bicycle steering geometry gives `tan(delta) = wheelbase × curvature`.
- Gabriel M. Hoffmann, Claire J. Tomlin, Michael Montemerlo and Sebastian Thrun, [Autonomous Automobile Trajectory Tracking for Off-Road Driving](https://ai.stanford.edu/~gabeh/papers/hoffmann_stanley_control07.pdf) (2007), separates steering geometry and the real vehicle's dynamic tyre constraints. The engine retains its physical tyres and gives pursuit a grip-dependent speed profile. Hans Pacejka and Igo Besselink, [Tire and Vehicle Dynamics](https://shop.elsevier.com/books/book-companion/9780080970165) (2012), and Jacob Svendenius, [Tire Modeling and Friction Estimation](https://lucris.lub.lu.se/ws/files/4401399/27004.pdf) (2007), cover force saturation under combined slip. A measured surface coefficient bounds the existing combined response inside `μ × normalLoad`. A wetness sample interpolates calibrated dry and wet limits.
- [FHWA horizontal curvature and superelevation](https://highways.fhwa.dot.gov/sites/fhwa.dot.gov/files/2022-06/fhwasa10001.pdf) (2010), Eq. 2, balances lateral acceleration with bank and friction in reduced form. Resolving both force components without the small-angle approximation gives `v²/R = g (sin β + μ cos β)/(cos β − μ sin β)` at limiting outward slip, for a positive inward bank `β`. RoadDriver propagates each upcoming bound backward with the constant-deceleration work relation `v² ≤ v_next² + 2 a Δs`.
- M. G. Bekker, [Introduction to Terrain-Vehicle Systems](https://books.google.com/books/about/Introduction_to_terrain_vehicle_systems.html?id=N694AAAAIAAJ) (1969), and J. Y. Wong, [Theory of Ground Vehicles](https://courses.minia.edu.eg/Attach/9775Theory%20of%20Ground%20Vehicles%20-%20J.%20Y.%20Wong%203rd%20Ed.pdf), Eq. 2.47 and Fig. 2.35 (2001), give `p = (k_c/b + k_phi) z^n` for a fitted plate. The engine supplies this effective stiffness and footprint from measured material data. It finds the pressure force and spring force at the same depth and applies the normal impulse at that contact point.

The collider uses the same visible road and bank geometry. A dynamic deck contributes its full contact-point velocity and inverse effective mass to traction, and receives the same impulse at the same position with the opposite sign. For wind the road assembly passes its chassis and the shared `Wind` field through the existing AirSolver and WindForce pair.

## Natural displacement and shoreline long waves (SEA-06)

- Yoshimitsu Okada, “Surface deformation due to shear and tensile faults in a half-space”
  (1985). This is a reference for generating externally supplied vertical deformation.
  The wave solver consumes registered bottom elevations. It does not compute Okada fault displacements.
  [NIED author paper](https://www.bosai.go.jp/sp/information/pdf/copy_of_Okada_1985_BSSA.pdf)
- Randall LeVeque, David George and Marsha Berger, “Tsunami modelling with adaptively
  refined finite volume methods” (2011). The depth-averaged Saint-Venant equations propagate
  long waves over variable depth and keep the wet boundary mobile. The optional solver
  uses a regular grid, wet/dry interface fluxes and world-clock substeps.
  [Author paper](https://faculty.washington.edu/rjl/pubs/AN2011/LeVequeGeorgeBerger-an11.pdf)
- Emmanuel Audusse, François Bouchut, Marie-Odile Bristeau, Rupert Klein and Benoît Perthame,
  “A fast and stable well-balanced scheme with hydrostatic reconstruction for shallow
  water flows” (2004), equations 2.6–2.9 and 3.1. Raise the interface bed to the higher cell
  bed, integrate the truncated hydrostatic columns and put the omitted hydrostatic pressure
  back on each cell's own side. The code combines that balance with HLL, minmod on water
  surface altitude and velocities, and SSP RK2. Ritter's 1892 wet/dry rarefaction checks the
  no-friction limit independently.
  [Audusse et al.](https://perso.math.u-pem.fr/bouchut.francois/publications/hydroproj_published.pdf) ·
  [Castro-Orgaz and Chanson (2017), Ritter benchmark](https://staff.civil.uq.edu.au/h.chanson/reprints/Castro-Orgaz_Chanson_efmc_2017.pdf)
  The extreme-scale regressions verify that the explicit CFL bound is retained when a requested
  tick is too expensive. The Coriolis implicit-midpoint rotation evaluates the same Cayley map in
  reciprocal coordinates when its squared half-angle overflows. The eikonal diagonal retains Zhao's
  two-neighbour quadratic by factoring its local transit time before squaring at extreme scales.
- An open side takes the outgoing shallow-water invariant `u_n + 2 sqrt(gh)` from the interior.
  A prescribed wave supplies the incoming invariant `u_n − 2 sqrt(gh)` from measured or authored
  exterior depth and normal speed. Both states meet within the same HLL flux and volume ledger.
  The flat-bed fixture compares the inward simple wave against its nonlinear characteristics from
  all four sides. Drähne's laboratory gauge and camera records provide separate forcing and holdouts.
  [Kristina, Bokhove and van Groesen, 2014, §3.2](https://doi.org/10.5194/npg-21-987-2014) ·
  [Drähne et al., 2016, §§2.2–2.4 and supplementary data](https://doi.org/10.3390/jmse4010001)
- Philip L.-F. Liu and Alejandro Orfila, “Viscous effects on transient long-wave propagation”
  (2004), treat the deep-column laminar bottom layer as a shear history. SEA-06 uses an optional
  single-frequency dissipative closure, derived from `iωu = G + νu''` with zero bed velocity and zero surface shear.
  For `q = h sqrt(iω/ν)` the depth-average admittance is `(1 − tanh(q)/q)/(iω)`. The real part of
  its inverse is the damping rate. It reduces to `3ν/h²` in a shallow viscous column and
  `sqrt(νω/2)/h` in the deep-column limit. Only this real rate attenuates both horizontal
  discharges, with an exponential update. The phase lag, turbulence and surface tension are separate.
  The regression independently sums the column's no-slip/free-shear eigenmodes.
  [Liu and Orfila, 2004](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112004001806) ·
  [Tanaka, Tinh and Sana, 2022](https://doi.org/10.3390/jmse10101433)
- The existing LeVeque–George–Berger regular-grid stencil reads a fixed Runge–Kutta stage.
  Splitting the X sweep by Z rows and the Z sweep by X columns gives each worker disjoint
  output cells in each sweep. JavaScript atomics publish the stage and join its ranges before
  the next sweep. The boundary ledger retains individual face contributions and sums them in
  the same order as the serial sweep. A browser window uses the serial path because its agent
  cannot block. [HTML Standard, agents](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#agents) ·
  [WebAssembly Threads specification, memory model](https://webassembly.github.io/threads/core/exec/relaxed.html)
- Kinjiro Kajiura, “The Leading Wave of a Tsunami” (1963). The rapid bottom-to-surface
  transfer at depth h is `sech(kh)`. The implementation uses its long-wave Padé approximation
  `1/(1 + (kh)²/2)`. The equivalent wet-cell Helmholtz system is symmetric and solved by
  diagonal PCG with zero normal flux. Its correction is evaluated as face divergence so that
  redistribution contributes zero net volume even with finite solve tolerance.
  [Author’s papers](https://tsunami-dl.jp/document/107)
- Hongkai Zhao, “A fast sweeping method for Eikonal equations” (2005), section 2.
  The static travel query uses alternating upwind sweeps of `|∇T| = 1/sqrt(gh)`, with no
  paths through dry cells. It estimates travel at the still-water depth. The dynamic
  inundation history comes from the finite-volume water state.
  [Author paper](https://www.math.uci.edu/~zhao/homepage/research_files/FSM.pdf)
- Valentin Heller and Willi H. Hager, “Impulse product parameter in landslide generated
  impulse waves” (2010). For natural subaerial granular slides in a prismatic channel,
  `P = F sqrt(S) M^(1/4) sqrt(cos(6α/7))` and `aMax/h = (4/9) P^(4/5)`. The solver exposes
  this empirical estimate independently of its conservative displacement and pressure
  input. The density in M is the water density and the length factor is the slide width
  times the square of the still-water depth.
  [ASCE paper](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)WW.1943-5460.0000037) ·
  [ETH follow-up, equation 2.4](https://ethz.ch/content/dam/ethz/special-interest/baug/vaw/vaw-dam/documents/das-institut/mitteilungen/2010-2019/244.pdf)

Natural source displacement adds or removes water by a normalized compact footprint. A
volume request outside the water budget is recorded as unplaced. Boundary volume uses the
same stage-weighted flux as the update. Diagonal native SIMD operations work in arena memory
without static writes.

## Thin accretion disks and Kerr geodesics (SPACE-03)

- Nikolai I. Shakura and Rashid A. Sunyaev, [*Black holes in binary systems. Observational appearance*](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1973A%26A....24..337S/abstract), 1973, equations (2.1), (2.4) and (2.6). A Keplerian disk has `Ω = sqrt(GM/r³)`. Combining its shear stress and the one-face energy balance gives `9 ν Σ Ω² / 8`. For steady mass supply and zero inner torque, this is `3 GM Ṁ [1 − sqrt(rInner/r)] / (8 π r³)`.
- James E. Pringle, [*Accretion Discs in Astrophysics*](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.aa.19.090181.001033), 1981, equations (2.9–2.10), (3.9–3.11) and (3.17). Multiply the diffusion equation by the annular area and set `x = sqrt(r)` to get the inward rate `3π ∂(νΣx)/∂x`. Each face flux leaves one annulus and enters the other. Differences in `x` preserve the linear steady torque profile on nonuniform meshes. A positive implicit tridiagonal solve advances the masses. Its residual fraction avoids a near cancellation in stiff pivots.
- Steven A. Balbus and John F. Hawley, [*A Powerful Local Shear Instability in Weakly Magnetized Disks. I. Linear Analysis*](https://doi.org/10.1086/170270), 1991. Outward-decreasing angular velocity and a weak magnetic field can excite local stress. The disk describes its averaged transport through a supplied viscosity.
- Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, [*The Mathematical Theory of Black Holes*](https://academic.oup.com/book/52805/chapter-abstract/421883824), 1983, chapter 7, and Ryuichi Fujita and Wataru Hikida, [*Analytical solutions of bound timelike geodesic orbits in Kerr spacetime*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.1420), 2009, equations (1–2). The Kerr Hamilton–Jacobi equation separates into radial and polar potentials. Differentiating the squared velocities advances signed Mino velocities through turning points. Divide by `dt/dλ` for observer time. Multiplying through by `Δ` and advancing `ln(r − r+)` removes the exterior radial coordinate singularity. Zero rest-mass normalization gives a null trajectory.
- James M. Bardeen, William H. Press and Saul A. Teukolsky, [*Rotating Black Holes: Locally Nonrotating Frames, Energy Extraction, and Scalar Synchrotron Radiation*](https://doi.org/10.1086/151796), 1972, equations (2.12–2.16) and (2.21). Direct and retrograde circular constants, frequencies and marginally stable radii supply exact references.

The implementation was written from the papers and existing Margo APIs.

## Depth-averaged lava and coastal displacement (EARTH-10)

- Robert W. Griffiths, [The Dynamics of Lava Flows](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.fluid.32.1.477), 2000. Sections 2–5 describe gravity-driven emplacement, the role of crystallisation and cooling in arrest, and how channels and crust shape the moving lava.
- G. Hulme, [The Interpretation of Lava Flow Morphology](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-246X.1974.tb05460.x), 1974. The ideal Bingham sheet has plug ratio χ = τᵧ/(ρ a h). Integration of its vertical velocity gives q = ρ a h³(1−χ)²(1+χ/2)/(3 μ) for χ < 1. The step solves q + Δt h a = |q*| by a bracketed scalar solve. The sub-yield case permits static balance and the zero-yield limit has a closed form. An independent test supplies the paper's discharge to the implicit update.
- Andrew J. L. Harris and Scott K. Rowland, [FLOWGO: A Kinematic Thermo-Rheological Model for Lava Flowing in a Channel](https://www.soest.hawaii.edu/earthsciences_archive/FACULTY/ROWLAND/pdfs/FLOWGO.pdf), 2001. The calibrated heat balance includes surface radiation and convection, basal conduction, and latent heat from crystallisation. The reference viscosity and yield rise exponentially with cooling below the liquidus. The depth-averaged implementation uses the apparent heat capacity across a specified solidus–liquidus interval.
- Antonio Costa and Giovanni Macedonio, [Numerical Simulation of Lava Flows Based on Depth-Averaged Equations](https://arxiv.org/pdf/physics/0504049), 2005. Equations 1–4 guide the conservative thickness, discharge and thermal transport across a variable bed. Radiation, convection and basal conduction appear separately in the thermal face and boundary model. The stationary thermal test uses the equal-and-opposite lateral conduction stencil.
- Amiram Harten, Peter D. Lax and Bram van Leer, [On Upstream Differencing and Godunov-Type Schemes for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws](https://doi.org/10.1137/1025002), 1983, section 3, and Emmanuel Audusse, François Bouchut, Marie-Odile Bristeau, Rupert Klein and Benoît Perthame, [A Fast and Stable Well-Balanced Scheme with Hydrostatic Reconstruction for Shallow Water Flows](https://perso.math.u-pem.fr/bouchut.francois/publications/hydroproj_published.pdf), 2004, equations 2.12–2.15. The numerical face uses the two bounding wave speeds and a shared-bed hydrostatic reconstruction. The liquid layer moves above ground plus stationary crust. The enthalpy flux is the upwind liquid enthalpy times the shared volume flux.

- David M. R. Hyman, Hannah R. Dietterich and Matthew R. Patrick, [Toward Next-Generation Lava Flow Forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022JB024998), 2022, §2.1, and Herbert E. Huppert, [The propagation of two-dimensional and axisymmetric viscous gravity currents over a rigid horizontal surface](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112082001797), 1982. The terminal tier uses the wide-sheet Bingham stress balance driven by the local pressure-head slope. It chooses the donor's reconstructed mobile depth and transfers its specific enthalpy. The explicit bound uses the Newtonian derivative of the yielded flux, and a separate donor-volume bound preserves nonnegative columns. The derivative is evaluated after factoring out the depth, avoiding division by a subnormal thin film.
- Andrew J. L. Harris and Scott K. Rowland, FLOWGO, 2001, and [Patrick et al., Okmok cooling](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003JB002537), separate conductive resistance from surface radiation and convection. The mixed-column mode removes the basal and lateral conductivity terms and applies the exposed-surface fluxes independently. Only active reservoirs bound the heat update. The skin temperature drives Weather's existing Planck/CIE emission, with no inferred hot cracks beneath the skin.

The marine output uses the exact geometric difference of consecutive occupied submerged volumes below a specified reference surface. The signed difference excites the existing SEA-06 and wake sources without creating lava mass. The ice interface transfers the actual absorbed power from ICE-05 before advecting the columns. Verification includes analytical laminar resistance, phase enthalpy and sub-yield arrest, conservative conduction and charted vent intervals, a confined channel, a live coastal heightfield, a measured absorbed heat ledger and browser replay in both Wasm memory modes. The implementation was written from these publications and the engine's field contracts.

### Rail running gear and wire interaction (DYN-05)

- J. J. Kalker, *Three-Dimensional Elastic Bodies in Rolling Contact* (1990) and
  [*On the rolling contact of two elastic bodies in the presence of dry friction* (1967)](https://repository.tudelft.nl/record/uuid%3Aaa44829b-c75c-4abd-9a03-fec17e121132).
  The small-slip tangent is calibrated by the linear rolling coefficient. The contact patch model
  uses one resultant tangent force per wheel.
  [Book](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-94-015-7889-9)
- Oldrich Polach, *Creep forces in simulations of traction vehicles running on adhesion limit*
  (2005), equations 2–7, 9, 11 and 12. The clean-room force uses the finite-contact integral,
  the paired reduction factors and the velocity-falling friction law. The small-creep slope
  and saturation inequality are verified directly. Independent axle spin creepage is outside
  this resultant-force approximation.
  [Paper](https://oldrich.polach.ch/data/object_4/Wear_2005.pdf)
- Simon Iwnicki (ed.), *Handbook of Railway Vehicle Dynamics* (2006), wheelset guidance and
  suspension chapters, and Iwnicki's *Manchester Benchmarks for Rail Vehicle Simulation*
  (1998). The reduced car uses two sprung bogies with four shared axle speeds. Hertz load follows
  the 3/2 power also verified in P. A. Montenegro and R. Calçada, *Wheel–rail contact model for railway
  vehicle–structure interaction applications* (2023), equation 11. Cant balance comes from
  resolving gravity and centripetal acceleration along the banked cross-section.
  [Handbook](https://www.iqytechnicalcollege.com/Handbook%20of%20Railway%20Vehicle%20Dynamics.pdf)
  [Manchester benchmark](https://doi.org/10.1080/00423119808969454)
  [Wheel–rail contact](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40534-023-00306-4)
- ENSCO for the Federal Railroad Administration, *High Speed Rail Tilt Train Technology* (1992),
  appendix A, equations A.1 and A.4 and figure A.10. The radial acceleration magnitude is speed squared
  over radius. Project it and gravity onto the canted section's right axis for bogie and carbody
  sway and roll. The survey curvature signs the radial term, which stays the same in reverse travel.
  [Federal Railroad Administration report](https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/10547/dot_10547_DS1.pdf)
- Gokul J. Krishnan, Jan Moraal, Zili Li and Zhen Yang, *An Experimental Study of Wheel–Rail Creep
  Curves Under Dry Contact Conditions Using V-Track* (2025). The contact comparison uses the prescribed
  angle, slip, speed and reported normal loads as inputs, and holds out the measured force coefficients
  in figures 9b and 11a/c. The engine defaults are fixed. A separate sensitivity uses Kalker's
  `G a b C22` on the reported ellipse, from his 1967 thesis §4.3 Table 3. No contact parameter uses
  the measured or CONTACT-fitted lateral force curves.
  [V-Track experiment](https://doi.org/10.3390/lubricants13070287)
- Colin Cole, Maksym Spiryagin, Qing Wu and Chris Bosomworth, *Practical Modelling and
  Simulation of Polymer Draft Gear Connections* (2017). The reduced connection has a measured
  centre spacing, a free-travel region and independent linear compression and tension branches.
  [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1061/9780784481257.041)
- Stefano Bruni et al., *The results of the pantograph–catenary interaction benchmark*
  (2015), and Andrea Collina, Stefano Bruni, Alan Facchinetti and Andrea Zuin, *PCaDA statement of methods* (2015).
  The moving contact is unilateral and drives the fixed-support wire in both transverse axes.
  Wave propagation follows the tensioned string's transverse balance in A. V. Metrikine and A. L. Bosch,
  *Dynamic response of a two-level catenary to a moving load* (2006). The implementation
  models one contact wire with linear wave propagation and a lumped collector.
  [Benchmark](https://doi.org/10.1080/00423114.2014.953183)
  [Method](https://re.public.polimi.it/retrieve/e0c31c0e-151d-4599-e053-1705fe0aef77/PCaDA%20statement%20of%20methods_11311-943365_Facchinetti.pdf)
  [String response](https://research.tudelft.nl/en/publications/dynamic-response-of-a-two-level-catenary-to-a-moving-load/)
- R. Courant, K. Friedrichs and H. Lewy, *On the Partial Difference Equations of Mathematical
  Physics* (1928), part II §1, and Gilbert Strang's MIT 18.086 lecture notes (2006),
  §5.3. Decomposing the centered tensioned-string difference into an ordered velocity update and
  a position update gives two independent passes. Each partition writes disjoint interior nodes.
  The joins preserve the stencil's old-neighbor values, and pantograph loads are accumulated in
  their original order before the passes.
  [Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cme324/classics/courant-friedrichs-lewy.pdf)
  [Strang lecture notes](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.086/2006/am53.pdf)
- Andrea Mariscotti, *Dataset of measured and commented pantograph electric arcs in DC
  railways* (2020), records the experimental association of detachment and powered arcing.
  The documented option emits a brief visual event after mechanically measured contact loss.
  [Dataset](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7378579/)

- Martin Lilleeng Saetra and Andre Rigland Brodtkorb, [Shallow Water Simulations on Multiple GPUs](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-28145-7_6), 2012, sections 2 and 4. Their separated face sweeps and row decomposition motivate the native inertial partition. Our X sweep owns whole rows and the Z sweep owns whole columns, with a join after each. The terminal tier assigns forward faces to their cells, gathers each cell's neighbours in serial arithmetic order, and reduces the per-cell source and cooling ledgers in that same order.

## Watertight inside test of a closed mesh (KB-SOFT-HOLLOWBOX1)

`packages/physics/src/soft-volume.ts`, `insideMesh` and `side`: a point is inside a closed mesh when a ray along +x crosses an odd number of triangles, each triangle tested by the sign of the point against its three edges seen along the ray.

- Sven Woop, Carsten Benthin and Ingo Wald, [*Watertight Ray/Triangle Intersection*](https://jcgt.org/published/0002/01/05/), Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques 2(1), 2013. The edge of two triangles is measured in one fixed direction so they get exactly opposite answers, and no ray passes between them.
- Herbert Edelsbrunner and Ernst Peter Muecke, [*Simulation of Simplicity: A Technique to Cope with Degenerate Cases in Geometric Algorithms*](https://doi.org/10.1145/77635.77639), ACM Transactions on Graphics 9(1), 1990. A ray exactly on an edge is moved by (d, d squared) in (y, z) for a vanishing d, so it lies on one side of every edge it touches.

The implementation was written from the papers.

## Colour enhancement and channel mixer: optional ColorEnhance (2026-11-26)

`@margoengine/tonemap/enhance`. The list of controls and their ranges (shadows and highlights -3..3, midtones,
vibrance and dehaze -1..1, mixer rows -2..2, applied to HDR colour before tone mapping) follows common
colour-grading controls; no other library's source was read.

Research compared:
- H. Koschmieder, *Theorie der horizontalen Sichtweite*, Beiträge zur Physik der freien Atmosphäre 12, 1924 (unread;
  the model as printed in the next paper). S. G. Narasimhan and S. K. Nayar, *Vision and the Atmosphere*, IJCV 48(3),
  2002, https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016328200723. Used: the haze image model I = J t + A (1 - t), inverted to remove
  haze and run forwards to add it.
- K. He, J. Sun and X. Tang, *Single Image Haze Removal Using Dark Channel Prior*, CVPR 2009,
  https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR.2009.5206515, and J.-P. Tarel and N. Hautière, *Fast Visibility Restoration from a
  Single Color or Gray Level Image*, ICCV 2009, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV.2009.5459251. Used: the minimum over the
  channels as the haze estimate, taken over one pixel. Not used: patch minima, guided or median filtering and a
  transmission map, which need extra passes and are an image restoration, not a colour control. The 0.5 strength cap is
  Margo's.
- A. R. Smith, *Color Gamut Transform Pairs*, SIGGRAPH 1978, https://doi.org/10.1145/800248.807361. Used: HSV
  saturation as the weight of vibrance. Adobe's public description of a vibrance control (dull colours move most,
  https://www.adobe.com/creativecloud/photography/discover/photo-saturation.html) is the behaviour aimed at; the
  formula x + (x - Y) v (1 - S) is Margo's, and keeps the order of saturations for every v in -1..1.
- ITU-R BT.709-6, 2015: the luma weights.
- Shadows, midtones and highlights: Margo's own, smoothstep weights in stops about 18% grey that sum to 1, applied as
  one gain so hue is kept. The 7-stop width makes the tone map monotone: the weights' slope is at most 1.5 / 7 per stop
  and neighbouring controls differ by at most 4 stops, 6 / 7 < 1 (`tests/enhance.test.js` walks every extreme setting).
  The channel mixer is a 3x3 matrix.

## Mesh data debug view: optional MeshDebugView (2026-11-26)

`@margoengine/inspector/mesh-debug`. The list of views and settings (wireframe, vertex dots, both, checkers on UV sets
0 and 1, vertex colours, material colours, a multiply switch, camera-lit shading colours, sizes and colours, a
replaceable material palette with a reset) follows common mesh
inspection views; no other library's source was read. Names, defaults
and behaviour are Margo's: lines and dots keep their own colour over the picture, `multiply` defaults by mode, and the
mesh is never rewritten to unshared vertices.

Research compared:
- J. A. Bærentzen, S. Munk-Lund, M. Gjøl and B. D. Larsen, *Two Methods for Antialiased Wireframe Drawing with Hidden
  Line Removal*, Spring Conference on Computer Graphics, 2008,
  https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/two-methods-for-antialiased-wireframe-drawing-with-hidden-line-re/ (abstract
  read). Used: the single-pass idea of an edge distance interpolated across the triangle, here a barycentric coordinate
  over the length of its screen gradient, so no distance is projected per triangle. Silhouette edges show half their
  width.
- NVIDIA, *Solid Wireframe*, Direct3D 10 SDK white paper, 2007,
  https://developer.download.nvidia.com/whitepapers/2007/SDK10/SolidWireframe.pdf (not read beyond its subject). Not
  used: it works in a geometry shader, which WebGPU lacks.
- W. Celes and F. R. Abraham, *Fast and versatile texture-based wireframe rendering*, The Visual Computer 27(10), 2011,
  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-011-0623-6 (abstract read). Not used: it carries edges in textures, which would take
  texture coordinates the view is there to show.
- A. Norton, A. P. Rockwood and P. T. Skolmoski, *Clamping: A Method of Antialiasing Textured Surfaces by Bandwidth
  Limiting in Object Space*, SIGGRAPH 1982, https://doi.org/10.1145/800064.801252 (abstract read). Used: the idea of
  replacing detail finer than the pixel by its local average; the checker is the product of each axis' square wave
  averaged over the pixel footprint, whose integral (a triangle wave) is elementary.
- J. F. Blinn, *Models of Light Reflection for Computer Synthesized Pictures*, SIGGRAPH 1977,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/563858.563893. Used: the half-vector highlight, with the light at the eye.
- S. Świerczkowski, *On successive settings of an arc on the circumference of a circle*, Fundamenta Mathematicae 46,
  1958, https://doi.org/10.4064/fm-46-2-187-189 (the three-distance theorem). Used: golden-ratio hue steps for material
  colours. The saturation 0.7 and the two alternating values are Margo's.

Vertex pulling by `vertex_index` from storage buffers follows the WebGPU and WGSL specifications
(https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/, https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/).

Size: new entry, absent to 6,877 B min+gzip, ceiling 7,133 B. No other entry grows; core and stage unchanged.

## Per-instance attributes (`@margoengine/materials/instance-attributes`, 2026-11-26)

- B. Dudash, [Animated Crowd Rendering](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems3/part-i-geometry/chapter-2-animated-crowd-rendering) (GPU Gems 3, chapter 2, 2007): per-instance data fetched in the vertex shader by instance index.
- F. Carucci, [Inside Geometry Instancing](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems2/part-i-geometric-complexity/chapter-3-inside-geometry-instancing) (GPU Gems 2, chapter 3, 2005): where per-instance data can live (constants, a second vertex stream) and what each limits.
- W3C, [WebGPU](https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/) and [WGSL](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/): the `instance_index` built-in, read-only storage buffers and flat interpolation.

Margo-own: one storage buffer with a block per attribute and a default row, `var<private>` values loaded per row, a flat
varying for fragment points, and cullers that leave row-indexed materials in place.

## Granular material points (EARTH-01)

- Yuanming Hu, Yu Fang, Ziheng Ge, Ziyin Qu, Yixin Zhu, Andre Pradhana and Chenfanfu Jiang,
  [*A Moving Least Squares Material Point Method with Displacement Discontinuity and
  Two-Way Rigid Body Coupling*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3197517.3197523) (2018),
  equations 15–19 and section 6. The quadratic spline has 27 neighbours and its
  moment tensor is `h² I / 4`. The nodal impulse includes the affine velocity and
  `−Δt V₀ τ (4/h²)` applied to the particle-to-node offset, where `τ` is the Kirchhoff
  stress. Gather the velocity and its affine gradient from the same weights.
- Gergely Klár, Theodore Gast, Andre Pradhana, Chuyuan Fu, Craig Schroeder, Chenfanfu
  Jiang and Joseph Teran, [*Drucker–Prager Elastoplasticity for Sand Animation*](https://doi.org/10.1145/2897824.2925906)
  (2016), and [technical supplement](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~cffjiang/research/sand/tech-doc.pdf),
  sections 4.1 and 6.1. The Kirchhoff principal stress uses the logarithms of
  principal elastic stretches, and the return map removes deviatoric strain until
  it reaches the Drucker–Prager cone. The zero-cohesion tension return goes to the
  cone tip. The optional cohesive shift adds cohesion to the admissible stress.
- Alexey Stomakhin, Craig Schroeder, Lawrence Chai, Joseph Teran and Andrew Selle,
  [*A Material Point Method for Snow Simulation*](https://media.disneyanimation.com/uploads/production/publication_asset/94/asset/SSCTS13_2.pdf)
  (2013), equations 1–2, section 7 and table 2. Snow uses fixed-corotated elastic
  stress, compression and stretch limits on the principal elastic stretches,
  and the determinant ratio for plastic hardening.
- Sachith Dunatunga and Ken Kamrin, [*Continuum modelling and simulation of granular flows
  through their many phases*](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2015.383) (2015), sections 2,
  3.2 and 4.4, and Pierre Jop, Yoël Forterre and Olivier Pouliquen,
  [*A constitutive law for dense granular flows*](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature04801)
  (2006), equation 2 and Figure 1. Use `I = d γ̇ₚ / sqrt(p/ρg)` and
  `μ(I) = μs + (μ2 − μs) I / (I0 + I)`. In the finite-strain adaptation, the
  Hencky elastic trace fixes pressure during plastic return. Kirchhoff pressure
  and shear have the same stress ratio as Cauchy pressure and shear. Divide
  Kirchhoff pressure by the full point volume ratio before evaluating `I`.
  Equations 25–29 give a quadratic for the updated shear. Shifting by the
  static yield `μs p` gives `x² − (a + b + c)x + ab = 0`, with `a` the trial
  excess, `b` the friction interval times pressure, and `c` the stress scale
  corresponding to `I0`. The scaled, rationalized smaller root is evaluated
  on loaded grains. The independent one-point oracle substitutes the realized
  shear and plastic rate into the original law and checks volume and restart.

The one-point manufactured tests evaluate the exact spline stress update followed by
the independent sand and snow returns. Free-fall uses the semi-implicit Euler
sum, including the half-step displacement. The incline test exercises a real terrain
bed and replays exactly in plain and shared memory. The fixed-camera collapse draws
the simulated material-point positions on both renderers.

Klár et al. (2016), section 6.2, equation 20, attributes a reference volume to
each particle for the discrete energy quadrature. For a full voxel cube of side
`L`, the handoff partitions its reference volume into `n³` congruent subcubes.
It uses their midpoints and volumes `(L/n)³`, which makes the constant-volume
and linear-position moments of a cube exact. This regular midpoint quadrature
uses the known voxel volume. The simulations in section 5.7 initialize positions
with Poisson disk sampling. The source cells are removed after registration and
all edits are applied before notifying voxel observers.

Éric Lajeunesse, Anne Mangeney-Castelnau and Jean-Paul Vilotte,
[*Spreading of a granular mass on a horizontal plane*](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1736611)
(2004), Figure 3, reports independent axisymmetric deposit profiles. The first
untuned comparison uses their low-aspect-ratio geometry and mass with the Jop
friction coefficients. It remains outside the observed central height at the
12 mm grid resolution. The manufactured constitutive test establishes the
implicit constitutive relation. Measured pile reconstruction remains open.

The shallow-layer output projects each particle's current volume
`V₀ det(F_E) det(F_P)` onto the three vertices of the existing terrain triangle.
Its barycentric weights sum to one, independently of the grid shape or cell
offset. The height change at a vertex is its volume change divided by the exact
vertex area from the terrain host. A uniform translation verifies the transferred
volume analytically and restores the previous layer state exactly.

The BB-7 adapter receives the published water-side impulse and follows the existing
swimming-sediment fixture's outward spread and shear fraction. Nallamuthu Rajaratnam,
[*Erosion by Plane Turbulent Jets*](https://www.iahr.org/library/infor?pid=6873) (1981),
and [*Erosion by Impinging Circular Turbulent Jets*](https://doi.org/10.1061/JYCEAJ.0004852)
(1976), show that a submerged impinging jet erodes through its bed wall jet. The
local MPM adapter resolves a compact radial shear profile and subtracts the
mass-weighted mean of its radial directions. The radial shear therefore redistributes
the layer without creating net horizontal impulse. The normalized quartic footprint
has area integral `πr²/3`; its vertical taper through the solid half-band gives
volume `πr²d/6`. If fewer grains occupy the footprint, only that covered share of the
incoming tangential impulse is applied. The test with a slower emitter proves the
exact accepted momentum and verifies that one publication is consumed once.

For the voxel fallback, the two-cell swap preserves the exact liquid amount and
metadata while sand descends. The conservation condition is independent of the
continuum yield law. Yongning Zhu and Robert Bridson,
[*Animating Sand as a Fluid*](https://doi.org/10.1145/1073204.1073298) (2005),
describes continuum material transport. The discrete packed-cell exchange is
Margo's own rule, covered by the two-layer falling-sand regression.

## Native strand guides (SOFT-03)

- Florence Bertails, Basile Audoly, Marie-Paule Cani, Bernard Querleux, Frédéric Leroy and
  Jean-Luc Lévêque, [*Super-helices for predicting the dynamics of natural hair*](https://doi.org/10.1145/1179352.1142012)
  (2006). The strand model retains independent curvature and twist about a moving material frame.
  This implementation discretizes space into segments with quaternion frames and rest rotations.
- Tassilo Kugelstadt and Elmar Schömer, [*Position and Orientation Based Cosserat Rods*](https://animation.rwth-aachen.de/media/papers/2016-SCA-Cosserat-Rods.pdf)
  (2016), section 6. The strain is the rotated centreline edge divided by its length minus the
  frame's third director. The bend and twist projection uses the vector of the relative quaternion
  against its natural rotation. The cylinder supplies axial and shear constants EA and GA and
  angular constants EI and GJ. Miklós Bergou et al., [*Discrete Elastic Rods*](https://www.lmm.jussieu.fr/~audoly/publi/BergouWardetzkyRobinson-Discrete%20Elastic%20Rods-2008-00.pdf)
  (2008), provides the frame-transport and natural-curvature comparison.
- Miles Macklin, Matthias Müller and Nuttapong Chentanez, [*XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics*](https://mmacklin.com/xpbd.pdf)
  (2016), equations 7–9. Each scalar projection uses compliance divided by the square of the
  time step and accumulates its multiplier within that substep.
- Matthias Müller, Nuttapong Chentanez and Tae-Yong Kim, [*Fast Simulation of Inextensible Hair and Fur*](https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/publications/FTLHairFur.pdf)
  (2012), sections 3.1–3.2. The fast pass follows the parent in root-to-tip order and subtracts
  the scaled child correction from the parent velocity. For a local ground plane, the admissible
  directions are the intersection of its positive half-space with the fixed-length link's sphere.
- Matthias Teschner et al., [*Optimized Spatial Hashing for Collision Detection of Deformable Objects*](https://cgl.ethz.ch/Downloads/Publications/Papers/2003/Tes03/Tes03.pdf)
  (2003). A separate ordered cell check rejects hash collisions; spacing is the largest point
  diameter. Consecutive points in an authored guide are excluded.
- Yang Yu et al., [*Structure and mechanical behavior of human hair*](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0928493116319208)
  (2017), and Kento Fujita and Hironori Tohmyoh, [*Effect of testing conditions on the tensile properties of a single human hair and the in-situ observation of cuticles during the tensile deformation by an optical microscope*](https://doi.org/10.1299/transjsme.20-00043)
  (2020), supply comparisons for diameter and the low-strain modulus. The default cylindrical
  guide uses an 80 μm diameter and a nominal 3 GPa material. The cross-flow drag coefficient is
  an exposed engineering estimate, and the drag step exactly integrates scalar quadratic
  relative-velocity decay for the sampled, fixed air value and coefficient.

The hanging-guide test compares extension with mgL / EA using the half-cylinder tip mass.
The curved no-load fixture independently checks invariance under a rigid transform. The fast
test measures every length during a wind reversal and contact with a live terrain bed. The
browser fixture draws the solved centreline and frame in a fixed view and repeats the same
gust against a still-air control.

### Lantern and low-wind leaf response

The courier lantern's single inextensible handle is validated against the finite-amplitude
pendulum. NIST's [*Digital Library of Mathematical Functions*](https://dlmf.nist.gov/22.19.i)
(Olver et al., 2010–present), equation 22.19.2, gives the period
`4 sqrt(L/g) K(sin(alpha/2))`; [section 19.8](https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.8.i) evaluates
`K` with the arithmetic-geometric mean. A separate reach differentiates the prescribed
hand path and checks the tip lag against the linear forced pendulum with a drive sampling
and small-angle error bound.

Frédérick P. Gosselin and Emmanuel de Langre, [*Drag reduction by reconfiguration of a
poroelastic system*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfluidstructs.2011.05.007) (2011), relates
bend and drag through the local flow and exposed section. The low-deflection fixture
uses a fixed air density and a 0.6 m/s reversing cross-flow. Its independent beam
reference starts with the distributed-load tip deflection `qL⁴/(8EI)`. The 24-link
reference accounts for the clamped first link and the exact quadratic-drag mean force
over each substep. The error combines the small-angle projection terms and a bound on
shear. This addresses motion of a narrow flexible leaf; the assets from the original
planter and workshop shots are separate.

### Feather and tapered strand sections

- Thomas Bachmann, Jens Emmerlich, Werner Baumgartner, Jochen M. Schneider and Hermann Wagner,
  [*Flexural stiffness of feather shafts: geometry rules over material properties*](https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.059451)
  (2012), equations 2–5 and table 1. The observed longitudinal change in stiffness follows
  the spatial variation in cross-section moment. Use the measured moment and modulus
  to set the curvature compliance rather than inferring both from the contact radius.
- Richard Bonser and Peter Purslow, [*The Young's modulus of feather keratin*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9318836/)
  (1995). Their comparative tension and dynamic bending tests distinguish material
  modulus from shaft geometry. Bin Wang and Marc André Meyers, [*Seagull feather shaft:
  Correlation between structure and mechanical response*](https://meyersgroup.ucsd.edu/papers/journals/Meyers%20428.pdf)
  (2017), section 4.4, similarly separates the effective flexural rigidity of a hollow
  shell and foam core.

A section supplies its axial area, transverse moment and torsion constant independently.
A frame joint spans half of each adjoining link, with total bending compliance
`L₁ / (2 E₁ I₁) + L₂ / (2 E₂ I₂)` and an analogous torsion compliance using `GJ`.
Weight distributes half of each link mass to each endpoint. The controlled beam tests
use the 9.7% and 18.8% station moments in Bachmann's barn owl and pigeon data. These
tests compare an independent sum of gravitational joint moments and report the
small-angle and shear terms in the allowed error. The other section properties describe
the test specimens. The GPU fixture uses tapered links against a still-air control.

### Swept strand and capsule contact

- Minchen Li, Danny M. Kaufman and Chenfanfu Jiang,
  [*Codimensional Incremental Potential Contact*](https://ipc-sim.github.io/C-IPC/file/paper.pdf)
  (2021), sections 5.3–5.4 and equation 10. Bound the change in separation by endpoint
  motions after subtracting common translation. A safe advance uses 90% of the available
  separation divided by its closing bound. The strand solver tightens that bound by
  projecting endpoint motion onto the current separating normal. Linear endpoints remain
  in the resulting half-spaces up to that advance.
- Robert Bridson, Ronald Fedkiw and John Anderson, [*Robust Treatment of Collisions,
  Contact and Friction for Cloth Animation*](https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/cloth-sig02/)
  (2002), sections 7.1–7.3. Edge witness weights distribute the normal and tangential
  impulse to all movable endpoints. The effective inverse mass is the sum of the squared
  weights times inverse mass. The tangential impulse is capped by the Coulomb friction
  budget and the impulse needed to stop sliding.

The crossing-link tests check the exact two-radius separation, equal and opposite
linear momentum and a pair count below the guide count for disjoint guides. The friction
test checks equal and opposite impulses including the anchored reactions, and less
kinetic energy after sliding. Separate
fixtures drive a kinematic capsule, a rigid capsule at 24 m/s and a second strand all
the way through an edge between sampled positions. The rigid fixture includes the
in-flight registry impulse and verifies an exact snapshot replay on both sides of contact.

David Baraff, [*Rigid Body Simulation II: Nonpenetration Constraints*](https://www.myphysicslab.com/develop/docs/Baraff_Siggraph_97_Course_Notes.pdf)
(1997), equations in section 6 and course slides D47–48, derives the normal impulse from
closing velocity and effective inverse mass. For a rigid contact arm `r` and normal
`n`, the rigid term is `1/m + (r × n) · I⁻¹(r × n)`. The link contribution sums each
endpoint's inverse mass times the square of its witness weight. The positional projection
uses the same relative mass for the strand share and does not generate an impulse.
Brian Mirtich and John Canny, [*Impulse-based Dynamic Simulation*](https://digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/134699/files/CSD-94-815.pdf)
(1994), sections 4.1–4.2, supplies the opposing tangent and Coulomb impulse limit.
The off-centre sphere regressions compare linear and angular impulse to the solid-sphere
inertia, including the impulse share carried by the anchor.

### Strand motion on the horse skin

The optional horse driver uses the authored joint hierarchy and applies the solved guides as
parent-relative transforms. The guide-to-bone calculation first maps the rest material frame
to the rest bone. It then composes the live frame with that offset and converts the result
through the live parent inverse. The weighted cards use the existing horse skinning path.

Bazarsad Bolormaa, Jean Yves Drean and Dorj Enkhtuya, [*A Study of the Diameter Distribution and
Tensile Property of Horse Tail Hair*](https://doi.org/10.1080/15440470801893281) (2008), measured
variation across horse tail fibres and along their lengths. The rig uses larger effective
bundles with independently controlled bending and drag settings. Those defaults are an
authoring approximation pending bundle-scale measurements. The existing equine gait follows
the references in the horses README.

### Physical spring-bone skin binding

The binding uses the glTF parent hierarchy, world transforms, weights and optional virtual
tips. It records each rendered joint's rest rotation relative to its native material frame.
