After simulation it composes that offset with the current frame and converts both world
position and rotation to the live parent frame. The avatar proof uses the authored ponytail
and selected colliders from the [VRM SpringBone 1.0 extension specification](https://github.com/vrm-c/vrm-specification/tree/master/specification/VRMC_springBone-1.0).
The avatar asset and license are listed in `examples/assets/vrm/README.md`.

### Reciprocal strand and rigid capsule contact

For each dynamic capsule projection, the strand's position correction contributes the
equivalent linear impulse from its lumped node mass and substep length. That impulse and
the moving-surface velocity correction enter the rigid row with opposite sign. The surface
point and rigid centre of mass give the angular impulse through their cross product. The
contact point uses the closest point on the capsule axis. The linear and angular convention
matches David Baraff, [*An Introduction to Physically Based Modeling: Rigid Body Simulation II*](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~baraff/sigcourse/notesd2.pdf)
(1997), equations 8–5 to 8–7 and C–11. The tests include the reaction still in the registry when closing
the initial impulse budget. They also check both memory variants and an origin-cell offset.

### Strand segment and capsule contact

Robert Bridson, Ronald Fedkiw and John Anderson, [*Robust Treatment of Collisions, Contact
and Friction for Cloth Animation*](https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/cloth-sig02/) (2002),
sections 7.1–7.3, derives the closest edge pairs and barycentric transfer to their endpoints.
Christer Ericson, [*Real-Time Collision Detection*](https://www.routledge.com/Real-Time-Collision-Detection/Ericson/p/book/9781558607323)
(2005), section 5.1.9, gives the finite-segment closest point problem including parallel segments.
The implementation minimizes the squared separation over the interior and boundaries of the
two segment parameters. The corresponding XPBD contact correction distributes by barycentric
inverse mass. The static test places a sphere completely between guide endpoints. The dynamic
test uses the published contact reaction to close the momentum of a moving rigid sphere.

### Direct strain solve for thin strands

Crispin Deul, Tassilo Kugelstadt, Marcel Weiler and Jan Bender, [*Direct Position-Based Solver
for Stiff Rods*](https://animation.rwth-aachen.de/media/papers/2018-CGF-Rods.pdf) (2018),
equations 18–20 and section 4.2, solve the coupled XPBD strain equation and alternate the
elastic system with contact. Margo eliminates the position and rotation updates first.
For a simple chain the resulting weighted gradient Gram matrix is block tridiagonal.
Its six-row Schur blocks are normalized and factored by Cholesky, with one forward solve
and one backward substitution per Newton pass. The compliant shear and axial strains and
rest quaternion bends are unchanged.

A repeated test uses Fujita and Tohmyoh's measured 3.45 GPa modulus for a cylindrical
30 mm fibre under its weight. The small-angle discrete bending response is the
Euler–Bernoulli uniform-load tip deflection times `(1 − 1/n)²` for `n` equally spaced
links with a clamped first segment and half endpoint mass. The test compares four
independent subdivisions against this discrete result with a bound for geometric
nonlinearity and shear. Its tip converges to the continuum solution.

## Image filter graph (2026-11-26)

`@margoengine/post/filter-graph`. The graph format, the access kinds, the fusion rule, the name prefixing, the
rounding of fused results, the runtime and every block's WGSL are Margo's, written from the research and web standards
below.

Research compared:
- Bo Qiao, Oliver Reiche, Frank Hannig and Jurgen Teich, *From Loop Fusion to Kernel Fusion: A Domain-Specific
  Approach to Locality Optimization*, CGO 2019, https://doi.org/10.1109/CGO.2019.8661176 (point and local operators;
  fusing a producer into a point reader repeats no work, which is the rule used; local-to-local pairs stay unfused).
- Jonathan Ragan-Kelley, Connelly Barnes, Andrew Adams, Sylvain Paris, Fredo Durand and Saman Amarasinghe, *Halide: A
  Language and Compiler for Optimizing Parallelism, Locality, and Recomputation in Image Processing Pipelines*, PLDI
  2013, https://people.csail.mit.edu/jrk/halide-pldi13.pdf (inlined against stored stages; here a stage with two
  readers or many taps is stored, never recomputed).
- Michael McCool, Stefanus Du Toit, Tiberiu Popa, Bryan Chan and Kevin Moule, *Shader Algebra*, ACM Transactions on
  Graphics 23(3), 2004, https://doi.org/10.1145/1015706.1015801 (connecting shaders as function composition).
- Mark Jarzynski and Marc Olano, *Hash Functions for GPU Rendering*, JCGT 9(3), 2020,
  https://jcgt.org/published/0009/03/02/ (the `noise` block uses the first component of pcg3d).
- W3C, *Compositing and Blending Level 1*, https://www.w3.org/TR/compositing-1/ (`composite` blend modes and source
  over); Rec. ITU-R BT.709 (luma and colour difference in the grey, key and mask blocks); Rodrigues' rotation formula
  (1840, `hue`); Irwin Sobel and Gary Feldman, *A 3x3 Isotropic Gradient Operator for Image Processing*, 1968
  (`edges`).
- W3C, *WebGPU Shading Language*, https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/ (`quantizeToF16`, explicit-level texture reads).

## Depth-integrated natural granular runout (EARTH-02)

The first native tier evolves vertical depth and horizontal discharges in X and Z. Its pressure flux and gravitational bed term use the shallow constant-gravity form in equations B18–B20 of Anne Mangeney, François Bouchut, Nicolas Thomas, Jean-Paul Vilotte and Marie-Odile Bristeau (2007), *Numerical modeling of self-channeling granular flows and of their levee-channel deposits*. Interface Coulomb friction projects the local driving impulse and mass-weighted velocity onto the friction disk. The normal component enters the apparent bed step as in B8–B14 and B22–B28. The first projection uses the single B12 projection generalized to both velocity components. [Mangeney et al. 2007](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006JF000469)

For a step across a face each reconstructed height subtracts the positive upward difference on that side, with zero as the lower bound. The flux applies one common conservative mass transfer and each side's pressure correction from equations 2.8–2.16 in Emmanuel Audusse, François Bouchut, Marie-Odile Bristeau, Rupert Klein and Benoît Perthame (2004), *A fast and stable well-balanced scheme with hydrostatic reconstruction for shallow water flows*. The homogeneous flux uses local Lax–Friedrichs and only reflected normal momentum crosses a closed boundary. A face drains at most its signal bound times the donor depth. The combined X/Z Courant fraction of 1/4 leaves at least half of every donor depth per substep even with both faces of an axis draining. [Audusse et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.1137/S1064827503431090)

Basal resistance adds turbulent Voellmy drag to the Coulomb contribution. In the horizontal shallow-bed form the acceleration is `g * speed² / (xi * depth)`. Integrating backward Euler gives the cancellation-safe positive root `2 * speed / (1 + sqrt(1 + 4 * g * dt * speed / (xi * depth)))`. The corrected equations 5 and 13 are in Marc Christen, Julia Kowalski and Perry Bartelt (2010), *RAMMS: Numerical simulation of dense snow avalanches in three-dimensional terrain*. A prescribed fraction of normal stress reduces the Coulomb contact load as in Richard Iverson and Roger Denlinger (2001), *Flow of variably fluidized granular masses across three-dimensional terrain I. Coulomb mixture theory*. This single-layer tier does not solve pore-pressure evolution. [Christen et al. 2010](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coldregions.2010.04.005), [equation erratum](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coldregions.2010.09.006), [Iverson and Denlinger 2001](https://doi.org/10.1029/2000JB900329)

The rough-incline balance and two-dimensional conservative update were compared with Stuart Savage and Kolumban Hutter (1989), *The motion of a finite mass of granular material down a rough incline*, and Roger Denlinger and Richard Iverson (2004), *Granular avalanches across irregular three-dimensional terrain: 1. Theory and computation*. Olivier Pouliquen and Yoël Forterre (2002), *Friction law for dense granular flows: application to the motion of a mass down a rough inclined plane*, gives measured depth- and speed-dependent friction and stopping. The roughness tier uses equations 3.5–3.9, including the published 0.136 Froude coefficient and the 0.001 intermediate exponent. The bundled profile uses measured angles of 21°, 30.7° and 22.2° and a 0.65 mm stopping length for 0.5 mm glass beads. Each face derives normal depth from the bed gradient and recovers along-plane speed from the horizontal velocity and its vertical projection. Two surface derivatives drive the vector Coulomb projection so a rotated plane uses one friction disk. [Savage and Hutter 1989](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112089000340), [Denlinger and Iverson 2004](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003JF000085), [Pouliquen and Forterre 2002](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112001006796)

The optional exponential stopping curve follows equations 3–4 in Olivier Pouliquen (1999), *Scaling laws in granular flows down rough inclined planes*. Table I supplies independently measured deposit fits for the 0.50 mm and 1.15 mm beads (systems 1 and 3). The recreated uniform chute holds the predicted normal-depth Froude speed, yielding normalized speeds of 0.9342 and 0.8505 at 24° and seven diameters. The corresponding measured values in Section III.B are 1.0 and 0.9. Both lie within the reported 10 percent upper bound on speed measurement. The layer obeys the 2002 start/stop bracket at 23.3°. No coefficient was fit to these front velocities. [Pouliquen 1999](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.869928)

Arrested cells can consolidate into the live bed in one transfer. The model follows Betty Sovilla, Jim N. McElwaine, Mark Schaer and Julien Vallet (2010), *Variation of deposition depth with slope angle in snow avalanches: Measurements from Vallée de la Sionne*. Its field profiles 816 and 817 give exponential stopping curves with (21.4°, 34.7°, 0.31 m) and (22.5°, 34.4°, 0.19 m), respectively. The tests separately bracket each 27° critical normal depth and reproduce the physical distinction between a stationary deposit and material above the stopping curve. The speed threshold is an explicit material option, and the solver does not infer a critical speed from the field measurements. [Sovilla et al. 2010](https://doi.org/10.1029/2009JF001390)

Projected cell area times vertical depth gives the mobile volume. The kernel converts its mass to bed volume using the density ratio applied to the Swiss scan profiles by Perry Bartelt, Yves Bühler, Othmar Buser, Marc Christen and Lukas Meier (2012), *Modeling mass-dependent flow regime transitions to predict the stopping and depositional behavior of snow avalanches*. That study compares 300 and 400 kg/m³ density cases. Each cell distributes one or two sixths to the corresponding vertices of the two bed triangles, then divides by the vertex support area for the height addition. The separate physical closure records the horizontal momentum and kinetic energy absorbed by the immobile ground. [Bartelt et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1029/2010JF001957)

Manon Robbe-Saule, Cyprien Morize, Robin Henaff, Yann Berthol, Alban Sauret and Philippe Gondret (2021), *Experimental investigation of tsunami waves generated by granular collapse into water*, measured the volume-driven piston effect of a collectively entering granular front. The first coastal transfer computes each cell's signed submergence change using its projected area times occupied vertical thickness below a fixed datum. SEA-06 consumes the same step volume through the existing SeaSource record. Preexisting submerged material establishes the initial reference. The carried deposit height is counted together with the mobile layer, so transfer into the bed emits only its net volume change. [Robbe-Saule et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2020.807)

P. Poulain, A. Le Friant, A. Mangeney, S. Viroulet, E. Fernandez-Nieto, M. Castro Diaz, M. Peruzzetto, G. Grandjean, F. Bouchut, R. Pedreros and J-C. Komorowski (2023), *Performance and limits of a shallow-water model for landslide-generated tsunamis: from laboratory experiments to simulations of flank collapses at Montagne Pelée (Martinique)*, compare bathymetry, topography and dispersive effects in depth-integrated models. The current witness validates the signed volume balance on the actual water receiver, including a crest caused by passage over a shoreline and a negative volume from submerged compaction. Water back-reaction and near-impact crest calibration require the full two-layer terms. [Poulain et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1093/gji/ggac482)

For ground shaking, the reference-frame inertial acceleration acts opposite the published horizontal support acceleration. The vertical support acceleration adds to the effective downward gravity, so the material shear threshold changes with the contact load. Nathan M. Newmark (1965), *Effects of Earthquakes on Dams and Embankments*, established the critical-acceleration concept. Jacques Ingles, José Darrozes and Jean-Claude Soula (2006), *Effects of the vertical component of ground shaking on earthquake-induced landslide displacements using generalized Newmark analysis*, show why horizontal and vertical support accelerations need separate components. The optional EARTH-08 edge puts the support force into the same apparent-step projection as slope and pressure. The flat wide-layer test checks both directions and the contact-load threshold against force balance with a derived first-order error in reconstruction. [Newmark 1965](https://doi.org/10.1680/geot.1965.15.2.139), [Ingles et al. 2006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enggeo.2006.02.018)

### SEA-11 hull slamming and accepted green water

The section bake uses the zero-gravity two-dimensional Wagner wetting condition, Hulin, Tassin and
Korobkin (2022) equation (2.3), to integrate the profile height at 32 midpoint angles. It preserves the
order of the sum and the 50 bisections for each uncapped depth while pairing independent angle samples in native
f64x2. The live load uses the momentum rate of the wetted added mass, as in the von Kármán water-entry
balance. Independent station ranges run in private Wasm memories and return in mesh order.
[Hulin, Tassin and Korobkin (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2022.448) · [von Kármán, NACA TN-321 (1929)](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19930081174)

The deck uses the existing Audusse et al. (2004) hydrostatic reconstruction, with the receiving cell
of each inlet found half a cell inside its inward normal. The exported surface copies accepted x-fast
height and depth in the hull frame. No particle emission or visible sheet is used as a load input.
[Audusse, Bouchut, Bristeau, Klein and Perthame (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1137/S1064827503431090)

The held-out force diagnostic records 12 isolated experimental markers from Fig. 4(g), (j) and (l)
of Tveitnes, Fairlie-Clarke and Varyani (2008). It uses reported width, length, deadrise and motor
speeds as inputs. Neither the measured force outcomes nor the paper’s fitted wetting and drag coefficients
set model parameters. The paper’s peak-relative repeatability, digitization and position allowances are
recorded separately in the script. The instrument did not measure the water-impact velocity of the face.
[Tveitnes, Fairlie-Clarke and Varyani (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oceaneng.2008.06.012)

### SEA-08 ordered panel workers

The three-dimensional panel response retains the original boundary-integral kernels and linearized reference
geometry. Each frequency system uses the same partial pivots and column order, with two complex row updates
per f64x2 calculation and an unpaired scalar tail. Participants solve independently with private Wasm heaps.
The caller joins them in frequency order. Runtime `HullSolver` continues to use the accepted radiation
table and finite memory over fixed ticks. The panel formulation references
[Aurélien Babarit and Gérard Delhommeau, 2015, *Theoretical and numerical aspects of the open source BEM solver NEMOH*](https://hal.science/hal-01198800),
and [William E. Cummins, 1962, *The Impulse Response Function and Ship Motions*](https://dome.mit.edu/handle/1721.3/49049).
The packaged browser and live world tests compare the coefficient tables and signed-origin replay. This change
distributes independent frequency solves and preserves the model’s limitations.

### SEA-08 ordinary-strip forward speed

The clean-room calculation follows [Salvesen, Tuck and Faltinsen (1970), *Ship Motions and Sea Loads*](https://trid.trb.org/View/495) as written in `8.3, equations 8.30–8.31 of [Journée and Massie (2001), *Offshore Hydromechanics*](https://ocw.tudelft.nl/wp-content/uploads/OffshoreHydromechanics_Journee_Massie_01.pdf). The engine uses bow-up pitch and vertical-up heave. In that convention the existing strip convolution gets the two terms `+U H(theta)` in heave and `-U H(zr)` in pitch, with `H = A33(infinity) d/dt + K33 *` and `dzr/dt = heaveVelocity - U theta`. The heave–pitch terms change sign with course direction. Pitch stiffness changes by `-U² A33` and damping by `+U² B33 / omega²`. Past relative displacement is reconstructed at each lag with a trapezoid. No indefinitely accumulated displacement enters the ledger.

The scope checks the complex amplitude of both coordinates in an 80 N, 3 rad/s vertical excitation at 2 m/s. The analytical 2×2 solve uses independently assembled integrated section loads, box inertia, and hydrostatic restoring. At 60 Hz the errors are 0.50% in heave and 2.07% in pitch. The test uses a 3% bound, just above the `omega dt / 2` step phase of 2.5% at this frequency. The broad-hull case verifies the static restoring limit from the zero-frequency Schur complement and the first moment of the finite radiation kernel. The fixed 0.05 rad trim case checks both inferred speed and a prescribed water-relative speed with a different horizontal body speed.

[Chang and Wellens (2024), *A generating absorbing boundary condition for simulating wave interaction with maritime structures in current or at forward speed*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compfluid.2024.106216) reports independently measured Wigley head-sea motion in §4.2.1, figures 20 and 22. The reserved outputs are 0.023 m heave and 2.45° pitch in run 77, and 0.018 m heave and 1.57° pitch in run 79. The authors report amplitudes to 0.001 m and 0.01°, without transducer uncertainty in that section. Neither run informed the model or its inputs. The present check uses a forced numerical reference and still water.

### SEA-08 waterplane radiation sources

[John N. Newman, *Marine Hydrodynamics*, 40th anniversary edition (2017), `6.10, equations 6.120–6.121](https://home.hvl.no/ansatte/gste/ftp/MarinLab_files/Litteratur/Marine_Hydrodynamics_Newman_2018.pdf) prescribes the rigid-body normal velocity on the wetted boundary. Closing that boundary with the still-water waterplane gives the opposite flux through the closure, by the divergence theorem for a translating and rotating rigid velocity field. The first-order source integrates `−(v_y + omega_z r_x − omega_x r_z) dA dt` on that plane. Each strip has two transverse Gauss points, so a rectangular strip transfers its roll dipole moment exactly. A symmetric hull at zero vertical velocity has zero volume flux even in forward motion. The receiving dispersive model advances the stamped volume and potential.

The box control produces `0.0333333333 m³` on its first tick from an 8 m² waterplane at 0.25 m/s downward. The source and wake-grid sums agree within the FFT's rounding. Symmetric pitch and roll controls check zero net volume, the signed dipole moments, and positive and negative wave lobes. A free hull sends a wave beyond its footprint and replays the same state in plain and shared arenas. Independent pressure and motion measurements are required for three-dimensional radiation amplitudes.

### SEA-08 forward-speed bare-hull roll damping

[Yoshiho Ikeda, Yoji Himeno and Norio Tanaka (1978), *Components of Roll Damping of Ship at Forward Speed*](https://doi.org/10.2534/jjasnaoe1968.1978.143_113) separates roll loss into wave, friction, eddy, lift and appendage contributions. The new course terms follow [ITTC (2024), *Estimation of Roll Damping*, revision 02, equations 33–36, 41 and 45](https://www.ittc.info/media/11942/75-02-07-045.pdf). The lift coefficient is linear in water-relative forward speed. The zero-speed friction is multiplied by `1 + 4.1 U/(omega L)`, and the eddy loss by `1 / (1 + (U/(0.04 omega L))²)`. The roll centre offset `OG` is positive below the surface. The same semi-implicit angular impulse used for still-water viscous damping keeps the added lift dissipative.

The numerical regression separates the independent box hydrostatics and the three published terms from the still-water radiation and six-coordinate added-mass fold. The held roll torque changes by 21.37840 N m at 1 m/s and 23.12493 N m at 2 m/s. The analytical differences are 21.37835 N m and 23.12484 N m. The bare rectangular control loses eddy damping faster than it gains lifting loss at those speeds. The Froude-number-specific water-relative override gives the same result at a different world speed.

[Han and Kinoshita (2012), *Stochastic Inverse Identification of Nonlinear Roll Damping Moment of a Ship Moving at Nonzero-Forward Speeds*](https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/769385) supplies independent measured bare-hull decay traces in figure 7(a). They are reserved for physical qualification. The roll check here is an analytical calculation using a separate rectangular hull.

### SEA-08 and DYN-01 contact on a rolling deck

The contact fixture transforms Newton's law into the heaving, rolling deck frame using [Widnall and Peraire (2009), *Relative Motion using Rotating Axes*](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/16-07-dynamics-fall-2009/resources/mit16_07f09_lec08/). It applies the Coulomb bound `|F_t| <= mu F_n`, as in [Stewart and Trinkle (1996), *An Implicit Time-Stepping Scheme for Rigid Body Dynamics with Inelastic Collisions and Coulomb Friction*](https://doi.org/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-0207%2819960815%2939%3A15%3C2673%3A%3AAID-NME972%3E3.0.CO%3B2-I). The scalar reference receives only the hull's pose and rates. It computes its own normal reaction and lateral slip, including the Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis terms. The discrete comparison allows the greatest reference slip in one sampling interval, and normal contact stays positive throughout.

### SEA-08 incident-wave excitation at forward speed

[J. M. J. Journée and W. W. Massie, *Offshore Hydromechanics*, 2001, §8.3, equations 8.45–8.48](https://ocw.tudelft.nl/wp-content/uploads/Part_2.pdf) give the ordinary-strip diffraction force per metre as `A(omega_e) a_w + [B(omega_e) − U dA/dx] (omega/omega_e) v_w`. Integrating the incident acceleration over encounter time gives the equivalent orbital velocity. Both terms of the damping coefficient multiply that velocity. The pitch moment is its first longitudinal moment in the engine's bow-up convention. The existing convolution sees the encounter rate in its memory but uses the physical water acceleration at each sample. The implementation adds the difference between the ordinary-strip excitation and the incident response of that moving convolution. Wake and current stay in the live velocity-field samples. The force is sampled at the equivalent mean draft, with finite-depth Airy transfer and gradients from a local quadratic on the actual stations.

Below the section table's first frequency, the truncated [Cummins (1962), *The Impulse Response Function and Ship Motions*](https://dome.mit.edu/handle/1721.3/49049) kernel gives a finite static added mass from its first time moment. The continuation uses even added mass and odd `B/omega_e` across zero. The gradient term continues the inverse encounter rate linearly below the first resolved frequency, `omega_e / omega_min²`. Both continuations meet their resolved values at the band edge and keep the load finite as a following wave comes to the ship’s speed. The tapered head-, beam- and following-wave regression evaluates the derivative term by integration by parts, leaving only endpoint masses and the integral of the original mass distribution. The exact stationary-encounter fluid field still needs a three-dimensional model.

The independent Chang–Wellens Wigley targets in figures 20 and 22 were never used for fitting. Figures 19 and 21 show that the tabulated periods are at the moving gauge. Using their measured incident amplitudes, speeds and depth, and the two-parameter Wigley draft with a vertical extension to the operating waterline, the corrected diagnostic gives 0.02137 m and 2.253° in run 77, and 0.01470 m and 1.300° in run 79. Their reported outputs are 0.023 m and 2.45°, and 0.018 m and 1.57° respectively. These differences leave tank qualification open.

### SEA-08 bilge keel roll damping

Read the [ITTC, *Estimation of Roll Damping*, 2024 revision 02](https://www.ittc.info/media/11942/75-02-07-045.pdf), §3.2.6–3.2.7, equations 48, 50–51, 54 and 58–59. The normal pressure uses Ikeda’s drag coefficient `22.5 / KC + 2.4`, with `KC = π l φₐ f / b`, breadth `b`, arm `l`, and local full-section velocity factor `f`. The Jones lift uses the wet plate breadth squared and the relative inflow with its angle of attack. Resolve the lift along the plate normal and apply its moment at the wet centroid. Both terms oppose the roll rate through the existing implicit damping impulse.

[Ikeda, Himeno and Tanaka, *Components of Roll Damping of Ship at Forward Speed*, 1978](https://doi.org/10.2534/jjasnaoe1968.1978.143_113) separates the keel’s normal force and forward lift from the hull pressure contribution. The plate test compares the normal and lift moments to the published component equations with the rigid port’s represented mass and inertia. The new implementation clips the wet span at two longitudinal quadrature points using the supplied water elevation. Hull pressure and plate added inertia are outside these terms.

[van ’t Veer, Schut and Pelerin, *Bilge Keel Loads and Hull Induced Pressures: Experimental Results and CFD Validation*, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1115/OMAE2015-41906), series A1 and Figure 10, provide independent first-harmonic drag observations and separately characterize fluid inertia and higher harmonics. Those observations are reserved for experimental comparison.

### SEA-08 normal drag at small bilge keel excursions

Read Sven Wassermann, Daniel Feder and Moustafa Abdel-Maksoud, [*Estimation of Force Coefficients for Normal Forces on Bilge Keels and Skin Friction Roll Damping of Ships by CFD Simulations*, 2016](https://www.shipstab.org/files/Proceedings/ISSW/ISSW_2016_Stockholm/Papers/6_1_Wassermann_et_al_ISSW2016.pdf), equations 1, 2 and 9–12 and Figures 2 and 6. Their original Equation 12 has the coefficient 0.47 on the squared natural logarithm. The 2024 ITTC recommendation prints 0.7 in Equation 49. Use 0.47 from the original paper, which derives its force coefficient from cycle energy. Its fit includes [Sarpkaya and O’Keefe, 1996](https://hdl.handle.net/10945/61972) as comparison data. That experimental series is in the fit’s evidence and is excluded as a held-out target.

Use the original fit from KC 4 upward and a cubic blend between the two fits for KC 3–4. For KC below 0.3, keep the drag coefficient at its finite low endpoint, so that force approaches zero quadratically at fixed immersion and oscillation frequency. The transition and low endpoint extension are engine choices. The held roll impulse is compared with direct evaluations of both published formulas across the applicable and transition ranges. Independent measured drag and free roll decay remain open.

### SEA-08 bilge keel pressure along the hull

Read Yoshiho Ikeda, Kiyoshi Komatsu, Yoji Himeno and Norio Tanaka, [*On Roll Damping Force of Ship: Effects of Hull Surface Pressure Created by Bilge Keels*, 1977](https://doi.org/10.14856/kansaiks.165.0_31), and the corresponding [ITTC 2024 procedure](https://www.ittc.info/media/11942/75-02-07-045.pdf), Figure 3 and equations 52–55. Pressure is separate from the plate force. The ahead coefficient starts at 1.2 and tapers to zero along the girth. The rear coefficient is `1.2 − C_D` with a length of `b(0.3 KC + 1.95)`. This implementation integrates the lever on the mesh cut at the two plate quadrature stations. It clips both arcs at the live wave and the half-section boundary, integrates the linearly varying moments exactly on each segment, and adds the closure to the implicit viscous roll impulse.

[van ’t Veer, Schut and Pelerin, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1115/OMAE2015-41906) tested the pressure on the separate rotating cylinder. Figure 13 reports an approximately KC-independent shape in front and substantial variability in the wake, including measured positive pressures behind the plate. It supports the mechanism and exposes the limitation of a uniform intervening suction region. None of those results were fitted. The reciprocal sign test and analytical moment in the rectangular case qualify the integration. The phase of the vortex pressure, finite-gap pressure, and quantitative fit to the independently observed pressure distributions remain open.
## Elastic rods: implicit springs, pins and drag in a multibody's direct solve, Morison loads and vortex lift (SOFT-02)

Clean room from papers, written from their equations. No other engine's or paper's code was read.

- Crispin Deul, Tassilo Kugelstadt, Marcel Weiler and Jan Bender, [Direct Position-Based Solver for Stiff Rods](https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13326), Computer Graphics Forum 37(6), 2018. Read in full. Taken:
  - the idea that a rod's stiff bending and twisting must be solved directly, on the tree of its segments in linear time, and not a joint at a time;
  - their compliance per constraint, K^-1 with K = diag(EI, EI, GJ) over the segment length.
  - Own work: Margo solves it as backward Euler springs inside its articulated-body projection, not their position-based Newton step.
- Tassilo Kugelstadt and Elmar Schömer, [Position and Orientation Based Cosserat Rods](https://doi.org/10.2312/sca.20161234), SCA 2016. Read for the Cosserat energy: stretch-shear and bend-twist measured between neighbouring segment frames, and the rest Darboux vector as the rest curvature. Margo's frames are its link bodies' rotations, and the rest turn between two links is the joint's frame.
- Roy Featherstone, Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms, Springer 2008, chapters 6 and 7 (the joint-space inertia matrix and the articulated-body recursion). The implicit spring is a term on the joint's own coordinate. It adds h d + h^2 k to D = S^T A S and h (k (theta - theta_0) - d qdot_0) to the right side.
- David Baraff, [Linear-Time Dynamics using Lagrange Multipliers](https://doi.org/10.1145/237170.237226), SIGGRAPH 1996. Read for linear-time solves of trees with loops closed by constraints. Margo closes a rod's pinned ends with stiff backward Euler springs on the end link, not multipliers. Its pin stiffness, h^2 k = 10^6 times the link's mass, is an own choice: the gap under a load F is F h^2 / (10^6 m), and the ratio stays far inside the 16 digits of the doubles the tree is solved in.
- J. R. Morison, M. P. O'Brien, J. W. Johnson and S. A. Schaaf, [The Force Exerted by Surface Waves on Piles](https://doi.org/10.2118/950149-G), Petroleum Transactions AIME 189, 1950. Taken: the force on a slender member is drag 1/2 rho C_D D |u| u plus inertia rho V (1 + C_a) a_water - C_a rho V a_body, taken across the member. Own choices:
  - the inertia split into the Froude-Krylov force on the whole water acceleration and the added mass across;
  - the added mass carried as mass on the link, with its weight pushed back up;
  - drag as a damping c |u_rel| toward the flow, taken by the tree's solve as backward Euler.
  - Since the loads moved to the loads entry, the coefficients are DNV's (C_A by KC, 1 in a steady current) and the drag the Reynolds number's below the crisis, in place of the rod's own fixed C_D 1.2 and C_A 1.
- R. D. Blevins, Applied Fluid Dynamics Handbook, 1984, and Flow-Induced Vibration, 2nd ed., 1990. Taken:
  - C_D about 1.2 for a smooth circular cylinder below the drag crisis (Re 10^3 to 2 x 10^5), the default `hydro.drag`;
  - the natural frequency of a pinned-pinned beam under tension, omega_1^2 = (pi / L)^2 T / mu + (pi / L)^4 EI / mu, checked in tests/rod.test.js.
  - The added mass coefficient 1 of a circular cylinder is potential-flow theory (J. N. Newman, Marine Hydrodynamics, MIT Press 1977, chapter 4).
- The tangential drag along a rod is Eames's, C_Dn (m + n sin phi) cos phi (as DNV-RP-C205 6.3.1.3 gives it, in the loads entry's morison.ts), here as the damping c_t = 1/2 rho C_Dn (m + n sin phi) D L |u| that gives it on the relative velocity. It replaces an own skin-friction choice of 0.01 the rod carried before its loads moved to the loads entry.
- F. M. White, Viscous Fluid Flow, 2nd ed., McGraw-Hill 1991: the curve fit C_D = 1 + 10 Re^(-2/3) for a circular cylinder, 1 < Re < 2e5, read. `reynoldsDrag` takes it below the drag crisis and DNV's post-critical C_DS(k / D) from Re 5e5, a straight line in log Re between (own choice; the crisis's dip is not followed). A hose or a tentacle is subcritical (Re of 10^2 to 10^4), where DNV's 0.65 would halve its drag.
- The segment loads (`segmentLoads`) share the loads entry's member physics, written by lane C from DNV-RP-C205 and Facchinetti et al.: one wake step (`wakeStep`) serves both, here with the coupling A y'' / D of the segment's own acceleration across the flow (Facchinetti, de Langre and Biolley 2004, eq. 2, A 12), there with none for a member held still. The water's velocity and acceleration are one sampler (water.ts) for both.
- M. L. Facchinetti, E. de Langre and F. Biolley, [Coupling of structure and wake oscillators in vortex-induced vibrations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfluidstructs.2003.12.004), Journal of Fluids and Structures 19(2), 2004. Taken: the wake variable q of a van der Pol oscillator at the shedding frequency, q'' + eps Omega_f (q^2 - 1) q' + Omega_f^2 q = (A / D) y'', with eps = 0.3 and A = 12 (their acceleration coupling), and the lift (C_L0 / 2) q with C_L0 = 0.3 and St = 0.2. Own choices:
  - the oscillator stepped in substeps of at most 0.05 rad of its own phase;
  - the link's acceleration across the flow read from its speed a step apart.
- A. Khalak and C. H. K. Williamson, [Motions, forces and mode transitions in vortex-induced vibrations at low mass-damping](https://doi.org/10.1006/jfls.1999.0236), Journal of Fluids and Structures 13, 1999. Read for the bounds the strumming test holds: lock-in near a reduced velocity of 1 / St = 5, a response that stays near the structure's frequency while the shedding frequency runs past it, and amplitudes up to about one diameter at low mass-damping.

### SEA-08 wet bilge keel virtual inertia

Read Turgut Sarpkaya and James L. O’Keefe, [*Oscillating Flow about Two and Three-Dimensional Bilge Keels*, 1996](https://hdl.handle.net/10945/61972), equations 1–2 and Figures 1–2. The reference volume per metre is `πb²/4` and their `K = U_m T / b` is twice the convention used in the drag fit. The wall-bounded plate’s first-harmonic inertia coefficient varies with excursion. The specimen spans 0.91 m, projects 0.102 m and was measured at frequency parameter β = 1845.

Calibrate a bounded Hill curve to 17 filled-circle observations in Figure 2. With `s = (K/10.1969)^2.1764` the coefficient is `1.1200 + 3.3528 s/(1+s)`. Digitization to about 0.03 in coefficient gives a largest absolute fit residual near 0.115. The normalized observed pairs, with K and coefficient rounded to 0.01, are (0.57, 1.12), (0.77, 1.15), (1.84, 1.17), (1.96, 1.24), (2.52, 1.27), (3.34, 1.42), (3.85, 1.48), (5.34, 1.72), (6.15, 1.93), (7.54, 2.19), (8.16, 2.51), (9.10, 2.65), (11.34, 2.99), (14.56, 3.39), (18.71, 3.71), (25.20, 4.05), (29.01, 4.21). Outside those observations use the low-end limit and hold the upper endpoint at K=30. Each wet plate contributes a positive normal rank-one inertia about the hull centre using its wet centroid. The carried-force solve rotates the resulting whole matrix into world coordinates.

The measured roll periods and decay cycles of Rasmus Byrdal Kjær, Yanlin Shao and Jens Honoré Walther, [*Experimental and CFD Analysis of Roll Damping of a Wind Turbine Installation Vessel*, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apor.2023.103857), Tables 7–8, were reserved. Their measured bare-to-keel period pairs are 1.22→1.26, 1.51→1.56, 1.84→1.89, 2.16→2.21 and 2.66→2.71 s, tabulated to 0.01 s. The paired difference includes damping as well as added inertia. These outputs determined neither engine inputs nor fitted coefficients. Full-model comparison needs the tank hull’s offsets and exact mass placement.

Read Mohsin A. R. Irkal, S. Nallayarasu and S. K. Bhattacharyya, [*CFD Approach to Roll Damping of Ship with Bilge Keel with Experimental Validation*, 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apor.2015.11.008), §3, Figures 1–3 and Tables 1–2 as inputs. ### SEA-08 three-dimensional surge end effects

John L. Hess and A. M. O. Smith, [*Calculation of Potential Flow about Arbitrary Bodies*, 1967](https://doi.org/10.1016/0376-0421(67)90003-6), establish constant-panel integration on arbitrary 3D shapes. A. van Oosterom and J. Strackee, [*The Solid Angle of a Plane Triangle*, 1983](https://doi.org/10.1109/TBME.1983.325207), supply the signed triple-product angle. The engine uses Green’s second identity with prescribed hull-normal velocity, constant surface potentials and centroid collocation. The single-layer edge integral is the contour sum of projected distances times logarithms plus height times signed solid angle. Near an edge the engine evaluates the mathematically identical signed inverse-hyperbolic-sine primitive to retain the perpendicular distance that cancels in the logarithm’s denominator.

Andrew Hulme, [*The Wave Forces Acting on a Floating Hemisphere Undergoing Forced Periodic Oscillations*, 1982](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112082001980), gives the high-frequency Dirichlet free-surface limit and the normalized axial added mass 0.273239 in §5 and Table 2. Odd images enforce that surface condition. J. N. Newman, [*Algorithms for the Free-Surface Green Function*, 1985](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00055041), distinguishes infinite and finite depth. Here the high-frequency mixed boundary has 12 alternating image pairs for a rigid bed with zero normal flow. A separate NumPy evaluation of the 198-face control at depth 1.15 radii gives 0.31571361 with 12 shells and 0.31571369 with 24 shells. The engine computation is built from those equations. Search results surfaced external implementations, which were unused.

The force-port test loads the closed hemisphere in axial translation with prescribed external force. Its refined body is within one percent of Hulme’s analytical limit, using surface geometry and water density only. Removing the 3D term gives effectively zero normalized axial added mass. The close-bed comparison is a numerical cross-check. Finite-frequency radiation, coupled panel motions and independent physical surge measurements remain open.

### SEA-08 course inference in a mean current

J. M. J. Journée and W. W. Massie, [*Offshore Hydromechanics*, 2001](https://ocw.tudelft.nl/wp-content/uploads/OffshoreHydromechanics_Journee_Massie.pdf), §6.2.1, give the encounter frequency by following the moving ship through the wave phase. Nils Salvesen, E. O. Tuck and Odd M. Faltinsen, [*Ship Motions and Sea Loads*, 1970](https://trid.trb.org/View/495), motivate the separate encounter and steady-advance terms of the strip model. A fixed-coordinate wave component retains its supplied phase and the body advances across it at world speed. The steady coefficients in radiation, diffraction and viscous roll use the projected water-relative speed.

When the author has omitted `course.speed`, read the existing `SeaSurfaceSample.current` at the hull centre’s horizontal location, then project the difference between hull and current velocity onto the horizontal hull axis. An explicit speed bypasses this inference. The contract separates the mean current from oscillatory orbital velocity. A plain elevation query gives zero inferred current. The coupled SpectralSea fixture compares the inferred 0.75 m/s with the explicit equivalent and the exact tide-drift control.

### SEA-08 displacement from a translating hull

J. H. Michell, [*The Wave-Resistance of a Ship*, 1898](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786449808621111), linearizes the flow boundary at the centre plane using each side’s longitudinal hull slope. J. N. Newman, [*Marine Hydrodynamics*, 1977](https://home.hvl.no/ansatte/gste/ftp/MarinLab_files/Litteratur/Marine_Hydrodynamics_Newman_2018.pdf), §6.13 and equation (116), state that the source strength is proportional to the longitudinal gradient of the half-beam. In the hull’s frame with positive x forward and an oncoming signed flow of `-U`, the two sides supply `-U ∂(full beam)/∂x`. Its integral over the wetted draft gives `-U dA/dx` when `A` is the immersed section area. Treating each midpoint section as piecewise constant gives the face source `U dt (A_before - A_after)`. The paired contributions at the ends sum to zero. The source first moment along x equals `U dt Σ (A Δx)`, independently of trim in the reference shape.

The engine projects each face onto the still-water plane and deposits this signed volume in the existing dispersive free-surface grid. At that stage it uses a finite patch to resolve a centred face on the grid. The depth-dependent exponential of the Michell wave integral is outside this approximation. Takao Inui and Hisashi Kajitani, [*Bow Wave Analysis of A Simple Hull Form*, 1968](https://doi.org/10.2534/jjasnaoe1968.1968.124_19), independently measured a 2.5 m Wigley hull with capacitive probes and report reduced bow-wave amplitude relative to thin-ship predictions at both ends of the angle range. Their measurements remain held out. The prism tests here derive the source, its moment and the sign of the first crest from pure volume conservation and verify the live renderer coupling. They establish neither an observed elevation match nor wave-breaking accuracy.

### SEA-08 PA-13 wake pressure returned to the moving hull

Thomas H. Havelock, [*The Theory of Wave Resistance*, 1932](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1932.0188), discusses resistance from distributed sources and sinks. J. N. Newman, [*Marine Hydrodynamics*, 1977](https://home.hvl.no/ansatte/gste/ftp/MarinLab_files/Litteratur/Marine_Hydrodynamics_Newman_2018.pdf), §6.12 and Chapter 7, equation (145), describe the pressure contribution to longitudinal wave resistance. The engine’s near-surface patch supplies the existing pressure law `p = ρg(η-y)` in the absence of incident waves. On a wall-sided prism at draft `T`, axial force is the difference between the two end integrals of `ρg(T+η)²/2`. The independent integration evaluates the piecewise-linear transverse wake height exactly between grid centres. The fixture aligns the hull subdivisions and wake sampling knots. The small force bound follows from the scale `ρg B D²` and binary64 roundoff.

A 4 m prism starts at 1 m/s with heave and rotation held, with the stern and bow driving the live dispersive grid. Sampling the actual patch through `SpectralSea` gives 0.71653 m/s after 60 ticks. The uncoupled pressure control stays at 1 m/s while emitting its wake. The coupled run transfers −1,161.086 N s and does −996.521 J of work on the hull. The independent force integral differs by at most 1.57 × 10⁻¹¹ N. Hull momentum and kinetic energy follow the pressure impulse and work to binary32 state-rounding bounds. Plain and shared memory reproduce `40dd15ba8b54585a` after restoring a snapshot. This qualifies the pressure feedback for this numerical prism. The coupled water-side energy balance and tank resistance remain open.

### SEA-12 depth and breadth of advancing hull sources

E. O. Tuck, D. C. Scullen and L. Lazauskas, [*Ship-wave patterns in the spirit of Michell*, 2000, Eq. 4](https://www.scullen.com.au/DSc/Publications/tuck_scullen_lazauskas_00e.pdf), give the deep-water source depth factor exp(k y), where y is up from the mean surface. J. Tessendorf, [*Simulating Ocean Water*, 1999–2004, Eqs. 20–21 and 51–52](https://jtessen.people.clemson.edu/reports/papers_files/coursenotes2004.pdf), uses linear free-surface potential dynamics and the finite-depth dispersion relation. In depth D, multiply the vertical Fourier equation (∂yy − k²)φ = q by G = cosh(k(y+D))/cosh(kD) and integrate by parts. Both bottom derivatives vanish, and G(0)=1. The surface condition therefore reads φ_y(0) = k tanh(kD) φ(0) + ∫Gq dy. For a uniform source in a band, the integral uses the interval mean of G. The k=0 mode retains all signed volume. The fixed-domain modal test checks the resulting transfer and time phase on three grids.

For the guided hull, each band uses the area and first lateral moment of the station section cut at its two depth edges. Green’s theorem gives the signed integrals z dy for section area and z²/2 dy for its first lateral moment. The waterline closing segment contributes zero to both. The two-point rule of [NIST DLMF §3.5(v), Gauss–Legendre Formula](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.5#v) uses the roots ±1/√3 of the quadratic Legendre polynomial, scaled to the equivalent span. The signed differences of adjacent spans telescope to zero volume over each band. A closed eccentric prism checks these moments, source work counts and replay. This is a linear reference-geometry source. It approximates disconnected spans by one and has no reciprocal body–wake work term. The literature source was used for its formulas, and the KCS signed elevation data were reserved for the comparison. [Geometry, resolution and measured residual](limits.md#ship-motion-on-the-wake-grid)

C. K. Birdsall and D. Fuss, [*Clouds-in-Clouds, Clouds-in-Cells Physics for Many-Body Plasma Simulation*, 1969, §3 and Fig. 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0021999169900588), give the area fractions of a square cloud over four grid sites. The projected wake forms the centred, area-normalized radial stencil and translates each tap by the four products of the fractional offsets to the adjacent centres. The weights sum to one and their first coordinate moments give the tap's translated location. Symmetry of the centred stencil gives zero first moment about its centre. This fixes a subcell position error caused by normalizing samples of a patch that touches only one centre. The focused wake test checks the signed complex modes and total volume against the exact stencil weights. Clipped patches keep their original volume-normalized edge treatment.

H. Kajitani, H. Miyata, M. Ikehata, H. Tanaka, H. Adachi, M. Namimatsu and S. Ogiwara, [*The Summary of the Cooperative Experiment on Wigley Parabolic Model in Japan*, 1983, §1 and Table I, p. 22](https://archive.org/details/DTIC_ADP003037), supply the 2.5 m University of Tokyo hull, 0.25 m beam, 0.156 m draft, 2.35 m tank depth and Froude numbers 0.267 and 0.316. The towing fixture holds sinkage and trim fixed. Table I reports measured `g ζ/U²` to 0.001, corresponding to 0.18 mm and 0.25 mm at the two speeds. The table supplies no separate uncertainty for these values. Its recorded elevations enter only the residual calculation. The numerical domain is 12 × 4 m with an absorbing edge, so it does not reproduce the laboratory’s 3.5 m reflective channel.

At the station `2x/L = -0.95`, where the paper’s axis points aft, the measured normalized heights are 0.358 and 0.312. At 50 mm grid spacing the solver gives 0.140 and 0.095, and at 25 mm it gives 0.177 and 0.132. The fine-grid predictions are about 31.5 and 33.0 mm versus measured 63.8 and 77.9 mm. The highest predicted point of the sampled bow profiles is farther aft in both cases. F. Noblesse, F. Huang and C. Yang, [*The Neumann–Michell Theory of Ship Waves*, 2013, §4.1 and Figure 1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10665-012-9568-7), distinguish the local flow from outgoing waves and report a similar bow deficit and phase shift in linear slender-ship models. The comparison records a residual in the waterline approximation. Closure against the 3D near-hull flow and production shot bindings remain open.

### SEA-08 mean axial load from short-wave reflection

Mariko Kuroda, Masaru Tsujimoto, Toshifumi Fujiwara, Shigeo Ohmatsu and Ken Takagi, [*Investigation on Components of Added Resistance in Short Waves*, 2008](https://doi.org/10.2534/jjasnaoe.8.171), equations (1), (2) and (8)–(10), give the axial reflected load from waterline shape, draft and wave encounter. The hull mesh is intersected at its still-water draft. Each incident segment with normal `n` contributes `n_x dl (-n·k̂)²` with its signed axial projection. This recovers Fujii–Takahashi's bow integral in heading waves and allows separate incident surfaces around the hull in oblique waves. The reflectance uses `x = ω_e² d/g` and `1/[1+(K₁(x)/(π I₁(x)))²]`. The incident frequency follows the sea depth and the encounter uses the course through the mean water.

Masaru Tsujimoto, Kazuya Shibata, Mariko Kuroda and Ken Takagi, [*A Practical Correction Method for Added Resistance in Waves*, 2008](https://doi.org/10.2534/jjasnaoe.8.177), Figure 7 and equations (9), (16), supply the conventional hull curve `C_U = max(10, 68 - 310 |B_f|)` and the linear sum over the spectral energy. The short-wave force uses `1+C_U |U|/sqrt(gL)`; it gives a signed axial momentum load with the original convention of opposing head waves. It uses the conventional chart, with no fitted vessel-specific input. The [NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, equations 10.25.2 and 10.31.1](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.31.E1), gives the two modified Bessel power series. The engine shares the positive terms and uses harmonic increments for integer digamma values. At very small draft-wavenumber product it uses the leading `π² x⁴/4`, and full reflection at 12 is within double-precision rounding.

The wall and diamond-prism fixtures derive contour projections analytically, compare the applied axial force with independently evaluated special functions, turn the actual rigid body through 90 degrees, and check drift-current, phase, dry and disabled cases. B. J. Guo and S. Steen, [*Evaluation of Added Resistance of KVLCC2 in Short Waves*, 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1001-6058(10)60168-0), measured a segmented ship to distinguish its bow contribution. Its segment forces remain held out. The present tests qualify the geometric and analytical components of the optional mean load.

The limiting branch squares `π x²/2` with IEEE 754 products. This follows from `I₁(x) ∼ x/2` and `K₁(x) ∼ 1/x`. A source regression applies the pinned-math check directly to the reflection calculation. [NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, equations 10.30.1–2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.30.i)

Dong-Min Park, Jaehun Lee and Yonghwan Kim, [*Uncertainty Study of Added Resistance Experiment*, 2014](https://doi.org/10.3744/SNAK.2014.51.5.396), Tables 1–2 and 12, supply the 3.2 m model, 0.58 m beam, 0.208 m draft, 0.016 m wave amplitude, `Fn = 0.142`, `λ/L = 0.5`, `g = 9.799 m/s²` and water density 997.8 kg/m³. It joins the shared midship point and samples every fourth point plus the stern, giving 41 half-contour points. The 21-point version retains every other point. Both extrude that outline to the nominal draft to isolate reflected waves.

Table 12 holds out the measured normalized mean resistance 2.932 and expanded 95% uncertainty 0.4643 from 16 runs, printed to 0.001 and 0.0001 respectively. The force-port differences yield 2.6965 and 2.7189 for the 21- and 41-point half contours. Both lie inside the reported band. This uses the source and coefficients already on public main without fitting to any reported force or motion. The experiment includes heave and pitch, while the short-wave fixture isolates axial reflection at the same initial body pose. Independent segmented pressure measurements remain open.

### SEA-08 launch effects from the carried hull

SEA-14 already evolves a cavity from the body's trajectory. A per-row `effectsOnly` preserves that observation and the existing splash and foam events. It returns before the duplicate surface pressure, impact pressure, slam mass and displacement solve. SEA-08 supplies those hull loads and wakes. The release reuses the existing cavity and crown laws. Duclaux et al. measure the dependence on wettability. Aristoff et al. measured the shape and entrained volume from decelerating entrants, and Gekle et al. followed the collapsing cavity into its upward jet. [Duclaux et al. (2007), *Dynamics of transient cavities*](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112007007343), [Aristoff et al. (2010), *The water entry of decelerating spheres*](https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2012/04/Aristoff-PoF.pdf), [Gekle et al. (2009), *High-Speed Jet Formation after Solid Object Impact*](https://ris.utwente.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/6901523/high-speed.pdf).

The 1 m coated launch hull enters at 0.09167 s and emits a crown height of 0.42479 m. Its WakeSolver still reaches a gauge at a peak of 6.035 mm. The snapshot reproduces the event record and the same state across plain and shared memory. The launch checks coupling and load ownership. The original experiments supply the water-entry laws.

### SEA-08 hull-launch cavity pressure

Duclaux, Caillé, Duez, Ybert, Bocquet and Clanet, [*Dynamics of transient cavities*, 2007](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112007007343), §3, model the ventilated transient cavity with constant air pressure. Duez, Ybert, Clanet and Bocquet, [*Making a splash with water repellency*, 2007](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys545), give the wettability dependence of air entrainment. The existing EntrySolver computes opening, direction from the motion relative to the water, and closure. Its optional field carries the direction and activity per rigid row. HullSolver clips the immersed hull polygons at the plane through the current center and integrates the remaining water pressure and form drag. Entry does not add a force or volume in observer mode. The submerged cube fixture integrates the load and moment in closed form on two triangulations.

A coated 60 kg launch model first changed the held vertical load by −585.661 N at step 6. The cavity sealed at 0.425 s and the air row cleared that step. Plain and shared memory matched and snapshot replay was exact. Both renderer backends returned the same state e2aac72c284cc1a6 and drew the active splash. This measures engine behavior in a controlled numerical scene.

### SEA-08 measured resistance and motion on the full KVLCC2 hull

The same solver runs the complete hull freely in heave and pitch under the published tow speed. Park, Lee and Kim's Tables 2 and 10–12 supply the test inputs and held-out output intervals. The original Gothenburg grid supplies both submerged hull halves. The full-length fixture samples every fourth point and every fifth row, retaining the last column, for a 41 by 13 half hull. An additional stride of two checks the 21 by 7 discretization. Waterplane extrusion closes the 0.082 m freeboard. Displacement, longitudinal and vertical centres of mass and pitch gyration radius come from the independent standard KVLCC2 geometry and model particulars. Neither the measured resistance nor measured motion enters the inputs. [Park, Lee and Kim (2014), *Uncertainty Study of Added Resistance Experiment*](https://doi.org/10.3744/SNAK.2014.51.5.396), [Original KRISO/NMRI Gothenburg 2000 geometry](https://www.nmri.go.jp/study/research_organization/fluid_performance/cfd/cfdws05/gothenburg2000/KVLCC/kvlcc_g%26c.htm), [Kim et al. (2017), *Numerical studies on added resistance and motions of KVLCC2 in head seas for various ship speeds*](https://pure.strath.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/66854791/Kim_etal_OE_2017_added_resistance_and_motions_of_KVLCC2_in_head_seas.pdf), [Yoo-Chul Kim et al. (2014), *Prediction of added resistance in waves using RANS-based analysis*, Table 1](https://publications.lib.chalmers.se/records/fulltext/204412/local_204412.pdf).

The solver integrates pressure on the moving wetted hull and takes its existing wave-reflection correction. ITTC equation G-32 separates the dominant motion contribution and the reflection correction. A prototype that added the Gerritsma–Beukelman relative-motion result independently counted the resolved motion resistance again and was discarded. The test integrates rigid force over two disjoint six-encounter windows after the 20 s radiation memory has filled and projects each motion onto the first encounter harmonic. [ITTC, *Preparation, Conduct and Analysis of Speed/Power Trials*, 2022, Annex G.4](https://www.ittc.info/media/10174/75-04-01-011-2022.pdf), [Gerritsma and Beukelman (1972), *Analysis of the resistance increase in waves of a fast cargo ship*](https://doi.org/10.3233/ISP-1972-1921701).

At `λ/L = 2.0`, 18 towing runs give normalized resistance 0.8099 ± 0.4922, heave 0.8799 ± 0.04024 and pitch 0.9735 ± 0.07355, with expanded 95% uncertainties. The two discretizations give resistance 0.8469 and 0.8660, heave 0.8899 and 0.8927, and pitch 0.9701 and 0.9719. Each is within its measured interval. At `λ/L = 1.1`, 15 runs give resistance 7.195 ± 0.7072, heave 0.7300 ± 0.03710 and pitch 0.5521 ± 0.04158. The refined hull gives 6.8958, 0.75550 and 0.58761, all within their separate 95% bands. The earlier 21 by 7 geometry gave heave 0.7719 and pitch 0.5949, both above their upper limits. It floated 4.17 mm above the nominal grid waterline at the published displacement. The 41 by 13 geometry floats 0.977 mm above nominal, within the 1 mm draft uncertainty in Table 1. Only the geometric resolution changed. The test checks the refined reference draft before stepping and retains the coarser 2.0 calculation as a discretization control. The refined pressure-only control gives resistance 5.5446 at 1.1.

## animation/deformed-points and per-instance morph weights (2026-11-26)

Row "Draw a skinned or morphed mesh as points" and row "Per-instance morph target weights on instanced meshes" of `docs/rival-parity-gaps.md`. Written from the papers and standards below and from Margo's own deformation pass (`packages/animation/src/shader.ts`, `batch.ts`, `instanced-skin.ts`), which both features reuse. The rival examples named in the gap rows were known by name and by what they show on screen only; no engine's or library's source, shader text or companion code was read.

- J. P. Lewis, M. Cordner and N. Fong, "Pose Space Deformation: A Unified Approach to Shape Interpolation and Skeleton-Driven Deformation", SIGGRAPH 2000, https://doi.org/10.1145/344779.344862 . Used: shape interpolation as the base shape plus a weighted sum of per-vertex target offsets, applied before the skeleton-driven blend (sections 2.2 and 2.3), which is the order of Margo's deformation pass and of the instanced one.
- N. Magnenat-Thalmann, R. Laperriere and D. Thalmann, "Joint-dependent local deformations for hand animation and object grasping", Graphics Interface 1988. Known by citation (through Lewis et al.): linear blend skinning.
- T. Lorach, "DirectX 10 Blend Shapes: Breaking the Limits", GPU Gems 3, chapter 3, Addison-Wesley 2007, https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems3/part-i-geometry/chapter-3-directx-10-blend-shapes-breaking-limits . Used: target offsets kept in one GPU buffer indexed by target and vertex, with the weights in a second buffer the vertex stage loops over, so the number of targets is not tied to vertex attributes.
- B. Dudash, "Animated crowd rendering", GPU Gems 3, chapter 2, Addison-Wesley 2007, https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems3/part-i-geometry/chapter-2-animated-crowd-rendering . Used: per-instance data read from a buffer by the instance index in the vertex stage; here a row of morph weights per instance beside the instance's matrix and clips.
- Khronos Group, glTF 2.0 specification, sections 3.7.2.2 (morph targets: POSITION and NORMAL displacements, weights per mesh or node) and 3.7.3 (skins), https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html . Used: what a target displaces and that morphing comes before skinning.
- M. Botsch and L. Kobbelt, "High-Quality Point-Based Rendering on Modern GPUs", Pacific Graphics 2003, https://www.graphics.rwth-aachen.de/publication/03118/ . Used: a point drawn as a screen-aligned quad whose extent is set in the vertex stage from the projection (a world-sized point's extent divided by its clip w, a pixel-sized one's multiplied by it), with the disc cut in the fragment stage. Their Gaussian blending pass and per-pixel depth correction are not used.
- W3C, WebGPU and WGSL specifications (instance-step vertex buffers, `@builtin(vertex_index)` and `@builtin(instance_index)`, `discard`), https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/ and https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/ .

Own derivations: the world-size extent from the view-projection matrix alone (the lengths of its x and y rows without their share along the w row, which is the projection's focal scale for a centred, off-axis or orthographic projection; `pointScale`, checked against direct projection in `packages/animation/tests/deformed-points.test.js`); the reader count that keeps a hidden model deforming.
## Batched mesh item culling and levels of detail (`@margoengine/materials/batched-lod`, 2026-11-26)

- J. H. Clark, [Hierarchical Geometric Models for Visible Surface Algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1145/360349.360354) (Communications of the ACM 19(10), 1976): a hierarchy of bounding volumes tested against the view, so a node outside drops everything under it and a node wholly inside keeps everything under it untested, and a level of detail chosen per object from how much of the screen it covers.
- U. Assarsson and T. Möller, [Optimized View Frustum Culling Algorithms for Bounding Boxes](https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.2000.10487517) (Journal of Graphics Tools 5(1), 2000): the box against plane test by the box's reach along the plane normal, with the three outcomes outside, crossing and inside that the walk uses.
- G. Gribb and K. Hartmann, [Fast Extraction of Viewing Frustum Planes from the World-View-Projection Matrix](https://www.gamedevs.org/uploads/fast-extraction-viewing-frustum-planes-from-world-view-projection-matrix.pdf) (2001): the six planes core's camera already keeps, read as they are.
- T. L. Kay and J. T. Kajiya, [Ray Tracing Complex Scenes](https://doi.org/10.1145/15922.15916) (SIGGRAPH 1986): the top-down build that splits each node's objects at the median along an axis.
- I. Wald, S. Boulos and P. Shirley, [Ray Tracing Deformable Scenes Using Dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchies](https://doi.org/10.1145/1189762.1189768) (ACM Transactions on Graphics 26(1), 2007): refitting the boxes of a tree as built when its objects move, and rebuilding once the refitted tree has degraded.
- T. A. Funkhouser and C. H. Séquin, [Adaptive Display Algorithm for Interactive Frame Rates During Visualization of Complex Virtual Environments](https://doi.org/10.1145/166117.166149) (SIGGRAPH 1993): discrete levels of detail per object with hysteresis, so an object at a switch point does not flicker between two levels.
- D. Luebke, M. Reddy, J. D. Cohen, A. Varshney, B. Watson and R. Huebner, [Level of Detail for 3D Graphics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9781558608382/level-of-detail-for-3d-graphics) (Morgan Kaufmann, 2002), chapter 4: distance-based selection and the hysteresis band around each switch distance.

Margo-own: each level is its own item of the batch with exactly one flag set, so the batch's compute pass, shadows and
picking need no change; the padded outside test whose pad never grows from a box to one inside it, so the walk keeps
exactly the items a test of every item keeps (packages/materials/tests/batched-lod.test.js); the rebuild rule (summed
node surface area doubled since the build); and the level choice shared with `LODSystem` as `packages/shared/lod-pick.js`
(coarser at once, finer only below `distance * (1 - hysteresis)` of the level on show). No other engine's source was
read.

### KB-BVH-SYNCPOSE1 synchronous raycasts on skinned and morphed meshes

Read as inputs: Ingo Wald, Solomon Boulos and Peter Shirley, [*Ray Tracing Deformable Scenes Using Dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchies*, 2007](https://doi.org/10.1145/1186644.1186650), for refitting a tree of fixed topology bottom-up each frame and for when that holds its quality; Christian Lauterbach, Sung-Eui Yoon, David Tuft and Dinesh Manocha, [*RT-DEFORM: Interactive Ray Tracing of Dynamic Scenes using BVHs*, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1109/RT.2006.280213), for the rebuild test on a node's box against its children's; Daniel Kopta, Thiago Ize, Josef Spjut, Erik Brunvand, Al Davis and Andrew Kensler, [*Fast, Effective BVH Updates for Animated Scenes*, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1145/2159616.2159649), for tree rotations during a refit; and the glTF 2.0 specification, [sections 3.7.2.2 (morph targets) and 3.7.3 (skins)](https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html). Only the papers and the specification were read, no code that accompanies them and no other engine's source.

Margo's own: the registry in `packages/shared/pose-source.js`, the CPU evaluation in `packages/animation/src/pose.ts` (written from Margo's deformation shader, `packages/animation/src/shader.ts`, term for term) and the posed entry in `packages/bvh/src/raycaster.ts`, which calls the `MeshBVH.refit` the package already had. The plain refit of the first paper is what is built; the rebuild test and the rotations are not, and docs/limits.md says so.

### SEA-08 three-dimensional radiation and diffraction at finite frequency

P. J. Rohrer et al., [*Applied Ocean Research* 152, 104198, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apor.2024.104198), Eqs. 21–29, give the deep-water free-surface Green function and the boundary integral for constant strength panels. The implementation integrates the direct and mirror Rankine terms analytically and uses three Gaussian points on the remaining wave part. The complex scaled E1 uses its convergent series near the origin and its least-term asymptotic expansion away from it; see [NIST DLMF §6.12](https://dlmf.nist.gov/6.12). The radiation and directional diffraction columns use one collocation matrix and one factorization. Incident wave diffraction prescribes minus the normal velocity of the Airy potential. HullSolver keeps the direct incident pressure in its existing wetted integration.

J. N. Newman, [*Algorithms for the Free-Surface Green Function*, 1985](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00055041), and Z.-M. Chen, [*New formulation of the finite depth free surface Green function*, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07754), give the constant-depth Hankel representation and distinguish the singular Rankine terms from the wave integral. The engine forms the even bed reflection of the deep solution in Hankel coordinates, solves the geometric series using the Robin reflection coefficient, extracts the nearest bed image analytically, and integrates under the outgoing poles. The finite-depth Green test checks both physical boundary conditions at three frequencies. Moving the bed from 1.2 to 30 radii recovers the reference deep-water limit in the projected loads.

A. Hulme, [*The wave forces acting on a floating hemisphere undergoing forced periodic oscillations*, 1982, Tables 1–2](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112082001980), supplies analytical comparison values at four positive frequencies for surge and heave. The 480-wet-panel refinement comes within 4 percent of all 16 coefficients and improves on 140 panels. At ka = 0.5 the surge added mass is 0.63699 versus 0.6439, and the heave radiation damping is 0.33731 versus 0.3391, in Hulme's normalized units. J. Falnes and A. Kurniawan, [*Fundamental formulae for wave-energy conversion*, 2015, §5 and §7](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.140305), relate the heave radiation and excitation of a floating axisymmetric body through Haskind reciprocity. The independent relation gives total excitation 16,903.15 N per metre at ka = 0.5. The wetted incident load plus the panel diffraction gives 16,905.99 N per metre.

W. E. Cummins, [*The Impulse Response Function and Ship Motions*, 1962](https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/citations/AD0288388), gives the time-domain radiation equation. The world uses the baked damping in the existing motion convolution and its infinite-frequency mass in the implicit added-inertia solve. A motion forced through five cycles transfers 2.76735 J out of the body, corresponding to 1,153.06 kg/s against the frequency-domain rate of 1,103.07 kg/s. Its replay is exact. On WebGPU and WebGL2 the coupled hull and rendered wake match at 1,362 vertices, with identical CPU replay. The remaining independent Wigley and S175 tank comparisons and the finite-speed free-surface terms are separate evidence items.

### SEA-08 pressure-free lateral inertia

The Lewis-form quadrant uses the antisymmetric potential and stream-function pair in J. M. J. Journée and W. W. Massie, [*Offshore Hydromechanics*, 2001, §7.3 and Eq. 7.106](https://ocw.tudelft.nl/wp-content/uploads/OffshoreHydromechanics_Journee_Massie.pdf). Taking the high-frequency free-surface condition first keeps the potential zero on both quadrant boundaries. If the boundary stream coefficient of motion i is P_i(m) in cos(2 m θ), the potential coefficient is minus P_i(m) in sin(2 m θ). Integrating their product with the contour stream derivative gives rho pi times the sum of m P_i(m) P_j(m). The sway coefficients follow from the first and third Lewis cosines. The roll coefficients follow from the squared distance to the roll point. The resulting matrix is reciprocal and positive semidefinite by construction.

The former extrapolation fit two finite-frequency solves even after their wave amplitude approached zero. A body-row inverse-mass roundoff moved the rectangular test hull's waterline about 6 nm and its apparent infinite-frequency sway mass from 193.1 kg to 499.1 kg. The direct solution gives 194.3 kg on both sides of the perturbation within the regression bound. For a half-circle of radius R, the analytical series sums to 2 rho R² / pi through the telescoping identity for m / (4 m² - 1)². The 128-term tail of that series is below 1.6e-5 relative.

### SEA-08 lateral course radiation

N. Salvesen, E. O. Tuck and O. M. Faltinsen, [*Ship Motions and Sea Loads*, 1970, Eqs. 43–54 and Appendix 1](https://trid.trb.org/View/495), give the speed corrections for sway, roll and yaw. For a tapered-ended hull, the engine uses the interior terms after the endpoint contribution vanishes. In the engine's y-up convention, positive yaw points the bow toward negative Z. The lateral slope is therefore minus yaw. The kinematic lateral velocity is the oscillatory sway velocity less the course speed times that slope. The same sway and roll Cummins responses supply the two angular cross terms and the quadratic yaw term. The existing radiation history supplies the past sway velocity and angular velocities. Integrating from the present reconstructs the delayed motions, keeping the finite history independent of the initial absolute location. A fixed heading and small angles define the ordinary-strip approximation. The correction does not provide a translating 3D Green function or blunt-transom end terms.

A forced-oscillation body port exercises the five retained corrections at known frequency and speed, using the frequency-domain lateral coefficients independently of the time-step reconstruction. All five complex amplitudes match within 0.33 percent. The actual hull and wake fixture restores to the same 92073e2cb54e0b8a state on WebGPU and WebGL2, with 11.869 mm at the distant gauge.

autopilot, track and `hull` paths of `src/ship/solver.ts`, written from papers only (no code of any autopilot or toolbox):

  https://skoge.folk.ntnu.no/prost/proceedings/cdc-2008/data/papers/1849.pdf (pages 573 to 574, eqs. 5 to 16, read): the
  cross-track error, lookahead-based steering χ_d = α_k + atan(-e / Δ) and the along-track switching of waypoints.
- J. Ackermann, "Der Entwurf linearer Regelungssysteme im Zustandsraum", Regelungstechnik 20, 1972 (as control textbooks
  restate it): the state feedback that places a controllable single-input system's poles.
- K. Nomoto, T. Taguchi, K. Honda and S. Hirano, "On the steering qualities of ships", International Shipbuilding Progress
  4, 1957 (known through textbook restatements): why a first-order steering model cannot be fitted to a course-unstable
  hull, so the gains are placed on the full sway-yaw linearisation instead.
- J. Holtrop and G. G. J. Mennen, "An approximate power prediction method", International Shipbuilding Progress 29, 1982,
  and J. Holtrop, "A statistical re-analysis of resistance and propulsion data", ISP 31, 1984 (already the record of
  `holtropMennen`).

The reference model easing into a new heading, the gain scheduling by a tenth of the speed, the integral's freeze while
the rudder is hard over and the drift low-passed over 10 L / U are this package's own arrangement. Proof:
`packages/physics/tests/ship.test.js` (the three autopilot and Holtrop tests).



## physics loose props on a moving deck: friction anchors on a turning body, smooth kinematic paths (2026-11-26)

Files: `packages/physics/kernel/src/solver.rs` (`tally_drift`), `packages/physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs` (`kinematic_pose`,
`smooth_velocity`, `kinematic_velocity`), `packages/physics/src/body.ts` (`setNextVelocity`). No rival engine source and no
paper's companion code was read.

- E. Catto, "Solver2D" (2024), https://box2d.org/posts/2024/02/solver2d/ . Used: the soft step with a relaxing pass, and
  friction anchors held fixed in each body over a step. The anchors' slide over a substep is our own derivation below.
- The exponential map of rotations (Rodrigues' formula; any rigid-body dynamics text, for example R. M. Murray, Z. Li and
  S. S. Sastry, *A Mathematical Introduction to Robotic Manipulation*, CRC Press 1994, chapter 2). Used: an arm turned by a
  rotation vector t moves by t x a + t x (t x a) / 2 + O(t^3). Measured from the arm after the turn, as the tally reads it,
  the second-order term changes sign: a - R(-t) a = t x a - t x (t x a) / 2.
- The Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff series, E. Hairer, C. Lubich and G. Wanner, *Geometric Numerical Integration*, 2nd ed.,
  Springer 2006, section III.4, https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-30666-8 ; and A. Iserles, H. Z. Munthe-Kaas, S. P. Norsett and
  A. Zanna, "Lie-group methods", *Acta Numerica* 9 (2000), https://doi.org/10.1017/S0962492900002154 . Used:
  log(exp(X) exp(Y)) = X + Y + [X, Y] / 2 + ([X, [X, Y]] + [Y, [Y, X]]) / 12 + ..., with the bracket of so(3) the cross
  product. With X = b and Y = -a, the turn between two poses on a rotation-vector path is b - a + (a x b) / 2 +
  (a + b) x (a x b) / 12 to third order (our own reduction). A fourth-order bound, |a|^2 |b - a| / 12, is what the
  regression allows.
- The cubic Hermite basis (any numerical analysis text). Used: the path of position and rotation vector from the step's
  pose to its target, with the speeds at both ends, so its speed is continuous across steps.

Own derivations: the friction demand of a prop on a ship's deck, R^T (a - g) at the prop, from the deck's motion in doubles
(`packages/physics/tests/deck-props.test.js`); the tipping criterion, half width over the height of the centre of mass
against that demand; the slow-heel onset at atan mu.

Calibration (2026-11-27). Fukui et al. print neither KCS's rudder roll lever nor its roll damping. The steady roll moment is a
near-cancellation: the hull's outward moment, about -0.13 q d, against the rudder's inward one, about +0.08. So both values

al. 2021, Table 5). That gives the lever 0.236 d below the water plane, where the rudder's geometric centroid is 0.54 d, and
the decay coefficient a = 1.0 in place of Yasukawa and Yoshimura's 0.035 for another hull.
Validated on data not fitted:
- KRISO's three model scales: largest roll 15.0 to 15.5 degrees, within 12 percent; steady 4.58 to 4.92, within 10 percent.
- The port turn.
- The advance and tactical diameter.
- The 20/20 and 10/10 zigzags' first overshoots.

  doi:10.21278/brod68401 (Ankudinov's factors give KVLCC2 overshoots far under KRISO's); G. Delefortrie, K. Eloot, E. Lataire,
  W. Van Hoydonck and M. Vantorre, 4th MASHCON, 273-286, 2016 (a fully measured model is also too course-stable at h/T 1.2).
No simulation code was read. Applying one tanker's measured interaction constants to another of the same form, reading
X'_vr's ratio as that of X'_vr + m'_y, and interpolating in (T/h)^2 are this package's own.

Calibration. One value is fitted: N'r at h/T 1.2, 2.4 times deep, where the captive tests disagree twofold (Esso Osaka 1.99,
KVLCC2's 1.4 m model 4.10), to KRISO's first 20/5 overshoot at h/T 1.2, 3.8 degrees. Validated on data not fitted:
- h/T 1.2: KRISO's 20/10; FHR's two 20/5 overshoots; the 35 degree turn's 40 degree reach.
- h/T 1.5: the reach and the 20/10.
- h/T 2.0: the reach.
Proof: `packages/physics/tests/ship.test.js`, "banks and shallows against measurement".
