  repulsion as 1 - Fr^2 times a ramp in T^2 / (h - T)^2, Y_A always attraction, both the displacement force times the
  inverse distance to the bank times the Tuck number with the influence width B (5 Fr_h + 5) and the limited blockage,
  and the boundary layer's influence thickness, eq. 9.11). His coefficients are per ship and not tabulated.
- J. T. Duffy, "Modelling of ship-bank interaction and ship squat for ship-handling simulation", PhD thesis, University of
  Tasmania, 2008 (read: the reversal from attraction to repulsion above a depth Froude number that falls as T / (h - T)
  rises; his +-5 to 10 percent uncertainty of the sway force and yaw moment).
- M. Vantorre, G. Delefortrie, K. Eloot and E. Laforce, "Experimental investigation of ship-bank interaction forces",
  MARSIM 2003 (Figs. 4 and 5, read off 250 dpi page renders: container carrier D, 1000 Y' and 1000 N' at y_B 0.28 to 0.78,
  h/T 1.07 to 1.5, Fn 0.032 to 0.081, to 2, 3 and 10 units at h/T 1.5, 1.2 and 1.1 or less; bulk carrier C2 to 4 and 2
  units; eq. 1, Norrbin's vertical-bank formula, for the deep-water moment; eqs. 12 to 18 kept for the propeller).
- G. Delefortrie, J. Verwilligen, K. Eloot and E. Lataire, "Bank interaction effects on ships in 6 DOF", Ocean Eng. 310,
  118614, 2024, doi:10.1016/j.oceaneng.2024.118614 (open manuscript; Table 3: A01's forward and aft forces, the validation;
  Table 4: R^2 0.47 to 0.94 of FHR's own fits, and 0.9 called sufficient).
- W. Van Hoydonck, S. Toxopeus, K. Eloot et al., "Bank effects for KVLCC2", J. Mar. Sci. Technol. 24, 174-199, 2019,
  doi:10.1007/s00773-018-0545-3 (Table 4, the validation).
No simulation code was read. The fit is this package's own:
- One set of constants for any hull. The forward force's Froude-dependent repulsion scales with C_B and its depth-only
  repulsion with 1 - C_B. Each hull's own fit gave these two in nearly those proportions: 1.35e-3 and 1.40e-3 per unit
  C_B, and 1.18e-3 and 1.13e-3 per unit 1 - C_B.
- The forward attraction is 0.8975 of the aft. That ratio gives Norrbin's deep-water ratio N / (L Y) = -0.0025 / 0.0926.
- The boundary layer's constant is 0.1.
- The fit is weighted least squares over both hulls' force and moment, each weighted by its reading error, and
  cross-validated by holding out each depth in turn.

### The ship's squat limit and default shaft depth (SEA-09, `SQUAT_FROUDE_LIMIT`, `shaftDepth`, 2026-11-27)

- The squat laws hold up to a depth Froude number of 0.7 (Huuska's limit, where the flow under the ship is still
  subcritical), as S. Serban and V. Panaitescu state it in their 2016 squat review (already read for `squat`). The solver
  holds a faster ship's squat at the limit's.
- The default shaft depth, the draught less 0.52 propeller diameters, is KCS's: its propeller centre 0.02913 L below the
  waterline (the Tokyo 2015 CFD workshop's KCS particulars, https://t2015.nmri.go.jp/kcs_gc.html, read), with L 230 m,
  draught 10.8 m and diameter 7.9 m (SIMMAN 2008's KCS particulars, read): (10.8 - 6.70) / 7.9 = 0.52.

## physics rods in air, direction and work counts (2026-11-27)

Files: `packages/physics/src/loads/segments.ts` (`segmentAirLoads`, `swayFlow`), `packages/physics/src/rod/index.ts`
(`setTarget`). No rival engine source and no paper's companion code was read.

- The independence (cross-flow) principle for an inclined cylinder (S. F. Hoerner, *Fluid-Dynamic Drag*, 1965, chapter 3):
  the drag across is the cylinder's at the flow's part across it. Used for the test's closed form of a cable hanging in a
  uniform wind, w sin(theta) = 1/2 rho C_D D (U cos theta)^2, a straight line because every load on it is uniform.
- International Standard Atmosphere (ISO 2533:1975), sea level at 15 C: density 1.225 kg/m^3 and kinematic viscosity
  1.4607e-5 m^2/s.
- Mulberry32, a 32-bit generator of integer operations (T. Ettinger, 2017; public domain description). Used for the sway's
  seeded phases and headings, so a seed gives the same bits on every engine.
- Own derivations: the target pull as a spring of natural frequency w and damping ratio zeta on each link's own mass, so a
  rod pulled as a whole moves as one critically damped mass, d (1 - (1 + w t) e^(-w t)); the step bound 2 pi f dt <= 0.5 for
  a force held over a step; the rod's work counts, 2n - 3 pairs looked at and n joints for n links.

## physics wrapped rope with capstan friction (2026-11-27)

Files: `packages/physics/src/rod/wrapped.ts` (`WrappedRope`). No rival engine source and no paper's companion code was read.

- S. Sueda, G. L. Jones, D. I. W. Levin and D. K. Pai, "Large-scale dynamic simulation of highly constrained strands",
  ACM TOG 30(4), 2011, https://doi.org/10.1145/2010324.1964934 (preprint read). Used: Eulerian nodes on a constraint
  (a circle on a cylinder) that the strand's material slides through, so a wrap is a place, not contacts; Lagrangian
  nodes as material points. Their wraps are frictionless or without slip; their limitations section leaves finite friction
  to future work.
- The capstan equation (L. Euler 1762; J. A. Eytelwein 1808): a rope sliding over a cylinder through an angle phi with
  friction mu has T_high = T_low e^(mu phi), and holds while the ratio is within it.
- Own derivations: the gradient of a tangent span plus its arc with respect to its node is the span's unit vector (the
  rope winds and unwinds as the node moves), so a wrap's sides are inextensible constraints along those vectors; held, each
  side keeps its material to an anchor fixed on the cylinder; sliding, one total-length constraint with the impulses split
  by the capstan ratio, T_A' = (rate + T_A0 w_A + T_B0 w_B) / (w_A + k w_B); a fixed node holds whatever the load unless a
  winch draws its side past its rope, when the rope slides toward it; for an Atwood machine over a capstan one step gives
  a = g (m2 - k m1) / (m2 + k m1) exactly.

## physics wrapped rope on moving bodies (2026-11-27)

Files: `packages/physics/src/rod/wrapped-solver.ts` (`WrappedRopeSolver`). No rival engine source and no paper's companion
code was read. Sources as for `WrappedRope` above (Sueda, Jones, Levin and Pai 2011; Euler 1762 and Eytelwein 1808), and
the staggered partitioned coupling of the physics framework (C. A. Felippa, K. C. Park and C. Farhat, "Partitioned
analysis of coupled mechanical systems", CMAME 190, 2001, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0045-7825(00)00391-1).

- Own derivations: on a drum that moves and turns, each side's stretch rate is u . (v_node - v_drum(T)), T the tangent
  point and u the span's unit vector, exact for the drum's rigid motion: a node carried with the drum moves from T at omega x
  (A - T), square to u as A - T lies along u, so it stretches nothing; the effective inverse mass of a side is the node's plus the drum's at T along u;
  each pull T u on a node toward T is matched by - T u on the drum at T, and as the node and T lie on one line along u the
  pair keeps angular momentum about any point, so the drum's torque R (T_high - T_low) comes from the two pulls; the
  anchor of a wrap's material is put back at the middle of the touching arc each step, the shift moved from one side's
  count to the other's, so a turning drum never carries it off the arc; for a winch drum slipping under the rope, the side
  the surface comes from is the tight one, T_A = k T_B, so A rises at a = g (k m_B - m_A) / (m_A + k m_B) whatever the drum's
  speed while it slips and whatever the deck's steady speed.

Files: `packages/physics/src/loads/segments.ts`, `packages/physics/src/loads/morison.ts` (`wakeStep`'s second harmonic),

  van der Pol oscillators", Ocean Engineering 53 (2012) 83-97, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oceaneng.2012.06.025 (open
  preprint, https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/41066/, read). Used: the in-line wake p'' + 2 eps_x w_f (p^2 - 1) p' + 4 w_f^2
  p = Lambda_x X'' / D (eq. 6, eq. 8), p = 2 C_D / C_D0 with C_D0 = 0.2, eps_x = 0.3, Lambda_x = 12.

  read, paywalled); its fit 1 + 1.043 (2 A_rms / D)^0.65 as given in SINTEF's VIVANA theory notes, "Drag coefficient

  vortex-induced vibration of a flexible pipe in steady flow", Marine Structures (2025),
  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marstruc.2025.103895, open as https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05748 (v3, read). Used: the

  paths with the axes' tick marks: the mean bow, RMS in-line and cross-flow displacement and their mode shapes; and the
  same figures' CFD and VIVANA curves, for how far the paper's own predictions sit from the measurement. Their companion
  repository was not read.

  notes on the time series files available on the VIV data repository" (University of Southampton, 9 March 2022), read for
  the riser series' tensions and still-water modal frequencies, for a second check once its data are available.
- Own derivations: the in-line wake on the segment's acceleration along the relative flow and its force along that flow;
  the swing for the drag growth measured across the water's own flow (across the relative flow it would count the bow);
  the growth as a steady load on the water's speed, not a damping, so a light segment stays stable; the lock-in frequency
  of a bowed cable at its raised tension, T (1 + (8 / 3) (delta / L)^2 / strain) for a parabolic bow delta.

### PA-88 open and inside-out triangle-mesh solid mass fallback (`estimateMeshMassProperties`)

Clean-room TypeScript implementation in `packages/physics/src/mesh-tools.ts`, using only deterministic f64 arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `Math.sqrt`, range-reduced odd-series `atan2`):

- B. Mirtich, [*Fast and Accurate Computation of Polyhedral Mass Properties*](https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.1996.10487458) (Journal of Graphics Tools 1(2), 1996): signed tetrahedron volume, first moment and second-moment covariance integration for closed meshes, automatically flipping sign when a closed surface is wound inside out.
- A. Van Oosterom and J. Strackee, [*The Solid Angle of a Plane Triangle*](https://doi.org/10.1109/TBME.1983.325207) (IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering 30(2), 1983): exact signed solid angle of a triangle subtended at an arbitrary query point.
- A. Jacobson, L. Kavan and O. Sorkine-Hornung, [*Robust Inside-Outside Segmentation using Generalized Winding Numbers*](https://doi.org/10.1145/2461912.2461916) (ACM Transactions on Graphics 32(4), 2013): generalized winding-number classification (`|w(p)| >= 0.5`) on a uniform voxel grid for open or non-manifold meshes, followed by parallel-axis voxel inertia accumulation and Jacobi diagonalization.

Only public papers were consulted; no rival or companion implementation source was read.

  difference categories), Annex F (12-bit DC and AC ranges), Table B.2 (precisions) and F.2.2.3 (Huffman decoding).
- A. Moffat and A. Turpin, "On the implementation of minimum-redundancy prefix codes", IEEE Transactions on
  Communications, 1997, https://people.eng.unimelb.edu.au/ammoffat/abstracts/mt97ieeecomm.html: decoding by a table
  indexed with the next bits, in place of a loop per bit.
- M. Liddell and A. Moffat, "Decoding prefix codes", Software: Practice and Experience, 2006,
  https://people.eng.unimelb.edu.au/ammoffat/abstracts/lm06spe.html: compares decoding methods and finds table methods
  fast while the table stays small; hence 9 bits, with the length search for longer codes.
- Adobe, "Digital Negative (DNG) Specification", version 1.7.1.0,
  https://helpx.adobe.com/camera-raw/digital-negative.html: a lossless tile may be coded as a frame of another shape
  (two components at half the width).
- NEMA, DICOM PS3.5, https://dicom.nema.org/medical/dicom/current/output/chtml/part05/sect_8.2.html: the JPEG transfer
  syntaxes and encapsulated pixel data the sample files use.

Rivals' feature list: DICOM and DNG lossless JPEG readers on the web take selection values 1 to 7, 8 to 16 bits and
interleaved components, and WebAssembly builds of libjpeg-turbo add 12-bit lossy data; this reader covers those and
the point transform, restart intervals and sampling factors. Arithmetic coding stays refused.

Evidence: libjpeg-turbo 3.2.1 (conda-forge win-64 package, run as programs) made the fixtures of
`tests/generate-jpeg-libjpeg-turbo.mjs`. The NEMA DICOM WG04 sample set
(ftp://medical.nema.org/MEDICAL/Dicom/DataSets/WG04/; compsamples_jpeg.tar SHA-256
df4487f691added9ed863424a166db31e954b2acf8efa299b2235259ab5b1883, compsamples_refanddir.tar.bz2
2477265a9b1435230f0288ae2a30e26de512f6c2b9cd5f6f04bc1a0d5b539c96) was checked whole with
`tests/jpeg-nema-corpus.mjs`: 13 of 13 lossless files equal the references; 10 of 10 12-bit lossy files differ from
`djpeg -dct float` by at most 1. ITU-T T.83's compliance data is sold with that standard and was not used.

A fixed bug found on the way: a file cut right after a 0xFF byte of entropy data read as endless zeros and decoded
without an error. The bit reader now counts every byte it reads past the data.

Rust and WebAssembly were measured and not used. A Rust prototype of the lossless loop (64-bit bit buffer, one
component), run in turns with the TypeScript decoder in one Node process, per-round minimum of 12: MG1 (14.3 million
samples) 144 ms against 90 ms, RG1 45 against 32 ms, SC1 45 against 29 ms, MR2 (1 million) 10.3 against 10.2 ms, CT1
(262,144) 2.6 against 3.8 ms, on a machine shared with other work. The gain, 1.4 to 1.6 times, appears only above about
1 MB of data, small slices and camera tiles are no faster, and the synchronous `decodeJPEG` and `parseTIFF` calls cannot
load a module on demand, so Wasm would mean a second, asynchronous decoder.

### SEA-12 work of a projected hull displacement

V. E. Zakharov, *Stability of periodic waves of finite amplitude on the surface of a deep fluid* (1968), §2,
uses wave energy as the Hamiltonian with gravitational potential energy quadratic in elevation. At the discrete
finite-depth WakeSolver kick the surface potential is unchanged and height changes by dη. The added energy is
ρg dx² Σ dη(η + dη/2). The meter applies the same depth-band projection as the receiving solver. With a straight
impermeable quay the image domain has equal energy on either side, so the wet domain takes half of the sum.
The test separately reads the live potential and computes its energy with the finite-depth modes k tanh(kD).
[Zakharov](https://zakharov75.itp.ac.ru/static/local/zve75/zakharov/1968/1968-03-art3A10.10072FBF00913182.pdf)

For free surge, take the transpose of the same displacement operator in the wave-energy pairing. Acting on
the hull with an opposite impulse evaluated at the midpoint exactly balances the rigid kinetic energy
for that same step. Bao, Donev, Griffith, McQueen and Peskin (2017), §2, provide the discrete adjoint
principle for reciprocal fluid–body work. Cooper (1987) derives the preservation of quadratic invariants
by implicit midpoint. [Bao et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.07169) · [Cooper](https://doi.org/10.1093/imanum/7.1.1)

On the finite domain, apply the same pairing to the four motion columns. Project the advancing column through
the finite volume operator, and stamp the three convex waterplane columns on the connected wet surface.
Use the elevation after the first half sponge when computing the transpose. For the combined kick
`dη = B ds`, the midpoint quadratic work is `ρg dx² (Bᵀη + BᵀB ds/2) · ds`. The test checks that expression
against the change in elevation and kinetic energy at the surface, including absorber losses.

### SEA-12 wake reflection at a straight quay

Un-Ryong Rim, Jun-Bom Ko, Chol-Jun Han and Fuad-Mahfud Assidiq, *An Exact Neumann-to-Dirichlet (NtD) Boundary
Condition for Three-Dimensional Wave Motion Over Piecewise Smooth Topographies Near a Vertical Breakwater*
(2025), §2, equations 1–3. The mirror pair in the incident potential gives zero normal gradient at the vertical
face. SEA-12 uses the same even continuation for its hull pressure and displaced-volume inputs on a symmetric
WakeSolver grid. The analytic regression checks an oblique finite-depth mode, and the coupled regression checks
real hull pressure and source fields, wet-side volume and snapshot replay. [Rim et al.](https://doi.org/10.1002/eng2.70041)

Van der Meer et al., *EurOtop Manual on Wave Overtopping of Sea Defences and Related Structures* (2018), chapter 7,
treat crest level and vertical-wall wave conditions separately from the transport over that crest. The Water
binding uses consecutive solver samples to locate a rising crest crossing and interpolate the liquid velocity.
The VFX particles visualize that crossing. An overtopping discharge, a wave-impact breakup or a measured droplet
size distribution is outside this Water binding. [EurOtop](https://www.overtopping-manual.com/assets/downloads/EurOtop_II_2018_Final_version.pdf)

## Rigid-body fields: gravity field, updraft and vortex (DYN-01, 2026-11-27)

`GravityField`, `Updraft` and `Vortex` in `packages/physics/src/fields.ts` are Margo's own, written from the behaviour
described in the Babylon.js documentation page "Physics Helpers" (doc.babylonjs.com, the features deep dive on
physics, read 2026-11-26 for the parity bar): a gravitational field that pulls bodies toward an origin within a
radius, an updraft that pushes bodies up inside a cylinder (straight up, or away from the centre of its base), and a
vortex that turns bodies about a cylinder's axis while pulling them in and lifting them. The force laws are Newton's
(a field acceleration toward a point, a force along a direction) with the falloffs Margo's `explosion` already used;
the step is explicit Euler on the impulse F dt (E. Hairer, S. P. Norsett and G. Wanner, *Solving Ordinary
Differential Equations I*, Springer 1993, section I.7). No Babylon, Havok, Ammo, three.js or other engine source was
read; the API names follow the documentation only so that code ports.

### SEA-12 eighth-order horizontal quay dispersion

The dimensionless uniform-grid symbol of the nearest-face horizontal graph is
`s = 4 sin²(k dx / 2)`. The expansion of `4 asin²(sqrt(s)/2)` gives
`s + s²/12 + s³/90 + s⁴/560` through degree four. This agrees with the
centred stencil from Bengt Fornberg (1988), *Generation of Finite Difference
Formulas on Arbitrarily Spaced Grids*, Table 1. See also W. A. Mulder (2024), *Temporal dispersion correction
for wave-propagation modelling with a series approach*, the spatial symbol
expansion. [Fornberg](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1988-0935077-0) ·
[Series expansion](https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2478.13411)

For each axis let `D` be the oriented face difference and `W` the face openings.
With `L = Dᵀ W D`, apply that polynomial as the divergence of a shared flux.
Starting from `W D u`, apply `I + A/12 + A²/90 + A³/560` with
`A = W D Dᵀ`, then multiply by the layer thickness. The symmetric volume
operator is positive semidefinite because `L` is and every polynomial
coefficient is positive. A closed face keeps zero flux in each pass. The
same polynomial supplies the normal velocity query and the projection.
On a row of seven fully open faces, four cell-pair differences with
weights `205/144, −127/720, 17/720, −1/560` evaluate the same polynomial.
A fractional or closed face in that row uses the aperture-weighted
polynomial. The flux regression compares both routes with separate
successive applications of the weighted face operator.
The layered mixed-aperture regression checks local volume balance, work
and replay. The uniform carrier test holds vertical resolution fixed.

The largest eigenvalue of the weighted nearest-face graph on either
axis is at most four. The eighth-order polynomial multiplies this graph
by at most `r = 1 + 4/12 + 16/90 + 64/560`. Each nearest-face graph is at most
twice its diagonal as a quadratic form, so the complete operator is
bounded by `2r M`, where `M` is the block-diagonal column preconditioner.
The two-sided Jacobi correction is positive when its weight is below
`1/r`. The eighth-order grid uses one half. The coarser corrections still
use their nearest-face graph. [Jinchao Xu and Ludmil Zikatanov, *Algebraic multigrid methods*, 2017, equations 4.3–4.6](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0962492917000083)

For large eighth-order volumes, the preconditioner adds the positive
column inverse and the symmetric Galerkin correction by acting on the
same residual. The sum stays positive definite and does not evaluate
the fine matrix between those two corrections. The finite projection
itself still applies the original eighth-order operator.
[James Bramble, Joseph Pasciak and Jinchao Xu, *Parallel multilevel preconditioners*, 1990](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1990-1023042-6)

### SEA-12 outgoing discrete quay boundary

The independent harmonic verification matches the uniform exterior to the
eighth-order interior graph. Separate its layer/Robin operator in depth
and its closed-wall cosine modes across the channel. For each generalized
eigenvalue `lambda`, the normal recurrence has
`L = 2 - r - 1/r` and `P(L) = -dx² lambda`, where
`P(L) = L + L²/12 + L³/90 + L⁴/560`. Keep the four outward factors
`r`, selecting the propagating phase by the `exp(-i omega t)` convention
and the evanescent ones by `|r| < 1`. Four inner columns determine the
four ghost columns by modal continuation. The discrete power in a
propagating mode is proportional to the derivative of its normal symbol.
This supplies the reciprocity weights independently of the solve.

[Porter and Evans, *Complementary approximations to wave scattering by
vertical barriers*, 1995, §2](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112095002849)
supply the finite-depth propagating and evanescent separation.
[Un-Ryong Rim, *Wave diffraction by floating bodies in water of finite
depth using an exact DtN boundary condition*, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oceaneng.2021.109711)
uses exterior elimination for finite-depth waves.
[Senganal Thirunavukkarasu and Murthy Guddati, *Absorbing boundary conditions
for time harmonic wave propagation in discretized domains*, 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2011.04.021)
explain why the continuation must match the discrete interior.

The [verification script](../packages/physics/scripts/measure-finite-quay-outgoing.py)
tests the empty channel, a finite-ended curtain with an open underside,
the sealed underside, a moved radiation boundary and two reversible
incident modes. It is an offline harmonic diagnostic with fixed lateral
walls, using NumPy and SciPy. The engine time step still uses its existing
perimeter sponge.

### SEA-12 finite quay wake

Craig and Sulem, *Numerical Simulation of Gravity Waves* (1993), express the gravity-wave variables as
surface elevation and a trace of the fluid potential. At the mean free surface their linear equations
are `height_t = G potential` and `potential_t = -g height`. The finite solver uses the symmetric normal
flux operator `G` on a fixed wet volume. Johansen and Colella, *A Cartesian Grid Embedded Boundary Method
for Poisson's Equation on Irregular Domains* (1998), motivate a shared flux over each open face. This
implementation uses a two-point cell-centred conductance. The exact rectangular depth recurrence and
thin-aperture series flux are independent discrete tests. The spread at wet faces retains only connected
weights from the subcell stencil.

Using the implicit midpoint update turns the top distance into `halfLayer + g dt² / 4`. The symmetric
volume matrix uses equal and opposite face fluxes. The volume kick changes surface potential energy by
`rho g A delta (height + delta/2)`. The held surface pressure does work `-p A deltaHeight`. Perimeter
damping removes elevation energy and records that change separately. The bulk and normal velocity at the
endpoint follow from twice the harmonic midpoint extension minus the old one. Summing the
finite-volume rows over one connected basin cancels every paired interior face. The remaining
Robin flux integral equals the sum of its signed volume sources. Recover the uniform potential
mode from that equation after the relative solve, using a compensated sum over the free surface
and signed sources. Closed basins have separate means. Porter and Evans,
*Complementary Approximations to Wave Scattering by Vertical Barriers* (1995), Table 1, is the continuum
reference for the half-depth plate. No companion code or measured elevation entered these equations.
[Craig and Sulem](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcph.1993.1164) ·
[Johansen and Colella](https://crd.lbl.gov/assets/pubs_presos/AMCS/ANAG/A135.pdf) ·
[Porter and Evans](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112095002849)

The larger systems use the Galerkin coarse-space energy `Pᵀ A P` following Vaněk, Mandel and Brezina,
*Algebraic Multigrid by Smoothed Aggregation for Second and Fourth Order Elliptic Problems* (1996).
This implementation aggregates connected 2 × 2 horizontal blocks within a single layer. Fixed curtain
edges remain between aggregates at every level. The coarse residual sums the fine flux work across each
edge, and paired smoothing gives a symmetric preconditioner for the unchanged fine system. The odd-grid
manufactured potential catches a wrong conductance or wet region merge.
[Vaněk, Mandel and Brezina](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02238511)

Lele, *Compact Finite Difference Schemes with Spectral-like Resolution* (1992), §2.2 and Eq. 3.1.10,
give the explicit fourth-order central second difference and its Fourier symbol. In a uniform layer
the implementation rewrites that stencil for each horizontal axis as `L + L²/(12 thickness)`, with
`L` the conductance graph Laplacian on that axis. Its correction adds `‖L u‖²/(12 thickness)` to
the volume operator's quadratic form. The same open-face mask appears twice in `L²`, so a second
difference stays on a wet connection and never crosses a sealed face. The shared flux reports the
gradient of `u + L u/(12 thickness)`. Vertical conductances and the base multigrid correction stay
as before. The fourth-order claim applies to the open uniform horizontal interior, with a separate
connection and work check at the aperture.
[Lele](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991%2892%2990348-8)

Haruo Yoshida, *Construction of higher order symplectic integrators* (1990), Eqs. 4.4–4.6,
composes a symmetric second-order flow into fourth order with two forward stages and one signed
backward stage. The midpoint rotation of a linear gravity mode has angle `2 atan(ω Δt/2)`.
The three coefficients sum to one and their cubes sum to zero, cancelling the cubic angle error.
Each stage preserves the quadratic invariant with the held pressure added as a constant shift of
elevation. The pressure work is therefore the sum of `-p A Δη` over the signed motion of the stages.
The surface impulse and absorber lie outside the conservative composition. The reported depth
pressure uses the accepted potential difference across the whole tick.
[Yoshida](https://doi.org/10.1016/0375-9601%2890%2990092-3)

Use the transpose of linear depth interpolation to distribute a point source between the wet layer
centres. The two weights sum to one, including at the mean surface. If the nearest depth neighbour
is solid, retain the full contribution in its connected wet layer. The finite harmonic extension pairs
the surface flux with the same weighted depth values. The mode test uses the
uniform-layer normal mode and its Neumann bed as an independent reference.
[Bao et al. (2017), §2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.07169)

The point publisher clips the mesh's wetted faces at the reference depth edges and each XZ bin.
It integrates the signed X component of panel area and its first moments. For each sign within a
bin, the centroid preserves the integrated longitudinal displacement and all three first moments.
Multiply the signed area by through-water speed and step length for volume. This follows the
normal component of the linear advancing-hull source distribution. The projection radius and
receiving depth grid are separate numerical choices.
[Zhang et al., Interference effects on the Kelvin wake of a monohull ship, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.euromechflu.2014.12.006)

The reference hull waterplane cuts the indexed triangle mesh into exact spans between adjacent
longitudinal knots. On each subdivided trapezoid use four-point Gauss–Legendre nodes in each
direction on `[0,1]`. The change of coordinates includes the local trapezoid breadth. The affine
vertical velocity is `heave + ωz (x − cmx) − ωx (z − cmz)`. Its area integral and the centroid
terms are exact for the polygon at the reference draft. Shorter panels converge the signed wave
coefficients independently of the receiver's mollifier. The tests use a closed-form rectangle
Fourier integral and a disconnected waterplane. [NIST DLMF §3.5(v)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.5.v)

## physics rod vortex-induced vibration calibrated and checked against towed and sheared pipes (2026-11-27)

Files: `packages/physics/src/loads/segments.ts`, `packages/physics/tests/rod-viv.test.js`, `packages/physics/tests/rod.test.js`,
`packages/physics/tests/loads-segments.test.js`. No rival engine source and no paper's companion code was read; measured
values are numbers read from the paper's figures, no data file.

- R. N. Govardhan and C. H. K. Williamson, "Defining the 'modified Griffin plot' in vortex-induced vibration: revealing the
  effect of Reynolds number using controlled damping", J. Fluid Mech. 561 (2006) 147-180,
  https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112006000310 (its fit, A* = (1 - 1.12 alpha + 0.30 alpha^2) log10(0.41 Re^0.36), as
  widely quoted; the paper itself not read). Used: the growth with Re, log10(0.41 Re^0.36), as a ratio to Re 5e4, scaling
  the wake's lift and fluctuating drag.
- N. Srinil and H. Zanganeh (2012), as above: their eqs. 3 to 5, the wake forces on the free-stream speed V with the motion
  turning their direction (F_x = F_D - F_L Y'/V, F_y = F_L + F_D Y'/V).
- X. Fu et al. (2025), as above, now also their section 3.2 and Table 2 (the linearly sheared pipe, 3.88 m, 28.41 mm,
  1.24 kg/m, EI 58.6 N m^2, EA 9e5 N, damping 2.58 %, 550 N) and their Figs. 9 and 12 (measured red curves and the CFD and
  VIVANA curves), read from the figures' SVG paths with their tick marks.
- Calibration (Scott, 2026-11-27: calibrate on part of the data, validate on the rest): the wake's lift 0.56 and fluctuating
  drag 0.53 at Re 5e4 were set on the uniform 1.6 m/s case's cross-flow (0.460 D) and in-line (0.175 D) RMS, by a grid of
  runs at 600 steps a second; sensitivity about 0.07 D across per 0.1 of lift and 0.17 D in line per unit of drag; the
  0.4 m/s case and the sheared cases are held out.
- Own derivations: the fluctuating drag as q^2 less its running mean over five shedding periods (2 cos 2 theta for the free
  wake q = 2 cos theta), so the drag fluctuates in the lift's phase at twice its frequency and a symmetric swing drives only
  symmetric in-line modes; the free-stream speed in the wake forces, as the relative speed with a wake locked to the
  motion gives them a mean -rho D U (C / 2) <v p> that took back the mean drag the in-line motion adds; the bow's growth with
  the in-line motion, U^2 + <x'^2>, from the drag on the relative flow.
- Found on the way: `Physics.step()` takes no step length (it steps its `fixedTimestep`), so the earlier test's
  `physics.step(1 / 600)` ran at 60 steps a second, three steps an in-line period; the test now sets `fixedTimestep`.

source (MoorDyn, MooDy, OrcaFlex) and no paper's companion code was read; the measured values are the paper's table.

  Ocean Engineering 104 (2015) 590-603, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oceaneng.2015.05.035 (abstract and the method as widely
  described; the paper not read). Used: the lumped-mass approach, mass in nodes, tension-only segments with internal
  damping, Morison loads per segment on its own normal and tangent, bottom contact.
- L. Bergdahl, J. Palm, C. Eskilsson and J. Lindahl, "Dynamically scaled model experiment of a mooring cable", J. Mar. Sci.
  Eng. 4(1):5 (2016), https://doi.org/10.3390/jmse4010005 (open, read). Used: the experiment (section 3, Fig. 3 for the

  drag across 2.5 and along 0.5 on the bar diameter, added mass 3.8 on the steel's volume, bed friction 0.3).

  for the test's closed form.

  k M v^2), from its energy.

## Audio phase vocoder (2026-11-27)

`@margoengine/audio/vocoder` is written from the papers only; no other library's code and no paper's companion code was
read. It replaces the "considered and not built" note of the 2026-11-10 spectrogram record.

- Z. Prusa and N. Holighaus, "Phase Vocoder Done Right", EUSIPCO 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07382 (read in full):
  phase integrated over time and frequency, largest magnitude first, trapezoidal steps, the 1e-6 magnitude tolerance
  with random phase below it. Chosen: no peak picking or transient detector.
- Z. Prusa and P. L. Sondergaard, "Real-Time Spectrogram Inversion Using Phase Gradient Heap Integration", DAFx 2016,
  https://dafx.de/paper-archive/details/KyhYU44R13wwkkqNs3bgPw : the heap integration.
- F. Auger and P. Flandrin, "Improving the readability of time-frequency and time-scale representations by the
  reassignment method", IEEE Trans. Signal Process. 43(5), 1995, doi:10.1109/78.382394: both phase derivatives from
  transforms with the derivative window and the time-weighted window. Used in place of Prusa's finite differences: no
  unwrapping, so it holds when compressing, where the analysis hop is long. Using them here, the rotation form that
  turns all channels together, and the phase reset for energy new in a frame are Margo's own choices.
- J. Driedger, M. Mueller and S. Ewert, "Improving Time-Scale Modification of Music Signals Using Harmonic-Percussive
  Separation", IEEE Signal Processing Letters 21(1), 2014, doi:10.1109/LSP.2013.2294023; D. Fitzgerald,
  "Harmonic/Percussive Separation Using Median Filtering", DAFx 2010; J. Driedger, M. Mueller and S. Disch, "Extending
  Harmonic-Percussive Separation of Audio Signals", ISMIR 2014: the split, 200 ms and 500 Hz medians, and a separation
  factor (2). With a separation factor of 1 a six-note chord lost up to 39 % of a partial to the percussive path. The split is
  used only when lengthening: compressing measured no better with it and lost noise energy.
- J. Driedger and M. Mueller, "A Review of Time-Scale Modification of Music Signals", Applied Sciences 6(2):57, 2016,
  doi:10.3390/app6020057: overlap-add for the percussive part.
- A. Roebel and X. Rodet, "Efficient Spectral Envelope Estimation and its Application to Pitch Shifting and Envelope
  Preservation", DAFx 2005: the true envelope.
- J. Laroche and M. Dolson, "New Phase-Vocoder Techniques for Pitch-Shifting, Harmonizing and Other Exotic Effects",
  IEEE WASPAA 1999, doi:10.1109/ASPAA.1999.810857: pitch shifting with formants held.
- Compared and not used: J. Laroche and M. Dolson, "Improved Phase Vocoder Time-Scale Modification of Audio", IEEE
  TSAP 7(3), 1999, doi:10.1109/89.759041 (phase locking around picked peaks; Prusa and Holighaus compare against the
  classic vocoder and commercial tools and their method needs no peak picker); A. Roebel, "A New Approach to Transient
  Processing in the Phase Vocoder", DAFx 2003 (detection and phase reset); L. Fierro and V. Valimaki, "Enhanced Fuzzy
  Decomposition of Sound into Sines, Transients, and Noise", J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71, 2023,
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14041 (a three-way split, not built).
- Foundations: J. L. Flanagan and R. M. Golden, "Phase Vocoder", BSTJ 45(9), 1966,
  doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1966.tb01706.x; M. Portnoff, IEEE TASSP 24(3), 1976 (the FFT phase vocoder).
## physics a taut tree's tension stiffness (2026-11-27)

Files: `packages/physics/kernel/src/multibody.rs` (`add_tension_stiffness`, `pin_tension`), `packages/physics/tests/rod.test.js`.
No rival engine source and no paper's companion code was read.

- M. Tournier, M. Nesme, B. Gilles and F. Faure, "Stable constrained dynamics", ACM TOG 34(4) 2015,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/2766969 (its idea, the geometric stiffness of a constraint's force taken into the implicit solve,
  as widely described; the paper not read).
- Own derivations: a taut string's energy (T / 2) sum l theta^2 over its links' turns, so each link carries T l on its turn
  across its axis, half from each end; a force F at the arm r turning with its link changes its moment by [F]x [r]x d theta,
  whose symmetric part (F . r) I - (r F^T + F r^T) / 2 is the pin's; taken in by rho / (1 + rho) of it, rho the tension's
  share of the joint's turning stiffness, so bending-held rods keep their explicit, undamped tension.
### GPU cloth (`@margoengine/physics/gpu-cloth`, SOFT-01, 2026-11-27)

Built from papers and texts only; no engine source was read (three.js's `webgpu_compute_cloth` and Ammo's cloth were
looked at as running examples and documentation, for what they offer, not how they are written).

- M. Müller, B. Heidelberger, M. Hennix and J. Ratcliff, "Position based dynamics", Journal of Visual Communication and
  Image Representation 18 (2), 2007, doi 10.1016/j.jvcir.2007.01.005: predict, project the constraints, take the
  velocity from the move; pins as particles of zero inverse mass.
- T. Jakobsen, "Advanced Character Physics", Game Developers Conference 2001: Verlet-style velocities from positions
  and cloth as particles joined by distance constraints relaxed in turn.
- M. Macklin, M. Müller and N. Chentanez, "XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics", Motion in
  Games 2016, doi 10.1145/2994258.2994272: the compliance alpha / dt^2 in the distance constraint's step, so stiffness
  is a material constant (m/N) and not an iteration count.
- M. Macklin, K. Storey, M. Lu, P. Terdiman, N. Chentanez, S. Jeschke and M. Müller, "Small Steps in Physics
  Simulation", Symposium on Computer Animation 2019, doi 10.1145/3309486.3340247: one constraint pass in each of many
  substeps rather than many passes in one step (30 substeps of 1/1800 s by default).
- M. Fratarcangeli and F. Pellacini, "Scalable Partitioning for Parallel Position Based Dynamics", Computer Graphics
  Forum 34 (2), 2015, doi 10.1111/cgf.12550: edges coloured so no two of a colour share a particle, each colour one
  parallel pass (Gauss-Seidel between colours, no atomics); here a greedy colouring, at most 2 x 16 - 1 colours.
- T. Kim, N. Chentanez and M. Müller, "Long Range Attachments - A Method to Simulate Inextensible Clothing in Computer
  Games", Symposium on Computer Animation 2012, doi 10.2312/SCA/SCA12/163-169: each free particle kept within its rest
  distance along the cloth (here the shortest path over the edges) of its nearest pin, with a slack.
- M. Macklin, M. Müller, N. Chentanez and T.-Y. Kim, "Unified Particle Physics for Real-Time Applications", ACM TOG 33
  (4), 2014, doi 10.1145/2601097.2601152: contacts as position constraints and Coulomb friction taken in position (the
  tangential slide relative to the surface cut back by mu times the depth).
- S. F. Hoerner, Fluid-Dynamic Drag, 1965: a flat plate's normal force coefficient, 1.17, applied per particle to the
  air's velocity through its faces (the force normal to the face carries both drag and lift).
- H. Gouraud, "Continuous shading of curved surfaces", IEEE Trans. Computers C-20 (6), 1971: vertex normals as the
  area-weighted sum of the faces'; E. Lengyel, "Computing Tangent Space Basis Vectors for an Arbitrary Mesh", 2001: the
  draw tangents from the texture coordinates.
- Closed-form signed distances from the geometry of a point and a sphere, a segment (capsule) and a box (C. Ericson,
  Real-Time Collision Detection, Morgan Kaufmann 2005, ch. 5); a mesh as a trilinear signed distance field with its
  exact in-cell gradient.
- Margo's own: the velocity kept as state (not (x - previous) / dt), so float32 positions far from the origin keep
  small accelerations; pins and colliders moved from their last pose to this one by each substep's share of the frame,
  with friction relative to the collider surface's own motion; the CPU twin runs the GPU's passes in the GPU's order so
  the WebGL2 layer and Node give the same cloth (since 2026-11-27 a Rust kernel, `packages/physics/cloth-kernel`, whose sin and
  cos reduce the argument by pi / 2 in two parts, W. J. Cody and W. Waite, Software Manual for the Elementary Functions,
  Prentice-Hall 1980, then sum the Taylor series on [-pi/4, pi/4]); gusts as products of sines (no spectrum).
- Checked against: XPBD statics of a particle on two compliant edges (bisection of the force balance, within the float32
  floor ulp alpha / (w dt^2)), a falling sheet's terminal speed sqrt(rho_A g / (rho Cd / 2)) to 1e-5, Coulomb's
  friction angle and g (sin - mu cos) sliding on a 20 degree slope to 0.2 percent, rest at the thickness on a sphere,
  capsule, box (1e-5 m) and a sphere's trilinear SDF (h^2 / (4 r)), tethers capping a soft strip at 1 + slack, bit-equal
  hashes across runs and a snapshot restore, and the GPU against the twin within 1e-4 m (measured 8.3e-7 m) on WebGPU.
- Own derivation (2026-11-27, `pin_spring`): a pin that gives holds across at a thousand times its give's stiffness, so its
  across gap is a thousandth of its half link's stretch under the same load and its stiffness does not grow as 1 / h^2.

## navmesh exact any-angle search (2026-11-27)

`@margoengine/navmesh/any-angle`, written from the papers' descriptions. No paper's companion code and no other engine's
source was read.

- M. Cui, D. D. Harabor and A. Grastien, "Compromise-free pathfinding on a navigation mesh", Proc. IJCAI 2017,
  https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2017/70 (Polyanya): search nodes (I, r) of an interval seen from a root, observable and
  non-observable successors, the f-value with the goal mirrored in the interval's line, root-level g pruning, dead-end
  pruning and the extra successor that arrives at the goal. Chosen: it is exact on any mesh of convex polygons, needs
  no preprocessing, and so serves meshes that rebuild at run time.
- D. Harabor, A. Grastien, D. Oz and V. Aksakalli, "Optimal any-angle pathfinding in practice", J. Artificial
  Intelligence Research 56, 2016, https://jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/11004 (Anya): the interval and root
  formulation Polyanya extends, for grids only.
- A. Nash, K. Daniel, S. Koenig and A. Felner, "Theta*: any-angle path planning on grids", AAAI 2007 and J. Artificial
  Intelligence Research 39, 2010, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3843, and A. Nash, S. Koenig and C. Tovey, "Lazy Theta*",
  AAAI 2010, https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/7566: not used. They are grid searches over vertices and
  their paths are not proved shortest.
- T. Lozano-Perez and M. A. Wesley, "An algorithm for planning collision-free paths among polyhedral obstacles",
  Comm. ACM 22 (10), 1979, https://doi.org/10.1145/359156.359164: the visibility graph the test compares against.
- Margo's own: the search over portals, not edges, so partial portals at tile seams and several portals on one edge are
  walked (a path bends at an interval's end and follows the edge); corners read from the walls of the whole fan round a
  vertex; one flood of the fan where a root lies on its interval; each view of a polygon or portal kept once per length,
  without which equal ways on grid-like meshes multiplied (556,203 nodes on a 798 polygon map, 841 after); off-mesh
  links as extra arrivals with the estimate scaled by the cheapest link's cost per metre (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael
  1968). Not built: the paper's intermediate pruning, which changes the work and not the path.

## navmesh weighted any-angle search (2026-11-27)

`@margoengine/navmesh/weighted-any-angle`, written from the papers' descriptions. No paper's companion code and no other
engine's source was read.

- J. S. B. Mitchell and C. H. Papadimitriou, "The weighted region problem: finding shortest paths through a weighted
  planar subdivision", J. ACM 38 (1), 1991, https://doi.org/10.1145/102782.102784: the problem, Snell's law of
  refraction and travel along edges at the cheaper weight. Its continuous Dijkstra is not built (polynomial of high
  degree, and approximate).
- J.-L. De Carufel, C. Grimm, A. Maheshwari, M. Owen and M. Smid, "A note on the unsolvability of the weighted region
  shortest path problem", Computational Geometry 47 (7), 2014, https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.5209: no exact algorithm
  with arithmetic and roots exists. So the search brackets the least cost.
- M. Lanthier, A. Maheshwari and J.-R. Sack, "Approximating shortest paths on weighted polyhedral surfaces",
  Algorithmica 30, 2001, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00453-001-0027-5: points on edges joined within each face and
  searched with Dijkstra. Used for the first path.
- L. Aleksandrov, A. Maheshwari and J.-R. Sack, "Determining approximate shortest paths on weighted polyhedral
  surfaces", J. ACM 52 (1), 2005, https://doi.org/10.1145/1044731.1044733: points placed closer near vertices for a
  proved factor. Not used: its guarantee is a worst case over the whole mesh, and the bound here is measured for each
  query.
- K. Daniel, A. Nash, S. Koenig and A. Felner, "Theta*: any-angle path planning on grids", J. Artificial Intelligence
  Research 39, 2010, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3843, section on non-uniform costs: not used, grid only and no bound.
- D. P. Bertsekas, "Projected Newton methods for optimization problems with simple constraints", SIAM J. Control and
  Optimization 20 (2), 1982, https://doi.org/10.1137/0320018: pulls a path tight inside its portals (a convex problem
  with a tridiagonal Hessian).
- S.-Q. Xin and G.-J. Wang, "Efficiently determining a locally exact shortest path on polyhedral surfaces",
  Computer-Aided Design 39 (12), 2007, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2007.08.001 (abstract only): an approximate path
  is made locally exact by changing which faces it goes through, pass by pass. Margo's own for weighted ground: where a
  pulled path ends up on a vertex, the faces round the vertex's other side replace those it used, a short stretch with
  held ends is pulled first, and the change stays only if the whole path costs less. Done on the first and final paths.
- N. Sharp and K. Crane, "You can find geodesic paths in triangle meshes by just flipping edges", ACM Trans. Graph. 39
  (6), 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01270: shortens a path at a vertex by taking the other side of its wedge. Not
  used: it rests on unweighted angles and changes the triangulation.
- Margo's own: the lower bound from pieces of portals (an arc costs the least distance between two pieces times the
  polygon's weight, so no real path costs less than its relaxed one). A piece has a state for each side it is reached
  across and is left through the other: two legs in a row through one convex polygon are never shortest, and the one leg
  that stays on a portal pays off only through a polygon cheaper than the one just crossed (the travel along edges of
  Mitchell and Papadimitriou). Without these rules relaxed paths slid along touching pieces and the bound stalled. Also
  dropping every piece whose cheapest relaxed path already costs `cost / (1 + tolerance)`; splitting only the pieces
  left, widest first, a width being length times the cube root of the weight (a piece's error grows with weight
  times length and the arcs with the square of the pieces, so sharing a given error at the least arcs puts lengths in
  inverse proportion to the cube root: the error equidistribution of adaptive meshing, C. de Boor, "Good approximation
  by splines with variable knots. II", Lecture Notes in Mathematics 363, 1974, https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0069121,
  bibliography checked, text not read; measured against width by weight, its square root, no weight and other split
  shares); and estimating what is left to walk by what the round before proved from the same piece,
  which a part of it cannot undercut (a heuristic from a coarser graph, admissible because every finer path maps to a
  coarser one that costs no more).
- Looked at for the tighter bound and not built: potentials with a Lipschitz bound on a triangulation (a certified dual
  bound, but its solver converges slowly from a point source and its gap on bent paths is unmeasured).

## weather wind field advected by the mean wind (KB-LOOK-TV-SHIMMER2, 2026-11-27)

`WindField.sample`, `drift`, `set(options, at)` and `resetDrift` in `@margoengine/weather`; no paper's companion code and
no other engine's source was read.

- G. I. Taylor, "The spectrum of turbulence", Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 164 (1938) 476-490,
  https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0032: the frozen-turbulence hypothesis; the eddies a fixed point feels are a pattern
  carried past it by the mean velocity, so the pattern's offset is the integral of the mean wind over time.
- J. Stam and E. Fiume, "Turbulent wind fields for gaseous phenomena", SIGGRAPH 1993,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/166117.166163: a small-scale turbulent field advected by the large-scale mean flow; the gusting
  of the large scale changes the velocity at a point, not where the small-scale pattern sits.
- The offset is a phase: carried by the instantaneous direction times the whole elapsed time (the defect), its rate is
  speed x (1 + t x d direction / dt), which half an hour into a 20 m/s gale is kilometres a second. The integral of the
  mean velocity is exact for a mean held between `set` calls, and `set(options, at)` rebases it so the integral stays
  continuous across a change.

## SEA-12 floating from a body's colliders (`floating`, `bodyLoad`, `debugRender`, 2026-11-27)

Margo's own design from the following public sources; no engine's or library's source was read (three.js's GPGPU water
examples were only run and their pages read, for the migration note).

- Archimedes' principle by the divergence theorem: a closed surface under the gauge pressure (eta - y) takes the
  displaced volume straight up, and under (eta - y)^2 / 2 the integral of (eta - y), which gives the centroid's height.
  G. K. Batchelor, *An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics* (Cambridge, 1967), §1.4 (hydrostatics), and any calculus text's
  Gauss theorem. Used for `bodyLoad`'s centre of buoyancy of a mesh and checked against the hull's triangle centroid.
- The wall-sided righting arm GZ = sin(phi) (GM + BM tan^2(phi) / 2) and BM = I / V: K. J. Rawson and E. C. Tupper,
  *Basic Ship Theory*, 5th ed. (Butterworth-Heinemann, 2001), vol. 1, ch. 4 (the wall-sided formula); the test's
  cylinder moment and GM.
- A regular n-gon of circumradius R has area (n / 2) R^2 sin(2 pi / n) and, about a centroidal axis, the second moment
  pi^2 r^4 (2 + cos(2 pi / n)) / (6 n sin(2 pi / n)) when its area is the circle's: the polygon second-moment formula
  (1/12) sum (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)(y_i^2 + y_i y_{i+1} + y_{i+1}^2), from W. D. Pilkey, *Formulas for Stress,
  Strain, and Structural Matrices*, 2nd ed. (Wiley, 2005), §2.3. The cylinder and cone prisms keep the circle's area.
- Heave and roll natural periods 2 pi sqrt((m + A33) / (rho g A_wp)) and 2 pi sqrt(I44 / (m g GM)): J. N. Newman,
  *Marine Hydrodynamics* (MIT Press, 1977), §6.16-6.17; the added mass A33 is Lamb's ellipsoid coefficient the solver
  already uses (H. Lamb, *Hydrodynamics*, 6th ed., 1932, art. 115).
- The energy-neutral pose of a held load over s symplectic-Euler substeps, (s - 1) / (2 s) of the step on, is the
  rigid solver's own derivation (`world/solvers/rigid.ts`, the hull solver's `seakeeping/solver.ts`): the update of
  a load -k x taken at x + theta v dt has determinant 1 + (omega dt)^2 (1 - theta - (s + 1) / (2 s)). E. Hairer, C.
  Lubich and G. Wanner, *Geometric Numerical Integration*, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2006), §I.1 and §VI.3 (symplectic Euler
  and its preserved area), for why the determinant 1 leaves the amplitude unchanged.

## Exact boolean output without cut points, and Float32 output (2026-11-27, KB-3MF-DOTS1)

Read as published descriptions only (search results and summaries of the papers); no source code or companion
repository was opened, CGAL's included.

- W. J. Schroeder, J. A. Zarge, W. E. Lorensen, "Decimation of triangle meshes", SIGGRAPH 1992,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/142920.134010: remove a vertex and retriangulate the loop around it.
- G. H. Meisters, "Polygons have ears", American Mathematical Monthly 82, 1975, https://doi.org/10.2307/2319703.
- B. Levy, "Exact predicates, exact constructions and combinatorics for mesh CSG", 2024,
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12949: clean the exact result, then round it, as rounding can create intersections.
- V. Milenkovic, E. Sacks, "Geometric rounding and feature separation in meshes", Computer-Aided Design 108, 2019,
  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2018.10.003: short edges and skinny triangles are removed with local mesh edits.
- M. Botsch, L. Kobbelt, "A robust procedure to eliminate degenerate faces from triangle meshes", VMV 2001,
  https://www.graphics.rwth-aachen.de/publication/188/: collapse needles, split the neighbor of a cap.
- O. Devillers, S. Lazard, W. Lenhart, "3D snap rounding", SoCG 2018, https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.SoCG.2018.30:
  rounding without any new self-intersection; not implemented, its worst case being far above the input size.

Design: vertex removal runs on the exact homogeneous points, with float filters and BigInt determinants, only where
one or two input triangles' parts meet at the point, so the point set of the surface does not change. Float32 output
reuses the Botsch and Kobbelt pass with a length that counts as nothing (2^-20 of the largest coordinate nearby). It
does not guarantee a result free of self-intersections after rounding.

## Automatic shoulder fit on thick upper arms (2026-11-27)

In a T pose, a large arm cross-section could make the shoulder ray reach the chest at a plausible location and then move the fitted joint too far inward. The fit now limits the final inset along the measured arm axis, reserving one measured arm radius outside the existing central torso band when there is room. The projected limit leaves the nominal inset alone when it fits or the ray is pointed away from that band. An original stand-in with tapered sleeves checks the shoulder placement on both sides at two grid resolutions.

- Ilya Baran and Jovan Popović, *Automatic Rigging and Animation of 3D Characters* (2007), [paper](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~jovan/papers/baran-2007-ara.pdf). The paper motivates fitting bones within a surface using shape measurements.
- Carel G. M. Meskers et al., *In vivo estimation of the glenohumeral joint rotation center from scapular bony landmarks by linear regression* (1998), [paper record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9596544/). This work distinguishes the joint center from the visible shoulder surface. The inset bound here is a geometric heuristic for mesh rigging.
### Measured cloth bending (`SoftBodyMaterial.bending`, `@margoengine/physics/soft`, SOFT-01, 2026-11-27)

`packages/physics/soft-kernel/src/bend.rs`, the bending rows of `rigid.rs`, `writeBends` in `packages/physics/src/soft.ts`.
Written from these papers; no engine's or companion code was read.

- M. Bergou, M. Wardetzky, D. Harmon, D. Zorin and E. Grinspun, "A quadratic bending model for inextensible surfaces",
  Symposium on Geometry Processing 2006, https://doi.org/10.2312/SGP/SGP06/227-230: the hinge's row vector
  K = (c03 + c04, c01 + c02, -c01 - c03, -c02 - c04) of rest cotangents, whose K x is zero on a flat placement, sums to zero
  and is |e| times the dihedral angle for an isometric bend. Their local matrix 3 / (2 (A0 + A1)) K^T K converges to the
  squared mean curvature (checked here: 3/2 kappa^2 per area summed over a cylinder), a plate of Poisson's ratio 1: a free
  cantilevered strip of it drooped 30 to 45 percent past a beam of the same B at any width (a linear solve of its Q on the
  strip, and the soft solver). So the hinge vectors are not summed directly.
- M. Wardetzky, M. Bergou, D. Harmon, D. Zorin and E. Grinspun, "Discrete quadratic curvature energies", Computer Aided
  Geometric Design, 2007, https://www.cs.columbia.edu/cg/pdfs/1166238667-bendingCAGD.pdf: the family of isometric bending models and their
  invariances (read for the conditions a discrete quadratic energy must meet).
- D. Cohen-Steiner and J.-M. Morvan, "Restricted Delaunay triangulations and normal cycle", Symposium on Computational
  Geometry 2003 (not read; its tensor as the discrete-curvature literature states it): a region's curvature tensor as the sum over edges of the dihedral
  angle times the edge length in the region times the edge's direction outer product, over the region's area. Here the region
  is a triangle, each hinge shared half and half, and the in-plane normal of the edge carries the curvature across it, so
  k_T = 1 / (2 A_T) sum (K_e x) n_e n_e^T, a vector per component, linear in the positions. The energy B/2 (k11^2 + 2 k12^2
  + k22^2) A_T is the plate with no Poisson coupling that a woven fabric's bending is.
- F. T. Peirce, "The 'handle' of cloth as a measurable quantity", Journal of the Textile Institute, 1930 (as Luible
  section 2.2 and ASTM D1388 state its cantilever): a strip whose tip reaches the 41.5 degree slope
  hangs out twice its bending length c = (B / w)^(1/3); the exact heavy elastica (solved in the test by shooting) agrees to
  0.02 degrees.
- E. Luible's thesis (above): Annex C's KES-FB2 B for the presets and the validation, section 4.2.2's FAST bending rigidity
  and weights for the four woven fabrics both instruments measured, section 4.3's face and back spread of up to 89 percent for
  the band, section 5.3.6 on why the two instruments differ.
- Clamp: two pinned columns half a cell either side of the clamp's edge hold the slope level at the edge (a central
  difference), checked on a finite difference beam, where a column at the edge and one behind it lengthen it by half a cell.

### GPU cloth CPU route on threads (`@margoengine/physics/gpu-cloth` `threads`, SOFT-01, 2026-11-27)

`packages/physics/cloth-kernel/src/lib.rs` (`cloth_step_part`), `src/cloth/kernel.ts`, `src/cloth/thread.ts`. Each pass of
a substep is split by a static schedule, thread t of T taking items [n t / T, n (t + 1) / T) of the particles, the pins and
each edge colour, with a counting barrier between passes (a shared arrived count and generation word, the last arrival
raising the generation): the bulk-synchronous model (L. G. Valiant, "A bridging model for parallel computation", CACM 33(8),
1990). No item of a pass writes what another item of it reads (a colour's edges share no particle: the graph colouring the
GPU route already uses), so the result does not depend on the thread count. The worker pattern is the explosive kernel's
(`src/explosive/thread.ts`).

## Crossing triangles after rounding an exact boolean (2026-11-27, KB-BOOL-F32CROSS1)

Read as published descriptions only (search results, abstracts and library manual pages); no source code or companion
repository was opened, CGAL's included. The publisher refused the Valque and Lazard page, so only its abstract-level
summary was read.

- J. D. Hobby, "Practical segment intersection with finite precision output", Computational Geometry 13(4), 1999:
  snap rounding in the plane.
- D. Halperin, E. Packer, "Iterated snap rounding", Computational Geometry 23(2), 2002,
  https://doi.org/10.1016/S0925-7721(01)00064-5: repeat until features are apart.
- O. Devillers, S. Lazard, W. J. Lenhart, "Rounding meshes in 3D", Discrete and Computational Geometry 64, 2020,
  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00454-020-00202-2: a 3D rounding with no new intersections, at a worst case far above the
  input size; not implemented.
- L. Valque, S. Lazard, "Resolving self-intersections in 3D meshes while preserving floating-point coordinates",
  Computer Graphics Forum 44(5), 2025, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf70192: round, find new crossings, repeat.
- J. R. Shewchuk, "Adaptive precision floating-point arithmetic and fast robust geometric predicates", Discrete and
  Computational Geometry 18, 1997, https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321: filtered exact orientation tests.
- P. Guigue, O. Devillers, "Fast and robust triangle-triangle overlap test using orientation predicates", Journal of
  Graphics Tools 8(1), 2003, https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.2003.10487580.
- M. Botsch, L. Kobbelt, 2001 (above): splitting a cap's neighbor, now also the repair's step after 64 rounds.

Design: pairs come from a sweep along one axis and are decided with a float64 filter and BigInt. For each crossing
pair, local edits that keep the mesh closed: join corners within a reach, put a corner into a nearby edge or face,
split two nearby edges at one point; then the thin-triangle pass, then test again. The reach doubles from 2^-23 to 2^-16
of the coordinates and the state with the fewest pairs is returned. It is not proven to reach zero.


## Float64 crossings and thin shells of an exact boolean (2026-11-27, KB-BOOL-CROSS64, KB-BOOL-F32SHEETS1)

The sources of the section above, read the same way, and:

- M. Attene, "As-exact-as-possible repair of unprintable STL files", Rapid Prototyping Journal 24(5), 2018,
  https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.07829 (read as a search summary only): self-intersecting and sheet-like parts are removed
  and the rest kept.
- C. Ericson, "Real-Time Collision Detection", 2005, section 5.1.5: the closest point of a triangle.

Design: float64 output goes through the same pair edits with reaches from 2^-52 to 2^-28, fourfold, and the validity
repair after each; only pairs with a corner that rounding, the repair or an edit moved are tested, so exact contact
stays. A connected part that still crosses is removed when twice its volume over its area, and the distance from seven
points of each of its triangles to a triangle facing the other way, are both within 2^-26 (float32: 2^-22) of its
largest coordinate. Derived here; not proven to reach zero.

  https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8659.1330233. Used: the Fresnel share the glass reflects.

The atlas projection (scale k / (k + z) with k = b / (1 - b) for a back wall share b) is one-point perspective, derived
here.

## SEA-12 the step's bound for a floating body (2026-11-28)

- E. Hairer, C. Lubich and G. Wanner, *Geometric Numerical Integration*, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2006), §I.1 and §IX.8:
  symplectic Euler on an oscillator keeps a shadow energy within (w h / 2) of the energy, and is stable for w h < 2;

## The pose checker: rigging/validate (2026-11-28)

Scope: `@margoengine/rigging/validate` (`checkPose`, `checkClip`, `checkProportions`, `assertPose`, `assertClip`,
`formatPoseReport`), the human table's proportion measures, body volumes, volume pairs and feet in
`@margoengine/rigging/anatomy/human`, and the pose sheet `packages/humans/test/pose-sheet.browser.mjs`. Written from the
sources below. No other engine's, tool's or paper's code was read.

Ranges and their tiers: the anatomy table's rows and `clampPose`, as in "Anatomy core and the human table" above; a pose
is checked on a copy, and the checker reports what the clamp would change.

Volumes and proportions: C. C. Gordon et al., "2012 Anthropometric Survey of U.S. Army Personnel: Methods and Summary
Statistics", NATICK/TR-15/007, 2014, https://tools.openlab.psu.edu/publicData/ANSURII-TR15-007.pdf (the flexed biceps,
flexed forearm, wrist, thigh, lower thigh, calf and ankle circumferences, the chest and waist depths and breadths, and the
heights and lengths the proportion bands are built on). A limb segment is a capsule of radius circumference / 2 pi; the
trunk uses half its depth. C. Ericson, "Real-Time Collision Detection", Morgan Kaufmann, 2005, section 5.1.9 (closest
points of two segments), from the book's description of the method.

Foot contact: L. Kovar, J. Schreiner and M. Gleicher, "Footskate cleanup for motion capture editing", ACM SIGGRAPH/
Eurographics Symposium on Computer Animation 2002, https://doi.org/10.1145/545261.545277 (a planted foot should not move;
contact read from a height and speed threshold). The three-frame plant, the 0.02 stature contact band and the 0.1 stature
per second slide are chosen here, stated in docs/limits.md.

Joint speeds: G. S. Fleisig et al., "Biomechanical analysis of weighted-ball exercises for baseball pitchers", Sports
Health 9(3):210-215, 2017, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5435148/ (shoulder internal rotation peaks of 6,594 to
6,756 degrees per second, SD 743 to 893). The default `maxSpeed` of 9,000 is their mean plus three SD.

Derived here: the step and blip tests for a capture pop (a speed four times both neighbours, or one frame far from two
close neighbours), the "looks locked back" warning for a hinge whose clinical range passes straight by under 10 degrees,
the asymmetry band of 5 percent, and the shrink of 0.7 that lets soft contact pass.

Scope: `@margoengine/animator/ik` (the fitted body as the solvers read it, the swivel-angle limb solver, the joint and
region limits), its use by `addFullBodyIK`, `addFootPlacement`, `addLookAt`, `addCCDChain`, `addWarping` and
`addStepping`, and by `solvePoseIK`, `solveSkeletonIK`, `addIKChain` and `solveContactIK` in
`@margoengine/rigging`. Written from the papers below. No other engine's, tool's or paper's code was read. Blender is
run as an outside referee by `packages/rigging/tests/ik-blender-check.mjs` through its Python interface; none of its
source was read.

The limb: D. Tolani, A. Goswami and N. I. Badler, "Real-time inverse kinematics techniques for anthropomorphic limbs",
Graphical Models 62(5):353-388, 2000, https://doi.org/10.1006/gmod.2000.0528 (the hinge angle from the distance to the
target, then one swivel angle about the line from the root to the target); M. Kallmann, "Analytical inverse kinematics
with body posture control", Computer Animation and Virtual Worlds 19(2):79-91, 2008, https://doi.org/10.1002/cav.176
(the swivel searched for the nearest value the joint ranges allow).

Joint ranges inside a solve: P. Baerlocher, "Inverse kinematics techniques for the interactive posture control of
articulated figures", EPFL thesis 2392, 2001 (swing and twist limits); P. Dobrowolski, "Swing-twist decomposition in
Clifford algebra", 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.05481 ; F. S. Grassia, "Practical parameterization of rotations
using the exponential map", J Graphics Tools 3(3):29-48, 1998, https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.1998.10487493 ;
J. Wilhelms and A. Van Gelder, "Fast and easy reach-cone joint limits", J Graphics Tools 6(2):27-41, 2001,
https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.2001.10487539 ; G. Wu et al., ISB recommendations on joint coordinate systems, J
Biomech 35(4):543-548, 2002 and 38(5):981-992, 2005 (the axes the angles are read on).

Chains: A. Aristidou and J. Lasenby, "FABRIK: a fast, iterative solver for the inverse kinematics problem", Graphical
Models 73(5):243-260, 2011, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gmod.2011.05.003 ; A. Aristidou, Y. Chrysanthou and J. Lasenby,
"Extending FABRIK with model constraints", Computer Animation and Virtual Worlds 27(1):35-57, 2016,
https://doi.org/10.1002/cav.1630 (each joint moved to its nearest allowed place between passes); A. Aristidou, J.
Lasenby, Y. Chrysanthou and A. Shamir, "Inverse kinematics techniques in computer graphics: a survey", Computer
Graphics Forum 37(6):35-58, 2018, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13310 (compared: analytic, Jacobian, CCD and FABRIK
families; the analytic limb was taken for arms and legs because only it fixes the hinge angle exactly and leaves the
swivel as one searchable number).

The default swivel: H. Cruse, E. Wischmeyer, M. Bruwer, P. Brockfeld and A. Dress, "On the cost functions for the
control of the human arm movement", Biological Cybernetics 62(6):519-528, 1990, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00205114
(a cost per joint with its minimum at a comfortable angle; here each angle of the shoulder or hip as a share of its
clinical range, squared and summed).

The whole body: P. Baerlocher and R. Boulic, "An inverse kinematics architecture enforcing an arbitrary number of
strict priority levels", The Visual Computer 20:402-417, 2004, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-004-0244-4 (the order
feet, balance, hands, gaze, kept here as weights of one damped least-squares solve, not as strict levels); S. R. Buss
and J.-S. Kim, "Selectively damped least squares for inverse kinematics", J Graphics Tools 10(3):37-49, 2005,
https://doi.org/10.1080/2151237X.2005.10129202 (clamping the error near the end of the reach).

Margo's own in this entry: the fitted body read through structural types so the animator package needs no import from
rigging; the flexion found by bisection on the true root-to-end length, which holds for bones that do not lie on a
line and for a hinge with a modelled carrying angle; a straight limb's bend side taken from the hinge axis crossed
with the limb's line; the rule that a bent pose keeps its side and a straight one takes the least-cost swivel; the
swivel search outward in 5 degree steps with a bisection back to the edge of the range; hinges stopped at straight
inside a solve while a played pose keeps the structural allowance past it; the gate of a twist read after the swing
is settled; and a shared region eased across only the bones a solver owns.

X. Yang, B. Guo and H.-Y. Shum, "Real-time rendering of plant leaves", SIGGRAPH 2005,
https://doi.org/10.1145/1073204.1073251 (leaves as a glossy reflective surface plus a transmitted term of their own

and P. Prusinkiewicz, "Generating Spatial Distributions for Multilevel Models of Plant Communities", Graphics

https://doi.org/10.1145/280814.280898 (plants of one species aggregate in patches, and plants thin where a dominant

### SEA-10 compartment volume tables and dry openings

Pekka Ruponen (2007), *Progressive flooding of a damaged passenger ship*, treats room permeability, the free-surface level, air pressure and mass balance in Chapters 3–5. A room with no water has no hydrostatic head, even when an aperture in a thick floor lies below the room's geometric lower bound. Hendrik Dankowski (2013), *A fast and explicit method for simulating flooding and sinkage scenarios of ships*, supplies the independent reconstruction of Case A geometry in Chapter 4. The early comparator uses Ruponen's own initial breach submergence and no fitted measurement outcomes. [Ruponen dissertation](https://urn.fi/urn:nbn:fi:tkk-010597) · [Dankowski dissertation](https://tore.tuhh.de/entities/publication/c9f6ab74-3ae3-4dae-8aa1-ff7bf96a86b2)

Ivan E. Sutherland and Gary W. Hodgman (1974), *Reentrant polygon clipping*, describe successive plane cuts. Brian Mirtich (1996), *Fast and Accurate Computation of Polyhedral Mass Properties*, derives volume integrals from the boundary. The optional native phase clips the same body-local triangle fan for each level as `volumeBelow`. It preserves triangle and fan summation order, with paired f64x2 geometry and private workers handling disjoint plane ranges. No companion code was read or imported. [Sutherland and Hodgman](https://doi.org/10.1145/360767.360802) · [Mirtich](https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.1996.10487458)

### SEA-15 native parcel diffusion and held-out jet scour

John K. Salmon, Mark A. Moraes, Ron O. Dror and David E. Shaw (2011), *Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1, 2, 3*, define the Philox4x32 transform in Section 4.3. George E. P. Box and Mervin E. Muller (1958), *A Note on the Generation of Random Normal Deviates*, give the independent Cartesian normal construction from two unit uniforms. The optional Rust stage uses the same key, parcel slot, tick words, pinned transforms and output order as the TypeScript entry. Its SIMD lanes act on independent parcel counters. Only the kernel that synthesizes those samples moves to Rust. The source, flow, bed, settling, oil and ledgers retain their original order. [Salmon et al.](https://doi.org/10.1145/2063384.2063405) · [Box and Muller](https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177706645)

Ahmad Mohamadiyeh, Jeffrey Peakall, Michael Fairweather, Martyn Barnes and Timothy N. Hunter (2026), *Impinging jet erosion of granular sediments*, supply independently measured nozzle discharge, bed properties and two ultrasonic final crater profiles. Numerical inputs use the source setup and measured materials. Neither crater profile sets an input parameter. The comparison integrates the below-baseline profile revolved about the nozzle axis, carries the published vertical readout resolution through the integration and reports the 10 mm to 5 mm model spacing difference separately. Leo C. van Rijn (1984), *Sediment Transport, Part II: Suspended Load Transport*, remains the source of the bed pickup and reference level used by the solver. [Jet scour experiment](https://doi.org/10.1002/aic.70336) · [Experimental data](https://doi.org/10.5518/1730) · [Van Rijn](https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9429(1984)110:11(1613))

## Rock structure, drainage and far fir crowns: terrain rock, biomes drainageStructure, procedural fir-sprays (2026-11-28)

Above the Treeline look round 4: steep faces, the summit dome and far mountains read as smooth grey felt, patches as
camouflage, and far firs as grey sticks. Sources read for it (papers only, no companion code):

- F. K. Musgrave, C. E. Kolb and R. S. Mace, "The synthesis and rendering of eroded fractal terrains", SIGGRAPH 1989,
  https://doi.org/10.1145/74333.74337 (thermal weathering to an angle of repose: why talus lies at 30 to 40 degrees
  below walls).
- O. Stava, B. Benes, M. Brisbin and J. Krivanek, "Interactive terrain modeling using hydraulic erosion", SCA 2008,
  https://doi.org/10.2312/SCA/SCA08/201-210 (water carving gullies where flow gathers).
- G. Cordonnier, J. Braun, M.-P. Cani, B. Benes, E. Galin, A. Peytavie and E. Guerin, "Large scale terrain generation
  from tectonic uplift and fluvial erosion", Computer Graphics Forum 35(2), 2016, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.12820
  (stream power: incision grows with drainage area times slope, so drainage area is the map of where gullies are).
- G. Cordonnier, M.-P. Cani, B. Benes, J. Braun and E. Galin, "Sculpting mountains: interactive terrain modeling based on
  subsurface geology", IEEE TVCG 24(5), 2018, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2017.2689022 (rock layers and joints shaping
  faces into ledges and blocks).
- E. Galin, E. Guerin, A. Peytavie, G. Cordonnier, M.-P. Cani, B. Benes and J. Gain, "A review of digital terrain
  modeling", Computer Graphics Forum 38(2), 2019, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13657 (survey; amplification of a coarse
  heightmap by procedural detail at the scales it cannot hold).
- H. Schott, A. Paris, L. Fournier, E. Guerin and E. Galin, "Large-scale terrain authoring through interactive erosion
  simulation", ACM TOG 42(5), 2023, https://doi.org/10.1145/3592787 (drainage area as the driver of eroded structure).
- B. Benes and R. Forsbach, "Layered data representation for visual simulation of terrain erosion", SCCG 2001,
  and A. Peytavie, E. Galin, J. Grosjean and S. Merillou, "Arches: a framework
  for modeling complex terrains", Computer Graphics Forum 28(2), 2009
  (beds of hard and soft rock stepping a face into risers and benches).
- S. Worley, "A cellular texture basis function", SIGGRAPH 1996, https://doi.org/10.1145/237170.237267 (F1 and F2 - F1
  of jittered cell points: blocks and their joints).
- T. G. Freeman, "Calculating catchment area with divergent flow based on a regular grid", Computers and Geosciences
  17(3), 1991, https://doi.org/10.1016/0098-3004(91)90048-I (the multiple-flow shares already in hydrology).
- I. Statham, "A scree slope rockfall model", Earth Surface Processes 1(1), 1976
  (rockfall from a wall travels down and stops where the slope falls under the angle of repose: talus fans and cones).
- K. Perlin, "An image synthesizer", SIGGRAPH 1985, https://doi.org/10.1145/325165.325247, and D. Ebert, F. K. Musgrave,
  D. Peachey, K. Perlin and S. Worley, "Texturing and Modeling: A Procedural Approach", 3rd ed. 2003, ch. 16 (domain
  distortion of noise: patch warp).
- M. Jarzynski and M. Olano, "Hash Functions for GPU Rendering", JCGT 9(3), 2020 (pcg3d for every cell value).
- C. Remolar, M. Chover, O. Belmonte, J. Ribelles and C. Rebollo, "Geometric simplification of foliage", Eurographics
  2002 short papers, and X. Zhang, F. Blaise and M. Jaeger, "Multiresolution plant models with complex organs", ACM
  GRAPHITE 2006 (a simplified crown keeps its foliage area by growing the
  leaves it keeps).
- Reference photographs looked at for the look (not copied, nothing kept): alpine granite faces, couloirs and talus
  cones of the Colorado Front Range and Rocky Mountain National Park.

Margo's own in this entry: the analytic bench and riser normal (the face's gradient times 0.25 on the top 30 percent of
a bed and (1 - 0.075) / 0.7 below, so the mean slope holds); level beds warped by two value noises and broken by a
third; two facet scales (`facets` and 4.1 times it at 0.7 strength), each block tilting the normal by its own hashed
direction; the slope fade and the pixel-footprint fades (facets from 0.12 to 0.4 of a block, beds from 0.1 to 0.3 of
a cycle, gullies from 0.25 to 0.6 of a structure texel); the gully carve as central differences of the drainage texel
added to the height gradient; the debris push that moves `terrainRockLoose` of every layer's weight to the debris
layer; the drainage scale (log catchment from 800 to 60,000 square metres), the wall (40 degrees), repose (34
degrees) and travel (half settles every 90 m) defaults and the 3 x 3 spread of settled debris; the patch warp (2.6 cell
noise, 1.1 cell reach, a 3.3 cell octave of weight 0.75) and contour terraces (a sine of the height a `terraces` cycle,
phase wandering by a 7 cycle noise, 2.1 radians per layer); and the fir spray ring growth factors (1.17 x 1.1 and
2.3 x 1.3) from the near ring's spray area.

### Craters (EARTH-06, `@margoengine/physics/crater`, 2026-11-27)

`packages/physics/src/crater/law.ts` and `solver.ts`, written from:

  4's explosion constants, eq. 6's formation time, read).
